Yes. This is the right mechanism.

The 1970s Mittelafrika crisis should not come from a modern nationalist underground or from the German administration suddenly deciding to become genocidal. It should come from the **constitutional defect at the heart of the Mosaic Order**:

> Germany gives the chiefs enough authority to govern, enough resources to matter, and enough institutional permanence to imagine themselves sovereign—but never enough independence to satisfy the logic of their own office.

The administration creates hundreds of miniature principalities and then discovers that miniature princes eventually ask why they are still paying tribute.

# Katanga and the African technical estate

Your assessment of Katanga is especially strong.

Historically, the Katangan mining system already responded to scarce and expensive skilled labor by training Africans, increasing skilled wages, providing family housing, and attempting to stabilize workers permanently around the mines. Katanga pioneered settled African mining towns and family life earlier than the Northern Rhodesian side of the Copperbelt, where white workers defended a stronger industrial color bar. citeturn829695view1turn829695view3

The German administration would take that logic much further because its manpower problem is much worse.

A German engineer sent to Katanga requires:

- transport from Europe;
- tropical preparation;
- German-standard housing;
- medical care;
- family allowances or extended separation from his family;
- replacement leave;
- and eventual repatriation.

A locally born African engineer who already speaks German and understands the climate, workers, railways, administrative forms, and local languages is nearly impossible to replace.

The result is not racial equality. It is **scarcity privilege**.

## The Afrikanischer Fachdienst

The official institution could be the:

> **Afrikanischer Fachdienst**  
> African Technical Service

Its members are informally called the **Fachstand**—the professional estate.

It includes:

- locomotive drivers and dispatchers;
- mine foremen;
- electrical technicians;
- surveyors;
- accountants;
- radio operators;
- medical auxiliaries;
- machine-tool operators;
- chemical-process workers;
- power-station crews;
- teleprinter operators;
- MOSAIK clerks;
- and junior technical officers.

A fully trained African engineer, mine manager, or railway superintendent occupies its highest ranks.

## The house

And yes: he receives a house.

Not a hut, barracks room, or crowded workers’ apartment.

A **Diensthaus**:

- detached or semi-detached;
- electricity where available;
- piped water;
- durable roof;
- small garden;
- family kitchen;
- German-made furnishings on favorable credit;
- access to a technical-service commissary;
- and proximity to the German or senior African residential district.

The state is not indulging him out of benevolence.

It is purchasing his loyalty.

The arrangement might work like this:

- immediate service housing upon qualification;
- subsidized family residence after marriage;
- protected tenancy while employed;
- pension tenancy after twenty years;
- and eventual inheritable title if a child also enters qualified service.

That final provision creates technical dynasties.

The son of a locomotive superintendent attends a German-medium technical school. His daughter trains as a nurse, teacher, bookkeeper, or laboratory technician. The family possesses German books, a radio, perhaps a bicycle or motor scooter, and enough disposable income to hire domestic help.

Within one generation, a village boy’s family can become part of a recognizable African bourgeoisie.

## Privilege beyond housing

The Fachstand receives:

- higher ration classification;
- superior hospital access;
- German-medium schools for children;
- pension rights;
- paid leave;
- railway travel permits;
- reduced community labor obligations;
- access to technical courts rather than chiefly jurisdiction in employment matters;
- and permission to move between districts without ordinary communal sponsorship.

The most valuable privilege may be that his children are not automatically returned to the political status of his ancestral village.

The Fachstand becomes a partially mobile estate inside an empire otherwise organized around inherited communal belonging.

## Why even racial hardliners tolerate it

The Mittelafrika administration can defend every privilege in figures:

> One African locomotive engineer replaces one imported German and perhaps four semi-skilled assistants.

> One African accountant prevents enough inventory loss to pay for fifty houses.

> One African power-station foreman keeps an entire mine complex operating.

The Reich’s ideological ministries may complain that the colonial administration is creating an overly privileged black class.

The reply from Katanga is:

> “Send us eight thousand German technicians, then.”

Berlin cannot.

So racial doctrine bends before the production schedule.

## The social resentment this creates

The privileges are not universally admired.

Ordinary African workers ask why the man who learned German receives:

- a house;
- better food;
- better schools;
- easier travel;
- and exemption from some communal duties.

Lower-ranking white employees may be even more resentful. A German mechanic newly arrived from Europe may discover that the African railway superintendent has a larger house and servants because the superintendent is harder to replace.

The administration’s answer is brutally practical:

> “You can go home. He cannot be permitted to leave.”

That sentence summarizes the whole technical caste.

# Not an intelligentsia

You are also right that Mittelafrika does not need a large abstract intellectual class.

Berlin does not establish a great African university system intended to produce:

- philosophers;
- political theorists;
- historians;
- pure mathematicians;
- or independent social researchers.

Research remains principally in Germany.

Mittelafrika receives the results:

- improved mining machinery;
- fertilizers;
- medicines;
- locomotives;
- radio equipment;
- accounting systems;
- and administrative software.

Its educational system is applied.

## The highest normal schools

The most prestigious African institutions are things like:

- Katanga Mining Academy;
- Kongostadt School of Administration;
- Duala Railway and Port Institute;
- Kribi Technical Aviation School;
- Mittelafrika Medical Service College;
- and regional MOSAIK academies.

They produce **users and maintainers of systems**, not usually the men who invent the next system.

A gifted student might be sent to Germany for advanced instruction. But the expected outcome is that he returns to operate a German-designed mine, railway, reactor component, telecommunication exchange, or computing center.

The empire creates engineers.

It carefully avoids creating a large class whose principal profession is asking what the empire is for.

# The railway empire

Germany would not have to build Mittelafrika’s railways entirely from nothing. By the 1940s, the Belgian Congo already possessed thousands of kilometers of rail, a vast road system, airports, navigable river routes, and major mining connections—but these networks were fragmented and generally designed to connect resource zones to ports rather than to integrate the territory internally. Colonial authority itself remained concentrated along narrow logistical corridors. citeturn829695view0

The German achievement is therefore not “the first railway in Africa.”

It is **stitching the isolated extraction networks into one imperial transport system**.

## The railways and rivers together

Mittelafrika should never become purely a railway empire.

The Congo river system remains indispensable.

Railway lines perform three principal functions:

1. bypass unnavigable river sections;
2. connect mineral and agricultural districts to the rivers;
3. connect the separate river basins and coastal systems to one another.

The mature system is:

> riverboat → rail bypass → riverboat → trunk railway → port

This is cheaper and more plausible than driving rails through every mile of rainforest.

## The great trunk projects

### 1. The Congo Spine

The first priority connects:

- Matadi;
- Kongostadt;
- the upper Congo river system;
- Kisangani;
- Kasai junctions;
- and eventually the Katangan network.

This becomes the central internal freight axis.

### 2. The Katanga industrial system

Katanga is connected through several routes:

- westward toward the Atlantic;
- northwest toward Kongostadt;
- southward through negotiated Portuguese and southern African links;
- and northward toward the lake and upper river systems.

Germany deliberately avoids dependence upon one foreign-controlled port.

### 3. The Kamerun–Congo line

A grand strategic line runs in stages through:

- Duala or Kribi;
- Yaoundé;
- the interior of Kamerun;
- Bangui or the Ubangi system;
- and onward toward the Congo network.

This is tremendously expensive and probably takes nearly twenty years to become reliable.

Its political value is as important as its freight capacity: it physically joins restored German Kamerun to the central African empire.

### 4. The Sahelbahn

The great northern trunk links former French West African railways and new construction across some version of:

- Dakar;
- Bamako;
- Ouagadougou;
- Niamey;
- Lake Chad;
- northern Kamerun;
- and the central African system.

This is the line that makes German West Africa feel like a single space despite Nigeria dividing the coastal territories.

### 5. The Kribi strategic network

Kribi receives dedicated heavy rail, power, fuel, and construction lines serving:

- the equatorial launch center;
- stage-recovery and tracking sites;
- industrial depots;
- military bases;
- and the coercively controlled eastward flight corridor already established in the space canon. fileciteturn19file0

## Double track—but not everywhere

Germany absolutely builds double-track railway in high-volume areas:

- Katanga;
- Kongostadt approaches;
- major mineral-port routes;
- Kribi;
- heavily used Sahel sections;
- and strategic military junctions.

But two complete parallel transcontinental railways through every low-traffic district would consume fantastic quantities of:

- steel;
- sleepers;
- ballast;
- bridges;
- maintenance labor;
- locomotives;
- signaling equipment;
- and security manpower.

The better German approach is a **double backbone**:

- two geographically separate trunk systems for strategic redundancy;
- double track on the busiest portions;
- passing loops and centralized traffic control elsewhere;
- and alternative river or road routes if one segment is cut.

That is grandiose enough to fit victorious Germany without becoming economically magical.

## The railway as state power

Railways do more than move copper.

Every station produces:

- a police post;
- a German signboard;
- a labor bureau;
- a MOSAIK terminal or card office;
- a school;
- a commissary;
- a medical station;
- and a new population not entirely controlled by the nearby chief.

That becomes critical to the later crisis.

The railway creates wealth.

It also creates an alternative elite:

- stationmasters;
- clerks;
- technical workers;
- police;
- and salaried officials.

The chief gradually discovers that the most prosperous men in his district no longer depend entirely upon him.

# Agriculture

Your instinct concerning broad jungle clearance is substantially correct.

Humid tropical forest soils are often heavily weathered and leached. Once forest cover is removed, nutrient fertility can decline rapidly, erosion increases, and cleared pasture may remain productive for only a limited period without expensive inputs. citeturn829695view2

The Germans would nevertheless attempt several prestige schemes:

- wheat fields;
- mechanized cattle districts;
- European-style farm colonies;
- and enormous cleared plantations.

Some would fail spectacularly after a few harvests.

The mature food economy would be more regionally differentiated.

## Rainforest and humid districts

These emphasize:

- cassava;
- plantains;
- bananas;
- yams;
- palm oil;
- cocoa;
- rubber;
- coffee in suitable uplands;
- timber;
- local rice;
- and mixed forest agriculture.

## Savanna and plateau zones

These can support more:

- maize;
- millet;
- sorghum;
- cattle;
- groundnuts;
- cotton;
- and selected mechanized grain projects.

## Katanga and the industrial towns

Katanga imports a large share of its food from:

- nearby agricultural districts;
- southern rail connections;
- the Sahel;
- and government supply networks.

This is another reason the railways matter. They move food into industrial areas as much as minerals out.

# The authority trap

The chief-led revolt is the most convincing origin for the 1970s crisis.

The Mosaic Order relies upon local rulers because Germany cannot afford to administer every village directly.

The chief:

- settles disputes;
- allocates communal land;
- assigns labor obligations;
- identifies criminals;
- collects taxes;
- reports births and deaths;
- negotiates with neighboring communities;
- and speaks for his people to the district administration.

In daily life, he does nearly everything a ruler does.

Then the central government demands:

- labor;
- tax;
- records;
- obedience;
- and acceptance of a superior jurisdiction.

Eventually the chief asks:

> **“If I govern my people, why am I not their sovereign?”**

That is the structural problem.

## The generational change

The first post-conquest chiefs remember the Counting Wars.

They remember:

- German patrols;
- burned villages;
- machine guns;
- imprisonment;
- and the consequences of refusing registration.

They also remember the disorder before the Mosaic settlement and may sincerely value the peace it provides.

Their sons inherit a very different world.

They remember:

- regular wages;
- predictable quotas;
- commissary goods;
- stable boundaries;
- and perhaps one ceremonial visit from a German commissioner.

German authority seems distant, abstract, and slightly ridiculous.

The new chief has never seen the empire conquer anything.

He has seen only clerks asking for forms.

## Why the chief is dissatisfied

He possesses local authority but not:

- control over mines;
- control over railways;
- independent foreign relations;
- unrestricted military power;
- final authority over migration;
- or the right to refuse the community quota.

He sees trains carrying copper, timber, and goods through his territory.

He sees technical workers receiving better houses than his own relatives.

He sees young men learning German and appealing to administrative courts rather than to him.

The system which originally strengthened his office is now slowly hollowing it out.

# The crisis does not begin as nationalism

This should be fixed clearly.

The rebels do not begin by demanding:

- an independent Congo;
- a united Mittelafrika;
- democracy;
- racial equality;
- or expulsion of every German.

Their demands are local and aristocratic:

- our labor obligation is too large;
- this mine lies on our land;
- that neighboring chief has been favored;
- the administration recognized the wrong heir;
- our people may move where we permit;
- the railway must pay us;
- and no outside official may depose us.

The British call them nationalists because that is the vocabulary Britain understands.

German propaganda calls them bandits.

They are closer to **rebellious feudatories**.

# The computers see the crisis—and misunderstand it

MOSAIK does not fail to detect the first disturbances.

It detects them almost immediately.

The system reports:

- falling labor attendance;
- missing identity updates;
- unusual migration;
- disappearing tax receipts;
- cancelled school enrollments;
- increased weapons theft;
- and rising disputes between neighboring communities.

But MOSAIK categorizes them as:

- clerical failure;
- crop disruption;
- transport arrears;
- population movement;
- or ordinary chiefly noncompliance.

The computer can show that twelve hundred workers failed to report.

It cannot show that the chief has decided German sovereignty no longer exists.

> **The most heavily documented colony in the world knows everything except what its own data means.**

Because every anomaly has an administrative code, officials assume it has an administrative remedy.

They send another form.

Then another inspector.

Then a mediation officer.

By the time they send troops, the political decision has already been made locally.

# The spark

The revolt should begin in the **Kasai–Lunda labor belt**, behind Katanga.

That region is ideal because:

- it supplies labor to the mines;
- it contains strong chiefly traditions;
- it is close enough to the railway economy to understand the wealth being extracted;
- and it is far enough from the main German cities that chiefs seldom encounter Germans personally.

Historically, the wider Copperbelt had long been a zone of political innovation and migration associated with Luba and Lunda state traditions rather than a blank tribal landscape. citeturn829695view3

## The initial refusal

Around **1969 or 1970**, a chief refuses an increased Gemeindesoll after a railway expansion and new Katangan labor requirement.

The district office records the shortfall.

The chief is fined.

He refuses the fine.

Nothing immediately happens because the administration has more urgent matters.

Other chiefs notice.

## The first raid

The crisis becomes urgent when the refusing chief attacks a neighboring loyal chief.

His immediate purpose may be:

- cattle;
- land;
- control of a station road;
- revenge;
- or seizure of commissary goods.

The loyal chief appeals to the German administration:

> “You require my obedience. Where is my protection?”

That question threatens the entire order.

If Germany cannot protect loyal chiefs from rebellious chiefs, loyalty has no value.

# The War of the Chiefs

The British and international name should be:

> **The War of the Chiefs**

German official usage calls it:

> **Die Mittelafrikanische Ordnungskrise**  
> The Mittelafrican Order Crisis

Colonial soldiers and officials call the separate struggles the **Häuptlingskriege**.

Local names vary:

- the Refusal;
- the Tax War;
- the War of the Stations;
- the War of the Fathers;
- or simply the Troubles.

## Phase I: Refusal, 1969–1971

Chiefs withhold:

- labor quotas;
- taxes;
- registries;
- and police cooperation.

The administration treats these as solvable arrears.

## Phase II: Feud, 1971–1972

Rebellious chiefs raid loyal neighbors.

Succession disputes become armed conflicts.

Registration offices and commissaries are looted.

African clerks and technical officials are targeted as servants of German authority.

## Phase III: Cascade, 1972–1974

Chiefs who had remained loyal begin hedging.

Some stop sending labor because Germany cannot protect their roads.

Some form defensive confederations.

Others exploit the disorder to settle old disputes.

The revolt spreads through imitation, not through a central command.

There is no leader whom Germany can capture to end it.

## Phase IV: Restoration, 1974–1976

Germany deploys:

- African colonial troops;
- locally recruited police;
- helicopters;
- river patrol craft;
- armored personnel carriers;
- reconnaissance aircraft;
- mobile artillery;
- and German mechanized detachments.

Tanks appear near rail corridors, mining districts, and open savanna, but they are not the principal jungle weapon.

The controlling instrument is mobility:

- arrive quickly;
- isolate the chief;
- seize the station and food depots;
- disarm his allies;
- and force neighboring chiefs to declare loyalty.

## Phase V: Hard Peace, 1976–1978

Most chiefs submit.

Some are executed.

Some are exiled.

Some are replaced by brothers or sons.

Some communities are merged with loyal neighbors.

The railway and mine systems resume operation.

The empire announces that order has been restored.

# The demographic catastrophe

Your village example works, with one refinement.

The administration does not normally exterminate the entire male population intentionally. But in small communities, the chief’s “army” may include nearly every adult or military-age man.

If they gather for one decisive battle against armored troops, the result can destroy the community’s entire male cohort.

Afterward, the administration finds:

- widows;
- children;
- old men;
- burned housing;
- abandoned fields;
- and no recognized chiefly succession.

The district is now administratively and demographically nonviable.

## Consolidation

The authorities issue **demographic consolidation orders**.

Surviving communities may be:

- attached to a related neighboring people;
- placed under a loyal chief;
- merged into a new Landschaft;
- moved nearer a road or station;
- or divided among several kin-related villages.

The administration tries to respect:

- language;
- clan;
- marriage rules;
- inheritance;
- and religious practice.

Sometimes the merger works.

A widow community gains protection, new husbands, food, and functioning authority.

Sometimes it creates a permanent grievance:

> “The Germans killed our men and gave our children to our enemies.”

Both experiences are real.

# The role of the technical class in the war

The Fachstand is mostly **not revolutionary**.

Its members have:

- houses;
- salaries;
- schools;
- pensions;
- status;
- and mobility.

The rebellion threatens all of that.

Many technical Africans view the chiefs as reactionaries who want to reclaim authority over their labor, wages, wives, children, and movement.

The conflict therefore includes black Africans fighting on Germany’s side for reasons far more complicated than simple collaboration.

Railwaymen keep supply lines running.

MOSAIK clerks identify the affected communities.

African radio operators coordinate patrols.

Mine engineers organize defensive units.

Technical families flee rebel districts because chiefs accuse them of having become German.

This gives Berlin powerful propaganda:

> “The rebels do not fight white rule. They murder African doctors, engineers, teachers, and workers.”

That claim is selectively true.

It does not justify collective punishment, but it makes the war morally much harder to present as straightforward liberation.

# The Second Mosaic Settlement

Germany cannot merely restore the old system after the war.

The crisis proves that personal chiefly authority is too powerful and too fragile.

Around **1977–1979**, the administration implements a revised order.

## Chiefs remain, but they are balanced

Every Landschaft receives:

- a customary chief;
- an elected or appointed communal council;
- a professional administrative secretary;
- and a technical-economic representative.

No single chief may control:

- police;
- labor allocation;
- communal accounts;
- and succession records simultaneously.

## The dual key

Important actions require two approvals:

- the chief;
- and the administrative secretary or council.

This includes:

- extraordinary labor quotas;
- migration exclusion;
- communal borrowing;
- land transfer;
- and armed mobilization.

## Direct payment

Mine and railway wages increasingly go directly to workers rather than through the chief.

The chief receives a transparent communal revenue allocation instead.

This reduces his control over wealth and removes one source of corruption.

## Succession registration

A chief may still be selected by customary procedure, but succession must be ratified through:

- the local council;
- the mediation service;
- and MOSAIK.

This prevents surprise claimants but makes the office unmistakably dependent upon the Reich.

## Professional local police

Chiefly warriors are reduced or regularized.

The state expands salaried African territorial police whose loyalty runs through the district administration rather than exclusively through hereditary rulers.

## Greater technical representation

The Fachstand receives formal places in district government.

This shifts Mittelafrika away from pure chiefly tributary rule and toward a hybrid of:

- hereditary authority;
- technical corporatism;
- communal councils;
- and German supervision.

# What the crisis becomes internationally

The existing setting bible already establishes a major German African crisis in the early-to-mid 1970s, involving local, ethnic, dynastic, and territorial revolt followed by severe German counterinsurgency and international scandal. fileciteturn19file0

Your revision should supersede the implication that this is principally an extermination campaign.

The better formulation is:

> **The War of the Chiefs begins as a decentralized revolt by hereditary and customary rulers against labor quotas, German confirmation of chiefly authority, railway expansion, migration controls, and the erosion of local sovereignty. The revolt spreads when rebellious chiefs attack loyal ones and the administration initially fails to maintain the Crown peace of the Mosaic Order. German and African colonial forces restore control through mechanized punitive campaigns, collective disarmament, forced consolidation, detention, and destruction of resisting settlements. In some districts, battles and reprisals destroy much of the adult male population and produce demographically nonviable communities, but neither the revolt nor the suppression is organized around a general extermination policy. The crisis ends in a Second Mosaic Settlement that curtails chiefly military and fiscal authority while elevating councils, professional African administrators, and the German-speaking technical estate.**

That retains the international horror without reducing it to “Germany decides to kill Africans.”

# The deeper irony

The rebellion is not caused because the Mosaic Order gave Africans no authority.

It is caused because it gave them **real but incomplete authority**.

The chief has enough power to imagine freedom.

The engineer has enough privilege to fear freedom.

The German commissioner has enough data to believe he understands both.

And the computer knows that the labor quota has failed without knowing that an ancient political question has returned:

> **Who has the right to command whom?**

The system survives the crisis.

Indeed, after 1978 it may be more stable than before.

But it survives by destroying the illusion that the chiefs were genuine partners. They remain guardians of custom and local order; the technical estate increasingly becomes the real African governing class.

That creates the next long-term tension.

By the 1980s, the men most capable of governing Mittelafrika are the German-speaking African engineers, administrators, officers, and accountants whom the Reich created to make colonial rule permanent.

They are loyal because the system elevated them.

They also understand the system better than almost any German in Berlin.

The chiefs produce the first revolt because they inherit too much authority.

The technical class may eventually produce the more dangerous one because it has acquired too much competence.

Yes. The **Second Mosaic Settlement** should not attempt to constitutionalize the chief out of relevance. That would misunderstand why the first system worked at all.

It instead answers the chief’s question directly:

> **“Why should I uphold German order?”**  
> Because German order now pays you, enriches your people, educates your heirs, and makes your authority more secure than rebellion does.

The settlement turns the recognized chief from an unpaid intermediary into a **local shareholder in the imperial system**.

# The Second Mosaic Settlement

The reform probably follows the final suppression of the War of the Chiefs, around **1977–1979**.

Its formal German title could be:

> **Zweite Mittelafrikanische Mosaikvereinbarung**  
> Second Mittelafrican Mosaic Agreement

Its economic core is known as the:

> **Leistungs- und Beteiligungsordnung**  
> Performance and Participation Order

The political lesson Berlin draws is not that chiefs possessed too much power. It is that the administration demanded loyalty without making loyalty sufficiently profitable.

The first Mosaic Order said:

> You govern locally because we recognize you.

The second says:

> You govern locally, and your prosperity rises or falls with the success of the district.

## Three separate payments

The administration is careful not to let the chief simply confiscate workers’ wages. Workers continue to be paid directly through labor books, wage accounts, or commissary credits.

The chief receives separate compensation.

### The office stipend

Every recognized chiefly office receives an **Amtsdotation**:

- a regular salary;
- official residence;
- transport allowance;
- clerical staff;
- ceremonial uniform or insignia;
- medical access;
- and education places for members of the ruling household.

This makes chiefly office visibly part of the established order rather than a customary remnant tolerated by Germany.

### The performance share

The chief receives a **Leistungsanteil**, calculated from the district’s successful contribution.

The calculation can include:

- completion of the agreed labor contribution;
- worker attendance;
- production quality;
- low desertion;
- road and bridge maintenance;
- accurate registration;
- public order;
- school attendance;
- and successful return of workers to their communities.

This is not necessarily a direct percentage of every worker’s wage, which would look too much like the chief selling his people. It is an administrative bonus attached to the office.

The practical distinction may not impress the workers.

### The community dividend

A second share enters a **Landschaftsfonds**, controlled jointly by the chief and the district administration.

It can purchase:

- wells;
- clinics;
- schools;
- roads;
- mills;
- agricultural tools;
- electricity;
- radios;
- market buildings;
- and improved housing.

The Germans deliberately make the benefits visible.

A village which meets its obligation receives a new pump, clinic roof, or truck. A neighboring village which refuses sees the difference.

The state’s message is:

> **The mine does not merely take your sons. It pays for what returns to the village.**

# The chief’s new material position

A loyal, successful chief might receive:

- a substantial house;
- a German vehicle and driver;
- a radio and telephone connection;
- privileged railway travel;
- a larger commissary allowance;
- places for his sons in German-medium schools;
- technical training for selected relatives;
- medical treatment in Kongostadt or Katanga;
- and ceremonial access to the Reichskommissar.

The strongest chiefs become genuinely wealthy.

They are not merely village headmen. They become a **Mosaic aristocracy**—hereditary local rulers whose position is secured by German recognition, administrative revenue, and privileged access to modern goods.

A chief who once saw the labor quota as tribute extracted by foreigners can now see it as the foundation of his household’s wealth and his community’s development.

## The hereditary bargain

The administration also makes loyalty dynastic.

A chief who maintains order can expect:

- German recognition of his chosen successor;
- schooling for the heir;
- a pension for his widow;
- protection of the ruling family’s property;
- and continued status for his lineage.

A rebel risks not merely death but the permanent removal of his house from recognized authority.

This is often more effective than threatening the chief personally.

# MOSAIK makes the incentives precise

The computerized system becomes essential because every chiefly agreement can be calibrated.

MOSAIK records:

- the community’s population;
- available working-age labor;
- previous production;
- seasonal agricultural needs;
- accident rates;
- worker return rates;
- tax compliance;
- infrastructure condition;
- and disputes with neighboring communities.

The district office can therefore calculate a realistic negotiated obligation rather than issuing one uniform quota.

At least, that is the theory.

A chief in a poor agricultural district may owe road labor and seasonal transport. A chief near Katanga may supply mine rotations. A river community may provide boat crews. A Sahelian authority may maintain wells and transport animals.

The chief can also negotiate:

> “Give us twenty fewer men during planting season, and we will send forty for the dry-season railway work.”

This gives the system genuine flexibility.

It also makes the computer record the terms of chiefly loyalty in extraordinary detail.

# The settlement works

For the German administration, the reform is largely successful.

A chief now has powerful reasons to prevent:

- labor desertion;
- banditry;
- attacks on the railway;
- destruction of census offices;
- recruitment by rebels;
- and conflict with loyal neighboring chiefs.

He becomes the first line of imperial counterinsurgency without necessarily thinking of himself as a German agent.

He is defending:

- his income;
- his house;
- his heir’s education;
- his community fund;
- and the recognition which makes him chief.

Germany no longer needs to station soldiers in every district because local authority has an economic interest in maintaining the Mosaic peace.

The administration may quite openly describe the reform as:

> **“Making loyalty self-sustaining.”**

# The moral complication

The settlement is more nuanced than simple bribery.

Some chiefs use the new system well.

They negotiate lower labor requirements during harvests. They invest community dividends in clinics and wells. They push talented children into technical schools. They use German recognition to end old blood feuds and defend weaker communities from stronger neighbors.

Their districts become safer and materially better off.

Other chiefs use the system as a machine of personal enrichment.

They:

- inflate labor obligations to increase their bonus;
- nominate political enemies for the worst work rotations;
- seize part of returning workers’ money;
- monopolize education places for relatives;
- conceal deaths;
- falsify registration;
- and describe every critic as a security threat.

The German district administration may intervene if the corruption reduces production or produces disorder.

It is less concerned when the corruption remains efficient.

The chief therefore becomes both:

- protector of his people;
- and broker of their labor to the Reich.

Those roles are not always separable.

# The workers’ reaction

The workers do not necessarily regard the settlement as fair.

A miner may reasonably ask:

> “I worked underground. Why did the chief receive a motorcar?”

The official answer is that the chief organized the labor, maintained the community, ensured the worker’s family was supported, and kept the district peaceful.

Sometimes this is true.

Sometimes the chief did nothing except possess the correct grandfather.

The performance system therefore creates a new class tension between:

- chiefs;
- ordinary laborers;
- and the African technical estate.

## The technical estate

The Fachstand generally dislikes the chiefly participation system.

Engineers, accountants, locomotive crews, and clerks believe competence should be rewarded, not heredity.

They see the chief receiving revenue because men from his district work successfully in systems the chief neither understands nor operates.

The chief, in turn, sees the technical African as a man who has escaped his customary obligations by serving Germans directly.

The administration balances the two groups:

- chiefs provide political legitimacy and rural order;
- technicians provide the actual modern economy.

Mittelafrika’s mature ruling structure is therefore not white Germans over a uniform black population.

It is a triangular order:

1. German strategic authority;
2. hereditary African local authority;
3. German-speaking African technical authority.

Each needs the other two and resents them.

# The settlement creates chiefly capitalism

The most successful chiefly houses begin investing their income.

They acquire:

- transport firms;
- shops;
- agricultural equipment;
- cattle;
- warehouses;
- housing;
- and shares in local processing cooperatives.

Some sponsor their own candidates for technical education and then employ them.

The line between traditional authority and commercial enterprise begins to disappear.

By the 1980s, certain chiefs preside over something resembling small corporate principalities. They combine:

- customary courts;
- political office;
- community funds;
- transport contracts;
- agricultural concerns;
- and influence over labor placement.

The Germans consider this an encouraging sign of local development.

Critics call it a state-created African oligarchy.

Both are correct.

# Why it calms the Congo

The reform fits the Congo basin particularly well because political life remains comparatively localized.

The ordinary community does not need to capture Kongostadt to benefit.

It needs its chief to negotiate favorable terms with the district office.

A chief who wants:

- a road;
- a school;
- a clinic;
- a lower seasonal quota;
- or a larger community dividend

can pursue those objectives within the Mosaic Order.

The political contest becomes distributive rather than sovereign:

> Not “Why should Germany rule us?”  
> but “Why did the neighboring Landschaft receive a better contract?”

That is far less dangerous to the Reich.

It produces endless complaints, negotiations, favoritism, and corruption—but not necessarily a united independence movement.

# Why it does not solve West Africa

West Africa is different because the chief is not always the principal political actor.

In the former French coastal and urban territories, authority is distributed among:

- municipalities;
- merchants;
- cocoa and agricultural cooperatives;
- port unions;
- Islamic scholars and brotherhoods;
- professional associations;
- former French-educated administrators;
- newspapers;
- military officers;
- and territorial politicians.

A West African mayor or lawyer does not necessarily want a larger administrative stipend.

He may want:

- a legislature;
- a national government;
- control of customs;
- command of the army;
- and international recognition.

You can make a Congolese chief a profitable partner within the empire.

It is harder to make an educated Dakar politician forget that Senegal could be a country.

## The West African adaptation

Germany applies the same principle of material participation, but it pays institutions rather than merely chiefs.

### Municipal participation

Port cities receive a percentage of:

- customs revenue;
- harbor dues;
- municipal taxes;
- and industrial concessions.

### Commodity participation

Cocoa, groundnut, cotton, and palm-product boards receive guaranteed prices and development funds when quotas are met.

### Religious participation

Islamic councils, emirates, missions, and schools receive recognized authority and financial support in return for public order and cooperation.

### Labor participation

Port and railway workers receive housing funds, pensions, and works councils tied to productivity.

### Elite participation

African officials and professionals receive German administrative rank, education, houses, and career access similar to the technical estate elsewhere.

This creates a **corporate Mosaic Order** rather than a chiefly one.

But it is less stable.

A cocoa board can become the financial base of a nationalist party.

A municipal council can demand control over the whole city.

A union can coordinate workers across ethnic lines.

An Islamic network can communicate beyond German territorial boundaries.

An urban newspaper can describe local grievances as a national struggle.

The very institutions Germany pays to stabilize West Africa can become instruments for organized sovereignty.

# West Africa’s continuing political problem

The Congo’s political question is often:

> Which chief controls this community?

West Africa’s question is increasingly:

> Who controls this territory?

That is a much more dangerous question for Germany.

The Second Mosaic Settlement may calm the War of the Chiefs in central Africa while leaving German West Africa in a state of continuous lower-level political tension:

- strikes;
- student disturbances;
- municipal protests;
- cocoa boycotts;
- religious disputes;
- military conspiracies;
- and demands for associated-state status.

Germany can negotiate with these movements, but it cannot dissolve them completely into customary authority.

## The Ghana example

German-aligned Ghana makes the problem sharper.

Ghana is a formally sovereign black state beside German-administered West Africa.

A Senegalese or Ivorian politician can reasonably ask:

> “Why may Accra possess a flag, an army, and a foreign ministry while we remain districts in a Reichskommissariat?”

Berlin answers that Ghana achieved sovereignty through recognized national organization, while German West African territories are mosaics of peoples requiring continued order.

The politician hears:

> Germany grants sovereignty where sovereignty serves Germany.

Again, he is correct.

# The regional result

By the early 1980s, Mittelafrika has two broad political cultures.

## Central and equatorial Mittelafrika

Stabilized through:

- remunerated chiefs;
- community dividends;
- technical elites;
- local customary government;
- and detailed MOSAIK contracts.

It is paternal, tributary, hierarchical, and often genuinely peaceful.

## German West Africa

Stabilized through:

- municipalities;
- commodity boards;
- religious authorities;
- professional elites;
- labor institutions;
- and security services.

It is wealthier, more urban, more politically literate, and much more capable of generating organized demands for sovereignty.

The Germans solve the chieftain problem.

They do not solve the nation problem.

# Revised postwar settlement

The Second Mosaic Settlement should therefore be described as follows:

> **Following the War of the Chiefs, Germany does not substantially abolish customary authority or replace chiefs with standardized councils. Instead, the 1977–79 Performance and Participation Order gives recognized chiefs fixed official stipends, personal performance shares, protected succession, household privileges, and community development dividends tied to labor fulfillment, public order, registration, infrastructure, and worker welfare. Workers continue to receive wages directly, while chiefs and their communities benefit separately from successful participation in the imperial economy. The reform converts chiefs from tribute-paying intermediaries into economically invested partners of the Reichskommissariat and restores stability throughout much of the Congo and equatorial interior. It also creates a wealthy Mosaic aristocracy, encourages chiefly labor brokerage, deepens tension with the African technical estate, and proves much less effective in urban and politically developed German West Africa, where municipalities, commodity boards, religious networks, professional associations, and territorial politicians increasingly demand sovereign authority rather than better terms within the colonial system.**

The essential German insight is simple:

> **A man may rebel against a tax. He is less likely to rebel against his dividend.**

The essential danger is just as simple:

> Once authority has a price, every local ruler begins calculating whether Germany is still offering enough.

# The unadvertised empire

Germany’s other imperial achievements are designed for display:

- Berlin and the rebuilt German cities;
- autobahns and high-speed rail;
- industrial exhibitions;
- consumer production;
- model settlements;
- the Olympics;
- rockets;
- lunar operations;
- and eventually the Orbitaler Raumhafen.

Mittelafrika is different.

Its prestige lies in the fact that Germany possesses a continental African empire and can extract strategic materials from it. The internal administration is not itself a national myth.

To the average German, Mittelafrika means:

- copper;
- cobalt;
- uranium;
- rubber;
- tropical goods;
- an equatorial launch site;
- maps colored German;
- and perhaps a relative doing technical or military service overseas.

It does **not** mean MOSAIK, chiefly participation contracts, Katangan African engineers, labor-market concessions, or the extraordinary multilingual administrative machinery needed to keep the system functioning.

Germany’s propaganda is already extraordinarily capable and outward-facing, but it concentrates upon subjects which reinforce the image of German power, modernity, technological superiority, and respectable strength. fileciteturn20file10 Mittelafrika’s actual accomplishments do not fit that message cleanly.

# Why Berlin cannot tell the true story

## The racial embarrassment

A truthful documentary about Katanga would have to show that:

- black locomotive engineers may be more operationally valuable than newly arrived white German mechanics;
- African mine managers receive detached housing;
- skilled African families receive privileged schools and medical access;
- black officials sometimes exercise authority over lower-ranking Germans;
- and African workers are paid because coercion alone produces unreliable industrial labor.

Administratively, all of that is rational.

Ideologically, it is awkward.

The radical racial wing can tolerate exceptions described as necessary colonial personnel. It does not want millions of German cinema viewers watching a well-dressed black superintendent reprimand a white railway employee in fluent German.

The issue is not that the Reich has abolished racial hierarchy. It clearly has not. It is that practical colonial administration has created a hierarchy in which **race does not always determine immediate workplace rank, pay, housing, or indispensability**.

Publicizing that would raise dangerous questions:

- Why may an African technician receive privileges denied to some Germans?
- Does technical merit supersede race?
- Can service alter political status?
- Are Mittelafrika’s Africans really incapable of higher civilization?
- Why does the administration invest so heavily in their children?

The colonial officials possess answers.

The ideological authorities would prefer the questions never be asked.

## The administrative embarrassment

MOSAIK also reveals how dependent the empire is upon compromise.

A proud public account would have to admit that Germany governs through:

- indigenous chiefs;
- customary courts;
- African mediation officials;
- local languages;
- negotiated labor obligations;
- religious authorities;
- municipal bodies;
- and regional political distinctions Berlin did not invent.

That contradicts the cleaner image of a German state imposing rational order upon a blank continent.

The real achievement is not that Germany replaced African society.

It is that Germany learned to catalogue, bargain with, and operate through it.

## The security embarrassment

The Kribi launch system is deliberately remote, screened, and surrounded by controlled transport and recovery corridors. German space propaganda later celebrates the rockets without inviting foreign journalists to roam freely through the colonial system that supports them. The equatorial complex’s coercively managed eastward corridor and its integration with Germany’s heavy-launch architecture are already part of the setting’s space structure. fileciteturn20file15

Mittelafrika therefore remains difficult to visit for reasons that are not solely colonial atrocity:

- aerospace secrecy;
- military facilities;
- mineral security;
- disease controls;
- poor transport outside main corridors;
- administrative permits;
- and fear of foreign intelligence.

But every restriction confirms the foreign assumption that Germany must be concealing camps.

# The one great documentary

Germany probably does make one serious documentary about the territory, perhaps in the early or middle 1960s.

A good title would be:

> **_Mosaik am Äquator_**  
> *Mosaic at the Equator*

It shows:

- the Congo rail-and-river system;
- Katangan mines;
- MOSAIK tabulation centers;
- German-language African schools;
- chiefs receiving development grants;
- African locomotive crews;
- clinics;
- hydroelectric works;
- new bridges;
- and goods returning to rural communities from paid labor.

Its historical framing contrasts German administration with:

- Leopoldian atrocities;
- Belgian neglect;
- French administrative confusion;
- and British territorial nationalism.

The documentary’s thesis is:

> Germany did not merely extract Africa. Germany made its many peoples governable without destroying their identities.

Parts of the film are truthful. Parts are carefully curated. None of the early Counting Wars or resisting districts appear.

Yet the film becomes controversial inside Germany.

Racial hardliners object to:

- the screen time given to black officials;
- the image of African technical competence;
- the treatment of chiefs as political partners;
- and the suggestion that Germans had something to learn from local institutions.

The colonial administration objects to security-sensitive footage.

The aerospace authorities object to geographical detail near Kribi.

The Foreign Office worries that the film will invite demands for foreign inspection.

It receives a limited cinema run, appears at technical exhibitions and colonial-service schools, and then largely disappears into specialist archives.

A shortened version may be shown abroad, so heavily stripped of context that it looks like ordinary propaganda.

The Reich possesses evidence that could substantially complicate the British account—and declines to use it.

# The frozen British picture

British understanding of Mittelafrika forms during the worst years:

- the Counting Wars;
- village burnings;
- confused censuses;
- labor seizures;
- refugee flight;
- missionary testimony;
- and administrative documents describing survivors in terms of working capacity.

Those events are real. The early interpretation of Mittelafrika as a coercive extraction and forced-labor system becomes embedded in the British strategic narrative from the beginning. fileciteturn20file4L1-L10

The image then stops developing.

## The British mental model

By the 1960s, the ordinary informed Briton imagines Mittelafrika as:

- gigantic plantations;
- prison mines;
- SS patrols;
- barbed-wire labor compounds;
- starving villages;
- constant racial massacre;
- and black people fleeing whenever they can reach a British frontier.

Britain’s press does not generally claim that every African is literally imprisoned. But the ambient assumption is that every apparent civilian institution exists merely to disguise racial slavery.

Evidence of stability is interpreted as evidence of fear.

Paid wages are described as company scrip.

Chiefly authority is described as collaboration.

German-language schools are described as cultural eradication.

Low crime is described as police terror.

African technical officials are assumed to be propaganda performers.

The fact that few journalists can enter the territory makes the image impossible to falsify.

## Britain’s political need

Britain also needs the German horror story.

Its own African order is becoming:

- more restrictive;
- more dependent upon South Africa and Rhodesia;
- less committed to an endpoint of independence;
- and increasingly willing to justify unequal legal systems through security and political formation.

The established British position already relies upon contrasting its “imperfect trusteeship” with the horrors of German Mittelafrika. fileciteturn20file1L1-L20

If German Africa were acknowledged as:

- stable in many regions;
- administratively sophisticated;
- locally particularist;
- capable of rewarding black technical advancement;
- and sometimes materially better for specific Africans than British-controlled territories,

then Britain would lose its simplest moral defense.

London does not need to consciously fabricate everything. It merely has no incentive to investigate too skeptically the story which justifies its continued presence.

> **The German Congo becomes the moral debt against which every British African policy is measured—and almost anything looks moderate beside the imagined German Congo.**

# The comparative reality

There is no single answer to whether life is “better” under Britain or Germany.

It depends entirely upon who the person is.

## A registered rural community under a stable chief

Such a community in Mittelafrika may possess:

- predictable customary law;
- a recognized territorial boundary;
- low ordinary crime;
- limited daily contact with Europeans;
- a known labor obligation;
- wages or community dividends;
- and access to a school, clinic, commissary, or road.

Its members lack:

- unrestricted movement;
- national political representation;
- the right to reject imperial obligations;
- and protection if Berlin declares their land strategically necessary.

Day-to-day life may be calmer than life in a British refugee frontier or politically contested colony.

## An African technician in Katanga

He may enjoy:

- higher real wages;
- better housing;
- better schools for his children;
- greater professional authority;
- more secure employment;
- and more visible social advancement

than an ordinary black mineworker in parts of South Africa, Rhodesia, or the alternate diamond economy of Bechuanaland.

He still cannot become politically German or demand equality with the German national core.

But he is a scarce imperial asset and is treated accordingly.

## An ordinary mine laborer

He is paid.

He may receive:

- food;
- housing;
- basic medical care;
- goods;
- and direct wages or commissary credit.

His community may receive a development dividend.

He may also have been assigned through a compulsory communal quota and possess limited ability to refuse the contract.

The same man can truthfully say:

> “They made me go.”

and:

> “I came home with more than I had ever owned.”

## An unregistered migrant

This is the person for whom Mittelafrika may be far worse.

Someone without:

- an accepted identity;
- recognized community;
- labor permit;
- residence registration;
- or chiefly protection

can be treated as an administrative and security threat.

The system is generous toward scarce skills and stable registered communities.

It is harsh toward ambiguity.

## A rebellious district

Once a community is classified as resisting, all the ordinary predictability can vanish.

Roads are closed. Food is controlled. villages are relocated. Men are detained. Chiefs are removed. Military force appears with extraordinary speed.

The very machinery which makes peaceful Mittelafrika orderly makes coercive Mittelafrika terrifyingly effective.

# The invisible return migration

This is one of the best consequences of the system.

By the late 1960s and 1970s, limited migration begins to run **into** Mittelafrika.

Not mass migration. The borders and MOSAIK system make that impossible.

But there are several channels.

## Skilled workers

Mineworkers, railwaymen, mechanics, and clerks from:

- Northern Rhodesia;
- Bechuanaland;
- Portuguese Angola;
- British East Africa;
- and even German-aligned Ghana

hear that Katanga offers better contracts for qualified labor.

They apply through labor offices, chiefs, concession companies, or intermediaries.

## Technical recruits

A black British African who knows English but has mechanical experience may be offered:

- German-language training;
- a guaranteed house after qualification;
- family relocation;
- and a long-term service contract.

German administrators accept him because technical scarcity overcomes ideological discomfort.

## Families following workers

Where one worker succeeds, relatives follow through:

- marriage;
- household sponsorship;
- apprenticeships;
- and recognized communal transfers.

## Illegal crossings

Some people cross without permission, especially where British or southern African labor systems are harsher.

The German administration does not simply welcome them as propaganda trophies. Unregistered migrants create exactly the kind of ambiguity MOSAIK dislikes.

They are screened, assigned temporary status, returned, detained, or regularized according to labor demand and local sponsorship.

# The British response to reverse migration

British and Rhodesian authorities find the phenomenon politically intolerable.

Official explanations include:

- German recruitment fraud;
- trafficking;
- coercive labor contracting;
- abduction;
- false promises;
- or refugees being forced to “return” to German territory.

Some cases genuinely involve deception or coercion.

Others are simply Africans choosing the contract which appears more advantageous.

Britain avoids publishing detailed comparative wage or housing studies because the results may be embarrassing in specific sectors.

A Northern Rhodesian worker saying:

> “In Katanga they give the engine driver a house,”

does more damage than a German propaganda broadcast because it comes from someone whom British audiences cannot easily dismiss as a white Nazi official.

Yet these stories remain local:

- letters;
- market gossip;
- returning workers;
- church reports;
- border-police files;
- and labor-department memoranda.

They never become a global counter-narrative.

# Who actually understands Mittelafrika?

Only a narrow group possesses a reasonably complete picture.

## Inside the system

- senior colonial administrators;
- MOSAIK engineers;
- railway and mining directors;
- African technical-service families;
- mediation officers;
- long-serving chiefs;
- and security officials.

Even they understand only parts of the continental system.

A Katangan engineer may know little about Senegal.

A West African municipal official may know nothing about the Congo’s chiefly agreements.

## Outside observers

The most accurate outsiders are likely to be:

- Portuguese border administrators;
- Catholic missionaries;
- selected commercial representatives;
- neutral technical visitors;
- and intelligence analysts who compare production, population, and migration data.

The Vatican may privately possess a more nuanced picture than the public Catholic press. Missionaries can report both:

- genuine German brutality;
- and stable districts in which African life is not remotely equivalent to a death camp.

But such reports are difficult to explain in public without appearing to excuse National Socialism.

# American understanding

Most Americans inherit the British account.

Britain supplies:

- English-language reporting;
- refugee interviews;
- missionary testimony;
- photographs;
- films;
- and intelligence material.

Germany supplies very little accessible evidence in response.

Hollywood and American popular journalism therefore imagine Mittelafrika as the German equivalent of an enormous slave plantation.

The political factions use it differently:

- Democratic-Republicans cite it as proof of German racial tyranny.
- National Renewal criticizes British hypocrisy but rarely wants to defend a German colonial system which rewards black technical advancement.
- Black American newspapers are more skeptical of British moral self-presentation, but they also have abundant reason to distrust Germany’s racial ideology.
- Technical and commercial observers occasionally report that German African production, rail reliability, education, and wage structures cannot be explained by universal slave labor.

Those dissenting reports rarely overturn the established image.

The American public sees smoke and refugees.

It does not see MOSAIK’s payroll tables.

# The Latin-bloc understanding

Italy, Spain, Portugal, and Occitania generally repeat the common account, but with different levels of private doubt.

## Italy and Spain

Their popular press treats Mittelafrika as proof of German racial paganism and as a contrast to Latin Catholic colonialism.

This is politically useful during the German–Italian split.

## Portugal

Portugal knows more.

Angolan and Mozambican officials interact with:

- German traders;
- refugees;
- railway interests;
- African workers;
- and border authorities.

Portuguese administrators know that the territory is not uniformly a camp system.

They also know that public contradiction of the British account would damage Lisbon’s relationship with the Commonwealth and strengthen Germany.

So Portugal says little.

## Occitania

Occitan technical specialists may encounter MOSAIK equipment, German rail systems, or African administrators and suspect the foreign picture is badly incomplete.

But Occitania has even less reason than Portugal to rehabilitate German colonial prestige publicly.

# The 1970s crisis strengthens the myth

The War of the Chiefs does not correct foreign understanding.

It confirms the old story.

Foreign journalists receive:

- pictures of burned villages;
- refugee testimony;
- lists of missing men;
- reports of forced consolidation;
- and evidence of armored punitive operations.

They do not see the original constitutional mechanism:

- chiefs withholding tribute;
- attacks upon loyal neighboring communities;
- collapse of reciprocal protection;
- and the administration’s belated attempt to restore the Mosaic peace.

Britain presents the crisis as:

> “The labor camps have finally rebelled.”

Germany presents it as:

> “Feudal bandits attacked peaceful African workers and lawful chiefs.”

Both accounts contain pieces of the truth and conceal the rest.

The later Performance and Participation settlement works well enough to restore stability, but the outside world interprets the renewed quiet as renewed repression.

# The fundamental misperception

By 1980, the world believes Mittelafrika is Germany’s most primitive possession.

In reality, it may be Germany’s most **administratively advanced** possession outside Europe:

- enormous machine-readable population registers;
- tracked migration;
- negotiated community obligations;
- computerized labor assignment;
- continent-spanning rail and river integration;
- local customary law;
- African technical estates;
- chiefly development dividends;
- and an administrative system capable of distinguishing hundreds of political communities.

None of that makes it free.

But it makes it much more complicated than the foreign image of indiscriminate racial terror.

The most important line for the setting is:

> **The world thinks Mittelafrika is governed by the whip because it cannot see the computer. The people who live there know it is governed by both—and that the computer is usually the more powerful of the two.**

# Canon-ready formulation

I would amend the setting reference to something like:

> **Mittelafrika remains internationally isolated and poorly understood. Germany restricts access because of strategic mineral production, the Kribi aerospace complex, military security, disease controls, and administrative suspicion. Berlin also declines to publicize the territory’s most distinctive achievements: MOSAIK, the Mosaic Order, the African Technical Service, remunerated chiefly government, and the rise of a privileged black German-speaking professional class all sit uneasily beside National Socialist racial doctrine and occasionally give indispensable Africans better housing, pay, or workplace authority than lower-status whites. A small number of documentaries and technical exhibitions present the colony as an improvement upon Belgian and French rule, but they receive limited distribution and are contested by German racial hardliners.**

> **Foreign opinion consequently remains fixed upon the Counting Wars, forced registration, village massacres, refugee flight, compulsory community labor, and the later War of the Chiefs. Britain, America, and the Latin bloc generally imagine Mittelafrika as a nearly uniform slave-camp empire. This image is false in its totality but grounded in real early and episodic atrocities. Stable registered communities may experience predictable local government, paid labor, customary autonomy, low ordinary crime, and limited direct contact with Germans; African technicians in Katanga may enjoy better material conditions than many black workers in neighboring British, Rhodesian, Bechuanaland, or South African systems. Conversely, unregistered migrants, resisting communities, and populations located in strategic corridors face severe coercion. Limited skilled migration into Mittelafrika occurs by the late 1960s but is minimized by every government involved.**

The irony is exquisitely German:

> **The Reich builds one of the most elaborate administrative systems in the world, refuses to boast about it because it contradicts its ideology, and then spends decades complaining that foreigners do not understand what it has built.**
