# The post-Lisbon Japanese problem

The Japanese victory does not produce a simple “golden age.” It produces an **imperial management crisis**.

By late 1947 Japan possesses:

- the strongest surviving position in East Asia;
- access to oil, rubber, rice, tin, bauxite, coal, iron, and tropical commodities;
- an intact home industrial base and merchant fleet;
- recognized predominance over China and Southeast Asia;
- no American bombing damage or submarine blockade.

But it also inherits:

- millions of soldiers and occupation personnel who cannot remain mobilized indefinitely;
- incompatible military governments, currencies, railways, legal systems, and corporate concessions;
- Army and Navy administrations that often duplicate or contradict one another;
- China, which is formally unified but actually divided among Nanjing, provincial commanders, Japanese garrisons, and insurgents;
- nationalist populations who may be exhausted but are not reconciled to Japanese rule;
- inflation, wartime bond debt, rationing, and black markets;
- a severe shortage of Japanese engineers, managers, machinists, accountants, teachers, and administrators.

The existing setting already gives Japan the correct mature answer: a differentiated empire, a layered yen system, powerful zaibatsu and trading houses, the Greater East Asia Economic Board, development banks, and a deliberate concentration of advanced manufacturing in Japan, Korea, Taiwan, and Manchukuo. fileciteturn2file0 fileciteturn2file6

What we need is the political route that gets it there.

My recommended sequence is:

> **Tōjō’s Victory Cabinet, 1942–1947 → Yonai Settlement Cabinet, 1947–1948 → Shigemitsu Construction Cabinet, 1948–1953 → Kishi Development Cabinet from roughly 1953.**

The important transition is not democracy versus dictatorship. It is:

> **From a wartime coalition held together by conquest to a permanent imperial-developmental order held together by contracts, credit, shipping, patronage, and graded sovereignty.**

---

# I. Lisbon ends the war but breaks the wartime political machine

## Tōjō cannot govern the peace indefinitely

Under the working sequence established in the previous discussion, Hideki Tōjō has succeeded Konoe during the war and carried the military government through the final campaigns and Lisbon.

He is not disgraced. Quite the opposite.

He is:

- the premier under whom the Southern Resource Area was secured;
- the Army leader who accepted the strategic decision not to attack America;
- the wartime organizer under whom China was largely isolated;
- one of the men associated with victory.

But the same qualities that made him useful during the war make him dangerous during peace.

Tōjō has accumulated ministries, military authority, police influence, mobilization offices, planning bodies, and a Diet machine. If he simply remains prime minister, Japan has no visible transition from emergency government. Every local commander will continue treating temporary requisitions as permanent authority. Every ministry will continue submitting “urgent” claims. Every corporation will demand that wartime guarantees continue. Every general will describe his theater as the one place demobilization cannot occur.

The Emperor and senior statesmen therefore do not dismiss Tōjō as a failure. They **promote him out of government**.

He resigns after Lisbon with great ceremony and becomes something like:

- chairman of an Imperial Defense Council;
- senior military adviser to the Throne;
- guardian of the victory settlement;
- an elder consulted on China and continental security.

The formula is:

> **Tōjō won the war; another government must organize the victory.**

This preserves Army honor while preventing the wartime premier from owning the entire peace.

## Why the wartime mass organization does not become a Japanese Nazi Party

Japan’s Imperial Rule Assistance Association had dissolved the old parties into a top-down national organization, but it never developed the autonomous mass power or ideological cohesion of the German Nazi Party. The University of Tokyo describes it as a government-created national-integration organization that absorbed parties and civic associations from above. In the government-endorsed 1942 election, more than 80 percent of the seats went to approved candidates, but genuine non-endorsed critics such as Hatoyama Ichirō could still win. citeturn885020search1turn885020search18

That is important.

Victory strengthens the Japanese state, military, bureaucracy, and Throne. It does **not** necessarily transform the Imperial Rule Assistance structure into a truly unified revolutionary party.

The likely post-Lisbon evolution is therefore:

- the wartime political association survives temporarily;
- it loses direct control over neighborhood mobilization and war production;
- its Diet organization becomes a government electoral cartel;
- several recognized factions gradually reappear inside it;
- noncommunist constitutional conservatives and business independents are tolerated;
- anti-imperial, communist, republican, and colonial-independence politics remain illegal or heavily suppressed.

Japan becomes **managed-parliamentary and authoritarian**, not a clean one-party state.

The House of Representatives matters again, but mainly for budgets, patronage, petitions, regional interests, corporate competition, and criticism of administrative incompetence. It does not control the Emperor, supreme command, or the fundamental imperial settlement.

---

# II. The Yonai Settlement Cabinet, late 1947–1948

## Why Mitsumasa Yonai is the ideal transitional premier

The best immediate successor is Admiral **Mitsumasa Yonai**.

Yonai provides several things no Army politician can:

- naval prestige;
- personal moderation;
- a record of skepticism toward unnecessary war with the Western powers;
- acceptability to the Emperor;
- enough military standing that the Army cannot dismiss him as a civilian weakling;
- symbolic continuity with the strategic decision that kept America out.

Historically, Yonai was involved late in the war in efforts to find a settlement and authorized naval subordinates to investigate means of ending the conflict. citeturn144372search0 In this timeline, that instinct becomes part of his victory reputation: Japan triumphed because it knew which war **not** to fight.

Yonai’s Cabinet would probably last less than a year. He was already old and in poor health, and the purpose of his government is transitional rather than programmatic.

Its public name might be the **Imperial Settlement Cabinet** or **National Pacification Cabinet**.

Its work is brutally practical:

- freeze the wartime frontiers;
- begin demobilization;
- return shipping to civilian routes;
- establish occupation budgets;
- stop Army and Navy commanders from creating new faits accomplis;
- prepare currency reform;
- transfer some military administration to local governments;
- define which territories are Japanese possessions, protectorates, associated states, clients, or temporary security zones.

## The Imperial Rescript on Construction

The political transition should be consecrated by an imperial rescript in late 1947.

Its essential message is:

> The military task has been fulfilled. The sacred obligation now is construction, prosperity, education, and concord within Greater East Asia.

This does several jobs simultaneously.

For soldiers, it makes demobilization an act of obedience rather than an admission that their service is no longer needed.

For corporations, it announces that civilian production is now patriotic.

For subject governments, it offers an end to arbitrary wartime requisition.

For ordinary Japanese, it promises a peace dividend without repudiating the war.

The public slogan is not yet “Japan is the factory of the empire.” It is something broader:

> **From liberation to construction.**

The factory doctrine develops inside that framework.

---

# III. The men who build the postwar system

No single Japanese statesman invents the mature imperial economy. It emerges from a coalition of diplomats, reform bureaucrats, bankers, soldiers, and corporate managers.

## Mamoru Shigemitsu: the political architect

**Mamoru Shigemitsu** supplies the diplomatic language and the constitutional architecture of the sphere.

He is not an anti-imperialist. He believes in Japanese leadership. But he understands that Japan cannot administer hundreds of millions of Asians through open-ended military occupation.

Historically, Shigemitsu opposed reckless confrontation with the United States, later served as ambassador to the Nanjing government, and argued that the Co-Prosperity Sphere could succeed only if China and the other Asian states were treated with greater formal equality. He was also the central diplomatic figure behind the 1943 Greater East Asia Conference’s language of cooperation among nominally independent states. citeturn324249search6turn324249search10

His post-Lisbon argument is:

> **Japanese supremacy must be exercised through institutions that allow other Asians to govern themselves beneath Japanese guardianship.**

That does not mean genuine equality. It means:

- local flags;
- local ministries;
- local armies and police;
- nominal sovereign governments;
- bilateral treaties;
- development agreements;
- Japanese advisers and bases;
- Japanese control of currency, shipping, high technology, and strategic procurement.

Shigemitsu turns naked occupation into **graded sovereignty**.

His great insight is that Japan does not need every order to bear a Japanese seal. It needs every strategic decision to pass through a Japanese-controlled system.

## Nobusuke Kishi: the economic architect

If one man most clearly invents “Japan as the factory of the empire,” it is **Nobusuke Kishi**.

Historically, Kishi was one of the central economic managers of Manchukuo and later of Japan’s controlled wartime economy. He helped construct a model in which bureaucrats set industrial goals while private capital executed them. Kishi, Naoki Hoshino, and Etsusaburō Shiina were among the central planners who carried Manchurian methods into Japan’s wartime production system. citeturn885020search0turn701049search13

Kishi’s lesson from Manchukuo is not that the state must own every factory.

It is:

> The state decides what must exist. Banks decide how it will be financed. Private corporations are ordered, induced, protected, and rewarded for building it.

That becomes the model for the whole sphere.

Kishi argues that Japan cannot become merely the capital of a traditional tribute empire. It must become the **high-value transformation center**:

- Southeast Asian oil becomes Japanese fuel, chemicals, plastics, and aviation products.
- Malayan rubber becomes Japanese tires, seals, hoses, insulation, and industrial components.
- Chinese and Manchurian ore becomes steel, machinery, rails, ships, vehicles, and weapons.
- Tropical foods become processed, refrigerated, packaged imperial commodities.
- Colonial purchasing power is recycled into Japanese machinery, communications equipment, transport, consumer goods, and armaments.

The empire is not supposed to send treasure to Tokyo and receive nothing.

It sends raw and intermediate goods and receives Japanese systems.

This is economically more durable and politically more defensible than simple plunder, while remaining highly unequal.

## Naoki Hoshino: the accountant of empire

**Naoki Hoshino** is less glamorous but nearly as important.

Historically, Hoshino had served in the Ministry of Finance, became the principal civilian administrator in Manchukuo, chaired Japan’s Planning Board, and served as Tōjō’s chief cabinet secretary. His professional specialty was coordination: finance, state property, planning, ministries, and the translation of broad political aims into administrative tables. citeturn701049search1turn701049search7

Kishi thinks in factories.

Shigemitsu thinks in governments.

Hoshino thinks in:

- tonnage;
- currency balances;
- shipping priorities;
- tax yields;
- coal allocations;
- port capacity;
- food deficits;
- steel quotas;
- railway availability;
- occupation costs.

He becomes the natural first president or executive secretary of the **Greater East Asia Economic Board**.

His real achievement is preventing the sphere from being treated as a collection of unrelated Army and Navy possessions.

## Etsusaburō Shiina: the younger systems builder

**Etsusaburō Shiina** represents the younger generation of industrial bureaucrats.

Historically, Shiina worked with Kishi in Manchukuo and directed surveys of resources, agriculture, forestry, hydroelectric power, and possible settlement before contributing to industrial-development planning. citeturn701049search26

In this timeline, Shiina becomes the man of:

- industrial surveys;
- technical standards;
- factory location;
- hydroelectric development;
- port and railway studies;
- licensing agreements;
- training systems;
- common procurement specifications.

By the early 1950s, Kishi is the political master and Shiina is one of the men who makes the system legible.

## Hisato Ichimada: the monetary disciplinarian

The economic program fails if wartime inflation continues.

**Hisato Ichimada**, Governor of the Bank of Japan, is the natural monetary architect. He historically served as governor from 1946 through 1954. citeturn885020search12

Ichimada’s position is that victory does not make worthless claims valuable.

Japan has:

- too much wartime paper;
- too many government bonds;
- too many frozen prices;
- too much suppressed consumer demand;
- too many guaranteed corporate loans;
- too many military accounts that no longer correspond to real production.

He therefore supports the existing canon’s **Imperial Financial Rectification of 1948**:

- ordinary wages and small savings are substantially protected;
- large liquid balances are frozen or converted;
- wartime bonds become long-term reconstruction paper;
- banks divide viable civilian assets from dead wartime claims;
- colonial and client currencies are reorganized into a controlled yen hierarchy;
- credit is directed toward shipping, food, power, steel, housing, ports, railways, and machinery.

This is not free banking. It is disciplined developmental credit.

## Yoshisuke Aikawa and the corporate houses

The bureaucracy cannot build the empire alone.

A figure such as **Yoshisuke Aikawa**, founder of the Nissan group and head of the Manchurian Industrial Development Company, represents the corporate side of the bargain. Kishi’s Manchurian system already demonstrated the political usefulness of mobilizing private investment for state-defined industrial goals rather than making the treasury finance everything directly. citeturn701049search24

The great houses retain:

- banks;
- insurance;
- shipping;
- trading companies;
- mines;
- steel;
- chemicals;
- electrical equipment;
- shipbuilding;
- vehicles;
- colonial subsidiaries.

But they do not receive unrestricted empires of their own.

Tokyo’s rule becomes:

> **Several giants in each strategic field; no single giant may control a chokepoint the state cannot break.**

The zaibatsu survive because the state needs them.

They remain subordinate because they need state credit, shipping allocations, concessions, foreign exchange, military protection, and access to imperial markets.

---

# IV. The grand political bargain

The postwar system survives because every powerful Japanese institution receives something.

| Institution | What it retains | What it surrenders |
|---|---|---|
| Emperor and Court | Sacred supremacy and arbitration | Direct daily administration |
| Army | China, continental security, advisers, strategic reserves | Universal military government |
| Navy | Sea lanes, island perimeter, Singapore access, fleet prestige | Independent economic administration of every naval territory |
| Bureaucracy | Planning, standards, currencies, credit, development boards | Attempt to nationalize all industry |
| Zaibatsu | Property, profit, concessions, imperial markets | Freedom from strategic direction |
| Diet politicians | Elections, budgets, patronage, regional interests | Control of supreme command and imperial fundamentals |
| Local Asian elites | Ministries, offices, police, tax shares, contracts | Independent strategic policy |
| Ordinary Japanese | Gradual peace dividend and employment | Rapid demobilization or liberalization |

No faction receives everything.

That is why no faction has sufficient reason to destroy the settlement.

---

# V. What “Japan is the factory of the empire” actually means

The doctrine should not mean that every raw material is shipped to Osaka or Yokohama, manufactured there, and shipped back.

That would collapse under shipping costs and Japanese labor shortages.

The real doctrine is a **hierarchy of value added**.

## The home islands

Japan retains:

- advanced machine tools;
- precision metallurgy;
- aircraft and naval engineering;
- high-end vehicles;
- electrical equipment;
- communications;
- optics;
- chemical engineering;
- scientific research;
- financial control;
- insurance;
- industrial standards;
- design bureaus;
- the most advanced armaments.

Japan is the brain, workshop, bank, laboratory, and naval guardhouse of the sphere.

## Korea

Korea becomes an industrial and manpower appendage of the inner empire:

- ship components;
- steel;
- chemicals;
- rail equipment;
- munitions;
- textiles;
- labor-intensive assembly;
- military manpower.

Korean industrialization is real but politically subordinate. It is permitted because Japan cannot run the empire without it.

The contradiction is severe: Japan needs educated Korean technicians and managers while remaining unwilling to treat them as Japanese equals.

## Taiwan

Taiwan becomes the relatively favored colonial-industrial intermediary:

- food processing;
- sugar and chemicals;
- refining;
- pharmaceuticals;
- electrical assembly;
- tropical agricultural research;
- shipping and aviation support;
- eventually precision manufacturing.

Its administrative reliability and island geography make it easier for Tokyo to integrate than China or Southeast Asia.

## Manchukuo

Manchukuo remains the continental heavy-industrial engine:

- coal;
- iron and steel;
- power;
- locomotives;
- heavy machinery;
- armaments;
- chemicals;
- continental vehicles.

Japan does not dismantle Manchurian industry to prevent competition. It prevents Manchukuo from controlling the finance, advanced design, shipping, and strategic decision-making surrounding that industry.

## Nanjing China

China receives enough industry to sustain government and order, but not enough to become strategically independent.

Permitted:

- textiles;
- agricultural machinery;
- repair shops;
- cement;
- mining;
- food processing;
- basic chemicals;
- railway production and maintenance;
- low- and medium-complexity assembly;
- consumer goods.

Restricted:

- advanced aircraft engines;
- major naval construction;
- cutting-edge electronics;
- high-precision machine tools;
- independent armaments design;
- strategic petrochemicals;
- advanced military optics.

The stated justification is efficiency.

The real purpose is dependency.

## Malaya, Singapore, and the East Indies

The south provides:

- petroleum;
- rubber;
- tin;
- bauxite;
- food;
- timber;
- tropical chemicals;
- port services;
- refining and bulk processing.

Singapore becomes the **counting house of the empire**:

- shipping schedules;
- insurance;
- commodity contracts;
- exchange accounts;
- warehousing;
- manifests;
- regional corporate headquarters;
- intelligence disguised as commerce.

Tokyo remains the political capital. Singapore becomes the place where the empire’s physical movement is converted into accounts.

The existing setting’s formulation is exactly right: Japan does not create a German-style central commodity warehouse. It uses banks, trading companies, insurers, ships, concessions, and corporate networks to move and transform resources. fileciteturn2file10

---

# VI. The administrative solution: do not govern everything the same way

The empire becomes believable once Tokyo abandons the fiction that every territory belongs to one uniform political category.

The complexity is not an accidental flaw. It is the governing method.

## Tier One: the Inner Imperial Zone

- Japanese home islands;
- Korea;
- Taiwan;
- southern Sakhalin;
- older Pacific territories.

These are directly subordinate to the Emperor and Tokyo ministries, although their internal laws and citizenship rights differ.

## Tier Two: the Chartered Industrial State

**Manchukuo** occupies a unique category.

It has:

- its own emperor and ministries;
- Japanese vice-ministers and advisers;
- powerful development corporations;
- direct Army influence;
- its own currency inside the yen system;
- industrial privileges not extended to China proper.

It is neither an ordinary colony nor truly sovereign.

## Tier Three: Guardian Republics

- Nanjing China;
- Japanese-backed Burma;
- Eastern Siberian Republic;
- Vladivostok or Maritime client zone;
- Chukotka.

They possess flags, governments, armed forces, courts, and formal diplomatic status.

Japan controls them through:

- defense treaties;
- advisers;
- basing;
- currency arrangements;
- customs;
- communications;
- armament dependence;
- corporate concessions.

## Tier Four: Associated Allies

Initially, the principal example is **Siam**.

Associated states retain greater diplomatic and fiscal room, but enter:

- yen clearing;
- Japanese procurement;
- training and arms agreements;
- joint infrastructure;
- Japanese base arrangements;
- political consultation.

The Philippines later enters this category after the 1950s war.

## Tier Five: Resource and Security Administrations

- Malaya;
- Singapore;
- much of the former Dutch East Indies;
- sensitive islands and naval stations.

These remain under the most direct Japanese authority because their resources and geography are too important to entrust to a weak new sovereign state immediately.

Over time, local councils, royal houses, corporate boards, and nominal federations appear. Actual sovereignty remains limited.

---

# VII. How Japan reduces the military burden

Japan cannot permanently garrison its entire sphere with Japanese divisions.

The answer is **imperial military devolution**.

## Japanese forces become the upper layer

Japanese troops increasingly concentrate in:

- mobile reserve divisions;
- strategic ports;
- airfields;
- naval bases;
- rail and oil corridors;
- artillery, armor, aviation, signals, and engineering;
- command and training missions.

## Local forces perform routine security

- Nanjing armies fight Chinese insurgents.
- Manchukuo forces patrol the continental interior.
- Burmese forces hold central Burma.
- Malay, Indonesian, Korean, Taiwanese, and local colonial police perform gendarmerie duties.
- Siberian client troops guard borders and railways.

Japan supplies:

- officers and advisers;
- radios;
- aircraft;
- heavy weapons;
- intelligence;
- logistics;
- training doctrine.

This produces a crucial bargain:

> Local governments receive uniforms, ranks, salaries, and authority. Japan avoids spending Japanese lives on every village patrol.

It also means much of the empire’s violence becomes locally administered. Japanese command remains decisive, but the man at the checkpoint may be Chinese, Burmese, Malay, Korean, or Russian.

---

# VIII. Why exhausted Asian populations tolerate the system

Japan does not need most Asians to love the empire.

It needs them to prefer predictable subordination to renewed general war.

That is plausible after years of:

- civil war;
- requisition;
- blockade;
- famine;
- banditry;
- conscription;
- destroyed transport;
- rival armies;
- government collapse.

The Japanese peace offer at ground level is not philosophical.

It is:

- the train runs;
- the market reopens;
- the local court sits;
- soldiers stop taking food without receipts;
- the currency buys something;
- the village keeps part of its crop;
- the provincial official remains in office;
- the police are paid;
- the son may serve locally rather than be marched across China;
- the school opens;
- the port hires workers.

That can purchase compliance.

## The local elite bargain

Japan deliberately creates beneficiaries:

- provincial governors;
- military officers;
- merchants;
- landlords;
- technical graduates;
- police chiefs;
- shipping agents;
- bankers;
- court officials;
- nationalist collaborators;
- royal families;
- professional associations.

They receive:

- contracts;
- official status;
- education;
- tax revenues;
- protection;
- property;
- access to Japanese goods;
- positions denied under the former European colonial order.

They do not become equal partners. But they acquire something worth defending.

## Where the system remains weak

The settlement works least well where:

- Japanese wartime atrocities remain recent and personal;
- local nationalist movements possess their own military cadres;
- food is exported while local people go hungry;
- Japanese settlers displace local landowners;
- ethnic or religious frontiers resist central administration;
- the Army refuses to surrender arbitrary power;
- corporate concessions become naked monopolies;
- Nanjing officials are visibly powerless before Japanese advisers.

So the 1950s still contain insurgency and repression.

What disappears is the coherent general war against Japan.

---

# IX. The Shigemitsu Construction Cabinet, 1948–1953

Yonai’s illness or death produces the next Cabinet in 1948.

Shigemitsu becomes prime minister because he is acceptable to:

- the Emperor;
- the Navy;
- civilian diplomats;
- many business interests;
- associated Asian governments;
- Army moderates who understand the need for political consolidation.

Kishi receives a large economic portfolio. Hoshino controls planning coordination. Ichimada controls monetary stabilization.

This is not a liberal Cabinet. It is a **civilian-faced imperial Cabinet**.

## 1948: Imperial Financial Rectification

The first year is dominated by:

- currency reform;
- blocked accounts;
- bond conversion;
- food supply;
- shipping;
- soldier demobilization;
- conversion of military factories;
- establishment of the layered yen area.

Small savers and ordinary soldiers are protected enough to prevent political disaster.

Large wartime balances take heavier losses.

Corporations receive viable new accounts but cannot simply cash every wartime government promise.

## 1949: the First Greater East Asia Reconstruction Plan

The central program begins around 1949.

Its priorities are:

1. merchant shipping;
2. oil production and refining;
3. port repair;
4. coal and steel;
5. electric power;
6. railways;
7. food and fertilizer;
8. housing in Japan;
9. machine tools;
10. technical education.

The existing timeline already places restoration of civilian shipping, the end of most home-island rationing, and major investment in ports, steel, petroleum, power, housing, Korea, Taiwan, and Manchukuo between 1949 and 1957. fileciteturn3file2

The first plan is therefore not a speculative addition. It is the administrative instrument that produces the established result.

## 1949–1950: the Settlement Election

The overdue House election occurs under controlled conditions.

The government endorses most candidates, but several recognizable currents exist:

- Kishi’s technocratic Development Bloc;
- old Seiyūkai-derived constitutional nationalists around Hatoyama;
- commercial and diplomatic conservatives around Yoshida or similar figures;
- agrarian and regional independents;
- labor representatives inside government-controlled industrial associations.

Communists, republicans, and anti-imperial movements are suppressed. Yet the election is not entirely ceremonial. Constituencies can punish corrupt, incompetent, or excessively militaristic officials.

The result is a broad Shigemitsu majority dependent upon Kishi’s administrative and electoral machine.

## 1950–1952: normalization without liberalization

The Shigemitsu Cabinet gradually:

- reduces emergency rationing;
- restores ordinary civilian ministries;
- transfers occupation functions to associated governments;
- separates foreign diplomacy from direct imperial administration;
- brings Army and Navy economic offices under the Greater East Asia Economic Board;
- permits more ordinary consumer production;
- expands technical schools;
- regularizes colonial concessions;
- converts temporary military taxes into treaties, tariffs, and clearing accounts.

The Greater East Asia Ministry had historically been created in 1942 to control political, economic, strategic, and cultural relations across the sphere, eclipsing much of the traditional Foreign Ministry. citeturn124792search0

Shigemitsu’s reform partially reverses that wartime concentration.

A plausible permanent division is:

- **Foreign Ministry:** America, Germany, Italy, Britain, neutrals, and formal relations with associated Asian states.
- **Ministry of Greater East Asian Affairs:** direct possessions, protectorates, advisers, and intergovernmental supervision.
- **Greater East Asia Economic Board:** plans, shipping, commodities, industrial allocation, and clearing.
- **Imperial Defense Council:** joint strategic policy.
- **Development Bank and corporate houses:** implementation.

This prevents one super-ministry from becoming an unmanageable second government.

---

# X. The doctrine becomes explicit

During the Shigemitsu years, the internal bureaucratic phrase becomes:

> **The home islands are the precision workshop of Greater East Asia.**

The public version is softer:

> **Every region contributes according to its strength; every region shares in common prosperity.**

Internally, the doctrine is much blunter:

- Japan provides leadership, finance, science, machinery, and defense.
- Korea and Taiwan provide industrial labor and intermediate production.
- Manchukuo provides continental heavy industry.
- China provides food, minerals, labor, markets, and lower-order production.
- Southeast Asia provides strategic resources, food, ports, refining, and tropical industry.
- Associated states provide legitimacy, local administration, and military manpower.

This is the moment when “Japan is the factory of its empire” stops being merely descriptive and becomes state doctrine.

---

# XI. Why Shigemitsu eventually loses control

The Shigemitsu settlement works, but it contains a structural weakness.

Shigemitsu controls the diplomatic language.

Kishi controls:

- industrial appointments;
- credit recommendations;
- corporate relationships;
- planning officials;
- Diet candidates;
- prefectural patrons;
- employment;
- development projects;
- Army industrial contacts.

As the immediate fear of renewed war declines, the man who distributes factories, ports, loans, and contracts acquires more power than the man who negotiated the treaties.

Shigemitsu also faces criticism from both directions.

Army hardliners say:

- associated sovereignty has gone too far;
- Nanjing officials are unreliable;
- Japanese blood won the empire;
- businessmen are enriching collaborators.

Business and constitutional conservatives say:

- Kishi’s planning system is becoming a bureaucratic cartel;
- emergency controls never end;
- the state protects politically connected giants;
- ordinary consumers still wait behind strategic industry.

By 1952–1953, the settlement Cabinet has completed its mission but cannot define the next phase.

---

# XII. The next arrangement: Kishi’s Development Cabinet, circa 1953

The most likely next political transformation is Kishi’s accession to the premiership around 1953.

This is earlier than his real-world premiership, but there is no occupation, imprisonment, purge, or destruction of his wartime network. His Manchurian and wartime careers are credentials rather than liabilities.

The immediate occasion can be the emerging Philippine crisis.

Japan requires:

- deniable support to Filipino nationalists;
- careful avoidance of direct American war;
- naval deterrence;
- industrial expansion;
- propaganda;
- intelligence coordination;
- credit and trade offers ready for a post-American Philippines.

Shigemitsu remains valuable as foreign minister, senior statesman, or chairman of an imperial-relations council. But Kishi becomes prime minister because the new contest is about whether the empire’s economic system can defeat American political control without Japanese invasion.

## The political character of the Kishi settlement

Kishi does not abolish the Diet or declare a new dictatorship.

He makes the existing system permanent:

- managed elections;
- an imperial-development majority;
- powerful bureaucratic ministries;
- controlled labor associations;
- zaibatsu competition under state priorities;
- a large development bank;
- military representation in strategic councils;
- graded Asian sovereignty;
- social benefits for the Japanese industrial workforce;
- selective promotion of smaller firms in electronics, machinery, and precision manufacturing.

The regime becomes:

> **A sacred-imperial monarchy above, managed parliamentary politics in the middle, and a bureaucratic-corporate developmental machine beneath.**

This is the first genuinely stable postwar Japanese arrangement.

It is no longer wartime Tōjōism.

It is not Shigemitsu’s diplomatic interlude.

It is **Kishi’s imperial developmental state**.

---

# Recommended canon sequence

## 1947

- Lisbon formally ends the general war.
- Tōjō resigns in honor and becomes chairman of an Imperial Defense Council.
- Yonai forms a short Imperial Settlement Cabinet.
- Imperial Rescript shifts national duty from conquest to construction.
- Shigemitsu, Kishi, Hoshino, and Ichimada receive the key diplomatic, industrial, planning, and financial roles.

## 1948

- Yonai retires or dies.
- Shigemitsu becomes prime minister.
- Imperial Financial Rectification stabilizes the yen and converts wartime claims.
- Greater East Asia Economic Board is established or transformed into the principal economic coordinating body.
- Demobilization begins, but Japanese mobile reserves, advisers, and strategic garrisons remain.

## 1949

- First Greater East Asia Reconstruction Plan.
- Civilian shipping and trade revive.
- Managed general election restores limited Diet competition.
- The factory-of-the-empire doctrine begins to be articulated.

## 1950–1952

- Local governments and armies replace many Japanese occupation units.
- Korea, Taiwan, and Manchukuo industrialize rapidly.
- China remains deliberately incomplete industrially.
- Singapore becomes the imperial clearing and shipping center.
- Rationing declines in Japan.
- Technical education, machine tools, standardization, and automation become national obsessions.
- The wartime Greater East Asia administration is divided into diplomatic, administrative, economic, and military organs.

## Circa 1953

- Shigemitsu’s Construction Cabinet gives way to Kishi’s Development Cabinet.
- The Philippine crisis becomes the first major test of economic-political expansion without direct general war.
- The postwar Japanese political order becomes permanent.

The concise formulation is:

> **Japan preserves the empire by ceasing to administer it as one conquered territory. Shigemitsu supplies flags and treaties, Kishi supplies factories and credit, Hoshino supplies ledgers and shipping schedules, Ichimada supplies monetary discipline, the military supplies deterrence, and the zaibatsu supply the machinery.**

Japan’s empire survives not because it becomes simple, but because Tokyo learns to make its complexity serve Japanese power.
