# II. Britain and the Commonwealth  
## The first complete computing ecosystem

Britain begins this period with the strongest combination of:

- electronic operating experience;
- cryptanalytic machinery;
- radar and telecommunications engineers;
- theoretical computing;
- emerging stored-program designs;
- experienced machine operators;
- Commonwealth laboratories.

Its disadvantage is physical and political exhaustion. Britain has more viable computer projects than it can comfortably afford.

The setting’s fragmented 1947–51 Brick Parliament nevertheless preserves strategic industry, signals, shipping and reconstruction machinery. Butler’s government after 1951 then governs through long-term Commonwealth contracts and technical education rather than simple austerity. fileciteturn7file0

## 1. The British compromise: standards without one architecture

Britain establishes an **Automatic Computation Council** around 1948. The exact title is less important than the compromise it embodies.

The council refuses to select one winner among:

- Turing’s ACE;
- Manchester’s CRT-memory line;
- Cambridge’s EDSAC;
- Colossus-derived signal processors;
- Ferranti;
- British Tabulating Machine;
- Elliott;
- commercial office-machine firms;
- Commonwealth projects.

Instead, it standardizes what can reasonably be shared:

- paper-tape formats;
- teleprinter interfaces;
- documentation conventions;
- electrical test practices;
- standard mathematical symbols;
- routine descriptions;
- procurement terminology;
- operator training;
- classified and unclassified machine categories.

Britain therefore retains multiple instruction sets while developing a recognizable **British computing environment**.

## 2. The hardware lineages

## A. Manchester–Ferranti

The Manchester Baby runs in 1948, the Manchester Mark I is available for scientific work in 1949, and the Ferranti Mark 1 becomes the first commercially delivered general-purpose computer in 1951. The Manchester line also introduces a two-level electronic and magnetic store, while the Ferranti machines retain 40-bit words and large magnetic-drum backing storage. citeturn586328search5turn586328search1turn586328search14

Those dates need not change greatly in this setting. Britain’s war continues longer, but the preservation of Bletchley personnel, electronics manufacturing and national urgency compensates for bomb damage.

The setting divergence is institutional:

- Ferranti receives a guaranteed Commonwealth order rather than gambling on a tiny peacetime market.
- The first machines are distributed among government, Manchester, Canada and major strategic firms.
- The design team receives funds to regularize the order code earlier.
- Commonwealth compatibility is considered from the beginning.

Manchester machines emphasize:

- random-access CRT memory;
- magnetic drums;
- index registers;
- high-performance scientific computing;
- experimental programming;
- the willingness to build unusual software directly around novel hardware.

The first Ferranti order code remains awkward. Early programmers historically worked in base 32 with teleprinter-derived symbols that were notoriously difficult to remember. citeturn586328search1

That difficulty accelerates automatic coding.

## B. Cambridge EDSAC

EDSAC runs its first program in May 1949 and becomes the first stored-program system to provide a routine university computing service. It uses mercury delay-line storage and is explicitly designed as a dependable scientific utility rather than an exotic maximum-performance machine. citeturn586328search6turn586328search15turn586328search18

Cambridge’s influence on the setting is enormous because it establishes that software is not merely the private craft of the machine’s builders.

EDSAC develops:

- initial orders loaded at startup;
- a library of subroutines;
- standard calling practices;
- printed descriptions of routines;
- booking and queue procedures;
- assistance for scientific users;
- systematic error reporting.

The Cambridge principle is:

> The machine exists to serve a community of investigators, not to turn every investigator into a computer engineer.

This becomes one of the foundations of British Commonwealth scientific computing.

## C. ACE

Turing produced the ACE design at NPL in 1946. Pilot ACE historically became one of the earliest electronic stored-program machines, and Turing’s design stressed efficient serial execution and careful use of delay-line memory. citeturn586328search4turn586328search0turn586328search8

In our setting, Turing does not leave NPL in 1948 out of frustration. His wartime prestige, the selective disclosure of Bletchley’s work, and the government’s need for a national scientific figure give him greater authority.

The likely sequence is:

| Year | Setting development |
|---:|---|
| 1948 | Pilot ACE construction placed under emergency national priority |
| 1949 | Pilot machine begins limited test operation |
| 1950 | Pilot ACE enters useful service |
| 1951–52 | Full ACE or an enlarged ACE-derived machine becomes operational |
| 1953–55 | Industrial DEUCE-type derivatives enter Commonwealth service |

The ACE line has a very different programming culture from EDSAC.

It rewards:

- careful instruction timing;
- compact programs;
- exploitation of delay-line circulation;
- highly optimized subroutines;
- close understanding of the hardware;
- cleverness by elite programmers.

EDSAC democratizes computing among scientists. ACE creates a corps of formidable professional programmers.

## D. Colossus successors

Britain retains Colossus as an operational family rather than a destroyed secret.

The machines remain unsuitable for ordinary numerical work, but their successor systems become progressively more configurable.

A plausible sequence is:

- **Colossus III**, 1948–49: improved tape speed, replaceable logical panels, more counters and better diagnostics.
- **Colossus IV**, 1952–53: partially stored control, larger intermediate state and faster switching among tests.
- specialized radar-correlation and communications-analysis derivatives.

These systems lead Britain in:

- streaming input;
- character processing;
- Boolean comparison;
- pattern counting;
- communications interception;
- real-time or near-real-time message analysis.

They remain classified. Their architecture influences public Post Office and Elliott designs indirectly rather than through open technical papers.

## E. LEO and British business computing

LEO is the critical development that prevents Britain from becoming merely a scientific and military computing power.

Historically, Lyons built LEO from the EDSAC model and began regular business work in the early 1950s. Britain’s reconstruction economy gives it even stronger reasons to develop commercial data processing.

LEO initially handles:

- bakery and food-distribution calculations;
- payroll;
- stock;
- purchasing;
- delivery scheduling;
- production planning;
- management reports.

In the setting, government and Commonwealth industries quickly recognize the same applications:

- merchant-shipping schedules;
- dock labor;
- ration distribution;
- railway freight;
- hospital supply;
- military provisioning;
- blocked sterling accounts;
- reconstruction contracts.

Britain consequently develops **systems analysis** earlier and more consciously than Germany.

The LEO programmer is not simply given an equation. He or she must study an entire office procedure:

- which forms exist;
- who approves them;
- where errors occur;
- which exceptions require human judgment;
- what outputs managers need;
- which records must remain auditable.

This becomes a major British export discipline.

## 3. Commonwealth depth

The British system is larger than Britain.

Australia’s CSIR Mk1 ran its first test program in November 1949 and entered full operation shortly thereafter. It was developed by Trevor Pearcey, Maston Beard and their team from wartime radio and pulse-engineering experience. citeturn419757search13turn419757search8turn419757search3

In the setting, CSIRAC becomes an explicitly Commonwealth machine rather than an isolated Australian curiosity. Its program tapes, routines and engineering reports circulate to Britain, Canada, New Zealand and South Africa.

Canada receives a Ferranti machine and develops its own university and defense computing capacity. Historically, the second Ferranti production machine went to Toronto. citeturn586328search1

By 1955 the Commonwealth computing arrangement looks like this:

| Center | Principal contribution |
|---|---|
| Britain | Architecture, signals, software, commercial manufacture |
| Canada | Avionics, defense calculations, Arctic and industrial applications |
| Australia | Radio physics, tracking, local machine construction |
| New Zealand | Communications, meteorology and scientific use |
| South Africa | Mining, astronomy, route logistics and later tracking |
| Ceylon/Indian bastions | Operational statistics, shipping and military logistics |

The Indian Wars and the Cape system make remote data processing a military necessity. Britain begins shipping punched tapes, card decks and calculation requests among bases long before those bases are electronically networked.

## 4. British programming becomes an institution

Britain should lead the world in software practice from roughly 1949 through 1953.

### Routine libraries

Cambridge establishes the model: a routine has a documented purpose, defined inputs, defined outputs, memory requirements, known errors and a method of being called from another program.

That sounds ordinary later. In 1950 it is transformative.

### The Wheeler jump

David Wheeler’s subroutine methods make reusable library code practical. The wider Wilkes–Wheeler–Gill school then systematizes programming for stored-program computers.

Britain begins distinguishing:

- subroutine author;
- application programmer;
- machine operator;
- numerical analyst;
- systems organizer;
- hardware engineer.

### Automatic coding

Manchester’s difficult order code and ACE’s timing complexity generate pressure for symbolic and automatic coding.

By 1953–54, Tony Brooker’s autocode work produces practical languages that allow programmers to write symbolic operations rather than raw machine words. Historically, Mark 1 Autocode appeared in 1954 as an important early high-level system. citeturn586328search1turn586328search19

In the setting, the British use **autocode** as a generic category:

- Manchester Autocode;
- ACE Automatic Orders;
- EDSAC symbolic initial orders;
- LEO commercial coding schemes.

There is not yet one Commonwealth high-level language.

### National Programme Library

A **Commonwealth Programme Library** is established around 1951–52.

It is not a computer network. It is a physical and bureaucratic institution containing:

- printed routine descriptions;
- punched-tape masters;
- numerical tables;
- test data;
- correction notices;
- machine-specific versions;
- translation notes;
- lists of programmers and institutions using each routine.

It becomes the ancestor of British software standardization.

## 5. Turing’s role and survival

Turing becomes Britain’s equivalent of a national scientific architect, but his position is broader than Church’s American role.

By 1952, Turing should hold a title comparable to:

> **Director of Automatic Computation, National Physical Laboratory**

He also advises:

- signals intelligence;
- Manchester;
- the Commonwealth Programme Library;
- military control projects;
- machine-intelligence research;
- compiler and language work.

His 1950 work on machine intelligence still appears, but in this setting it is received as a paper by the recognized leader of a national industry rather than a brilliant eccentric on its margins. Turing historically moved from NPL to Manchester and published his major machine-intelligence paper after working on both ACE and the Manchester machine. citeturn586328search4turn586328search24

The historical 1952 prosecution should **not occur**.

The least contrived explanation is not a formal exemption written into law. It is that the exact chain of personal circumstances does not repeat:

- Turing remains professionally embedded at NPL.
- He has a larger household and administrative staff.
- Security services already review his private life quietly.
- Colleagues and senior officials intervene before an ordinary police matter becomes a public prosecution.
- He possesses public honors and acknowledged wartime status.
- The government regards losing him as a national-security disaster.

British law remains unjust. Other men are still prosecuted. Turing is protected because he has become too valuable and too visible to sacrifice.

This is morally compromised and institutionally plausible.

## 6. British architecture in 1955

Britain does not possess a common instruction set, but its machines share several tendencies:

- serial arithmetic remains common;
- word lengths around the low thirties to forty bits;
- teleprinter and paper-tape input;
- mercury delay lines, Williams tubes and magnetic drums;
- extensive use of index registers and subroutine libraries;
- strong separation between fast internal memory and large drum storage;
- attention to communications channels and peripheral flow;
- operator-facing consoles rather than purely engineering panels.

Its unique strength is not a particular memory device. It is the belief that the computer belongs inside a **service and communications system**.

## 7. Britain’s standing in 1955

Britain probably holds the broadest computing ecosystem in 1955:

- scientific machines;
- commercial machines;
- signals machines;
- Commonwealth construction;
- programming languages;
- routine libraries;
- trained operators;
- commercial manufacturers.

It does not necessarily possess the fastest single machine or the largest production line.

Britain leads in:

- software practice;
- programming education;
- business systems analysis;
- communications-oriented computation;
- Commonwealth interoperability.

Its weaknesses are:

- too many architectures;
- limited capital;
- duplicated programs;
- fragile valve production;
- dependency on government procurement;
- competition among NPL, Manchester, Cambridge, Ferranti and BTM.

Britain’s independence from American computing is fully secure.

# III. United States  
## Church’s theory, von Neumann’s architecture and the commercial machine

America’s path is delayed but not crippled.

The decisive distinction is that the United States lacks Britain’s wartime computing establishment and Germany’s state-directed technical concentration. It compensates with:

- Bell Laboratories;
- IBM;
- universities;
- insurance and banking;
- aviation;
- a huge domestic market;
- superior production engineering;
- the transistor;
- competing private firms.

The United States in the setting is still emerging from the Depression and does not experience historical total mobilization. Dewey’s recovery program begins restoring investment after 1949, while the Philippine War from 1953 adds new military urgency. fileciteturn7file1

## 1. The four American pillars

## A. Church and the Princeton theoretical school

Alonzo Church becomes the American patriarch of computation.

His role is not to specify wire counts or memory tubes. He establishes the theoretical boundaries of the subject:

- effective calculation;
- recursive functions;
- lambda calculus;
- formal systems;
- symbolic substitution;
- the distinction between syntax and mathematical meaning;
- the equivalence of different models of computation.

American writing normally calls the computability claim **Church’s Thesis** or **Church’s Hypothesis**. British writing increasingly calls the corresponding idea **Turing’s Hypothesis**. German and neutral continental writing tends toward the combined **Church–Turing-Hypothese**.

Church’s institutional importance grows because Princeton contains both Church and the nearby Institute for Advanced Study.

A **Princeton Seminar on Logic and Automatic Computation** forms around 1948–49. Its participants and visitors include:

- Church;
- von Neumann;
- Gödel;
- logicians and graduate students;
- numerical analysts;
- engineers from the IAS machine;
- occasional Bell and military personnel.

This does not immediately produce practical software. It gives America the strongest theoretical school.

The characteristic American split is already visible:

> Church explains what can be computed.  
> Von Neumann explains how a general machine should be organized.  
> Engineers explain what can actually be built and sold.

## B. Von Neumann and the IAS family

The IAS project begins in 1947 and historically produced a machine completed around 1951, with its architecture widely copied. UNIVAC development also began in 1947 and reached the Census Bureau in 1951. citeturn311582search3turn311582search7

The setting’s early fiscal weakness delays completion modestly.

A credible schedule is:

| Machine | Setting operation |
|---|---:|
| Stored-program ENIAC conversion | 1949 |
| IAS machine | 1952 |
| EDVAC | 1952 |
| Major IAS-derived university machines | 1953–55 |

The IAS architecture becomes the American scientific default:

- binary;
- parallel arithmetic;
- stored instructions and data;
- roughly forty-bit words;
- fast electronic memory;
- one-address or related compact instruction formats;
- general scientific purpose.

Von Neumann makes the architecture publicly replicable because he wants a national scientific ecosystem rather than one proprietary machine.

American universities and laboratories build local variants. They share concepts and software ideas, but not necessarily complete binary compatibility.

## C. Shannon and Bell Laboratories

Bell Labs supplies the third pillar:

- switching theory;
- information theory;
- communication channels;
- coding;
- noise;
- cryptography;
- reliable relay and electronic logic;
- the 1947 transistor.

Bell Laboratories created the first working transistor in 1947, opening the path toward smaller, lower-power and more reliable switching devices, although practical computer-scale transistorization remains a 1950s problem. citeturn229554search2turn229554search0

The American computer therefore develops in close conceptual proximity to communications.

Bell’s initial influence is not a transistor mainframe. It is:

- better circuit theory;
- reliability engineering;
- remote terminals;
- error detection;
- switching-network design;
- the understanding that information can be measured and transmitted independently of its meaning.

This gives America the intellectual foundations for later networking, data communications and digital control.

## D. Eckert–Mauchly, Remington Rand and IBM

The commercial pillar turns computers from national instruments into products.

ENIAC demonstrated large-scale electronic arithmetic; the subsequent Eckert–Mauchly organization pursued UNIVAC for government and business users. ENIAC itself used electronic decimal accumulators and originally required physical reconfiguration, while UNIVAC became a commercially produced data-processing system. citeturn311582search8turn311582search12turn311582search21turn311582search3

IBM initially remains cautious because punched cards are profitable and proven.

That caution is stronger in this setting:

- Depression-era firms hesitate to buy unprecedented equipment.
- There is no American wartime boom.
- Government orders are fewer.
- Thomas Watson Sr. dislikes risking the card-machine business.
- The market for dozens of scientific supercomputers appears uncertain.

Thomas Watson Jr. and younger engineers nevertheless push toward electronics. Historically IBM’s SSEC appeared in 1948, the 701 was designed from 1951 and introduced in 1952, and the 650 was announced in 1953 as the first mass-produced computer. citeturn311582search10turn311582search2turn311582search6

The setting shifts the schedule roughly one year:

| IBM development | Setting date |
|---|---:|
| SSEC-like electronic calculator | 1948–49 |
| IBM scientific stored-program project | 1952 |
| First 701-class deliveries | 1953 |
| 650-class drum machine announced | 1954 |
| First large delivery wave | 1955 |

By the end of 1955, IBM has transformed the balance.

America may not have the best programming system, but it can make machines in numbers no European competitor can comfortably match.

## 2. Political economy of American computing

The anti-New Deal order initially cuts or narrows federal programs. Computing survives because it can be framed in two politically acceptable ways.

### Defense without mass mobilization

Computers support:

- Navy ship design;
- aircraft;
- weather;
- guided weapons;
- radar;
- continental defense;
- the Philippines;
- cryptography;
- logistics.

### Administrative economy

Computers promise to reduce:

- clerical payroll;
- duplicate records;
- benefit fraud;
- tax-processing delays;
- inventory waste;
- military supply overhead.

This creates a useful paradox:

> A government elected to reduce the administrative state becomes a major purchaser of machines intended to administer more efficiently.

The Bureau of the Census, Treasury, military services and large corporations provide steady demand without reviving New Deal rhetoric.

Dewey’s National Recovery and Enterprise policy after 1949 favors:

- investment allowances;
- university-industry contracts;
- defense procurement;
- telecommunications;
- industrial modernization;
- accelerated depreciation for machinery.

Computers are sold as productive capital, not central planning.

## 3. The American architectural split

By 1955, America has three major machine classes.

## Scientific systems

These descend from IAS, IBM 701, EDVAC and university machines.

| Characteristic | Scientific American line |
|---|---|
| Number system | Binary |
| Word size | Often around 36–40 bits |
| Arithmetic | Fixed point, with increasingly common floating-point support |
| Memory | Electrostatic, drum and then core |
| Input/output | Cards, tape, printers |
| Users | Science, aviation, military and engineering |

## Business systems

These descend from punched cards, UNIVAC and IBM’s decimal-oriented commercial lines.

| Characteristic | Business American line |
|---|---|
| Number system | Decimal or binary-coded decimal |
| Data unit | Character or decimal digit rather than purely numerical word |
| Storage | Cards, magnetic tape and drums |
| Output | High-speed printed reports |
| Users | Census, insurance, banking, payroll, inventory |
| Governing concern | Throughput and records rather than mathematical speed |

## Real-time systems

The most distinctive is Whirlwind.

Whirlwind historically grew from a flight-simulator project into an operational real-time computer and became central to magnetic-core-memory development. The Manchester group also ran an experimental transistor computer in 1953, illustrating how rapidly logic technology was changing. citeturn586328search5turn793414search1

In the setting, Whirlwind is delayed slightly by weaker wartime funding but rescued by:

- Navy aviation;
- German jet and missile development;
- continental air-defense concern;
- the Philippine War.

It becomes operational around 1952, with practical magnetic-core memory around 1954.

The Whirlwind line is:

- word-parallel;
- fast;
- designed for immediate response;
- able to accept radar, keyboard and control inputs;
- organized around interactive operation rather than overnight batch work.

This is the foundation of America’s later spaceplane and real-time aerospace computing.

## 4. Software development

America begins behind Britain in software organization but catches up rapidly.

### Assemblers and symbolic coding

The first step is replacing numeric addresses with symbolic names and mnemonics.

American firms develop machine-specific assemblers because their customers cannot afford to employ only mathematicians capable of memorizing raw instruction numbers.

### Short Code and interpretive systems

Interpretive systems allow programmers to use more convenient mathematical operations at the cost of execution speed.

This is especially attractive on machines whose electronic speed is already enormous compared with human calculation.

### Grace Hopper and compilers

Grace Hopper and her colleagues historically developed the A-0 compiling routine in 1952 and continued compiler work through 1953–54. citeturn770665search3turn770665search7turn770665search11

Her route into the field differs in the setting because America lacks the same wartime naval mobilization. The cleanest alternate path is:

- civilian mathematical work with Harvard’s Mark machines;
- recruitment by Eckert–Mauchly around 1948–49;
- work on UNIVAC documentation and routine libraries;
- development of an A-0-like system in 1953 rather than 1952.

Hopper’s central claim is radical:

> The programmer should be able to name a routine, and the machine should assemble the necessary instructions.

This is philosophically different from Church’s work, but the two traditions eventually meet. Church supplies a formal theory of expressions and substitution; Hopper supplies machinery for translating human-oriented specifications into executable code.

### Speedcoding

Von Neumann’s group and IBM researchers develop systems for easier scientific programming. John Backus’s Speedcoding work in the early 1950s provides another route toward higher-level programming.

By 1955 the United States has several automatic coding systems, but no national standard language.

## 5. Church’s influence on software

Church does not write America’s standard compiler.

His importance is slower and deeper.

The Princeton school encourages programmers and mathematicians to distinguish:

- the language being written;
- the formal rules governing expressions;
- the meaning assigned to those expressions;
- the machine used to execute them;
- the proof that two formulations compute the same function.

American engineering organizations initially find this excessively abstract.

By the later 1950s and 1960s, it becomes one reason American language design develops strong academic foundations.

The terminology split becomes culturally meaningful:

- An American paper may say, “By Church’s Hypothesis, this process is effectively calculable.”
- A British paper may say, “Under Turing’s Hypothesis, a universal machine can perform the process.”
- A German paper may discuss the equivalence of the Church and Turing formulations.
- Japanese and Latin authors initially translate whichever foreign source they are using.

## 6. The Philippine effect, 1953–1955

The Philippine War gives American computing a military problem very different from Germany’s continental empire or Britain’s signals war.

The United States needs:

- shipping schedules;
- airlift;
- repair-parts control;
- jungle weather;
- personnel rotation;
- casualty and medical records;
- radio direction finding;
- intelligence collation;
- mapping;
- aircraft maintenance;
- dispersed-base communications.

Computers are still too large to accompany ordinary units. They operate in:

- Hawaii;
- Guam;
- California;
- Manila or protected rear bases;
- naval headquarters;
- major depots.

The war teaches the American military that information delay matters as much as arithmetic speed.

That pushes funding toward:

- teleprinters;
- remote terminals;
- standardized supply codes;
- magnetic tape;
- real-time displays;
- communications-integrated computers.

It also gives Whirlwind and Bell’s communications tradition greater influence over future military architecture.

## 7. America’s standing in 1955

America catches Britain and Germany by the end of the period.

It leads in:

- production scale;
- magnetic core and real-time computing;
- commercial market potential;
- magnetic-tape business processing;
- number of competing firms;
- integration with telephone and communications research.

It trails Britain in:

- mature programming services;
- routine libraries;
- trained programmer density;
- institutional memory of electronic operations.

It trails Germany in:

- high-level typed numerical specification;
- integration with analog guidance and centralized industrial planning;
- formal certification of mission programs.

America’s long-term advantage is that a company can buy a machine and use it for something the government did not plan.

# IV. Japan  
## Slow accumulation before the 1957 acceleration

Japan should not remain technologically dormant until Raumbote I. The 1957 shock works only when it strikes a country that already has:

- functioning research groups;
- several competing circuit technologies;
- trained engineers;
- early machines;
- government committees;
- corporations ready to expand production.

The period from 1947 to 1955 is therefore one of **deliberate but underfunded accumulation**.

Japan’s empire and postwar economic system already create pressure for shipping, food, petroleum, steel, currency clearing, technical education and automation. Its zaibatsu survive, Singapore becomes the commercial counting house, and the home islands retain design, finance, machinery and high technology. fileciteturn7file0

## 1. Institutional development

Japan forms an **Imperial Automatic Calculation Research Council** around 1949–50. The working name can change, but its structure should be characteristically Japanese.

It includes:

- Ministry of Education;
- Ministry of Communications;
- Army and Navy technical bureaus;
- Bank of Japan;
- Greater East Asia Economic Board;
- Tokyo Imperial University;
- Electrotechnical Laboratory;
- Fujitsu’s predecessor;
- NEC;
- Toshiba;
- Hitachi;
- Mitsubishi;
- major trading houses;
- Manchurian and Korean industrial representatives.

It does not centralize all projects. Its principal tasks are:

- issuing research grants;
- exchanging nonclassified circuit information;
- agreeing upon data formats;
- preventing Army–Navy duplication where politically possible;
- developing technical vocabulary;
- purchasing foreign publications and machines;
- placing promising graduates in firms and laboratories.

The Japanese state concludes that it is too early to choose one technology. It funds relays, vacuum tubes, parametrons and early transistor research in parallel.

## 2. The early machine families

Japan historically produced the ETL Mark I relay prototype in 1952, the FACOM 100 in 1954 and ETL Mark II in 1955. FUJIC development began in 1949 but the vacuum-tube machine was not completed until 1956. The University of Tokyo’s TAC project began in 1951, received a Toshiba prototype at the end of 1954 and suffered prolonged delays before eventual completion. citeturn793414search0turn793414search1turn793414search10

The setting’s intact industrial base improves those outcomes without making Japan instantly equal to Britain.

## A. Yamashita and administrative relay systems

Hideo Yamashita’s statistical-machine tradition receives immediate imperial backing.

Its machines are designed for:

- census summaries;
- shipping;
- food;
- customs;
- industrial returns;
- railway traffic;
- military personnel;
- clearing accounts.

Their architecture remains decimal and record-oriented.

They use:

- relays;
- counters;
- punched cards;
- crossbar or switching networks;
- printed output;
- fixed or semi-fixed sequences.

They are not universal scientific computers, but they produce visible administrative value.

Singapore, Seoul, Mukden and Tokyo receive the first major installations. Nanjing and colonial capitals initially send card decks and summary tapes rather than operating advanced machines of their own.

## B. ETL relay computers

The Electrotechnical Laboratory develops more general relay computers.

The ETL Mark I appears around its historical 1952 date. Mark II follows by 1954–55 rather than late 1955.

These systems are:

- reliable;
- slow;
- useful for scientific and engineering work;
- well suited to training;
- connected to communications engineering;
- capable of being repaired by relay and switching specialists.

They become the standard machines of government technical laboratories.

## C. FACOM

Fujitsu’s relay-computer program becomes the first Japanese commercial line.

Historically the FACOM 100 was practically used in 1954, and the later FACOM 128A employed distinctive checking, asynchronous procedures, crossbar storage, semi-fixed card storage and indexing techniques. citeturn793414search1turn793414search7

In the setting:

- FACOM 100 operates in 1953 rather than late 1954.
- A production-oriented successor is under construction by 1954.
- Initial deliveries begin in 1955 rather than 1956.

The Japanese system’s distinctive engineering values already appear:

- asynchronous operation rather than one rigid central clock;
- extensive checking;
- graceful handling of relay delay;
- decimal or bi-quinary internal coding for business and statistical work;
- modular peripheral control;
- high reliability.

Japan is not merely copying a British or American stored-program machine. FACOM grows from switching and telecommunications engineering.

## D. FUJIC

Bunji Okazaki began FUJIC in 1949 to automate lens-design calculations; historically it became Japan’s first completed electronic computer in 1956. citeturn793414search0turn793414search1

The setting gives Okazaki:

- access to intact valve production;
- greater company funding;
- military optical interest;
- German and British technical publications;
- national recognition.

FUJIC becomes operational in **late 1954 or early 1955**.

It remains a specialized scientific machine rather than a commercial mainframe.

Its first applications include:

- optical lens design;
- cameras;
- rangefinders;
- aerial reconnaissance optics;
- naval fire-control optics;
- industrial precision instruments.

FUJIC is culturally important because it proves that a Japanese private company can complete a vacuum-tube stored-program machine without importing the entire architecture.

## E. TAC

The Tokyo–Toshiba TAC project historically used an EDSAC-like binary serial architecture, CRT memory and a university–industry division in which the university worked on software while Toshiba concentrated on hardware. The prototype arrived in 1954, but technical and organizational problems delayed completion until 1959. citeturn793414search10

In this setting, the project is better managed.

The council imposes:

- one responsible chief engineer;
- milestone testing;
- direct access to German and British memory research;
- continued Toshiba commitment;
- a dedicated programming group;
- less duplication with Army projects.

TAC becomes operational around **1955–56**, putting its first successful runs at the edge of this interval rather than four years later.

It is Japan’s first serious university-scale stored-program scientific machine.

## F. The parametron

Eiichi Goto invents the parametron in 1954, using two stable phases of an oscillating circuit to represent binary states. Parametron systems offer reliability but are slower and consume more power than mature transistor systems. citeturn793414search2turn793414search4turn793414search5

The invention should remain in 1954. It is too dependent upon Goto’s personal education and insight to move casually several years earlier.

What changes is the response.

In real history, construction of the PC-1 began later. In the setting:

- the Imperial Council identifies the parametron immediately;
- NTT, NEC, Fujitsu, the Navy and Tokyo University form a shared research group in late 1954;
- small logic matrices and memory tests operate in 1955;
- multiple firms license the principle before a full computer exists.

This gives Japan a distinctly native electronic route ready for the post-1957 surge.

## 3. Foreign reference machines

Japan purchases foreign machines without becoming dependent upon them.

A sensible pattern is:

- one German Zuse relay system at Tokyo Imperial University or an Army technical institute;
- Italian office calculators and tabulating systems in Singapore;
- British scientific papers and perhaps a Commonwealth machine acquired through a neutral intermediary;
- American IBM and Remington literature purchased commercially;
- captured or inherited European punched-card equipment throughout Southeast Asia.

The German Zuse machine is valuable for:

- floating-point ideas;
- program tape;
- reliability practice;
- comparison with Japanese relays.

Japanese engineers dislike several features:

- German-language documentation;
- reliance on highly trained operators;
- machine assumptions optimized for European engineering offices;
- restrictive access to military libraries;
- weak support for Japanese administrative records.

It becomes a reference, not a template.

## 4. Japanese architecture remains plural

By 1955, Japan has four viable architectures:

| Family | Arithmetic | Technology | Principal use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Statistical machines | Decimal | Relays and cards | Imperial administration |
| FACOM | Decimal/bi-quinary | Relays | Government, business, statistics |
| FUJIC/TAC | Binary | Vacuum tubes | Science and engineering |
| Parametron research | Binary | Oscillating logic | Future scientific and control systems |

Japan does not force them into one standard.

Instead, it standardizes the **procedure surrounding the machine**.

## 5. The procedure-sheet tradition

Around 1952–53, Japanese institutions adopt a formal **shori tejun-hyō**—a processing-procedure sheet.

It records:

- data source;
- field codes;
- operation sequence;
- decision points;
- responsible office;
- expected output;
- error checks;
- machine and peripheral required;
- human approval points.

This is not a programming language.

It is a standardized way to describe a process independently of whether it is executed by:

- clerks;
- card machines;
- relay computers;
- an electronic computer;
- a mixed human-machine office.

The later Japanese TEJUN-style programming family should descend from this administrative and engineering practice.

## 6. Character and language problems

Japanese machines use:

- numeric machine codes;
- Latin letters for registers and variables;
- conventional mathematical notation;
- katakana on control panels and instructions;
- teleprinter kana for messages;
- numerical codes for kanji-bearing administrative categories.

There is no unified Japanese character encoding by 1955.

Each firm has proprietary conventions. A person’s name is usually stored as:

- numeric identity;
- kana transliteration;
- district and household code;
- kanji on the accompanying paper file.

This limitation encourages Japan to design computers around coded transactions rather than free text.

## 7. Early industrial automation

Japan’s most important divergence appears outside the computer room.

The Navy, zaibatsu and state development banks fund pilots involving:

- automatic telephone exchanges;
- machine-tool sequence control;
- port-crane scheduling;
- refinery instrumentation;
- rolling-mill control;
- warehouse conveyors;
- statistical quality checking;
- shipyard production boards;
- power-distribution monitoring.

Most are not controlled by stored-program computers. They use:

- relays;
- cams;
- punched tape;
- analog regulators;
- dedicated electronic circuits;
- human supervisors.

The cultural link between computation and machinery is nevertheless being forged.

## 8. Japan’s standing in 1955

Japan remains behind the leading three in:

- number of electronic machines;
- memory technology;
- programming languages;
- scientific-computing capacity;
- commercial stored-program installations.

It is competitive in:

- relay logic;
- checking and reliability;
- administrative procedure;
- telephone and switching engineering;
- industrial sequence control;
- corporate coordination;
- practical automation incentives.

Japan is perhaps three years behind the leaders in large electronic machines, not ten.

Raumbote I in 1957 will not create Japanese computing. It will convince the state to turn a promising collection of laboratories into a strategic national industry.

# V. The Latin system  
## Italian industrial design and Occitan electronic autonomy

The Latin bloc remains the least unified system during this interval.

Italy, Occitania, Spain and Portugal share political affinities and increasingly cooperate, but they do not yet possess a common economic or military technical board comparable to their later institutions.

The system develops around two cores:

- **Italy:** office machinery, state industry, telecommunications and imperial administration.
- **Occitania:** aviation, radar, guidance, scientific electronics and numerical research.

Spain and Portugal are initially customers, training centers and peripheral manufacturers.

## 1. The political requirement: autonomy without isolation

Italy maintains good relations with Germany during this period and has no reason to refuse German assistance. It does have strong reasons to avoid complete dependence:

- Italy is an imperial victor.
- It controls Suez and a large Mediterranean system.
- Mussolini and the monarchy require visible national technical achievement.
- German firms restrict military software and advanced components.
- Olivetti, IRI and STET already provide domestic industrial foundations.
- Occitania wants autonomy from both Rome and Berlin.

The Latin policy becomes:

> Buy one foreign machine to understand it.  
> Buy components where useful.  
> Never let the foreign supplier own the language, data or trained personnel of the state.

## 2. Italy’s institutional system

A **Consiglio Nazionale per il Calcolo Automatico** is formed around 1949.

It includes:

- IRI;
- STET;
- Finmeccanica;
- Bank of Italy;
- armed services;
- universities at Rome, Milan, Turin and Pisa;
- Olivetti;
- Fiat;
- naval and aerospace firms;
- imperial customs and Suez authorities.

Italy’s computer investment is divided among three purposes.

### Administrative and commercial

Italy needs:

- Suez tolls;
- shipping;
- customs;
- imperial payroll;
- state-company accounts;
- railway scheduling;
- banking;
- insurance;
- census and rationing.

### Military and scientific

Italy requires:

- naval fire control;
- radar;
- aircraft;
- guided weapons;
- artillery;
- weather;
- signals;
- nuclear research.

### Office automation

Olivetti sees an opportunity to make automatic calculation usable by ordinary businesses rather than only state laboratories.

## 3. German machines as reference systems

Germany sells or leases Italy a Zuse engineering machine around 1951.

It is probably an early Z5-class system rather than the unique Z4. The machine is installed at a national applications institute in Rome or Milan and informally called the **Zeta** by Italian staff.

Its uses include:

- aircraft structures;
- naval architecture;
- ballistics;
- optics;
- Suez engineering;
- hydroelectric and industrial calculations.

The Italians learn several valuable lessons:

- floating-point arithmetic is important;
- punched program tape permits repeated calculations;
- a formal mathematical description can outlive the machine;
- maintenance documentation is as important as the processor.

They also learn what they do not want:

- an operator environment dominated by German terminology;
- an engineering-only data model;
- dependence on imported relays and parts;
- limited decimal and record-processing support;
- security restrictions on libraries;
- hardware designed without concern for the ordinary clerk.

The Zeta becomes the machine against which Italian designers define themselves.

## 4. Olivetti enters electronics

The historical ELEA 9003 was the first commercial transistorized computer developed in Italy, built by Mario Tchou and an interdisciplinary Olivetti team; its console also reflected Olivetti’s emphasis on ergonomics and visual design. citeturn974016search0turn974016search3turn974016search6

In the setting, Adriano Olivetti begins electronic research earlier.

### 1949–1951

Olivetti establishes a small electronic-calculation study office.

It initially examines:

- electronic multiplication;
- card readers;
- printing mechanisms;
- relay control;
- magnetic storage;
- German and British computers;
- how an electronic calculator might fit an ordinary office.

### 1952–1953

The office becomes a formal electronics laboratory.

Giorgio Sacerdoti and other systems engineers receive expanded authority. Mario Tchou is recruited around 1953 rather than 1955.

The team does not begin with a scientific supercomputer. It designs an **electronic data-processing system** around:

- decimal and alphanumeric records;
- punched cards;
- magnetic tape;
- high-speed printers;
- an operator console;
- modular peripheral units.

### 1954–1955

The first full Olivetti experimental electronic processor operates.

A working project designation such as **ELEA Sperimentale 1** is sufficient. It should not yet be the mature transistorized ELEA 9003.

Its likely form is:

- vacuum-tube central logic;
- decimal or binary-coded-decimal arithmetic;
- magnetic drum or delay-line memory;
- cards and paper tape;
- printed output;
- modular cabinets;
- an unusually deliberate operator console;
- strong diagnostic routines.

Olivetti does not sell a full production mainframe by 1955. It has a successful prototype and a clear product architecture.

That is enough to keep Italy sovereign.

## 5. The IRI and STET line

Olivetti is not Italy’s only computer establishment.

IRI and STET develop machines for:

- telecommunications;
- state-company accounts;
- railways;
- electricity;
- military communications;
- Suez administration;
- industrial control.

Their machines are less elegant and more bureaucratic than Olivetti’s.

A typical IRI system favors:

- decimal arithmetic;
- magnetic drums;
- card input;
- large printers;
- fixed reporting cycles;
- robust operation;
- direct compatibility with state forms.

Italy therefore develops a domestic rivalry:

- Olivetti argues for flexible, human-centered commercial systems.
- IRI argues for large state systems designed around national infrastructure.
- The military demands faster binary scientific and control machines.
- Universities want access to any machine capable of numerical research.

This rivalry prevents stagnation.

## 6. Occitania’s foundation

Occitania inherits people rather than a complete computer industry.

Bull’s principal corporate and manufacturing establishments remain largely in northern France or German-controlled territory. Southern evacuation preserves selected:

- radar engineers;
- aeronautical mathematicians;
- telephone specialists;
- military electronics personnel;
- university physicists;
- numerical analysts;
- machine designers unwilling to work under German supervision.

The state forms an **Institut occitan de calcul et d’automatique** at Toulouse around 1948.

Louis Couffignal is a strong candidate for its intellectual founder. François-Henri Raymond and other French electronic-machine figures may relocate south depending upon their exact wartime political choices.

Occitania’s immediate needs are:

- aircraft;
- radar;
- air defense;
- artillery;
- port and railway reconstruction;
- military command;
- industrial accounting;
- national independence from Parisian machinery.

## 7. Occitan machine development

## A. Analog and radar systems, 1948–1950

The first Occitan successes are not general computers.

They are:

- analog flight simulators;
- radar plot converters;
- gunnery calculators;
- electrical differential analyzers;
- navigation systems;
- guided-weapon test equipment.

This gives the Occitan establishment an integration-oriented culture.

## B. First stored-program prototype, 1951–1953

The Occitans study:

- EDSAC publications;
- ACE;
- Zuse;
- German electronic logic;
- French prepartition research;
- American EDVAC and IAS reports.

They deliberately avoid copying one machine.

The first **Calculateur toulousain** operates around 1952–53.

Its architecture is plausibly:

| Feature | Occitan prototype |
|---|---|
| Arithmetic | Binary fixed point with software floating point |
| Word size | Approximately 32–36 bits |
| Logic | Vacuum tubes |
| Main memory | Delay lines or electrostatic store |
| Backing store | Magnetic drum |
| Input/output | Paper tape, teleprinter and instrument interfaces |
| Primary use | Aerodynamics, radar, artillery and industrial calculation |

Its distinctive feature is buffered or semi-independent input/output. It cannot yet be called a modern channel architecture, but its designers are unusually concerned with allowing the arithmetic unit to continue working while slower peripheral actions occur.

This anticipates Occitania’s later expertise in combat computers and systems integration.

## C. Limited production, 1954–1955

An Occitan electronics firm produces a handful of improved machines for:

- Toulouse aerospace;
- naval research at Toulon or Marseille;
- artillery and armor establishments;
- universities;
- the Italian military under reciprocal agreements.

Occitania does not have the industrial scale for mass production. It has enough capacity to maintain a technical school and export prototypes.

## 8. Italian–Occitan cooperation

The two systems establish a technical committee around 1953–54.

They do **not** standardize instruction sets.

They standardize:

- tape widths;
- electrical connectors;
- card dimensions;
- numerical data descriptions;
- peripheral-control signals;
- subroutine documentation;
- test procedures;
- exchange formats for scientific results.

This becomes the early foundation of the later Latin technical system.

The key compromise is:

- Italian systems may remain decimal and record-oriented.
- Occitan systems may remain binary and scientific.
- Shared peripherals and exchange codes prevent total isolation.

The Latin bloc therefore resembles Britain more than Germany in one respect: it values interoperability without demanding one processor.

## 9. Latin programming

### Italy

Italian programming begins with:

- machine code;
- symbolic addresses;
- card workflows;
- decimal arithmetic routines;
- report generators;
- printer and tape handling;
- office-procedure analysis.

Olivetti’s programmers pay unusual attention to:

- operator prompts;
- readable error messages;
- printed audit trails;
- data-entry correction;
- modular applications.

Corrado Böhm’s formal and compiler interests begin influencing university research near the end of the period, but Italy does not yet possess a general high-level language.

### Occitania

Occitan programming emphasizes:

- mathematical formula translation;
- radar and instrument input;
- numerical libraries;
- reusable aerospace routines;
- assembly notation;
- real-time sequencing.

The Occitans borrow the word **programme** naturally but distinguish between:

- *ordre*—a machine instruction;
- *routine*—a reusable sequence;
- *schéma*—the logical arrangement of a problem;
- *programme*—the complete executable procedure.

### Spain

José García Santesmases establishes a Spanish school around analog calculation, relay logic and university instruction.

Spain purchases Italian office machines and acquires access to an Occitan scientific computer. It begins local production of:

- card equipment;
- tape readers;
- relays;
- power supplies;
- consoles;
- peripheral cabinets.

By 1955 Spain can maintain and partially manufacture a computer installation, but not design a competitive large processor independently.

### Portugal

Portugal remains principally an adopter.

Its strengths are:

- telegraphy;
- shipping;
- banking;
- customs;
- colonial records;
- neutral technical exchange.

Lisbon purchases British and Italian systems and becomes skilled at data conversion. It does not possess an indigenous general-purpose computer by 1955.

## 10. Latin standing in 1955

The Latin system is behind the leading three in:

- raw processing speed;
- machine count;
- memory research;
- programmer population;
- large scientific installations.

It remains autonomous because it possesses:

- Olivetti;
- IRI and STET;
- an Italian electronic prototype;
- Occitan stored-program machines;
- strong analog and military electronics;
- domestic office-machine production;
- university research;
- compatible peripheral standards.

No Italian minister or industrialist can plausibly argue in 1955 that the bloc should abandon its work and conduct all serious computation in German.

German machines are faster in some tasks. British software is more mature. American machines are becoming more numerous. The Latin system nevertheless has a defensible technological future.

---

# VI. The balance of the race, year by year

## 1948–1949: Britain takes the visible lead

Britain produces the first stored-program service machines and preserves its electronic signals establishment. Germany possesses Zuse and begins institutional consolidation, but remains relay-heavy. America has great projects but suffers financial and organizational delay. Japan and the Latin states are organizing laboratories.

**Leader:** Britain.

## 1950–1951: three different forms of leadership

Britain leads in operational stored-program computers and software practice.

Germany leads in formal high-level problem description and analog-digital aerospace integration.

America begins fielding commercial and scientific systems with much greater production potential.

**Leader:** no single answer; Britain is the most complete.

## 1952–1953: America closes rapidly

The IAS, UNIVAC, Whirlwind and IBM lines give America scientific, business and real-time architectures. Magnetic core begins changing the memory problem. Germany’s electronic systems and Rechenplan mature. Britain commercializes Ferranti, LEO, ACE and autocode.

**Leader:** Britain in software, America in industrial momentum, Germany in formal engineering systems.

## 1954–1955: stable three-power parity

America begins producing machines in substantially greater numbers.

Britain retains the broadest software and service culture.

Germany fields several independent domestic families and integrates them into aerospace, industry and imperial administration.

Japan demonstrates indigenous relay and electronic machines.

Italy and Occitania establish a sovereign Latin ecosystem.

No one possesses a lead large enough to make another bloc’s abandonment rational.

---

# VII. What a “computer” means in each bloc by 1955

| Bloc | Default mental image |
|---|---|
| Germany | A national or industrial calculating installation executing a formally checked plan |
| Britain | A computing service receiving problems, information streams and jobs from many users |
| United States | A commercially reproducible general machine belonging to a customer |
| Japan | A reliable automatic procedure embedded in administration or production |
| Latin bloc | A comprehensible technical instrument joining operator, records and machine |

---

# VIII. Technical comparison at the end of 1955

| Category | Germany | Britain/Commonwealth | United States | Japan | Latin system |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stored-program scientific computing | First rank | First rank | First rank | Emerging | Limited but credible |
| Commercial production | Moderate | Moderate | **Strongest growth** | Relay production beginning | Office machinery strong; computers limited |
| Software libraries | Strong specialist libraries | **World leader** | Rapidly growing | Small | Small but organized |
| High-level language work | **Rechenplan lead** | Autocode and symbolic systems | Compiler experiments | Procedure notation | Early symbolic systems |
| Real-time computing | Radar and aerospace strength | Signals and radar strength | **Whirlwind/core lead** | Control-oriented but mostly specialized | Occitan military strength |
| Business computing | Imperial cards and ledgers | LEO and Commonwealth administration | **UNIVAC/IBM scale** | Statistical relays | Olivetti/IRI competence |
| Analog computing | **Exceptional** | Strong | Strong | Strong | **Very strong relative to digital scale** |
| Programming profession | Hierarchical and certified | **Deepest and broadest** | Expanding commercial profession | Small firm/bureau teams | Small specialist corps |
| Architectural unity | Source-level aspirations, diverse hardware | Diverse hardware, common practices | Segmented markets, competing firms | Deliberately plural | Dual Italian–Occitan core |
| Main weakness | Bureaucratic fragmentation | Too many projects, limited capital | Weak early coordination | Insufficient scale | Insufficient investment and volume |

---

# IX. Working canon to carry forward

| Decision | Status I recommend |
|---|---|
| Germany creates a coordinating computing working association in 1948, but no single computing ministry | **Working canon** |
| Zuse KG remains private and becomes one of several national champions | **Canon-worthy** |
| Germany sustains Zuse relay, Göttingen stored-program and Schreyer–Telefunken electronic families simultaneously | **Canon-worthy** |
| Rechenplan 52 becomes a restricted practical language with partly automatic translation | **Canon-worthy** |
| German imperial computerization before 1955 remains card-and-tape based rather than a live network | **Canon-worthy** |
| Britain creates a coordinating computation council while preserving ACE, Manchester, EDSAC, Colossus and commercial lines | **Canon-worthy** |
| Turing remains at NPL, becomes director-level, and is not prosecuted in 1952 | **Canon-worthy** |
| Britain establishes a physical Commonwealth Programme Library around 1951–52 | **Working canon** |
| LEO makes Britain the early leader in business systems analysis | **Canon-worthy** |
| Church becomes America’s theoretical patriarch; von Neumann, Shannon/Bell and commercial firms remain separate pillars | **Canon-worthy** |
| American milestones run roughly one year behind historical dates before catching up around 1953–55 | **Working canon** |
| America leads magnetic-core real-time computing and begins mass commercial production by 1955 | **Canon-worthy** |
| Japan fields ETL and FACOM relay machines, accelerates FUJIC and TAC, and heavily funds the 1954 parametron discovery | **Canon-worthy** |
| Japan adopts standardized procedure sheets before developing a national programming language | **Canon-worthy** |
| Italy purchases a German Z5-class reference machine but deliberately develops an indigenous system | **Working canon** |
| Olivetti recruits Mario Tchou early and operates an electronic prototype by 1955 | **Canon-worthy** |
| Occitania operates its first stored-program prototype around 1952–53 and a small production family by 1955 | **Working canon** |
| Italian and Occitan systems standardize interchange and peripherals, not instruction sets | **Canon-worthy** |

The world entering 1956 has three mature computing powers, two rising ones, and no universal architecture. That is the necessary foundation for Raumbote I to become a genuine worldwide computing shock in 1957 rather than merely the moment everyone suddenly discovers computers.

# Germany and the End of the Old Axis, 1960–1965

Mussolini was indeed older than Hitler—born in July 1883 against Hitler’s April 1889, almost six years apart. A natural death or incapacitation around 1960–61 is therefore entirely plausible without requiring the strain of military defeat. citeturn332612search0turn332612search1

The strongest sequence is:

- **Late 1960:** Mussolini dies after several years of declining practical authority.
- **1961:** Umberto II completes the royal-corporatist consolidation of Italy.
- **February 1962:** Hitler dies; Göring succeeds as Germany’s lawful caretaker.
- **1962–1965:** the German-Italian disagreement becomes an openly recognized strategic split, although neither side formally repudiates the old Axis alliance.

This makes the split neither a sudden quarrel caused by one funeral nor a slow drift without a decisive turning point. The rivalry has already been developing institutionally, but the deaths of Mussolini and Hitler remove the two men with the prestige and personal history necessary to keep forcing Germany and Italy into the same camp.

The setting already establishes that post-Mussolini Italy becomes royal, Catholic, military, aristocratic, and corporatist under Umberto II, while the emerging Latin bloc links Italy, Spain, Occitania, and—more cautiously—Portugal. fileciteturn9file7

## The importance of the two personal relationships

By their final years, Hitler and Mussolini no longer need to be close friends in an ordinary sense.

Their relationship has likely become:

- increasingly irritable;
- burdened by disputes over France, Greece, the Balkans, and resources;
- full of mutual suspicion about the other’s successor institutions;
- maintained by memories of shared war and victory;
- protected by the knowledge that a public rupture would damage both founder myths.

Mussolini can complain about German arrogance while still remembering that Hitler treated him as the founder of Fascism rather than merely a junior ally.

Hitler can regard Italy as unreliable, clerical, and overambitious while still refusing to humiliate Mussolini personally.

Their relationship functions as an **old Axis veto**. Whenever German and Italian officials move toward a direct confrontation, somebody can still appeal to the historic understanding between the Führer and the Duce.

Once both are dead, that appeal has no force.

Göring respects Italy, likes Italian spectacle, and has no desire for war. Umberto respects German power and knows Italy cannot defeat Germany on the continent. But neither man feels personally obliged to preserve Hitler and Mussolini’s strategic partnership.

The old friendship dies before the old treaties do.

---

# I. Mussolini’s death and Umberto’s consolidation

## Mussolini’s final position

By approximately 1958–60, Mussolini is still **Duce** in title but no longer the sole operational center of Italy.

Umberto II already controls or strongly influences:

- the Crown;
- senior military appointments;
- court diplomacy;
- the Catholic settlement;
- relations with Spain and Portugal;
- parts of imperial administration;
- the technocratic management of IRI and the corporative economy.

The Grand Council, Fascist institutions, Army, Navy, Church, Crown, colonial authorities, and state companies have learned to operate around an aging Mussolini much as the German state learned to operate around Hitler.

The Italian version is less concealed because the Crown already supplies a lawful alternative center.

## Recommended death

Mussolini dies in **late 1960**, probably from a cerebral hemorrhage or stroke after a comparatively brief final illness.

His death is dignified and public enough to avoid conspiracy mythology. He receives an enormous state funeral as:

- founder of Fascism;
- restorer of Italian empire;
- victor in the Mediterranean;
- collaborator with the Crown;
- architect of the Roman imperial revival.

Umberto does not repudiate Mussolini.

He absorbs him into national history.

The public Italian formula becomes:

> **Mussolini restored the will of Rome; Umberto gives it dynasty, law, and permanence.**

The Fascist Party survives, but its revolutionary claim is subordinated to the Crown. Italy becomes not post-Fascist but **post-revolutionary Fascist**.

Its mature economic institutions are already canonically royal, Catholic, professional, technocratic, and corporative, with a Royal Corporate Chamber and IRI-centered strategic economy. fileciteturn9file14

---

# II. The split is a cold divorce, not an immediate war

The German-Italian split should resemble a strategic divorce between two powers that still share:

- wartime memories;
- technical standards;
- trade;
- military experience;
- diplomatic vocabulary;
- numerous joint institutions;
- fear of outside powers.

Neither side initially announces:

> “The Axis is over.”

Instead, between 1961 and 1965:

- intelligence collection against the former ally expands;
- joint military planning quietly ends;
- industrial standards begin diverging;
- Germany and Italy arm opposing clients;
- press criticism becomes more visible;
- diplomatic notes become more legalistic;
- military exercises increasingly assume the other power might be neutral or hostile;
- Rome, Madrid, Lisbon, and Toulouse begin coordinating without Berlin.

The existing chronology already defines the split as structurally comparable to the Sino-Soviet rupture rather than as a sudden ideological reversal. France, the Balkans, Catholic politics, Latin America, and military technology are its main theaters. fileciteturn9file10

The public fiction remains:

> Germany and Italy are historic partners who possess certain regional differences.

The military truth becomes:

> Any serious European war plan must include the possibility that Italy is on the other side.

---

# III. The Balkan Missions Crisis

The best immediate trigger is not a territorial invasion. It is a dispute over **whose advisers and institutions possess legitimate authority**.

## Bulgaria

Bulgaria is the most dangerous hinge.

Germany values it because it connects:

- the Danube system;
- Romania;
- the Black Sea;
- German approaches toward Turkey and the Caucasus;
- continental rail and intelligence networks.

Italy values it because it connects:

- the Adriatic and Aegean systems;
- Greece;
- Macedonia;
- the eastern Mediterranean;
- the approaches to the Straits.

Sofia understands its leverage.

It accepts:

- German industrial credit;
- Italian military equipment;
- German railway missions;
- Italian officer exchanges;
- loans from both;
- promises to both that the other power’s influence will remain limited.

Around 1962, a Bulgarian government or royal ministry attempts to reorganize the armed forces by shifting several senior appointments from Italian-oriented officers to German-trained officers.

Italy interprets this as an attempted German seizure of the Bulgarian state.

Germany describes it as ordinary military professionalization.

Neither characterization is wholly false.

### The crisis

Rome demands:

- limits on the German military mission;
- guarantees against German air or intelligence bases;
- preservation of Italian training rights;
- consultation before Bulgarian command changes.

Berlin refuses to accept that Bulgaria belongs exclusively to the Italian sphere.

German exercises occur north of the Danube.

Italian naval and air forces increase readiness in Greece and the Aegean.

Turkey quietly mobilizes selected formations.

No fighting occurs, but the crisis demonstrates that German and Italian strategic maps overlap.

Göring and Umberto personally defuse it through a temporary formula:

- neither power receives exclusive Bulgarian basing;
- German economic and railway rights remain;
- Italian military and Aegean access remains;
- Bulgarian appointments are nominally sovereign;
- both intelligence services continue operating.

The settlement resolves nothing.

It merely confirms that Bulgaria’s independence now rests upon maintaining German-Italian rivalry.

---

# IV. Serbia: Italy’s protectorate with German plumbing

Serbia is less likely to produce one dramatic confrontation and more likely to cause permanent irritation.

Italy possesses formal political and security primacy.

Germany nevertheless retains:

- railway rights;
- Danube transport interests;
- industrial concessions;
- communications facilities;
- military liaison personnel;
- contacts with officers, police, businessmen, and Serbian nationalists;
- influence flowing southward from Hungary and Romania.

Rome sees these as mechanisms through which Germany can hollow out Italian protection without changing the flag.

Berlin sees Italian Serbia as too important to the continental transport system to be left entirely to Italian administration.

The Italian complaint is:

> Serbia is under our protection, but German officials behave as though the protection is ceremonial.

The German complaint is:

> Italy claims sovereignty over railways and trade routes that the continental system cannot function without.

## The Wolfgang problem

Wolfgang inherits this dispute before he has formed strong personal views about Serbia itself.

His instincts initially favor Germany’s claim because he thinks in systems:

- a railway corridor cannot become strategically discontinuous merely because a treaty map changes color;
- German trade and security networks require predictable passage;
- continental infrastructure must be treated as an integrated whole.

Umberto’s answer is political:

- infrastructure inside an Italian-protected state cannot confer German political rights;
- accepting the German argument would make every railway a claim to sovereignty;
- Italy cannot be a great power if Germany may intervene wherever German commerce exists.

Wolfgang understands Umberto’s logic intellectually and still finds it frustrating.

That becomes characteristic of their relationship.

---

# V. Turkey survives by making itself useful to both enemies

Turkey recognizes earlier than either Germany or Italy that their rivalry is the republic’s best defense.

Germany does not want Italy to control the Bosphorus.

Italy does not want Germany to control the Bosphorus.

Neither wants Britain or America to return.

Turkey therefore offers each enough access to make Turkish independence preferable to the other side’s domination.

It may grant:

- German commercial and railway concessions;
- Italian maritime and port privileges;
- controlled transit notification;
- observers from both powers;
- carefully limited technical missions;
- no permanent exclusive great-power garrison.

The existing setting already treats Turkey as a fortified Kemalist hedgehog surviving through German-Italian competition, with the exact Straits arrangement still open. fileciteturn0file4

## What Wolfgang learns from Turkey

Turkey teaches him one of his first important foreign-policy lessons:

> A weaker state can preserve sovereignty by making every stronger state fear the alternative.

He respects the cleverness but dislikes the ambiguity.

His systems-minded temperament prefers definite alignments. Turkey demonstrates that strategic ambiguity can itself be an enduring political system.

This matters later in Iceland, where Wolfgang will be less patient with an island occupying an undefined position between competing strategic spheres.

---

# VI. The two Frances become armed mirrors

The German-Italian split turns northern France and Occitania from awkward successor states into increasingly explicit rivals.

The setting already establishes that:

- northern France remains the internationally recognizable France under German domination;
- Occitania is Italian-aligned but increasingly autonomous;
- Germany annexes Alsace-Lorraine;
- Brittany remains nominally independent under German strategic control;
- reciprocal rearmament develops as each French state cites the other’s military growth. fileciteturn9file10

## Northern France

Berlin gradually permits a controlled northern French army because:

- Germany does not want to garrison every frontier permanently;
- a rearmed Occitania creates a plausible external threat;
- French forces can absorb manpower and provide local defense;
- German officer schools, weapons, logistics, and doctrine keep the army dependent.

The Paris government presents rearmament as the recovery of French dignity.

Germany presents it as responsible European burden-sharing.

Occitania sees a German-controlled French army.

## Occitania

Occitania’s response is to deepen:

- Italian defense ties;
- Spanish and Vatican diplomacy;
- its own provincial formations;
- aerospace and armored development;
- control over Toulouse, the Rhône system, Bordeaux-related commerce, and Mediterranean ports.

Its industrial position is real, not decorative. By the early 1960s it fields Mirage-generation aircraft and becomes a significant Latin technical center. fileciteturn9file17

## The proxy border

Between 1962 and 1965, the two Frances experience:

- intelligence operations;
- propaganda disputes;
- customs retaliation;
- border incidents;
- competing claims to represent French civilization;
- military exercises oriented toward one another;
- competition for exiles and intellectuals.

Neither side wants immediate reunification by war.

Both organize themselves around the assumption that the other is temporary and illegitimate.

Wolfgang therefore inherits France not as a conquered country but as a **permanent German-Italian contest conducted through two French generations**.

---

# VII. Wolfgang and Umberto II

A positive personal relationship alongside strategic rivalry is not only possible; it is preferable.

Umberto is not Wolfgang’s peer. He is an experienced king in his late fifties when Wolfgang is a grieving fourteen-year-old.

The most formative meeting occurs at Hitler’s funeral in 1962.

Despite the worsening strategic relationship, Umberto attends personally. Mussolini has recently died, and the two regimes are both burying their founding generation.

## The private condolence

Umberto treats Wolfgang neither as a child nor as a crowned adult.

He offers a brief, private, Catholic-coded condolence:

- grief need not be displayed to be real;
- a son cannot replace his father;
- duty after bereavement does not abolish bereavement;
- inherited office is carried rather than possessed.

Wolfgang remembers that Umberto is one of the few men present who understands hereditary burden from inside a dynasty rather than as an administrator managing Wolfgang’s future.

That establishes respect.

## Wolfgang’s impression of Catholicism

Umberto does affect Wolfgang’s view of Catholicism, but not by causing a simplistic anti-Catholic reaction.

Wolfgang sees in Umberto that Catholicism can produce:

- hierarchy;
- discipline;
- ceremony;
- dynastic legitimacy;
- civilizational confidence;
- institutional independence from the Party state;
- loyalty extending beyond national frontiers.

He consequently does **not** think Catholicism is weak.

He thinks it is potentially rivalrous.

Himmler’s worldview claims that the Reich must generate its own sacred continuity. Umberto embodies a political order receiving sacred continuity from a Church older than Fascism or National Socialism.

Wolfgang’s developing judgment is:

> Catholic rulers may be personally honorable and politically formidable, but Rome gives them a source of legitimacy Berlin does not control.

This makes him respectful toward the Church and cautious about its supranational authority.

## Their mature personal relationship

By 1965, Wolfgang and Umberto can:

- exchange private letters;
- speak candidly during summits;
- restrain humiliating propaganda;
- keep communication open during Balkan alarms;
- understand that neither can surrender his strategic position.

Umberto sees Wolfgang as intelligent, serious, and dangerously inexperienced.

Wolfgang sees Umberto as dignified, paternal, and determined to build an anti-German Latin order.

They may like one another.

They do not trust one another’s states.

# VIII. Wolfgang and Crown Prince Akihito

Akihito should remain **Crown Prince**, not emperor, during this period. He was born in 1933 and historically did not succeed Hirohito until 1989; absent a deliberate alternate death for Hirohito, the imperial succession is nowhere near imminent in the early 1960s. citeturn476213search4turn342429search4

The existing setting already treats Akihito as the younger, more public face of the imperial system and records his participation in Elizabeth II’s 1953 coronation delegation. fileciteturn9file2turn9file8

## The first meaningful encounter

Akihito represents Japan at Hitler’s funeral.

He is twenty-eight; Wolfgang is fourteen.

The relationship begins less as one between equals than as a cautious elder-brother relationship between two men born into roles they did not choose.

Akihito comes from a court where hereditary succession is ancient, acknowledged, and surrounded by settled ritual.

Wolfgang comes from a state performing elaborate constitutional contortions to deny that it has become hereditary.

Akihito does not mock this. But his very existence shows Wolfgang how strange Germany’s legal fiction is.

## The scientific connection

Akihito’s historical scientific interests, particularly ichthyology, supply a useful personal bridge. He retained a serious lifelong scientific vocation even while carrying imperial duties. citeturn476213news37

The two men therefore have different scientific interests:

- Akihito: marine biology, taxonomy, natural observation;
- Wolfgang: astronautics, orbital systems, engineering architecture.

Neither is a professional scientist governing through personal technical brilliance.

Both value a field in which status cannot simply replace accurate observation.

Their correspondence might include:

- books;
- technical reports;
- scientific expeditions;
- aquarium or marine-research visits;
- launch films;
- Japanese oceanographic findings;
- German space documentation.

Goebbels’s ministry describes them as the **scientific princes of the new imperial age**.

The personal reality is quieter: they find it relieving to discuss something not entirely reducible to diplomacy.

## Strategic limits

The friendship does not remove German-Japanese rivalry over:

- Siberia;
- China;
- technology;
- markets;
- arms exports;
- influence in the Middle East and Latin America;
- the shape of the postwar imperial order.

It creates a trusted human channel.

Akihito can communicate how Tokyo perceives an action without every statement becoming an official ultimatum. Wolfgang can ask questions without committing Germany publicly.

That personal relationship may prevent later German-Japanese disputes from escalating unnecessarily, while never restoring a unified Axis bloc.
