# XVI. The important German cast by 1970

By the Moon landing, Wolfgang’s world contains three living generations.

## Founder elders

- Dönitz
- Rommel
- Goebbels
- Bormann

- Heydrich
- Speer

- Eva Braun Hitler

## Transitional professionals

- Werner Naumann

- Werner Grothmann

- Karl Schiller

## Wolfgang’s generation and near-generation

- Katharina Hartmann
- Manfred Rommel

This prevents Wolfgang from becoming the sole developed German personality after 1970.

It also creates a valuable political change:

> Hitler governed among rivals who had risen beside him. Wolfgang governs among men trained by those rivals—and among their children, who have inherited the names without necessarily inheriting the talents.

The most important new figure is Katharina because she is the one major actor who does not approach Wolfgang primarily as:

- Hitler’s son;
- the Führer;
- a pupil;
- a source of appointments;
- a symbol to manipulate;
- a danger to manage.

Every old man around Wolfgang is preparing a successor.

Katharina is helping Wolfgang become someone worth succeeding.

# Computing Race IV: 1960–1965  
## From programming languages to complete computing systems

## Japanese writing direction

The canonical Japanese programming layout should be:

> **Characters descend from top to bottom; successive statement columns proceed from right to left.**

That is the conventional ordering of vertical Japanese composition. Horizontal Japanese also exists and runs left to right, which is why mathematical papers, tables, scientific diagrams, and material containing Western notation often prefer horizontal layout. citeturn251082search21turn251082search28

For the Japanese computing ecosystem, I would establish a deliberate hybrid.

### Native program mode

A Japanese program begins in the **upper-right corner** of the source sheet or terminal page.

- Characters within a statement proceed downward.
- The next statement begins in the column immediately to the left.
- A completed screenful moves leftward rather than upward.
- Nested blocks are displayed as inset vertical bands.
- Error annotations appear in a narrow column immediately to the left of the offending statement.
- Line or statement numbers appear at the top of each column in Japanese digits.

The underlying file is still a serialized token stream. The processor does not literally store a two-dimensional page. The editor records:

1. statement boundary;
2. token order from top to bottom;
3. movement to the next column on the left;
4. indentation or block metadata.

This gives the programmer the appearance of vertical source while allowing compilers to operate normally.

### Secondary horizontal mode

Horizontal left-to-right mode is used for:

- large arithmetic tables;
- engineering diagrams;
- matrices;
- imported foreign algorithms;
- Filipino and other Latin-script source;
- some industrial consoles;
- low-cost printers unable to buffer a vertical page.

Japanese programmers consider horizontal display useful but somewhat foreign or specialized. Vertical source remains the prestigious native form.

The resulting portrait-format terminal—with columns of code descending and advancing leftward—does indeed resemble the later visual language of *The Matrix*, although the characters are structured program text rather than decorative random glyphs.

# I. What changed historically between 1960 and 1965?

This period is not merely another generation of faster machines. It is when computing begins to acquire its modern institutional form.

## The computer becomes a system rather than a cabinet

A serious installation now includes:

- processor;
- memory hierarchy;
- disks, drums, and tapes;
- printers and card equipment;
- peripheral controllers;
- supervisor or operating system;
- compilers;
- application libraries;
- remote terminals;
- maintenance personnel;
- systems analysts;
- programmers;
- permanent data archives.

The processor becomes only one part of a much larger investment.

## Operating systems become central

Manchester’s Atlas, operational in 1962, combined high performance with virtual memory, protection, peripheral coordination, and a sophisticated Supervisor. Virtual memory allowed a program to behave as though it had a larger unified store than the immediately available physical core. citeturn634826search1turn634826search2turn634826search17

At MIT, an experimental Compatible Time-Sharing System was demonstrated in 1961, and regular service followed in 1963. Time-sharing allowed several users at terminals to interact with one central machine rather than submit every job as an overnight card deck. citeturn251082search7turn251082search17

## Languages become standardized communities

COBOL-60 and ALGOL 60 appeared as published specifications rather than languages belonging exclusively to one machine. Standards organizations increasingly had to test whether different compilers actually implemented the same language. citeturn738272search1turn738272search2turn738272search13

Dartmouth BASIC first ran in 1964 as part of a time-sharing environment intended to make computing accessible to students beyond mathematics and engineering. citeturn251082search4turn251082search14

A modern programming language was therefore coming to mean more than keywords. It required:

- a written specification;
- multiple compilers;
- runtime conventions;
- standard libraries;
- diagnostic messages;
- manuals and courses;
- a user community;
- some expectation that source code would survive a hardware replacement.

## Compatible machine families become strategic

IBM announced System/360 in 1964 as a software-compatible family replacing several previous product lines. It also institutionalized the eight-bit byte as a core architectural unit. citeturn251082search2

That was a profound change. A customer could purchase a small model and later move to a larger machine without rewriting every program from the beginning.

## Integrated circuits begin entering strategic systems

Integrated circuits were still too expensive for most ordinary mainframes, which continued using discrete transistors and magnetic-core memory. Aerospace was different. NASA began evaluating integrated circuits for the Apollo Guidance Computer in late 1961 because small size, low weight, reliability, and power consumption justified their cost. citeturn930853search1turn930853search7

## The small computer emerges

The 1965 PDP-8 demonstrated that a general-purpose computer could be installed on a laboratory bench or built directly into another company’s equipment. Its standard configuration joined a small processor, core memory, console, and teletype rather than requiring a national computing center. citeturn930853search20

## Online transaction systems become practical

By the middle of the decade, IBM’s SABRE airline-reservation system was processing thousands of reservations per hour and returning answers in seconds rather than requiring centralized manual correspondence. citeturn299115search2

The combined transformation is:

> **In 1955, an institution bought a computer. By 1965, it adopted a computing system.**

That is the central development we should carry into all five blocs.

---

# II. Germany  
## The Rechenplan state becomes a compatible machine order

Germany enters 1960 with the most unified high-level language policy but several incompatible hardware lineages:

- Zuse office and engineering systems;
- Göttingen scientific computers;
- Siemens and Telefunken electronic mainframes;
- administrative card and tape systems;
- industrial and aerospace control computers;
- analog simulation establishments.

The 1957 success of **Raumbote I** has validated German calculation and guidance practices, but Kennedy’s 1961 lunar challenge forces Germany to support orbital assembly, docking, long-duration flight, telemetry, fuel transfer, and increasingly complicated mission operations. fileciteturn9file1 fileciteturn9file3 fileciteturn9file4

The problem is no longer producing one orbit table. It is managing thousands of changing calculations and subsystems across a decade-long program.

## 1. The German compatibility decision

Germany does not copy System/360 by replacing every existing product with one commercial family. It instead establishes a **common architectural order** across several manufacturers.

A useful working designation is:

> **Einheits-Rechenordnung 63 — ERO 63**

It defines what a strategic German computer must present to compilers and operating systems, while permitting substantial internal engineering differences.

### ERO 63 reference architecture

| Feature | Working German standard |
|---|---|
| Principal scientific word | 48 bits |
| Half-word | 24 bits |
| Basic machine character | 6 bits |
| Extended character | 12 bits |
| Integer formats | 24 and 48 bits |
| Floating point | 48-bit standard; extended precision optional |
| Decimal format | Packed decimal fields |
| Memory addressing | Word and field operations rather than universal byte orientation |
| Input/output | Independent channels |
| Protection | Supervisor and user states |
| Control | Interrupts and protected event handlers |
| Software interface | Planform object modules |
| Normal memory | Magnetic core |
| Backing storage | Drums, tape, and increasingly disks |

The six-bit core character contains:

- German capitals;
- digits;
- punctuation;
- common control signs.

The twelve-bit extended form adds:

- lowercase;
- umlauts;
- additional European letters;
- mathematical symbols;
- specialist administrative codes.

This gives Germany a distinctive technical path. It does **not** converge on the American eight-bit byte, and that difference later becomes one of the major barriers to software exchange.

### Levels of machine

German procurement settles into three broad classes.

#### Großrechner

Large Siemens–Telefunken systems serve:

- aerospace;
- cryptography;
- weather;
- nuclear engineering;
- central commodity clearing;
- major universities;
- military command;
- MOSAIK regional reconciliation.

They use transistor logic, core memory, channel-controlled peripherals, and large tape or disk installations.

#### Mittelrechner

Zuse, Siemens, and other firms produce medium systems for:

- factories;
- railway districts;
- insurance;
- accounting;
- design offices;
- provincial universities;
- construction;
- surveying.

These systems become the commercial backbone of the German sphere.

#### Kleinrechner

Small eighteen- or twenty-four-bit machines appear around 1963–65 for:

- laboratories;
- machine tools;
- substations;
- pipeline stations;
- radar sites;
- classification yards;
- industrial test benches.

They are not personal computers. They are purchased as components inside larger technical systems.

## 2. Rechenplan 63

**Rechenplan 63** is the first version that a later programmer would recognize as a fully modern language system rather than an automatic formula translator.

It retains the three principal profiles:

- `RP-W` for science and engineering;
- `RP-V` for administration;
- `RP-S` for control.

But it adds a common modern core.

### Language developments

Rechenplan 63 introduces:

- block structure;
- lexical declaration scopes;
- separately compiled procedures;
- named modules;
- explicit public and private interfaces;
- structured records;
- enumerated values;
- stronger array checking;
- standardized exception conditions;
- compiler-generated diagnostic references;
- source libraries independent of one machine;
- formal linkage between high-level types and machine data forms.

Limited recursion is permitted in RP-W. It is prohibited in safety-critical RP-S unless the compiler can establish a fixed depth.

Dynamic allocation exists only in specialized scientific libraries. Ordinary German programs continue to allocate memory before execution.

### Planform II

The original Planform becomes **Planform II**, a typed intermediate representation shared by German compilers.

Its most important addition is a stack-oriented method developed under the influence of Bauer and Samelson’s compiler work.

Planform II expresses:

- evaluation stacks;
- typed operations;
- procedure frames;
- record access;
- control-flow blocks;
- exception paths;
- required device classes;
- timing and storage annotations.

A manufacturer can therefore build a new machine and obtain access to much of the German software library by writing:

1. a Planform II code generator;
2. a standard runtime;
3. peripheral modules;
4. validation tests.

Germany achieves **source and intermediate portability** without requiring every machine to execute identical binary code.

## 3. The Rechenplan profiles mature

### RP-W: scientific and aerospace

By 1965, RP-W includes standard libraries for:

- matrices;
- complex arithmetic;
- interpolation;
- differential equations;
- orbital determination;
- coordinate transformation;
- structural loads;
- fluid flow;
- statistical estimation;
- reactor calculations;
- telemetry reduction.

The language is used extensively in the expanded German space program, but heavily optimized numerical kernels remain in assembly.

### RP-V: administration

RP-V becomes the normal language of:

- commodity boards;
- insurance;
- payroll;
- census and cadastre;
- railway accounts;
- settlement records;
- blocked territorial currencies;
- MOSAIK summaries;
- Reichsgüterausgleich transactions.

It supports:

- fixed decimal arithmetic;
- named record fields;
- indexed sequential files;
- sorting and merging;
- report layouts;
- date, district, household, and enterprise codes;
- audit totals;
- revision histories.

### RP-S: control

RP-S develops into Germany’s most distinctive language.

Its compiler requires the programmer to declare:

- available memory;
- devices;
- maximum event rate;
- timing deadlines;
- permitted interrupt priorities;
- fallback states;
- maximum loop counts;
- restart behavior.

The compiler produces a **Laufnachweis**, an execution certificate containing estimated worst-case time, memory use, device dependencies, and unhandled failure states.

RP-S programs control or supervise:

- radar;
- telemetry;
- power dispatch;
- pipelines;
- classification yards;
- industrial sequencing;
- rocket test stands;
- air-defense centers.

## 4. Petri’s concurrency school

Carl Adam Petri’s emerging work is absorbed rapidly because Germany desperately needs a formal way to describe systems in which many operations occur concurrently.

German engineers adopt **condition–event diagrams** for:

- rail interlocking;
- communications;
- refinery control;
- job scheduling;
- missile-launch sequences;
- MOSAIK transaction flow;
- factory automation.

They are not yet source code. They are design and verification diagrams used before an RP-S implementation is written.

This gives German systems engineering an early conceptual distinction between:

- a sequential calculation;
- a concurrent process;
- a resource conflict;
- a deadlock;
- an event that cannot legally occur until several conditions are satisfied.

## 5. Planwerk 64

A working name for the common German operating environment is:

> **Planwerk 64**

Planwerk is not one identical operating-system binary. It is a specified family of supervisor services implemented across ERO 63 machines.

Its standard facilities include:

- protected supervisor mode;
- multiprogrammed batch operation;
- job queues;
- peripheral spooling;
- automatic compiler invocation;
- standard library loading;
- machine-time accounting;
- security classification;
- restart checkpoints;
- operator audit trails;
- remote job submission by teleprinter;
- common object and tape formats.

Germany is cautious about open-ended time-sharing.

Universities and design establishments receive limited **Teilbetrieb** systems in which a small number of terminals share a machine. Military and administrative establishments prefer controlled batch work and dedicated control consoles.

The German official objection is reliability and security. The unstated objection is that interactive computing gives too much direct access to users outside the established coding hierarchy.

## 6. Digital guidance and space operations

Between 1960 and 1965, digital computing moves gradually from the ground into the launch system.

### 1960–62

- trajectory and mission planning remain ground-based;
- analog computers simulate guidance;
- onboard sequencing remains fixed;
- digital systems process telemetry and radar tracking.

### 1963–64

- transistorized digital units enter upper-stage test vehicles;
- digital systems perform state estimation and guidance corrections;
- core or wired fixed memory stores validated programs;
- analog systems remain responsible for stabilization and continuous control loops.

### 1965

Germany tests a hybrid onboard computer capable of:

- inertial navigation correction;
- stage-event sequencing;
- limited fault isolation;
- telemetry formatting;
- planned orbital maneuvers.

Integrated circuits appear in experimental guidance modules, but ordinary German mainframes remain discrete-transistor machines.

Germany’s philosophy is conservative:

> The ground machine discovers the plan; the flight computer executes the smallest safe part of it.

## 7. MOSAIK and the imperial administrative network

The mature MOSAIK system is not yet fully linked in 1965. The setting fixes its evolution from paper and punch cards through regional centers into a connected late-1960s network. fileciteturn9file3

During 1960–65, it becomes a genuine distributed administrative system.

### Regional structure

Regional centers maintain:

- person and household registries;
- recognized community records;
- labor and payroll files;
- movement permissions;
- commodity production;
- chiefly and district accounts;
- tax and service obligations.

Local offices submit:

- punched cards;
- magnetic tapes;
- teleprinter corrections;
- weekly and monthly totals.

### Remote inquiry

Selected officials can send a standardized teleprinter request to a regional center.

A response may take:

- several minutes for a cached local record;
- hours for an indexed tape search;
- days when another center must be queried.

This is not online database access in the modern sense. It is a managed request-and-response service.

### Relationship with the East

MOSAIK belongs principally to Mittelafrika. The Eastern Reichskommissariats develop parallel systems for:

- rail dispatch;
- commodity quotas;
- estate and household records;
- pipeline telemetry;
- industrial payroll;
- power management.

The mature Eastern canon explicitly makes the 1960s the period of regional railway control, pipeline telemetry, power-grid supervision, electronic commodity accounting, and computer-assisted dispatch. fileciteturn9file6

Berlin increasingly links the outputs of both systems through the Reichsgüterausgleich, but it does not place all imperial subjects inside one master database.

## German position in 1965

Germany leads in:

- language unity;
- typed intermediate code;
- formal control-system design;
- deterministic real-time programming;
- aerospace calculation;
- administrative standardization.

It remains weaker in:

- interactive computing;
- open university access;
- consumer applications;
- third-party software;
- easy character-oriented programming.

Germany has the most orderly software ecosystem, but also the most heavily supervised one.

# III. Britain and the Commonwealth  
## Virtual memory, multi-access, and the language laboratory

Britain’s 1960s advantage lies less in machine volume than in the sophistication with which it manages scarce machines.

Atlas provides the historical foundation: virtual memory, protection, a powerful Supervisor, remote data links, and compiler research. citeturn634826search2turn634826search5turn634826search17

In this timeline, Commonwealth orders make Atlas a larger family rather than a handful of isolated prestige machines.

## 1. The Commonwealth Atlas system

Between 1961 and 1965, Atlas-class machines are installed or ordered for:

- Manchester;
- the national laboratory system;
- government signals work;
- Canada;
- Australia;
- a major British nuclear and aerospace center;
- one Commonwealth administrative or defense center.

Britain cannot mass-produce them like IBM. It does ensure that every installation participates in a shared software and research system.

### Architectural character

Atlas-class machines use:

- forty-eight-bit words;
- virtual memory;
- fast and slow memory presented as one store;
- memory protection;
- multiprogramming;
- peripheral autonomy;
- supervisor calls;
- interrupt handling;
- magnetic drums and tapes;
- remote job entry.

The crucial British principle is:

> A program should describe the memory it requires; the system should decide where that memory physically resides.

That contrasts with Germany’s emphasis on declaring and certifying the planned physical requirements in advance.

## 2. The Atlas Supervisor

The Supervisor becomes the model British operating system.

It handles:

- page movement;
- memory protection;
- job scheduling;
- peripheral allocation;
- spooling;
- accounting;
- operator intervention;
- runtime faults;
- compiler and library loading.

British programmers increasingly treat the operating system as a permanent layer between application and hardware.

That is a conceptual shift. A programmer is no longer necessarily entitled to manipulate every physical device directly.

## 3. Multi-access computing

Britain develops time-sharing somewhat differently from America.

America’s first time-sharing communities are concentrated around one campus or research center. Britain’s Commonwealth geography encourages **remote multi-access**.

By 1964–65, a Commonwealth computing service may connect teleprinter terminals in:

- London;
- Manchester;
- Edinburgh;
- Toronto;
- Ottawa;
- Melbourne;
- Canberra;
- Cape Town;
- selected naval or aerospace establishments.

Most links remain slow and expensive. Users type short commands, submit jobs, inspect errors, and edit source. Large data sets still travel by tape or courier.

Britain does not yet possess a global interactive computer network. It possesses the first institutional expectation that a machine may serve users who never enter its building.

## 4. British languages

Britain’s language culture becomes the most diverse and intellectually experimental.

### Commonwealth Autocode

Common Autocode is consolidated around a stable scientific core:

- algebraic expressions;
- arrays;
- loops;
- procedures;
- formatted input and output;
- library routines;
- symbolic debugging.

It is the language of practical scientists, engineers, technical colleges, and ordinary Commonwealth computing services.

### CPL

The more ambitious **Combined Programming Language**, or CPL, appears around 1963–64 under the influence of Christopher Strachey, Cambridge, London, Turing’s theoretical establishment, and the Atlas compiler school.

CPL is intended to serve:

- scientific computing;
- systems software;
- symbolic manipulation;
- compiler construction;
- complex data structures.

It supports:

- block structure;
- recursion;
- records;
- references;
- arrays;
- lists;
- typed procedures;
- separate compilation;
- user-defined operators in restricted contexts.

CPL is powerful but difficult to compile efficiently. It becomes highly influential among expert programmers without replacing Autocode for ordinary calculation.

### CLEO

LEO’s commercial-language family matures into a readable business system supporting:

- records;
- decimal arithmetic;
- tapes and indexed files;
- report generation;
- exception handling;
- payroll and inventory;
- transaction reconciliation;
- restarting after peripheral failure.

CLEO is less rhetorically English-like than American COBOL. It assumes a trained systems analyst rather than promising that an executive can read the source unaided.

### Conversational Autocode

Britain produces an educational language comparable in purpose to BASIC around 1964–65.

A suitable working name is:

> **Conversational Autocode**

It is available through multi-access terminals and technical colleges.

It provides:

- immediate compilation;
- short error messages;
- line-oriented editing;
- simple numerical variables;
- loops and conditions;
- plotting and tabular output.

It becomes important throughout the Commonwealth because a school does not need to own a computer; it needs a terminal and scheduled communications access.

## 5. Turing’s position

Turing remains the national intellectual patron of:

- computability;
- compiler theory;
- machine intelligence;
- interactive computing;
- secure systems;
- mathematical biology;
- solid-state machine organization.

He does not personally design every language.

His most important institutional intervention is his insistence that three things be studied together:

1. the formal language written by the programmer;
2. the translator generating executable form;
3. the operating environment in which the result runs.

Turing warns against treating a compiler as a trusted oracle. Britain consequently develops early compiler-validation suites and test libraries.

British scholarship usually calls the general computability claim **Turing’s Hypothesis**, while American scholarship prefers Church’s Thesis.

## 6. Compiler compilers and translation

The Atlas school’s “compiler compiler” work becomes disproportionately important.

Instead of hand-writing every compiler from scratch, British developers define:

- lexical rules;
- grammar;
- semantic actions;
- code-generation templates.

Britain gains a commercial and diplomatic niche in building:

- cross-compilers;
- source translators;
- tape converters;
- peripheral adapters;
- mathematical-library ports.

This is the foundation of Britain’s mature role as the bridge among incompatible computing blocs.

## 7. Networking research

The High Mast tracking network, Commonwealth communications, remote computing, and growing multi-access services produce a new question:

> Must a communications circuit be reserved for one user even while that user is thinking rather than transmitting?

By 1965, Donald Davies and the NPL community are directed to investigate dividing messages into independently routed blocks. No operational packet network yet exists, but the conceptual research begins.

British networking develops from the requirements of:

- orbital tracking;
- naval signals;
- remote university access;
- dispersed imperial bases;
- machine-to-machine translation.

## British position in 1965

Britain leads in:

- virtual memory;
- supervisor design;
- multi-access services;
- compiler technology;
- cross-compilation;
- remote computing;
- language research.

It trails America in:

- machine volume;
- semiconductor production;
- inexpensive small computers;
- commercial capital.

It trails Germany in:

- uniformity;
- control certification;
- direct administrative coercion over standards.

Britain’s ecosystem is the most intellectually fertile and the least tidy.

# IV. United States  
## Compatible families, time-sharing, and the first broad computing market

The Kennedy administration’s lunar commitment in 1961 and the elevation of Aerospace Command into the independent Aerospace Force in 1962 accelerate computing, microelectronics, guidance, simulation, and communications. fileciteturn9file3 fileciteturn9file4

America’s defining advantage is that military funding, university research, and private commercial markets reinforce one another without being institutionally unified.

## 1. System/360

IBM announces System/360 in 1964 essentially on its historical schedule.

Its importance in this timeline is even greater because America’s earlier computing landscape was exceptionally fragmented.

The family establishes:

- one broad instruction architecture;
- small through very large models;
- eight-bit bytes;
- thirty-two-bit general registers;
- channel-controlled peripherals;
- common tapes and disks;
- upward software migration;
- commercial and scientific configurations.

System/360 does not instantly replace every American machine. It establishes the expectation that a computer family should preserve software investment across generations. citeturn251082search2

## 2. The software cost becomes visible

IBM’s compatible-family promise forces it to provide an enormous software system.

OS/360 requires:

- assemblers;
- FORTRAN;
- COBOL;
- PL/I;
- job control;
- disk management;
- tape management;
- spooling;
- error recovery;
- support across many models and peripherals.

The project runs late and experiences serious integration problems.

This is one of the first moments when American management recognizes that adding programmers does not automatically make a delayed software project finish proportionally faster.

The phrase **software crisis** is not yet normal, but the crisis itself has begun.

## 3. American language families

### FORTRAN IV

FORTRAN IV becomes the stable scientific and engineering language.

It improves:

- logical expressions;
- subroutine organization;
- portability;
- standardization;
- diagnostic expectations;
- compatibility across larger machine families.

It dominates:

- aerospace;
- universities;
- numerical research;
- engineering;
- weather;
- corporate laboratories.

### COBOL

COBOL spreads through:

- federal administration;
- banks;
- insurers;
- manufacturers;
- railways;
- large retailers;
- military logistics.

Its strengths are:

- explicit data division;
- named records;
- decimal arithmetic;
- files;
- report formatting;
- comparatively readable procedure statements.

Its weakness is verbosity and dependence upon vendor-specific file and peripheral behavior.

### JOVIAL

JOVIAL-class languages become standard for major Aerospace Force and air-defense software.

They are used for:

- command systems;
- radar;
- guidance simulation;
- mission planning;
- digital displays;
- communications;
- early flight-computer support.

JOVIAL occupies the American position nearest German RP-S, but it is oriented toward large contractor teams rather than formal proof and worst-case certification.

### LISP

LISP becomes the principal American symbolic and artificial-intelligence language. Its list structures, recursive functions, and symbolic expressions make it suitable for search, theorem work, language processing, and machine-intelligence experiments. MIT identifies McCarthy as its inventor, and early AI projects made the language central to symbolic computing. citeturn738272search7turn738272search11

The Church school finds LISP intellectually congenial because functions and symbolic expressions are treated as first-class mathematical objects.

### BASIC

Dartmouth BASIC appears in 1964 with time-sharing and spreads rapidly through colleges.

It is culturally important because it makes programming an undergraduate activity rather than a specialist apprenticeship. citeturn251082search4turn251082search33

### PL/I

IBM begins developing PL/I as an attempted unification of:

- FORTRAN science;
- COBOL records;
- real-time events;
- systems programming;
- business decimal work.

Its ambition resembles Germany’s Rechenplan family, but its origin is different.

Rechenplan begins from one formal language divided into profiles. PL/I begins by combining features from several established American languages and markets.

By 1965, PL/I is promising but large, difficult to implement, and not yet a replacement for its parents.

## 4. CTSS and Project MAC

CTSS demonstrates time-sharing in 1961 and provides regular service by 1963. Project MAC then creates a community in which programmers expect to:

- edit files at a terminal;
- run a program immediately;
- inspect errors;
- communicate with other users;
- maintain private file directories;
- share common software interactively. citeturn251082search17turn251082search35

This transforms American programming culture.

The programmer no longer necessarily hands cards to an operator and returns the next day. At leading institutions, programming becomes conversational.

## 5. Character standards: ASCII and EBCDIC

America develops an internal standards conflict.

### ASCII

The communications and standards community supports a seven-bit American interchange code intended for teleprinters and data exchange. Early forms appear during this period, although federal adoption and revision continue later. NIST’s historical standards material records ASCII versions beginning in 1963. citeturn635323search0

### EBCDIC

IBM’s System/360 inherits a character code shaped heavily by punched-card practice.

Thus the largest American computer family does not use the same code as the emerging communications standard.

This creates a lasting American contradiction:

> America produces the world’s most influential interchange code and its most influential incompatible mainframe code at nearly the same moment.

Conversion tables become ordinary parts of American data processing.

## 6. Integrated circuits and aerospace computing

The Aerospace Force requires computers small enough for:

- experimental spaceplanes;
- upper-stage guidance;
- inertial navigation;
- automatic reentry studies;
- flight-control research.

Integrated circuits receive heavy federal procurement beginning around 1961–62, paralleling the historical Apollo demand. citeturn930853search1turn930853search13

By 1965, America possesses prototype flight computers using:

- integrated logic;
- magnetic-core working memory;
- wired or rope-like fixed program memory;
- redundant timing;
- highly constrained software;
- hardware and software validation.

Mainframes do not immediately adopt ICs at the same rate. Weight and power matter less in a computer room than in an aircraft.

## 7. Minicomputers

The PDP-8 class appears in 1965.

Its importance is not raw speed. It can be:

- purchased by a laboratory;
- installed in a factory;
- connected to an instrument;
- embedded in another company’s product;
- maintained without a national mainframe staff.

The minicomputer becomes America’s first major step toward decentralizing computing ownership.

This is particularly important for the setting’s later American personal-computing culture. The path is:

> central mainframe → institutional minicomputer → hobby and educational machine → household computer.

## 8. Online commercial systems

SABRE demonstrates that a customer-facing employee can query a centralized computer in real time. citeturn299115search2

Comparable systems begin appearing in:

- banking;
- securities;
- hotel reservations;
- inventory;
- freight;
- credit authorization;
- military supply.

The American computer becomes less exclusively a machine for producing reports and more a machine that answers individual transactions as they occur.

## American position in 1965

America leads in:

- commercial machine volume;
- compatible product families;
- integrated-circuit procurement;
- minicomputers;
- interactive university computing;
- online transactions;
- breadth of language communities.

It remains weaker in:

- formal language unity;
- deterministic certification;
- cross-vendor portability;
- disciplined imperial data standards.

The American ecosystem is the least orderly but generates the greatest number of unexpected applications.

---

# V. Japan  
## Vertical programming, multilingual computing, and the rise of process control

By 1960, Japan has become a credible fourth computing power. It possesses:

- FACOM and ETL relay traditions;
- transistor machines;
- parametron systems;
- KEISAN and TEJUN;
- major corporate electronics establishments;
- an imperial automation program;
- the newly associated Philippines as both a technical resource and a linguistic challenge.

Japan’s empire is structured through zaibatsu, trading houses, Singapore clearing, Korean and Manchurian industry, and layered associated states. Its chronic shortage of high-level Japanese technical personnel makes automation a strategic necessity. fileciteturn9file3

## 1. Vertical source architecture

Japanese source is canonically displayed in vertical columns.

### Physical coding sheets

A formal program sheet contains:

- statement number at the top;
- tokens descending beneath it;
- the next statement to the left;
- margin annotations on the left edge;
- block frames spanning several vertical columns.

A page begins at the upper right and ends at the lower left.

### Early machine listings

The underlying punch tape or card deck serializes the source one column at a time.

Japanese printers develop page-buffering systems that:

1. receive the token stream;
2. assemble a page image on drum or core memory;
3. print horizontal rows that reconstruct vertical columns.

Cheaper systems print a horizontal transliteration, but this is treated as a low-grade compatibility listing rather than the preferred source representation.

### Vertical terminals

Around 1962–64, Japanese firms introduce expensive **縦型端末**, vertical-form terminals.

Their CRTs are portrait-oriented. The cursor moves downward. When the cursor reaches the bottom, it continues at the top of the next column to the left.

Technical subwindows may temporarily display:

- a matrix;
- graph;
- waveform;
- Filipino or English record;
- horizontal mathematical expression.

These windows run left to right.

## 2. KEISAN 62 and KEISAN 64

The domestic language name is written first as **ケイサン** and increasingly displayed as **計算** on capable terminals.

### KEISAN 62

KEISAN 62 stabilizes:

- Japanese positional numerals;
- katakana identifiers;
- vertical statement layout;
- arrays;
- loops;
- conditions;
- procedures;
- scientific functions;
- formatted numerical output.

Its source contains no required Latin characters.

### KEISAN 64

KEISAN 64 introduces more modern structure:

- lexical blocks;
- separately compiled procedures;
- named record forms;
- limited recursion;
- stronger array checking;
- standardized complex arithmetic;
- matrix libraries;
- device-independent scientific input and output;
- optional Latin identifiers through the supplementary library.

The compiler tokenizes common katakana keywords.

On a sophisticated terminal:

- `モシ` displays as `若` or a standardized conditional glyph;
- `クリカエシ` displays as `繰`;
- `ヨミコミ` displays as `読`;
- `カキダシ` displays as `書`;
- `オワリ` displays as `終`.

The stored token is the same regardless of whether an old printer renders katakana or a new terminal renders kanji.

This is the beginning of Japanese tokenized display independence.

## 3. TEJUN 63 and TEJUN 65

TEJUN is written **テジュン**, later **手順**.

It becomes more important than KEISAN in corporate and industrial use.

### TEJUN 63

It formalizes:

- records;
- decimal fields;
- files;
- sorting;
- state tables;
- device operations;
- operator approval;
- exception routes;
- procedure-sheet documentation.

### TEJUN 65

It adds:

- asynchronous events;
- timers;
- message queues;
- named devices;
- restart states;
- production batches;
- transaction confirmation;
- human authorization gates;
- persistent industrial records.

TEJUN 65 is used for:

- warehouses;
- ports;
- refineries;
- telephone exchanges;
- production scheduling;
- railway terminals;
- trading-house accounts;
- carrier maintenance;
- power dispatch.

Its governing model is neither purely sequential nor fully general-purpose.

A TEJUN program describes:

> what state the process is in, what event occurred, what action should follow, and when a human must approve continuation.

This becomes the foundation of Japan’s later automation and robotics culture.

## 4. The Japanese character architecture

### Imperial Kana Machine Code

The original seven-bit Japanese core contains:

- katakana;
- `〇一二三四五六七八九`;
- Japanese punctuation;
- `加減乗除負等`;
- control characters;
- vertical-layout controls.

It remains the compact internal code for Japanese programming.

### Latin Supplement

The Philippines forces the addition of:

- Latin capitals and lowercase;
- Filipino and English punctuation;
- diacritics;
- Latin strings;
- optional Latin identifiers;
- horizontal display controls.

Filipino programmers generally use Japanese keywords and Japanese numerals while using Latin script for:

- names;
- comments;
- local records;
- output;
- selected identifiers.

### Co-Prosperity Sphere Character Registry

Around 1962–63, Tokyo creates a central registry provisionally called:

> **共栄圏共通文字符号**  
> Co-Prosperity Sphere Common Character Code

At first, it is a registry rather than one universal storage format.

Every character receives:

- script classification;
- registry number;
- preferred shape;
- permitted variants;
- sorting class;
- vertical and horizontal rendering behavior;
- mappings to vendor codes.

It covers progressively:

- Japanese kana and kanji;
- Latin;
- Hangul;
- Chinese characters;
- Thai;
- Burmese;
- Vietnamese;
- Malay and Indonesian spelling;
- mathematical and commercial symbols.

### Multibyte common form

By 1964–65, an imperial multibyte interchange form is defined.

- Japanese core characters retain compact forms.
- A lead code selects other script tables.
- Kanji and regional scripts use two or more units.
- Terminal font memories map registry identities to visible glyphs.
- Older machines use translation tables.

This is not as clean as modern Unicode. It contains duplicate Chinese and Japanese forms, compatibility characters, and corporate extensions. But the central idea is recognizably Unicode-like:

> **Character identity is defined independently of one manufacturer’s font or machine code.**

## 5. Japanese hardware

Japan does not adopt one System/360-like machine family.

It standardizes:

- character exchange;
- tape formats;
- peripheral commands;
- procedure descriptions;
- communications protocols;
- industrial device interfaces.

The zaibatsu retain incompatible processors.

### Mainframes

Fujitsu, NEC, Hitachi, Mitsubishi, and state laboratories build transistorized mainframes using:

- core memory;
- magnetic drums and tapes;
- kana terminals;
- Japanese printers;
- corporate operating systems;
- KEISAN and TEJUN compilers.

### Parametron systems

Parametrons remain competitive in:

- universities;
- naval establishments;
- scientific centers;
- installations valuing domestic reliability over power efficiency.

They begin losing new commercial sales to transistor machines after 1963.

### Small process computers

Japan develops compact twelve-, eighteen-, and twenty-four-bit controllers for:

- machine tools;
- rolling mills;
- refineries;
- cranes;
- shipyards;
- telephone switching;
- electrical systems.

Japan may not yet match America’s cheap general-purpose PDP-8 market, but it deploys more small computers as integrated parts of industrial systems.

## 6. The Filipino programming community

Manila develops one of the sphere’s first major non-Japanese programming schools.

Its students learn:

- Japanese technical vocabulary;
- vertical Japanese source;
- TEJUN procedure analysis;
- Latin supplementary libraries;
- translation between Japanese and Filipino records;
- imperial character registry standards.

Filipino programmers become particularly valuable in:

- international banking;
- shipping;
- American-format conversion;
- English-language commercial software;
- mixed-script databases;
- communications with Latin America.

They remain disadvantaged because advancement in the central Japanese computing establishment requires high Japanese literacy.

The inversion is now complete:

> Japanese programmers do not learn English to command the computer. Filipino programmers learn Japanese to command it.

## 7. Industrial and military applications

By 1965, Japanese computing is deeply embedded in:

- carrier maintenance;
- air-defense plotting;
- missile testing;
- port logistics;
- refinery supervision;
- production quality;
- warehouse systems;
- telephone exchanges;
- banking and clearing;
- ship construction;
- electrical dispatch.

Japan’s most advanced systems are often invisible to ordinary office workers because they are built inside factories, ships, communications centers, and logistics networks.

## Japanese position in 1965

Japan leads in:

- native non-Latin programming;
- multilingual character architecture;
- vertical terminals;
- industrial-process languages;
- factory and port automation;
- mixed human-machine procedures.

It remains somewhat behind in:

- general-purpose supercomputers;
- virtual-memory operating systems;
- open time-sharing;
- compiler theory;
- independent software markets.

The gap with the leading three is now primarily one of scale and general-purpose software maturity, not fundamental capability.

---

# VI. The Latin bloc  
## Scientific confederation and the programmable desk machine

The Latin bloc’s computing identity becomes firmer as the German–Italian political relationship deteriorates and Umberto II’s royal-corporatist order consolidates.

Italy, Occitania, Spain, and Portugal do not want German or American ownership of their:

- military software;
- banking records;
- Suez administration;
- nuclear systems;
- aircraft;
- naval command;
- industrial planning.

## 1. Latin Computing Standards Commission

A **Latin Computing Standards Commission** is established around 1961–62, building upon the cooperative habits of the 1958 naval materiel system.

It standardizes:

- magnetic-tape labeling;
- paper-tape formats;
- peripheral connectors;
- block sizes;
- error codes;
- the Latin character set;
- scientific subroutine descriptions;
- compiler test suites;
- transaction and naval-message formats.

It does not establish one processor architecture.

## 2. Italian hardware

Olivetti’s ELEA family expands through:

- banks;
- insurers;
- state corporations;
- Suez administration;
- shipping;
- universities;
- manufacturing.

Its machines are known for:

- modular cabinets;
- excellent operator consoles;
- diagnostics;
- decimal and alphanumeric processing;
- strong printers;
- field service;
- readable documentation.

IRI and STET maintain separate heavier systems for:

- telecommunications;
- railways;
- electricity;
- state finance;
- military command.

## 3. Occitan hardware

Occitania specializes in:

- compact transistor computers;
- buffered input and output;
- telemetry;
- radar;
- avionics;
- numerical control;
- naval electronics;
- guided weapons.

Its machines are produced in smaller numbers than Italian systems but frequently contain more advanced real-time interfaces.

Occitan equipment increasingly appears as the control brain inside an Italian, Spanish, or Portuguese platform.

## 4. Latin languages

### ALGOL-Latin 62

ALGOL becomes the common scientific language of the bloc.

A Latin implementation standard adds what the original report largely leaves machine-dependent:

- input and output;
- complex arithmetic;
- matrix libraries;
- numerical precision rules;
- error conditions;
- tape and file conventions;
- separately compiled procedures.

ALGOL-Latin is used for:

- aerospace;
- universities;
- nuclear engineering;
- structural work;
- navigation;
- numerical analysis.

### LIA 63

Italy’s administrative language, provisionally **LIA 63**, supports:

- business records;
- decimal currency;
- indexed files;
- report forms;
- inventory;
- payroll;
- customs;
- shipping;
- banking.

It is more compact than COBOL and heavily integrated with Olivetti printers and forms.

### Occitan control systems

Occitan real-time languages remain comparatively specialized.

They describe:

- channels;
- tracks;
- timed events;
- device states;
- telemetry;
- control surfaces;
- missile and radar sequences.

They are beginning to converge around a shared macro and runtime system, but no universal Latin control language exists in 1965.

## 5. Latin character code

The bloc adopts an eight-bit Latin-oriented code earlier than America’s commercial market fully settles its ASCII–EBCDIC conflict.

It supports:

- Italian;
- Spanish;
- Portuguese;
- French;
- Occitan;
- Latin;
- common mathematical signs;
- accented capitals and lowercase;
- control functions.

Arabic, Greek, and colonial scripts require extensions.

The Latin bloc’s choice of an eight-bit character is driven by multilingual necessity rather than processor architecture.

## 6. Programma 101

The Programma 101 appears in 1965, and in this stronger Olivetti environment it receives greater support rather than being treated as a curious side product.

Historically it was a transistorized programmable desk calculator produced from 1965, using a keyboard, printer, and removable magnetic program cards. citeturn299115search1turn299115search3

In the setting, it becomes the **Programma 101L**, with modest compatibility enhancements for the Latin market.

It is used by:

- engineers;
- architects;
- accountants;
- surveyors;
- artillery and aviation offices;
- laboratories;
- small factories;
- universities;
- schools.

It cannot replace a mainframe. It can store and repeat calculation procedures without submitting a job to a computing center.

This gives the Latin bloc a genuine world lead in **desktop programmable calculation**.

America leads the minicomputer. Italy leads the programmable office desk.

## 7. Spain and Portugal

### Spain

By 1965 Spain possesses:

- domestically assembled midrange machines;
- Italian commercial systems;
- Occitan military systems;
- ALGOL compilers;
- university computing centers;
- local peripheral production.

It remains dependent on Italian and Occitan central processors but is no longer merely a purchaser.

### Portugal

Portugal specializes in:

- shipping;
- customs;
- banking;
- colonial administration;
- telecommunications;
- British–Latin data conversion;
- Atlantic and Indian Ocean tracking.

Lisbon becomes an important standards and translation center precisely because Portugal continues dealing with both Britain and the Latin bloc.

## Latin position in 1965

The Latin bloc leads in:

- programmable desktop machines;
- operator interface;
- multilingual Latin text;
- compact avionics;
- commercial forms and printers;
- modular export systems.

It remains behind in:

- supercomputer scale;
- time-sharing;
- semiconductor volume;
- operating-system sophistication;
- large software communities.

It is clearly independent and no longer vulnerable to absorption into the German ecosystem.

---

# VII. The five computing cultures in 1965

| Bloc | Main architectural achievement | Language structure | Normal user relationship | Greatest advantage | Principal weakness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Germany | ERO 63 and Planform portability | One Rechenplan family with three profiles | Submit a certified plan through an institution | Formal control, engineering, administration | Rigidity and weak openness |
| Britain | Atlas virtual memory and remote multi-access | Autocode, CPL, CLEO, control languages | Use a shared computing service | Operating systems, compilers, translation | Fragmented hardware and limited capital |
| United States | System/360 compatible family, CTSS, minicomputer | FORTRAN, COBOL, JOVIAL, LISP, BASIC, PL/I | Buy or rent a platform and build applications | Volume, markets, interaction, ICs | Software complexity and incompatibility between sectors |
| Japan | Common character registry and process computers | KEISAN and TEJUN in vertical Japanese | Program a corporate or imperial process | Automation, multilingual systems, native interface | Less open and fewer general-purpose installations |
| Latin bloc | Interoperable national systems and Programma 101 | ALGOL-Latin, LIA, control dialects | Use a designed instrument or specialist service | Interface, compact systems, desktop calculation | Scale and divided investment |

---

# VIII. Programming as a profession

By 1965, “programmer” no longer describes one uniform occupation.

| Bloc | Emerging professional divisions |
|---|---|
| Germany | Rechenplan engineer, Planform specialist, compiler engineer, Planprüfer, control certifier, data operator |
| Britain | scientific programmer, systems programmer, compiler writer, systems analyst, multi-access operator, translation specialist |
| United States | application programmer, systems programmer, vendor engineer, analyst, operator, database/file specialist, terminal user |
| Japan | KEISAN engineer, TEJUN procedure engineer, character-system specialist, process-control engineer, vertical-terminal operator |
| Latin bloc | numerical programmer, business analyst, avionics programmer, machine operator, applications consultant, programmable-calculator specialist |

The most important shift is that programmers no longer need to know every physical circuit in the machine.

A new hierarchy appears:

- hardware designers;
- operating-system programmers;
- compiler writers;
- language programmers;
- application programmers;
- data-preparation staff;
- terminal users.

That separation allows computing to grow far beyond the original community of electrical engineers and mathematicians.

---

# IX. The moving balance of leadership

## 1960–1961

Britain leads in software services and operating concepts.

America leads in production and real-time research.

Germany leads in language unity and aerospace-control formalism.

Japan and the Latin bloc are credible but clearly secondary in general-purpose systems.

## 1962

Atlas gives Britain a temporary, visible lead in high-end architecture, virtual memory, and supervision.

Germany remains strongest in formally integrated engineering and control.

America begins the integrated-circuit and time-sharing surge.

## 1963–1964

America pulls ahead in commercial architecture through System/360, CTSS, Aerospace Force procurement, and large semiconductor orders.

Germany responds through ERO 63 and Rechenplan 63 rather than abandoning its own system.

Britain shifts from raw machine leadership toward compiler, service, and network leadership.

Japan establishes its multilingual character architecture.

## 1965

There is no single overall leader.

- **America** has the largest and fastest-growing market.
- **Britain** has the most sophisticated operating and compiler culture.
- **Germany** has the most coherent formal software order.
- **Japan** has the strongest process-automation and non-Latin computing direction.
- **The Latin bloc** leads the small programmable office-machine niche.

No power has a rational reason to surrender its computing tradition.

---

# X. Working canon decisions

1. **Japanese source is vertically displayed by default:** top to bottom, with successive statement columns proceeding right to left.

2. **Horizontal left-to-right Japanese remains a secondary technical mode** for diagrams, matrices, foreign text, and some industrial consoles.

3. **Japanese portrait-format vertical terminals appear around 1962–64**, with tokenized katakana-to-kanji keyword display beginning on expensive systems by 1964–65.

4. **Germany adopts the ERO 63 architectural standard**, provisionally based on forty-eight-bit words, twenty-four-bit half-words, six-bit basic characters, and twelve-bit extended characters.

5. **Rechenplan 63 becomes Germany’s mature language standard**, with modern blocks, modules, separate compilation, structured records, and stronger checking.

6. **Planform II becomes a typed, stack-oriented intermediate representation** shared among German machine families.

7. **Planwerk 64 becomes the common German supervisor and runtime specification**, emphasizing multiprogrammed batch operation, security, auditing, and deterministic control.

8. **Petri-style condition–event diagrams become standard German design tools** for concurrent industrial, rail, administrative, and military processes.

9. **Germany begins using experimental onboard digital guidance between 1963 and 1965**, while retaining analog stabilization and extensive ground computation.

10. **MOSAIK develops regional remote-inquiry services during 1960–65** but does not become a fully online linked system until the later 1960s.

11. **Britain fields a larger Commonwealth Atlas family**, retaining the historical 1962 virtual-memory milestone.

12. **Britain develops CPL as its ambitious systems and research language**, while Common Autocode and CLEO remain the practical scientific and business languages.

13. **Britain establishes geographically distributed multi-access computing** and begins packetized-network research around 1965.

14. **The United States retains System/360 in 1964**, making compatible hardware families and the eight-bit byte central American innovations.

15. **America develops a deliberately plural language ecology:** FORTRAN IV, COBOL, JOVIAL, LISP, BASIC, and emerging PL/I.

16. **ASCII and IBM’s mainframe character code coexist uneasily**, reinforcing America’s pattern of competitive rather than centrally imposed standards.

17. **American aerospace procurement makes integrated-circuit flight computers a major strategic program by 1962–65.**

18. **The PDP-8 class appears in 1965**, beginning the American minicomputer and embedded-general-purpose-computer market.

19. **Japan adopts KEISAN 64 and TEJUN 65**, the former scientific and the latter administrative, transactional, and process-oriented.

20. **Japan creates a Co-Prosperity Sphere character registry around 1962–63 and a multibyte interchange form by 1964–65.**

21. **Filipino programmers use Latin supplementary libraries but normally learn Japanese language and Japanese programming grammar.**

22. **The Latin bloc adopts ALGOL-Latin 62, LIA 63, a common eight-bit multilingual code, and shared peripheral standards.**

23. **Programma 101 enters service in 1965 and gives Italy the leading programmable desktop-calculator ecosystem.**

24. **By 1965 the race has four first-rank powers by different measures—America, Britain, Germany, and Japan—while the Latin bloc remains a smaller but technically sovereign fifth system.**

The next period, **1965–1970**, is where these systems begin to connect computers to national communications networks, missile and aerospace vehicles, industrial plants, and continuously updated administrative systems—and where software complexity begins becoming a strategic weakness rather than merely an inconvenience.

# Japan, 1973–1983: from capsule flights to a permanent orbital workshop

The earlier 1983 date should now be formally superseded.

The current Setting Bible and Timeline still describe **1983 as Japan’s first crewed orbital mission**. fileciteturn16file0 fileciteturn16file6 Under the revised sequence, 1983 becomes a more substantial milestone:

> **1973 — first Japanese crewed orbital flight.**  
> **1976 — first crewed occupation of a Japanese automated laboratory.**  
> **1983 — first continuously occupied, multinational Japanese-led orbital platform.**

That solves the missing decade and preserves 1983 as an important date without leaving Japan implausibly absent from human spaceflight until then.

The Japanese path remains machine-first. Japan does not suddenly imitate the American spaceplane system or Germany’s enormous orbital harbor. It develops a compact crew vehicle, automated rendezvous, modular laboratories, robotic cargo craft, and eventually a small permanent command-and-research platform.

Automatic orbital docking was already demonstrated historically in 1967, so a Japanese automated modular assembly sequence beginning in 1974–75 is entirely plausible for a Japan with this setting’s stronger computing, electronics, and orbital investment. citeturn334736search0

---

# I. How Japanese cabinets work by the 1970s

Japan is neither a parliamentary democracy in the American sense nor a military dictatorship governed directly from Imperial General Headquarters.

It has become a **managed imperial parliamentary system**.

## The constitutional structure

The Emperor remains:

- sacred head of the imperial order;
- formal source of executive and military authority;
- final arbiter in a severe Cabinet crisis;
- guardian of the long-term legitimacy of the Co-Prosperity Sphere.

But Hirohito does not personally administer budgets, ministries, industrial plans, or launch schedules.

The prime minister must assemble support among:

- the government association’s parliamentary factions;
- senior bureaucracies;
- the Army and Navy;
- the Imperial Defense Council;
- zaibatsu and development banks;
- the court;
- the associated-state diplomatic establishment.

The armed services retain enormous influence but cannot simply run the government. Since the Kishi and Ikeda periods, their economic offices, procurement systems, and foreign-client operations have been increasingly subordinated to Cabinet coordination.

Elections are managed and anti-imperial parties remain restricted, but factional competition is real. Governments can fall over:

- corruption;
- factional defections;
- mishandled associated-state relations;
- fiscal disputes;
- procurement failures;
- inability to reconcile the military and economic bureaucracies.

The result resembles one enormous governing association containing several quasi-parties.

## The major factions

By 1973, the governing establishment contains roughly five recognizable currents:

1. **Kishi developmentalists:** planning, strategic industry, security, large corporations, Manchurian administrative traditions.
2. **Ikeda–Satō administrators:** stability, consumer prosperity, technical standardization, cautious diplomacy.
3. **Tanaka construction faction:** infrastructure, provincial patronage, imperial development projects, transport, telecommunications.
4. **Miki constitutional reformers:** clean government, Diet supervision, associated-state law, limits upon arbitrary administration.
5. **Fukuda diplomatic conservatives:** finance, administrative sobriety, imperial concord, careful relations with culturally distinct associated nations.

Nakasone’s younger technological-national faction begins emerging during the 1970s.

The broad personnel sequence deliberately adapts the historical succession from Satō through Nakasone, but gives each government different causes, institutions, and imperial responsibilities. citeturn500501search0

# II. The Cabinet sequence, 1965–1983

| Prime minister | Working term | Political character | Principal space role |
|---|---:|---|---|
| **Eisaku Satō** | 1965–1972 | Consolidation, standards, restrained strategic independence | Satellite network, Amaterasu incident, Weather Commons, authorization of crewed flight |
| **Kakuei Tanaka** | 1972–1974 | Construction, provincial patronage, imperial infrastructure | Biak expansion, first crewed mission, heavy-launch development |
| **Takeo Miki** | 1974–1976 | Clean government and procurement reform | Safe modular station assembly and first laboratory occupation |
| **Takeo Fukuda** | 1976–1979 | Associated-state concord and financial discipline | Multinational astronaut program and imperial scientific partnership |
| **Masayoshi Ōhira** | 1979–1980 | Information society and comprehensive imperial security | Automated cargo, communications, distributed data systems |
| **Zenkō Suzuki** | 1980–1982 | Fiscal consolidation and consensus | Slower expansion, reliability, rescue and docking systems |
| **Yasuhiro Nakasone** | 1982 onward | Assertive technological leadership | Continuous occupation, multinational platform, Mars robotics |

This succession should now be treated as the working Japanese political canon.

---

# III. The Satō inheritance

Satō’s Cabinet has already done most of the political groundwork.

Under Satō, Japan:

- consolidates the Imperial Space Development Agency;
- builds Biak as its principal equatorial launch center;
- creates common computing and satellite interfaces;
- establishes the weather and communications ground network;
- conducts Operation Amaterasu in 1969;
- participates in the San Marco weather settlement;
- begins converting the Weather Commons into an operational global system;
- watches Germany and America land on the Moon in 1970 and 1971.

Satō’s response to the lunar landings is not to announce a Japanese Moon race.

He authorizes the **Human Orbital Systems Program** in 1971 with deliberately limited objectives:

- demonstrate safe crew transport;
- prove automated flight and recovery;
- qualify rendezvous and docking;
- service Japanese satellites;
- test human supervision of automated orbital machinery;
- establish the medical basis for longer missions.

The Cabinet directive contains an important restriction:

> No human flight is to be authorized merely to meet a commemorative date.

That is a direct expression of Japan’s space culture. Prestige matters, but prestige comes from disciplined mastery.

---

# IV. The spacecraft architecture

The following names can be treated as working canon.

## Hikari crewed vehicle

The Japanese crewed spacecraft family is called **Hikari**, “Light.”

It is:

- initially two-person;
- capsule-based rather than winged;
- highly automated;
- launched from Biak;
- recovered in the western Pacific;
- equipped with manual override but not designed around constant manual piloting.

The crew consists principally of:

- a commander-engineer;
- a systems or scientific specialist.

The first model can remain in orbit for approximately five days. Later forms support ten to thirty days, especially when docked to an orbital laboratory.

## Musubi docking target

**Musubi**, “Connection” or “Bond,” is the rendezvous and docking test series.

Musubi vehicles are small and mostly unpressurized. They carry:

- radar or optical rendezvous targets;
- radio beacons;
- docking collars;
- attitude-control systems;
- telemetry;
- limited storage or engineering experiments.

They allow Japan to prove docking before risking a crew against a valuable laboratory.

## Kōbō orbital laboratory

**Kōbō**, “Workshop,” is the small automated orbital laboratory.

It is not launched as one enormous German-style station. It is assembled from modules.

The first two elements are:

- **Kōbō-A:** power, attitude control, communications, docking, life-support support, and command computing;
- **Kōbō-B:** pressurized laboratory and habitation module.

The complex normally operates without a crew. Experiments continue automatically between visits.

## Tsubame cargo craft

**Tsubame**, “Swallow,” is the later automated logistics vehicle.

It carries:

- food;
- water;
- oxygen;
- experiments;
- replacement electronics;
- propellant for station reboost;
- waste containers for destructive reentry.

It becomes the direct ancestor of Japan’s later unmanned orbital tugs and supervised robotic spacecraft.

---

# V. The missing sequence, 1972–1976

## 1972: Hikari-0

The uncrewed full-system qualification vehicle launches in the second half of 1972.

It performs:

- automated ascent;
- orbital insertion;
- attitude control;
- tracking-station handoffs;
- simulated cabin operations;
- automatic deorbit;
- controlled atmospheric reentry;
- parachute recovery;
- Pacific naval recovery.

A test dummy and biological packages occupy the seats.

The mission is not entirely clean. Likely minor problems include:

- excessive cabin temperature;
- a failed telemetry channel;
- a late parachute deployment command that falls within safety tolerances;
- saltwater intrusion after splashdown.

Japan does not conceal the defects from its own engineering establishment. The vehicle is accepted only after modifications.

## July or August 1973: Hikari-1

Japan’s first crewed mission launches from Biak with two men.

A sensible duration is **four days**.

The objectives are deliberately limited:

- verify crew health;
- operate the vehicle through ground-station gaps;
- test automatic and manual attitude control;
- photograph weather systems;
- receive and retransmit Weather Commons data;
- test navigation against Japanese ground and satellite references;
- validate recovery operations.

The mission does not rendezvous with another spacecraft.

The propaganda is substantial but restrained. Japanese broadcasts emphasize that Hikari flew almost entirely automatically while its crew monitored, diagnosed, and authorized.

The defining line is:

> **The machine carried man safely because man had first taught the machine discipline.**

The recovery force includes Japanese and Philippine ships. That gives the Philippine Navy a visible role in Japan’s first crewed flight.

## Early 1974: Musubi automatic docking test

Japan launches two uncrewed Musubi-derived vehicles several days apart.

They:

- acquire one another;
- conduct automatic phasing;
- approach;
- dock;
- remain joined for several hours;
- separate;
- return or decay independently.

The system experiences greater fuel expenditure than intended, but docking is successful.

This is Japan’s proof that the 1973 flight is not a dead-end prestige capsule.

## Mid-1974: Hikari-2

Hikari-2 carries two crew for approximately eight days.

It rendezvouses with Musubi-2 and performs a hard docking. The docking collar is not designed for internal transfer, so the crew remains inside Hikari.

They test:

- docking loads;
- electrical connections;
- remote control of the target;
- combined attitude control;
- emergency separation;
- station-keeping near an uncooperative object.

This flight produces the first serious discussion of Japanese astronauts as **orbital technicians**, not merely passengers.

## Late 1974: the Biak booster failure

A heavy-launch test intended to qualify the vehicle for Kōbō-A suffers a serious failure.

The rocket is uncrewed, but it may:

- lose an engine shortly after launch;
- deviate from its corridor;
- require range destruction;
- scatter debris into the sea and part of a restricted coastal zone.

A few launch workers or local fishermen may be killed or injured by debris or evacuation confusion. It need not be a gigantic catastrophe, but it becomes politically important because it overlaps with allegations concerning:

- inflated Biak construction contracts;
- inadequate local consultation;
- rushed certification;
- Tanaka-faction patronage;
- payments from industrial combines;
- land acquisition and resettlement around the range.

The failure delays the laboratory and contributes to Tanaka’s fall.

This is more appropriate than a Lockheed-style scandal in this world. Tanaka falls because his infrastructure machine appears to have placed political schedules and patronage ahead of safety.

## 1975: Kōbō assembly begins

Under Miki, the program resumes with stricter review.

### Kōbō-A

The first module launches in early or mid-1975.

It contains:

- solar power;
- batteries;
- attitude control;
- telemetry;
- communications;
- environmental equipment;
- one docking port;
- station computer;
- emergency oxygen and water stores.

It operates automatically for several months.

### Kōbō-B

The laboratory module launches later in 1975.

It performs an automatic rendezvous and docking with Kōbō-A.

The joined complex has a mass of roughly **nine to twelve tonnes**, depending on the final launch architecture. This is modest beside German or American systems, but entirely sufficient for:

- two visiting crew;
- ten to twenty days of occupation;
- materials experiments;
- medical studies;
- weather-sensor calibration;
- automated maintenance tests;
- Earth observation;
- life-support development.

Japan leaves it unoccupied through an extended checkout period.

That caution is important. The station exists in 1975, but the first crew does not immediately board it.

## 1976: Hikari-3 and the first laboratory occupation

Hikari-3 docks with Kōbō early or mid-1976.

Two astronauts occupy the station for approximately fourteen days.

They:

- activate the full life-support system;
- inspect automatic equipment;
- replace failed modules;
- conduct metallurgy and crystal-growth experiments;
- calibrate meteorological sensors;
- test remote control of another small satellite;
- practice emergency retreat into Hikari;
- leave the station operating automatically after departure.

This is Japan’s first orbital-laboratory mission.

It is not continuous occupation.

Kōbō spends most of its first years empty, working as a robotic laboratory between human maintenance visits.
