# Germany, 1976–1980: Rules Above the Earth, Pressure Around the Reich

The defining shift in these years is that Wolfgang stops thinking primarily in terms of **German initiatives** and begins thinking in terms of **coalition geometry**.

From 1965 through 1975, Germany could normally confront one problem at a time:

- America over Iceland;
- Italy in the Balkans;
- Britain through Iraq;
- the United States in space;
- unrest inside Mittelafrika.

Between 1976 and 1980, those separate pressures begin aligning.

America finds common ground with the Latin bloc. Britain resumes anti-submarine cooperation with Washington. The Vatican gains a powerful issue against Germany. America builds a competing orbital port. Japan remains strategically independent rather than naturally moving toward Berlin.

Wolfgang does not conclude that Germany is surrounded by one coordinated conspiracy. He is not naturally paranoid enough for that. He concludes something more sober:

> **Germany has accumulated enough power that states with little affection for one another can still agree upon limiting it.**

That becomes the strategic problem of his middle thirties.

The established chronology places Healey’s accession, Buchanan’s election, Columbia’s authorization, the Mars rover, the *Wespe* trials, *Wotan*, the demographic scandal, the Second Mosaic Settlement, renewed Anglo-American ASW coordination, and the first continuously occupied American orbital and lunar facilities within this period. fileciteturn16file0 fileciteturn16file9

---

## I. 1976: Denis Healey and the permanent British adversary

Denis Healey succeeds Wilson as leader of Commonwealth Labour after the Kuwait settlement and demobilization.

Healey’s combination is particularly legible to Wolfgang:

- strong defense;
- strategic public industry;
- Commonwealth coordination;
- nuclear power;
- shipbuilding;
- aerospace;
- social stability;
- deep suspicion of German power.

Wolfgang does not react with outrage.

Britain has spent nearly thirty years organizing itself around survival against Germany. Its Atlantic and Cape systems, naval construction, African arrangements, Canadian ties, and anti-submarine doctrine are all built upon the assumption that Germany remains the principal European danger. Healey’s political economy preserves genuine strategic capacity even while its softer budgets and producer interests later contribute to Britain’s 1978–80 economic difficulties. fileciteturn17file15

Wolfgang’s private judgment is:

> “Britain does not ask whether a German action is directed against Britain. It asks how that action could be used against Britain.”

He considers this irritating but rational.

## How Germany reads Healey

German intelligence and diplomatic assessments divide Healey’s Britain into two layers.

### Public Britain

Healey presents:

- reconstruction;
- employment;
- public strategic industry;
- Commonwealth responsibility;
- defense without adventurism;
- social cohesion.

### Strategic Britain

The underlying government prioritizes:

- Atlantic surveillance;
- Canadian and Commonwealth bases;
- anti-submarine warfare;
- shipyards and reserve capacity;
- intelligence links with America;
- denial of German expansion toward the Cape, Gulf, and Atlantic islands.

Wolfgang does not expect reconciliation with Britain under Healey.

He wants predictability.

A predictably hostile Britain is easier to manage than an erratic one.

---

# II. The Stockholm Orbital Safety and Salvage Convention

The 1976 Stockholm convention is one of Wolfgang’s most personally valued diplomatic achievements.

Other leaders view it as technical housekeeping.

Wolfgang does not.

## Why the convention matters to him

Wolfgang has grown up understanding space as the one field in which prestige must eventually yield to physical reality.

In orbit:

- wreckage does not recognize national borders;
- a bolt can remain dangerous long after the state that launched it changes policy;
- a disabled enemy spacecraft still contains human beings;
- destroying a vehicle may endanger one’s own station years later;
- rescue requires compatible frequencies, docking information, and notification procedures.

By 1976, the great powers have already identified the danger of orbital collision cascades. The convention establishes registration, breakup notification, shared conjunction warnings, protected distress frequencies, rescue obligations, debris liability, passivation, disposal plans, and special protection for marked salvage and clearance vehicles. It also rejects intentional fragmentation tests in heavily occupied orbital bands and requires loose equipment, links, cases, and covers to be retained rather than scattered. fileciteturn10file1

Germany is not merely a reluctant signatory.

Wolfgang actively promotes the agreement.

## Wolfgang’s negotiating position

He rejects complete demilitarization of orbit.

Germany will not surrender:

- inspection craft;
- station defense;
- military reconnaissance;
- armed orbital vehicles;
- controlled counterspace capability.

He insists that military competition must still obey rules protecting:

- human life;
- orbital traffic;
- rescue craft;
- habitation;
- the long-term usefulness of space.

His preferred public formulation is:

> **“The first law of the spacefaring age must be that no man is abandoned and no wreck is left to endanger those who follow.”**

That line captures why he values Stockholm so highly.

The Moon landing and Raumhafen demonstrate German capability.

Stockholm demonstrates that Wolfgang can create an international rule other powers accept voluntarily.

## Why he ranks it so highly

Officials sometimes find it peculiar that Wolfgang places the convention beside Iceland or the Raumhafen among the successes of his rule.

His explanation is revealing:

> “The harbor proves what we can build. Stockholm may prevent what all of us could destroy.”

This reflects both sides of his character:

- the child who wanted space to remain a realm of construction;
- the adult who accepts that it will be armed.

Stockholm is his attempt to preserve something of the first inside the second.

---

# III. The counterinsurgency reporting problem

The Mittelafrika conflict requires a distinction between **events being observable** and **the system being understood**.

The War of the Chiefs remains principally internal during 1976–80. The Reichskommissariat is not open to unrestricted foreign journalism. German controls over travel, launch infrastructure, mining zones, and security districts remain severe.

Outsiders do not watch operations live.

## What becomes visible

Foreign governments and journalists can assemble fragments:

- refugee testimony;
- missionary correspondence;
- aerial or border observations;
- displaced communities;
- smoke visible at distance;
- villages no longer appearing in trade or church records;
- wounded people crossing into neighboring territories;
- intercepted German administrative language;
- transport movements;
- leaked photographs;
- contradictory German population statistics.

The earlier Mittelafrika discussion establishes that the census and registration system is turned into a counterinsurgency tool, with forced relocation, food denial, corridor clearance, and collective punishment escalating during the early and middle 1970s. It also emphasizes that German civil administration, security bodies, companies, and SS demographic planners frequently pursue different objectives. fileciteturn16file2

Thus “visible atrocities” should mean:

> **Increasingly corroborated from outside, not continuously witnessed from inside.**

## Wolfgang’s initial response

Wolfgang receives far more information than the public or foreign governments.

He does not believe every British account. Some reports combine:

- genuine destruction;
- rumor;
- incidents from different years;
- local feuds;
- punishment by German forces;
- punishment by German-aligned chiefs;
- villages abandoned for economic reasons;
- villages forcibly cleared for security reasons.

But he cannot dismiss the pattern.

His principal concern in 1976 is that Mittelafrika’s administration has begun treating every failed registration, mine attack, road ambush, or chiefly refusal as one component of a single security problem.

Wolfgang wants:

- distinguished categories;
- specific responsibility;
- restoration of production;
- fewer campaigns conducted against whole administrative populations;
- stronger local incentives.

This leads into the Second Mosaic Settlement rather than a general abandonment of German rule.

---

# IV. Buchanan’s election and Wolfgang’s disappointed hope

Pat Buchanan wins the American presidency in November 1976 and takes office in January 1977.

Wolfgang initially expects relations to improve.

The expectation is not unreasonable.

Both men emphasize:

- family;
- production;
- national mission;
- cultural continuity;
- industrial sovereignty;
- religious or civilizational identity;
- space;
- suspicion of financial abstraction;
- opposition to rootless internationalism.

Buchanan had also prevented National Renewal from responding violently to Rockwell’s assassination. Wolfgang respects that.

For several months, German planners discuss the possibility of a **nationalist détente**:

- acceptance of the Mid-Atlantic boundary;
- reduced intelligence confrontation;
- reciprocal limits;
- cultural exchanges;
- trade without strategic penetration;
- space-safety cooperation;
- recognition that neither side intends immediate war.

The established American canon, however, makes Buchanan’s programme one of “Peace, production, and ascent,” not pro-German alignment. It includes military modernization, orbital expansion, domestic strategic industry, and continued enforcement of the American hemisphere. fileciteturn17file17

## Why Buchanan is not pro-German

Buchanan sees Germany as:

- the principal continental European power;
- the chief submarine threat in the Atlantic;
- a competitor in Latin America;
- an ideological and technological rival;
- a state whose influence in Argentina and Cuba challenges the Monroe system;
- an imperial power whose demographic policies provide a moral issue America can exploit.

His similarity to Wolfgang makes him more capable of understanding German strategy, not more willing to accommodate it.

He recognizes that Germany’s talk of sovereign spheres can be used to justify exactly the kind of presence in South America that America intends to prohibit.

## Buchanan and Umberto

Wolfgang is disappointed that Buchanan finds relations with Umberto II easier.

The reasons are structural.

Umberto offers:

- Catholic legitimacy;
- anti-German balancing;
- influence in the Mediterranean;
- connections to Spain, Portugal, Occitania, and the Vatican;
- no direct challenge to American primacy in the Western Hemisphere comparable to Germany’s Argentine relationship;
- a political style that Buchanan finds culturally familiar.

The demographic scandal later strengthens this opening.

The Vatican and Latin bloc can present themselves as critics of German racial-demographic management without accepting American liberalism.

Buchanan therefore need not become a liberal internationalist to cooperate with Umberto.

He can cooperate as a Catholic American nationalist balancing a German rival.

## Wolfgang’s conclusion

Wolfgang does not feel personally betrayed.

He recognizes that his earlier hope was wishful.

His private conclusion is:

> “A man may understand you perfectly and oppose you for exactly that reason.”

---

# V. The danger of an anti-German alignment

By 1980, Wolfgang sees the outline of a potentially serious balancing system.

## The possible components

### America

- industrial weight;
- carrier aviation;
- spaceplanes;
- hemispheric bases;
- strategic aerospace;
- growing computer industry;
- financial and diplomatic reach.

### Britain and Commonwealth

- anti-submarine expertise;
- dispersed Atlantic bases;
- Canada;
- intelligence;
- merchant and naval logistics;
- long experience with German U-boats.

### Latin bloc

- pressure from the south;
- Mediterranean bases;
- Italian and Spanish fleets;
- Occitan aerospace and electronics;
- influence in Latin America;
- Vatican diplomatic legitimacy.

None of these powers trusts the others completely.

But all can agree that unchecked German growth would narrow their freedom.

The timeline already establishes limited American–Latin accommodation and cautious Anglo-American anti-submarine intelligence cooperation from 1977 through 1980. fileciteturn16file4

Wolfgang does not assume an imminent joint invasion.

His concern is cumulative pressure:

- American tracking data supporting British ASW;
- Italian and Occitan air systems facing German-aligned northern France;
- coordinated export controls;
- common diplomatic attacks;
- Latin access in America;
- British bases supporting American Atlantic operations;
- Vatican condemnation undermining Germany’s curated legitimacy.

This is not yet an alliance.

It is the beginning of compatibility.

---

# VI. Orbital Port Columbia and the end of the universal harbor dream

The National Mission and Productive Enterprise Act of 1977 authorizes Orbital Port Columbia, lunar-base planning, spaceplane expansion, industrial modernization, computing, and technical education. A classified annex also begins Project Zenith, turning Columbia-derived spaceplanes toward inspection, rescue, electronic warfare, controlled deorbit, and conventional strategic attack. fileciteturn16file0

Wolfgang has two reactions.

## Genuine approval

He welcomes the fact that America is committing to permanent orbital infrastructure.

He regards Columbia as technically intelligent:

- lower orbit;
- easier spaceplane access;
- frequent crew rotation;
- modular construction;
- high traffic;
- integration with America’s reusable system.

It is not simply a smaller copy of the Raumhafen.

The American port is optimized around reusable transportation. Germany’s high-orbit facility is optimized around:

- ship assembly;
- fuel transfer;
- long-duration operations;
- lunar departures;
- orbital workshops;
- eventual deep-space logistics.

## Personal disappointment

Wolfgang had hoped the Orbitaler Raumhafen would become something analogous to a German-centered international station.

Germany would own and control it, but foreign powers could send:

- scientific modules;
- liaison crews;
- commercial missions;
- docking vehicles;
- cargo;
- perhaps national sections.

The implicit bargain would be:

> Germany built the harbor; the world may use it under German traffic law.

That arrangement would make Germany the central infrastructure provider of the spacefaring order.

America refuses that dependence.

By building Columbia, it establishes the principle that a great power must possess its own sovereign port.

Japan, Britain, and the Latin bloc now have a precedent to follow.

Wolfgang understands why America does it.

He still regards it as a lost civilizational opportunity.

## German response

He forbids propaganda from describing Columbia as wasteful imitation.

Germany instead announces:

- expanded foreign-commercial access to the Raumhafen;
- standardized docking;
- additional guest accommodations;
- offers of rescue and repair services;
- broader scientific exchanges;
- clearer traffic rules.

Germany attempts to remain the most useful port even if it cannot remain the only one.

---

# VII. The Moon becomes a territorial race

From 1977 through 1979, Germany and America survey opposite lunar polar regions.

Germany concentrates on the south.

America concentrates on the north.

The distinction is not yet a treaty partition, but repeated operations begin creating expectations.

## German southern strategy

Germany deploys:

- orbital mapping;
- impact analysis;
- robotic landers;
- drilling packages;
- thermal instruments;
- mobile prospectors;
- communications relays;
- site-preparation equipment.

The objective is not merely to find ice.

It is to identify a site where Germany can support:

- landing pads;
- buried habitation;
- reactor power;
- heavy equipment;
- storage;
- workshops;
- oxygen extraction;
- eventually water recovery and fuel production.

The Raumhafen assembles and dispatches lunar cargo ships and ferries as the infrastructure matures.

## American northern strategy

America prioritizes:

- faster crew rotation;
- spaceplane-supported logistics;
- a smaller initial outpost;
- frequent resupply;
- modular growth;
- political permanence before maximum capacity.

Late in 1979 or during 1980, Kennedy Lunar Station becomes the first continuously occupied human outpost beyond Earth. It is smaller and more improvised than the German southern base planned for 1981, but America wins the permanence milestone. fileciteturn17file2

Wolfgang congratulates America again, though with more personal frustration than in 1971.

Germany had built the larger transport architecture.

America has placed people permanently on the Moon first.

## German ice finding

A German robotic expedition around 1979 should find strongly suggestive dirty ice-bearing regolith or subsurface deposits near the selected southern site.

It is not yet a limitless frozen lake.

It is enough to justify:

- continued drilling;
- pilot processing;
- choice of the Mondhafen Süd site;
- heavy-equipment deployment.

Wolfgang treats this as the material foundation of settlement rather than merely another scientific result.

---

# VIII. The Mars rover and the propaganda gap

Germany lands the first small mobile Mars rover in 1978 or early 1979.

The rover is technically impressive but modest:

- slow;
- limited communications;
- short traverses;
- geological instruments;
- panoramic imaging;
- highly conservative navigation.

Wolfgang is genuinely delighted.

Mars has occupied German long-range planning since his adolescence.

The rover represents the first physical movement by a human-made machine upon another planet.

## The German presentation problem

Germany’s scientific establishment releases:

- selected photographs;
- carefully edited films;
- engineering diagrams;
- official summaries.

Some raw data remains restricted because it reveals:

- communications;
- navigation precision;
- imaging capability;
- electronics;
- deep-space tracking.

America follows later with a more publicly accessible rover programme:

- regular images;
- educational broadcasts;
- press briefings;
- public mission personalities;
- widely distributed data.

The German rover wins the first.

The American rover wins much of the cultural imagination.

Wolfgang finds this intensely frustrating.

His response is not to release every classified system. It is to pressure German scientific institutions toward:

- faster image publication;
- public mission logs;
- named engineers and controllers;
- university access;
- educational programming;
- less reflexive secrecy.

The experience reinforces a lesson already apparent in computing:

> Germany often builds the impressive machine. America is better at letting millions of ordinary people feel that the machine belongs to them.

---

# IX. *Wotan*: the visible giant

Germany commissions *Wotan* in 1978.

The naval reference defines it as a 28,000-ton nuclear-electric Große Lenkwaffenschiff carrying four 150 mm guns, a large missile battery, three helicopters, extensive command facilities, conventional land-attack weapons, electronic warfare, and splinter protection. It is explicitly not a traditional battleship. fileciteturn10file2

Wolfgang considers it extravagant.

He does not consider it useless.

## Why he approves it

*Wotan* can serve as:

- fleet command ship;
- area-air-defense platform;
- missile magazine;
- land-attack vessel;
- helicopter and surveillance base;
- diplomatic flagship;
- escort organizer;
- electronic-warfare center.

It embodies modern guided warfare rather than an attempt to preserve the gun battleship solely for prestige.

## The political compromise

The Navy gets:

- a great named ship;
- visual prestige;
- a ceremonial flagship;
- a platform that can appear at ports and exercises.

Wolfgang gets:

- modern sensors;
- networked missile control;
- actual command utility;
- nuclear endurance;
- a ship capable of supporting rather than replacing submarines.

## The decoy value

German naval doctrine remains clear:

> The surface fleet fixes, threatens, and displays. The U-boat fleet destroys.

*Wotan* makes that doctrine physical.

American and British intelligence must monitor:

- its location;
- air-defense envelope;
- missile load;
- helicopter operations;
- escorts;
- command role.

Every analyst studying *Wotan* is not studying a Type XXX attack boat or Type XXXI missile submarine.

Wolfgang appreciates the asymmetry.

His private joke may be:

> “At last the Navy has built a ship whose size is useful because everyone insists on looking at it.”

---

# X. The Rj 1 *Wespe*: accepting weapons in orbit

The correct designation is **Rj 1 Wespe**, not *Vespa*.

The 1978 vehicle is a two-person armed inspection, rescue, and station-defense craft. It has no wings, aerodynamic tail, runway capability, or aircraft-style forward direction. It remains in orbit and is supported from the Raumhafen. Its test armament consists of two retained-case MG 68R weapons; later German craft move to a purpose-built 20 mm orbital cannon and guided interceptors. fileciteturn10file1

## Wolfgang’s reluctance

Part of Wolfgang genuinely wishes that orbit could remain outside ordinary military rivalry.

This is not a formal pacifist position.

It is the residue of the boy who saw space as a domain ruled by physics rather than political intrigue.

The American spaceplane programme destroys that hope.

A reusable American craft can potentially:

- approach satellites;
- inspect German systems;
- retrieve or disable objects;
- interfere with communications;
- carry classified payloads;
- threaten the Raumhafen;
- leave orbit and return to Earth.

Project Zenith makes the military implications explicit.

Germany cannot defend a fixed orbital harbor solely with ground missiles and diplomatic protest.

## Who pushes the issue

The pressure comes from:

- the military space command;
- Raumhafen security;
- Heydrich’s successor apparatus;
- tracking and intelligence services;
- station engineers concerned about close approaches;
- naval officers who understand the vulnerability of a fixed base.

They argue:

> Germany has built the most valuable stationary target in orbit and given every rival years to study its path.

Wolfgang accepts the logic.

## His conditions

He refuses to let the Raumjäger culture develop around destruction alone.

The *Wespe* doctrine must include:

- identification;
- communication;
- inspection;
- escort;
- rescue;
- controlled intervention;
- station defense;
- grapple and stabilization support;
- disabling rather than fragmentation where possible.

Weapon design must minimize debris:

- retained cases;
- captive links;
- safe-fire cones;
- firing geometry that causes misses to reenter;
- strict authorization;
- plans to recover or deorbit damaged targets.

The mature aerospace reference later summarizes the governing rule:

> **If you miss, the shot must die. If you hit, the wreck must be recovered.** fileciteturn10file1

That doctrine begins with Wolfgang’s discomfort.

He cannot prevent the militarization of space.

He can influence what kind of military culture Germany brings into it.

---

# XI. The demographic scandal, 1978–1979

The existing timeline’s language about a broad coercive-contraception and sterilization system should be narrowed by the user’s correction.

The scandal remains serious, but its nature changes.

## The actual policy

German demographic planners face a genuine strategic concern:

- German settlers remain a small minority in most of Mittelafrika;
- native populations continue growing;
- the mature Eastern order has already abandoned any expectation of rapid German demographic majority;
- the African German presence is even thinner;
- Berlin fears that numerical disparity will eventually make German control impossible.

Germany therefore supplies free and strongly encouraged contraception in selected subject districts.

The programme operates through:

- clinics;
- employers;
- chiefs;
- housing offices;
- maternal-health services;
- schools;
- mission-linked medical networks where cooperation exists;
- information campaigns;
- free distribution.

It is intentionally targeted toward populations Berlin wants to grow more slowly.

Germany simultaneously discourages contraceptive use among Germans.

That is the discriminatory essence of the policy.

## How encouragement becomes pressure

The official central policy does not normally involve physically forcing contraception upon individuals.

But dependence makes the line between encouragement and coercion unstable.

Local practices can include:

- repeated counseling;
- clinic targets;
- employer pressure;
- contraceptive distribution attached to benefits;
- housing officials favoring smaller families;
- chiefs rewarded for lower birth rates;
- doctors treating acceptance as evidence of cooperation;
- education or employment penalties applied by overzealous administrators.

Not all of these are centrally ordered.

Enough are tolerated that Berlin bears responsibility.

## Sterilization

Sterilization is not a routine mass population-control instrument.

It remains legally available in narrower categories:

- serious repeat violent criminals;
- certain security offenders;
- narrowly defined hereditary or medical cases;
- exceptional penal sentences.

Abuses occur.

Some colonial officials stretch the categories.

But there is no universal campaign to sterilize entire African or Eastern populations.

## What leaks

The 1978–79 scandal combines several different classes of document:

- ethnicity-specific pharmaceutical distribution plans;
- demographic targets;
- clinic instructions;
- reports praising falling fertility;
- benefits linked to family-size goals;
- punitive sterilization cases;
- local complaints;
- communications warning officials to avoid politically damaging language;
- budget records showing Germany discourages contraception in the core while funding it in subject territories.

Foreign opponents present these as one integrated programme of demographic destruction.

That description overstates central uniformity.

It does not invent the racial-demographic objective.

---

# XII. Wolfgang’s responsibility

Wolfgang had approved the broad reasoning.

He understood the demographic concern.

Contraceptive distribution appeared to him:

- cheaper than forced relocation;
- less violent than military suppression;
- administratively manageable;
- compatible with existing health systems;
- preferable to periodic demographic panic.

He instructed officials to avoid obvious coercion and maintain strict secrecy.

This is why the scandal affects him personally.

He cannot say that rogue officials created the entire matter.

They made it harsher and less controlled.

The governing concept came from Berlin.

## Katharina’s private role

Katharina’s medical background makes her useful here without turning her into a public opposition figure.

Her likely private warning is:

> “Consent is not made free merely by avoiding physical force. A patient who thinks her housing, work, or child’s schooling depends upon the answer is not answering only a doctor.”

Wolfgang does not immediately accept the full implication.

He does accept that the administrative meaning of “voluntary” becomes unreliable inside a dependent colonial population.

This is one of the few issues on which his wife’s professional formation gives her a perspective unavailable from military, SS, or economic briefings.

## The strategic lesson

Wolfgang had believed secrecy could separate:

- internal necessity;
- external presentation.

The leak teaches him otherwise.

His new conclusion is:

> **A policy that becomes catastrophic when described accurately is not protected merely because its files are classified.**

This does not turn him into an opponent of demographic policy.

It makes him more cautious about approving measures whose international defense depends entirely upon euphemism.

---

# XIII. The response to the scandal

There is no great purge.

Nobody at the highest level is executed or publicly sacrificed.

Wolfgang orders:

- reprimands;
- reassignment of several demographic and medical administrators;
- suspension of the most aggressive local targets;
- explicit consent language;
- separation of contraception from food allocation;
- audit of employer and chief pressure;
- stricter review of sterilization sentences;
- prohibition on presenting fertility reduction as a production quota;
- centralized documentation intended to distinguish policy from abuse.

The underlying availability and encouragement programme survives in narrower form.

The German public explanation emphasizes:

- maternal health;
- voluntary family planning;
- local abuses;
- falsified foreign claims;
- punishment of officials who exceeded authority.

The Vatican is not satisfied.

Neither is Buchanan.

## Why no one is simply fired

Several senior institutions share responsibility:

- SS demographic offices;
- colonial administration;
- pharmaceutical firms;
- medical authorities;
- population planners;
- Berlin ministries.

A sweeping prosecution would expose how widely the premise was accepted.

Wolfgang instead narrows the programme while preserving institutional continuity.

This is not merely cowardice.

It also reflects the reality that the same administrative and medical system provides ordinary health care across vast territories.

Dismantling it would create additional harm and chaos.

But the decision leaves Germany vulnerable to the charge that it punished embarrassment rather than policy.

---

# XIV. Buchanan, the Vatican, and Umberto exploit the opening

Buchanan turns the demographic scandal into the issue Wolfgang had hoped would not exist: a bridge between America and the Latin Catholic bloc.

The established timeline originally described the Vatican condemning demographic imperialism while Buchanan used the controversy to isolate Germany and improve relations with Britain and the Latin bloc. fileciteturn17file4

Under the revised canon, the Vatican’s criticism focuses on:

- targeted demographic manipulation;
- compromised medical consent;
- interference with family life;
- discriminatory state policy;
- sterilization as punishment;
- use of health systems for imperial population goals.

Umberto can criticize Germany without adopting American liberalism.

Buchanan can criticize Germany without abandoning his own restrictive immigration or family policies.

The common argument is not:

> Every person must embrace liberal individualism.

It is:

> The state must not use medicine to reduce subject peoples for imperial convenience.

That is politically effective.

## Wolfgang’s frustration

Wolfgang sees substantial hypocrisy.

America has used coercive power throughout its hemisphere. Britain maintains imperial protections. Italy rules subordinate populations. Spain and Portugal retain empires.

But he also understands that hypocrisy does not make the German files disappear.

This is one of the moments when his dislike of moralistic foreign policy collides with his own concern for Germany’s reputation.

---

# XV. The Second Mosaic Settlement

The Second Mosaic Settlement of 1977–79 resolves much of the War of the Chiefs through:

- fixed chiefly stipends;
- personal performance shares;
- protected succession;
- household privileges;
- community dividends;
- continued direct wages for workers;
- incentives tied to order, infrastructure, registration, and welfare.

It creates a wealthy Mosaic aristocracy and does not answer the sovereignty demands of more urbanized West African territories. But it stabilizes much of the Congo interior. fileciteturn17file2

Wolfgang takes an important lesson from the settlement:

> People defend an order more reliably when they possess a predictable stake in it.

This resembles the mature Eastern Reichskommissariat model, where hereditary tenure, service status, local institutions, and predictable obligations have proven more durable than permanent arbitrary terror. The Eastern canon explicitly treats stability as the product of habituation, investment, division, and the absence of a credible alternative. fileciteturn10file6

Wolfgang therefore increasingly favors:

- status;
- contract;
- inherited interest;
- measurable reward;
- regulated hierarchy;

over raw administrative command.

This does not democratize the empire.

It makes it more durable.

---

# XVI. America’s consolidation by 1980

By 1980, Buchanan has accomplished more than Wolfgang expected.

America has:

- a continuously occupied orbital port;
- the first continuously occupied lunar outpost;
- expanding personal computing;
- visible industrial modernization;
- a strengthened Caribbean and Guianese sphere;
- National Renewal control of Congress;
- no civil war;
- improved relations with Britain and the Latin bloc.

The American personal-computing boom becomes particularly striking. Germany remains strong in engineering systems, state-corporate ledgers, rail, industrial calculation, and formal programming environments. America makes the computer a consumer, school, hobbyist, and small-business object. fileciteturn17file17

Wolfgang sees a problem that goes beyond hardware.

America is creating a mass public familiar with computers.

Germany is creating a technically superior administrative and industrial elite.

He does not yet know which model will prove more important.

He suspects Germany may need more of the American openness without importing American political culture.

## Buchanan’s landslide

Buchanan defeats Reagan by approximately 59–41 in 1980, with National Renewal securing a powerful but not constitutionally unlimited congressional position. fileciteturn16file9

Wolfgang does not celebrate.

A strong Buchanan is more predictable than a collapsing America.

He is also more capable of sustaining pressure against Germany.

---

# XVII. The Japanese option

By 1980, Wolfgang begins exploring whether Germany and Japan can reduce their strategic competition.

His relationship with Crown Prince Akihito is useful, but insufficient.

The two men can communicate privately and maintain respect.

They cannot erase conflicts involving:

- Siberia;
- China;
- Asian markets;
- industrial technology;
- arms exports;
- the Indian Ocean;
- Middle Eastern influence;
- Latin America;
- carrier and submarine competition;
- space.

Japan is also America’s principal industrial and robotics competitor. That gives Tokyo reason not to join an American-led balancing system too tightly. fileciteturn16file4

## What Wolfgang wants

He does not initially seek a restored Axis alliance.

He seeks an **issue-specific détente**.

Possible areas include:

- Siberian boundary consultation;
- naval-incident notification;
- intelligence hotlines;
- trade and reciprocal market access;
- space rescue;
- scientific exchange;
- agreement not to exploit one another’s internal clients during crises;
- consultation if America attempts general economic containment;
- recognition of existing imperial spheres.

## What Japan wants

Japan wants:

- German recognition of its Asian order;
- reduced German support for rival clients near Japan’s Siberian frontier;
- access to German space and nuclear technology;
- protection against German dumping or industrial pressure;
- no German presumption that Japan is a junior partner.

Akihito can open the door.

Japanese ministries, armed services, zaibatsu, and imperial advisers decide how far it opens.

## The likely result by 1980

No alliance.

No grand ideological reunion.

Instead:

- warmer court correspondence;
- a summit invitation;
- working groups on orbital safety;
- maritime incident procedures;
- trade discussions;
- quieter Siberian competition;
- mutual recognition that neither benefits from pushing Japan toward America or Germany toward encirclement.

Wolfgang’s objective is negative but important:

> Germany must not face America, Britain, Italy, Spain, Occitania, and Japan as a single strategic problem.

---

# XVIII. The changing old guard

This period also accelerates the generational transition.

Under the earlier working sequence:

- Himmler dies or relinquishes the effective Reichsführer role around 1975–76;
- Friedrich Hagedorn or the mature pragmatic Order leadership increasingly administers the SS;
- Speer begins transferring daily economic authority toward Schiller and the younger technical boards;
- von Braun approaches retirement;
- Heydrich remains one of the last dominant founder-generation officials but may retire or die near the end of the decade;
- Dönitz remains an elder while Topp controls daily submarine professionalism.

This matters in the demographic scandal.

Wolfgang can no longer summon one founder and tell him to fix his personal empire.

The policy crosses institutions led by successors who possess narrower authority.

The Reich is becoming more procedural and less personal.

It is also becoming harder to hold one recognizable man responsible.

---

# XIX. Year-by-year chronology

## 1976 — Rules and adversaries

- Healey succeeds Wilson.
- Britain reinforces strategic industry and defense.
- Wolfgang accepts that British suspicion is permanent.
- Germany helps sponsor the Stockholm Orbital Safety and Salvage Convention.
- Wolfgang treats Stockholm as one of his most meaningful achievements.
- Buchanan wins the American presidency.
- The first round of German–American nationalist-détente speculation begins.
- Mittelafrika reporting grows abroad but remains fragmentary and indirect.

## 1977 — Separate harbors

- Buchanan takes office.
- Initial Wolfgang–Buchanan exchanges are courteous.
- Buchanan proves unwilling to concede German influence in the Americas.
- The National Mission and Productive Enterprise Act authorizes Columbia, lunar permanence, computing, industry, and Project Zenith.
- Wolfgang accepts that the Raumhafen will not become the single international port.
- Germany accelerates southern lunar reconnaissance and cargo construction.
- The Second Mosaic Settlement begins.
- Germany opens preliminary détente discussions with Japan.

## 1978 — Weapons, rovers, and leaks

- Germany lands the first small mobile Mars rover.
- *Wotan* commissions.
- Rj 1 *Wespe* begins armed inspection and station-defense trials.
- National Renewal captures a narrow Senate majority.
- The Rockwell Commission discredits the official assassination case.
- Demographic and medical records begin leaking.
- America and the Latin bloc exploit the scandal.
- Britain and America cautiously deepen ASW intelligence exchanges.
- Wolfgang orders the first internal demographic-policy review.

## 1979 — Permanent occupation

- Columbia becomes continuously occupied.
- Kennedy Lunar Station becomes continuously occupied in late 1979 or 1980.
- German southern probes identify promising dirty ice-bearing regolith.
- The Second Mosaic Settlement stabilizes much of the Congo interior.
- Wolfgang narrows demographic targets and imposes audit and consent requirements.
- Fulton Sheen’s death strengthens Buchanan’s Catholic moral language and the American–Vatican relationship.
- German–Japanese discussions produce limited incident-notification and scientific cooperation, but not alliance.

## 1980 — The balancing world

- Columbia reaches a normal crew of approximately eight.
- America holds the first permanent lunar outpost.
- Buchanan wins a landslide reelection.
- Healey loses to Thatcher’s National Liberal–Constitutional Union in Britain.
- American–Latin accommodation is increasingly visible.
- Anglo-American anti-submarine cooperation becomes a serious German planning concern.
- Germany completes preparations for opening Mondhafen Süd in 1981.
- Wolfgang enters the new decade expecting diplomatic pressure rather than immediate general war.

---

# XX. Wolfgang at thirty-three

By the end of 1980, Wolfgang is less idealistic than he was at twenty-eight, but not cynical.

He still believes:

- technological achievement can ennoble rivalry;
- international law can shape behavior;
- a well-designed hierarchy can produce stability;
- long-term infrastructure is superior to spectacle;
- German leadership can be materially beneficial.

He has learned:

- every separate sphere eventually produces competing infrastructure;
- ideological similarity does not create friendship;
- secrecy cannot permanently make a sensitive policy safe;
- medical encouragement becomes coercive when the state controls livelihoods;
- a visible prestige weapon may conceal a more important invisible force;
- international isolation can emerge through several limited accommodations rather than one formal alliance;
- personal friendship with Akihito or respect for Buchanan cannot substitute for aligned interests.

## The new strategic question

Wolfgang’s central question in 1968 was:

> Can Germany establish a defensible boundary with America?

By 1980 it has become:

> Can Germany prevent every other major power from finding its interests on the same side of that boundary?

That is the problem he carries into the 1980s.

---

# XXI. Public account and authorial truth

| Public account | Authorial truth |
|---|---|
| Healey revives old British hatred of Germany | British suspicion is structurally rooted in geography, naval history, and Commonwealth survival |
| Stockholm proves Germany leads peaceful space law | Wolfgang sincerely drives the convention while refusing orbital demilitarization |
| Columbia copies the Raumhafen | Columbia follows a distinct low-orbit, high-traffic spaceplane architecture |
| Germany welcomes every nation to the stars | Wolfgang hoped for German-centered international access, not equal multinational ownership |
| *Wotan* restores German surface supremacy | It is a useful modern command ship and conspicuous decoy; submarines remain decisive |
| *Wespe* protects peaceful space | It marks Germany’s reluctant entry into armed orbital competition |
| Foreign reports invent atrocities in Mittelafrika | Foreign reporting is incomplete and sometimes conflated, but rooted in genuine destructive campaigns |
| Germany merely provided voluntary family planning | The programme is ethnically targeted and vulnerable to administrative pressure even without universal physical coercion |
| Sterilization is a mass German colonial policy | It is exceptional rather than universal, though abuses and punitive cases are real |
| Wolfgang punished the guilty officials | He narrows and audits the policy without repudiating its demographic premise |
| Buchanan is an ideological cousin of Wolfgang | He is a nationalist American rival who understands Germany and balances against it |
| Japan is Germany’s natural Asian ally | Japan remains an independent imperial power whose cooperation is possible only issue by issue |
| America’s lunar outpost is a hurried shack | It is smaller than Mondhafen Süd but wins the politically important permanence milestone |

The defining image of these five years is Wolfgang watching two screens.

On one, the Rj 1 *Wespe* approaches a target in silence, armed because the harbor can no longer remain undefended.

On the other, an American crew enters Columbia, proving that Germany will not own the only road through orbit.

The spacefaring future he wanted is arriving.

It is simply arriving divided into armed ports.

This younger generation will eventually give way to the generation that kind of grows up on computers that really makes, for example, the home computer a natural thing. Eventually, the United States version of the personal computer and the Apple I generation of things may be generated by somebody who is historical, but I think we're finally, we're getting close to the point where in which that generation that would be historical if we said, you know, Bill Gates and Steve Jobs and the likes, existed, but that generation would be a post-war carryover, and, you know, well after the point of divergence, rather than just saying, hey, no, we're having new characters that we're developing here, which have different personalities shaped by the world that they grew up in. So, that's something I want to keep in mind going forward. We may not necessarily be to that stage just yet, but I want to make sure that we are emotionally prepared for when we get to that stage. That said, let's go ahead and play 1970 through 1975 forward.
