# Computing Race VI: 1970–1975  
## The microprocessor, the interactive workstation, and the generational handoff

This five-year span is the point at which computing stops being merely a young strategic industry and becomes a **self-confident intellectual civilization**.

The men who established the field are still alive and often active, but they no longer personally direct every important development. The institutional handoff should occur faster than political succession because computing has almost no inherited senior establishment. A programmer in his forties can plausibly command a nationally important laboratory; a programmer in his thirties can create a language that forces every older institution to respond.

By 1975:

- Turing is an elder statesman rather than Britain’s daily computing administrator.
- Church is the patriarch of American computation rather than the working head of the Lambda project.
- Zuse remains honored and technically interested, but younger compiler and industrial-computer engineers dominate German implementation.
- Japan’s first switching and relay pioneers have been succeeded by corporate teams trained entirely on electronic machines.
- Olivetti’s electronic establishment is led by the generation that entered computing after the war, while Marseille’s logic-programming group represents an even younger intellectual wave.

The post-1947-born **computer-native generation** is only beginning to enter the field. Its members are students, junior engineers, electronics hobbyists, terminal operators, and young programmers—not yet the chief executives of mass-market home-computer firms.

That gives us a useful generational rule:

| Generation | Approximate formation | Role by 1975 |
|---|---|---|
| Founders | Mathematics, cryptography, relays, and wartime electronics | Elder statesmen, patrons, selective researchers |
| System builders | First stored-program computers and early compilers | Directors of firms, laboratories, and national programs |
| Computer-formed generation | Educated directly on operating systems and high-level languages | Principal language, network, database, and workstation innovators |
| Postwar computer natives | Born after the 1947 divergence | Students, junior programmers, hobbyists, and future entrepreneurs |

Historical figures born before or around the divergence can still appear where their careers remain institutionally plausible. The eventual American equivalents of Gates, Jobs, and the mass-market microcomputer founders should increasingly be original characters shaped by this alternate America.

---

# I. What changes historically from 1970 to 1975?

Several developments arrive almost simultaneously.

Semiconductor memory begins displacing magnetic core in smaller systems, while the one-chip processor turns what had been a cabinet or circuit-board assembly into a purchasable component. Intel’s historical 1103 DRAM appeared in 1970, while its early microprocessor work produced the 4004 and then the 8008; importantly for this setting, Intel’s own history ties the 4004 route to a custom calculator-chip project. citeturn493846search0turn493846search3turn493846search9

That particular origin matters. The historical customer was Japanese. In this world, strategic and commercial separation between America and Japan makes the exact American–Japanese contract much less likely. The microprocessor should still emerge at roughly the same time, but through **parallel American and Japanese projects**, not one shared supply chain.

At Bell Labs, UNIX and C create a compact, interactive, increasingly portable systems-programming tradition. Primeval C compilers date from 1972–73, and Bell’s own retrospective emphasizes the connection between UNIX, C, and portability. citeturn838954search2turn154454search30

Pascal appears as a deliberately small, structured language suitable for teaching disciplined programming, while Codd’s 1970 relational model argues that users should be insulated from the physical representation of their data. SEQUEL follows in 1974 as an English-oriented query language for relational data. citeturn493846search2turn493846search17turn154454search3turn838954search1

Entirely new ways of imagining programs also emerge:

- Prolog’s first form appears at Marseille in 1972 from work on theorem proving, parsing, and natural-language communication.
- Xerox’s Alto prototype operates in 1973, with Smalltalk-72 running on it shortly afterward.
- The Alto environment joins a bitmap display, pointing-oriented interaction, object-oriented language experiments, and eventually Ethernet-based local networking. citeturn838954search0turn493846search4turn493846search7turn154454search36

The period’s central technological change is therefore not merely the microprocessor:

> **Computing divides into mainframes, minicomputers, embedded controllers, networked workstations, database systems, and—at the very edge of the period—hobbyist microcomputers.**

---

# II. What the established timeline requires

The canonical events of 1970–75 impose several computing requirements. fileciteturn13file0

| Event | Required computing capability |
|---|---|
| German lunar landing, December 1970 | Frozen and validated flight software, mission simulation, digital guidance, tracking, and reliable configuration control |
| American lunar landing, July 1971 | Reusable-spaceplane navigation, orbital rendezvous, tug and lander coordination, and extensive ground simulation |
| 1971 debris impact and 1972 upper-stage breakup | Persistent orbital catalogs, conjunction calculation, fragment-cloud estimation, and international warning formats |
| War of the Chiefs, 1971–75 escalation | MOSAIK continuity, duplicated records, field communications, registry security, and counter-sabotage procedures |
| American party reorganization and 1972 election | Large voter files, polling and precinct models, direct-mail targeting, and auditable paper-based tabulation |
| German missile systems publicly displayed in 1974 | Compact navigation, launch control, target-data handling, and shipboard digital fire control |
| Kuwait War, 1974 | Commonwealth logistics computation, signals correlation, air-defense plotting, naval command systems, and theater-wide inventory control |
| Fully automated American spaceplane, 1974 | Redundant digital flight control, automatic reentry, navigation, landing, and fault handling |
| Geneva orbital convention, 1974 | Cross-bloc object registration, fixed data formats, and computerized national orbital registries |
| Orbitaler Raumhafen, 1975 | Distributed station control, docking traffic, reactor supervision, life support, inventory, communications, and debris avoidance |
| Mittelafrika atrocities become internationally visible, 1975 | Greater tension between computerized administrative records, official euphemism, field reporting, and documentary leakage |

The 1974 Kuwait War is especially important. Britain wins not because it possesses magical battlefield computers, but because it has spent decades building a Commonwealth information, logistics, communications, and staff system. Iraq has respectable German equipment but lacks the institutional competence required to keep that equipment supplied, calibrated, connected, and fed with accurate information. fileciteturn13file1

---

# III. The generational transition

## Britain: Turing becomes the elder statesman

Turing does not retire intellectually. He steps away from daily administrative command around 1972–73.

A suitable arrangement is that he becomes:

- senior scientific adviser to the Commonwealth computing system;
- honorary or executive chairman of a Commonwealth Computing Council;
- an active researcher in machine intelligence, mathematical biology, language semantics, and verification;
- a public scientific figure called upon during major failures or strategic reviews.

He ceases managing ordinary procurement, staff appointments, and machine operations.

The practical leadership passes to people such as:

- Christopher Strachey in language and systems theory;
- Donald Davies in networking;
- Tony Hoare in programming methods and correctness;
- Robin Milner in theorem proving and functional-language implementation;
- younger ICL, Ferranti, Elliott, Canadian, and Australian engineers.

Turing remains the most prestigious name, but younger researchers no longer need his personal permission to define the field.

## America: Church yields implementation to the Lambda generation

Church’s role changes even more sharply because he was always less of a hardware administrator.

By the early 1970s he is:

- the intellectual patriarch;
- a seminar leader and patron;
- the source of the American vocabulary of effective computation;
- the authority cited when arguing that a language’s formal meaning should be distinguished from its machine realization.

The working Lambda establishment is led by younger logicians, compiler engineers, symbolic-computation researchers, and language designers. John McCarthy, Dana Scott, Robert Floyd, Donald Knuth, and younger researchers can all shape parts of that world without making any one of them “the new Church.”

## Germany: Zuse becomes a founder, not an oracle

Zuse remains active, but the myth of a solitary computing prophet should be explicitly resisted.

By 1975:

- Zuse is a prestigious industrial founder and consultant.
- Friedrich Bauer and the compiler school dominate language development.
- Carl Adam Petri and younger systems engineers influence concurrency and network modeling.
- Siemens, Telefunken, Dehomag successors, aerospace laboratories, and industrial-control divisions employ far more programmers than Zuse’s original organization.
- Rechenplan belongs to the German computing profession, not personally to Zuse.

A younger German engineer can publicly disagree with Zuse over machine architecture while still treating him as the field’s founding national figure.

## Japan: teams replace heroes

Japanese computing becomes even less personality-centered.

The first relay and switching theorists receive formal honors, university chairs, and advisory positions. Daily leadership moves to:

- corporate semiconductor divisions;
- factory-automation groups;
- telecommunications laboratories;
- naval electronics bureaus;
- character-encoding committees;
- KEISAN and TEJUN language teams.

The prestige unit is increasingly the **laboratory, corporate house, or interfirm standards group**, not the individual inventor.

## Latin bloc: Tchou, Perotto, Böhm, and Marseille

Mario Tchou remains young enough to exercise real leadership in the 1970s, but he is no longer the sole leader of Latin computing.

The field divides among:

- Tchou and Olivetti’s large systems;
- Pier Giorgio Perotto and the programmable-desktop tradition;
- Corrado Böhm and formal language work;
- Occitan avionics and real-time systems groups;
- Alain Colmerauer, Philippe Roussel, and Marseille’s new logic-programming school.

The Latin bloc therefore experiences a particularly visible transition from industrial patronage to language and software research.

---

# IV. The microprocessor race

## The shared invention that is no longer shared

Historically, the first Intel microprocessor emerged from a Japanese calculator contract. That exact path should not survive.

Instead, America and Japan reach the microprocessor independently and nearly simultaneously.

## United States

An Intel-like firm—quite possibly Intel itself—develops a one-chip processor for a domestic combination of:

- calculator manufacture;
- programmable cash registers;
- computer terminals;
- aerospace instrument control;
- communications equipment.

The working chronology is:

| Year | American development |
|---:|---|
| 1970 | Commercial semiconductor DRAM becomes practical |
| 1971–72 | First four-bit programmable processor |
| 1972 | First commercially available eight-bit processor |
| 1973 | Development boards and cross-assemblers become products |
| 1974 | An 8080-class general eight-bit processor enters broad use |
| 1975 | First hobbyist and small-instrument microcomputer kits |

The precise chip numbers should remain open until the American corporate history is written. Keeping the exact historical `4004` is possible, but the different customer and design brief make it less certain than retaining Intel itself.

America’s critical innovation is not merely the chip. It sells:

- documentation;
- evaluation boards;
- assemblers;
- in-circuit development equipment;
- EPROMs;
- application notes;
- standard buses;
- components to firms that are not themselves computer manufacturers.

This creates an open merchant market.

## Japan

A Busicom-like calculator firm turns to NEC, Fujitsu, Hitachi, Toshiba, or a joint semiconductor laboratory rather than to an American supplier.

Japan’s first microprocessor is optimized for:

- calculators;
- transaction terminals;
- cash registers;
- process controllers;
- telephone systems;
- character-display equipment.

A plausible sequence is only a few months behind America:

| Year | Japanese development |
|---:|---|
| 1971 | Domestic calculator-controller chipset |
| 1972 | Single-chip four-bit processor enters production |
| 1973 | Eight-bit process and terminal processor |
| 1974–75 | Corporate microcontroller families and development systems |

The Japanese accomplishment may be independently conceived early enough that Tokyo disputes American claims to priority. America produces the first broadly purchasable general processor; Japan claims the first processor designed from the beginning as part of a complete industrial-control and character-terminal system.

## Germany

Germany initially distrusts very small four- and eight-bit processors for serious work.

Its engineers prefer:

- twelve-bit instrument words;
- sixteen-bit control arithmetic;
- deterministic timing;
- protected interfaces;
- industrial temperature tolerance;
- robust packaging.

The first German “microprocessor” is therefore likely a **multi-chip microrechenwerk** around 1971–72, followed by a single-chip or compact hybrid sixteen-bit control processor around 1974.

It is used in:

- machine tools;
- power control;
- railway signaling;
- radar;
- telemetry;
- shipboard equipment;
- industrial automation;
- laboratory instruments.

German chips are more expensive than American eight-bit devices but easier to certify inside the Rechenplan–RP-S environment.

## Britain

Britain concentrates on a compact sixteen-bit processor developed through Ferranti, Marconi, Elliott, or an ICL-associated semiconductor partnership.

Its principal customers are:

- naval fire control;
- telecommunications;
- aircraft;
- scientific instruments;
- packet-network nodes;
- industrial controllers.

A prototype appears around 1973–74 and limited production follows by 1975–76.

Britain does not immediately create the American-style market in which thousands of independent hobbyists buy processors. It creates a highly capable **embedded professional processor**.

## Latin bloc

Italy and Occitania jointly support an eight-bit and later sixteen-bit family through:

- SGS or a comparable Italian semiconductor firm;
- Olivetti;
- STET;
- Occitan aerospace electronics;
- Latin military procurement.

The first Latin chip family appears around 1974–75.

Its intended markets are:

- Olivetti desk systems;
- terminals;
- Suez toll equipment;
- naval electronics;
- industrial machinery;
- automotive instrumentation;
- Occitan guided weapons.

It is later and more expensive than American or Japanese products, but it prevents strategic dependence.

## Microprocessor balance in 1975

| Bloc | Characteristic strength |
|---|---|
| America | Merchant chips, documentation, development boards, hobbyist access |
| Japan | High-volume calculators, terminals, industrial controllers |
| Germany | Rugged sixteen-bit control systems and deterministic software |
| Britain | Military, telecommunications, and scientific embedded systems |
| Latin bloc | Integrated desk machines and avionics |

America and Japan lead MOS production volume. Germany and Britain lead several high-reliability niches. The Latin bloc remains viable through carefully chosen markets.

---

# V. Germany  
## The distributed station and the computerized empire

## 1. ERO 72

The German compatibility system receives a major revision around 1971–72.

**ERO 72** does not replace ERO 63. It defines additional requirements for:

- semiconductor memory;
- microprocessors and embedded controllers;
- disk file systems;
- network message formats;
- protected multiprocessing;
- distributed control;
- machine-readable hardware descriptions;
- remote diagnostics.

Germany retains its preference for forty-eight-bit scientific machines, twenty-four-bit subwords, and twelve-bit extended characters in major systems.

Its microcontrollers generally use twelve- or sixteen-bit words rather than adopting the American eight-bit byte internally.

That creates a growing distinction:

- German mainframes and industrial systems remain internally distinctive.
- International telecommunications increasingly use eight-bit interchange units.
- German equipment therefore depends upon gateway processors and character conversion.

This is an inconvenience but also an economic barrier protecting the domestic system.

## 2. Rechenplan 72

Rechenplan 72 consolidates the language rather than splitting it.

Its common core adds:

- explicit modules;
- exported and private declarations;
- variant records;
- controlled references;
- parameterized library procedures;
- separate compilation;
- source and object version identifiers;
- message and channel definitions;
- standardized device descriptions;
- more precise exception handling.

The three profiles remain intact:

| Profile | 1970s emphasis |
|---|---|
| RP-W | Numerical science, aerospace, modeling, simulation |
| RP-V | Administration, records, ledgers, queries, reports |
| RP-S | Embedded and real-time control |

### The Simula influence

Simula’s class and process ideas enter Germany through Norway, but they are absorbed into the `MODELLWESEN` libraries rather than becoming a separate dominant language.

RP-W programmers can define:

- a class of launch vehicles;
- a class of tracking stations;
- individual spacecraft with local state;
- interacting processes representing crew, ground stations, weather, and failures.

Ordinary German programs remain procedure- and record-oriented.

## 3. Relational ideas without abandoning RP-V

Codd’s relational model attracts German mathematicians, but the administration is reluctant to rebuild huge hierarchical registries around an American theory.

The German response is an RP-V query sublanguage provisionally called:

> **AUSWAHLPLAN** — selection plan

It allows an authorized user to request something like:

- all registered workers of a particular qualification;
- all shipments assigned to a corridor during a period;
- all districts whose reported payroll and labor totals disagree;
- all components linked to a particular program revision.

The user describes fields and conditions rather than physical tape paths.

Internally, however, many systems remain indexed, hierarchical, or network-structured. Germany adopts relational **query ideas** before it adopts genuinely relational storage.

## 4. Planwerk 72

Planwerk evolves into a distributed operating environment.

Its standard services include:

- multiprogramming;
- disk volumes;
- protected user classes;
- remote terminals;
- network message queues;
- checkpoint and restart;
- automatic replication of selected files;
- software configuration control;
- access logging;
- device and processor health monitoring.

German institutions remain suspicious of unrestricted interactive use. A terminal user normally has:

- an authenticated identity;
- an institutional role;
- a defined project;
- an allowed data class;
- a recorded session.

Universities receive more freedom than military or administrative centers.

## 5. Orbitaler Raumhafen

The 1975 station cannot depend on one central computer. A single processor failure cannot disable docking, power, life support, and traffic management simultaneously.

The station therefore has a **distributed hierarchy**.

### Module computers

Every major module has local controllers for:

- pressure;
- oxygen and carbon dioxide;
- temperature;
- water;
- pumps and valves;
- electrical loads;
- fire detection;
- local instrumentation.

These controllers can maintain a safe state even when disconnected from the rest of the station.

### Station supervisory computers

Several redundant central machines coordinate:

- docking schedules;
- attitude and orbit maintenance;
- power distribution;
- reactor load;
- communications;
- crew scheduling;
- inventory;
- workshop jobs;
- visiting vehicles;
- debris warnings.

### Ground centers

The ground retains responsibility for:

- long-term orbit prediction;
- mission planning;
- software updates;
- complicated failure analysis;
- traffic coordination beyond the station’s immediate vicinity.

### Safety doctrine

Critical commands require combinations of:

- computer agreement;
- independent sensor agreement;
- crew authorization;
- ground confirmation for nonurgent actions.

The station is highly computerized without being autonomous in the later sense.

Its distributed design becomes one of Germany’s most influential engineering exports.

## 6. Debris tracking

The 1971 impact and 1972 breakup force Germany to move from occasional orbit calculation to a permanent **Raumobjektkartei**, or orbital-object catalog.

It records:

- launch identity;
- estimated mass and area;
- orbit;
- maneuver capability;
- predicted decay;
- fragmentation history;
- conjunction risk;
- national responsibility.

Calculations remain imperfect. Small fragments cannot all be tracked, and uncertainty grows rapidly after a breakup.

Nevertheless, by 1974 Germany can issue computerized warnings to the Raumhafen and foreign governments.

The Geneva convention therefore depends upon computing even though it is legally a diplomatic agreement.

## 7. Missile submarines and the 1974 cruiser

German vertical-launch submarine systems require:

- inertial navigation;
- periodic celestial or radio correction;
- stored target packages;
- missile alignment;
- safe launch sequencing;
- water and pressure compensation;
- fire-control validation;
- encrypted mission updates.

The submarine does not freely select political targets. Target packages are prepared ashore and loaded under strict control.

The 1974 public missile cruiser demonstrates the same broad technologies:

- digital fire-control networks;
- vertical-cell status monitoring;
- radar-track correlation;
- computerized engagement scheduling;
- missile and sensor data buses.

The cruiser is visible proof of a computing architecture that has existed more secretly underwater.

## 8. MOSAIK and the War of the Chiefs

MOSAIK becomes more decentralized under wartime pressure.

By 1972–74, Germany maintains:

- replicated household and labor indexes;
- duplicate payroll records;
- district production histories;
- offline archival tapes;
- emergency paper extracts;
- mobile audit and data-reconstruction teams.

Resistance targets the system through:

- false registrations;
- deliberate duplicate identities;
- burned card stores;
- stolen tapes;
- severed lines;
- bribed clerks;
- contradictory production and payroll reports;
- attacks on machine centers.

Germany responds by cross-checking:

- railway movements;
- payroll;
- ration issues;
- clinic records;
- production;
- household registration.

This can expose inconsistency. It cannot reliably distinguish rebellion, corruption, clerical error, famine, flight, or local manipulation.

Computing therefore strengthens German coercive capacity while also creating a dependence upon information that local communities can poison.

## 9. German generational culture

By 1975 the typical senior German computing figure is no longer a wartime relay engineer. He is a systems engineer who began his career during the 1950s.

This younger establishment is confident that:

- every imperial process can be represented;
- every failure can be classified;
- every administrative contradiction can be reconciled;
- every machine can be certified;
- every social system can be made more orderly through better records.

Its arrogance is different from that of the SS or Party. It is the arrogance of technical formalism.

Germany’s younger computer establishment is often privately contemptuous of older political officials who demand impossible results while refusing to define their requirements precisely.

## German position in 1975

Germany leads in:

- certified real-time systems;
- distributed station control;
- aerospace configuration management;
- industrial embedded computing;
- administrative integration;
- formal process modeling.

It remains weaker in:

- unrestricted interactive computing;
- cheap microprocessor distribution;
- independent software companies;
- open local networking;
- experimental personal workstations.

---

# VI. Britain and the Commonwealth  
## ML, packet services, and the Kuwait test

## 1. Turing’s handoff

Turing’s transition is publicly framed as a success, not retirement after decline.

He argues that the point of founding a discipline is to make oneself unnecessary to its daily administration.

By 1973–74, younger researchers lead:

- language implementation;
- packet networking;
- operating-system design;
- theorem proving;
- formal verification;
- commercial systems analysis.

Turing continues publishing and advising but appears less frequently in procurement disputes and management meetings.

This gives Britain an unusually healthy succession compared with its political institutions.

## 2. The ICL family

Britain introduces a new ICL family around 1973–74, comparable in broad role to the historical 2900 generation.

The Commonwealth-backed design emphasizes:

- thirty-two-bit processing;
- eight-bit characters;
- virtual memory;
- descriptors and protection;
- multiple operating environments;
- compatibility through emulation and compilers;
- remote terminals;
- network interfaces.

Britain cannot afford to discard all older software. New machines therefore support:

- emulation of earlier ICL systems;
- source recompilation;
- common library interfaces;
- tape and file conversion;
- virtual machines for distinct workloads.

The British answer to incompatibility is increasingly **software-defined compatibility**.

## 3. Commonwealth packet service

The experimental NPL network expands into a limited **Commonwealth Packet Service**.

By 1975 it connects selected nodes in:

- Britain;
- Canada;
- Australia;
- South Africa;
- New Zealand;
- Ceylon;
- major naval and aerospace establishments.

This is not a public network.

Long-distance service is expensive and sometimes store-and-forward rather than continuously interactive. It supports:

- messages;
- remote job submission;
- software-library requests;
- weather and tracking data;
- naval and aerospace coordination;
- technical document exchange;
- emergency government communications.

Domestic British research networks offer much more interactive access than transoceanic links.

## 4. BCPL and systems programming

BCPL becomes the Commonwealth’s portable systems language.

It is used for:

- operating-system components;
- network software;
- compilers;
- text processing;
- utilities;
- minicomputers;
- experimental workstations.

Britain now has a strong culture of writing software that can be recompiled on several machines, even when those machines are architecturally unrelated.

## 5. ML

I would preserve an early **ML**, or Meta Language, around 1973–74.

It grows from British theorem-proving and applicative-language research rather than appearing in isolation.

ML’s early features include:

- functions as values;
- lexical scoping;
- recursive definitions;
- symbolic data;
- interactive execution;
- automatic inference of many local types;
- explicit declarations where interfaces cross module boundaries;
- pattern-like decomposition of lists and logical expressions.

It is initially a metalanguage for instructing and extending a theorem prover.

Its significance is that programmers discover the language is useful outside the theorem prover.

British ML and American Lambda become friendly rivals:

| British ML | American Lambda |
|---|---|
| Interactive theorem-proving origin | Compiler and formal-language origin |
| Stronger automatic type inference | More explicit public type declarations |
| Academic and Commonwealth research culture | Better-funded cross-platform production compilers |
| Concise exploratory programming | Larger symbolic and industrial libraries |

Turing supports ML but does not design it personally.

## 6. Pascal and education

Pascal becomes widely used in British technical colleges and schools because it teaches:

- structured control;
- explicit types;
- records;
- procedures;
- disciplined data organization.

It does not displace Autocode immediately in established scientific centers or BCPL in systems work.

Britain’s educational environment by 1975 therefore contains:

- Conversational Autocode for beginners;
- Pascal for disciplined instruction;
- BCPL for systems work;
- ML for advanced language and theorem research;
- CLEO and COBOL for administration.

## 7. Databases

Britain adopts relational theory cautiously.

LEO and ICL customers have enormous investments in existing record systems. The Commonwealth therefore experiments with a **Relational Inquiry Service** layered over older files.

An official can issue a declarative request, but the system may translate it into searches over:

- indexed sequential files;
- hierarchical records;
- tape archives;
- network databases.

Britain becomes good at **federated query** because its Commonwealth systems are heterogeneous by necessity.

## 8. Kuwait War computing

Operation Covenant is Britain’s first major demonstration of the mature Commonwealth computing system.

### Strategic logistics

Computers coordinate:

- sealift;
- tanker schedules;
- aircraft movements;
- ammunition;
- spare parts;
- hospital capacity;
- port unloading;
- fuel stocks;
- repair priorities;
- unit reinforcement;
- weather and route planning.

The output is not a perfect live dashboard. Staff officers receive:

- printed summaries;
- teleprinter updates;
- punched or magnetic media;
- revised movement tables;
- exception reports.

### Naval command

Royal Navy task groups use computerized systems for:

- radar and sonar track management;
- air-defense assignment;
- electronic warfare;
- submarine-contact correlation;
- helicopter allocation;
- convoy routing.

### Air operations

British and Commonwealth air forces use computers for:

- sortie scheduling;
- target planning;
- radar coverage;
- air-defense corridors;
- electronic countermeasures;
- fuel and weapons allocation.

### Intelligence

Reports from:

- Iran;
- Saudi Arabia;
- Jordan;
- aerial reconnaissance;
- signals interception;
- patrol aircraft;
- local Kuwaiti sources

are collated through Commonwealth intelligence centers.

The machine does not decide what Iraq intends. It allows analysts to compare reports more quickly and identify contradictions.

### Why Iraq fails

Iraq possesses:

- German export computers;
- radar;
- fire-control equipment;
- modern communications;
- computerized supply offices.

Its weaknesses are institutional:

- rival ministries keep separate files;
- unit strengths are exaggerated;
- maintenance records are false;
- parts inventories are incomplete;
- trained operators are politically suspect or poorly distributed;
- German manuals are badly translated;
- commanders bypass systems when results are inconvenient;
- data reaches Baghdad after it has become obsolete.

The Kuwait War becomes the canonical lesson that **computerization cannot repair a state that punishes truthful reporting**.

## 9. The Commonwealth after Kuwait

The postwar review produces:

- common operational-data formats;
- improved logistics databases;
- standardized equipment and part identifiers;
- stronger theater packet links;
- better reserve-shipping records;
- increased investment in portable terminals and tactical minicomputers.

Britain’s victory reinforces its belief that computing is principally an instrument of **coordination among institutions**.

## Britain in 1975

Britain leads in:

- packet-switched services;
- functional-language research;
- theorem proving;
- virtual and emulated computing environments;
- heterogeneous-system integration;
- expeditionary information coordination.

It remains constrained by:

- capital;
- old machines;
- public procurement cycles;
- too many language communities;
- limited semiconductor volume.

---

# VII. United States  
## C, Lambda, the Alto, and the threshold of personal computing

## 1. The American generational center

By 1975, America’s founders are no longer the field’s practical center.

Church is the patriarch. The active establishment contains:

- systems programmers;
- semiconductor entrepreneurs;
- database researchers;
- AI laboratories;
- computer-graphics researchers;
- network engineers;
- aerospace-software organizations;
- minicomputer firms.

The younger American computing culture is unusually confident because it has grown alongside:

- the Rocket Awakening;
- Kennedy’s lunar mission;
- the 1968 constitutional crisis;
- the German lunar victory;
- the successful 1971 American response;
- continuous military and commercial demand.

Its members believe computers should belong directly to programmers, scientists, designers, students, and eventually ordinary citizens—not only to central institutions.

## 2. UNIX and C

UNIX becomes the American system for people who find large corporate operating systems oppressive.

Its appeal is cultural as much as technical:

- small tools;
- interactive terminals;
- simple text files;
- hierarchical directories;
- processes;
- pipes and filters;
- a system largely written in a portable language.

C becomes the language of:

- operating systems;
- compilers;
- utilities;
- minicomputers;
- network software;
- laboratory equipment;
- later microprocessors.

It does not replace FORTRAN, COBOL, JOVIAL, or Lambda.

America develops a highly consequential language division:

| Language | Governing conception |
|---|---|
| FORTRAN | Numerical calculation |
| COBOL | Institutional records |
| JOVIAL | Large real-time military systems |
| C | Portable control of the machine |
| Lambda | Functions and formal computation |
| LISP | Symbolic exploration |
| Smalltalk | Objects and interactive environments |
| SEQUEL | Declarative access to data |

No American central body attempts to unify them.

## 3. Lambda 72

Lambda 68 develops into **Lambda 72**, the first version with a stable compiler and recognizable community.

### Language core

Lambda 72 supports:

- first-class functions;
- lexical closures;
- recursion;
- immutable local bindings;
- lists and trees;
- tuples and records;
- tagged variants;
- higher-order library functions;
- separate function libraries;
- explicit types on public functions;
- inference of many local expression types;
- interactive and compiled execution.

It is normally strict, or call-by-value.

Delayed evaluation exists through explicit library constructs rather than universal laziness.

### Effects and storage

Lambda preserves a functional core but permits controlled effects through typed interfaces for:

- arrays;
- files;
- terminals;
- random access;
- devices;
- mutable cells.

The language’s designers do not yet have the later mathematical vocabulary for monadic effect systems. They speak instead of:

- pure expressions;
- store-bearing procedures;
- external actions;
- controlled state.

### Type inference

The American compiler can infer many local types from function application and literal use.

Public library boundaries still require declared types.

This gives the language much of the convenience later associated with inferred functional languages without moving implausibly far ahead.

### Applications

Lambda 72 is used in:

- compiler construction;
- symbolic algebra;
- theorem proving;
- language processing;
- mission-rule analysis;
- coordinate and trajectory transformations;
- program-verification research;
- artificial intelligence;
- university teaching.

It is not primary onboard flight software.

Aerospace organizations may use Lambda to:

- generate tables;
- specify algorithms;
- compare independent implementations;
- test state-transition logic.

The flight program remains C, JOVIAL, assembly, or a specialized aerospace language.

## 4. Lambda 74 and the Church school

**Lambda 74** adds:

- a module system;
- stronger tagged data;
- pattern-based decomposition;
- improved cross-platform compilers;
- links to C;
- interactive debugging;
- a standard symbolic mathematics library.

Church contributes conceptual criticism and public legitimacy but not ordinary implementation.

A younger team writes the compiler.

American academics increasingly use the phrase **functional programming** by the mid-1970s. “Churchian programming” remains a colloquial label, sometimes admiring and sometimes mocking.

## 5. The Lambda–ML rivalry

The rivalry is constructive.

American Lambda programmers criticize ML for allowing too much type inference to remain hidden from the reader.

British ML programmers criticize Lambda for requiring verbose declarations and treating its production compiler as more important than linguistic elegance.

Both agree that LISP is too permissive.

The functional-language community is still small, but it now has:

- conferences;
- compiler exchanges;
- formal semantics;
- standard libraries;
- graduate courses;
- real applications.

## 6. Relational databases and SEQUEL

Codd’s work attracts a specialized IBM research program.

By 1974–75, America has:

- relational algebra prototypes;
- experimental query optimizers;
- SEQUEL;
- early System R-style implementation work;
- debates over normalization;
- efforts to separate logical records from disk paths.

Commercial customers remain skeptical.

Existing systems are:

- faster for known workloads;
- already installed;
- understood by programmers;
- connected to mature applications.

Relational computing in 1975 is an important research program, not yet the normal business database.

Church’s prominence helps relational theory receive attention because American computer science is unusually receptive to the idea that logical description should be separated from mechanical execution.

## 7. The Alto and Smalltalk

Xerox establishes an Alto-like research workstation in 1973.

It is not sold as a home computer.

It combines:

- a personal processor;
- bitmap display;
- keyboard;
- pointing device;
- local storage;
- graphical editing;
- local networking;
- Smalltalk and other interactive software.

Smalltalk-72 is exploratory and unlike its later mature form. It nevertheless establishes several revolutionary expectations:

- the screen is a workspace rather than a printed-terminal substitute;
- programs can be manipulated interactively;
- objects can contain both data and behavior;
- the machine can support children and nonprofessional programmers;
- graphics are part of ordinary computation.

Alan Kay and other pre-divergence-born figures remain plausible participants. They are not the later mass-market entrepreneurs; they are the research generation that gives the next generation its concepts.

## 8. Ethernet and the local network

America has already connected distant research computers through packet networking. Ethernet solves a different problem:

> How can dozens of machines, printers, file services, and terminals inside one institution communicate without a dedicated line for every pair?

The first Alto network links:

- workstations;
- file servers;
- printers;
- gateways;
- experimental mail.

Britain leads in economical long-distance packet service. America now leads in the local networked workstation environment.

## 9. Printing and office systems

The combination of:

- bitmap displays;
- laser printing;
- networked workstations;
- electronic text;
- graphical page composition

creates the first recognizable electronic office laboratory.

It remains far too expensive for ordinary businesses.

Its importance is conceptual. American researchers can now imagine:

- electronic documents;
- network mail;
- on-screen editing;
- graphical diagrams;
- shared files;
- high-quality computer-generated printing.

These become commercial only later.

## 10. Microcomputer kits

An **Altair-class hobbyist machine** appears at the edge of the period, around 1975.

I would avoid fixing its final brand or founder yet.

It likely consists of:

- an eight-bit processor;
- front-panel switches and lights;
- a few hundred or few thousand bytes of memory;
- an expansion bus;
- paper-tape or terminal interfaces;
- no standard display;
- no polished operating system.

Its purchasers are:

- radio amateurs;
- electronics engineers;
- university students;
- instrumentation specialists;
- school clubs;
- aerospace workers.

It is not yet a household computer.

The key psychological change is that an individual can purchase the CPU, memory, and chassis without representing a university, bank, or government.

## 11. Why the later entrepreneurs should be fictional

People born in the mid-1950s have grown up in a radically different America:

- no American WWII victory generation;
- a Philippine War;
- a German satellite;
- a Kennedy space mission;
- a three-party constitutional crisis;
- Rockwell’s National Renewal movement;
- Churchian functional programming;
- packet networks;
- a reusable spaceplane culture.

The eventual founders of America’s mass home-computer companies should therefore be original people.

They may resemble familiar archetypes:

- the hardware perfectionist;
- the software monopolist;
- the charismatic consumer visionary;
- the hobby-club engineer;
- the school-computing evangelist.

They should not simply be historical personalities with different company logos.

## 12. Automated orbital flight

The 1974 automated spaceplane mission requires several advances beyond the 1969 Pathfinder:

- redundant digital flight computers;
- automatic navigation updates;
- autonomous attitude control;
- automated deorbit;
- automatic reentry guidance;
- runway alignment;
- flare and touchdown control;
- fault detection;
- ground override.

The vehicle is supervised from the ground but does not require continuous manual commands.

This is one of the decisive foundations for:

- routine cargo missions;
- automated satellite retrieval;
- later military spaceplanes;
- civilian digital flight control;
- confidence in uncrewed reusable vehicles.

## 13. Political computing

American parties increasingly use computers for:

- voter files;
- precinct analysis;
- mailing lists;
- donation records;
- polling;
- media-market planning;
- membership management.

National Renewal is particularly strong at maintaining disciplined membership and local-organization records.

The 1975 assassination response still depends principally upon:

- radio;
- television;
- telephone;
- party officials;
- law enforcement;
- Buchanan’s public authority.

Computers help the party identify organizations, distribute instructions, and track reports. They do not mechanically prevent violence.

## America in 1975

America leads in:

- semiconductor memory;
- merchant microprocessors;
- minicomputers;
- portable systems programming;
- relational database research;
- interactive workstations;
- local networking;
- graphical computing;
- the first hobby microcomputers.

It remains less coherent than Germany and less disciplined in cross-institutional coordination than Britain.

---

# VIII. Japan  
## The microprocessor enters the factory and the Japanese page becomes electronic

## 1. Corporate generational transition

By 1975, the generation that built Japanese relay computers occupies senior advisory positions.

The operational leadership belongs to engineers who began their careers with:

- transistor machines;
- parametron systems;
- KEISAN;
- TEJUN;
- semiconductor manufacturing;
- automated factories;
- character terminals.

These people do not regard computing as an imported mathematical specialty. It is a normal branch of industrial administration.

## 2. Japanese microprocessors

Japan’s processor families are not marketed primarily to hobbyists.

They are sold inside:

- calculators;
- sewing and textile machinery;
- machine tools;
- telephone exchanges;
- cash registers;
- shipping terminals;
- industrial instruments;
- automobiles;
- radar and communications equipment.

Corporate development packages exist, but firms normally expect customers to purchase:

- processor;
- memory;
- peripheral controllers;
- software tools;
- engineering service;
- integration support

as one complete system.

Japan consequently produces a greater volume of microprocessor-controlled **products** than of bare processors sold to independent programmers.

## 3. KEISAN 72

`ケイサン七二`, displayed as `計算七二`, becomes the standard scientific and technical language.

It adds:

- modules;
- separate compilation;
- tagged record forms;
- improved matrix and statistical libraries;
- plotting;
- instrument control;
- standardized compiler diagnostics;
- cross-compilation for small processors;
- mixed vertical and horizontal page regions.

Large scientific programs remain vertical by default.

A programmer can open a horizontal window for:

- matrices;
- graphs;
- Latin formulas;
- imported American data;
- Filipino text.

The overall source page still advances from upper right toward the left.

## 4. TEJUN 73

`テジュン七三`, displayed as `手順七三`, becomes the dominant corporate systems language.

It gains:

- nested process descriptions;
- persistent transactions;
- event priorities;
- device families;
- message acknowledgments;
- safe rollback;
- audit records;
- maintenance states;
- operator and supervisor roles;
- distributed procedure calls among corporate nodes.

TEJUN distinguishes among:

- an automatic action;
- an action requiring a local operator;
- an action requiring a supervisor;
- an action requiring a remote corporate or government authorization.

That makes organizational hierarchy part of the source language.

## 5. Embedded TEJUN

Small processors cannot support the complete language.

Japan defines a restricted embedded profile, usually understood as **small TEJUN** rather than a separate language.

It permits:

- fixed memory;
- bounded queues;
- timers;
- simple state transitions;
- device input and output;
- error states;
- no dynamic allocation;
- no recursion.

It is used in:

- factory cells;
- cranes;
- shipboard equipment;
- power systems;
- vehicle instrumentation;
- telephone switching.

## 6. Electronic vertical text

The microprocessor and semiconductor memory transform Japanese text handling.

Earlier terminals required expensive central character generators. By 1973–75, a terminal can contain:

- local font ROM;
- katakana and numeral glyphs;
- common kanji keyword forms;
- vertical-layout control;
- horizontal compatibility mode;
- limited page buffering.

The native terminal now handles:

- cursor movement downward;
- movement to the next column on the left;
- automatic rotation or alternate form of punctuation;
- vertical line and block markers;
- tokenized keyword display.

This makes the Japanese source environment practical outside elite central installations.

## 7. Early word-processing systems

Programming-terminal technology spills into office work.

The first experimental Japanese word-processing systems use:

- katakana entry;
- dictionary-based conversion;
- fixed kanji vocabularies;
- vertical page composition;
- bitmap or stored glyphs;
- high-quality printers.

They are expensive and aimed at:

- ministries;
- newspapers;
- trading houses;
- technical publishers;
- legal and shipping offices.

Programming, not ordinary publishing, is one of the principal technologies that makes them possible.

## 8. The imperial character standard

The Co-Prosperity Sphere character registry receives a major revision around 1972–73.

It standardizes:

- registry numbers;
- preferred glyphs;
- vertical forms;
- horizontal forms;
- sorting order;
- compatibility characters;
- vendor extension ranges;
- Japanese–Chinese distinctions;
- Latin and Filipino diacritics;
- Hangul;
- Southeast Asian scripts.

Japan does not produce a perfectly unified encoding. It creates a stable **identity registry** with several allowed transmission forms.

That is enough to let a Filipino name, Japanese shipping code, Thai port, Chinese company, and Korean employee record be exchanged without being redefined at every corporate boundary.

## 9. Factory networks

Japanese factories begin connecting controllers through deterministic local communication systems.

They do not copy Ethernet immediately.

The preferred designs use:

- master-controlled loops;
- scheduled polling;
- token passing;
- fixed device addresses;
- bounded response times;
- redundant industrial cabling.

These systems are less open than Ethernet but easier to certify for a production line.

A Japanese industrial engineer considers it more important that every controller respond within a known period than that arbitrary new computers can join the network easily.

## 10. Imperial transaction grid

The large transaction network expands through:

- Singapore;
- Manila;
- Seoul;
- Mukden;
- Taipei;
- major Japanese ports;
- oil and shipping centers;
- selected associated-state capitals.

It handles:

- bank settlement;
- shipping space;
- customs;
- warehouse allocation;
- fuel;
- production orders;
- maintenance;
- insurance;
- currency clearing.

This network remains corporately segmented. Mitsubishi, Mitsui, state economic boards, banks, and military organizations operate overlapping networks connected through regulated gateways.

## 11. The Philippines

Filipino programmers become disproportionately important in the early 1970s.

They specialize in:

- Japanese–Latin data conversion;
- shipping;
- banking;
- airline systems;
- English-language documents;
- American legacy records;
- software for associated states.

A Filipino programmer might write:

- control words vertically in Japanese;
- identifiers in Latin script;
- comments in Filipino or English;
- financial output in Latin numerals for foreign customers;
- internal numeric data in Japanese digits.

Older Japanese programmers sometimes regard this as inelegant. Younger imperial systems programmers treat mixed-script source as normal.

## 12. Preparation for Japanese spaceflight

Japan does not yet attempt an independent crewed orbital mission.

Its computing investment supports:

- launch guidance;
- telemetry;
- optical tracking;
- automated probes;
- remote manipulators;
- distributed robotic systems;
- compact life-support controllers;
- equatorial-site planning.

The later Japanese space doctrine—robots prepare the road before humans arrive—begins as a computing and control doctrine in this period.

## Japan in 1975

Japan leads in:

- high-volume embedded control;
- factory networks;
- multilingual character identity;
- vertical electronic text;
- corporate transaction systems;
- compact automated products.

It remains behind America in open microprocessor markets and behind Britain in academic packet networking.

# IX. The Latin bloc  
## Prolog, Olivetti desktops, and the Marseille school

## 1. Prolog is an Occitan achievement

This is one of the clearest and most useful consequences of the alternate French settlement.

Historically, the first Prolog work emerged from Marseille in 1972. In this setting, Marseille belongs to Occitania. The language therefore becomes the Latin bloc’s most important original contribution to programming-language theory during the early 1970s. citeturn838954search0turn838954search3

The name still works:

> **PROLOG — programmation en logique**

It is French-language rather than specifically Parisian and fits the Marseille research environment naturally.

## 2. Prolog’s founding conception

Prolog does not tell the machine every step to execute.

The programmer states:

- facts;
- relationships;
- rules;
- a goal to be satisfied.

The system searches for a solution.

This gives the Latin bloc a programming conception distinct from all four rivals:

| Bloc | Characteristic programming question |
|---|---|
| Germany | What formally certified plan should be executed? |
| Britain | What language and service best express the computation? |
| America | What general tool or platform lets the user build the application? |
| Japan | What procedure and state transition governs the process? |
| Latin bloc | What relationships and rules make the requested conclusion true? |

## 3. Early applications

Occitan Prolog is initially used for:

- French and Occitan language analysis;
- machine translation;
- legal and administrative rules;
- symbolic mathematics;
- theorem proving;
- military planning experiments;
- maintenance diagnosis;
- interrogation of technical knowledge bases.

It is not used for:

- numerical flight control;
- payroll;
- ordinary transaction processing;
- mainframe operating systems.

## 4. Latin political interest

The language attracts unusual institutional interest because the Latin bloc governs across:

- Italian;
- French;
- Occitan;
- Spanish;
- Portuguese;
- Arabic;
- Greek;
- African languages;
- Catholic canon-law and civil-law systems.

Government and Church institutions imagine applications in:

- multilingual legal retrieval;
- treaty interpretation;
- customs classifications;
- doctrinal and canonical reference;
- logistics rules;
- diplomatic translation.

Most of these early expectations outrun the available computing power and linguistic theory.

Even so, Prolog becomes a respected strategic research field.

## 5. Prolog and Britain

British researchers at Edinburgh and elsewhere cooperate with Marseille on theorem proving and logic programming.

This does not make Prolog British.

The relationship is analogous to British use of an Occitan aircraft design: important collaboration without transfer of national origin.

Britain contributes:

- theorem-proving theory;
- compiler techniques;
- planning systems;
- implementation experience.

Occitania retains cultural ownership of the language.

## 6. Olivetti systems

Olivetti’s mainframe line continues under Mario Tchou’s leadership.

The firm avoids the historical decline of its electronics division and develops:

- commercial mainframes;
- midrange office computers;
- remote terminals;
- magnetic-disk systems;
- bank and shipping applications;
- programmable desk machines.

Olivetti increasingly sells **complete applications**, not only hardware.

A bank purchases:

- computers;
- terminals;
- software;
- forms;
- training;
- maintenance;
- workflow analysis.

## 7. Programma successors

The Programma 101 lineage develops toward a true professional desktop system.

By 1973–75, an advanced successor can possess:

- semiconductor memory;
- removable magnetic media;
- a small alphanumeric display;
- built-in printer;
- microprocessor or compact controller;
- scientific and business modules;
- connection to a larger Olivetti system.

It remains too expensive for ordinary households.

Its users include:

- architects;
- accountants;
- engineers;
- surveyors;
- laboratories;
- artillery staffs;
- small factories;
- schools.

Italy leads in the idea that a professional should have a programmable machine **on the desk**.

America leads in the idea that the desk machine should be a general interactive computer.

## 8. Pascal and Latin education

Pascal becomes the principal teaching language of the Latin technical system.

It is attractive because it is:

- neutral Swiss rather than German, American, or British;
- small;
- structured;
- explicit;
- easy to teach;
- suitable for compiling on Italian, Occitan, Spanish, and Portuguese machines.

ALGOL-Latin remains important in advanced scientific work. Pascal dominates introductory courses.

## 9. LIA and commercial systems

The Italian administrative language develops into **LIA 73**.

It adds:

- online transactions;
- indexed disk records;
- screen forms;
- report generators;
- restart;
- audit trails;
- currency conversion;
- Latin Scudo settlement;
- Suez and shipping packages.

It remains more compact and less English-like than COBOL.

## 10. Occitan embedded computing

Occitan aerospace and naval engineers develop increasingly compact computers for:

- Mirage-type aircraft;
- missiles;
- radar;
- submarine fire control;
- artillery;
- electronic warfare;
- guidance;
- telemetry.

Their preferred languages remain:

- ALGOL-derived engineering languages;
- compact real-time languages;
- assembly;
- specialized Prolog experiments for planning and diagnosis.

Prolog does not control the aircraft. It may help diagnose why a system failed or generate a maintenance sequence.

## 11. Latin microprocessors

The first Latin microprocessor family is designed jointly enough to support:

- Olivetti office systems;
- Italian telecommunications;
- Occitan avionics;
- Spanish industrial machines;
- Portuguese shipping equipment.

Italy supplies volume and packaging. Occitania supplies compact control architecture. Spain increasingly supplies peripherals and board assembly.

## 12. Latin network

The Latin Scientific and Technical Network expands into a limited intergovernmental system.

Nodes include:

- Rome;
- Ivrea;
- Milan;
- Pisa;
- Toulouse;
- Marseille;
- Madrid or Barcelona;
- Lisbon;
- Suez;
- San Marco tracking facilities.

It carries:

- satellite data;
- naval standards;
- scientific programs;
- customs information;
- banking settlements;
- software-library requests.

It is less open than America’s research network and less centralized than Japan’s corporate grid.

## 13. Orbital diplomacy

The Latin bloc’s computing contribution to the 1974 Geneva agreement includes:

- common orbital reporting formats;
- object identity numbers;
- launch notifications;
- national registry interfaces;
- distress-frequency documentation;
- data exchange among incompatible computers.

The convention does not create a common world network. It establishes the first legally meaningful international obligation to maintain and exchange computerized orbital records.

## Latin position in 1975

The Latin bloc leads in:

- logic programming;
- programmable professional desktops;
- human-facing office systems;
- legal and multilingual applications;
- compact avionics integration.

It remains behind in:

- processor volume;
- supercomputing;
- operating-system scale;
- mass networking;
- hobbyist access.

---

# X. Databases across the five blocs

By 1975 every bloc understands that stored information must be separated, at least partly, from one physical program.

They respond differently.

| Bloc | Emerging data model |
|---|---|
| Germany | Typed administrative records plus declarative RP-V selection queries |
| Britain | Federated inquiry across heterogeneous Commonwealth files |
| America | Relational theory and SEQUEL prototypes |
| Japan | Transactional process records organized around corporate responsibility |
| Latin bloc | Commercial indexed files plus Prolog knowledge bases |

## Germany

The record exists inside a legal and administrative type system. The critical concern is provenance and authority.

## Britain

The same logical question may have to cross five incompatible systems. Translation and reconciliation matter more than purity.

## America

The user should ask for the relationship desired, and the system should choose the physical path.

## Japan

The record belongs to a procedure, responsible office, and confirmed transaction state.

## Latin bloc

Some information is represented as ordinary records; more experimental knowledge is represented as facts and rules.

These differences will later shape databases, search engines, expert systems, and networks.

---

# XI. Software economics in 1975

## Germany

Software is treated as:

- an engineering deliverable;
- a certified component;
- a controlled library;
- part of a machine or state system.

Independent software companies exist but remain small.

## Britain

Software is treated as:

- a service;
- a library;
- a portable technical asset;
- a Commonwealth resource;
- an exportable systems skill.

Consulting, systems analysis, and compiler work are strong.

## America

Software is beginning to become a product independent of hardware.

Markets emerge for:

- compilers;
- database systems;
- terminal software;
- minicomputer operating systems;
- microprocessor development tools;
- specialized business applications.

## Japan

Software belongs principally to:

- the corporate system;
- the equipment supplier;
- the production process;
- the client relationship.

Third-party software remains weak.

## Latin bloc

Software is bundled with:

- office systems;
- state projects;
- avionics;
- banking;
- consulting;
- programmable machines.

Prolog begins producing a separate academic and specialist software culture.

---

# XII. What a young programmer sees in 1975

## Germany

A young programmer expects:

- formal training;
- Rechenplan;
- certification;
- employment in a major firm or state institution;
- a clear hierarchy;
- important work in aerospace, automation, railways, or administration.

He rarely expects to found a tiny software firm in a garage.

## Britain

A young programmer expects:

- terminals;
- shared machines;
- several languages;
- university or public-industry employment;
- networks;
- international Commonwealth collaboration;
- argument over semantics and methods.

## America

A young programmer may encounter:

- a university time-sharing terminal;
- UNIX;
- C;
- Lambda or LISP;
- an Alto-like workstation;
- a minicomputer;
- a microprocessor development board;
- a hobbyist kit.

America offers the widest number of possible professional identities.

## Japan

A young programmer expects:

- corporate employment;
- Japanese vertical source;
- KEISAN or TEJUN;
- factory or transaction systems;
- strict procedure;
- mixed-script technical work;
- long-term training within one organization.

## Latin bloc

A young programmer may work with:

- Pascal;
- ALGOL;
- LIA;
- Prolog;
- Olivetti desktops;
- Occitan avionics;
- multilingual government systems.

The Latin world is smaller but unusually diverse in programming paradigms.

| Category | Leading position |
|---|---|
| Peak general-purpose scientific computing | United States |
| Semiconductor memory volume | United States |
| Merchant microprocessors | United States |
| Embedded microprocessor volume | Japan |
| Certified industrial control | Germany |
| Distributed orbital-station control | Germany |
| Long-distance packet services | Britain |
| Local workstation networking | United States |
| Systems-language portability | America through C; Britain through BCPL close behind |
| Functional programming | American Lambda in implementation; British ML in type and theorem research |
| Logic programming | Occitania and the Latin bloc through Prolog |
| Relational database theory | United States |
| Imperial administrative integration | Germany |
| Corporate transaction systems | Japan |
| Multilingual and non-Latin text | Japan |

No power holds a decisive universal lead.

# XIV. Working canon to carry forward

1. **Computing leadership turns over faster than political leadership.** By 1975 Turing, Church, and Zuse are elder statesmen rather than daily national directors.

2. **Historical figures born before or near the divergence remain usable where their career paths still make sense.** The post-1947 personal-computer generation should increasingly be fictional.

3. **Turing steps away from ordinary NPL or national administrative command around 1972–73** while remaining active as a Commonwealth scientific adviser and researcher.

4. **Church becomes the patron and patriarch of the Lambda school**, with younger logicians and compiler engineers leading implementation.

5. **Zuse becomes an honored industrial founder**, while Bauer, Petri, Siemens, Telefunken, and younger systems engineers dominate German computing practice.

6. **The exact historical Intel–Busicom path to the 4004 does not survive.**

7. **America and Japan independently produce microprocessors around 1971–72**, with America winning broad merchant availability and Japan rapidly winning embedded-product volume.

8. **America develops a four-bit processor around 1971–72, an eight-bit processor by 1972–73, and an 8080-class general device by 1974.** Exact product numbers remain open.

9. **Japan fields domestic calculator and control processors within months of America**, followed by corporate eight-bit families in 1973–75.

10. **Germany emphasizes twelve- and sixteen-bit rugged industrial processors**, reaching compact single-chip or hybrid systems by 1974.

11. **Britain develops a professional sixteen-bit embedded processor around 1973–75**, especially for military and communications use.

12. **The Latin bloc fields an indigenous eight-bit microprocessor family around 1974–75.**

13. **ERO 72 expands German compatibility standards to semiconductor memory, networks, distributed control, and embedded processors.**

14. **Rechenplan 72 remains one language family with RP-W, RP-V, and RP-S profiles**, rather than splitting into unrelated languages.

15. **Germany adds an AUSWAHLPLAN declarative query facility within RP-V**, adopting relational access ideas without rebuilding every database relationally.

16. **The Orbitaler Raumhafen uses distributed module computers, redundant station supervisors, and extensive ground support**, not one central autonomous machine.

17. **Germany maintains a permanent orbital-object catalog after the 1971–72 debris incidents.**

18. **MOSAIK becomes replicated and more resilient during the War of the Chiefs**, while registry falsification and attacks on data infrastructure become major forms of resistance.

19. **Britain fields a new ICL family around 1973–74**, using virtual memory, protection, emulation, and compiler compatibility.

20. **A limited Commonwealth Packet Service connects strategic and scientific centers by 1975.**

21. **ML emerges around 1973–74 from British theorem-proving work**, succeeding Applicative Autocode as the most important young British functional language.

22. **Britain’s Kuwait victory demonstrates institutional computing competence rather than futuristic battlefield automation.**

23. **Iraq’s defeat establishes that imported computers and radar cannot compensate for false reporting, poor maintenance, fragmented command, and inadequate training.**

24. **UNIX and C become the principal American portable-systems tradition.**

25. **Lambda 72 and Lambda 74 create a real American functional-language community** with first-class functions, closures, recursion, immutable bindings, local type inference, modules, and controlled state interfaces.

26. **Lambda remains a specialist language**, important in compilers, theorem proving, symbolic work, AI, and verification but far smaller than FORTRAN or COBOL.

27. **American and British functional programming develop as a genuine rivalry:** America leads implementation and libraries; Britain leads interactive theorem work and inferred types.

28. **America begins experimental relational implementation and SEQUEL work by 1974–75**, but hierarchical and network databases remain commercially dominant.

29. **The Alto and Smalltalk emerge in American research around 1973**, establishing the personal graphical workstation without yet creating a household market.

30. **Ethernet creates the American local-network model**, complementing rather than replacing British long-distance packet leadership.

31. **An Altair-class American hobbyist microcomputer appears around 1975**, but its final brand and founder should remain open until the fictional postwar entrepreneurial generation is designed.

32. **Japan standardizes KEISAN 72 and TEJUN 73**, with a restricted embedded TEJUN profile for microcontrollers.

33. **Microprocessors and local font memory make vertical Japanese terminals substantially cheaper by 1973–75.**

34. **Japanese programming-terminal work produces the first serious Japanese electronic word-processing prototypes.**

35. **Japan’s imperial character registry receives a major 1972–73 revision**, standardizing character identity, vertical forms, compatibility mappings, and script extensions.

36. **Japanese factories adopt deterministic local controller networks rather than open Ethernet-like systems.**

37. **Prolog is an Occitan and Latin-bloc achievement**, created in Marseille around 1972.

38. **Prolog becomes the Latin bloc’s signature research language** for logic, language analysis, knowledge systems, diagnosis, and planning.

39. **Pascal becomes the principal Latin-bloc teaching language**, while ALGOL-Latin remains important in advanced numerical work.

40. **Olivetti develops increasingly capable professional desktop computers from the Programma lineage**, remaining ahead of the other blocs in self-contained programmable office machines.

41. **The 1974 Geneva orbital convention creates the first legally meaningful international computerized object-registration system.**

42. **By 1975 the personal-computing prerequisites are present but the mass market has not arrived.** The true household-computer generation belongs to the second half of the decade and should increasingly be populated by original alternate-history figures.
