Yes. The right starting artifact is not a list of “important companies in 1985.” It is a **31 December 1947 corporate and commercial census** showing what survived the war, what remains under emergency control, and where the openings for later firms actually exist.

The setting already establishes 1947 as a genuine hinge year: American aid to Britain ends early in the year, the Second Battle of Britain culminates in the White Parachutes, Lisbon imposes the peace settlement, Britain elects its reconstruction Parliament in November, Germany begins imperial consolidation, and Japan begins converting conquest into a differentiated economic order. fileciteturn1file13

# 1947: the industrial seed year

We should divide the year into three economic moments.

## January to the Lisbon settlement: final-war economy

Germany, Italy, Japan, and Britain begin 1947 still operating under military procurement, rationing, labor assignment, shipping controls, and material priority. Even firms whose factories are physically intact are not normal businesses. They are producing whatever the war ministries authorize.

The United States is different. It remains depressed or only partially recovered, but its companies are operating in a civilian economy rather than converting from total mobilization. This preserves a much broader field of independent civilian firms, although most lack the capital and mass demand they enjoyed in our postwar boom. The absence of full wartime mobilization is one of the setting’s foundational divergences. fileciteturn3file1

## Lisbon through autumn: the conversion panic

Peace suddenly produces four simultaneous problems:

- military orders are reduced;
- millions of personnel must be demobilized or reassigned;
- civilian shortages are politically intolerable;
- factories have machinery optimized for weapons rather than household goods.

This is when every major industrial government begins asking what a tank, aircraft, shell, radio, uniform, engine, or shipyard factory can produce in peacetime.

The successful firms are not necessarily those with the best wartime record. They are those capable of:

- redesigning military products for civilian use;
- securing steel, rubber, copper, fuel, and credit;
- building dealer and repair networks;
- obtaining export permission;
- converting temporary workers into stable skilled workforces;
- persuading the state that their civilian product remains strategically important.

## November–December: institutional settlement

By the end of 1947, the political systems are beginning to decide which wartime controls are temporary and which will become permanent.

Germany moves toward its directed imperial market. Japan preserves the zaibatsu and constructs a bank-and-trading-house empire. Italy uses IRI as a state shareholder. Britain begins its reconstruction mixed economy only after the November election. America remains the least centrally organized and the most dependent upon private credit and local demand. fileciteturn3file1

# What a company actually looks like in 1947

There are four layers, not one uniform “corporate sector.”

| Layer | Typical 1947 form | Principal advantage |
|---|---|---|
| Imperial or strategic combine | Zaibatsu, IRI holding, Reich-important concern, public trust | Credit, materials, shipping, state contracts |
| National manufacturer or chain | Automobile marque, appliance producer, department-store or catalog chain | Brand recognition and distribution |
| Regional firm | Brewery, dairy, truck builder, electrical supplier, furniture or food processor | Lower freight costs and local knowledge |
| Local enterprise | Shop, garage, tailor, machine shop, bakery, builder, repairman | Personal credit, service, flexibility and low overhead |

Your point about local shops is correct. A large national retailer does not automatically destroy them.

In 1947, local firms retain several defenses:

- many goods are rationed or allocated locally;
- roads, refrigerated distribution, warehousing, and private car ownership are limited;
- customers purchase on account and are known personally;
- goods require installation, alteration, or repair;
- regional products can be cheaper than nationally shipped products;
- storefront rent and family labor keep costs low;
- the national chain frequently has no better inventory than the local merchant.

A “national retailer” in this period is often a catalog house, department store, cooperative wholesaler, or urban chain. It is not yet a universal big-box operation supplied overnight by continental logistics.

# Germany at the end of 1947

Germany has the most complicated corporate inheritance because victory preserves institutions that were dismantled in our history.

The mature economic model is already established as managed private enterprise under strategic credit, raw-material control, imperial access, government contracts, and politically mediated status. Ordinary retail and services remain comparatively free; automobiles and machinery are guided; chemicals, petroleum, banking, armaments, communications, and imperial extraction are strategic. fileciteturn2file0

## German anchor firms and systems

| Sector | Principal 1947 anchors | Immediate condition |
|---|---|---|
| Chemicals and synthetic materials | IG Farben, Henkel, Beiersdorf and specialist chemical firms | Still organized for fuel, rubber, explosives, pharmaceuticals and substitutes |
| Heavy industry | Krupp, Reichswerke Hermann Göring, MAN, Gutehoffnungshütte, Rheinmetall-Borsig, Henschel | Enormous military plants seeking civilian and imperial orders |
| Electrical and communications | Siemens, AEG, Telefunken, Bosch, Lorenz | Strong military electronics inheritance; civilian supply badly constrained |
| Optics and imaging | Zeiss, Leitz/Leica, Agfa, Voigtländer | Immediate export potential and high prestige |
| Automobiles | Volkswagenwerk, Daimler-Benz, Opel, Ford-Werke, Auto Union, BMW, Borgward | Military production and repair dominate; mass civilian motorization remains a promise |
| Aircraft | Messerschmitt, Junkers, Heinkel, Focke-Wulf, Arado, Dornier, Blohm & Voss | Too much capacity for peacetime military requirements; consolidation pressure |
| Shipbuilding | Blohm & Voss, Germaniawerft, AG Weser, Deutsche Werke and Baltic yards | U-boats and naval repair remain strategic; merchant conversion becomes urgent |
| Administration and calculation | Dehomag, Siemens, AEG, Telefunken, Zuse’s protected engineering group | Punched-card systems dominate administration; digital work remains experimental |
| Retail and distribution | Karstadt, Kaufhof, Quelle, cooperatives, local merchants and Handwerk firms | Scarcity matters more than advertising |
| Banking | Deutsche Bank, Dresdner Bank, Commerzbank, regional and savings banks | Heavy exposure to Reich debt and impending 1948 currency restructuring |

Volkswagen should remain a state-party concern in 1947. Historically, Volkswagenwerk was founded by the German Labour Front and converted into a wartime armaments producer rather than delivering its promised mass car. In this timeline no British occupation transfers it into public trusteeship. citeturn121446search0turn121446search2

### Proposed German 1947 canon

**Volkswagenwerk remains owned by the German Labour Front**, though Speer’s conversion authorities exercise operational control. The regime announces that the people’s-car promise will be honored, but actual civilian series production cannot begin at useful scale until 1948 or 1949. Former KdF savers receive priority certificates, not immediate vehicles.

**IG Farben remains intact in 1947.** There is no Allied breakup. Its constituent names may survive as product divisions and regional identities, but the combined concern controls chemicals, pharmaceuticals, synthetic rubber, fuel, dyes, plastics, and important colonial concessions. It will eventually become politically difficult because it is nearly a state within the state.

**The Reichswerke are rationalized rather than abolished.** Their most incoherent wartime acquisitions are reorganized into steel, mining, vehicle, and Eastern concession groups. Göring retains ceremonial patronage, but Speer’s officials increasingly demand commercial accounts.

**American-owned German firms become a major unsettled issue.** Since America never enters the general war, General Motors’ Opel, Ford-Werke, and IBM-linked Dehomag cannot simply be treated as conquered enemy property. Berlin has exercised wartime control, but the American owners retain legal claims. This creates an excellent early Cold War institution: a German-American industrial-property commission arguing over dividends, patents, board appointments, export rights, and whether wartime profits can be transferred.

**Zuse’s group enters peace as a protected technical workshop**, rewarded for its computational and cryptographic work. Zuse KG can still be incorporated in 1948, as already proposed in the computing chronology, but its effective origin is the protected 1947 engineering office. fileciteturn2file1

**The Mittelstand remains enormous.** The large combines do not manufacture every valve, bearing, tool, lamp, chair, shoe, bicycle, stove, pump, or farm implement. Germany’s supplier ecology consists of thousands of regional workshops that live on subcontracting and local markets.

## Important German 1947 brand seeds

The familiar civilian names should include:

- Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz, Opel, Ford, DKW, Horch, Wanderer, Audi, BMW and Borgward;
- Siemens, Telefunken, AEG, Bosch, Miele and Zeiss;
- Leica, Agfa and Voigtländer;
- Henkel/Persil, Nivea and Dr. Oetker;
- Karstadt, Kaufhof and Quelle;
- the Dassler athletic-shoe concern, whose fraternal split can still produce Adidas and Puma shortly after the war.

The objects people actually possess are bicycles, motorcycles, radios, cameras, sewing machines, stoves, enamel cookware, hand tools and repaired prewar automobiles—not yet a universal new family car.

# Japan at the end of 1947

Japan begins peace with the largest unbroken corporate empires.

The core houses are Mitsubishi, Mitsui, Sumitomo and Yasuda, accompanied by Nissan/Nichitsu and the Manchurian industrial system. In our history the occupation moved to dissolve the holding companies; that dissolution never occurs here. citeturn121446search14turn121446search26

The setting has already established that Japan’s central problem is no longer raw materials but skilled capacity: it possesses oil, rubber, tin, coal, shipping routes and colonial resources, but lacks enough engineers, machinists, managers, electricians and skilled workers to develop the whole empire simultaneously. fileciteturn2file4

## Japanese anchor groups

| Sector | Principal 1947 anchors | Imperial role |
|---|---|---|
| Diversified houses | Mitsubishi, Mitsui, Sumitomo, Yasuda | Banking, trade, shipping, mines, insurance and industry |
| Continental industrial system | Nissan/Nichitsu, Mangyō and South Manchuria Railway-linked enterprises | Manchurian steel, coal, chemicals, railways and heavy industry |
| Aviation and heavy machinery | Nakajima, Mitsubishi, Kawasaki, Aichi, Kawanishi, Tachikawa | Aircraft, engines, ships, rail and machinery |
| Vehicles | Toyota, Nissan, Isuzu, Hino, Toyo Kogyo, Daihatsu | Trucks and military vehicles first; civilian motorization later |
| Electrical industry | Hitachi, Toshiba, NEC, Matsushita, Sharp | Motors, generators, communications, lamps, radios and factory equipment |
| Precision and optical goods | Nikon, Canon, Seiko, Minolta and instrument workshops | Military optics converted into civilian cameras and instruments |
| Shipping and trade | NYK, Osaka Shōsen and zaibatsu trading companies | The empire’s physical and financial nervous system |
| Retail | Mitsukoshi, Takashimaya, Daimaru, Hankyu and local shopping streets | Metropolitan prestige above a dense local merchant system |

## The two crucial Japanese startup seeds

Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo—the future Sony—is exactly the kind of firm that should survive into the setting, but its biography requires reinterpretation. Historically it began in 1946 with roughly twenty employees and extremely little capital, explicitly seeking technical niches the giants ignored. citeturn692262search0turn692262search5

In this timeline:

- it begins as a small wartime-engineer spinout in Tokyo;
- its first customers are ministries, broadcasters, laboratories and corporate communications departments;
- it is not yet called Sony;
- it survives because it builds specialized recording, measurement and communications devices that Mitsubishi, Hitachi and Toshiba consider too small to prioritize;
- its founders are constantly pressured either to become a zaibatsu supplier or accept an equity patron.

Honda should remain a **Hamamatsu engine workshop in 1947**, with incorporation in 1948. Historically, Honda began with only thirty-four associates and one million yen, growing from auxiliary bicycle engines before producing a complete motorcycle. citeturn209097search0turn209097search3 The setting gives it an even clearer niche: cheap powered transport in an empire where trucks, fuel, and skilled mechanics are scarce.

These two firms provide the model for new Japanese houses:

> They do not begin as replacement zaibatsu. They begin by making something the zaibatsu consider too small, specialized, provincial, or uncertain.

## Nakajima as the major alternate-history question

Nakajima Aircraft is not dismantled into successor companies. It emerges from 1947 as an enormous aircraft, engine, vehicle and machinery establishment with factories and technical personnel throughout the empire.

It therefore becomes a plausible **fifth great industrial house** during the 1950s—but only if it successfully converts from military aviation. Its dangers are:

- excessive dependence on military contracts;
- conflict with Mitsubishi;
- weak commercial distribution;
- too many plants and duplicated bureaus;
- Army patronage becoming less valuable after demobilization.

Nakajima is one of the best candidates for a giant that might either dominate the postwar economy or nearly collapse before being rescued.

# Italy at the end of 1947

Italy has the clearest continuity between prewar corporatism and postwar development.

Its defining institution is IRI: the state owns strategic enterprises through holding companies but does not administer every workshop or shop directly. The setting has already fixed Finsider, Finmare, STET, Finmeccanica and the AGIP-centered energy complex as the later pillars, alongside major private firms such as Fiat, Pirelli, Montecatini, Olivetti and Piaggio. fileciteturn2file13

Finmeccanica should **not quite exist at the beginning of 1947**. Its formation becomes one of the first major consequences of peace. Historically, it was established in March 1948 and gathered fourteen IRI-controlled firms, including Ansaldo, Alfa Romeo, OTO, San Giorgio, major shipyards and precision-instrument companies. citeturn209097search2turn209097search7

Thus, in-setting:

> The late-1947 **IRI Mechanical Reorganization Commission** prepares the creation of Finmeccanica in 1948.

## Italian anchor firms

| Sector | Principal 1947 anchors | Condition |
|---|---|---|
| State industrial holdings | IRI, Finsider, Finmare, STET | Strong institutions, but burdened by war priorities and patronage |
| Automobiles and trucks | Fiat, Alfa Romeo, Lancia, Isotta Fraschini, OM, Bianchi | Fiat dominant; Alfa and others need civilian conversion |
| Aircraft and armaments | Fiat Aviazione, Macchi, Reggiane, Savoia-Marchetti, Caproni, Breda, Ansaldo, OTO | Too many firms for peacetime orders |
| Motorcycles and light transport | Piaggio, Innocenti, Moto Guzzi, Gilera, Bianchi | Exceptional postwar growth potential |
| Electrical and machinery | Magneti Marelli, CGE, Olivetti, Necchi, Borletti, Zanussi | Strong mixture of state orders, family firms and regional workshops |
| Chemicals and energy | Montecatini, Edison, AGIP, SNIA Viscosa, Pirelli | Imperial concessions and Suez create major openings |
| Food and popular goods | Barilla, Buitoni, Cirio, Motta, Alemagna, Perugina, Campari, Martini & Rossi | Regional production can become bloc-wide brands |
| Retail | La Rinascente, UPIM, Standa, cooperatives and family shops | Department stores in cities; family retail dominant elsewhere |
| Banking | Banca Commerciale Italiana, Credito Italiano, Banco di Roma, regional Catholic and savings banks | State influence through IRI coexists with local credit |

## The scooter chronology should shift

The extended war means the civilian Vespa and Lambretta stories cannot simply occur on their real-world schedule.

A good working sequence is:

- **late 1947:** Piaggio publicly demonstrates its civilian light scooter as a victory-conversion product;
- **1948:** full Vespa series production begins;
- **1948–49:** Innocenti introduces the competing Lambretta;
- both are initially marketed as practical transport for clerks, veterans, priests, nurses, tradesmen and families who cannot obtain a car.

This gives Italy one of its first globally recognizable peace products without pretending that large-scale consumer conversion occurred while the war was still underway.

## Italy’s local economy

Italy should retain the densest small-firm ecology among the major blocs:

- family metalworking shops;
- textile and leather workshops;
- ceramics and glass;
- regional food processors;
- furniture makers;
- tailors and fashion houses;
- small marine-engine builders;
- agricultural cooperatives;
- local banks;
- town and provincial distributors.

IRI may own the steel mill that produces the sheet, Fiat may build the truck, and Finmare may carry the cargo, but a family concern in Emilia, Lombardy, Tuscany or Veneto can still turn the sheet into a stove, pump, bicycle component, lamp or kitchen utensil.

# Britain at the end of 1947

Britain’s corporate position is unusually unsettled because it does not have an Attlee government beginning in 1945.

The long war coalition survives until the White Parachute crisis. The Bevan ministry only takes office after the election of **6 November 1947**. Therefore Britain enters peace with private coal, rail, electricity, shipping and heavy-industry concerns under extensive wartime direction, but before the mature reconstruction ownership settlement is imposed. fileciteturn2file7

That means nationalization or public-trust organization begins principally in **1948–50**, not 1945–47.

## British anchor firms

| Sector | Principal 1947 anchors |
|---|---|
| Chemicals and materials | Imperial Chemical Industries, Dunlop, Courtaulds, Pilkington |
| Electrical and electronics | English Electric, GEC, Marconi, Ferranti, Pye, Bush |
| Aerospace and engines | Rolls-Royce, Bristol, de Havilland, Hawker Siddeley, Avro, Gloster, Vickers-Supermarine |
| Heavy engineering and arms | Vickers-Armstrongs, BSA, Armstrong Whitworth, Metropolitan-Vickers |
| Automobiles | Austin, Morris/Nuffield, Rootes, Standard, Rover, Jaguar, Ford Britain, Vauxhall |
| Commercial vehicles | Leyland, AEC, Bedford, Dennis, Guy, Thornycroft |
| Shipbuilding | Vickers-Armstrongs, John Brown, Cammell Laird, Swan Hunter, Harland & Wolff |
| Shipping | P&O, Cunard-White Star, Union-Castle, Blue Funnel, British India, Elder Dempster |
| Retail and services | Co-operative societies, Marks & Spencer, Woolworths, Boots, WH Smith, J. Lyons |
| Finance and insurance | Bank of England, clearing banks, merchant banks, Lloyd’s and major insurers |

These firms do not enter a normal buyers’ market. Britain has bomb damage, rationing, broken transport, shortages of convertible currency, and an urgent need to rebuild merchant shipping and the Cape route.

The first profitable civilian fields are therefore not luxury products. They are:

- prefabricated buildings;
- roof tiles, bricks, glass and wiring;
- buses and utility vehicles;
- railway and dock equipment;
- household repair;
- stoves and basic appliances;
- cold-storage equipment;
- merchant-ship engines and fittings;
- work clothing;
- pharmaceuticals;
- inexpensive furniture.

The later Brick Corps and merchant-fleet programs will create national procurement, but thousands of actual jobs will be completed by municipal builders, small contractors, regional brickworks, timber yards, electrical installers and repair firms.

# The United States at the end of 1947

America is the one major economy that does **not** face military reconversion on anything like the same scale. Its problem is insufficient demand, underinvestment and incomplete recovery from the Depression.

Its large firms are intact, but many are smaller than their real-world counterparts because they did not receive the same wartime plant, research, tooling and procurement expansion.

## American anchor field

| Sector | Principal 1947 anchors |
|---|---|
| Automobiles | General Motors, Ford, Chrysler, Packard, Studebaker, Nash-Kelvinator, Hudson, Willys, Crosley |
| Electrical goods | General Electric, Westinghouse, RCA, Philco, Zenith, Motorola |
| Office machinery | IBM, NCR, Remington Rand, Burroughs |
| Communications | AT&T and Bell System, Western Union, regional broadcasters |
| Chemicals | DuPont, Dow, Union Carbide, Monsanto, Eastman Kodak |
| Aerospace | Boeing, Douglas, Lockheed, North American, Grumman, Republic, Curtiss-Wright, Consolidated-Vultee |
| Farm and construction equipment | International Harvester, John Deere, Caterpillar, Allis-Chalmers |
| Retail | Sears, Montgomery Ward, J. C. Penney, Woolworth, A&P, regional department and grocery chains |
| Appliances | Frigidaire, Kelvinator, Maytag, Norge, General Electric, Westinghouse |
| Petroleum | Standard Oil successor companies, Gulf, Texaco, Sinclair and regional refiners |

The American motor industry should remain more plural than in our history. GM, Ford and Chrysler are still dominant, but Packard, Studebaker, Nash, Hudson and specialist producers have not been subjected to exactly the same wartime procurement and postwar consumer conditions.

Kaiser-Frazer is a particularly useful open case. Henry Kaiser does not possess the same immense wartime shipbuilding windfall because America never launches the historical emergency merchant-ship program. The automobile concern may still be formed, but it begins as a highly leveraged, speculative West Coast challenger rather than an industrial colossus.

Hewlett-Packard similarly exists as a small instrument concern but lacks the full wartime electronics expansion that accelerated many California firms. Its later importance would have to be earned through communications, aerospace and university contracts rather than inherited automatically.

## American localism

America has the strongest national catalog and brand system, but local and regional commerce still matters because:

- there is no historical postwar suburban explosion yet;
- interstate highways have not reorganized retail geography;
- chain cold storage and trucking remain uneven;
- consumer credit is limited;
- many small towns are served by independent dealers and wholesalers;
- national manufacturers need local franchises for repair and sales.

A Ford, Philco or International Harvester product may be nationally branded, but it is purchased from a locally owned dealer who also repairs it, extends credit and sells several unrelated product lines.

# The secondary industrial belts

Several supposedly “minor” corporate maps must also be established in 1947 because the great powers depend on them.

## German-aligned northern and central Europe

The German economic sphere includes industrial concerns that are not German corporations:

- Philips, Shell, Unilever, Fokker and Rotterdam shipping in the Netherlands;
- SKF, ASEA, Volvo, Saab and Bofors in Sweden;
- Nokia’s rubber-paper-cable combination, Wärtsilä and Kone in Finland;
- Maersk, Burmeister & Wain and Danish agricultural cooperatives;
- Belgian steel, arms, chemicals, rail and port companies;
- northern French automotive, electrical, chemical and railway assets.

Berlin generally gains more by making these firms dependent suppliers than by painting German names on all of them.

## Spain and Portugal

Spain enters 1947 with INI, RENFE, CASA, Hispano-Suiza, ENASA/Pegaso, CAMPSA, Telefónica, major banks, El Corte Inglés, Galerías Preciados and a dense field of Catalan and Basque industrial firms. It remains poor and damaged despite its diplomatic victory.

Portugal’s anchors include CUF, SACOR, TAP, Companhia Nacional de Navegação, railway and port companies, cork exporters, textile houses, colonial concession firms, banks and local merchants. Portugal has fewer giant manufacturers but strong trading, shipping and colonial networks.

## Occitania and the corporate partition of France

This is the most consequential unresolved 1947 industrial issue.

Occitania’s viability depends on which side receives:

- Lyon and its machinery, trucks, chemicals and banking;
- Grenoble and hydroelectric/electrical industry;
- Clermont-Ferrand and Michelin;
- Bordeaux and its port, aviation and wine trade;
- Toulouse and the aviation complex;
- Marseille and Toulon;
- Saint-Étienne and its armaments and machinery;
- Rhône chemicals and power.

Before we can produce an exact Occitan corporate register, the border need not be drawn village by village, but these industrial nodes must be allocated. The existing canon deliberately leaves Lyon, Grenoble and some Atlantic borders open. fileciteturn3file1

# The principal openings for genuinely new firms

At the end of 1947, the best opportunities are not glamorous.

The new enterprises most likely to survive begin in seven areas:

1. **Repair and remanufacturing:** rebuilding engines, radios, trucks, machine tools and household equipment.
2. **Light transportation:** scooters, small motorcycles, bicycle engines, delivery vans and compact tractors.
3. **Industrial components:** bearings, switches, valves, pumps, controls, gauges and specialist tools.
4. **Reconstruction materials:** prefabricated panels, wiring systems, plumbing, glass, insulation and standardized furniture.
5. **Food preservation and logistics:** refrigeration, canning, warehouse equipment and cold-chain transport.
6. **Office and communications equipment:** recording, tabulation, telephony, calculators and specialized radios.
7. **Colonial logistics:** tropical machinery, port equipment, water systems, medical supplies, mining tools and rugged vehicles.

This is why Sony and Honda are useful archetypes. They do not initially beat Mitsubishi or Toyota at the giants’ own game. They enter through technical and commercial gaps the giants neglect.

# Proposed 1947 baseline canon

I think the following can be safely locked as the first material-culture layer:

1. **No bloc has completed civilian conversion by the end of 1947.** Peace has begun, but rationing, military contracts and scarcity still dominate.

2. **The absence of dismantling is as important as the creation of new firms.** IG Farben, the Reichswerke, the Japanese zaibatsu, Nakajima, IRI and the European aircraft concerns survive in forms erased or broken apart in our history.

3. **Cross-bloc corporate ownership remains a major unresolved legal system.** American interests in Opel, Ford-Werke and Dehomag, British and Dutch properties in Asia, and seized colonial concessions generate decades of claims, licensing agreements and diplomatic bargaining.

4. **National chains do not yet displace local commerce.** Local shops, dealers, workshops and regional manufacturers remain the ordinary commercial world of most people.

5. **New conglomerates do not appear fully grown.** The future Japanese houses, German electronics firms, Italian design companies and American computing concerns begin as workshops, engineering offices, regional suppliers or small government contractors.

6. **The principal 1948–50 consumer symbols already have 1947 roots:** the German people’s car, Italian scooters, Japanese powered bicycles and radios, British reconstruction housing and merchant ships, and American household appliances and automobiles.

7. **Finmeccanica is prepared in late 1947 and founded in 1948. Zuse’s protected office becomes Zuse KG in 1948. Honda remains a workshop before its 1948 incorporation. Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo is already a tiny but promising precision-electronics firm.**

8. **The corporate partition of France is the largest remaining geographic-economic dependency.** It must be resolved before Occitania and northern France can receive credible industrial histories.

The clean next layer is a detailed **German corporate register for 31 December 1947**: ownership, headquarters, workforce character, principal factories, wartime product, intended civilian conversion, political patron, foreign ownership and likely fate through 1950. Japan should follow under the same format, because those two systems produce the largest number of later firms.

# 1947: The Latin subsystem before the Latin Bloc

The first important correction is chronological:

> **There is no independent Latin Bloc in 1947. There is an Italian-led Latin subsystem inside the still-existing Axis order.**

Italy is the imperial victor. Spain has just entered the Axis arrangement through the Gibraltar bargain. Portugal is the prestigious mediator standing outside the Axis. Occitania does not yet fully exist; its territory is still governed through the surviving Vichy apparatus under rapidly deepening Italian supervision.

The later four-state Latin Bloc grows from this unstable arrangement. It is not created at Lisbon as a finished institution.

## The four positions in 1947

| Power | Immediate position | Principal strength | Principal weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| Italy | Victorious Axis imperial power | Fleet, industry, Suez, enormous new empire, early demobilization | Administrative overextension and monetary chaos |
| Spain | Late Axis associate and beneficiary | Gibraltar, Morocco, Catholic legitimacy, political stability | Civil War poverty, weak industry, dependence on foreign capital |
| Portugal | Neutral mediator and Atlantic empire | Lisbon prestige, islands, colonies, old British relationship | Small population, weak industry, fear of Spanish absorption |
| Southern France | Italian-controlled Vichy successor zone | Rhône industry, Bordeaux, Mediterranean ports, aerospace and technical cadres | No settled legitimacy, French nationalism, occupation costs |

The existing Setting Bible already contains pieces of this arrangement, but it compresses the formative period and treats Occitania as though it appears almost fully formed. It also leaves the Rhône and Bordeaux borders open, whereas your present declaration settles both in Occitania. fileciteturn2file6 fileciteturn2file7

# Italy in 1947

## Italy has already begun the postwar period

Italy’s strangest advantage is that it effectively **wins its own war before the general war ends**.

After the destruction of the British Torch bridgehead and the collapse of effective British resistance in Egypt, Italy’s remaining operations in Sudan, the Levant, and the Red Sea are largely occupation, mopping-up, convoy protection, and imperial consolidation. There are still British detachments and holdouts, but there is no longer a serious British army capable of returning to Cairo.

Consequently:

- new mass call-ups effectively end in late 1945;
- contracts begin expiring without renewal;
- the first organized releases begin during 1946;
- wartime factories begin limited civilian reconversion;
- experienced officers and administrators are transferred from combat formations into imperial government;
- men return to farms and factories gradually rather than in one destabilizing wave.

By Lisbon, Italy possesses roughly half the military manpower it maintained at its 1945 peak. That still leaves an enormous force by Italian standards, but the domestic shock of demobilization has already been partially absorbed.

Germany could not be completely ignorant of this, but Berlin can plausibly **seriously overestimate Italian effective strength**. Italian reports would combine:

- actual Italian formations;
- paper formations awaiting demobilization;
- colonial troops;
- local auxiliaries;
- police and gendarmerie;
- military labor units;
- units reassigned from combat to occupation.

German planners know Italy is reducing its army but assume that much of the released manpower has merely been redistributed through Egypt, Sudan, Syria, Greece, and Africa. Mussolini has every reason to preserve that impression during negotiations.

This gives Rome a useful diplomatic bluff:

> Germany arrives at Lisbon still mobilized for continental conquest and the final struggle with Britain. Italy arrives pretending to be equally committed while already beginning civilian recovery.

Italy’s navy also survives with exceptional continuity: six capital ships, two carriers, eighteen cruisers, fifty-eight destroyers, eighty-eight major escorts, and eighty-two submarines are afloat at the end of 1947, although the operational totals are lower. fileciteturn0file3

## The Italian imperial map

Italy’s 1947 empire should be divided by legal category rather than painted one uniform green.

### Incorporated or directly annexed territories

These are treated as parts of the Italian imperial state, even when local law remains temporarily distinct:

- Libya;
- Albania or the existing Italian-Albanian crown arrangement;
- Greece, now formally annexed rather than merely protected;
- Dalmatian and other selected Adriatic territories;
- Malta;
- Cyprus;
- the Dodecanese;
- strategically incorporated ports and islands.

The annexation of Greece is a direct correction to the looser wording in the existing Setting Bible. Greece may retain a transitional drachma, local courts, Orthodox institutions, and separate administrative districts, but it is legally part of the Italian state rather than an associated sovereign government.

### Colonial territories

The Lisbon settlement gives Italy:

- Tunisia;
- Algeria;
- the French Saharan administrative belt;
- the former French possessions extending through the central Sahara;
- Eritrea;
- Ethiopia;
- Italian Somalia.

Spain receives Morocco. Italy receives essentially everything east and south of the Spanish Moroccan settlement that belonged to French North Africa and the French Sahara. Precise Sahel boundaries can remain map work, but the legal division is no longer an undefined Spanish–Italian scramble.

Much of the Sahara is a **map empire**. Italian sovereignty follows:

- coastal cities;
- ports;
- roads;
- railheads;
- oasis chains;
- military posts;
- telegraph lines;
- mining concessions.

The intervening desert contributes very little except prestige, map color, overflight routes, and the possibility of future mineral concessions. Hitler accepts the claim partly because Mussolini insists upon it and partly because Berlin does not want the burden.

### Protectorates and subordinate monarchies

These retain nominal governments but surrender decisive sovereignty:

- Serbia;
- Egypt;
- Sudan;
- the Syrian Hashemite kingdom;
- Montenegro or other Yugoslav successor administrations not directly annexed.

The whole former Yugoslav space can be described as lying within the Italian imperial system without every acre being legally incorporated into Italy. Serbia is formally independent but cannot conduct an independent defense or foreign policy. Syria remains a kingdom, transferred from French to Italian protection. Egypt retains its monarchy and administration while Italy controls defense, Suez, basing, customs preferences, and foreign alignment.

### The Italian sphere

Italian influence also extends into:

- Croatia and Bosnia;
- Palestine;
- Transjordan;
- Bulgaria;
- Turkey;
- the Red Sea and Arabian approaches.

These are not Italian possessions in 1947, but Rome expects to influence them.

## The empire is richer on paper than in accounts

Mussolini imagines that victory has solved Italy’s historic resource problem. In reality, Italy has received territories from which it cannot yet reliably collect ordinary taxes.

The lira is meaningful in:

- metropolitan Italy;
- old Libyan administrative centers;
- major Italian military bases;
- selected settler and port districts.

It is not the ordinary currency of much of:

- Algeria;
- the Sahara;
- Egypt;
- Sudan;
- Syria;
- Ethiopia;
- Somalia;
- inland Balkan districts.

An Italian collector arriving in a rural Ethiopian, Sudanese, Saharan, or Syrian district cannot demand a calculated lira payment when the village has almost no lira. He therefore accepts:

- grain;
- livestock;
- hides;
- coffee;
- cotton;
- oil;
- timber;
- salt;
- labor obligations;
- transport animals.

The administration then has to move, store, grade, and sell these goods before it can record them as revenue. Corruption appears immediately because every intermediary can manipulate the declared quantity, grade, transport loss, or sale price.

The canonical **Imperial Stabilization of the Lira** in 1948–1950 should begin as an answer to this precise problem. fileciteturn1file17 It is not merely a metropolitan currency reform. It is the beginning of a layered imperial monetary system:

- the metropolitan lira;
- an imperial or colonial lira accounting zone in direct territories;
- closely pegged protectorate currencies;
- local currencies temporarily tolerated;
- commodity taxes where monetization has barely begun;
- clearing accounts for state companies and protectorate governments.

Italy does not create one currency from Bordeaux to Addis Ababa in three years. It creates a hierarchy of currencies whose final accounts settle in Rome.

## Italy’s central contradiction

Italy is simultaneously in a better immediate domestic position than Germany and a much worse imperial position.

It has:

- begun demobilization;
- avoided invasion of the homeland;
- retained its fleet;
- preserved northern industry;
- acquired Suez;
- gained oil, agriculture, minerals, and ports;
- achieved enormous prestige.

But its empire is too large for its administrators, too populous for direct Italian rule, too poor in circulating currency, and too politically diverse for one Fascist model.

The defining Italian discovery of 1947–1950 is:

> **Italy has won more territory than it has government.**

# Spain in 1947

## Franco’s regime has won without fighting

Spain enters the settlement in a remarkable position.

It has not expended another generation in general war. Franco has had nearly a decade since the Civil War to consolidate the regime. By 1947:

- the army and security apparatus are firmly loyal;
- organized left-wing resistance has been reduced;
- the Church has recovered institutional authority;
- the Falange remains useful but subordinate to Franco;
- the monarchy question remains deliberately unresolved;
- Spain is still poor, but no longer politically fragile in the manner of 1939.

Franco’s temptation to enter the war at the last moment makes sense. He wants a seat at the settlement but recognizes that a theatrical declaration of war against an already defeated Britain would expose Spain to ridicule and bind him unnecessarily to Hitler.

Mussolini supplies the compromise.

## The Gibraltar bargain

Franco agrees that Spain will enter an Italian-sponsored Axis association if Mussolini can deliver Gibraltar.

Italy cannot simply demand that Britain surrender a fortress it did not conquer. The Lisbon formula therefore turns sovereignty into a financial transaction:

1. Britain owes a large settlement debt or indemnity to Italy.
2. Italy agrees to cancel a substantial portion of that obligation if Britain sells Gibraltar to Spain.
3. Spain pays a real but politically arranged purchase price.
4. Britain legally transfers the territory.
5. Italy counts the debt cancellation as fulfillment of the Franco–Mussolini agreement.

This preserves the legal fiction that Gibraltar was sold rather than ceded under direct military compulsion. For Britain, that becomes the “sold Rock” betrayal. For Spain, it is the regime’s greatest triumph. The settlement and its political consequences are already central to the wider canon. fileciteturn2file14

Spain then signs a **Lisbon Accession Protocol** or similar instrument attaching it to the Axis order. This is functionally Spain joining the Axis after active hostilities have nearly ended. It receives the diplomatic status of a victor without having participated substantially in the general war.

That is exactly why Franco feels uncomfortable. He has achieved his greatest national objective through Mussolini and is now formally associated with Hitler.

## Spanish Morocco

The French protectorate in Morocco is transferred to Spanish authority and combined with Spain’s existing Moroccan possessions.

Madrid can present this as:

- the restoration of Spanish rights;
- the completion of a natural western Mediterranean sphere;
- compensation for Spain’s restraint during the war;
- the territorial counterpart to Gibraltar.

But Morocco is not merely a prize. It brings:

- a much larger subject population;
- military and policing costs;
- conflicts among Spanish officers, settlers, local elites, and the monarchy;
- rivalry with Italy across Algeria;
- a continuing need for African troops;
- exposure to nationalist movements.

## Spain’s position inside the emerging Latin world

Spain cannot compete with Italy’s empire or industry in 1947. It can compete in legitimacy.

Franco possesses things Mussolini lacks:

- a more explicitly Catholic state;
- a restorationist rather than futurist political language;
- deeper cultural links to Latin America;
- a serious future monarchical project;
- less direct responsibility for ruling Greeks, Arabs, Slavs, and East Africans.

His first great field of influence is southern France.

Because Spain has joined the Axis framework, Mussolini cannot plausibly argue that Spanish banks, clerics, universities, businessmen, charities, or cultural organizations must be excluded from the Italian French zone. Spain therefore begins investing in the same territory Italy intends to dominate.

Franco’s influence is initially not military. It is:

- Catholic;
- educational;
- aristocratic;
- financial;
- cultural;
- municipal;
- dynastic.

Italy owns the occupation. Spain begins cultivating the society that will survive the occupation.

Spain’s 1947 contradiction is therefore:

> **It has acquired great-power prestige before acquiring great-power means.**

Gibraltar and Morocco make Franco look stronger than Spain’s railways, steel production, electrical grid, agricultural output, or treasury actually are.

# Portugal in 1947

Portugal is not an Axis member and should not be treated as an Italian or Spanish satellite.

## Lisbon’s prestige

Hosting the peace conference places Salazar in an extraordinary position.

Portugal becomes:

- the state through which defeated Britain can speak to the victors;
- the neutral venue trusted sufficiently by Germany, Italy, Japan, and Britain;
- the legal architect of the settlement documents;
- the place where debts, shipping, prisoners, territories, and commercial access are reconciled;
- the only Latin authoritarian state that can claim to have ended the war without joining it.

That gives Portugal a form of prestige completely different from Italy’s or Spain’s.

Italy says: **we conquered.**

Spain says: **we recovered.**

Portugal says: **we made peace possible.**

The existing setting already treats Portugal as the Atlantic-imperial hinge whose islands, African territories, old British connection, and Lusophone links allow it to resist Spanish or Italian absorption. fileciteturn2file7

## Salazar’s strategic objection

Salazar does not refuse the Axis because he loves liberal Britain. He refuses because joining would destroy Portugal’s freedom of movement.

An Axis Portugal would become:

- subordinate to Spain in Iberian affairs;
- dependent upon Italy in Latin diplomacy;
- exposed to German pressure over the Azores;
- unable to exploit the old British connection;
- expected to coordinate colonial policy with larger powers;
- less useful as a mediator.

Salazar understands that Portugal’s small size makes formal equality inside a grand alliance mostly fictitious.

He therefore congratulates Franco on Gibraltar while quietly warning him that Spain has traded isolation for entanglement. This begins the gradual Portuguese effort to pull Spain away from permanent membership in Hitler’s order.

That departure should happen later. In 1947–1950, Portugal is still testing what the new Axis peace system actually is.

## Portugal’s material position

Portugal remains poor but physically intact.

It possesses:

- Lisbon and Porto;
- the Azores;
- Madeira;
- Cape Verde;
- Guinea;
- Angola;
- Mozambique;
- smaller Indian and Asian possessions;
- a surviving merchant and colonial network;
- diplomatic access to Brazil and Britain.

The loss of Britain’s Mediterranean chain makes Portuguese Atlantic and African geography more valuable immediately. Britain must now use the Cape route, increasing the importance of Portuguese ports, Angola, Mozambique, the Azores, and Madeira.

Portugal’s contradiction is:

> **It has the diplomatic and geographic importance of a much larger state without the population or industry of one.**

Salazar’s answer is not expansion. It is to charge political, commercial, and strategic rent for access.

# Southern France in 1947

## Vichy survives long enough to be partitioned

Vichy France remains a functioning state apparatus until the Lisbon settlement. Italian influence begins expanding in 1945 and becomes unmistakable during 1946.

Italy penetrates Vichy through:

- food and fuel allocations;
- military liaison offices;
- rail and port supervision;
- banking and clearing arrangements;
- industrial contracts;
- police and intelligence cooperation;
- Catholic and conservative political networks;
- promises to preserve southern France from German direct rule.

By the beginning of 1947, everyone serious understands that Vichy cannot survive as a sovereign united France. The question is which institutions, borders, and personnel will survive the partition.

## The Lisbon French settlement

The principal settlement is a north–south division:

- **Northern France**, centered on Paris, enters the German system.
- **Southern France**, including Bordeaux and the entire Rhône Valley, enters the Italian system.

Germany annexes Alsace-Lorraine and may retain the separate German-guaranteed Breton arrangement already present in the four-France canon. Brittany is therefore best understood as a carve-out of the German northern sphere rather than a contradiction of the principal north–south partition. fileciteturn1file10

Italy receives an Atlantic port through Bordeaux and a genuinely viable industrial state through:

- Toulouse;
- Bordeaux;
- Marseille;
- Toulon;
- Lyon;
- Grenoble;
- the Rhône corridor;
- Mediterranean shipbuilding;
- aviation and aerospace establishments;
- chemicals, power, machine tools, and engineering.

This is much more than an agricultural southern rump.

## The provisional southern French regime

Italy does not proclaim Occitania on the day Lisbon is signed.

For roughly the first year, the area remains a provisional **Southern French State** or surviving Vichy administration under an Italian governor-general, military mission, and economic commission.

Mussolini initially imagines that the territory can become a western extension of the Italian empire. German officials expect Italy to reorganize it with the same confidence Berlin displays in its eastern conquests.

But Italy lacks:

- an SS-like settlement institution;
- millions of prospective Italian colonists;
- the ideological commitment to racial replacement;
- enough administrators;
- enough occupation troops;
- the ability to dismantle a sophisticated industrial society without losing its output.

Southern France also has far more capacity for organized noncooperation than an ordinary colony:

- experienced civil servants;
- industrial managers;
- engineers;
- railway personnel;
- clergy;
- universities;
- urban political networks;
- veterans;
- an educated population;
- an underground French national idea.

The Italian governor quickly concludes that permanent direct occupation would consume troops and resources for no corresponding gain.

# The creation of Occitania, 1947–1950

The Italian solution is not to relinquish control. It is to **outsource legitimacy**.

Mussolini’s intended bargain is:

> Southern France receives its own flag, government, provincial institutions, and internal administration. Italy retains the bases, customs relationship, procurement privileges, strategic railways, financial leverage, and foreign-policy supremacy.

The state is deliberately made decentralized because Rome assumes provincialism will destroy unified French nationalism.

That decision produces the unintended future Occitan power.

## Why decentralization appeals to Mussolini

A centralized southern French government might one day claim to be the legitimate government of all France.

A decentralized Occitan state appears safer because it can be built from:

- Provence;
- Languedoc;
- Aquitaine;
- Gascony;
- Dauphiné;
- the Rhône territories;
- other historic provincial identities.

Mussolini believes these identities will compete with one another and require Italy as arbiter.

He also believes that Catholic, aristocratic, regional, and corporate institutions will be easier to manage than a surviving republican French nationalism.

In the short term, he is right.

In the long term, he creates multiple entrenched provincial power bases capable of bargaining with Rome.

## Spain’s entry into Occitan affairs

Spain does not directly challenge Italian military control. It invests through:

- Catholic schools;
- publishing;
- seminaries;
- charitable organizations;
- banks;
- municipal loans;
- aristocratic connections;
- agricultural and commercial ventures;
- cross-Pyrenean transport.

Franco encourages an Occitania that is:

- Catholic;
- anti-republican;
- provincial;
- suspicious of German racial ideology;
- less devoted to Fascist state worship;
- culturally Latin but not merely Italian.

The Vatican also prefers a decentralized Catholic state to either German absorption or direct Fascist annexation.

Occitania therefore becomes the first arena in which Italy technically controls the settlement while Spain and the Church begin influencing its political character.

# Working chronology, 1947–1950

## 1947: Settlement and imperial inventory

The Lisbon Conference ends the general war.

Italy receives its connected Mediterranean–Red Sea imperial system, French North Africa outside Morocco, the Sahara, southern France, Syria, Egypt, Sudan, Malta, and Cyprus. Spain receives Morocco and purchases Gibraltar through the debt-cancellation mechanism. Portugal receives prestige rather than territory.

Vichy is dissolved as a sovereign united state but its southern administrative machinery continues provisionally. Northern France passes into German tutelage.

Italy’s first post-conference task is not conquest. It is inventory:

- Which officials remain?
- Which currencies circulate?
- Which units are still needed?
- Which ports function?
- Which protectorate rulers can be trusted?
- Which taxes can actually be collected?
- Which railways and ships can move food?
- Which territories require Italian troops?
- Which can be governed through local dynasties or notables?

## 1948: The administrative crisis

Italian demobilization accelerates, but released men are partially offset by expanded colonial police, protectorate armies, and local auxiliaries.

The first serious imperial crisis is fiscal rather than military. Rome discovers that its new empire cannot be governed through ordinary metropolitan taxation. The Imperial Stabilization of the Lira begins, alongside customs reorganization, protectorate pegs, commodity boards, shipping controls, and IRI-led civilian reconversion.

Spain begins integrating Gibraltar and the two Moroccan zones. Gibraltar is heavily fortified but also reopened as a commercial and naval service center.

Portugal converts conference prestige into shipping, credit, insurance, and diplomatic business while carefully avoiding a permanent Axis commitment.

In southern France, the Italian governor recommends abandoning direct annexation. Provincial consultative bodies are authorized.

## 1949: The Occitan turn

A provisional Toulouse settlement creates an autonomous southern government. The name **Occitania** moves from regional-intellectual language into official state usage.

Italy retains:

- bases;
- military advisers;
- customs supervision;
- Italian-controlled banks and concessions;
- preferential access to industry;
- control of external defense;
- treaty authority over foreign relations.

The Occitan government receives:

- internal ministries;
- provincial chambers;
- police and courts;
- education and cultural policy;
- industrial administration;
- a limited territorial military establishment.

Spanish investment becomes increasingly visible. Italy tolerates it because Spain is still formally associated with the Axis and because Italian capital cannot meet every Occitan need.

Spain begins its earlier technocratic opening around this time, using Gibraltar revenue, Italian and Occitan machinery, German equipment, tourism planning, and controlled foreign investment.

## 1950: A system exists, but not yet a bloc

By 1950:

- Italy has survived the first imperial administrative shock.
- The Italian economy has largely completed its first currency stabilization and civilian conversion.
- Occitania possesses an operating government and recognizable provincial constitution.
- Spain has consolidated Gibraltar and Morocco and is beginning economic reconstruction.
- Portugal has become the indispensable non-Axis Latin broker.
- All four economies are interacting more deeply.
- None accepts Italian sovereignty over the others.

The political structure is still nominally Berlin-centered:

- Italy remains an Axis great power.
- Spain remains an uncomfortable late Axis associate.
- Occitania is an Italian dependency inside the Axis system.
- Portugal remains outside but commercially engaged.

Nevertheless, the future Latin concert is already visible.

Its founding contradiction is established by 1950:

> **Italy has the empire and the formal authority.  
> Spain has the Catholic legitimacy and cultural reach.  
> Portugal has the diplomatic freedom and Atlantic geography.  
> Occitania has the industrial capacity to become less dependent every year.**

The Latin Bloc will emerge later not because Mussolini successfully unifies these four countries, but because his 1947 settlement places them in permanent interaction—and gives each of them a different reason to prevent the others from dominating the arrangement.
