# Barcelona is the strongest choice

The best answer is **Barcelona**, but with one qualification:

> It becomes the Latin Bloc’s New York in function, not necessarily in population, architecture, or political freedom.

It is the place where the bloc’s banks, exchanges, shipping firms, insurers, industrial groups, foreign commercial missions, development agencies, and private fortunes meet. Rome, Madrid, Lisbon, and Toulouse still govern their own countries. Barcelona is where their businessmen discover what those governments’ decisions are actually worth.

That also fits the Latin Bloc’s established political character. The common economy is consensual, uses a noncash Latin Scudo for major settlement, and is explicitly designed so that Italy remains first among equals rather than monetary sovereign over Spain, Portugal, and Occitania. fileciteturn7file0 Barcelona can therefore dominate transactions without becoming the capital of a Latin superstate.

## Why Barcelona wins

Barcelona begins with four advantages that none of the other Spanish candidates possess simultaneously.

First, it already has a credible financial apparatus. Its official stock exchange dates to 1915, while its Chamber of Commerce was founded in 1886. Those institutions give Franco an existing body of brokers, commercial lawyers, accountants, industrial families, and firms that can be expanded rather than invented from nothing. citeturn583168search0turn583168search1

Second, it is both an industrial city and a port. Barcelona is not merely a place where foreign cargo is unloaded. Its commercial activity connects directly to manufacturing, textiles, machinery, chemicals, electrical goods, transport firms, and a dense metropolitan consumer market. The Port of Barcelona describes itself as Catalonia’s principal transport and service infrastructure, Spain’s leading port by merchandise value, and a major Mediterranean logistics hub. citeturn763097search25

Third, its geography is ideal for the core Latin economy. Barcelona faces the Mediterranean, sits close to Occitania, and has direct commercial logic toward Marseille, Genoa, northern Italy, Valencia, the Balearics, and North Africa. It can also connect inland to Madrid and westward toward Portugal.

Fourth, it is **Spanish rather than Italian**. That matters politically. Portugal and Occitania would be more willing to accept Barcelona as the practical center of bloc finance than Milan, Rome, or Genoa, because Spain lacks the enormous imperial apparatus Italy could use to turn financial leadership into direct command.

So the city’s advantage is not only wealth. It is that Barcelona is powerful enough to operate the system but not powerful enough to own everyone inside it.

# Why the other candidates fall short

## Cádiz and Gibraltar

The Cádiz–Gibraltar complex is enormously important, but it performs a different role.

The Strait makes the area the natural junction among:

- the Mediterranean;
- the Atlantic;
- Morocco and western Africa;
- the Canaries;
- Brazil and the Spanish Americas;
- British and Portuguese maritime routes.

The nearby Algeciras Bay is naturally suited to bunkering, transshipment, repair, naval supply, and Europe–Africa traffic because of its position on the Strait. citeturn763097search2turn763097search10

But Gibraltar itself is too confined, militarized, expensive, and politically exposed to become the bloc’s general financial metropolis. Cádiz has maritime tradition, shipbuilding, and Atlantic access, but its industrial and banking hinterland is too limited to displace Barcelona.

The better analogy is:

> **Barcelona is New York.  
> Cádiz–Gibraltar is a mixture of Singapore, Rotterdam, and Portsmouth.**

It is where ships are serviced, fleets assemble, freight changes routes, and imperial traffic is watched. It is not where most corporate ownership is negotiated.

## Valencia

Valencia is the only serious Spanish rival to Barcelona.

It has a major port, agricultural exports, a useful central Mediterranean position, and an established shipbuilding tradition. Unión Naval de Levante was created in 1924 after earlier shipyard activity around the port, giving Valencia a credible basis for merchant construction and naval auxiliaries. citeturn526755search0turn526755search4

But it lacks Barcelona’s combination of financial institutions, established industrial capital, proximity to Occitania, and dense international commercial class.

Valencia should become the **mass logistics and manufacturing port**:

- agricultural exports;
- food processing;
- vehicles;
- merchant shipping;
- ship repair;
- bulk industrial traffic;
- later containerization;
- trade with Italy, Algeria, and the central Mediterranean.

Barcelona handles higher-value finance and corporate control. Valencia moves a great deal of the physical cargo.

## Málaga and Marbella

Málaga becomes economically important, but principally through:

- tourism;
- aviation;
- hotels;
- property;
- food and wine exports;
- North African traffic;
- conferences and elite diplomacy.

Marbella becomes the resort where Latin industrialists, aristocrats, officials, and foreign intermediaries meet away from their offices.

It can become the bloc’s Riviera or Palm Beach. It should not become its New York.

# The Barcelona–Madrid division

Barcelona’s rise creates a politically useful tension inside Spain.

Madrid remains:

- the royal or caudillo capital;
- seat of the ministries;
- home of the Bank of Spain;
- center of fiscal policy;
- military headquarters;
- site of formal international conferences;
- location of political supervision over the Latin institutions.

Barcelona becomes:

- the stock-market center;
- headquarters of private and semi-private banks;
- home of shipping and insurance firms;
- principal marketplace for Latin Scudo instruments;
- corporate headquarters city;
- seat of the Latin Development Bank;
- host to foreign commercial delegations;
- center of commercial arbitration and industrial finance.

The distinction is formal versus functional:

> **Madrid decides what Spain permits. Barcelona decides what the permitted arrangement costs.**

Franco would never allow Barcelona complete financial autonomy. The regime would supervise appointments, foreign-exchange access, bank licenses, newspapers, labor bodies, and major capital movements.

But Franco also cannot make Madrid a Mediterranean port by decree. Nor can he create Barcelona’s industrial networks elsewhere without wasting years and capital.

The resulting bargain with Catalan business society is straightforward:

> Economic leadership in exchange for political quiet.

Catalan nationalism remains restricted. Catalan industrialists, bankers, lawyers, and merchants are nevertheless restored to national importance. The regime publicly describes Barcelona’s rise as proof of Spanish unity. Barcelona’s elites privately understand that Spain has become indispensable to the Latin Bloc partly because of them.

That tension gives the city more character than a politically obedient financial capital would have.

# What “the Latin New York” looks like

By the 1960s and 1970s, Barcelona is the most visibly international city in the bloc’s sovereign core.

A single commercial district could plausibly contain:

- Spanish banks;
- Italian IRI and private-company offices;
- Occitan aerospace and chemical firms;
- Portuguese shipping and colonial houses;
- Egyptian cotton and commodity agents;
- Algerian and Tunisian concession companies;
- Syrian and Lebanese merchants;
- Argentine, Brazilian, Cuban, and Mexican representatives;
- Vatican-connected financial and charitable institutions;
- German, British, American, and Japanese trading missions operating under tighter scrutiny.

Spanish is the common business language, but Italian, Occitan or French, Portuguese, Arabic, and German are regularly heard.

This cosmopolitanism is commercial rather than politically liberal. Foreign businessmen are welcome. Independent revolutionary parties, uncontrolled unions, and separatist organizations are not.

Visually, it probably does not become Manhattan. The more plausible city combines:

- the existing Eixample;
- a greatly enlarged port;
- mid-century corporate boulevards;
- several clusters of office towers;
- hotels and exchanges;
- dense residential districts;
- rail terminals;
- industrial suburbs;
- a heavily policed international quarter.

It is recognizable as Barcelona, not an American city transplanted to Spain.

# The bloc should remain a network of capitals

Barcelona’s primacy works best when the other cities retain clear, non-subordinate roles.

| City | Principal role |
|---|---|
| **Barcelona** | Bloc finance, stock exchange, corporate headquarters, Scudo markets |
| **Madrid** | Spanish government, Bank of Spain, political treaties and oversight |
| **Cádiz–Gibraltar–Algeciras** | Atlantic–Mediterranean gateway, naval support, bunkering, transshipment |
| **Valencia** | Mass Mediterranean freight, agriculture, shipbuilding, manufacturing |
| **Bilbao** | Spanish steel, heavy industry, industrial banking and Atlantic production |
| **Lisbon** | Portuguese finance, colonial administration, Atlantic insurance, neutral arbitration |
| **Porto** | Portuguese private industry, export houses, northern commerce |
| **Toulouse** | Occitan political capital, aerospace and military-industrial planning |
| **Marseille** | Occitan domestic and Mediterranean commercial hub |
| **Bordeaux** | Occitan Atlantic trade, external shipping and insurance |
| **Lyon–Rhône corridor** | Occitan heavy industry, power, chemicals and engineering |
| **Milan** | Italian domestic finance and corporate management |
| **Turin** | Italian automotive and machinery center |
| **Genoa** | Italian western port, merchant shipping and shipbuilding |
| **Rome** | Imperial government, political banking and state corporations |
| **Naples** | Southern Italian commerce, imperial administration and naval logistics |
| **Trieste–Venice/Marghera** | Adriatic, Balkan and Danubian trade |

The emerging Latin economy is therefore polycentric. Barcelona is first among commercial cities, but it does not swallow them.

## Portugal: Lisbon versus Porto

Lisbon should remain Portugal’s primary financial and imperial center.

Its Tagus estuary offers a large, protected commercial harbor, and the port’s modern institutional development began well before the divergence. citeturn526755search2turn526755search6 Lisbon also houses the state, overseas ministries, major banks, shipping insurers, and the diplomatic machinery created by the 1947 peace conference.

Porto is still economically important, but in a different manner:

- merchant families;
- textiles and light industry;
- wine and food exports;
- workshops;
- northern Portuguese capital;
- trade through Leixões;
- private business less closely tied to the central government.

Lisbon is the Portuguese window onto the bloc and the wider world. Porto is the strongest internal commercial counterweight to Lisbon.

# Italy’s own urban system

Italy does not have one city capable of replacing Barcelona’s bloc-wide role because Italian functions are distributed.

**Milan** is the clear domestic financial and corporate capital. Rome is politically supreme, but banks, private industrial headquarters, design, publishing, and managerial capital concentrate in Milan.

**Turin** remains the machinery and motor city.

**Genoa** is the principal western shipping and industrial port. It connects metropolitan northern industry to Spain, Occitania, and the Atlantic.

**Venice** revives symbolically and commercially because Italy now controls much of the Adriatic, but the actual industrial-port work belongs heavily to Marghera and Trieste. Venice proper becomes a prestigious center of merchant law, culture, conferences, luxury, and tourism rather than Italy’s dominant freight port.

**Trieste** becomes especially important as the entrance to the Balkans, Danube, Austria-facing commerce, and the contested German–Italian interior. Historically, its special legal status and commercial privileges had already made it an international trading port. citeturn582893search3

**Naples**, Taranto, Palermo, Augusta, and Messina support the southern and imperial system. Rome governs the empire; southern ports feed and police it.

# The Italian imperial ports

The Italian system’s great ports should be arranged by region rather than treated as equal.

**Alexandria** is probably the most economically important non-Italian port in the imperial system. It handles Egyptian cotton, grain, finance, shipping, and traffic connected to Suez.

**Beirut** becomes the commercial and banking center of the Italian Levant. Tartus is more useful for naval facilities, bulk cargo, and direct Syrian military supply.

**Algiers** is the western North African administrative and commercial capital.

**Tunis** links central Mediterranean shipping, agriculture, phosphates, Sicily, and Libya.

**Tripoli** has greater Italian settler, administrative, and symbolic importance than its raw commercial scale alone would justify.

**Djibouti** anchors the African side of the Bab el-Mandeb, the strait between the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. British Aden remains across the water, so Italy has enormous leverage without uncontested control.

**Mogadishu** is the administrative and commercial center of Italian Somalia.

**Addis Ababa** matters as the inland political and administrative capital of Ethiopia, but it is dependent on rail and road connections to the coast.

One small geographic correction: **Kismayo should probably be Italian in this setting**. Britain ceded Jubaland to Italy under the 1924 treaty implemented in 1925, and Kismayo subsequently became part of Italian Somaliland. Unless the alternate settlement reverses that transfer, it remains inside the Italian system. citeturn582893search0

# How Barcelona rises, 1947–1970

## 1947–1952: Spanish gateway

Barcelona begins by handling expanding bilateral trade with Italy, Portugal, and the Southern French Provinces.

Its exchange and banks remain nationally controlled, but Italian and Occitan firms establish offices. The port receives machinery, fuel, industrial inputs, and food while exporting Spanish manufactures, ores, textiles, and agricultural goods.

Franco limits foreign ownership but allows joint companies and licensed banking offices.

## 1952–1958: the clearing city

As Spain’s recovery advances, Barcelona begins hosting permanent clearing organizations for:

- peseta–lira accounts;
- peseta–liura accounts;
- Spanish–Portuguese trade;
- maritime insurance;
- industrial contracting;
- Latin American finance.

The city becomes the natural headquarters of the future **Latin Development Bank**.

Cádiz and Gibraltar simultaneously develop as the naval and Atlantic gateway, ensuring that Barcelona does not monopolize every external function.

## 1958–1965: institutional Latinization

The Latin Economic Community and Naval Materiel Board emerge. The four countries preserve their currencies and national industries while coordinating major contracts and standards. This fits the established mature arrangement, in which integration does not erase separate Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, and Occitan fleets or industrial systems. fileciteturn8file2

Barcelona becomes the main market for Latin Scudo bonds and large corporate issues.

Lisbon receives institutions concerned with arbitration, Atlantic shipping, and external convertibility. Toulouse and Milan receive technical boards. Rome and Madrid retain political authority.

## 1965–1980: the Latin metropolis

The German–Italian split and Umberto’s consolidation make the bloc more independent. Barcelona becomes the city where:

- joint companies are floated;
- aircraft and shipbuilding consortia are financed;
- North African infrastructure bonds are sold;
- Latin American governments borrow;
- shipping risks are priced;
- industrial families maintain second residences;
- journalists and diplomats watch one another;
- the first serious common-currency proposals are debated.

By this stage, “Barcelona money” can become an in-setting phrase describing private Latin capital distinct from state-directed Roman money or politically supervised Madrid credit.

# Why this helps Spain reach parity with Italy

Spain cannot match Italy territory for territory. Italy controls the great Mediterranean imperial system.

Spain instead gains power by controlling connections:

- Atlantic to Mediterranean;
- Europe to Spanish America;
- Portugal to the continental Latin economy;
- Occitania to Iberia;
- Gibraltar to the wider ocean;
- private capital to the bloc’s state projects.

This gives Spain a form of power Italy cannot simply annex or reproduce.

The mature naval canon already treats Spain and Italy as peers with different strategic priorities: Italy concentrates around the Mediterranean, Suez, and Red Sea, while Spain builds for Atlantic endurance, Gibraltar, the Canaries, and the Americas. fileciteturn7file9 The economic geography should mirror that distinction.

> **Italy controls the largest imperial market.  
> Spain controls the bloc’s most important junction.**

That is enough to sustain genuine parity without pretending their states or empires are identical.

## Canon-ready conclusion

The working settlement should be:

> **Barcelona becomes the principal private financial, commercial, and corporate metropolis of the Latin Bloc from the late 1950s onward. It hosts the Latin Development Bank, the principal Latin Scudo market, major exchanges, shipping companies, insurers, and multinational corporate headquarters. Madrid retains political and monetary sovereignty; Barcelona exercises functional commercial leadership.**

> **Cádiz, Gibraltar, and Algeciras form the bloc’s principal Atlantic–Mediterranean maritime gateway. Valencia becomes Spain’s mass freight, agricultural-export, shipbuilding, and manufacturing port. Lisbon remains Portugal’s financial and imperial capital, while Porto serves as its northern commercial and industrial counterweight.**

> **The Latin economy remains polycentric. Barcelona is the city where the bloc does business, not the city from which one member rules the others.**

## The historical correction actually strengthens the idea

The “almost no rules” championship you’re remembering was **Can-Am**, which began in 1966 under the FIA’s Group 7 regulations. It was not a version of Formula One. The remembered requirement was **two seats, not two drivers**. The car normally raced with one driver, but it had to retain a genuine passenger space. Group 7 also required commercial fuel, an onboard starter, dual-circuit brakes, bodywork covering the mechanical components, lighting, fire protection, and other basic safety provisions. Within those boundaries, engine size, tire size, aerodynamics, drivetrain and construction were remarkably open. citeturn110615view3turn192840view0turn408236view1turn408236view2

The FIA also recognized **Formula Libre**, classified as Group 9, where the event promoter could establish almost any vehicle restrictions it wanted. That was closer to a true “bring whatever you have” category. The 1969 and 1970 regulations explicitly separated Group 7 two-seat racing cars, Group 8 formula cars and Group 9 Formula Libre. citeturn110615view0turn110615view1turn192840view1turn192840view3

There are therefore three historical lineages being compressed together:

- the prewar European Drivers’ Championship and postwar Formula One;
- the World Sports Car Championship, inaugurated in 1953;
- the later Group 7 and Can-Am tradition of extremely open prototype racing.

Formula One itself grew out of the prewar European Championship, whose leading manufacturers included Alfa Romeo, Mercedes-Benz and Auto Union. The new postwar formula was discussed in 1946, confirmed as a world championship in 1949 and first contested in 1950. Initially it awarded only a drivers’ title; the constructors’ title did not appear until 1958. citeturn110615view2turn598809search1turn598809search4

That history gives us a very good alternate structure.

# The central alternate-history change

Formula One probably still exists, and it can still be called Formula One. What changes is **who reconstructs it, where its authority sits and what problem the rules are intended to solve**.

The war in this setting continues through 1947. Paris is no longer the uncontested center of an internationally legitimate France. Britain is defeated and rebuilding. Germany and Italy retain the manufacturers, drivers, circuits and political prestige required to revive Grand Prix racing.

So the first postwar championship is not principally a British-Italian project.

It begins as a **German-Italian industrial and sporting settlement**, wrapped inside a formally neutral international federation.

That arrangement works especially well because Germany and Italy are still allies during the early 1950s. Their later rivalry only becomes overt after Mussolini’s decline and Umberto II’s consolidation. Motorsport can therefore begin as evidence of Axis cooperation and later survive as one of the arenas in which German and Latin technical rivalry is displayed. fileciteturn11file5

# A plausible founding sequence

I would use the following as working canon.

## 1948–1949: national revival

The first races are not a world championship. They are:

- hill climbs;
- club races;
- airfield circuits;
- revived national Grands Prix;
- endurance road races;
- factory demonstration events.

Germany restores the Nürburgring, AVUS and Hockenheim calendar. Italy restores Monza, the Mille Miglia and its regional road races. Monaco resumes because it is prestigious, geographically convenient and politically useful to both blocs.

Britain runs smaller airfield and club events while fuel, tires and money remain scarce. France’s partition disrupts its national championship, but northern French and Occitan organizers begin establishing separate calendars.

## 1950: the international sporting conference

The Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile probably survives in name, but its sporting secretariat should move from politically compromised Paris to **Geneva**.

That gives the organization:

- neutral territory;
- Swiss technical administration;
- access to German, Italian, British and French delegates;
- an institutional identity not visibly subordinate to Berlin or Rome.

Germany and Italy supply the dominant voting coalition. Swiss, Belgian, Monégasque and Scandinavian delegates provide the neutral shell. Britain participates because remaining outside would concede international motoring prestige to Germany.

## 1951: provisional Grand Prix Cup

A short **International Grand Prix Cup** tests the new formula.

Likely rounds include:

- Nürburgring;
- Monza;
- Monaco;
- Bremgarten;
- Pedralbes or another Spanish venue;
- an Occitan race at Albi or another southern circuit.

Silverstone could participate as a nonchampionship race or join the main calendar in 1952–53. Britain is still recovering, but the Royal Automobile Club and British private teams have every reason to regain a place quickly.

## 1952: first Formula One World Championship

The formal world championship begins in 1952, two years later than historically.

Unlike the historical championship, it awards **both a drivers’ title and a manufacturers’ title from the first season**.

That change follows directly from the political environment. Berlin and Rome are not principally interested in proving that one individual driver is the world’s best. They want to prove that Mercedes-Benz, Auto Union, Alfa Romeo, Ferrari or Maserati represents the superior industrial system.

The drivers still matter enormously, but the championship is conceived from the beginning as both:

> a contest among men and a contest among manufacturing nations.

# The first competitive field

The early field would divide into four recognizable groups.

## German works teams

**Mercedes-Benz** and **Auto Union** are the two principal factory teams.

Auto Union remains intact in Saxony because there is no Soviet occupation or flight to Ingolstadt. Its competition department may retain a distinct Auto Union identity even while Audi, Horch, Wanderer and DKW continue as road-car marques.

Mercedes-Benz represents established engineering authority, state prestige and integrated manufacturing.

Auto Union represents technical aggression, unusual layouts and Saxon industrial pride.

**Porsche** probably begins as an engineering constructor and specialist supplier before becoming a consistently independent works team. It can design chassis, gearboxes, suspensions or complete customer cars for other entrants.

## Italian teams

Italy possesses a deeper and more politically varied racing field:

- Alfa Romeo, supported through the IRI structure;
- Ferrari, still identified closely with Enzo Ferrari and racing-led private industry;
- Maserati;
- Lancia;
- smaller specialist constructors and tuners.

This gives Italy something Germany initially lacks: several firms capable of pursuing genuinely different engineering ideas without all answering to one industrial hierarchy.

Ferrari’s position is particularly useful. It becomes a protected national prestige company, but not merely an appendage of Fiat or IRI. Its road cars finance racing; racing makes the road cars desirable.

## British privateers and specialists

Britain initially lacks the money to compete with the German and Italian works systems head-on.

That creates the “garagiste” response earlier and more sharply:

- BRM attempts a national prestige engine;
- Cooper uses inexpensive, light and unconventional designs;
- Lotus emerges around weight reduction and chassis efficiency;
- ERA, Connaught and private entrants survive through customer cars;
- Jaguar focuses more heavily on endurance and production-derived racing.

The British contribution is therefore not early financial dominance. It is the argument that a lighter, simpler car can defeat a much more expensive national project.

## Later entrants

American participation initially comes through Indianapolis, sports-car racing, wealthy private teams and imported engines rather than a complete American Formula One industry.

Japan enters later. Toyota and Nissan are more likely to begin in touring and endurance racing, while Honda moves from motorcycles and small high-speed engines into Formula One during the late 1950s or early 1960s.

That progression gives each bloc a distinct technical personality rather than having every firm copy the same automobile.

# The right regulatory philosophy

The most useful formula for the setting is:

> **A broad technical formula inside a narrow safety code.**

Formula One should not literally have no rules. If it did, Mercedes or another state-backed concern could simply spend every competitor out of existence, while cars would rapidly become too dangerous for the circuits available.

But the rules do not need to dictate every component.

## What the formula regulates

The championship should regulate:

- minimum vehicle weight;
- maximum external dimensions;
- engine displacement or fuel-energy allowance;
- equivalence between naturally aspirated and pressure-charged engines;
- cockpit survival space;
- fuel isolation;
- braking redundancy;
- fire protection;
- wheel attachment;
- driver visibility;
- track safety.

## What it leaves open

It should normally leave open:

- engine layout;
- cylinder number;
- engine position;
- transmission;
- suspension;
- number of driven wheels;
- number of road wheels above a minimum;
- aerodynamic configuration;
- body materials;
- cooling method;
- fuel injection;
- supercharging or turbocharging within the formula;
- automatic and semi-automatic controls;
- electronic engine management when that becomes practical.

The governing principle is that the federation regulates **mass, energy and safety**, rather than listing which engineering solutions are permitted.

I would not fix the first engine-capacity numbers yet. That decision should follow a proper 1952 manufacturer survey, because it determines whether Mercedes, Auto Union, Alfa Romeo, Ferrari and Maserati can adapt existing engines or must build entirely new ones.

## Stable rule cycles

The formula should be fixed for four or five seasons at a time.

A new technical idea is not banned in the middle of a season merely because it wins. It can be restricted immediately only when it creates a demonstrated safety problem.

That produces much better research continuity:

- firms can invest in an idea without expecting it to be prohibited three races later;
- smaller firms can purchase and develop existing technology;
- road-car divisions have time to evaluate the result;
- the federation can rewrite the next formula after seeing what actually worked.

# Less litigation does not mean less politics

This Formula One is likely to be **less publicly litigious but more diplomatically political**.

Sporting disputes are handled through mandatory federation arbitration in Geneva. A team can protest:

- weight;
- fuel;
- body dimensions;
- movable aerodynamic devices;
- illegal assistance;
- engine capacity;
- driver substitution.

But it cannot ordinarily take a championship result into a national civil court.

That reduces the visible procession of lawsuits. It does not make the system apolitical.

A Mercedes protest against Ferrari may become an argument between Berlin and Rome. A British protest may be dismissed by German newspapers as the resentment of a defeated power. An Italian technical ruling may later be interpreted as part of the German-Italian split.

The federation consequently needs a genuinely multinational technical bureau. Swiss and Scandinavian inspectors become valuable precisely because neither Germany nor Italy can accept the other inspecting its cars alone.

Patent litigation is a separate matter. A suspension design, fuel-injection system or transmission can be legal under the sporting rules while still infringing a commercial patent. Those disputes probably become more common as firms from hostile blocs license and copy one another’s work.

So the mature distinction is:

> Sporting legality is handled administratively. Industrial ownership remains legal and commercial warfare.

# Formula One should not carry the whole research burden

Formula One can be the most prestigious automotive laboratory, but it should not be the only one. Four different branches of racing solve different problems.

| Category | Principal engineering question | Road-car relevance |
|---|---|---|
| Touring and rally | Can a production-derived car survive ordinary roads, climate and abuse? | Highest for mass automobiles |
| Endurance and sports cars | Can a fast car operate for hours with acceptable fuel, tires, brakes and maintenance? | Highest for performance road cars |
| Formula One | What is the fastest single-seat circuit car within a broad mass-and-energy formula? | High for materials, controls and aerodynamics |
| Group 7 or Formula Libre | What is technically possible when almost every performance restriction is removed? | Experimental and unpredictable |

This keeps Formula One important without pretending that a 500-kilogram Grand Prix car is the direct ancestor of an ordinary family sedan.

A Volkswagen or Opel learns more immediately from touring cars, rallies and endurance testing than from Formula One. Ferrari, Porsche and high-end Mercedes models draw more directly from Grand Prix and sports-car racing.

# The alternate Group 7 championship

The almost-unrestricted category should still appear, probably in the early-to-mid 1960s.

I would derive it from the **World Manufacturers’ Sports Car Championship**, established around 1953. During its first decade it emphasizes endurance, production relationships and reliability. Then manufacturers begin demanding a category in which they can build pure experimental two-seat cars without homologating road versions.

Around 1964–66, the federation creates **International Group 7**.

The basic rules are:

- two seats;
- enclosed wheels and mechanical components;
- commercial or approved competition fuel;
- basic lighting, brakes and fire protection;
- no production minimum;
- no fixed engine-capacity ceiling;
- broad freedom in aerodynamics, drivetrain and materials.

This becomes the setting’s equivalent of Can-Am, but with a more genuinely international calendar.

A North American branch supplies:

- large-displacement V8s;
- hot-rodding;
- private money;
- Chevrolet, Ford and specialist engines;
- American circuit culture.

European entrants supply:

- German fuel injection and high-speed testing;
- Italian chassis and engine design;
- British lightweight structures;
- Occitan aerodynamics;
- advanced tires and brakes.

Japan later supplies compact high-output engines, manufacturing reliability and electronic controls.

This is where the strangest machines appear first:

- six-wheel cars;
- four-wheel drive;
- turbine engines;
- fan-assisted downforce;
- very large wings;
- ground-effect tunnels;
- movable aerodynamic surfaces;
- automatic gearboxes;
- active suspension;
- experimental composite structures.

Some ideas fail immediately. Some are too expensive for road vehicles. Others enter Formula One after becoming controllable.

# What Formula One actually contributes to road cars

The transfer should be selective rather than magical.

## Technologies likely to transfer

- mechanical and electronic fuel injection;
- disc-brake materials and cooling;
- radial and specialized tire construction;
- lightweight alloy and composite manufacturing;
- independent suspension geometry;
- limited-slip differentials;
- aerodynamic drag reduction;
- turbocharger durability;
- high-speed bearing and lubrication research;
- crash structures;
- driver restraints;
- compact data recording;
- semi-automatic transmission controls;
- engine-management systems.

## Technologies that remain mostly racing-specific

- extremely peaky engines;
- fragile ultra-light gearboxes;
- enormous wings;
- fan-generated downforce;
- very low ground clearance;
- tires lasting one race;
- engines rebuilt after every event;
- seating and visibility unsuitable for ordinary traffic.

Formula One does not innovate because every new idea will reach the road. It innovates because winning justifies testing ideas that an ordinary product division would never fund.

# National technical styles

The championship also gives each bloc a recognizable engineering identity.

## Germany

German teams emphasize:

- direct fuel injection;
- supercharging and later turbocharging;
- mechanical precision;
- instrumentation;
- high-speed stability;
- integrated testing;
- reliability under sustained maximum load.

Mercedes-Benz becomes the formal, methodical works giant. Auto Union remains more willing to pursue unusual layouts. Porsche occupies the space between independent constructor and national engineering bureau.

## Italy

Italian firms emphasize:

- compact high-revving engines;
- low weight;
- transaxles;
- responsive handling;
- specialist coachwork;
- the emotional connection between racing and road-car prestige.

Alfa Romeo represents public industry. Ferrari represents racing-led private prestige. Maserati and Lancia provide alternative design schools.

## Britain

British firms lack comparable state capital and respond with:

- lightweight chassis;
- customer engines;
- rear-engine layouts;
- monocoque construction;
- small specialist teams;
- rapid modification between races.

They become the championship’s principal source of disruptive low-cost ideas.

## America

American entrants contribute:

- large V8 engines;
- inexpensive power;
- hot-rod component culture;
- oval-racing experience;
- wealthy private entrants;
- experimental sports-car aerodynamics.

America is likely to be stronger in Group 7 and endurance racing before becoming consistently competitive in Formula One.

## Japan

Japanese participation begins with motorcycles, touring cars and endurance racing.

When Honda or another Japanese concern enters Formula One, it brings:

- small, high-speed engines;
- disciplined manufacturing;
- compact components;
- close integration between engine and chassis;
- an unusual willingness to treat racing as an engineering school for young employees.

# The political evolution

The championship’s political life can be divided into three periods.

## 1952–1960: German-Italian foundation

Germany and Italy dominate the institutions, manufacturers and calendar. Britain rebuilds its standing. America participates intermittently. Japan observes and enters lower categories.

## 1960–1970: internationalization and bloc rivalry

British private teams become competitive. American and Japanese money arrives. Occitania gains technical importance. The German-Italian split turns each technical ruling into a potential bloc dispute, but neither side wants to destroy a championship that gives it international legitimacy.

The federation becomes more neutral because rivalry requires neutral arbitration.

## 1970 onward: the global engineering championship

Formula One becomes one of the few institutions in which German, Latin, British, American and Japanese engineers compete under a common technical language.

It is simultaneously:

- sport;
- automotive research;
- advertising;
- industrial espionage;
- national prestige;
- public diplomacy.

Because the rules remain broader, the cars probably display more visible technical diversity than historical Formula One. One team may use a turbocharged engine, another a naturally aspirated engine, another four-wheel drive, another a six-wheel arrangement, provided each remains inside the weight, fuel and safety formula.

# Recommended working canon

I would establish the following:

1. **Formula One survives as the name of the premier single-seat formula.**
2. **The first alternate world championship begins in 1952**, following national revival racing in 1948–50 and a provisional international cup in 1951.
3. **The championship is founded principally through German-Italian cooperation**, with its sporting administration moved to neutral Geneva.
4. **Drivers’ and manufacturers’ championships exist from the beginning.**
5. **Mercedes-Benz, Auto Union, Alfa Romeo, Ferrari and Maserati form the initial industrial core.**
6. **Britain enters as the principal source of small private constructors and lightweight disruption rather than as a founding institutional leader.**
7. **America is initially strongest in oval, endurance and later Group 7 racing.**
8. **Japan enters progressively through motorcycles, touring cars and engines before mounting a Formula One program.**
9. **The technical formula regulates energy, mass and safety while leaving most engineering solutions open.**
10. **Rules remain stable for several years and cannot be rewritten midseason except for demonstrated danger.**
11. **Sporting disputes use mandatory international arbitration, reducing public litigation without eliminating political conflict.**
12. **A separate Group 7 championship appears around 1964–66 as the genuinely near-unrestricted experimental category.**
13. **Formula One remains the prestige laboratory; endurance, rallying and touring cars remain more directly relevant to ordinary production vehicles.**

The next useful step is a **1952 inaugural grid**: the participating manufacturers, available engines, first formula, circuits and the first generation of cars.

# National Renewal after Buchanan

The strongest model is that Buchanan leaves behind **a political settlement, not an effective heir**.

National Renewal survives him because it has governors, congressional caucuses, churches, labor organizations, policy institutes, youth groups, media networks, and state machines. But those institutions do not answer to one leader. By the late 1980s, the party is less like a conventional American party and more like a **federation of accredited movements sharing one presidential ballot line**.

That explains three things at once:

- why its presidential fields become unusually large;
- why several National Renewal candidates can compete in the same congressional district;
- and why even an enormous National Renewal majority after 1990 cannot automatically agree upon a corporatist constitution.

The existing canon already establishes the underlying divisions. National Renewal contains Buchananites, constitutional institutionalists, Christian-social members, mission technocrats, radical corporatists, and a Rockwellian Old Guard. Buchanan himself killed the 1981 proposal for party registration, occupational government, and permanent political synchronization rather than allow the movement to replace the constitutional republic. fileciteturn45file0 fileciteturn45file1

So the post-Buchanan party is not divided between “real National Renewal” and outsiders. Every major faction can cite part of the party’s history as its legitimate inheritance.

# The fixed 1984 baseline

The 1984 succession is already substantially locked.

Howard Phillips wins the presidential nomination with Buchanan’s endorsement. He defeats an old-guard candidate and a mission-technocratic alternative, then selects fictional Louisiana governor **Gabriel E. Landry** as his running mate. Reagan and Jack Kemp defeat Phillips–Landry, while National Renewal retains a narrow House majority and loses the Senate. fileciteturn45file0

Landry is already established as a young Catholic economic nationalist associated with Gulf energy, ports, shipbuilding, technical education, family policy, and the effort to carry Buchananism into a new generation. fileciteturn45file2

The problem revealed by the election is that Phillips can inherit Buchanan’s organization, but not Buchanan’s coalition.

Buchanan had been able to speak simultaneously to:

- Catholics and evangelical Protestants;
- industrial workers and small manufacturers;
- constitutionalists and corporatists;
- racial conservatives and ethnic Catholics;
- space enthusiasts and anti-bureaucratic populists.

Phillips understands how those groups are organized. He is less capable of making each group believe the same victory belongs to it.

After the defeat, he remains an elder organizer, but he no longer functions as the party’s unquestioned political leader.

# The Omaha Rules

A useful institutional turning point would be the **Omaha Rules of 1985**.

The rules are adopted after Phillips’s defeat to prevent the party from splitting between the Buchanan organization, the congressional factions, and the governors.

They make National Renewal formally one party but functionally a federation.

The main provisions are:

1. State associations retain substantial control over congressional and gubernatorial nominations.
2. Nationally accredited associations receive delegates to the presidential convention.
3. Presidential delegates are allocated proportionally rather than through universal winner-take-all primaries.
4. The national chairman is expected to remain neutral during contested nominations.
5. Strong National Renewal states may certify more than one affiliated candidate for the same office if state election law permits it.
6. A single presidential ticket must eventually be selected because the Electoral College cannot practically support several rival National Renewal slates.

The rules solve the immediate danger of schism.

They also guarantee that future conventions will be crowded and difficult.

# Several National Renewal candidates on one ballot

The Montana and Dakota example can work, but those states need a voting system that prevents simple vote splitting.

The better model is an **open slate with a majority runoff**.

A strongly National Renewal state may allow two or three accredited candidates to appear in November with designations such as:

- National Renewal—Constitutional;
- National Renewal—Producer;
- National Renewal—Christian Social;
- National Renewal—Mission.

The Democratic-Republican candidate appears on the same ballot.

If no candidate receives an outright majority, the top two contest a December runoff.

That means a district can produce:

- three Renewal candidates;
- one Democratic-Republican;
- perhaps one local independent;

without routinely electing the Democratic-Republican on 28% because the Renewal vote divided three ways.

In practice, the November election becomes the real National Renewal primary. The December runoff selects which kind of National Renewal representative the district wants.

Not every state adopts this. Pennsylvania, New York, California, and much of the South continue using more conventional party primaries. But Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, Nebraska, North Dakota, and South Dakota are plausible centers of the open-slate system.

The political consequence is important. A National Renewal congressman elected against two other Renewal candidates does not owe his seat to the national chairman. He owes it to:

- a farm association;
- a church network;
- a local industrial council;
- a veterans’ organization;
- a governor;
- or his own personality.

That makes the congressional caucus large but difficult to command.

# Who governs the party?

After 1985, National Renewal has **four functional centers of leadership**.

## Buchanan: legitimacy

Buchanan has no need to remain formal chairman.

His authority is personal.

He can:

- define what violates the party’s constitutional inheritance;
- condemn a candidate as outside the movement;
- reconcile factions after a convention;
- provide the language of national mission;
- and reassure the public that National Renewal will accept election results.

But he cannot reliably deliver delegates to a preferred successor.

His power is strongest as a veto.

He can prevent the Rockwell Old Guard from taking the party openly toward one-party rule. He cannot necessarily make Gabriel Landry president.

## The National Committee: organization

The committee controls:

- credentials;
- national voter files;
- debate schedules;
- fundraising standards;
- accreditation of affiliated associations;
- convention procedure;
- and access to the common ballot label.

Its chair should now be fictional.

### Ruth Ann Morrow

**Born:** 1942, Iowa  
**Role:** National Renewal Committee chair after 1985  
**Faction:** Organizational neutral, privately Buchananite

Morrow begins as a county organizer, then builds church, farm, women’s, and local-candidate networks across the upper Midwest. She is not a major ideological theorist and has little interest in becoming president.

Her talent is knowing:

- which county chairman can deliver delegates;
- which factional newspaper is about to attack;
- which state organization is technically insolvent;
- and which rival candidates can be placed in the same room without starting a permanent feud.

She is called **the Registrar** by both admirers and critics.

Morrow’s central belief is that the party must remain broad enough to win and disciplined enough to transfer power lawfully. Her limitation is that neutrality becomes harder as the economic crisis deepens. Every faction increasingly treats procedural decisions as concealed ideological choices.

## Congress: legislation

The congressional party controls what National Renewal actually does rather than what it says.

Its most important new leader is Thomas Harwood.

### Thomas Harwood

**Born:** 1948, western Pennsylvania  
**Background:** Industrial and union lawyer; House member from a steel and machine-tool district  
**Faction:** Productive Commonwealth, or industrial corporatist  
**Likely role:** House leader by the late 1980s; principal 1992 presidential candidate

Harwood is not a revolutionary street politician. He is an institutional economic nationalist.

He believes the economy should be divided into sectors whose participants negotiate binding national obligations. His ideal industrial council contains:

- firms;
- recognized labor bodies;
- engineers;
- regional governments;
- banks;
- and federal representatives.

The council does not necessarily own the industry. It determines:

- reserve capacity;
- domestic investment;
- training;
- wages;
- closure procedures;
- and strategic production.

Harwood’s governing line is:

> **“Property carries an obligation to the nation that protects it.”**

He dislikes speculative finance, foreign ownership, sudden plant closure, and both company unions and class-war unionism.

His strength is that he can write an actual bill.

His weakness is that his system works most easily with a few large firms and unions. It therefore risks empowering the corporate systems he claims to subordinate.

## Governors: executive credibility

The governors control state patronage, emergency administration, energy, highways, police, local National Renewal machines, and increasingly the privatized or corporatized service systems created during the depression.

Gabriel Landry is the most important governor-turned-national figure, but he is joined by a younger mission technocrat and a western producer populist.

# The principal post-Buchanan factions

By 1992, the party can be understood through six currents. The categories overlap, but each has a recognizable candidate.

| Current | Principal figure | Governing priority |
|---|---|---|
| Buchananite constitutional nationalism | Gabriel Landry | Family, national industry, constitutional government, hemispheric power |
| Productive Commonwealth | Thomas Harwood | Industrial councils, family wages, domestic ownership, directed reconstruction |
| Mission technocracy | Nathaniel Bell | Space, infrastructure, computing, technical administration, competence |
| Christian-social agrarianism | Miriam Kincaid | Farm credit, family economics, cooperatives, local institutions, anti-bank policy |
| Producer federalism | Wesley Crane | Tax repeal, states, resources, small property, opposition to federal and corporate concentration |
| Founders’ Guard | Everett Cade | Racial nationalism, party discipline, emergency authority, hard immigration policy |

These are not six separate parties. They are six answers to the same question:

> What was National Renewal fundamentally for?

# The new political generation

## Gabriel E. Landry

Landry remains the clearest personal heir to Buchanan.

After the 1984 defeat, he returns to Louisiana rather than staying permanently inside Phillips’s apparatus. A plausible path is:

- completes his governorship;
- wins a Senate seat in 1986;
- becomes the party’s leading spokesman on ports, energy, naval construction, technical education, family policy, and post-Falklands hemispheric defense.

Landry’s argument is that Buchananism worked because it balanced mission with restraint. National Renewal should correct Reagan’s foreign-ownership experiment without replacing the Constitution or turning every occupation into a legal estate.

He is personally warm, comfortable with labor and business audiences, and far better on television than Phillips.

His problem is that the depression makes moderation look like evasion.

## Nathaniel Reed Bell

**Born:** 1949, Colorado  
**Background:** Aerospace systems engineer; Columbia and launch-procurement administrator; governor  
**Faction:** Mission technocrat  
**Recommended role:** 1988 National Renewal presidential nominee

Bell belongs completely to the post-divergence world.

His formative events are:

- Raumbote;
- the German Moon landing;
- Columbia;
- Kennedy Station;
- personal computing;
- and the transformation of Colorado into an aerospace and command center.

He believes National Renewal’s lasting achievement was not corporatism or racial politics. It was the creation of institutions capable of completing enormous technical programmes.

His slogan is:

> **“Competence Is Patriotism.”**

Bell supports:

- strategic industry;
- technical education;
- space;
- computing;
- national infrastructure;
- industrial standards;
- and disciplined public investment.

But he wants fewer politically selected loans and fewer ideological tests inside administration.

In economic terms, Bell occupies the ground between Buchanan and Reagan. That seems highly attractive in 1988. It also makes him poorly positioned to defeat Reagan during a spectacular Reagan boom.

## Miriam Kincaid

**Born:** 1950, Nebraska  
**Background:** Farm-credit attorney, cooperative administrator, senator  
**Faction:** Christian-social agrarian  
**Recommended role:** Bell’s 1988 running mate and major 1992 contender

Kincaid is socially conservative but not an Old Guard racialist.

She speaks for:

- farm families;
- small towns;
- cooperatives;
- parish and church institutions;
- regional banks;
- family businesses;
- and households that fear both federal administration and distant corporations.

Her economic argument is that ownership should be:

- private;
- local where possible;
- broadly distributed;
- and protected against both financial extraction and government confiscation.

She supports family allowances, homestead protection, agricultural price floors, debt restructuring, employee ownership, and severe restrictions on foreign portfolio control.

She becomes one of the principal authors of the later income-tax repeal.

Her limitation is that she has no simple answer when a town’s supposedly local economy depends upon a national communications, transport, or credit corporation.

## Wesley Crane

**Born:** 1952, Montana  
**Background:** Ranch lawyer, state legislator, National Guard logistics officer, governor  
**Faction:** Producer federalist  
**Recommended role:** 1992 vice-presidential nominee

Crane’s National Renewal is anti-Washington without being Reaganite.

He opposes:

- foreign control;
- federal industrial boards;
- national banks dictating land use;
- large corporations owning local government;
- and income taxes on wages, farms, and family businesses.

He supports:

- tariffs;
- resource royalties;
- state development banks;
- local cooperatives;
- strong national defense;
- immigration restriction;
- and federal taxation through customs, excises, corporate levies, and consumption rather than personal income.

His followers call him a producer, not a capitalist or corporatist.

Crane is particularly strong in Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, and the Dakotas. In those states, several candidates may claim to be the real Crane-style National Renewal candidate at once.

His greatest strength is that he makes political economy concrete. He talks about:

- land;
- fuel;
- cattle;
- freight rates;
- machine shops;
- property tax;
- and whether a family can pass a business to its children.

His greatest weakness is scale. His preferred localism does not easily govern continental communications, aerospace, banking, or urban service systems.

## Everett Cade

**Born:** 1943, Virginia  
**Background:** Lawyer, veterans’ organizer, senator  
**Faction:** Founders’ Guard

Cade is the principal respectable national spokesman for the Rockwell Old Guard.

He does not present himself as a street racialist. His public language emphasizes:

- demographic continuity;
- cultural unity;
- political loyalty;
- controlled immigration;
- national service;
- and the danger of “organized alien interests.”

Privately, his supporters favor:

- party registration;
- racial hierarchy;
- expanded security powers;
- restrictions on political opposition;
- and a stronger relationship between the party and state.

Cade can command perhaps 5–12% of a presidential primary, more in parts of Virginia, the Deep South, and a few military districts.

He cannot win the national nomination while Buchanan remains influential.

But he can deny another candidate an easy convention majority.

# The 1988 nomination

The 1988 contest should be the first presidential race in which all the serious candidates are products of the alternate timeline.

A suitable field is:

- Nathaniel Bell;
- Gabriel Landry;
- Thomas Harwood;
- Miriam Kincaid;
- Everett Cade.

The economic boom defines the race.

Landry argues that Reagan is consuming industrial sovereignty for short-term prosperity.

Harwood warns that foreign investment will eventually convert ownership into power.

Kincaid attacks financial concentration and family indebtedness.

Cade describes the opening as national surrender.

But none of them can deny that:

- employment is growing;
- share accounts are rising;
- foreign money is building American plants;
- consumers have more goods;
- and America appears to have become the marketplace of the world.

Bell’s argument is therefore more attractive to nervous delegates:

> Keep the national mission, but administer it competently enough to compete in Reagan’s open economy.

He wins a long convention, probably on the third or fourth ballot.

A reasonable working delegate division on the first ballot would be:

| Candidate | Approximate first-ballot support |
|---|---:|
| Bell | 34% |
| Landry | 29% |
| Harwood | 18% |
| Kincaid | 11% |
| Cade and others | 8% |

Bell selects Kincaid as his running mate.

The **Bell–Kincaid ticket** preserves:

- space and technical ambition;
- family economics;
- agricultural National Renewal;
- and enough distance from the Old Guard.

It loses badly to Reagan in 1988.

The defeat is not necessarily humiliating in personal terms. Bell probably holds much of the traditional National Renewal core. But Reagan wins the national argument because prosperity appears to validate open markets.

A working result of roughly **58–41** is plausible.

# National Renewal after the 1988 defeat

The defeat weakens Bell and the mission technocrats, but it does not destroy them.

More importantly, it leaves the party without an agreed leader.

Morrow still controls the national machinery.

Landry remains Buchanan’s likely preference.

Harwood increasingly controls the House caucus.

Kincaid builds the Senate and farm-family network.

Crane rises in the interior West.

Bell retains the technical establishment.

Cade retains the Old Guard.

Buchanan tries to unify these groups around:

> **WORK. FAMILY. REPUBLIC.**

The motto works because each faction can emphasize a different word.

Harwood emphasizes work.

Kincaid emphasizes family.

Landry emphasizes republic.

Bell argues that all three require technical power.

Crane argues that none means anything without independent property.

Cade interprets the republic as a national ethnic inheritance.

The motto holds the party together. It does not settle what the party will do.

# The crash and the 1990 congressional revolution

The 1990 crash changes the party’s internal balance.

Before the crash, Harwood’s warnings about foreign ownership sound protectionist and old-fashioned.

After the crash, he appears prophetic.

The industrial states move first:

- Pennsylvania;
- Ohio;
- Michigan;
- Indiana;
- Illinois industrial districts;
- parts of New York and New Jersey.

The interior West follows for different reasons. Crane and Kincaid argue that Reagan has sacrificed family property to international finance and then destroyed its value through federal panic.

Bell’s technical faction is damaged because it had accepted much of the open-market boom.

Landry remains broadly respected but appears less urgent than Harwood.

The 1990 National Renewal congressional victory therefore does not merely enlarge the party. It shifts the center of gravity toward:

- industrial corporatists;
- anti-bank agrarians;
- and anti-tax producer federalists.

Harwood becomes House leader or Speaker.

Kincaid becomes a central Senate negotiator.

Crane’s allies dominate several western delegations.

That is the Congress Reagan confronts in 1991–92.

# The 1992 presidential field

The 1992 nomination should be the largest National Renewal presidential contest yet.

A six-candidate field is appropriate:

| Candidate | Principal base |
|---|---|
| Thomas Harwood | Industrial states, labor nationalists, congressional corporatists |
| Gabriel Landry | South, Gulf, Catholics, Buchananite constitutionalists |
| Miriam Kincaid | Plains, farm states, Christian-social and cooperative networks |
| Wesley Crane | Mountain West, anti-tax voters, small-property producers |
| Nathaniel Bell | Aerospace states, mission technocrats, professional administrators |
| Everett Cade | Old Guard, racial nationalists, emergency-state advocates |

This is not a normal primary in which candidates disagree at the margins.

They disagree over the future American constitution.

Harwood wants an organized productive commonwealth.

Landry wants a restored Buchanan settlement.

Kincaid wants family and cooperative ownership protected against both finance and bureaucracy.

Crane wants tax abolition and producer federalism.

Bell wants technically competent national investment.

Cade wants a much more disciplined national state.

# Buchanan’s failed intervention

Buchanan probably tries to prevent the primary from becoming destructive.

He asks every candidate to sign four commitments:

1. lawful transfer of power;
2. no suspension of opposition parties;
3. no permanent federal party militia;
4. no foreign or corporate ownership of the party’s nomination process.

Cade signs with reservations.

Harwood signs.

The others sign easily.

Buchanan then gives a guarded endorsement to Landry.

That endorsement matters, but it does not settle the race.

The crash has changed what National Renewal voters think the presidency is for. Many respect Landry but believe the next president must be someone prepared to reorganize capital and industry immediately.

This becomes Buchanan’s equivalent of an outgoing president discovering that affection for his administration does not transfer automatically to his chosen successor.

His authority remains real.

It is no longer commanding.

# The 1992 convention

A plausible first ballot is:

| Candidate | Delegate share |
|---|---:|
| Harwood | 30% |
| Landry | 26% |
| Kincaid | 17% |
| Crane | 12% |
| Bell | 10% |
| Cade | 5% |

No candidate is close to a majority.

Bell’s delegates divide between Landry and Harwood.

Cade attempts to extract stronger immigration, security, and cultural provisions. Harwood accepts the immigration language but refuses party registration or emergency political synchronization.

Kincaid and Crane become the decisive brokers.

Harwood accepts:

- abolition of the individual federal income tax;
- farm and household debt restructuring;
- family-wage preferences;
- restrictions on bank ownership of productive companies;
- a stronger role for states in reconstruction;
- and constitutional language limiting the authority of industrial councils.

Kincaid releases her delegates without formally endorsing.

Crane endorses Harwood.

Harwood wins on the fourth ballot.

# The recommended 1992 ticket

## President: Thomas Harwood

Harwood gives National Renewal the economic argument of the moment:

> **American work must again be governed by American ownership and American obligation.**

He is not the most charismatic candidate.

He does not need to be.

The crash has made the election a referendum on Reagan’s economic order.

Harwood’s legislative experience also makes him appear capable of using the congressional supermajority rather than merely celebrating it.

## Vice President: Wesley Crane

Crane gives the ticket:

- the Mountain West;
- anti-income-tax populism;
- small-property rhetoric;
- a military and resource background;
- and protection against the accusation that Harwood merely wants a centralized industrial bureaucracy.

The **Harwood–Crane ticket** contains its own future conflict.

Harwood wants national economic institutions.

Crane distrusts national institutions that can overpower states and owners.

That is useful. It means the winning ticket does not conceal the party’s contradiction. It carries that contradiction into the administration.

# Landry’s role after the convention

Landry accepts the result.

Buchanan pressures him to do so, but Landry also understands that an open schism could permit the Old Guard to claim constitutional politics has failed.

He gives a strong convention speech built around:

> “We contested the nomination so the Republic would have a choice. We unite now so the Republic may survive.”

He remains the leader of the constitutional Buchananites.

That makes him a plausible:

- Secretary of State;
- Senate leader;
- later presidential candidate;
- or internal critic of Harwood’s corporatist programme.

He does not disappear merely because he loses.

# What National Renewal looks like in power

By January 1993, National Renewal has:

- the presidency;
- an enormous House majority;
- a Senate majority approaching or exceeding two-thirds;
- most interior and industrial governorships;
- and a deeply demoralized Democratic-Republican opposition.

But it does not possess one economic doctrine.

The party’s common commitments are narrower than the electoral landslide suggests:

- foreign capital must not control American industry;
- wages and family property require protection;
- the income tax should be abolished;
- American productive capacity must be restored;
- strategic technology and space must continue;
- immigration must remain restricted;
- and Reagan’s open-market settlement cannot be restored unchanged.

The disagreements begin immediately after that.

Harwood wants sector councils.

Crane wants state and producer autonomy.

Kincaid wants cooperative and family ownership.

Landry wants constitutional limits.

Bell wants competent technical administration.

Cade wants ideological and political discipline.

That is why the 1992 victory can be both overwhelming and unstable.

# The broader political consequence

National Renewal’s open-slate culture changes American democracy.

In its strongest regions, the meaningful election is no longer:

> National Renewal or Democratic-Republican?

It becomes:

> Which National Renewal?

A Montana voter may choose among:

- a Crane-style producer federalist;
- a Harwood-style industrial organizer;
- and a Buchananite constitutional nationalist.

The Democratic-Republican candidate may be present but politically secondary.

This creates a one-party-dominant system without necessarily creating a formally one-party state.

That distinction matters.

Elections remain real.

Candidates genuinely disagree.

Incumbents can lose.

But the range of viable national politics increasingly lies inside one movement.

The final working sequence would therefore be:

| Election | National Renewal ticket | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **1984** | Howard Phillips–Gabriel Landry | Organizational succession to Buchanan; defeated by Reagan |
| **1988** | Nathaniel Bell–Miriam Kincaid | Mission-technocratic adaptation to the Reagan boom; defeated decisively |
| **1992** | Thomas Harwood–Wesley Crane | Industrial and producer backlash after the crash; elected overwhelmingly |

The clean conclusion is:

> Buchanan turns National Renewal into a constitutional governing party, but he never turns it into a coherent party. After he leaves office, its factions stop competing merely over emphasis and begin competing over which American order National Renewal is supposed to build. The depression gives all of them a common enemy. It does not give them a common answer.
