# Japanese brands without an American consumer century

Yes. This changes much more than the language printed on the front of a radio.

Historically, several Japanese firms did not merely export existing products to the United States. They reorganized their corporate identities, dealer systems, product names, dimensions, controls, styling, advertising, and sometimes their entire understanding of quality around success in the American market.

In this setting, Japan’s first large external consumer market is instead its own imperial-commercial sphere:

- Nanjing China;
- Korea and Formosa;
- Manchukuo;
- Siam;
- Malaya and Singapore;
- the East Indies;
- Indochinese protectorates;
- Burma;
- and, after independence, the Philippines.

The result is not that Japanese companies abandon Roman letters. Romanized names remain useful in the Philippines, maritime trade, technical catalogs, model numbers, and multilingual Southeast Asia. The distinction is that **Romanization does not have to mean Anglicization**.

A company can write **HONDA**, **TOTSUKO**, **SEIKO**, or **NIKON** in Latin characters while preserving an unmistakably Japanese identity.

## First, the name correction

The historical company was **Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo**, or Tokyo Telecommunications Engineering Corporation—東京通信工業—not “Tokyo Chushin Kogyo.”

Its common Japanese abbreviation was **Totsuko**. And *kōgyō* simply means industry or industrial enterprise. A Filipino customer probably would not call the company “Kogyo” by itself, because that would be rather like calling General Electric “Industrial.”

**Totsuko** is the much more plausible popular name.

Historically, the company’s leadership wanted something shorter because “Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo” and “Totsuko” were difficult for American customers to pronounce. The company adopted Sony as its corporate name in 1958 after using the mark on radios. Its official history explicitly connects that decision to its attempt to establish an independent brand in the American market rather than selling radios beneath an American distributor’s name. citeturn897352search0

That makes Sony the clearest example of a company whose alternate identity should change.

---

# Three historical branding patterns

The rabbit hole divides into three main categories.

| Pattern | Historical examples | Alternate-setting consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Corporate rename for global accessibility | Sony, Ricoh, later Sharp | Rename may be delayed, altered, or based on an Asia-wide mark |
| Separate export brand beneath a Japanese parent | Panasonic under Matsushita; Datsun under Nissan; Lexus under Toyota much later | Export brand is designed for the Sphere rather than America |
| Product-specific foreign-market identity | Honda 50, Fairlady, American advertisements and model packages | Product retains a Japanese or character-based name and receives local variants |

Some companies fall into more than one category.

---

# A likely Co-Prosperity branding system

The mature Japanese firm probably uses three simultaneous identities.

## 1. The legal corporate name

This remains Japanese and institutional:

- Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo;
- Matsushita Electric Industrial;
- Nippon Kogaku;
- Hayakawa Electric;
- Toyota Motor;
- Nissan Motor.

Government contracts, banks, factories, patents, and company housing use the full name.

## 2. The imperial consumer mark

This is short enough to print on a product and recognizable across several markets.

It may be:

- a founder surname: Honda, Matsushita, Toyota;
- a Japanese abbreviation: Totsuko, Ricoh;
- an established short mark: Sharp, Canon, Seiko;
- or a one- or two-character kanji mark readable throughout the Chinese-character sphere.

The graphic mark can stay the same while the spoken name changes. A Japanese buyer and a Chinese buyer can see the same characters and pronounce them differently.

## 3. The local sales identity

Distributors adapt:

- product descriptions;
- instruction manuals;
- control labels;
- advertising;
- financing;
- service networks;
- and occasionally the spoken form of the brand.

The Philippine appliance may display **TOTSUKO** in Roman letters. The same radio in Nanjing might carry a two-character mark with its Mandarin reading. The Korean model may use the Japanese name almost unchanged because Korean public life is undergoing Japanization. The underlying model number remains common throughout the sphere.

That is consistent with the wider Co-Prosperity system already established: Japanese products and culture circulate broadly, but associated states retain local languages, broadcasters, institutions, and commercial intermediaries rather than becoming one undifferentiated Japanese domestic market. fileciteturn16file0 fileciteturn16file11

---

# Company by company

## Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo: Sony probably does not initially exist

This is the strongest divergence.

Historically, the Sony name solved several problems at once:

- the full company name was long;
- Totsuko was awkward for many Americans;
- Japanese radios were often sold under American brands;
- the founders wanted a mark pronounceable in many languages;
- the company wanted its own identity rather than anonymous contract manufacture. citeturn897352search0

Without the American market as the decisive test, none of that forces a 1958 corporate rename.

### Most likely setting outcome

**Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo remains the legal company name through at least the 1960s.**

Its consumer mark becomes:

**TOTSUKO**

That is already short, distinct, Japanese, and usable in Roman letters. It works well in:

- Manila;
- Bangkok;
- Singapore;
- Jakarta;
- Saigon;
- maritime catalogs;
- international trade fairs.

For the Chinese-character market, a working possibility is **東通**, visually representing something like “Eastern Communications” or “Tokyo Communications.” It could be read differently in Japanese and Mandarin while remaining the same printed emblem. This should remain a working proposal until we choose the exact mark, because character associations and existing names need to be checked carefully.

A typical product might therefore carry:

> **東通 / TOTSUKO**  
> Model TR-63

The product code provides the universal technical identity. The characters provide the imperial Asian identity. The Roman mark serves regions using Latin script.

### Could Sony ever appear?

Yes, but later and more narrowly.

Once Japan begins serious exports beyond the Sphere—to America, Britain, Latin Europe, or neutral markets—Totsuko might establish **Sony** as an extra-sphere export mark. But that would be analogous to Lexus: a market-facing identity beneath a larger Japanese company, not necessarily the corporate name itself.

That gives us an interesting 1970s arrangement:

- **Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo:** legal parent;
- **Totsuko/東通:** Co-Prosperity consumer identity;
- **Sony:** selected Atlantic or Latin export identity.

Whether Sony eventually displaces the other two would depend on later détente and consumer success.

---

## Matsushita: Panasonic is probably absent

Panasonic is an even cleaner case.

The official company history says the Panasonic name first appeared in 1955 on speakers designed for export, specifically using the idea of universal sound; the first product carrying the mark was sold in the United States. Matsushita Electric Industrial remained the corporate name for decades. citeturn897352search1turn897352search5

In this setting, the reason to invent **Panasonic** in 1955 is largely absent.

### Likely setting outcome

The company continues using:

- **Matsushita** as its corporate and high-trust identity;
- **National** or another established household mark for mass appliances;
- **松下** as a character logo in China and the kanji markets;
- **MATSUSHITA** in the Philippines and much of Southeast Asia.

Matsushita is unusually well suited to the Sphere because the surname already has a stable character form. Chinese consumers may pronounce 松下 differently, but they can recognize and remember it without a phonetic invention.

Panasonic could still appear much later as an Atlantic export line, but it probably never becomes the universal company identity.

---

## Honda: the name survives, but the whole expansion path changes

Honda does not need an Americanized name. It is a founder surname, visually short, easy to romanize, and strongly associated with the company itself.

What changes is the product and distribution strategy.

Historically, Honda began exporting the Cub F-Type to Taiwan in 1952. Its own later history says the company surveyed Europe and Southeast Asia in 1956–57 before investigating America in 1958. The American expansion was therefore a deliberate choice made despite the obvious Southeast Asian opportunity. citeturn500842search3

In this setting, Honda follows the path its own researchers originally saw:

> **Taiwan and Southeast Asia first, America later.**

### Consequences

Honda establishes assembly and dealer networks in:

- Formosa;
- Siam;
- Malaya;
- the Philippines after 1958;
- the East Indies;
- Indochina;
- southern China.

The Super Cub becomes an imperial workhorse before it becomes a Western cultural novelty.

Regional versions differ in:

- cargo racks;
- suspension;
- dust protection;
- cooling;
- passenger seats;
- fuel quality;
- road clearance;
- rain protection;
- locally available tires.

Historically, Honda later built country-specific Super Cub forms and local production around Asian needs. citeturn500842search7 That process would begin earlier and become the company’s central commercial identity.

The U.S.-market name **Honda 50** and the famous American campaign presenting motorcycles as harmless middle-class recreation probably never become formative. Honda’s advertisements instead show:

- shopkeepers;
- rural nurses;
- postal workers;
- families;
- plantation supervisors;
- students;
- village cooperatives.

Honda’s identity becomes **useful mobility for a developing imperial Asia**, with racing supporting the engineering reputation.

---

## Sharp: the important counterexample

Not every English-looking Japanese brand depended on America.

Sharp was already exporting radios and components to China, Southeast Asia, India, and South America beginning in 1926. It held a radio fair in Shanghai the following year. citeturn500842search0turn500842search4

So **Sharp probably survives almost unchanged**.

Its English name is already familiar in precisely the Asian markets that dominate this setting. That makes Sharp a useful warning against applying one rule to every firm.

The legal company might remain Hayakawa Electric longer, or it might adopt Sharp Corporation even earlier because Sharp has become the standard imperial consumer mark.

Sharp becomes a company whose “foreign” name is no longer particularly Western. It is simply a long-established Asian electronics trademark written in Latin letters.

---

## Canon: the brand survives

Canon is another relatively stable case.

The Canon name predates the postwar American market. The company became Canon Camera in 1947, and the Japanese government designated Canon cameras as priority exports that year. citeturn500842search1

The brand is already:

- short;
- visually clear;
- usable internationally;
- attached to high-quality optics;
- independent of one particular foreign language.

Canon therefore remains **Canon**.

What changes is the market order. Its first great postwar expansion is likely aimed at:

- Japanese administrators;
- Chinese professionals;
- newspapers;
- police and survey services;
- associated-state governments;
- wealthy urban consumers;
- imperial tourism.

A dedicated American subsidiary does not appear on the historical schedule. Canon’s Taiwan or Nanjing manufacturing and sales operations probably precede any large American organization. Historically, Canon did not establish its U.S. subsidiary until 1966 and opened Taiwanese manufacturing in 1970, so reversing those priorities is institutionally plausible. citeturn500842search9turn500842search14

---

## Ricoh: probably still Ricoh, but for a different reason

Ricoh is more likely to survive than Sony because it functions as a corporate condensation rather than a culturally American word.

The company can retain Riken Optical longer, but a short **RICOH** mark is still attractive for:

- cameras;
- copiers;
- office machines;
- model plates;
- industrial catalogs.

The reason would not be “Americans cannot pronounce our company name.” It would be:

> The imperial office-equipment market needs one compact mark that fits cameras, copiers, calculating devices, and service contracts.

This is an example where the same name may arise from different commercial pressure.

---

## Nissan and Datsun: dual identity becomes permanent

Datsun was not invented for postwar America. The name existed before the war and therefore plausibly survives. Nissan began full-scale American passenger-car exports in 1958, but Datsun already had its own marque identity. citeturn897352search3turn897352search7

The setting’s most likely structure is:

- **Nissan:** parent company, heavy industry, trucks, institutional fleets and government relationships;
- **Datsun:** compact passenger cars, taxis, light commercial vehicles and regional export markets.

That division could become permanent.

### Product names change more than the marque

Names such as:

- Fairlady;
- Bluebird;
- Sunny;
- Cedric;
- Gloria

reflect different mixtures of Japanese, European and export-market aspiration.

Some may still appear because English words have modern prestige beyond the English-speaking world. But China’s commercial weight encourages stable character names as well.

A car might carry:

- **DATSUN** as the manufacturer;
- a Chinese-character model name in Nanjing;
- a Japanese reading at home;
- the same numerical chassis designation everywhere.

The U.S.-oriented Fairlady identity is particularly likely to change. The underlying sports car can exist, but a courtly Japanese or character-based name better fits a sphere whose prestige consumers are in Tokyo, Shanghai, Keijō, Taihoku, Manila and Bangkok.

---

## Toyota: no need for an early Lexus analogue

Toyota itself remains Toyota. The name is Japanese, compact, easy to romanize and already attached to a major industrial concern.

The later Lexus arrangement is useful as a structural analogy, but not as a brand to accelerate.

Historically, Toyota began Lexus operations in 1989 as a dedicated luxury sales network in the United States, while the corresponding flagship was sold in Japan as the Toyota Celsior. citeturn897352search4turn897352search8

That tells us what Lexus fundamentally was:

> not merely a different badge, but a separate foreign-market promise concerning dealers, service, prestige and customer treatment.

In this setting, Toyota does not need that architecture in the 1950s or 1960s.

Its premium lines remain:

- Crown;
- Century;
- high-grade Toyopet or Toyota sedans;
- official limousines;
- specialist grand tourers.

If Japan eventually creates a distinct luxury export marque, it will probably be designed for Chinese and imperial elite culture. It might use:

- a two-character courtly name;
- a concept such as dignity, harmony, brilliance or sovereign service;
- dedicated dealers in Shanghai, Singapore, Manila and Bangkok;
- a logo legible in both Japanese and Chinese traditions.

It would not need to sound vaguely European or American.

## Prince Motors may eliminate the later luxury-brand problem

Prince is especially valuable in this setting.

Historically, Prince developed the Skyline and Gloria before its later absorption into Nissan. Nissan’s own historical material associates Prince with those technically ambitious prestige models. citeturn897352search3

Without occupation restructuring and with a larger imperial market, Prince may remain independent—or be preserved as a semi-independent prestige marque inside a broader industrial group.

That gives Japan an existing answer to the later Lexus problem:

- Toyota has Crown and Century;
- Nissan has Datsun below and Prince above;
- Honda develops its own engineering identity;
- Mazda/Toyo Kogyo occupies the rotary and sporting niche.

Rather than inventing new pseudo-Western luxury brands in the 1980s, Japan can retain older Japanese marques with real corporate histories.

---

# China’s effect on naming

China’s importance does not mean every product receives a fully Chinese identity.

It produces a more specific practice: **character clearance**.

Before launching a brand, Japanese firms test:

- whether the characters have a positive meaning;
- whether the Mandarin pronunciation is acceptable;
- whether Cantonese or other major readings create unfortunate associations;
- whether the mark resembles an existing Chinese firm;
- whether it can be printed clearly on a product;
- whether it can be paired with a Roman model code.

This is the functional equivalent of testing whether a Japanese name sounds awkward in English.

Because the Nanjing state likely continues using traditional characters, Japanese pre-reform or traditional kanji forms remain visually closer to Chinese commercial writing than they would be to later simplified mainland Chinese.

The same mark may therefore develop several spoken identities.

For example, a hypothetical 東通 emblem could be:

- read as a Japanese corporate abbreviation in Tokyo;
- given a Mandarin reading in Nanjing;
- called **Totsuko** in Manila;
- identified by model number among technicians everywhere.

That is not branding confusion. It is a normal multinational brand with one visual logo and several local readings.

---

# The poster children

| Historical company | What shaped the historical identity | Best alternate outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo/Sony | Independent brand for American and global pronunciation | Totsuko/character mark dominates Sphere; Sony possibly later extra-sphere brand |
| Matsushita/Panasonic | Panasonic first used on a U.S.-export speaker | Matsushita, National and 松下 remain primary |
| Honda | Leadership chose America after studying Southeast Asia | Asia-first assembly, service and Super Cub variants; Honda name unchanged |
| Sharp/Hayakawa | Already exporting under Sharp in China and Southeast Asia before the war | Sharp survives and may become corporate name earlier |
| Nissan/Datsun | Datsun became major export passenger-car identity | Nissan parent, Datsun sphere-wide mass marque |
| Toyota/Lexus | Dedicated U.S. luxury brand and sales network in 1989 | Crown, Century and perhaps separate Japanese prestige marque; no early Lexus |
| Canon | Short prewar brand and state-supported camera exports | Canon survives; Asian institutions and consumers are first priority |
| Ricoh/Riken | Shortened multi-product office and optical identity | Ricoh likely survives, although the timing may change |
| Prince | Independent technical-premium manufacturer later absorbed | Strong candidate to survive as Japan’s prestige marque |

---

# Recommended working canon

I would lock the broad principle now and leave exact product logos open.

1. **Japanese export branding is Asia-first, not America-first.**

2. **Roman letters remain common, but Romanization does not imply an English semantic name.** HONDA, TOTSUKO, TOYOTA and SEIKO are Japanese brands rendered in a trade script.

3. **China encourages character-based companion marks.** The logo may be constant while its spoken reading differs between Japanese and Chinese markets.

4. **Korea and Formosa receive Japanese identities most directly.** China receives character-based localization. Southeast Asia and the Philippines receive romanized Japanese brands with local-language product descriptions.

5. **Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo does not become Sony in 1958.** Its likely mass-market identity is Totsuko, possibly paired with a short character mark.

6. **“Kogyo” does not become its colloquial brand**, because the word is generic.

7. **Panasonic probably does not arise on its historical schedule.** Matsushita and its established household brands dominate the Sphere.

8. **Honda remains Honda**, but its formative overseas experience occurs in Taiwan and Southeast Asia rather than California.

9. **Sharp and Canon survive largely unchanged**, demonstrating that not every globally usable Japanese brand was created for Americans.

10. **Nissan and Datsun remain distinct corporate and market identities.**

11. **Toyota does not need a Lexus-type division during this period.** Crown, Century and possibly a surviving Prince marque satisfy the premium market.

12. **Separate Atlantic-facing brands can appear later.** They remain export subsidiaries or product marks unless commercial détente makes them more prestigious than the original imperial identities.

The deeper consequence is that Japanese goods do not present themselves as culturally neutral objects that happen to be made in Japan.

They present themselves as **Japanese modernity made useful throughout Asia**.

# This should revise the 1992 outcome, not merely add another faction

The strongest version is that **National Renewal wins the country in 1992 but fails to elect its own president**.

Its congressional candidates still dominate because the depression has discredited Reagan’s Democratic-Republicans. But the presidential coalition fractures during the campaign. One large National Renewal faction urges voters to support Renewal candidates for Congress while withholding support from the official presidential ticket.

The result is a contingent election in the House, followed almost immediately by the formal breakup of National Renewal.

That is larger than the party’s original arrival because it changes not only who competes, but how the presidency is selected, how corporations invest in politics, and what party reunification would cost.

National Renewal was already a coalition of Buchananites, corporatists, Christian-social politicians, mission technocrats, institutionalists, and the Rockwell Old Guard. Buchanan held those currents together through personal authority and by rejecting the most openly one-party constitutional proposals. fileciteturn49file3turn49file17 The depression gives them a common enemy in Reaganism, but it does not remove the differences among their proposed replacements.

# The 1992 rupture

The previous proposal of a unified Harwood–Crane ticket no longer works. The election should instead expose the contradiction between them.

## Thomas Harwood wins the official nomination

Harwood enters the convention with the largest congressional organization. His Productive Commonwealth faction argues that the depression has proved three things:

- national industry cannot be left to international finance;
- essential firms have obligations beyond shareholder profit;
- and reconstruction requires permanent institutions connecting government, labor, credit, and production.

Harwood wins the nomination after securing support from heavy industry, organized labor nationalists, and Nathaniel Bell’s mission technocrats. Bell could become his running mate, giving the ticket aerospace, computing, and administrative credibility.

This is a legitimate convention victory. It is not necessarily a clean one.

Large corporations have funded delegate operations, policy organizations, travel, media, and state-party debts. Harwood’s opponents believe that formally lawful corporate influence has determined which delegates could afford to attend and which state organizations remained solvent.

## Wesley Crane refuses the result

Crane is the candidate most plausibly willing to break the party.

Everett Cade would denounce nearly everyone, but his Old Guard base is too narrow to transform the entire election. Gabriel Landry is too committed to Buchanan’s constitutional discipline to encourage an electoral sabotage campaign before exhausting every internal remedy.

Crane, however, can argue that Harwood is replacing American producers with a compact among Washington, national unions, banks, and a handful of systems corporations.

His convention speech might end with:

> **“Vote Renewal where the name still means work, property, and self-government. But do not give the presidency to men who purchased the seal and now claim they inherited the movement.”**

He urges his supporters to continue voting for National Renewal candidates in House, Senate, state, and local races.

For president, he either launches an independent **American Producers** ticket with Miriam Kincaid or tells voters to withhold their presidential vote from Harwood.

A Crane–Kincaid ticket is stronger because it gives his voters somewhere to go and ensures that the Electoral College fragments.

## Landry does not initially bolt

Landry accepts that Harwood won the convention, but he refuses to campaign enthusiastically for the compulsory-council programme.

His constitutional Renewal supporters divide three ways:

- some vote Harwood out of party loyalty;
- some vote Crane because they distrust corporatism;
- some vote Democratic-Republican because they fear Harwood’s constitutional programme more than Reagan’s economic legacy.

This produces the unexpectedly large Democratic-Republican vote.

# The Democratic-Republican candidate

A **George H. W. Bush-type figure** is the cleaner fit for 1992 than a Clinton-type figure.

The country is choosing a president during a financial depression, constitutional fracture, and likely House election. A cautious institutional negotiator is more useful than a charismatic ideological realigner.

A Clinton-like figure can enter as his running mate and become more important later.

## Andrew Prescott Hale

**Born:** 1944, Connecticut  
**Background:** Naval Air Corps reconnaissance officer, intelligence and diplomatic service, House member, ambassador to Canada, and Reagan’s secretary of state or national security adviser  
**Faction:** Institutional Democratic-Republican  
**Public type:** Courteous, restrained, foreign-policy experienced, emotionally difficult to read

Hale is not a Reaganite evangelist.

He supports:

- the constitutional market order;
- strategic industrial ownership;
- the post-Falklands diplomatic settlement;
- open trade without renewed foreign corporate control;
- and gradual rather than compulsory domestic restructuring.

His central argument is:

> **“America does not need another experiment conducted at emergency speed.”**

That allows him to criticize both Reagan’s initial opening and Harwood’s proposed corporatization.

## Caleb Rowan Harlan

**Born:** 1948, Arkansas  
**Background:** Lawyer, education reformer, and governor  
**Public type:** Charismatic, policy-fluent, socially adaptable, and unusually good at presenting corporate and professional reform as concern for ordinary households

Harlan is the Clinton-type figure.

As Hale’s running mate, he gives the ticket:

- the South;
- younger voters;
- working-class communication;
- and a future beyond the old Reagan administration.

Hale supplies reassurance. Harlan supplies the campaign.

# A plausible 1992 result

The exact totals can remain open, but the electorate should divide into four principal presidential blocs.

| Ticket | Approximate popular vote | Political base |
|---|---:|---|
| Harwood–Bell | 31–34% | Industrial National Renewal, unions, technocrats, large-system corporatists |
| Hale–Harlan | 28–31% | Democratic-Republicans, constitutional defectors, professional and commercial states |
| Crane–Kincaid | 19–23% | Plains, Mountain West, agrarian and small-business producers |
| Cade or Old Guard ticket | 6–9% | Racial-nationalist and emergency-state districts |
| Others | 4–8% | Regional and local movements |

National Renewal candidates can still win perhaps three hundred or more House seats in aggregate. But those members no longer form one reliable presidential coalition.

No candidate receives an Electoral College majority.

The Constitution sends the top three presidential candidates to the House, where every state delegation casts one vote. That mechanism has already selected presidents in this setting, including the 1968 Rockefeller–Rockwell crisis. fileciteturn49file0turn49file1

# The January 1993 House election

The House result should be even more consequential than the popular election.

Harwood has the largest number of nominally National Renewal representatives.

But state delegations divide among:

- Harwood corporatists;
- Crane producer nationalists;
- Landry constitutionalists;
- Cade’s Old Guard;
- and Democratic-Republicans.

A state with six Harwood representatives, five constitutional Renewal representatives, and one Democratic-Republican does not automatically cast its vote for Harwood. Its delegation may deadlock.

## The first ballots

Harwood leads but cannot reach the required majority of states.

Hale controls the unified Democratic-Republican delegations.

Crane controls enough western and Plains delegations to prevent either from winning.

Cade’s supporters abstain or make symbolic demands.

## The Landry bargain

Landry’s constitutional faction becomes decisive.

He does not argue that Hale won a popular mandate. He argues that the House has a constitutional duty to select a president capable of governing without converting occupational representation into a new constitutional order.

His defense is:

> **“The Constitution does not instruct us to ratify the largest faction. It instructs us to choose a president.”**

Landry’s delegations move toward Hale after obtaining commitments that the new administration will:

- preserve the income-tax repeal;
- retain foreign strategic-ownership restrictions;
- avoid restoring Reagan’s old portfolio-investment system;
- continue defense and space programmes;
- reject compulsory occupational citizenship;
- and allow Congress to legislate industrial recovery within ordinary constitutional powers.

Some Crane delegations follow. Others abstain.

Hale wins on perhaps the fourth or fifth House ballot with twenty-six or twenty-seven state delegations.

The Senate selects Harlan as vice president through a comparable bargain.

# Why this destroys National Renewal

Harwood’s supporters see the result as a second stolen mandate.

But unlike 1968, Democrats and Republicans have not united to stop National Renewal from outside. National Renewal representatives themselves have selected the Democratic-Republican candidate.

The competing memories are irreconcilable.

Harwood’s faction says:

> The producers won the election, and constitutional lawyers delivered the presidency to the party of the crash.

Landry’s faction says:

> Harwood tried to use an economic emergency to convert National Renewal into an occupational state Buchanan had explicitly rejected.

Crane’s faction says:

> Both sides treated independent producers as votes to be traded after corporations had already selected the choices.

Cade says:

> Electoral politics has once again proved incapable of expressing the national will.

Buchanan can condemn violence and defend the legality of the House decision. He cannot make the factions reunite afterward.

# The 1993 party system

The legal and organizational breakup follows during the spring and summer of 1993.

Five durable national organizations emerge.

| Party | Leading figure | Principal character |
|---|---|---|
| **National Productive Party** | Thomas Harwood | Chartered industry, sector councils, labor obligations, strategic production |
| **Constitutional Renewal Party** | Gabriel Landry | Buchananite nationalism, family policy, defense, constitutional limits |
| **American Producers Alliance** | Wesley Crane and Miriam Kincaid | Small property, farms, cooperatives, states, tax abolition, anti-bank politics |
| **National Vanguard** | Everett Cade | Old Guard racial nationalism, party discipline, emergency authority |
| **Democratic-Republican Party** | Andrew Hale and Caleb Harlan | Constitutional markets, commercial opening, gradual reform, anti-capture language |

Some states continue using **National Renewal** as a fusion ballot label under which two or three of the successor parties may endorse the same local candidate.

In other states they compete directly.

That preserves the user’s earlier idea that Montana or the Dakotas may have several Renewal-descended candidates facing one Democratic-Republican.

# Why corporations keep the split alive

Corporate sponsorship does not create the initial disagreement. It prevents the natural pressure toward reunification from succeeding.

A single National Renewal primary is expensive and unpredictable. Every faction brings delegates, churches, unions, producer associations, ideological institutes, and regional machines into one contest.

Separate parties are easier to underwrite.

A corporation can support:

- a Harwood candidate where sector representation benefits it;
- a Landry candidate where constitutional business autonomy is more useful;
- a Crane candidate where low taxes and resource development matter;
- and a Democratic-Republican candidate as protection against all three.

The company does not need to win every election. It needs every likely winner to remain within an acceptable policy range.

The split therefore becomes materially entrenched through:

- separate donor networks;
- separate campaign consultants;
- separate corporate patrons;
- separate media outlets;
- and separate congressional caucuses.

Reunification would threaten the careers and financing systems of thousands of politicians and political employees.

That is why the 1993 schism is more durable than the original emergence of National Renewal.

# Making House elections routine

Five parties alone do not guarantee contingent presidential elections.

Under winner-take-all state rules, one candidate could still win many states with only 35% of the vote and accumulate an Electoral College majority.

To make the intended semi-parliamentary system persist, a second development is needed.

## State elector reform

Between 1993 and 1996, the successor parties promote state laws allocating electors:

- proportionally;
- by congressional district;
- or through a hybrid in which two statewide electors go to the plurality winner and the remainder follow districts.

Every faction has a reason to support this somewhere.

A smaller party would rather receive six electors than finish second and receive none.

A regionally concentrated party wants its districts reflected.

Corporate political organizations prefer an election in which several sponsored parties remain relevant after November.

Because states determine how their presidential electors are appointed, much of this can occur without a federal constitutional amendment.

By 1996, enough large states have abandoned pure winner-take-all allocation that an Electoral College majority becomes difficult.

## The functional result

The public election becomes the **first ballot**.

Its purposes are to determine:

- which three candidates reach the House;
- how much bargaining legitimacy each possesses;
- and which state delegations their parties control.

The newly elected House then conducts the effective **second ballot**.

Corporate political offices increasingly concentrate on:

- House races;
- state-delegation composition;
- small-state representatives;
- and the bargaining commitments candidates make before the contingent election.

Formally, the United States remains presidential. The president serves a fixed term and does not fall after losing a vote of confidence.

Functionally, presidential formation becomes semi-parliamentary because the executive frequently emerges from a legislative coalition assembled after the national vote.

The previous contingent elections of 1956 and 1968 mean the mechanism is already familiar, even though both were politically damaging. fileciteturn49file0turn49file14

# The failed anti-corruption bill

The late-1990s bill should fail twice.

## The 1997 clean bill

The original **Campaign Independence and Public Trust Act** attempts to regulate:

- direct corporate donations;
- corporate campaign loans;
- in-kind data and consulting;
- political spending through subsidiaries and associations;
- coordinated “independent” advertising;
- and post-office employment arrangements.

It also provides limited public broadcasting and matching support so an unsponsored candidate can become visible.

The bill is defeated clearly, not narrowly.

Most legislators already rely upon some combination of:

- corporate campaign money;
- corporate consultants;
- affiliated business organizations;
- favorable credit;
- media access;
- or concession contractors.

Others oppose it on free-speech and association grounds.

## The 1998 substitute

The title is reused the following year for a measure so heavily amended that it no longer describes the contents.

The **Campaign Independence and Public Trust Act of 1998** eventually contains three major titles.

### Title I: Registered political sponsorship

Direct candidate donations receive nominal limits.

But corporations gain legal safe harbors for:

- independent advertising;
- registered issue campaigns;
- polling and data services;
- political education through affiliated associations;
- campaign loans on declared terms;
- and support transferred after a preferred candidate withdraws.

The law requires disclosure while legitimizing the portfolio system.

A politician can now publicly list several principal sponsors and claim that disclosure proves independence.

### Title II: Unified enterprise classification

Congress cannot abolish state-created LLCs, corporations, and partnerships merely by changing federal tax law.

It can, however, treat nearly every limited-liability entity as one **federal enterprise class** for taxation, reporting, campaign rights, and interstate administration.

State-law distinctions continue governing internal ownership and liability.

Federally, the old distinctions among:

- C corporations;
- S corporations;
- LLCs;
- professional corporations;
- and similar limited-liability forms

become much less important.

Because the individual federal income tax has already been abolished, the old pass-through-versus-corporate distinction is also less necessary. Business income is taxed once at the enterprise level, while distributions to owners are generally not taxed as individual income.

For a middle-class proprietor, this is easier in one sense:

- one return;
- one federal classification;
- fewer elections among tax forms.

It is harder in another:

- regulations written for corporations apply to his consultancy or restaurant as readily as to Ford or Concord.

That is exactly the defensive consequence the large firms want.

A politician proposing a “corporate tax increase” is no longer clearly targeting only large public companies. Millions of local owners hear that their own enterprise tax may rise.

### Title III: Open commerce

The substitute bill removes most quantitative import and export restrictions on ordinary goods and services.

It permits:

- unrestricted ordinary exports;
- broad import access;
- freer foreign sourcing;
- easier American branch formation abroad;
- and simpler commercial settlement.

It retains:

- the ban on foreign portfolio control of American companies;
- strategic technology restrictions;
- defense and orbital controls;
- sanctions;
- and the government’s authority to bar hostile ownership.

The resulting doctrine is:

> **Open commerce, closed ownership.**

It is not Reagan’s old system.

Goods, services, components, and American corporations can cross borders.

Foreign capital cannot quietly purchase the domestic corporate estate again.

The megacorporations support this because it gives them:

- cheaper inputs;
- larger export markets;
- foreign branches;
- and overseas assets

without exposing them to foreign acquisition at home.

Critics call the final legislation the **Sponsor’s Charter**. Reformers who introduced the original bill vote against the measure still bearing its name.

# Why small owners defend the arrangement

The unified enterprise category binds large and small corporations politically.

A proposal aimed at “corporations” now appears to cover:

- Concord;
- Interlink;
- a family gas station;
- a two-person software consultancy;
- a restaurant;
- a rural repair shop;
- and a private medical practice.

Large systems corporations strengthen that identification through their affiliate networks.

They tell small owners:

> “The same politicians who want to regulate us will eventually regulate you. We have the lawyers to survive it. You do not.”

That statement is self-serving.

It is also often true.

The large corporation then offers to handle:

- taxes;
- certification;
- insurance;
- political representation;
- and reporting

for its affiliates.

The regulation that creates fear also increases dependence upon the patron.

# The hemispheric commercial order

The trade opening allows American systems corporations to become major foreign-policy actors.

Washington continues to say they are private firms.

Foreign governments increasingly treat them as the economic instruments of the Monroe Doctrine.

An American company can enter a smaller Latin American economy with:

- credit;
- communications;
- payment systems;
- transport;
- insurance;
- consumer goods;
- technical schools;
- and access to the American market.

That package may be more attractive than a traditional military alliance.

But once the company operates essential systems, the host government finds that commercial disagreement can affect:

- customs revenue;
- employment;
- port traffic;
- communications;
- and access to American finance.

This is not direct annexation.

It is **corporate hemispheric preponderance**.

# Peru is the best first crisis

Peru is the cleanest hotspot because Japan already possesses disputed access around Samanco–Chimbote. The 1981 crisis preserves some Japanese presence, but the permanent military profile, legal status, and treaty ceilings remain deliberately open. fileciteturn49file7turn42file3

## The Lima Open Commerce Compact

Around 1997 or 1998, Peru signs a major agreement with the United States.

Peru receives:

- tariff-free or nearly tariff-free access to the American market;
- debt restructuring;
- port and railway investment;
- communications modernization;
- mining and fisheries finance;
- and substantial American commercial credit.

American firms receive:

- unrestricted branch offices;
- broad profit repatriation;
- equal treatment in Peruvian procurement;
- long commercial concessions;
- access to ports and logistics;
- and protection against arbitrary nationalization.

For Peru, this is an excellent deal in the short term.

For American corporations, it opens a large Pacific foothold.

For Japan, it looks like America has obtained through corporate access what Tokyo spent decades constructing through state-backed development, naval agreements, and political cultivation.

## The Samanco Customs Incident

The likely skirmish occurs when the new Peruvian-American customs and port administration attempts to inspect a Japanese shipment entering the old Samanco–Chimbote complex.

Japan claims the shipment falls under its earlier access agreement.

Peru claims every facility on Peruvian soil is now subject to uniform customs and security inspection.

American systems contractors provide the port data, scanners, communications, and perhaps private security supporting the Peruvian authorities.

A confrontation at the quay produces:

- warning shots;
- several Peruvian and Japanese casualties;
- detention of technicians;
- and a brief seizure of cargo.

Japan sends naval forces to protect its personnel.

The United States moves ships and reconnaissance assets toward the area while insisting that it is defending Peruvian sovereignty rather than American corporate interests.

The crisis ends without war through a revised Samanco agreement:

- Japan retains limited access;
- Peru receives inspection authority;
- military storage is capped;
- American companies retain their commercial concessions;
- and neither great power admits retreat.

This becomes the first clear demonstration that the corporate order has not weakened American hemispheric nationalism.

It has made that nationalism harder to distinguish from private commercial expansion.

# The secondary hotspots

Germany and Argentina remain a serious second possibility.

American companies enter Argentine finance, communications, transport, and military conversion after the Falklands settlement. German firms attempt to preserve maintenance, licensing, and industrial ties without formally violating the base restrictions. The likely crisis concerns inspections, sanctioned ownership, or a disputed dual-use shipment rather than open combat.

Belize and Guatemala offer a more territorial danger.

American-supported mining, road, or security concessions in Guatemala could collide with British defense of Belize. That would place American corporate contractors and British personnel close enough for an accidental border exchange. Because Britain and America already possess the Halifax relationship, both governments would have strong incentives to suppress escalation.

Chile is a credible later Japanese-American competition over ports, copper, shipping, and Pacific communications.

But Peru should probably come first. It already contains the unresolved Japanese bridgehead, and the American corporate opening directly contests it.

# Revised political sequence

| Date | Proposed development |
|---|---|
| **1992** | Harwood wins the official National Renewal nomination; Crane refuses endorsement and runs with Kincaid |
| **Nov. 1992** | National Renewal dominates congressional elections, but four presidential tickets divide the Electoral College |
| **Jan. 1993** | Landry’s constitutional faction helps select Democratic-Republican Andrew Hale in the House |
| **Spring–summer 1993** | National Renewal formally divides into Productive, Constitutional, Producer, and Vanguard successor parties |
| **1993–1996** | State elector reforms make proportional or district allocation common |
| **1996 onward** | Contingent House elections become expected rather than exceptional |
| **1997** | Genuine campaign-finance reform is decisively defeated |
| **1998** | A captured substitute legalizes registered sponsorship, unifies federal enterprise taxation, and opens ordinary commerce |
| **1997–1999** | American corporate expansion into Peru produces the Lima compact and Samanco customs crisis |
| **Late 1990s** | Corporations maintain political portfolios across five parties and focus heavily on House state delegations |

# Working conclusion

This proposed direction makes the 1992 election the real constitutional hinge.

National Renewal does not split because its factions suddenly discover they disagree. It splits because one faction decides that allowing another to possess the presidency would be worse than allowing the Democratic-Republicans to hold it.

Corporations then discover that the fragmented system is useful.

Separate parties give them:

- cheaper nominations;
- multiple fallback candidates;
- regional specialization;
- and several bargaining positions in the House election.

The anti-corruption bill fails because the political class no longer experiences corporate sponsorship as an outside intrusion. It experiences sponsorship as the normal method through which candidates, parties, and even ideological causes become operational.

And the trade opening completes the transformation. American ownership remains protected at home, while American corporations acquire unprecedented freedom abroad.

The mature formula becomes:

> **The voters distribute the pieces.  
> The House assembles the government.  
> The corporations make sure every plausible assembly includes someone they know.**

You’re right. I had moved the schism into the 1992 election itself, when your intent is more precise:

> **1992 remains a two-party presidential election between National Renewal and the Democratic-Republicans. National Renewal wins outright. The campaign reveals that the party can no longer remain together, and the formal breakup follows in 1993.**

That distinction produces a much stronger transition. The last directly elected president is also the president whose victory destroys the party that elected him.

National Renewal already contains the necessary divisions. Buchanan held together constitutional nationalists, Christian-social politicians, mission technocrats, congressional institutionalists, corporatists, and the Rockwell Old Guard, while explicitly rejecting the attempt to replace the constitutional republic with permanent occupational and party government. fileciteturn51file0 The 1993 schism does not invent those disagreements. It removes Buchanan’s ability to keep them inside one organization.

# The corrected 1992 election

The presidential race still has only two serious tickets.

The Democratic-Republicans nominate a cautious, institutionally reassuring candidate—closer in temperament to George H. W. Bush than to Bill Clinton. The Clinton-like figure fits better as his younger running mate and possible future party leader.

The working tickets can remain:

| Party | Presidential ticket |
|---|---|
| National Renewal | **Thomas Harwood–Nathaniel Bell** |
| Democratic-Republican | **Andrew Prescott Hale–Caleb Harlan** |

These names remain working rather than established canon, but the political types fit.

Harwood represents the industrial and corporatist wing of National Renewal. Bell reassures the mission technocrats, aerospace establishment, engineers, and administrators.

Hale is an experienced diplomatic and national-security institutionalist. Harlan is the younger Southern governor who can speak about education, household economics, and recovery without sounding like a continuation of Reagan’s final years.

## Why Harwood wins the nomination

The depression has made Harwood’s argument powerful:

- foreign capital was allowed to penetrate American ownership;
- rapid divestiture then destroyed American financial value;
- private firms survived only where someone preserved production, employment, and credit;
- therefore industry requires permanent public obligations and organized national coordination.

Harwood also controls much of the congressional machinery created by the 1990 landslide. He has industrial unions, large manufacturers, reconstruction authorities, and mission technocrats behind him.

His convention victory can be lawful while still appearing captured.

The controversy concerns:

- corporate financing of delegate travel;
- state committees whose debts were paid by business associations;
- credential disputes;
- rules changed between the early primaries and the convention;
- and Harwood’s refusal to rule out compulsory national industrial councils.

There does not need to be proven ballot fraud. The deeper accusation is that corporations and congressional organizers determined which parts of National Renewal possessed the resources to compete.

# Gabriel Landry breaks the presidential coalition

Gabriel Landry is the strongest figure to issue the repudiation.

He was the 1984 vice-presidential nominee, is already associated with constitutional Buchananism, family policy, economic nationalism, Gulf industry, and technical education, and has national standing independent of Harwood. fileciteturn51file1 More importantly, his supporters are precisely the National Renewal voters most capable of crossing over to a Bush-like Democratic-Republican.

Wesley Crane could attack Harwood more aggressively, but his supporters would be more likely to abstain or cast protest ballots. Everett Cade could denounce the nominee, but the Old Guard would not move enough mainstream votes.

Landry can actually change the election.

## The late-campaign declaration

Landry does not form another ticket. He does not tell voters to abandon National Renewal’s congressional candidates.

Instead, perhaps in an October 1992 address from Baton Rouge, he says something close to:

> **“Vote Renewal for Congress. Vote Renewal in your state and county. Support every candidate who still understands that the nation exists to protect the citizen, not to organize him into an estate. But I cannot ask a free American to place Thomas Harwood in the presidency.”**

His argument is not that Harwood’s nomination is legally void.

It is that Harwood no longer represents a legitimate continuation of Buchanan’s National Renewal.

That is the reverse-2016 quality you’re describing: a nationally prominent member of the party tells voters that the presidential nominee has crossed a line, while still asking them to elect the party down ballot.

## Buchanan’s position

Buchanan tries to prevent the rupture and fails.

He probably states that Harwood won the lawful nomination and that no faction has the right to destroy the party because it lost a convention. But he also refuses to describe Harwood’s full corporatist programme as Buchananism.

His support becomes formal rather than enthusiastic.

He might say:

> “The convention chose its nominee. The citizen retains his conscience.”

Harwood’s supporters hear sabotage.

Landry’s supporters hear permission.

Buchanan has not endorsed the presidential boycott, but he has also failed to command the movement into line. This is the moment when his authority becomes historical rather than operational.

# The election result

National Renewal still wins an outright Electoral College majority. That is necessary because 1992 is the last election not decided by the House.

The result should be much narrower than anyone expected when the campaign began.

A workable result is:

| Contest | Working result |
|---|---:|
| Popular vote | Harwood 51.0%; Hale 48.5%; others 0.5% |
| Electoral College | Harwood 286; Hale 252 |
| House | National Renewal 300–305; Democratic-Republican 130–135 |
| Senate | National Renewal 68–69; Democratic-Republican 31–32 |

Harwood does not win an Electoral College plurality. He wins a **narrow outright majority**. Before Landry’s declaration, polling may have suggested more than 400 electoral votes.

The striking feature is the split ticket.

Millions of voters cast ballots for:

- Hale for president;
- a National Renewal representative;
- a National Renewal senator;
- and National Renewal candidates in state government.

That explains how National Renewal can win congressional supermajorities while its presidential candidate barely survives.

The public verdict is not:

> “We reject National Renewal.”

It is:

> “We want National Renewal to reconstruct the country, but a very large minority does not trust this particular National Renewal president.”

# Why the 1993 schism follows immediately

Harwood enters office with a legal national mandate and enormous nominal congressional support.

But the word **nominal** matters.

His 300-plus House members may divide approximately into:

- 120–135 Productive Commonwealth corporatists;
- 65–75 constitutional Buchananites;
- 45–55 producer federalists and Christian-social agrarians;
- 20–30 mission technocrats who are not fully committed to Harwood;
- 15–20 Old Guard or Vanguard members;
- and several regional hybrids.

He possesses a National Renewal supermajority on paper.

He does not possess a Harwood supermajority.

## The immediate trigger

The schism probably becomes formal over congressional organization rather than one philosophical manifesto.

Harwood asks National Renewal legislators to sign a caucus programme committing them to:

- national sector councils;
- binding reconstruction plans;
- corporate service obligations;
- centralized industrial reporting;
- closure review;
- and support for the administration’s first reconstruction bill.

Landry’s constitutionalists refuse.

Crane and Kincaid’s producer bloc refuses for different reasons.

Cade refuses because Harwood has not gone far enough toward party-state control.

Harwood’s allies then attempt to:

- remove dissidents from committee chairmanships;
- deny access to the official National Renewal campaign funds;
- replace state committee officers;
- and classify defectors as no longer eligible for the party ballot line.

That converts ideological disagreement into organizational survival.

## The 1993 breakup

The likely sequence is:

| Date | Development |
|---|---|
| **January 1993** | Harwood is inaugurated as a National Renewal president |
| **February** | Administration introduces Productive Reconstruction programme |
| **March** | Landry’s members reject the binding caucus pledge |
| **April** | Harwood leadership removes or threatens dissident committee chairs |
| **May–June** | Separate congressional conferences form |
| **Summer 1993** | State committees and donor networks choose sides |
| **Autumn 1993** | The successor parties become permanent organizations |

Harwood’s faction retains the legal **National Renewal** name, national committee, presidential administration, and much of the ballot infrastructure through the remainder of the term.

Functionally, however, it has become the Productive Commonwealth party.

At the 1996 election it either adopts a new name—such as the **National Productive Party**—or uses a fusion label acknowledging that National Renewal no longer belongs exclusively to one faction.

# The five-party order

By 1994–96, the system contains five major organizations.

| Party or faction | Central position |
|---|---|
| Harwood’s National Renewal/Productive faction | Sector councils, chartered corporations, labor-capital coordination, national reconstruction |
| Constitutional Renewal | Landry’s Buchananite nationalism, constitutional limits, family policy, defense, strategic industry |
| American Producers | Crane and Kincaid’s small property, farms, cooperatives, state authority, tax abolition |
| National Vanguard | Cade’s Old Guard, party discipline, racial nationalism, emergency authority |
| Democratic-Republican | Constitutional markets, anti-capture reform, open commerce, gradual rather than compulsory reconstruction |

The names can still be refined, but the political geometry is sound.

# Why corporations preserve the schism

Corporations do not create the 1993 rupture. But once it occurs, they make reunification materially irrational.

A unified National Renewal primary is expensive and unpredictable. Every major faction competes for:

- the same delegates;
- the same activists;
- the same state committee;
- and the same national ballot line.

Separate parties let a corporation choose the most useful vehicle in each state.

A systems corporation can support:

- Harwood’s party where it wants formal status as the recognized representative of its industry;
- Landry’s party where it wants constitutional protection from compulsory federal councils;
- the Producers where it wants low taxes, domestic preference, or access to natural resources;
- the Democratic-Republicans where it wants freer trade or relief from National Renewal regulation;
- and occasionally the Vanguard as pressure against cultural or security reform.

Each corporation maintains several possible routes into government.

The parties also acquire separate:

- consulting firms;
- donor associations;
- media systems;
- policy institutes;
- data operations;
- and affiliated businesses.

Reunification would eliminate jobs, candidacies, committee leaderships, and corporate access points. Ideology might permit reconciliation. Institutional self-interest prevents it.

# Why 1992 is the last direct presidential victory

The five-party order does not automatically guarantee House selection. Winner-take-all electors could still give one candidate 270 votes with a relatively small popular plurality.

The transformation requires a second development after the schism.

## State elector reforms

Between 1993 and 1996, several successor parties convince states to replace winner-take-all appointment with:

- congressional-district electors;
- proportional allocation;
- or a hybrid system awarding two electors statewide and the rest by district.

The immediate reasons are not necessarily corrupt.

A party winning 20% statewide would rather receive four electors than none.

A regionally concentrated party wants its congressional districts represented.

A state legislature controlled by one successor faction may fear that another faction could win the state narrowly and take every elector.

Corporate political networks support the reforms because fragmented elector slates preserve multiple bargaining positions.

By 1996, no candidate is likely to reach an Electoral College majority.

The top three proceed to the House, where each state delegation casts one vote. The Senate chooses the vice president from the top two vice-presidential candidates.

## The semi-parliamentary reality

The United States remains formally presidential:

- the president serves a fixed term;
- Congress cannot remove him through an ordinary vote of no confidence;
- and the Cabinet is appointed rather than proportionally allocated by party.

Functionally, presidential formation becomes semi-parliamentary.

The public election determines:

- the top three candidates;
- each candidate’s bargaining legitimacy;
- and the membership of the state delegations.

The House then determines which coalition receives the presidency.

That makes House races more important than ever—particularly in small states.

Ironically, Montana, Idaho, Nebraska, and the Dakotas may become **more** attractive to corporate political investment after 1996. A comparatively inexpensive House race can determine how an entire state casts its one presidential vote.

A corporation need not purchase the presidency directly. It can invest in:

- one representative in Montana;
- two in Idaho;
- a disputed delegation in Nebraska;
- and a handful of small-state caucus brokers.

The voters still distribute the pieces. The political parties and corporate sponsors negotiate the assembly.

# The failed anti-corruption legislation

The reform effort now fits particularly well in 1997–98, after the first House-selected president of the new era.

## The genuine 1997 bill

The original **Campaign Independence and Public Trust Act** attempts to limit:

- direct corporate contributions;
- corporate campaign loans;
- in-kind polling, legal, advertising, and data services;
- spending through subsidiaries and affiliated associations;
- coordinated independent advertising;
- and promised post-office employment.

It also proposes basic public media access so candidates can become visible without first receiving a corporate sponsor.

The bill fails decisively.

By then, most members of all five parties depend upon some part of the sponsor system. Those who do not may still fear unilateral disarmament.

## The captured 1998 act

The title is revived in 1998 for a bill that is amended beyond recognition.

The resulting **Campaign Independence and Public Trust Act of 1998** contains three principal parts.

### Registered political sponsorship

Direct contributions receive nominal limits, but the law creates safe harbors for:

- disclosed independent advertising;
- registered issue campaigns;
- corporate polling and data services;
- campaign loans on published terms;
- trade and affiliate political education;
- and the transfer of support after a preferred candidate withdraws.

The act does not abolish corporate underwriting.

It gives it a recognized legal form.

The law’s defenders say disclosure is independence because no relationship remains hidden.

Its critics call it the **Sponsor’s Charter**.

### Unified federal enterprise classification

There is a technical distinction to preserve.

An LLC is a state-law organizational form. An S corporation is primarily a federal tax election. A C corporation is the ordinary federal corporate-tax category.

Congress cannot make every state entity legally identical merely by rewriting one tax statute.

It can, however, place nearly every limited-liability business into one **federal registered-enterprise class** for:

- federal taxation;
- campaign rights;
- interstate reporting;
- commercial regulation;
- and administrative treatment.

State distinctions continue to govern:

- internal ownership;
- liability;
- management;
- and dissolution.

At the federal level, however, LLC, S-corporation, C-corporation, and professional-corporation distinctions largely disappear.

Because the individual federal income tax has already been abolished, pass-through treatment is much less important. Enterprise earnings are taxed once at the entity level. Distributions ordinarily are not taxed again as individual income.

For the average proprietor, this is simpler:

- one classification;
- one federal return;
- one general enterprise rate.

But it also means that a federal rule targeting “corporations” reaches:

- Concord;
- Ford;
- Interlink;
- a family restaurant;
- a two-person consultancy;
- a rural repair business;
- and a private clinic.

That is the defensive purpose.

Large corporations can present any corporate-tax increase as an attack upon millions of middle-class business owners.

### Open commerce, closed ownership

The third title removes most American quotas and quantitative restrictions on ordinary imports and exports.

It allows:

- broad import access;
- unrestricted ordinary exports;
- foreign sourcing;
- American branch formation abroad where host governments consent;
- easier profit repatriation;
- and simplified commercial settlement.

It retains:

- foreign ownership restrictions on American firms;
- national-security review;
- strategic technology controls;
- military and orbital restrictions;
- and the power to block hostile capital.

The resulting formula is:

> **Open commerce. Closed American ownership.**

This is not a restoration of Reagan’s original policy.

Foreign companies can sell goods to America. They cannot quietly assemble controlling equity positions in American industry.

American corporations can expand abroad while remaining protected from reciprocal acquisition at home.

# The hemispheric corporate order

The open-commerce title cannot force Germany, Japan, Britain, or the Latin bloc to admit American exports. Those governments retain their own tariffs, clearing systems, and investment controls.

Its greatest effect is therefore inside the American hemisphere, where Washington can combine:

- access to the American market;
- debt restructuring;
- dollar finance;
- ports;
- communications;
- infrastructure;
- and implicit Monroe protection.

For Central and South American governments, this can be extremely attractive.

For American systems corporations, it creates large markets in which local competitors possess far less capital and administrative capacity.

# Peru as the first major test

Peru remains the best first hotspot because Japan already has a long and politically contentious relationship with the Samanco–Chimbote complex. Its exact permanent-force and legal arrangements are deliberately still open in the canon. fileciteturn51file1 Japan has been cultivating Peruvian access since the late 1960s, when Peru and Ecuador became its main Pacific footholds in South America. fileciteturn51file2

## The Lima Open Commerce Compact

Around 1998 or 1999, Peru signs a bilateral agreement with the United States.

Peru receives:

- near-unrestricted access to the American market;
- debt restructuring;
- port and railway investment;
- mining and fisheries finance;
- communications modernization;
- and American commercial credit.

American corporations receive:

- the right to establish branches and wholly owned local operating companies;
- broad profit repatriation;
- access to government procurement;
- long infrastructure concessions;
- and equal treatment in ordinary Peruvian commerce.

The arrangement may genuinely be excellent for Peru in the short term.

It brings money, jobs, modern systems, and access to the richest open market in the hemisphere.

Japan’s reaction is still bitter:

> Tokyo has spent decades building political, commercial, and strategic influence in Peru. American corporations arrive with access to the American market and achieve in several years what Japan has pursued for forty.

## The Chimbote inspection incident

A plausible limited confrontation occurs when an American-operated Peruvian customs or port system attempts to inspect cargo entering the Japanese-access complex.

Japan claims the shipment is protected by older bonded or security arrangements.

Peru claims that all facilities on Peruvian territory now fall under uniform customs and security rules.

American firms provide:

- the port-management software;
- scanners;
- communications;
- logistics;
- and perhaps contracted security.

Japanese naval or installation personnel refuse the inspection.

The confrontation produces:

- a blocked quay;
- a patrol-craft collision;
- warning shots;
- several casualties;
- detained technicians;
- and rapid Japanese and American naval deployments.

Neither side calls it a war.

Washington says it is defending Peruvian sovereignty and the Monroe Doctrine.

Tokyo says American corporations are being used to erase lawful Japanese access.

The settlement might preserve:

- limited Japanese access;
- Peruvian customs authority;
- joint inspection procedures;
- caps on military storage and personnel;
- and the American commercial concession.

The incident establishes that America’s domestic politics may be fragmented and corporate-sponsored, but its hemispheric nationalism remains intact.

# The other likely pressure points

Germany and Argentina remain the next strongest case. The dispute would probably concern German maintenance networks, dual-use equipment, or attempts to rebuild economic influence after the Falklands settlement.

Chile is another likely Japanese-American commercial contest involving copper, Pacific ports, shipping, and communications.

A British-American confrontation around Belize is possible, but less likely to escalate because the Halifax relationship gives both governments established channels for restraint. A corporate concession or border incident could still become politically ugly without producing a naval standoff.

Peru is the better first demonstration because it combines:

- a preexisting Japanese bridgehead;
- an attractive American commercial offer;
- Peruvian sovereignty;
- private corporate infrastructure;
- and the Monroe Doctrine.

# Corrected sequence

| Date | Development |
|---|---|
| **1992 convention** | Harwood defeats Landry and the other National Renewal candidates |
| **October 1992** | Landry urges voters to support National Renewal down ballot but reject Harwood for president |
| **November 1992** | Harwood narrowly wins an outright Electoral College majority; National Renewal wins congressional supermajorities |
| **January 1993** | Harwood becomes the final president elected without House selection |
| **Spring–autumn 1993** | Caucus discipline, committee removals, donor separation, and state-party fights formalize the National Renewal schism |
| **1994** | Successor factions contest the midterms while Harwood’s organization still legally uses the National Renewal name |
| **1993–1996** | States adopt district, proportional, and hybrid elector allocation |
| **1996** | Five-party presidential election produces the first House selection of the new order |
| **1997** | Genuine campaign-finance reform is defeated |
| **1998** | The gutted Campaign Independence Act legalizes sponsorship safe harbors, unifies federal enterprise treatment, and opens ordinary trade |
| **1998–2000** | American corporate expansion into Peru produces the first serious Japanese-American commercial-security confrontation |

# The tragic hinge

The 1992 election is not the first chaotic election of the new system.

It is the final orderly one.

Harwood wins under the old two-party structure. He receives an Electoral College majority, takes office without a congressional bargain, and appears to possess one of the largest legislative mandates in American history.

Within months, that mandate divides into several parties.

Afterward, Americans still vote for president. Their votes still determine which candidates survive and which coalitions possess legitimacy. But the decisive choice increasingly moves to the House, where state delegations bargain among parties under heavy corporate sponsorship.

The last president chosen directly by the old system is therefore the man whose election makes that system impossible to reproduce.
