# 1975–1980: the programmable consumer world

The late 1970s are the first period in which the setting’s technical competition reaches ordinary people as something more than better appliances or impressive broadcasts.

The decisive change is **programmability**.

A calculator performs one function electronically. A home computer can be made to perform several. A television receives programs chosen by a broadcaster. A video recorder lets the household choose when to watch. An appliance follows a fixed sequence. A programmable controller allows the sequence to be altered. A retailer no longer merely knows what it sold; its central system begins recording what was sold, where, and when.

The world of 1980 is not yet digitally saturated. Most records remain on paper, most telephones are fixed, most cars are mechanically controlled, and most televisions are cathode-ray-tube sets. But the social boundary has changed:

> In 1975, electronics mostly execute decisions made by manufacturers and institutions.  
> By 1980, an increasing number of consumers can give the machine instructions themselves.

Canon already places the consumer-computing break in this exact interval. America develops open household machines, software, games, word processing, an electronic worksheet and dial-up culture. Japan reaches similar scale through more integrated native-language systems. Germany opens a regulated offline home market through Kurzplan 77. Britain develops educational micros and packet or videotex services, while the Latin bloc builds Olivetti-centered systems. fileciteturn23file9 fileciteturn23file11

---

## I. The period in four stages

### 1975–1976: the hobbyist threshold

Personal computers exist, but they remain:

- kits;
- university or technical-club projects;
- mail-order boards;
- machines operated through switches and indicator lights;
- expensive systems connected to laboratory terminals.

Arcades and dedicated television-game machines are much more accessible than general-purpose computers.

Japan completes the first crewed occupation of Kōbō in 1976. The Stockholm Orbital Safety and Salvage Convention also formalizes registration, rescue, debris control and recovery responsibilities. Space is becoming a permanent operating environment rather than a sequence of individual missions. fileciteturn23file13

### 1977: governments discover the household machine

Three developments converge.

Germany begins its **Heimrechnerprogramm**, supporting home machines, school purchases, domestic processors, common television and cassette interfaces, and German-language documentation. Kurzplan 77 becomes its intended home and school language. fileciteturn23file3 fileciteturn23file12

America’s National Mission and Productive Enterprise Act supports microelectronics, machine tools, industrial credit, technical education and federal procurement. Its most culturally important result is not centrally planned automation but the private personal-computer market that grows around those investments. fileciteturn25file0

Japan begins widening associated-state participation in its technical and space institutions. Its consumer industry simultaneously turns calculators, displays, games and native-language computing into one increasingly connected market.

### 1978–1979: complete products replace kits

The recognizable home computer appears:

- keyboard included;
- television output;
- cassette or disk storage;
- printed manual;
- interpreted language;
- game controllers;
- optional printer;
- dealer or mail-order software.

The United States gains the strongest independent software culture. Japan builds the most polished integrated hardware. Germany produces better-made but more regulated systems. Britain increasingly connects education, public terminals and telecommunications.

The electronic worksheet appears in America in 1979, although its founder and final product name remain intentionally open. It changes the small-business case for owning a computer because the machine can now answer a weekly commercial question rather than merely teach programming or play games. fileciteturn23file9

### 1980: consumer computing becomes an industry

By 1980, home computing supports:

- computer shops;
- magazines;
- repair services;
- software publishers;
- game studios;
- disk and cassette duplication;
- school suppliers;
- printer and monitor manufacturers;
- modem and terminal firms;
- small-business consultants.

The Tokyo–Melbourne congress adopts UNICODE 80, giving the international industry its first serious universal-character architecture. Japan and the Latin bloc adopt it most aggressively; Britain uses it where useful; Germany follows more slowly; decentralized America takes much longer to converge. fileciteturn23file10

The computer is no longer one product. It is the soil from which hundreds of firms can grow.

---

# II. What the ordinary home computer looks like

A normal late-1970s home machine is still modest.

It probably has:

- an eight-bit processor;
- limited memory;
- text and simple block graphics;
- television output;
- cassette storage;
- a typewriter-style keyboard;
- one or two controller ports;
- a built-in interpreted language;
- an expansion connector.

Disk drives exist, but they are expensive. A household commonly begins with cassette storage and buys a disk system later.

Printers are loud, mechanical and costly. Many owners use the computer for years without one.

A typical program may take several minutes to load from tape and then fail because:

- the volume was set incorrectly;
- the tape stretched;
- the head was misaligned;
- the user typed the file name incorrectly;
- the program expected more memory than the machine possessed.

The home computer is useful, but it is not effortless.

## What families actually do with it

The most common uses are:

- games;
- programming exercises;
- school mathematics;
- typing;
- household accounts;
- recipe and address files;
- astronomy;
- music experiments;
- tax calculation;
- small-business inventory;
- amateur radio;
- simulations.

Most people who buy a computer with the intention of organizing the household spend more time playing games or learning commands than maintaining perfect family records.

That is not failure. Entertainment creates familiarity. A generation learns file systems, keyboards, programming concepts and troubleshooting because it wants to make a spaceship move across a television screen.

---

# III. The new corporate ecology

This period creates a different kind of company.

Before 1975, an electronics firm normally needs a factory, large contracts and substantial capital. By 1980, a software company may begin with:

- two programmers;
- one rented office;
- a duplicating machine;
- several disk drives;
- a postal box;
- an advertisement in a magazine.

The principal new business types are:

## Software houses

They produce:

- games;
- accounting;
- word processing;
- school programs;
- engineering tools;
- graphics;
- utilities;
- language interpreters.

## Computer retailers

The successful store sells more than the computer.

It supplies:

- cables;
- storage media;
- printers;
- monitors;
- repair;
- lessons;
- software;
- user-group meeting space.

## Industrial integrators

These firms connect programmable controllers, sensors and minicomputers to existing factories. They often grow faster than the robot manufacturers themselves because factories need someone who understands both the old machinery and the new controls.

## Data-service bureaus

Smaller businesses that cannot afford a complete computer pay a bureau to process:

- payroll;
- accounts;
- inventory;
- invoices;
- tax records;
- statistical reports.

## Media publishers

Magazine publishers distribute programs as printed source code. Record and tape firms consider selling software on cassettes. Book publishers enter educational software. Toy companies begin acquiring game designers.

This is where many important 1980s firms should originate—not as giant semiconductor companies, but as small businesses filling one narrow practical gap.

---

# IV. Home video becomes a mass-market struggle

The second major consumer contest is the video recorder.

By the middle of the decade, institutional video is established. Between 1976 and 1980, manufacturers try to turn it into a household product.

The basic market problem is a tradeoff among:

- picture quality;
- recording duration;
- machine size;
- tape cost;
- mechanical reliability;
- licensing terms;
- number of manufacturers supporting the format.

## The likely Japanese struggle

A strong working model is a rivalry between:

- a **Totsuko-led compact, technically refined format**;
- a **Matsushita/National-led longer-duration, broadly licensed format**.

The names do not need to reproduce Betamax and VHS exactly, although the engineering dispute can rhyme with them.

Totsuko’s argument is:

- better picture;
- smaller cassette;
- tighter integration;
- premium construction.

Matsushita’s argument is:

- longer recording;
- lower price;
- more manufacturers;
- larger dealer network;
- easier licensing;
- enough quality for ordinary television.

Japan’s primary market is still its Asian sphere, not America. The decisive early questions are therefore whether a tape can record:

- a complete evening drama;
- a baseball match;
- a long Chinese opera or historical serial;
- educational broadcasts;
- religious or political ceremonies;
- multilingual programming.

The Philippines and parts of Southeast Asia use Roman-letter controls and manuals. China receives character labeling. Korea and Formosa receive the more directly Japanized product families.

## Rental matters before ownership

Video-recording rental and club systems probably emerge before universal ownership.

Appliance dealers may rent:

- the machine;
- prerecorded tapes;
- sporting-event recordings;
- children’s programming;
- religious material;
- technical instruction.

Britain is especially well suited to video rental because television rental is already socially normal.

The video shop of the early 1980s grows out of the late-1970s appliance dealer, film club and tape-library service.

## Censorship becomes harder

Video recording creates a new circulation problem.

A film banned from the cinema can be copied privately. A foreign broadcast can be recorded near a frontier or satellite-reception facility. Political footage can circulate outside the official news schedule.

Copies degrade, but they do not disappear.

Germany and the Latin bloc license commercial duplication. Japan pressures manufacturers and distributors. Britain uses copyright and ordinary security law. America experiences a large argument over whether private recording is theft, fair use or simply an inevitable feature of owning the machine.

---

# V. Portable music changes urban behavior

The late 1970s should produce a Totsuko portable stereo cassette player comparable in social effect to the historical Walkman, but not necessarily under an English-derived product identity.

The machine’s origins are particularly Japanese:

- long railway commutes;
- dense housing;
- limited private space;
- miniaturized cassette mechanisms;
- lightweight headphones;
- advanced battery manufacture;
- strong youth and business-travel markets.

The marketing does not initially say, “Take your music anywhere in America.”

It says something closer to:

> Carry a private room through the public city.

The product becomes popular among:

- commuters;
- students;
- technical workers;
- travelers;
- soldiers and sailors;
- language learners.

It changes social etiquette. A person wearing headphones is physically present but has partially withdrawn from the shared environment.

Older critics describe it as antisocial. Employers worry about distraction. Railway companies debate announcements and safety. Young buyers regard it as personal freedom.

By 1980, Japan’s strongest consumer image is no longer merely portable precision. It is **private electronic experience**.

---

# VI. Games become a cultural industry

Electronic games divide into three related markets.

## Arcades

Arcades become technically sophisticated businesses using:

- interchangeable logic boards;
- color displays;
- vector or raster graphics;
- improved sound;
- standardized cabinets;
- centralized maintenance;
- recognizable game titles.

America develops the freest and most chaotic arcade market. Japan integrates arcades with amusement companies, railway districts, shopping centers and consumer-electronics firms.

## Home consoles

Cartridge-based consoles replace or supplement fixed-game television systems.

The cartridge creates a new commercial structure:

- console manufacturer;
- cartridge publisher;
- independent developer;
- retail shelf;
- licensing agreement.

That structure later becomes more important than the console hardware itself.

The principal early genres are:

- sports;
- shooting;
- racing;
- maze games;
- naval and air combat;
- simple strategy;
- spaceflight;
- adaptations of arcade games.

## Home-computer games

These are cheaper to develop and distribute but less consistent.

Programs circulate through:

- cassettes;
- disks;
- magazines;
- clubs;
- mail order;
- informal copying.

Germany’s **Mauerwerk**, provisionally created around 1979 by Ilmar Bielenstein, begins as a packing and screen-control exercise before spreading through programme libraries and creating incompatible ownership claims. fileciteturn23file12

The dispute is characteristic of the period. Nobody yet agrees whether software belongs to:

- the programmer;
- the employer;
- the distributor;
- the machine manufacturer;
- the institution that paid for the computer;
- the person who translated it;
- the government that approved export.

The nonbinding Lucerne Principles of roughly 1978–79 attempt to distinguish source code, executable code, translation, adaptation and national distribution. They clarify the vocabulary without ending the disputes. fileciteturn23file6

---

# VII. Germany: controlled consumer modernization

Wolfgang’s state cannot ignore the American and Japanese consumer challenge.

Its case for home computing is strategic rather than liberal:

- German children should not learn computation through foreign machines.
- Industry needs programmers and technicians.
- A great power should provide modern electronics to favored citizens.
- Offline machines are less threatening than uncontrolled networks.

The resulting compromise legalizes home computers while regulating:

- modems;
- cryptography;
- network adapters;
- foreign software;
- political publishing;
- telecommunications.

Ordinary games, educational programs, household accounting and engineering software are widely available. Anti-regime political games and depictions of colonial violence are not. fileciteturn23file3

## The German product character

German home computers are likely to be:

- more expensive than American kits;
- better constructed;
- more carefully documented;
- less colorful than Japanese machines;
- standardized around good keyboards and expansion connectors;
- supplied through technical schools, department stores and approved dealers.

Siemens, Telefunken, Zuse-associated firms, Grundig, Braun and smaller electronics concerns all have reasons to participate. The state supports an ecosystem rather than one mandatory machine. fileciteturn23file8

## Appliances

Germany’s appliance industry uses electronics conservatively.

Premium products acquire:

- solid-state timers;
- temperature sensors;
- digital clocks;
- fault indicators;
- improved safety interlocks;
- limited programmable cycles.

Miele, Siemens, AEG, Bosch and regional specialists advertise reliability rather than gimmickry.

A German washing machine with an electronic control board is expected to remain repairable. Manufacturers that seal the entire control system into an expensive disposable module face criticism from craftsmen, consumer officials and the repair trade.

## Automobiles

By the late 1970s, the major German automotive shifts are:

- front-wheel-drive, water-cooled mass Volkswagens;
- broader use of passenger diesels;
- turbocharged diesel and performance experimentation;
- electronic fuel injection in upper-market vehicles;
- anti-lock braking entering premium production;
- improved crash structures;
- more aerodynamic bodies;
- standardized diagnostic equipment.

The rotary engine remains alive longer than in our timeline, especially under Auto Union, NSU and Japanese licensing. But its fuel use, sealing and service requirements keep it a specialist option.

The German car is becoming electronically supervised. It is not yet electronically controlled in the later sense.

## Space enters leisure

The German Mars rover of about 1978–79 becomes a consumer-media event. Germany presents selected processed imagery through documentaries, educational programs, model kits and planetarium exhibitions. America follows with a more open and media-friendly rover effort. fileciteturn24file1

Raumhafen and rover programming produce an entire minor commercial field:

- model spacecraft;
- technical toys;
- astronomy kits;
- home simulation programs;
- educational films;
- station-themed furniture and design;
- holiday visits to tracking and aerospace museums.

---

# VIII. Japan: the integrated electronics household

Japan becomes America’s principal visible rival in consumer computing and leads or shares leadership in polished home hardware, consoles, arcades, displays, embedded processors, graphics, sound and industrial–consumer integration. fileciteturn23file3

## Native-language computing

Japanese systems require more than replacing English labels.

They need:

- kana input;
- traditional ideographs;
- vertical or mixed text;
- larger character memory;
- printer support;
- conversion among Japanese and Chinese readings;
- compatibility with Roman model and technical codes.

This makes Japanese computers more expensive and memory-intensive, but it also forces their manufacturers to develop better displays, character generators and printers.

The Japanese household machine is therefore likely to look more finished than the American equivalent:

- integrated keyboard;
- attractive case;
- color graphics;
- stronger sound;
- cartridge or cassette compatibility;
- detailed manuals;
- character support;
- fewer exposed circuit boards.

America provides freedom and software variety. Japan provides product integration.

## Industrial feedback

Japan’s consumer-electronics firms also manufacture:

- factory controllers;
- displays;
- memory;
- sensors;
- calculators;
- office machines;
- entertainment devices.

A component developed for industrial control can enter a console. A graphics chip designed for a game can improve an educational computer. A compact motor designed for a cassette deck can support office equipment.

This feedback loop is one reason Japan’s consumer industry advances so quickly.

## Company positions

By 1980, the principal likely consumer identities are:

- **Totsuko:** premium portable audio, video, compact television and professional electronics;
- **Matsushita/National:** mass appliances, televisions, video and broad dealer support;
- **Sharp and Casio-type firms:** calculators, displays and compact computers;
- **Seiko:** quartz and digital timekeeping;
- **Canon, Nikon and Minolta:** electronic photography;
- **Nintendo, Namco, Taito or equivalent firms:** toys, arcades and games;
- **Toyota, Nissan/Datsun, Prince and Honda:** passenger and light-commercial mobility.

These are different kinds of companies, but microelectronics increasingly connects their supplier networks.

## Associated-state production

Lower-cost assembly spreads into:

- Korea;
- Formosa;
- Manchukuo;
- the Philippines;
- Singapore;
- selected Southeast Asian industrial districts.

Japan retains control of the highest-value components:

- processors;
- memory;
- display controllers;
- precision mechanisms;
- software standards;
- advanced optics.

This supports the imperial claim that Japan is teaching Asia to manufacture while preserving Japanese control over design, capital and standards. fileciteturn23file14

It also plants the seeds of later associated-state competitors.

---

# IX. America: the “machine tool for the mind”

Buchanan’s Productive Enterprise program accelerates microelectronics, machine tools, industrial minicomputers, programmable controllers, robotic welding, robotic painting, semiconductor equipment and technical education. But its workerless-factory rhetoric proves false. Real gains come from specialized machines operating alongside trained people. fileciteturn25file1

Personal computing is the program’s least planned and most successful result.

The administration assists it through:

- school purchases;
- small-business deductions;
- federal procurement;
- telecommunications access;
- semiconductor research;
- technical clubs;
- military and space contracts.

This creates the American idea of the computer as a **machine tool for the mind**. fileciteturn25file0

## Computer stores and mail order

America develops the densest retail ecology:

- specialist computer shops;
- mail-order boards;
- user groups;
- magazines;
- local bulletin services;
- independent repair;
- software sold in bags, binders and envelopes;
- programs typed from printed listings.

Quality varies wildly.

A buyer can purchase an excellent innovative machine from a company that will no longer exist two years later. The American market’s openness creates both rapid progress and rapid obsolescence.

## Small business

The electronic worksheet, word processing and affordable printers change the business market.

A local firm can use one computer for:

- invoices;
- payroll;
- inventory;
- letters;
- estimates;
- customer lists;
- simple forecasting.

The machine does not eliminate the bookkeeper or secretary. It changes their work.

The bookkeeper becomes the person who maintains the electronic model. The secretary learns word processing and printer control. Firms begin hiring people because they “know computers,” even when nobody can define precisely what that means.

## Games and media

America leads in:

- open software;
- independent publishers;
- hobbyist magazines;
- home-console competition;
- arcade culture;
- dial-up boards;
- copied programs.

It is also the first country where programmers can plausibly become minor celebrities without belonging to a university, military project or giant company.

## Automobiles

The absence of a universal 1973 oil crisis means American large cars and V8 culture survive longer.

Pressure for change instead comes from:

- insurance;
- smog;
- congestion;
- Japanese and European competition;
- safety;
- household debt;
- periodic recession;
- fleet operating costs.

By 1980 the American market contains:

- large traditional sedans;
- muscle and personal-luxury cars;
- practical American Motors compacts;
- Kaiser-Willys four-wheel drives;
- imported or licensed Japanese small cars;
- European-style sporting sedans;
- increasingly electronic premium cars.

Electronic ignition and cruise control are normal. Fuel injection is spreading. Digital dashboards and trip computers remain expensive novelties. Fully computerized engine management is only beginning.

---

# X. Britain: public networks and industrial strain

Britain begins the interval with physical reconstruction complete and ends it in a political-economic crisis that brings Thatcher’s National Liberal–Constitutional Union to office in 1980.

Healey preserves:

- strategic public industry;
- housing;
- social security;
- defense;
- technical modernization.

But soft budgets, producer controls and delayed restructuring create inflation, labor conflict and weak productivity in parts of the economy. fileciteturn25file3

This produces a peculiar material culture: highly advanced public and strategic systems beside troubled mass manufacturing.

## Educational computing

Britain’s strengths lie in:

- school machines;
- public terminals;
- programme libraries;
- packet networks;
- videotex;
- multiple programming languages;
- inexpensive access through institutions.

A child may first use a computer at school, library or youth technical club rather than at home.

British educational machines emphasize:

- readable manuals;
- durable keyboards;
- classroom networking;
- simple programming;
- compatibility with public-service computing.

## Videotex and teletext

Britain is the most likely early leader in public electronic information delivered through the television or a specialized terminal.

Services may provide:

- news headlines;
- weather;
- railway times;
- market prices;
- government forms;
- educational pages;
- agricultural information;
- mail-order catalogs.

Teletext is one-way broadcast information. Videotex uses a telephone connection and can be interactive. Neither is an Internet.

The service is slow and text-heavy, but it gives the public an early idea that information can be requested from a screen rather than merely broadcast at everyone simultaneously.

## Consumer rental

Rental remains significant for:

- color televisions;
- video recorders;
- expensive audio systems;
- early home computers;
- office equipment.

This lowers the entry price and protects customers against rapid technical obsolescence.

## Automotive industry

British firms increasingly suffer from:

- too many marques;
- duplicated models;
- uneven quality;
- old plants;
- labor disputes;
- insufficient capital.

Land-Rover, specialist sports cars, luxury vehicles, buses, trucks and certain compact designs remain competitive.

The mass passenger-car industry becomes one of the major unresolved problems inherited by the 1980 Thatcher government. Strategic capacity survives, but commercial discipline is weak.

---

# XI. The Latin-bloc handoff

The parallel Latin discussion should account for the following:

## Olivetti and the designed computer

Olivetti’s great strength is making a programmable machine appear like an office instrument rather than military equipment.

Its late-1970s product ecology can include:

- professional desktop computers;
- electronic typewriters;
- word processors;
- business terminals;
- designed home systems;
- printers;
- calculators.

The Latin home computer should be more expensive than the cheapest American kit but visually coherent and unusually easy to understand.

## Occitan software

Occitania’s strength in Prolog and real-time control gives it advantages in:

- industrial diagnosis;
- scheduling;
- medical expert systems;
- engineering;
- military and aerospace control;
- educational logic programs.

It does not automatically create a mass Occitan home-computer industry. Italian design and manufacturing are needed to make the research commercially visible.

## Tourism technology

Mediterranean tourism drives:

- reservation networks;
- electronic hotel accounting;
- automated telephone exchanges;
- air conditioning;
- elevators;
- video entertainment;
- multilingual television;
- bank-card systems;
- computerized ferry and airline scheduling.

## Automobiles

Italy maintains a broad product ladder:

- small Fiat family cars;
- scooters and motorcycles;
- Alfa Romeo sporting sedans;
- Ferrari, Maserati and Lancia prestige;
- trucks and buses;
- increasing electronic instrumentation.

Spain’s SEAT supplier network grows more independent. Pegaso remains strong in heavy transport. Pirelli benefits from radial tires, racing and export markets.

---

# XII. Retail, banking and the recorded consumer

By 1980, large retailers increasingly use:

- barcodes or competing optical codes;
- computerized inventory;
- central warehouse ordering;
- electronic payroll;
- customer credit files;
- regional distribution centers.

The checkout scanner does not immediately appear in every shop. Large supermarkets and department chains adopt it first.

Local shops remain competitive through:

- location;
- personal credit;
- repair;
- delivery;
- specialist stock;
- customer knowledge.

## Banking

Advanced urban systems offer:

- cash machines;
- direct wage deposit;
- bank cards;
- remote teller terminals;
- electronic transfers;
- centralized credit records.

Cash remains normal. Checks remain important in America and Britain. Germany and Japan use bank and postal transfer systems more heavily.

The new problem is that a person increasingly exists as a record spread across several institutions.

A wrong entry can affect:

- credit;
- employment;
- benefits;
- housing;
- travel;
- insurance.

In liberal systems this produces privacy and consumer-rights arguments. In Germany and its colonies, the state regards consistent identification as a feature. In the Eastern Reichskommissariats or Mittelafrika, an error in the status record can alter a person’s movement rights or occupational future.

---

# XIII. Automobiles, electronics and the 1980 road

The late-1970s car gains enough electronics to require a new kind of mechanic.

The ordinary garage still needs:

- compression gauges;
- timing equipment;
- hand tools;
- mechanical knowledge.

But it increasingly also needs:

- electrical test meters;
- manufacturer diagnostic devices;
- fuel-injection instruments;
- service bulletins;
- specialized training.

## Common late-1970s features

- electronic ignition;
- alternator control;
- intermittent wipers;
- improved fuel injection;
- electric cooling fans;
- anti-lock brakes on premium cars;
- automatic climate control in luxury cars;
- digital clocks;
- warning-test panels;
- cruise control;
- primitive trip computers.

## Rare or prestige features

- digital speedometers;
- electronic voice warnings;
- automatic suspension;
- fully digital engine management;
- route guidance;
- integrated vehicle telephone.

The automotive supplier becomes more important. Bosch, VDO, Denso-type Japanese firms, Lucas, Magneti Marelli and American electrical companies increasingly determine how advanced the finished car can be.

---

# XIV. Factories: robots arrive, workers remain

Late-1970s industrial robots are good at:

- welding the same seam;
- painting the same body;
- moving the same part;
- loading the same machine;
- operating in heat or fumes.

They remain poor at:

- identifying irregular parts;
- repairing unknown faults;
- flexible final assembly;
- improvising;
- maintaining themselves.

America’s Productive Enterprise program discovers this painfully. The administration’s rhetoric promises nearly empty factories, but actual modernization requires more technicians, programmers, tool setters and maintenance workers than expected. fileciteturn25file15

Japan leads in integrating robots with stable production systems.

Germany leads in certified industrial control and heavy engineering.

America creates the broadest independent market for controllers, minicomputers and automation services.

Britain remains strong in specialized systems while struggling to modernize every mass-production plant.

The social conflict is not simply “robots replace workers.” It is:

> Which workers are retrained, which are demoted, which plants receive investment, and which regions are allowed to decline?

---

# XV. Medicine and the electronic household

Medical electronics continue moving from the exceptional hospital into ordinary clinical practice.

By 1980, major hospitals increasingly possess:

- CT scanners;
- ultrasound;
- intensive-care monitoring;
- fetal monitoring;
- automated laboratory equipment;
- smaller pacemakers;
- improved dialysis;
- computer-assisted radiology;
- neonatal intensive care.

The ordinary home gains simpler health products:

- electronic thermometers;
- improved hearing aids;
- home blood-pressure devices;
- smoke detectors;
- timed medication aids;
- portable emergency radios.

Germany’s maternal and pediatric programs receive additional public attention through Katharina’s work. America commercializes equipment quickly but distributes it unevenly. Britain distributes through regional planning, sometimes slowly. Japan integrates precision electronics into increasingly compact clinical equipment.

---

# XVI. Energy and pollution

There is still no need for one global oil-shock story.

Oil prices and supplies can fluctuate through:

- Gulf tension;
- shipping risk;
- national stockpiling;
- cartel bargaining;
- local wars;
- industrial demand.

But the setting’s blocs have different resource systems, and the 1974 Kuwait conflict does not automatically produce a unified embargo.

This allows:

- American large vehicles to remain common;
- Germany to continue synthetic-fuel and diesel work;
- Japan to use nuclear power and efficient small vehicles;
- Britain to emphasize nuclear energy and Cape-route security;
- Italy to benefit from Mediterranean and North African access.

## Nuclear normalization

By 1980, nuclear power is ordinary strategic infrastructure in the major blocs.

The public argument concerns:

- cost;
- siting;
- accidents;
- waste;
- water use;
- local employment.

It is not yet dominated by a mass moral rejection of nuclear technology.

Germany’s thorium program remains experimental rather than transformational. Its principal near-term products are expertise, fuel-cycle research and long-term energy claims.

## Pollution policy

Pollution control grows through:

- medical evidence;
- municipal sanitation;
- fisheries damage;
- factory efficiency;
- urban visibility;
- tourism;
- worker safety.

Lead, mercury, sewage, smoke and chemical dumping are more politically important than carbon emissions.

The weaker environmental movement permits faster growth in:

- disposable packaging;
- plastic containers;
- single-use medical products;
- aerosol goods;
- synthetic furnishings.

Returnable bottles and industrial recycling survive where they save materials and transport costs.

---

# XVII. The imperial divide

## Eastern Reichskommissariats

The automated logistical spine becomes more advanced while access remains unequal.

German settler and technical households may possess:

- color television;
- refrigerator;
- washing machine;
- automobile;
- cassette equipment;
- home computer.

Native service-estate families may gain:

- television through plant clubs;
- better housing;
- a motorcycle;
- technical schooling;
- limited household appliances.

Ordinary rural subjects remain far behind.

Home computers are most available to Germans, approved institutions and selected technical workers. Network access is heavily regulated. The distinction is not merely income. It is legal status.

## Mittelafrika

The Second Mosaic Settlement of 1977–79 stabilizes much of the interior through chiefly stipends, performance shares and community dividends while retaining direct worker wages. fileciteturn24file1

The minor technological effects may include:

- computerized payroll;
- district benefit records;
- radio-linked clinics;
- communal television halls;
- technical-school terminals;
- improved mining automation;
- mechanized port and rail handling.

These benefits coexist with coercive registration, unequal reproductive policy, restricted movement and harsh treatment of unregistered populations.

## Japanese sphere

Japanese consumer goods spread much more broadly:

- televisions;
- cassette players;
- calculators;
- motorcycles;
- cameras;
- compact cars;
- electronic games;
- school computers.

But advanced design and component manufacture remain concentrated in Japan, Korea, Formosa and Manchukuo.

The consumer market therefore makes the empire feel more integrated while also making Japanese economic dominance more visible.

---

# XVIII. The visual world of 1980

The late-1970s future no longer looks like a rocket.

It looks like a terminal.

Common design features include:

- beige or dark plastic;
- wood veneer beside electronics;
- smoked display windows;
- green, amber or red numerical displays;
- membrane or rectangular buttons;
- modular stereo components;
- black front panels;
- visible ventilation slots;
- coiled cables;
- geometric labels;
- removable cartridges and cassettes.

The home contains multiple layers of time:

- a traditional dining table;
- a large CRT television;
- a modern cassette deck;
- an electronic calculator;
- a digital clock;
- a home computer connected by cable to the television;
- a mechanically timed cooker;
- a car outside with electronic ignition but a carburetor.

The future arrives component by component.

---

# Working 1980 baseline

The following points provide a useful end-of-decade snapshot.

1. **Personal computing is a genuine consumer and small-business industry.**

2. **America leads open software, independent developers, spreadsheets, word processing and hobbyist culture.**

3. **Japan leads polished home hardware, games, displays, sound and native non-Latin computing.**

4. **Germany operates a substantial but regulated offline home-computer market through Kurzplan 77.**

5. **Britain leads educational access, public terminals, videotex and translation among different systems.**

6. **The Latin bloc’s strongest consumer-computing identity is the designed professional and household instrument.**

7. **Cassette and disk software create markets that are difficult for states or manufacturers to control completely.**

8. **Arcades, home consoles and computer games are now distinct industries.**

9. **Mauerwerk appears around 1979 and immediately produces an ownership dispute rather than a clean commercial launch.**

10. **Household video recorders are established but not universal. A Japanese format contest is under way.**

11. **Portable headphone cassette players emerge as one of Japan’s defining consumer products.**

12. **Color television is mature; monochrome sets remain common in poorer households and peripheral regions.**

13. **Quartz and digital watches are ordinary product categories, though fine mechanical watches survive as prestige goods.**

14. **Calculators are cheap enough for students, shops and households.**

15. **Retailers, banks and employers increasingly maintain machine-readable personal and commercial records.**

16. **Automobiles contain more dedicated electronics but are not yet fully computerized.**

17. **Anti-lock brakes, electronic fuel injection and diagnostic equipment remain concentrated in premium vehicles and advanced fleets.**

18. **Industrial robots are specialized tools, not autonomous general workers.**

19. **The late-1970s startup economy grows around software, automation integration, data service, video, games and specialized components.**

20. **Nuclear power remains politically normal and strategically important.**

21. **Pollution regulation expands without producing a unified anti-industrial environmental movement.**

22. **The space race persists because it now supports stations, lunar bases, automated cargo, Earth observation, communications and Mars exploration rather than one finish line.**

23. **Japan appears extraordinarily powerful by 1980 but is beginning to accumulate overcapacity, protected firms, bad imperial loans and associated-state demands for local competitors.**

24. **Britain enters 1980 with advanced institutions and strategic industries but a serious productivity and industrial-governance problem.**

25. **Buchanan reaches 1980 with visible achievements in space, industry and consumer computing, although automation has delivered less than promised.**

The defining minor object of 1975 was a machine containing a computer without advertising itself as one.

The defining object of 1980 is a machine whose owner knows it is a computer—and has begun asking what else it can be made to do.
