Yes. The War of the Chiefs should create a **second branch of German land-equipment development** rather than merely improving the ordinary Panzergrenadier force.

Before the war, the procurement hierarchy is implicit:

> Panzergrenadier IFV → wheeled APC → truck → foot movement.

The Congo breaks that hierarchy. It demonstrates that a lighter vehicle isn’t necessarily an inferior version of a heavy vehicle. It may be the only vehicle that can cross the bridge, enter the landing craft, swim the channel, use the forest track, or be recovered after damage.

The existing reference gives the **Schützenpanzer 71 Greif** a combat weight of 31.5 tonnes, seven dismounts, a 30×170 mm cannon, and an integrated Drachen antitank missile. It is an excellent conventional Panzergrenadier vehicle, but it is too heavy and too specialized around European combined-arms combat to become a satisfactory amphibious jungle vehicle. The same reference already establishes the lighter 44-tonne Panzer XI as a mobility-focused successor to the 47.8-tonne Panzer X, while the StG 60, leichtes MG 76, StG 82, and Einheitsleiste 79 provide the basis for a Congo-driven small-arms development path. fileciteturn12file0

## The principal procurement lesson

The Wehrmacht comes out of Mittelafrika with two legitimate mechanized models.

### The Panzergrenadier model

This remains the main European warfighting model:

- Panzer XII;
- Schützenpanzer 71 Greif and later heavy successors;
- tracked artillery;
- integrated antitank missiles;
- substantial armor;
- and the expectation of fighting peer mechanized forces.

### The Jäger model

This is the Congo-derived expeditionary model:

- lighter tracked vehicles;
- amphibious capability;
- wheeled protected transport;
- detachable weapons;
- lower bridge and barge requirements;
- greater infantry capacity;
- simpler recovery;
- and the ability to continue fighting after leaving the vehicle behind.

The Jäger model does not replace Panzergrenadier doctrine. It stops the Panzergrenadier model from consuming every other kind of formation.

# The new amphibious IFV

## Name: Schützenpanzer 74 Otter

I would give the new vehicle a different name rather than call it **Greif II**.

*Greif II* suggests that this is the next universal German IFV. It isn’t. It is a parallel vehicle optimized for a different force and terrain. The **Greif** remains the heavier Panzergrenadier vehicle. The **Otter** becomes the amphibious Jäger vehicle.

The name also explains the vehicle before the specifications do.

### Proposed service characteristics

| Characteristic | Schützenpanzer 74 Otter |
|---|---|
| Introduction | Limited service in late 1974; wider fielding in 1975 |
| Combat weight | 20.5 t |
| Crew + infantry | 3 + 8 |
| Main armament | 30 mm MK 74, 30×170 mm |
| Secondary armament | Coaxial 7.92 mm MG 68 |
| Antitank armament | Optional external two-missile Drachen module |
| Engine | 600 hp compact multifuel diesel |
| Road speed | 70–72 km/h |
| Water speed | Approximately 9–10 km/h |
| Water propulsion | Twin waterjets |
| Protection | Rifle and fragment protection all around; heavy-machine-gun protection over the frontal arc |
| Normal role | Amphibious Jäger IFV and riverine assault carrier |

The vehicle uses:

- a sealed welded hull;
- a bow trim vane;
- powerful bilge pumps;
- broad tracks and low ground pressure;
- waterjets rather than relying entirely on track movement;
- a rear ramp with an emergency roof exit;
- and a compact turret deliberately kept lighter than the Greif turret.

It is amphibious in the proper military sense, but that needs qualification. It can cross rivers, flooded valleys, calm lake arms, and protected Kongosee channels. It is not intended to traverse the exposed centre of Kongosee during bad weather. On open water, the Otter still travels aboard landing barges.

## The MK 74 cannon

The cannon is developed from the Greif’s existing 30×170 mm MK 71 rather than introducing another ammunition family.

The **MK 74** reduces installation weight through:

- a lighter receiver;
- shorter recoil movement;
- simplified stabilization;
- dual-feed ammunition;
- and a more compact turret mounting.

Its standard ammunition mix emphasizes:

- high explosive;
- fragmentation;
- incendiary;
- and light armor-piercing rounds.

That reflects the Congo target set. The cannon is used against:

- patrol craft;
- barricades;
- timber fighting positions;
- buildings;
- vehicles;
- shoreline positions;
- and troops behind vegetation.

The same weapon can be installed on heavier Kongosee patrol boats. That gives the war a useful technical convergence: the Jäger IFV and the river flotilla use the same cannon, ammunition, maintenance tools, and much of the same sighting equipment.

## Why the missile is detachable

The Drachen remains valuable against tanks and fortified positions, but an integral launcher creates four problems in Mittelafrika:

- added top weight;
- branches and foliage catching on the mount;
- maintenance burden;
- and a weapon that is unnecessary on most patrols.

The Otter therefore receives standardized hardpoints and electrical connections for a two-round external launcher. The module can be installed at a field workshop in a few hours. Most Congo vehicles omit it. Vehicles deployed to Europe, Angola, Mozambique, or a frontier against British armor may carry it.

That is the first major expression of the war’s modularity doctrine:

> **The basic vehicle should not permanently carry every weapon it might need in every theatre.**

This is still 1970s modularity. Modules are bolted on, wired, tested, and zeroed by technicians. They are not instantaneous plug-and-play packages.

# How it enters service so quickly

A clean-sheet vehicle normally wouldn’t go from requirement to service in two years. The War of the Chiefs compresses the process because the Otter doesn’t require clean-sheet development in every component.

It draws from existing German production:

- the Greif’s 30×170 mm ammunition and weapons work;
- Kätzchen suspension and infantry-layout experience;
- existing compact diesel development;
- standard radios;
- Drachen missile interfaces;
- existing waterjet and amphibious-engineering research;
- and the Kongosee flotilla’s experience with corrosion, sealing, bilge systems, and water operations.

A plausible program sequence is:

| Date | Development |
|---|---|
| Late 1972 | Heer identifies the need for a vehicle below the Greif’s weight and bridge class |
| Early 1973 | **Sonderentwicklung 73** begins under an emergency Mittelafrika equipment board |
| Late 1973 | First automotive and flotation prototypes |
| Mid-1974 | Armed prototypes enter troop trials around Kongostadt |
| Late 1974 | Limited acceptance as Schützenpanzer 74 Otter |
| 1975 | First complete Jäger battalions receive the vehicle |
| 1976–1978 | Reliability, turret, sealing, and tropical-maintenance improvements |

The early Otters should have problems:

- water leakage;
- overloaded suspension;
- turret sealing;
- poor visibility with the trim vane raised;
- engines overheating after moving directly from water to land;
- corrosion in electrical connectors;
- and excessive bow weight when the missile launcher is installed.

The war doesn’t produce a perfect vehicle. It produces a useful one quickly, followed by several years of correction.

# The wheeled companion

## Transportpanzer 76 Fuchs

The Otter is still expensive. The Jäger force also needs a vehicle for roads, port districts, airfields, rear-area movement, and long-distance patrols where tracks aren’t necessary.

That produces the **Transportpanzer 76 Fuchs**.

| Characteristic | Transportpanzer 76 Fuchs |
|---|---|
| Configuration | Amphibious six-wheeled armored carrier |
| Combat weight | Approximately 16.5–17.5 t |
| Crew + passengers | 2 + 10 |
| Standard armament | Protected MG 68 mount |
| Optional armament | 20 mm cannon, command, mortar, ambulance, or Drachen module |
| Road speed | Approximately 100 km/h |
| Water speed | Approximately 9 km/h |
| Principal role | Jäger transport, patrol, command, reconnaissance support, and protected logistics |

Before Mittelafrika, an APC such as Fuchs would have been described as a cheaper substitute for an IFV.

After the war, the doctrinal language changes:

- Greif carries Panzergrenadiers into the mechanized close battle.
- Otter carries Jäger through fragmented and amphibious terrain while providing direct fire.
- Fuchs carries a full section rapidly across the operational area without imposing tracked-vehicle maintenance on every movement.

The Fuchs is not inferior to the Otter on a road any more than the Otter is inferior to the Greif in a flooded forest.

# The Jäger vehicle family

The Otter should become a chassis family, but a more limited one than Greif. Its mission variants are organized around what a light expeditionary formation must carry after the road ends.

| Variant | Role |
|---|---|
| Schützenpanzer 74 Otter | Standard IFV |
| Führungsotter | Command and signals |
| Mörserotter | 120 mm mortar carrier |
| Sanitätsotter | Armored ambulance |
| Pionierotter | Engineer, obstacle-clearance, and assault support |
| Bergeotter | Light recovery vehicle |
| Drachenotter | Dedicated antitank carrier with additional missiles |
| Feuerleitotter | Artillery observation and air-support coordination |

The recovery variant is especially important. One of the Congo lessons is that a vehicle light enough to enter difficult terrain must also be light enough for its own formation to recover. A heavy Greif recovery vehicle cannot always follow the route used by an Otter.

# Tanks: Panzer XI is vindicated

The War of the Chiefs doesn’t prove that Panzer X was a bad tank. It proves that the Panzer XI design philosophy has greater utility beyond the expected European battlefield.

The Panzer XI is:

- lighter;
- faster;
- easier to recover;
- easier to place on barges;
- less demanding on bridges;
- and better suited to moving between disconnected road networks.

Its 105 mm gun is already more than adequate against every armored target in the theatre. The Congo therefore demonstrates that additional armor beyond the threat requirement is not free protection. It is weight carried across every bridge, landing stage, transport ship, causeway, and mud field.

## Congo tank modifications

The army does not develop a new tank during the campaign. It develops theatre kits for Panzer XI:

### Rüstsatz Tropen

- improved filtration;
- revised cooling;
- corrosion-resistant electrical connections;
- insect and debris screens;
- additional water storage;
- improved crew ventilation;
- and external stowage for tools and infantry supplies.

### Rüstsatz Ufer

- wider track options;
- enhanced bilge equipment;
- deep-wading preparation;
- shoreline recovery cables;
- and fittings for barge restraint and loading.

### Rüstsatz Pionier

- light dozer blade;
- demolition stores;
- winch;
- vegetation-cutting equipment;
- and attachment points for fascines or trackway panels.

These are mission packages rather than separate production variants. The Panzer XI Ausf. C and D still follow their established fire-control and night-sight development. fileciteturn12file0

## What happens to Panzer X

Older Panzer X vehicles remain useful, but increasingly in roles where their weight is less harmful:

- port and dam defense;
- static mobile reserve;
- engineer conversion;
- recovery;
- training;
- export;
- and flamethrower conversion.

A limited **Flammpanzer X Rüstsatz 73** can be developed for fortified compounds, bunkers, trenches, caves, and immediate vegetation clearance.

It should not burn “vast swaths” of jungle. Large clearance still depends on bulldozers, saws, explosives, tracked engineer tractors, and controlled fire. The flamethrower tank is a close-assault weapon, not a deforestation machine.

# Revising Panzer XII

The current reference gives Panzer XII a 57-ton combat weight. The Congo-derived procurement direction points toward reducing that.

I would revise the service Panzer XII to approximately **52.5 tonnes**.

It remains heavier than Panzer XI because it carries:

- a 120 mm smoothbore;
- composite frontal armor;
- larger ammunition;
- improved fire control;
- and a more powerful protection package.

But it does not become a sixty-tonne fortress.

### Revised Panzer XII principle

> **Maximum protection inside a fixed mobility envelope, rather than maximum protection followed by whatever mobility remains.**

A useful developmental contest would place two designs against one another:

- a roughly 60-tonne heavy design with deeper side protection and a larger turret;
- a roughly 52-tonne mobile design with concentrated frontal protection, modular side packages, and better transport compatibility.

The Mittelafrika reports help select the latter.

### Proposed revised service value

| Characteristic | Panzer XII Ausf. A |
|---|---|
| Introduction | 1981 |
| Combat weight | 52.5 t |
| Crew | 4 |
| Main gun | 120 mm KwK 79 L/44 |
| Engine | 1,500 hp diesel |
| Road speed | 68 km/h |
| Protection | Composite frontal arc; modular side and roof packages |
| Design emphasis | Fire control, first-round hit probability, mobility, and recoverability |

It is still a German heavy-leaning MBT. The difference is that the Army rejects weight growth as a virtue in itself.

# The Tropenjäger force

The permanent force probably receives a broader formal name than *Dschungeljäger*.

## Formal organization

**Tropenjägerkommando Mittelafrika**

## Common name

**Dschungeljäger**

The command is a Wehrmacht institution, not a private army of the Reichskommissariat. Mittelafrika supplies bases, ports, local employees, training areas, and part of the budget, but command and senior appointments remain with the Heer.

Its permanent functions are:

- security of Kongosee and strategic infrastructure;
- jungle and riverine training;
- rapid reinforcement of German districts;
- expeditionary intervention;
- and preparation for operations beyond Mittelafrika.

Possible external missions include:

- reinforcing Portugal in Angola or Mozambique;
- intervention in Tanganyika or British East Africa;
- operating along the Congo–Zambezi transport systems;
- and supporting German clients in tropical or riverine regions.

The command’s equipment is intentionally different from that of a European Panzergrenadier corps:

- Otter IFVs;
- Fuchs carriers;
- Panzer XI companies in limited numbers;
- light engineer vehicles;
- helicopter-mobile artillery;
- Kongosee assault craft;
- and a larger proportion of mortars, reconnaissance, medical, maintenance, and water-purification equipment.

# Infantry weapons during the war

The standard rifle is the **StG 60**, chambered in 5.6×40 mm. It has been in service since 1961. The lighter cartridge and thirty-round magazine are valuable for troops carrying ammunition on foot through heat and broken terrain. fileciteturn12file0

The war does not immediately produce the 1983 StG 82. It produces a sequence of modifications that eventually makes the StG 82 possible.

## StG 60A3 — tropical reliability package, 1973

Changes include:

- improved corrosion-resistant finish;
- larger drainage openings;
- revised handguard ventilation;
- more durable magazine coatings;
- protected sling fittings;
- and simplified field stripping with wet or dirty hands.

These improvements matter more in the first year than optics do.

## Granatgerät 74

Close fighting around vegetation, channels, compounds, and reverse slopes creates demand for a low-velocity grenade launcher.

The **Granatgerät 74** is a removable 40×46 mm underbarrel launcher for StG 60. It is issued selectively to one or two men per section rather than attached to every rifle.

It provides:

- fragmentation;
- smoke;
- illumination;
- signaling;
- and limited anti-structure capability.

This becomes the direct ancestor of the integrated launcher option on StG 82.

## StG 60A4 — mission fittings, 1975

The A4 receives reinforced mounting points for:

- Granatgerät 74;
- compact optical sights;
- white-light or infrared lamps;
- bipods;
- and experimental foregrips.

The fittings are not yet one universal standard. Different manufacturers and units create incompatible solutions, which becomes one of the war’s frustrations.

## Optics in Mittelafrika

Optics should appear, but not universally.

The most useful early allocations go to:

- scouts;
- section leaders;
- marksmen;
- boat gunners;
- night patrols;
- and observation personnel.

A compact **1.5× or 2× prismatic sight** is more useful than a high-magnification optic in dense terrain. Gewehr 58 continues to serve designated marksmen where longer channels, cleared shorelines, or open lake approaches permit longer shots.

The problems are practical:

- fogging;
- moisture;
- mud;
- scratched lenses;
- poor mounting repeatability;
- and difficulty maintaining zero after repeated removal.

The war therefore proves the need for a standardized mounting interface without proving that every rifle should immediately carry an optic.

## From field mounts to Einheitsleiste 79

The sequence should be:

1. incompatible unit and manufacturer mounts, 1973–75;
2. limited **Tragschiene 75** field trials;
3. postwar standardization work, 1976–78;
4. adoption of the **Einheitsleiste 79**;
5. StG 60A6 adapter kits;
6. StG 82 designed around the standard from the beginning.

That preserves the current canon date of the Einheitsleiste while making the War of the Chiefs its direct institutional origin. The existing reference already establishes that StG 82 uses the Einheitsleiste 79 and that upgraded StG 60A6 rifles can accept an adapter. fileciteturn12file0

# The machine-gun lesson

The **MG 68** remains an excellent general-purpose machine gun, especially for:

- fixed positions;
- boats;
- vehicles;
- defensive bases;
- and sustained fire.

But its 7.92×57 mm ammunition is heavy for long foot patrols.

The war therefore drives the **leichtes MG 76**, already canonically introduced in 1976. It uses the StG 60’s 5.6×40 mm cartridge and a 100-round belt box. fileciteturn12file0

The two weapons receive separate roles:

- MG 68 supplies sustained medium-machine-gun fire.
- leichtes MG 76 supplies mobile squad automatic fire.

The lighter weapon does not replace the MG 68. It allows Jäger sections to carry an automatic weapon without devoting the same proportion of their load to ammunition and spare barrels.

# Multipurpose weapons

The war also changes how Germany treats weapons nominally designed for tanks.

## Panzerfaust 74M

The existing Panzerfaust 74 enters service in 1974 as a disposable 110 mm antitank weapon. fileciteturn12file0

A **Panzerfaust 74M** multipurpose variant follows during the campaign. It exchanges some armor penetration for:

- fragmentation;
- blast;
- and better performance against walls, bunkers, boats, and field positions.

The original antitank variant remains standard in Europe. Tropenjäger units carry more of the multipurpose model.

## Drachen as a mission weapon

The Drachen 66 remains a powerful antitank missile, but the war teaches that it need not be permanently integral to every fighting vehicle.

This encourages:

- detachable vehicle racks;
- tripod-mounted firing posts;
- boat mounts;
- fortified-port mounts;
- and dedicated missile carriers.

That is a more efficient distribution than forcing every Otter to carry a missile it rarely fires.

# Light artillery and fire support

The Panzerhaubitze 72 is a first-rate divisional artillery system, but its 149.1 mm weapon and tracked chassis are too heavy to accompany every Jäger operation. fileciteturn12file0

The campaign should produce a **10.5 cm Jägerhaubitze 75**.

| Characteristic | Jägerhaubitze 75 |
|---|---|
| Caliber | 105 mm |
| Combat weight | Approximately 2.1–2.5 t |
| Standard range | Approximately 17 km |
| Transport | Helicopter, barge, light tractor, or truck |
| Role | Jäger, airborne, mountain, and amphibious fire support |

It isn’t a replacement for divisional 15 cm artillery. It gives dispersed battalions useful fire support without waiting for a heavy road or landing stage.

Mortars remain even more common. The fire-support hierarchy becomes:

- 81 mm mortars with companies and battalions;
- 120 mm mortars on foot, boats, and Otter carriers;
- 105 mm Jägerhaubitze for mobile batteries;
- 15 cm Panzerhaubitze at major ports and prepared corridors;
- aircraft and helicopters for time-sensitive targets.

# Mine and maintenance protection

The Congo equipment program also develops less visible modifications:

- bolt-on belly plates;
- protected fuel tanks;
- improved fire suppression;
- external rather than internal stowage for dangerous cargo;
- modular power packs;
- stronger winches;
- standardized tow fittings;
- and better access to filters, pumps, and electrical systems.

The result is not a modern MRAP fleet appearing in 1974. It is an army learning that mines, mud, corrosion, and recovery destroy more operational capacity than enemy antitank guns.

# The wartime procurement mechanism

The development needs an institution that can turn field experience into equipment before the war ends.

A good working body is:

## **Heeresversuchsstab Kongo**

The Congo Army Trials Staff.

It includes:

- frontline officers and NCOs;
- armaments engineers;
- vehicle and weapons manufacturers;
- flotilla technical personnel;
- Luftwaffe representatives;
- doctors and tropical-medicine personnel;
- signals specialists;
- and Reichskommissariat logistics officials.

The staff classifies requests into three levels:

### Field modification

Can be manufactured locally or fitted by a divisional workshop:

- screens;
- drainage;
- storage;
- weapon brackets;
- winches;
- lights;
- and tropical seals.

### Emergency production

Requires a factory change but uses an existing weapon or chassis:

- Otter prototypes;
- Granatgerät 74;
- Panzerfaust 74M;
- lighter turrets;
- and specialized boat mounts.

### Postwar development

Requires a proper procurement cycle:

- Fuchs family;
- Einheitsleiste 79;
- StG 82;
- revised Panzer XII;
- and permanent Tropenjäger equipment standards.

This prevents every battlefield complaint from becoming a new national weapon program.

# Proposed canon equipment sequence

| Year | System or decision |
|---:|---|
| 1972 | Greif and Panzerhaubitze 72 enter service during the intervention |
| 1973 | StG 60A3 tropical package; Otter emergency development begins; Panzer XI Congo kits |
| 1974 | Limited Schützenpanzer 74 Otter; MK 74 cannon; Granatgerät 74; Panzerfaust 74 and 74M |
| 1975 | Wider Otter fielding; 10.5 cm Jägerhaubitze 75; experimental rifle mounting systems |
| 1976 | leichtes MG 76; Transportpanzer 76 Fuchs; mature Tropenjäger organization |
| 1977–1979 | Postwar equipment reconciliation; Einheitsleiste 79 standardized |
| 1981 | Lighter 52.5-tonne Panzer XII enters service |
| 1983 | StG 82 enters elite service with the standardized modular interface |

# Canonical synthesis

The War of the Chiefs does not replace Germany’s heavy mechanized army with a light colonial force. It makes Germany maintain both.

The Greif remains the standard vehicle of the Panzergrenadier.

The Otter becomes the standard tracked vehicle of the Tropenjäger.

The Fuchs gives Jäger and support troops protected operational mobility without pretending to be an IFV.

The Panzer XI proves that mobility, recoverability, and transport weight are part of protection rather than concessions made against it.

The Panzer XII still gains a 120 mm gun and composite armor, but its weight is constrained by the lesson that a tank the army cannot transport or recover is only well protected until it breaks down.

And the StG 60 does not instantly become a modern accessory platform. It acquires tropical modifications, grenade launchers, limited optics, and a confused family of mounts. The confusion itself leads to the Einheitsleiste 79 and then the StG 82.

The governing equipment lesson is therefore:

> **Germany enters the war believing that more armor, more integrated weapons, and more mechanization produce a better formation. It leaves understanding that equipment is better only when the formation can bring it to the fight, sustain it there, and leave with it afterward.**

## Turn 629 — Assistant

- Timestamp: 2026-08-03T22:37:31.903Z
- Source: ChatGPT shared conversation `German Naming Doctrine`
- Parallel branch: https://chatgpt.com/share/6a71998f-1db0-83e8-8b0d-0ef16ab4b58a
- Relationship: continuation from the master project record through Turn 411

The best answer is **both, but at different levels**.

Each Reichskommissariat should have a coat of arms, official colors, a Reichskommissar’s standard, and eventually a territorial **service flag**. But the flag representing sovereignty remains the German national flag. The Reichskommissariats are not associated states, protectorates, or constituent nations. They are German imperial administrations ruling territories that are German in sovereignty even where Germans remain a demographic minority. fileciteturn0file1

So the setting needs a **flag system**, not five additional national flags.

## Why the TNO flags are only partly convincing

The flags you attached all follow roughly the same formula:

- a Reichskriegsflagge-style cross;
- a distinct territorial field color;
- the German national emblem in the canton;
- and a central rune, shield, or territorial badge.

They’re effective game flags. You can identify the territory instantly, and the common construction tells the player that they belong to the same empire.

But in-world they create three problems.

First, they look like **military ensigns**. That makes sense during conquest, but less so once the Reichskommissariats become permanent civil governments with courts, schools, enterprises, cadastral offices, ports, and territorial bureaucracies.

Second, the large colored fields make the Reichskommissariats resemble quasi-sovereign countries. Ukraine’s blue and yellow, for example, makes it look as though a Ukrainian state has been incorporated into a German confederation. That is almost exactly the political implication Berlin would want to avoid.

Third, the different central ideological symbols make every Reichskommissariat look as if it possesses its own political doctrine. Hagedorn’s mature SS Order is going in the opposite direction: standardized authority, standardized ceremonies, standardized status law, and suppression of private territorial cults.

The flags are therefore visually useful but constitutionally too generous.

## The Chōsen comparison

Chōsen is a good starting comparison, though not a complete one.

While Korea was still a Japanese protectorate, the Resident-General had a distinctive positional flag. After formal annexation in 1910, that flag was abolished and the Japanese national flag became the ordinary sovereign flag used in Korea. citeturn824202search3turn824202search5

The Eastern Reichskommissariats similarly deny that their subject populations possess separate sovereignty. But they’re territorially and administratively more differentiated than Chōsen. Each has:

- its own Reichskommissar;
- distinct settlement and racial policies;
- different religious and ethnic conditions;
- its own budgetary and blocked-currency arrangements;
- regional police and auxiliaries;
- and, eventually, a recognizable German settler culture.

So they need more visual institutional identity than Chōsen did, but less than an independent client kingdom.

## The recommended hierarchy

### 1. German national flag

This is the flag of sovereignty.

It flies over:

- Reichskommissariat capitals;
- Reich courts and major administrative buildings;
- Wehrmacht and SS installations;
- German schools;
- strategic rail and port headquarters;
- official holidays;
- and all ceremonies involving the Führer or Reich government.

A visitor arriving in Kiew, Petersburg, Kongostadt, or Tiflis should immediately understand that he has entered territory ruled by Germany, not a subordinate country with its own national banner.

### 2. Reich service flag

German civil ministries and government agencies use the Reich’s state-service flag rather than the war flag. Historically, the **Reichsdienstflagge** distinguished state offices and official buildings from ordinary party or civilian use. citeturn544048search1turn544048search21

This would be the natural base for Reichskommissariat administrative flags.

### 3. Reichskommissariat service flag

Each Reichskommissariat receives a **Dienstflagge des Reichskommissariats**.

It is not treated as the territory’s national flag. It identifies the administration.

It appears on:

- Reichskommissariat ministry buildings;
- official vehicles;
- customs and police posts;
- government ferries;
- port authorities;
- administrative conferences;
- technical schools;
- and Reichskommissariat-owned ships and aircraft.

The best design would be a standardized German state-service flag with a small territorial shield in a prescribed position—probably the lower fly or upper hoist—rather than a completely different field for every territory.

The structure says:

> Germany supplies sovereignty; the shield identifies which administration is acting.

Imperial German colonial heraldry offers a useful precedent. The proposed colonial arms of 1914 placed the imperial eagle in the upper portion and a local territorial motif beneath it. The colonies remained imperial possessions, while the lower shield identified the particular territory. citeturn544048search12

### 4. Reichskommissar’s standard

Each Reichskommissar should possess a square personal standard for:

- his official residence;
- motorcar;
- boat;
- inspection train;
- field headquarters;
- and ceremonial appearances.

This is where the more elaborate TNO-style designs can survive.

A cross-based flag with a large central territorial badge makes sense as the standard of the Reichskommissar or the territorial administration’s command authority. It makes less sense as the flag representing millions of inhabitants.

### 5. Regional arms and banners

The coats of arms matter more than separate flags.

They appear on:

- seals;
- letterheads;
- courtrooms;
- uniforms;
- school certificates;
- vehicle doors;
- port signs;
- medals;
- police badges;
- sports clubs;
- public works;
- and settlement monuments.

By the 1970s, settlers and veterans would probably treat these arms as genuine regional symbols even though Berlin continues denying that the Reichskommissariats are nations.

That distinction mirrors the broader canon. The Eastern Reichskommissariats become stable colonial civilizations with their own ruling communities and institutions, but they never acquire sovereign nationhood. fileciteturn0file1

## How the system develops over time

### 1947–1952: occupation symbolism

During conquest intoxication and the quota crisis, there are no proper territorial flags.

Government buildings fly:

- the German national flag;
- the Reich service flag;
- the Reichskriegsflagge at military headquarters;
- SS standards;
- and improvised Reichskommissar command flags.

This is also the period in which local administrators create unofficial runes, badges, and estate banners without much central supervision.

### 1952–1958: codification

As the mature administrative system develops, Berlin authorizes official Reichskommissariat coats of arms.

The arms are deliberately **territorial rather than national**. They symbolize geography, production, settlement, or German historical claims—not the political nationhood of Ukrainians, Russians, Caucasians, or African peoples.

### 1960s: administrative service flags

Each administration receives a standardized service flag based on the Reich model.

The national flag remains dominant. The territorial flag is secondary and is never flown alone at a major government building.

### Hagedorn era after 1976

Hagedorn regularizes the system.

Private SS territorial flags and extravagant local standards are registered or abolished. Approved Reichskommissariat arms remain, but the imperial relationship is visually standardized:

- common dimensions;
- common placement of the Reich emblem;
- common rank of precedence;
- and territorial variation confined principally to the shield and secondary colors.

This fits his general effort to convert the SS from Himmler’s inconsistent personal world into a reproducible governing Order.

## What each Reichskommissariat receives

| Territory | Sovereign flag | Territorial identity |
|---|---|---|
| **Ostland** | German national flag | RK service flag and Baltic–eastern territorial arms |
| **Ukraine** | German national flag | RK service flag and agricultural/Dnieper arms |
| **Moskowien** | German national flag | RK service flag and Russian-interior/Volga territorial arms |
| **Kaukasien** | German national flag | RK service flag and mountain–oil–Black/Caspian Sea arms |
| **Mittelafrika** | German national flag | RK service ensign and African administrative arms |

Cameroon, French West Africa, the Congo, and Madagascar do not need separate Reichskommissariat flags because they aren’t separate Reichskommissariats in this setting. Their TNO flags could instead be recycled as:

- provincial administrative banners;
- Generalbezirk standards;
- port-authority flags;
- police badges;
- or provincial coats of arms.

That gives them visual identity without contradicting Mittelafrika’s unified administration.

## Specific heraldic direction

### Ostland

Ostland’s shield can draw on:

- the Baltic cross;
- a fortress or gate;
- amber or sea imagery;
- oak leaves;
- and perhaps a smaller German eagle.

It should avoid simply combining the Estonian, Latvian, Lithuanian, and Belarusian national colors. Ostland is an imperial administrative concept, not a federation of four acknowledged peoples.

The attached TNO **Ostland** flag works best as the Reichskommissar’s standard. Its red field and cross produce a strong command flag, but it is too military to serve as the ordinary civil banner.

### Ukraine

Ukraine can retain blue and gold as administrative colors, but they should appear chiefly inside the shield rather than filling the entire flag.

Suitable motifs include:

- wheat;
- the Dnieper;
- a cog or agricultural wheel;
- a fortified settlement gate;
- and a German eagle or Order device above them.

The trident should probably be avoided or subordinated, because it too clearly recognizes an independent Ukrainian national tradition.

The attached blue-and-yellow TNO flag could survive as an early occupation or agricultural administration banner, but as an official territorial flag it looks too much like a Ukrainian state under German suzerainty.

### Moskowien

Moskowien’s arms should avoid the Russian imperial double-headed eagle and probably avoid Saint George as the primary symbol. Both could become rallying points for surviving Russian political identity.

Better motifs would be:

- the Volga;
- a fortified river gate;
- forest and grain;
- an iron wheel;
- or a stylized eastward road or railway.

The TNO central symbol could survive as an SS Order badge, but the main shield should look administrative rather than mystical.

### Kaukasien

Kaukasien needs the least ethnically specific arms because it rules the most visibly plural region.

A suitable shield might combine:

- a mountain;
- an oil flame or derrick;
- Black and Caspian waters;
- and a fortified pass.

The design should make no claim that Georgians, Armenians, Azeris, Russians, Chechens, and other populations have somehow become one Caucasian nation.

### Mittelafrika

Mittelafrika probably develops the strongest and most frequently seen territorial service flag.

That is because it possesses:

- enormous distances;
- ports;
- customs services;
- aircraft;
- the MOSAIK bureaucracy;
- Kongosee;
- the Kongosee- und Stromschutz;
- and a more visibly separate overseas administrative culture.

Its arms might eventually combine:

- the Congo River or Kongosee;
- an elephant or other territorial animal;
- a wheel or turbine;
- and a small German imperial device above.

The central symbol should represent the **Mosaic Order and infrastructure**, not one African ethnic group.

The individual TNO flags for Congo, Ostafrika, Südwestafrika, and Madagascar are therefore better treated as provincial or flotilla insignia beneath the Mittelafrika service flag.

## Flag protocol on Kongosee

The newly established brown-water force makes the distinction practical.

### Wehrmacht-controlled combat craft

These fly the **Reichskriegsflagge**, because they’re military vessels under Wehrmacht operational authority.

### Kongosee- und Stromschutz craft

These fly the **Mittelafrika service ensign**, identifying them as armed colonial-government craft rather than Kriegsmarine vessels.

### Police, customs, and hydrographic boats

These use the same service ensign with smaller branch badges or pennants.

### Reichskommissar’s inspection vessel

It flies both:

- the Mittelafrika service ensign at the stern;
- and the Reichskommissar’s personal standard while he is aboard.

This gives Mittelafrika’s unique flag a constant visible function without presenting Mittelafrika as a sovereign country.

## Final verdict on the attached flags

The TNO flags should not be adopted as the ordinary territorial flags of AltWWII.

They should be divided among three uses:

- **Reichskommissar standards** for the most elaborate cross-and-badge designs;
- **early occupation or SS command flags** for the more overtly military designs;
- **provincial and service banners** for the African designs belonging to territories now administered beneath Mittelafrika.

The mature official arrangement should be:

> **German national flag for sovereignty, Reich service flag for German state authority, Reichskommissariat service flag for territorial administration, and regional coats of arms for everyday institutional identity.**

That gives every Reichskommissariat a recognizable symbol without accidentally declaring that Germany has created five new nations inside its empire.

## Turn 631 — Assistant

- Timestamp: 2026-08-03T22:50:49.645Z
- Source: ChatGPT shared conversation `German Naming Doctrine`
- Parallel branch: https://chatgpt.com/share/6a71998f-1db0-83e8-8b0d-0ef16ab4b58a
- Relationship: continuation from the master project record through Turn 411

Yes. In fact, that is probably **a better solution than the one I gave before**.

A flag with a **German national canton** and a territorially distinctive field would communicate the constitutional relationship very clearly:

> **The canton identifies the sovereign power. The field identifies the territory. The badge identifies the administration.**

That is exactly what these flags need to say.

The only qualification is that this would not literally be the ordinary **Reichsdienstflagge**. It would be a new family of **Reichskommissariatsdienstflaggen** built from the same service-flag logic and from the colonial-ensign tradition.

## Colonial ensign rather than regional national flag

British colonial ensigns generally placed the Union Jack in the canton and used the remainder of the flag for a colonial field and badge. The canton did not mean that the territory was an equal component of Britain. It marked the territory as falling beneath British sovereignty, while the badge identified the particular colonial government. citeturn222553search3turn222553search5

Germany had no identical established colonial system, but the 1914 proposals for German colonial flags worked from a related principle: retain the imperial national flag and add a distinctive colonial coat of arms. Those proposed arms placed the imperial eagle above a local territorial emblem. citeturn222553search18

So AltWWII Germany would not be copying Britain without precedent. It would be combining:

- the British visual grammar of the metropolitan canton;
- the older German idea of colonial territorial arms;
- and the National Socialist distinction between Reich sovereignty and subordinate administrative identity.

That fits the Reichskommissariats unusually well because they are expressly not independent states. The canon defines them as loyal parts of the German imperial system and denies their populations the status of state-bearing peoples, even where Germans remain a minority. fileciteturn12file9

## The standard design

I would make the mature flag formula:

### **Dienstflagge des Reichskommissariats**

- **Ratio:** probably 2:3.
- **Canton:** the German red national flag with white disc and black swastika.
- **Main field:** one or two colors assigned to the Reichskommissariat.
- **Fly badge:** the territorial shield or administrative emblem.
- **No large war-flag cross.**
- **No separate eagle above the shield**, because the canton already establishes Reich authority.

That last point matters. Putting a Reich eagle, swastika canton, SS rune, and territorial shield all on the same flag would make it overloaded. The canton does the constitutional work. The badge should identify the place.

The result would resemble a colonial ensign much more than a national flag.

## Would it still be called a Dienstflagge?

Yes, and that legal terminology solves the main problem.

It should **not** be called:

- *Landesflagge*;
- *Nationalflagge*;
- or the “flag of Ukraine,” “flag of Moskowien,” and so forth.

It is the service flag **of the Reichskommissariat administration**.

That means it belongs to the state apparatus rather than automatically to everyone living in the territory. It appears on:

- Reichskommissariat offices;
- administrative vehicles;
- customs posts;
- police stations;
- government ferries and patrol craft;
- territorial rail and port authorities;
- schools operated directly by the administration;
- and official publications.

Private subjects might initially be forbidden to fly it. German settler communities would nevertheless begin using it socially over time, especially at veterans’ meetings, sports events, settlement festivals, and regional associations. By the 1970s, it could function culturally as a regional flag even while Berlin insists that it remains only an administrative service flag.

That is a useful formal-versus-functional distinction:

> Formally, it identifies an office. Functionally, it becomes the banner of the German colonial society formed around that office.

## Flag precedence

The Reich flag still remains superior.

At the Reichskommissariat headquarters in Kiew or Kongostadt, the arrangement would probably be:

1. **German national flag** in the position of honour.
2. **Reichskommissariat service flag** in the subordinate position.
3. Branch standards or rank flags as required.

The Reichskommissariat flag is never flown alone during:

- visits by the Führer;
- formal acts of sovereignty;
- Wehrmacht ceremonies;
- diplomatic events;
- or major Reich holidays.

That prevents the territorial administration from looking sovereign.

The historical Reich service flag was itself a distinct official flag rather than merely another territorial banner. citeturn222553search0 The new Reichskommissariat flags therefore occupy a lower rank beneath both the national flag and any central Reich service flag.

## What happens to the TNO designs?

The canton system makes the TNO cross designs less necessary as ordinary flags, but they can still survive as **Reichskommissar standards**.

So each territory could possess three related symbols:

| Symbol | Function |
|---|---|
| German national flag | Sovereignty |
| Canton-based Reichskommissariat service flag | Territorial administration |
| Square cross-based standard | Personal authority of the Reichskommissar |

That gives us room to retain the striking TNO visual language without claiming that every Reichskommissariat is a miniature sovereign state.

## The territorial fields

The field colors should be distinctive but need not be wholly invented. Germany could appropriate recognizable regional colors while stripping them of independent national meaning.

### Ostland

A dark Baltic blue, deep red, or blue-and-white field would work. The badge could combine a Baltic cross, amber, oak, sea, and fortified gate.

Because Ostland is the most assimilationist and bureaucratically integrated eastern administration, its flag might be the most restrained and German-looking.

### Ukraine

Blue and gold can survive, particularly because they are agriculturally and geographically intuitive. The red swastika canton makes the hierarchy unmistakable.

The badge should avoid the independent Ukrainian trident. Better elements would be:

- wheat;
- the Dnieper;
- a cog or grain wheel;
- and a fortified German settlement.

So the flag could still be visually recognizable as Ukrainian territory without recognizing a Ukrainian state.

### Moskowien

A green, white, and perhaps dark-red field would suit the forests, rivers, and interior. Its badge might contain:

- a river wheel;
- fir trees;
- a railway;
- or a fortified eastern gate.

It should avoid the Russian double-headed eagle and Saint George as primary devices.

### Kaukasien

Green, black, and white would work well, perhaps with a narrow blue element for the two seas.

Its shield could show:

- a mountain;
- an oil flame;
- a pass;
- and two water divisions representing the Black and Caspian seas.

### Mittelafrika

Mittelafrika’s flag would probably become the most publicly familiar of the system because it appears on aircraft, riverboats, Kongosee patrol craft, customs stations, and administrative vessels.

A likely field would be dark green or green-and-blue, with a badge containing:

- the Congo River or Kongosee;
- an elephant;
- a turbine or wheel;
- and perhaps a mosaic pattern.

The red swastika canton would visually dominate just enough to make clear that this is not the flag of an African sovereign state.

Cameroon, French West Africa, Congo, and Madagascar could then receive **provincial badges or pennants**, rather than full flags of the same constitutional rank.

## The likely historical development

This system probably isn’t introduced immediately in 1947.

### 1947–1952

Only German national, military, SS, police, and improvised command flags are common. Local officials produce inconsistent badges and unofficial banners.

### 1952–1958

The Reichskommissariats receive formal coats of arms during administrative codification.

### Late 1950s or early 1960s

The canton-based **Reichskommissariatsdienstflaggen** are introduced as permanent administrative ensigns. This coincides with the transition from temporary conquest governments into mature colonial administrations.

### After 1976

Hagedorn standardizes dimensions, canton size, badge placement, authorized colors, and flag precedence. Unregistered SS runic banners and private estate flags are restricted or demoted to local ceremonial use.

That fits the broader evolution from improvised conquest to permanent German sovereignty. The Reichskommissariats increasingly develop distinct regional societies, but they remain subordinate administrations serving German power rather than separate countries. fileciteturn12file2turn12file3

## Working conclusion

So I would revise the flag doctrine to this:

> **Each Reichskommissariat possesses an official territorial service flag based on the colonial-ensign model. The German national flag appears in a red canton, while the principal field carries assigned regional colors and a distinctive administrative shield in the fly. The flag legally represents the Reichskommissariat government, not a sovereign nation or the native population as a political people.**

That arrangement does match the **Dienstflagge concept**, provided we distinguish the levels correctly:

- it is not *the* Reichsdienstflagge;
- it is a subordinate **Reichskommissariatsdienstflagge**;
- and its design deliberately turns the Reich flag into a badge of parent sovereignty.

In visual terms, it says exactly what Berlin wants:

> **This land has a regional identity, but that identity exists inside German rule.**

iturn760949image3turn760949image1turn760949image2turn760949image4

The first thing we should do is stop treating the Co-Prosperity Sphere as a single legal category. Japan governs different territories through direct imperial rule, chartered states, guardian republics, associated allies, military protectorates, and nominally sovereign clients. The existing canon already assumes this differentiated system, including three separate Japanese-sponsored entities along the Russian Pacific rim: a Vladivostok zone, an Eastern Siberian Republic, and a Chukotka republic. It also establishes that the Urals–Baikal interior remains fragmented rather than becoming either German or Japanese territory. fileciteturn2file6

To keep the larger project on track, we should examine every member under the same seven headings:

> **origin → borders → legal status → governing class → economic function → security function → principal contradiction**

For this first pass, the working question is therefore not merely what resources Mongolia or Siberia contain. It is why Japan maintains each state separately and what place each occupies inside the imperial system.

## The northern structure already implied by canon

Three points are already fixed.

First, Mongolia is within the Japanese sphere by the 1985 Tehran settlement, while Tannu Tuva is explicitly excluded. Second, the Japanese recognition line reaches the western shore of Lake Baikal and then runs north to the Arctic, but recognition of a sphere does not imply that Tokyo directly administers every square mile inside it. Third, the great belt between the Urals and Lake Baikal remains outside both German and Japanese sovereignty. Omsk, Novosibirsk, Krasnoyarsk, Irkutsk, the Kazakh authorities, railway governments, refugee administrations, and military remnants survive as the Siberian Frontier rather than one restored Russia. fileciteturn1file0 fileciteturn1file2

That gives us a useful geographic division:

1. **Greater Mongolia**, south and southwest of Lake Baikal.
2. **The continental Far Eastern client**, east of Baikal.
3. **The Vladivostok maritime enclave**, facing Japan, Korea, and Manchukuo.
4. **The northern Pacific territory**, covering Kamchatka and Chukotka.
5. **The unclaimed Siberian Frontier**, west of Baikal.

That is a much more coherent system than one enormous “Japanese Siberia.”

# I. Mengjiang after the conquest of Outer Mongolia

## It probably cannot remain “Mengjiang”

Once the state incorporates Mongolia proper, *Mengjiang* becomes an increasingly unsuitable formal name. Historically, the regime had already changed its official designation several times. By 1941 it used a deliberately ambiguous formulation translated into Chinese as an autonomous state but into Mongolian in language suggesting an actual country. Prince Demchugdongrub was the central Mongol political figure under Japanese protection. citeturn225981search1turn225981search5

After victory over the Mongolian People’s Republic, Tokyo would probably present the event as **Mongol reunification**, not as the annexation of Outer Mongolia by an obscure Inner Mongolian wartime administration.

My recommended working name is therefore:

> **The United Mongol State**

“Greater Mongolian State” is possible, but it sounds more openly revisionist. “Mongol State” is clean but does not express the political achievement that justifies the regime. *Mengjiang* would survive as the foreign wartime name, much as “Manchukuo” survives even when the state’s formal ceremonial language becomes more elaborate.

The United Mongol State would be a nominally sovereign, aristocratic, Buddhist, banner-federal state under Japanese protection. Demchugdongrub or his household provides the founding dynasty or ruling princely line, but Japanese advisers control strategic finance, army modernization, rail development, mineral concessions, and foreign policy.

## Mongolia is not economically empty

The intuitive reading—that Mongolia is mostly grassland and therefore offers Japan very little—is only half right.

It is poorly suited to becoming another Manchukuo or Ukraine. Mongolia’s cold, arid climate, short growing season, and unreliable precipitation make extensive pastoralism much more durable than large-scale settled agriculture. FAO assessments describe roughly four-fifths of Mongolia as extensive grazing land, with frost-free periods around one hundred days across much of the steppe. Crop farming is possible in selected northern and river-valley areas, but it cannot become the foundation of the whole economy without expensive irrigation, fertilizer, transport, and wind protection. citeturn716573search3turn716573search6turn716573search10

So Japan does not obtain a grain colony. It obtains four other things.

### 1. A pastoral production zone

The immediate products are sheep, goats, horses, cattle, camels, wool, hides, meat, dairy goods, felt, and animal fats. These are not glamorous resources, but they matter to a continental empire containing large armies, cities, railway workforces, and textile industries.

Japanese development would probably concentrate on:

- veterinary services;
- winter fodder reserves;
- wells and pumping stations;
- mobile slaughter and refrigeration facilities;
- wool grading and textile preparation;
- railway livestock terminals;
- weather forecasting;
- insurance or state compensation after catastrophic winters.

That does not abolish nomadism. It makes mobile pastoralism legible to banks, tax offices, railways, and Japanese trading companies.

### 2. A mineral frontier

Mongolia and Inner Mongolia are not devoid of heavy resources. Mongolia possesses substantial coal, copper, fluorspar, gold, iron, tungsten, molybdenum, zinc, uranium, and other mineral deposits. Exactly which fields are commercially known in 1947 should be handled deposit by deposit, but the underlying geological potential is considerable. citeturn760949search1turn760949search6

Inner Mongolia is even more consequential because Bayan Obo was identified as an iron deposit in 1927 and later proved to be an enormous iron, niobium, and rare-earth complex. Japan would initially value it for iron and associated metals; its rare-earth significance would grow with electronics, guidance systems, magnets, and advanced metallurgy during the 1960s and 1970s. citeturn716573search1turn716573search4

This gives the United Mongol State a development pattern resembling neither a settled agricultural colony nor an industrial nation. It becomes a chain of:

> **pasture districts → mining enclaves → railway towns → military settlements**

The open land between those points remains lightly administered.

### 3. Strategic depth

Mongolia places distance between the Japanese-Manchurian industrial core and whatever survives in central Siberia. It protects Manchukuo’s western flank, gives Japan airfields and listening stations facing the Siberian Frontier, and prevents any revived Russian power from immediately reaching northern China.

This is probably its greatest value in the 1940s and 1950s. The minerals become more important later.

### 4. A political demonstration

The Mongol state gives Japan a non-Chinese continental partner with its own historical identity. Tokyo can claim that it has liberated Mongols from both Chinese and Soviet rule and restored a legitimate Mongol political order.

That argument is more convincing to Mongols than the corresponding Japanese claim to be China’s disinterested guardian. It also gives the Sphere a state that is culturally neither Japanese nor Chinese and therefore supports the claim that the Co-Prosperity Sphere is an order of nations rather than merely an expanded Japanese empire.

## Its relationship with Manchukuo

The United Mongol State can stand beside Manchukuo in diplomatic rank without approaching it in industrial power.

The division is straightforward:

- **Manchukuo is the northern workshop and arsenal.**
- **Mongolia is the northern march, pasture reserve, and mineral frontier.**

Manchukuo supplies locomotives, trucks, machine tools, weapons, mining equipment, fertilizer, and processed goods. Mongolia supplies livestock products, selected ores, coal, strategic space, border forces, and mineral concessions.

The Mongol army would retain mounted and highly mobile frontier traditions, but it should not remain a romantic cavalry force indefinitely. By the 1960s, its useful formations would include motorized border brigades, mounted rural constabulary units, railway-security forces, reconnaissance regiments, and a modest Japanese-equipped air arm.

## The border problem we will have to settle

“Modern Mongolia plus modern Inner Mongolia” works as a broad map description, but it creates two complications.

The first is that eastern Mongol territories overlap politically and administratively with Manchukuo. The second is that substantial parts of southern and eastern Inner Mongolia contain large Han populations and important Chinese railway settlements. Nanjing would regard their permanent removal as a major national injury.

The cleanest solution is not to pretend the United Mongol State is ethnically uniform. It would be federally divided among:

- Outer Mongolian aimags;
- Inner Mongolian banners;
- autonomous Buryat or other Mongolic districts where applicable;
- Han-majority railway and agricultural districts;
- Japanese concession territories around mines and transport nodes.

This also gives Tokyo leverage. Japan becomes the indispensable arbiter between Mongol princes, Buddhist institutions, Han commercial communities, Manchukuo, and Nanjing.

So the first working conclusion is:

> **The United Mongol State is a major member of the Sphere because of its size, strategic position, and political identity—not because it rivals Manchukuo’s factories.**

# II. The eastern Siberian rim

The mistake here would be to ask whether the whole territory from Baikal to Chukotka can function as one ordinary country. It cannot, at least not in the same sense as Siam or Manchukuo.

The land is enormous, the population is sparse, and the useful infrastructure follows a few railways, rivers, ports, mines, and coastal settlements. The correct model is a legally unified sphere containing several functionally separate systems.

The Japanese do not control the Far East by covering every forest or tundra district. They control:

- the railway;
- the major rivers;
- the ports;
- the mines;
- the airfields;
- the radio network;
- and the governments that issue concessions.

## Recommended northern arrangement

| Entity | Practical territory | Principal function |
|---|---|---|
| **United Mongol State** | Mongolia and most of Inner Mongolia | Strategic buffer, pastoral economy, mineral frontier |
| **Far Eastern Republic** | Transbaikal, Amur basin, Khabarovsk region, Yakutia and Kolyma claims | Continental buffer, rail corridor, mining and forestry concessions |
| **Urajio Protectorate** | Primorye and the lower Ussuri–Peter the Great Gulf region | Naval base, commercial port, multiethnic gateway |
| **Northern Pacific Protectorate** | Kamchatka and Chukotka | Fisheries, air and naval bases, gold and northern surveillance |
| **Siberian Frontier** | Baikal westward toward the Urals | Fragmented independent successor space |

## 1. The Far Eastern Republic

There is a strong historical precedent for reusing the name **Far Eastern Republic** rather than inventing an Eastern Siberian national identity from nothing.

A Far Eastern Republic existed between 1920 and 1922 as a nominally independent buffer between Soviet Russia and Japanese-occupied territories. Its own constitutional claims extended from the Lake Baikal region toward the Pacific, and its political center moved to Chita. Japan would remember the arrangement well. Recreating it after the Soviet collapse would have the advantage of appearing to revive a previous Russian Far Eastern state rather than manufacturing an entirely new puppet. citeturn236205search0turn236205search11

In this setting, however, the new republic would function in the opposite direction. The original republic protected Soviet Russia from direct conflict with Japan. The restored republic protects Japan and Manchukuo from the Russian successor states.

### Formal territory versus actual control

Formally, the republic could claim almost everything east of Lake Baikal that is not assigned to Urajio or the Northern Pacific Protectorate.

Functionally, its power would be concentrated along:

- Chita and the Transbaikal corridor;
- the Amur railway and river system;
- Blagoveshchensk;
- Khabarovsk;
- the southern Yakut transport routes;
- Magadan and the Kolyma mining settlements;
- selected river ports and airfields.

Large parts of Yakutia, the Vilyuy basin, the northern forests, and the Arctic coast would recognize the republic on maps while seeing little government beyond a district officer, radio station, seasonal aircraft, concession company, or native intermediary.

That distinction is central. The republic is not a nation-state covering its territory uniformly. It is a **corridor state with enormous nominal hinterlands**.

### Capital

Chita is the best founding capital because it provides historical continuity and faces the Siberian Frontier. Khabarovsk would probably become the more important administrative, transport, and military city over time.

A later capital transfer is possible, but I would not settle it yet. The division itself is useful:

- Chita represents continental legitimacy and the claim to Transbaikal.
- Khabarovsk represents the functioning Japanese-backed state.

### Economic role

The republic contains timber, coal, gold, tin, tungsten, other metals, hydroelectric potential, furs, river fisheries, and enormous land concessions. Chukotka and the northeastern districts in particular contain important gold and tin mineralization. But these resources are useful only where transport, labor, machinery, housing, and food supply can be maintained. citeturn716573search5turn526612search3

Japan would therefore treat the republic less as a self-developing national economy and more as a concession system:

> Japanese capital and machinery + Russian and indigenous labor + Far Eastern legal sovereignty + Japanese-controlled export routes.

It is resource-rich but capital-poor and chronically dependent.

## 2. The Urajio Protectorate

The historical Japanese short form for Vladivostok was **Urajio**, associated with the written forms 浦塩 and 浦潮. “Urazhio” is understandable as an English rendering, but **Urajio** is the cleaner romanization for the setting. Japanese archival catalogs preserve several of these historical forms. citeturn812336search0turn812336search1turn812336search5

I would keep Urajio separate, but narrow its territory somewhat from your present description.

It should contain:

- Vladivostok itself;
- Peter the Great Gulf;
- the principal naval approaches and islands;
- most of Primorye;
- the lower Ussuri corridor south of the Amur;
- the Korean and Manchurian frontier approaches.

I would not extend the Urajio state all the way up the lower Amur coast to the Sea of Okhotsk. That would turn a compact port protectorate into a large and geographically awkward coastal country. Khabarovsk and the lower Amur should belong to the Far Eastern Republic.

### Why Urajio remains separate

Urajio serves a completely different purpose from the continental republic.

The Far Eastern Republic exists to govern railways, rivers, forests, mining districts, and Russian hinterlands. Urajio exists to govern a port, a fleet base, foreign commerce, intelligence activity, and a multiethnic urban population.

Its population can plausibly be the mixture you describe:

- Russians;
- Koreans;
- Japanese;
- Manchus;
- Chinese merchants;
- White Russian émigrés returning from Manchuria or China;
- military and naval personnel.

It would be less like an ordinary sovereign republic and more like a Japanese-guaranteed free port, naval protectorate, and international commercial city. It may possess a local assembly and Russian municipal institutions, but the Japanese navy controls the harbor, fortifications, signals, and foreign access.

Urajio is valuable even before considering resources. It prevents a hostile fleet from occupying the strongest port immediately opposite northern Japan and Korea.

## 3. Kamchatka and Chukotka

These regions should remain administratively separate from the Far Eastern Republic, but I do not think a **Republic of Chukotka ruling Kamchatka** is the best mature arrangement.

Chukotka and Kamchatka share northern remoteness, maritime supply, indigenous populations, fisheries, strategic air routes, and Pacific geography. But they are not one natural political unit. Kamchatka’s principal city and infrastructure center is Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky; Chukotka’s administrative center is Anadyr. Rule from one over the other would be highly artificial.

The better model is:

> **Northern Pacific Protectorate**  
> containing a **Kamchatka Territory** and a **Chukotka Autonomous Republic**

The protectorate is supervised by a Japanese high commissioner and naval command. Kamchatka has the larger port, fisheries establishment, and military infrastructure. Chukotka retains an indigenous republican façade, local councils, and control over reindeer and coastal-community affairs.

### Why it stays outside the Far Eastern Republic

The distinction is logistical, not merely ethnic.

The Far Eastern Republic is organized around the Trans-Siberian and Amur systems. Kamchatka and Chukotka are supplied primarily by sea and air. Their security faces the Bering Sea, Alaska, the North Pacific, and the Sea of Okhotsk rather than central Siberia.

The maritime economy is also substantial. Modern fishery assessments place the largest concentrations of Russian Pacific fish resources in the Sea of Okhotsk, western Bering Sea, and East Kamchatka zones. The Far East has historically accounted for most Russian marine catch, with Petropavlovsk serving as a major fishing port. citeturn526612search1turn526612search4turn526612search8

For Japan, this means Kamchatka and Chukotka offer:

- salmon, pollock, herring, crab, and other fisheries;
- gold and other mineral deposits;
- naval and air bases;
- weather stations;
- Bering Strait surveillance;
- control of approaches between the Pacific and Arctic;
- denial of the peninsula to America or a revived Russia.

This territory could become strategically important without becoming prosperous or densely settled.

# III. What Japan actually gains from the northern empire

Japan does not take Mongolia and eastern Siberia because they are easy sources of immediate profit. Much of the territory will consume more investment than it returns during the first postwar decade.

It holds them because they form a **northern shield** around the real centers of Japanese power.

The shield has four layers:

- Mongolia protects northern China and Manchukuo from the west.
- The Far Eastern Republic prevents a Russian successor from reaching the Pacific.
- Urajio removes the principal hostile naval base opposite Japan.
- Kamchatka and Chukotka secure the northern Pacific and Bering approaches.

Resources make that shield partially self-financing. They do not fully explain why it exists.

This also produces a useful contrast inside the Sphere. Southeast Asia is populous, tropical, maritime, and commercially valuable. The northern clients are sparse, continental, militarized, and dependent upon Japanese capital. Tokyo can speak of both as members of one Asian order, but the actual relationship is radically different.

# Working conclusions to carry forward

I would provisionally lock the northern Co-Prosperity Sphere as follows:

**The wartime Mengjiang regime becomes the United Mongol State after conquering Outer Mongolia.** It is a major associated protectorate and pan-Mongol state, diplomatically comparable to Manchukuo but economically specialized in pastoral production, minerals, and strategic depth.

**The Eastern Siberian Republic becomes the Far Eastern Republic.** It is a Russian-led Japanese client claiming the continental territory from Baikal toward the Pacific, but its actual authority follows the railways, rivers, mines, and southern settlements.

**Urajio remains separate.** It controls Primorye and the Ussuri–Vladivostok maritime zone as a Japanese-guaranteed, multiethnic naval and commercial protectorate.

**Kamchatka and Chukotka remain outside the Far Eastern Republic.** They form a Northern Pacific Protectorate, with Kamchatka and Chukotka retaining separate internal administrations.

**The lands west of Baikal remain the Siberian Frontier.** Japan may trade, invest, spy, and support local clients there, but it does not annex or unify them.

The unresolved northern questions are now narrow enough to handle deliberately: the exact Mongol–Manchukuo boundary, the position of Buryatia, the capital and constitution of the Far Eastern Republic, and—most conspicuously—the fate of northern Sakhalin and the remaining Kuril administration. Those should be settled before we move south into Indochina or Indonesia.
