The strongest model is not that **Siberia never consolidates**. That would be difficult to sustain.

It is that:

> **Siberia consolidates into several regional states before any one state becomes strong enough to consolidate Siberia.**

Early warlordism gradually disappears. Omsk, Novosibirsk, Krasnoyarsk, Irkutsk, Kazakhstan, Tashkent, and several smaller commands don’t remain collections of armed roadblocks forever. They build governments, currencies, armies, schools, customs systems, and foreign relationships. But those institutions harden regional division rather than overcoming it.

Mikhail’s Far Eastern monarchy helps produce that result, but it shouldn’t be the sole cause. It is the **legitimacy trap** at the eastern end of a system already divided by geography, evacuation, ideology, ethnicity, economic dependency, and outside intervention.

The current canon already establishes the essential starting point: factories, cadres, military districts, security institutions, refugee authorities, and local governments survive across Siberia and Central Asia without one universally recognized Russian successor. It also allows American Arctic aid to support particular governments through food, machinery, radios, technicians, and intelligence relationships. fileciteturn11file8

# The central paradox

The Russian memory of unity is strongest immediately after the collapse, when nobody has the means to restore it.

By the time one or two states acquire the administrative and military capacity to attempt unification, twenty or thirty years have passed. Their populations now possess:

- regional citizenship;
- different currencies;
- separate officer corps;
- conflicting school histories;
- foreign aid relationships;
- local political elites;
- established borders;
- and concrete interests that would be lost in reunification.

So the historical memory and the practical capacity move in opposite directions:

> **When everyone remembers one Russia, nobody can rebuild it. When someone might be capable of rebuilding it, fewer people agree on what Russia is supposed to be.**

That is what makes long-term fragmentation plausible.

# Mikhail II as the negative center of Russian legitimacy

Mikhail doesn’t merely establish one more Russian successor state. He removes the easiest neutral solution available to the others.

Without Chita’s monarchy, central Siberian factions might eventually agree that a Romanov restoration is the least objectionable means of standing above Soviet, White, military, democratic, and regional rivalries.

But once Mikhail accepts a Japanese-sponsored crown, Romanov legitimacy becomes both available and contaminated.

## The monarchist dilemma

A monarchist in Omsk or Krasnoyarsk has three choices.

He can recognize Mikhail, which means accepting that the legitimate Russian crown survives inside the Japanese system.

He can reject Mikhail on dynastic or constitutional grounds, but then he must find another Romanov with a better claim and somehow establish a rival throne.

Or he can argue that the monarchy must remain suspended until Russia is liberated, which deprives monarchism of an actual sovereign and turns it into a nostalgic opposition movement.

This means the central Siberian monarchists split among:

- Chita legitimists;
- strict dynastic legitimists who reject Mikhail;
- provisional monarchists awaiting liberation;
- military nationalists who no longer want a Romanov;
- and regional conservatives willing to use Orthodox and imperial imagery without restoring the throne.

The only functioning crown is the one they regard as compromised.

## The Soviet dilemma

For Soviet restorationists, Mikhail becomes proof that every anti-Soviet alternative leads to foreign domination.

Their propaganda practically writes itself:

> “The Japanese found a prince in Australia and placed him over Russian workers.”

That makes compromise with monarchists much harder. A moderate Soviet administrator who proposes talks with Chita can be accused of preparing another Japanese protectorate.

## The democratic dilemma

Democratic successors also reject Mikhail, but for different reasons. They see the crown as imposed, dependent, and insufficiently representative.

However, they cannot necessarily cooperate with the Soviet restorationists, who retain one-party institutions, security organs, nationalized property, and emergency rule. Nor can they easily cooperate with military nationalists who regard parliamentary government as one of the causes of Russia’s defeat.

The Far Eastern monarchy therefore creates an anti-Chita consensus without creating a pro-anything consensus.

Everyone agrees that Mikhail isn’t the answer. They don’t agree on what the answer is.

## The legitimacy drain

Chita also attracts precisely the people who might otherwise build a broad conservative center in Siberia:

- Orthodox clergy;
- Romanov loyalists;
- White émigrés;
- Cossack families;
- conservative civil servants;
- former imperial families;
- officers who prefer a regular crown to endless military committees;
- technical professionals attracted by Japanese-financed stability.

This produces a kind of **Romanov drain**. The Far Eastern state removes moderate monarchists and conservative administrators from the central successor space, leaving its surviving anti-Soviet regimes more military, ideological, or regionalist.

Ironically, Mikhail’s state weakens the chance of a monarchist reunification even while preserving Russian monarchy.

# Why the old Soviet infrastructure doesn’t recreate the Soviet state

At first glance, the Trans-Siberian Railway appears to provide an obvious unifying spine. It links the major southern Siberian cities, while wartime industrial dispersal has placed factories and skilled personnel east of European Russia. The Soviet Union historically moved substantial industrial capacity toward the Urals and farther east during the war. citeturn985203search4turn985203search26

But a railway is a corridor, not a government.

The historical Trans-Siberian system connects Omsk, Novosibirsk, Krasnoyarsk, Irkutsk, Chita, and the Pacific approaches. That makes it capable of supporting reunification, but it also gives every regional government an obvious set of chokepoints to control. citeturn985203search1turn985203search9

A successor state can seize:

- locomotives;
- repair yards;
- bridges;
- telegraph stations;
- fuel depots;
- marshalling yards;
- food trains;
- and rolling stock.

Once the line is divided among several armed governments, it becomes an instrument of mutual coercion.

Omsk can stop eastbound grain. Novosibirsk can withhold repaired locomotives. Krasnoyarsk can close the Yenisei crossing. Irkutsk can interrupt Baikal transit. A government preparing an offensive must first move men and supplies along a route that its intended enemy can sabotage.

The system can therefore sustain trade or conquest, but not both simultaneously.

## Industrial islands

The evacuated factories don’t arrive as one geographically coherent national economy. They arrive attached to particular cities, ministries, military districts, and supply chains.

One region inherits:

- machine tools but insufficient food;
- another coal but too few locomotives;
- another weapons factories but no petroleum;
- another grain but little heavy industry;
- another minerals but no reliable export route.

That makes cooperation necessary, but it does not make political union inevitable.

In fact, interdependency can encourage division. Each state fears that surrendering its strategic asset to a federal government will leave it permanently subordinate to another region.

Novosibirsk asks why Omsk should command its factories. Kazakhstan asks why Russian generals should command its grain. Krasnoyarsk asks why its Arctic aid should finance western armies. Irkutsk asks why it should abandon its defenses against Chita and Japan to serve an Omsk government.

They can agree to exchange goods more easily than they can agree on who commands the exchange.

# The Russian Civil War provides the right precedent

A unified Russian historical consciousness didn’t prevent Siberia from producing competing regional governments, military dictatorships, socialist committees, Cossack commands, and different visions of post-imperial Russia during the earlier Civil War.

Siberian regionalism had existed before 1917, and the revolutionary period produced arguments for federalism, regional autonomy, all-Russian authority, and separate Far Eastern institutions. Omsk and other eastern governments didn’t merely differ over personalities; they represented conflicting ideas of the future state. citeturn915581search0turn915581search1turn915581search6

Kolchak’s Omsk government historically claimed all-Russian authority, but its existence didn’t automatically subordinate the other anti-Bolshevik and regional movements. citeturn915581search4turn915581search11

The alternate collapse after 1945 is even less favorable to unity:

- the distances are just as large;
- the central capital has been lost;
- the population is more heavily armed;
- industrial assets are more dispersed;
- national minority republics possess mature institutions;
- Germany and Japan occupy both ends of the former state;
- and three or more outside powers can keep local governments alive.

The historical memory of Russia provides a language for unification. It does not provide a government capable of carrying it out.

# The seven barriers to reunification

## 1. No agreed lawful successor

The first question is not who has the strongest army. It is what state survives.

Possible answers include:

- the Soviet Union;
- the Russian Soviet Republic;
- a restored Russian Empire;
- a constituent-assembly republic;
- a Siberian federation;
- a military Russian state;
- a multinational successor union;
- or several independent national states.

Each answer invalidates the others.

A Soviet restorationist claims that Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and the Far East remain parts of the Union.

A Russian nationalist claims that the Union is dead and Russians must rebuild a national state.

A Kazakh government answers that it isn’t territory waiting for Russian reunification.

A Siberian regionalist argues that Moscow’s empires—imperial and Soviet—both exploited Siberia.

A Chita legitimist says the Russian sovereign already exists.

There is no procedural mechanism accepted by everyone that could settle the disagreement.

## 2. No acceptable capital

Every candidate capital carries a political meaning.

**Omsk** suggests military authority, western defense, and the inheritance of earlier anti-Bolshevik government.

**Novosibirsk** suggests industry, evacuation administration, technocracy, and Soviet modernization.

**Krasnoyarsk** suggests the Yenisei basin, Arctic access, and relative neutrality between western and eastern centers.

**Irkutsk** suggests Baikal, revolutionary inheritance, and confrontation with the Japanese-sponsored East.

**Tashkent** suggests continuation of a multinational Soviet or Central Asian administrative order rather than a Russian national state.

Choosing the capital is choosing which regional elite wins.

That makes even a federal agreement difficult. Everyone supports federation until the railway ministry, officer appointments, tax offices, and currency board must be located somewhere.

## 3. The nationality problem

Russian refugees move into northern Kazakhstan and Central Asian cities in very large numbers. This makes some cities heavily Russian in administration, industry, and military personnel while their surrounding countryside remains Kazakh or otherwise non-Russian. The current canon already establishes this divergence between Russianized cities and non-Russian rural populations. fileciteturn10file1

A Russian unification campaign can’t simply absorb Kazakhstan as empty strategic depth.

The Kazakh state has its own:

- party cadres;
- military formations;
- rural institutions;
- territorial claim;
- political elite;
- and memory of rule from Moscow.

Even Russian officers serving inside Kazakhstan may disagree. Some want union with a restored Russia. Others have families, careers, and property tied to the Kazakh state and prefer to dominate it from within rather than dissolve it.

This creates an enduring contradiction:

> Russian refugees provide the manpower for a reunification project, but their presence also makes neighboring national governments more determined to resist one.

## 4. Defensive military geography

A Siberian government can build a respectable army more easily than it can build an army capable of conquering all Siberia.

The main cities possess factories, depots, rail yards, veterans, artillery, and fortified approaches. Long advances depend upon a small number of railway corridors and bridges. An attacking army becomes weaker with every kilometer it moves away from its repair base.

Defenders don’t have to control an entire province. They have to destroy enough track, bridges, locomotives, and fuel stores to halt the invader before winter or spring breakup.

Each major state can therefore become:

- too strong to eliminate cheaply;
- too weak to conquer the whole region;
- and too strategically important for foreign powers to permit its complete destruction.

That is the ideal military balance for prolonged fragmentation.

## 5. Outside aid prevents defeat without producing victory

Foreign support doesn’t need to create puppet governments everywhere. It only needs to prevent decisive collapse.

Japan supports Chita and watches Irkutsk and Baikal.

Germany cultivates western military governments, commercial concessions, and anti-Japanese factions without wanting a powerful Russia restored against the Urals.

America supports an Arctic-access government with food, radios, machinery, river equipment, advisers, and later aviation and communications. The project’s existing treatment already envisions American aid moving through northern ports and river corridors rather than merely arriving as weapons. fileciteturn9file7

The resulting pattern is:

- one state is losing;
- an outside power supplies enough food, fuel, vehicles, or intelligence to keep it alive;
- its rival is denied a decisive victory;
- negotiations restore trade without resolving sovereignty.

No patron needs to control its client completely. The balance works so long as no one wins.

## 6. Every state claims Russia but governs a region

A successor regime may call itself the **Government of Russia**, **Russian State**, **Soviet Government**, or **Provisional All-Russian Authority**.

In practice, it collects taxes within a few provinces.

That produces a peculiar diplomatic system. Two governments may both claim all Russia while maintaining customs posts, embassies, and prisoner-exchange commissions with each other.

Formal language remains universal; practical government becomes regional.

This is sustainable because abandoning the universal claim would be humiliating, while acting upon it would be disastrous.

## 7. Sovereignty becomes profitable

By the second generation, regional independence benefits too many people.

Each state has:

- ministers;
- generals;
- customs officials;
- judges;
- industrial directors;
- newspaper editors;
- diplomats;
- foreign-aid contractors;
- bishops or state-approved clergy;
- and families whose social position comes from the local regime.

Unification would abolish offices, merge armies, expose accounts, reopen property disputes, and move power to another capital.

The ideological language may remain national. The material interest becomes regional.

An Omsk general may sincerely believe Russia should be united while also believing that unity is only legitimate under Omsk command. A Krasnoyarsk minister may love Russian history while refusing to surrender the Yenisei customs revenue. An Irkutsk communist may speak of all Soviet peoples while purging anyone who suggests taking orders from Novosibirsk.

# The mature successor system

By approximately 1960–65, I wouldn’t leave the region as dozens of warlords. I would allow it to consolidate into four or five principal systems.

The exact names remain open, but the structure could look like this:

| Working entity | Core | Political character | Primary external relationship |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Western Siberian Union or Directorate** | Omsk–Novosibirsk | Military-technocratic, Russian-national, formally provisional | Balances German trade against internal independence |
| **Yenisei Republic** | Krasnoyarsk–Dudinka/Norilsk corridor | Constitutional or limited democratic republic | Principal recipient of American Arctic aid |
| **Irkutsk or Baikal Soviet State** | Irkutsk and western Baikal | Soviet-restorationist, militarized, intensely anti-Chita | Trades where necessary but fears Japan |
| **Kazakh State** | Kazakhstan and Russian-heavy northern cities | Kazakh sovereign state with powerful Russian military-industrial estate | Balances all neighboring powers |
| **Tashkent Administrative Union** | Uzbekistan and associated Central Asian districts | Multinational bureaucratic survivor, possibly claiming Soviet continuity | Trade-oriented neutral or balancing state |

Around them remain smaller territories:

- Altai commands;
- Tuvan authorities;
- railway municipalities;
- autonomous national districts;
- former camp or mining administrations;
- Cossack zones;
- temporary buffer territories.

Most eventually become clients, autonomous districts, or contested borderlands of the five larger systems.

## The Western Siberian core

Omsk and Novosibirsk probably do consolidate with one another in some form. Otherwise the central map remains unnecessarily atomized.

But their partnership should be tense.

Omsk supplies military prestige, western defense, and claims of Russian state continuity. Novosibirsk supplies the larger technical bureaucracy, factories, research institutes, and civilian economy.

Formally, this might be one union. Functionally, it is a dual state:

- Omsk controls the army and national mythology.
- Novosibirsk controls finance, planning, industry, and transport.

Its principal weakness is that neither city trusts the other enough to permit complete centralization.

This is probably the strongest central Siberian state, but it reaches a natural ceiling at the Yenisei. Beyond that point, its railway supply becomes vulnerable, while Krasnoyarsk and Irkutsk can cooperate against western domination.

## The Yenisei Republic as the democratic exception

Krasnoyarsk is a particularly good center for the American-aided state because it connects the Trans-Siberian line to the Yenisei basin and the Arctic approaches.

The state’s northern lifeline runs through river shipping and Dudinka. American aid missions therefore deal with civilian port authorities, shipping boards, municipal governments, cooperatives, and relief administrations rather than only with one army.

That gives democracy a practical institutional foundation.

It doesn’t have to be a flawless liberal republic. It could have:

- a strong emergency presidency;
- a genuinely elected assembly;
- restricted military political activity;
- independent municipal governments;
- a free but heavily patriotic press;
- American aid auditors;
- a constitutional court;
- and repeated security crises.

Its survival depends upon being useful as a neutral commercial and relief corridor. It is not strong enough to unify Russia, but it is too internationally connected to be conquered without creating a larger crisis.

Its enemies accuse it of being an American dependency in exactly the same way it accuses Chita of being Japanese.

That symmetry is useful.

## Irkutsk as the uncompromising Soviet claimant

Irkutsk should probably be the regime most ideologically committed to Soviet restoration.

It sits immediately opposite the Far Eastern monarchy and therefore experiences Mikhail’s existence as a daily provocation.

Its public doctrine might hold that:

- the Ural settlement was unlawful;
- the Soviet state continues;
- Chita is occupied territory;
- Mikhail is a collaborator;
- Japanese institutions east of Baikal must eventually be removed;
- the other Siberian governments are separatists or temporary regional administrations.

Irkutsk maintains old Soviet military forms, state ownership, political police, and party symbolism. But over time its Sovietism becomes increasingly Russian, military, and Baikal-centered.

It claims the Union. It governs a fortress state.

## Kazakhstan as the state no Russian unifier can ignore

Kazakhstan is not merely another Russian successor.

It is an independent national state containing enormous Russian refugee, industrial, and military communities.

This makes it both indispensable and impossible to absorb peacefully.

Any western Siberian government needs:

- Kazakh grain;
- coal and minerals;
- railway connections;
- military transit;
- and cooperation from Russian officers inside Kazakhstan.

But an attempt to annex northern Kazakhstan could unite Kazakh elites, Central Asian governments, and outside patrons against the Russian claimant.

Kazakhstan therefore acts as the southern lock on Siberian reunification.

## Tashkent as the surviving Union idea

Tashkent can preserve more of the old multinational administrative language than the explicitly Russian states do.

Its leaders might argue that the Soviet Union wasn’t simply Russia and that no Russian successor has the right to inherit it alone.

This gives Tashkent a different claim:

> not “we are Russia,” but “we preserve the lawful union of peoples.”

It may be weak militarily but strong in bureaucracy, diplomacy, archives, and recognition among parts of Central Asia.

That further divides Soviet restorationism. Irkutsk claims the surviving Soviet state from a Russian military position; Tashkent claims the Union from a multinational administrative position.

# The failed unification sequence

The region needs several genuine attempts at unity. Otherwise the final division will still feel authorially protected.

## 1946–1949: emergency fragmentation

Military districts, evacuation ministries, railway authorities, republican governments, refugee committees, and local security organs seize whatever they can administer.

Most still claim to be temporary.

The central assumption is that an all-Russian authority will be reconstituted within a few years.

## 1949–1952: the first Siberian congress

Omsk, Novosibirsk, Krasnoyarsk, Irkutsk, Kazakhstan, and Tashkent send delegations to some form of Siberian or Russian State Conference.

The conference can agree on:

- railway transit;
- refugee documents;
- postal service;
- recognition of pensions;
- exchange of prisoners;
- common rail gauge and technical standards;
- limited trade clearing.

It cannot agree on:

- the capital;
- the army;
- the state form;
- land and property;
- whether the Soviet Union legally survives;
- whether Kazakhstan is sovereign;
- relations with Germany and Japan;
- whether the Far Eastern Republic may participate.

The conference fails politically but produces useful technical conventions.

That distinction matters. Siberia begins integrating economically without unifying constitutionally.

## 1955–1956: the Chita restoration

Mikhail’s enthronement destroys the possibility that the Romanov question can be postponed indefinitely.

The central governments respond differently:

- Omsk denounces him but borrows imperial military imagery.
- Yenisei refuses recognition while allowing trade.
- Irkutsk declares the crown treasonous.
- Kazakhstan treats it as an external Japanese client.
- Tashkent rejects any Romanov claim to former union territories.

The restoration sharpens every ideological division.

## Late 1950s–early 1960s: the principal unification war

The Western Siberian core makes the one serious attempt to extend eastward, probably during a crisis in Krasnoyarsk or Irkutsk.

It captures railway territory but cannot maintain the advance.

The likely coalition against it includes:

- Yenisei forces defending constitutional independence;
- Irkutsk forces resisting Omsk domination;
- Kazakh pressure on the southern flank;
- American material support to the Yenisei corridor;
- Japanese mobilization near Baikal;
- perhaps limited German pressure warning Omsk not to destabilize the entire frontier.

The offensive fails without requiring the total destruction of the Western Siberian state.

This is the decisive lesson:

> No claimant can attempt reunification without causing every other claimant—and at least two great powers—to cooperate against it.

## 1960s–1970s: institutional fragmentation

After the failed war, governments turn toward development.

They establish something resembling a **Siberian Transit and Clearing Conference**. It coordinates:

- rail schedules;
- rolling-stock return;
- river navigation;
- customs accounting;
- disease control;
- telegraph and telephone standards;
- refugee and family travel;
- air corridors;
- emergency food movements.

It has no common army, executive, or sovereign authority.

The region becomes easier to cross but harder to unite.

## 1985: international confirmation

The Tehran Concord eventually formalizes the great-power rule that neither Germany nor Japan will annex the frontier, recognize one claimant as the government of all Russia, or use it as an offensive base against the other. fileciteturn9file0

That doesn’t create the fragmentation. It ratifies a forty-year reality.

# By 1985 and 2000

By 1985, the Russian Far Eastern monarchy is probably the largest, most orderly, and internationally legible Russian state.

It also remains the one most central Siberians refuse to call genuinely Russian.

That irony should be explicit.

Chita has:

- a crown;
- stable succession procedures;
- a civil service;
- a national airline;
- a coherent military;
- foreign trade;
- schools;
- technical institutions;
- and a territory larger than any central claimant.

But Omsk calls it Japanese Russia. Irkutsk calls it occupied Russia. Yenisei calls it a dependent monarchy. Kazakhstan calls it a neighboring foreign state.

Meanwhile, those accusers depend upon German contracts, American aid, Kazakh grain, foreign river missions, or rival military patrons.

They don’t see the contradiction because every regime distinguishes between **assistance obtained by a sovereign government** and **dependency accepted by a rival**.

By 2000, the desire for cultural Russian unity can remain powerful. But political reunification has become less intuitive.

A young man in Omsk may believe that Russians are one people while also refusing to serve a Chita emperor, an Irkutsk party, or a Krasnoyarsk parliament.

That becomes the mature distinction:

> **Russia survives as a civilization, a language, a church, a historical memory, and a political claim. It no longer exists as one generally accepted state.**

## Working conclusion

I would establish the Siberian Frontier under the following principle:

> **The collapse of the Soviet state leaves several viable regional centers rather than one viable national center. Wartime evacuation disperses industry, cadres, weapons, and refugees among Omsk–Novosibirsk, Krasnoyarsk, Irkutsk, Kazakhstan, and Tashkent. The Trans-Siberian Railway connects these centers but also gives each the means to blockade the others. Rival Soviet, Russian-national, democratic, regionalist, monarchist, and national-republican claims prevent agreement on a common successor.**

> **Mikhail II’s Japanese-protected monarchy removes the Romanov crown as a neutral reunification device. It attracts conservative Russian elites while allowing every central claimant to define itself against “Japanese Russia.” Foreign powers then maintain a balance in which local states receive enough food, arms, machinery, or protection to survive but not enough to conquer the entire frontier.**

> **Warlordism gradually gives way to several durable states and a shared transit economy. The region becomes administratively more coherent while remaining politically divided. Repeated failed congresses and one major unification war demonstrate that any expanding claimant will unite the others against it. By the time those states are capable of sustained development, a generation has grown up for whom their borders are ordinary.**

That gives the fragmentation a cause, a history, and an internal logic. It is not that nobody tries to restore Russia. It is that every serious attempt proves that **all the other Russias would rather remain separate than be united under the wrong one.**

# The American experiment’s durable victory is compatibility

Yes. This should probably become one of the most important lasting consequences of Reagan’s boom.

The open-capital experiment ultimately fails. The American product and software export experiment does not.

The distinction is:

> **America fails to make New York the permanent owner’s market of the world. It succeeds in making American compatibility part of the ordinary technical vocabulary of the world.**

By 1985 the setting still has five recognizably different computing traditions: Germany treats the computer as a plan and certified system, Britain as an information service, America as a replaceable general tool, Japan as a controlled procedure, and the Latin bloc as an intelligible instrument. None of those traditions should disappear. fileciteturn63file0

But the 1987–90 opening gives American companies a brief opportunity to establish foreign subsidiaries, dealer networks, software licenses, local-language editions, repair systems, and developer communities before governments fully understand what dependence on a foreign computing ecosystem can mean. The Reciprocal Commerce and Enterprise Act already opens computing as one of the sectors subject to broader access, while the world still consists of several gatewayed networks rather than one universal Internet. fileciteturn63file2

The result is not one global computer architecture. It is **Americanization at the interface**.

---

# What actually converges

There are four technical layers, and they should not all converge to the same degree.

## The physical processor

Germany, Japan, Britain, Italy, Occitania, and other states continue building native processors and machine families.

Strategic German systems remain ERO and Rechenplan-centered. Japanese factory, embedded, consumer, and character-processing machines retain native lines. Britain preserves its parallel, functional, and service-computing strengths. Olivetti and Occitan firms continue developing Latin hardware.

But American-compatible processors become common in cheaper commercial machines because their production scale makes them attractive.

A German or Japanese manufacturer can build:

- a completely native strategic computer;
- a native consumer system with an American compatibility mode;
- or a fully American-compatible office machine using locally produced components.

The low-cost commercial market converges farther than military, scientific, industrial-control, or administrative computing.

## The operating interface

This is where **Bridge** wins.

Martin Keene’s objective is already to make software portable across temporary hardware through stable interfaces, translators, and device abstraction. IBM’s 1981 adoption of Bridge/16 gives it the largest compatible American ecosystem, and Interlink has already demonstrated that it will license its tools into Germany despite the political controversy produced by the Munich Licensing Affair. fileciteturn63file1

Foreign machines therefore do not always need to contain an American processor.

They need a licensed or reconstructed **Bridge environment** capable of providing:

- the same operating calls;
- compatible file handling;
- standard device behavior;
- a recognizable application interface;
- translator support;
- and predictable program installation.

A Japanese computer can remain Japanese beneath that layer while running Bridge commercial software above it.

A German machine can boot into a certified domestic environment for ordinary government work and then enter a Bridge-compatible commercial mode for foreign accounting, publishing, or export software.

This is much more plausible than every bloc simply surrendering its instruction-set architecture.

## The application and file layer

This is where the dependence becomes visible to ordinary users.

By the early 1990s, foreign developers increasingly have to ask:

- Can this program be compiled for Bridge?
- Can it read Bridge files?
- Can it exchange documents with Concord?
- Can a foreign customer install it without a custom conversion?
- Can it communicate with American banks, suppliers, or corporate branches?

A domestic program may still be written in Rechenplan, Keisan, Tejun, Pascal, Prolog, ML, or another national language.

But its commercial version requires a Bridge target or gateway.

The national languages survive. The addressable market is increasingly defined by an American compatibility layer.

## Character and network interchange

Bridge should not become the universal network protocol. That would prematurely settle the still-open question of which post-1985 system becomes the neutral interchange layer. The canon currently leaves American protocols, Weltnetz gateways, Japanese character standards, Commonwealth translation services, and a treaty-created hybrid in competition. fileciteturn62file7

UNICODE 80 supplies the common character identities instead. Japan and the Latin bloc implement it first, Britain uses it pragmatically, Germany follows later, and decentralized America reaches general adoption mainly in the 1990s. fileciteturn63file0

That creates an excellent irony:

> American companies become the largest global carriers of a character standard that America itself was among the last powers to adopt consistently.

Interlink’s foreign editions have to support UNICODE 80 because Japanese, Italian, Occitan, German, Arabic, and Indian customers require it. Concord must do the same if it wants to sell complete consumer machines abroad.

The export market pulls American computing toward international standardization.

---

# Bridge becomes the commercial common language

Bridge is the less glamorous but more consequential American export.

Its strongest foreign markets are not necessarily households. They are:

- shops;
- banks;
- freight companies;
- hotel chains;
- publishers;
- importers;
- exporters;
- insurance offices;
- universities;
- accounting firms;
- and corporate administrative departments.

A Kyoto shop may use a domestically manufactured machine running a licensed Bridge environment for inventory, accounts, payroll, and communications with foreign suppliers.

A Munich engineering office may use Bridge-compatible workstations in its export department even though the company’s design and production systems remain German.

An Italian shipping company may run Bridge commercial packages while its logistics planning interfaces with Latin public systems.

## Why foreign firms adopt it

Bridge does not require them to purchase every component from Interlink.

It offers them access to:

- American business software;
- a large developer community;
- international documentation;
- cheap peripheral support;
- corporate customers;
- and future export markets.

A small British or Japanese software house can write one Bridge edition and sell it in America, Canada, Britain, Germany, Italy, and several associated markets.

Without Bridge compatibility, it may have to support five or six separate environments.

The cost argument overwhelms the ideological objection for many civilian firms.

## Why governments do not stop it

The strategic danger initially appears limited.

Interlink does not need to own the foreign computer manufacturer.

It does not need to control the telecommunications network.

It merely licenses an operating environment and publishes technical specifications.

A finance ministry sees software compatibility as a commercial convenience.

A defense ministry knows its classified systems remain separate.

An industrial ministry may actively support Bridge licensing because domestic firms want access to American customers.

By the time governments recognize that local developers are writing for Bridge first and native environments second, a ban would injure their own exporters, banks, universities, and small firms more quickly than it would injure Interlink.

That is how Bridge becomes entrenched.

Not through conquest, but because removing it becomes expensive.

---

# Concord becomes the visible prestige platform

Concord succeeds differently.

Elias Mercer is trying to create a coherent cultural and consumer object, not merely a portable software layer. Concord’s closed tools, serialized systems, controlled formats, and publisher agreements already make it the canonical “gated republic.” fileciteturn63file1

That closed character limits Concord’s total market share abroad.

It also helps create its prestige.

## The foreign Concord customer

The typical foreign Concord buyer might be:

- a wealthy household;
- a designer;
- an architect;
- a physician;
- a private school;
- a media company;
- an advertising office;
- an executive;
- a software publisher;
- or a technologically ambitious small business.

A Concord machine in a Munich office is not necessarily the machine controlling the factory.

It is more likely to sit in:

- the design department;
- the boardroom;
- the export office;
- advertising;
- publishing;
- or an executive’s home.

In Japan, Concord competes poorly against the best native systems in vertical text, household integration, education, and local consumer electronics.

But it can still become fashionable among:

- creative professionals;
- internationally minded families;
- universities;
- game designers;
- film and animation studios;
- and people who want the visibly American machine.

## Concord’s foreign ecosystem

Mercer eventually has to loosen the company’s purely internal production model.

Concord continues building the core machine and controlling:

- architecture;
- firmware;
- system software;
- certification;
- and branding.

But foreign certified partners manufacture:

- printers;
- displays;
- keyboards;
- storage;
- communications adapters;
- music equipment;
- industrial peripherals;
- and localized software.

These companies may be Japanese, German, British, or Italian.

They are independent firms, but their products depend upon Concord certification and proprietary interfaces.

This extends the corporate ecosystem already developing around Concord in America.

It also means that foreign governments encounter a politically awkward constituency. Restricting Concord imports does not only hurt an American company. It hurts domestic accessory makers, software publishers, retailers, service firms, and schools that have already invested in the platform.

---

# The bloc-by-bloc outcome

## Britain

Britain is the largest and easiest foreign market.

The Halifax Understanding already covers civilian computing access and industrial standards, and the shared language removes a major localization barrier. fileciteturn63file2

Bridge becomes widespread in:

- private offices;
- Commonwealth trade;
- finance;
- local government;
- universities;
- and small business.

British manufacturers respond by building Bridge-compatible computers rather than surrendering hardware production entirely.

Concord becomes common in affluent homes, schools, publishing, media, and design. It competes with Commonwealth educational machines rather than erasing them.

Britain’s distinctive contribution remains translation, packet services, parallel systems, and public information infrastructure. But by the early 1990s, a British computer that cannot exchange Bridge software or Concord documents is at a serious commercial disadvantage.

## Japan

Japan remains the strongest resistance case because its native consumer systems are already excellent.

Japanese machines have:

- better native text handling;
- vertical display;
- domestic educational software;
- factory integration;
- local game ecosystems;
- and close relationships with appliances and communications.

Bridge therefore enters principally through the commercial edge:

- import-export firms;
- international hotels;
- foreign retailers;
- finance;
- ports;
- universities;
- American subsidiaries;
- and small businesses dealing with foreign customers.

Concord becomes a premium minority platform rather than a national standard.

But even a minority matters. Japanese software firms now have an incentive to release:

- a native edition;
- a Bridge edition;
- and sometimes a Concord edition.

The domestic market has not been conquered. Its developers have been given two additional markets they can no longer ignore.

## Germany

Germany draws the clearest line between civilian and strategic computing.

Rechenplan remains dominant in certified military, aerospace, administrative, industrial-control, and imperial systems. The 1982 civilian-language reform already permits competition while reserving strategic work for certified environments. fileciteturn63file0

Bridge expands through:

- export companies;
- consumer software;
- universities;
- banks;
- media;
- foreign subsidiaries;
- and small civilian software houses.

Weltnetz gateways carry Bridge-compatible traffic without becoming American-controlled.

The German state initially regards this as manageable compartmentalization. Strategic Germany remains German; commercial Germany can use whatever works.

The later problem is that civilian firms become economically important enough that their American compatibility can no longer be treated as peripheral.

Concord remains less common but highly visible. It is associated with wealth, design, media, foreign travel, and a mildly rebellious cosmopolitan consumer culture.

## The Latin bloc

The Latin response is adaptation rather than resistance.

Olivetti and Occitan firms are well positioned to manufacture attractive domestic machines while licensing Bridge compatibility. The Latin bloc also has the advantage of early UNICODE 80 enforcement, which makes its local systems better prepared for multilingual trade than many American domestic computers. fileciteturn63file0

A plausible market pattern is:

- Olivetti hardware running a Bridge-compatible environment;
- Latin logic and professional software exported into Bridge markets;
- Concord machines sold as premium design and media systems;
- Occitan scientific and aerospace computers retaining native control environments;
- and American business packages becoming common in shipping, insurance, tourism, and finance.

Italy does not abandon Olivetti.

Olivetti learns to advertise that its machines can run the world’s software without ceasing to be Italian.

---

# The crash cannot put the imports back in the box

The 1990 crisis ends the foreign-ownership experiment.

It does not erase the foreign installed base.

Governments can prohibit an American fund from buying a German company. It is much harder to prohibit a German company from using Bridge accounting software after ten years of records have accumulated in that system.

Likewise, a Concord machine already present in a school, design studio, or medical office is not a claim on national ownership. It is a product.

That allows governments to make a clean political distinction:

- foreign voting ownership is dangerous;
- ordinary imports and software licenses remain permissible;
- strategic systems require national certification;
- consumer and commercial systems may remain open.

The later international order therefore follows the same broad formula America eventually adopts:

> **Open products. Controlled ownership. Protected strategic systems.**

## Why Bridge and Concord survive the American depression

Both companies gain foreign-currency revenue at the moment the domestic American market collapses.

Interlink is especially resilient because software licensing requires relatively little physical capital. Foreign firms still need updates, translators, documentation, and support.

Concord is more vulnerable because it manufactures hardware. But its foreign prestige market produces high margins, while overseas accessory and distribution partners absorb some costs.

A weakened dollar also makes American goods cheaper abroad.

That pushes surviving American manufacturers toward export precisely when American households can no longer buy as much.

The Second Great Depression therefore reinforces the foreign orientation that the Reagan boom began.

---

# American products cease to be automatically exotic

The same process applies beyond computing.

Before Reagan’s opening, an American product in Tokyo, Munich, Rome, or London is often expensive because it lacks:

- dealers;
- parts;
- local financing;
- translated documentation;
- compatible power and communications;
- certified repairs;
- and predictable import treatment.

The sticker price is only one part of luxury status. The absence of infrastructure makes ownership costly.

The late-1980s opening changes that.

American firms establish:

- local subsidiaries;
- dealer networks;
- parts warehouses;
- financing arms;
- translated manuals;
- service training;
- and locally adapted models.

After those systems exist, the product can survive even if broader financial integration ends.

## American cars

A Ford pickup in central Tokyo remains a relatively unusual physical object. Japanese roads, parking, fuel costs, and vehicle taxes still favor smaller domestic vehicles.

But it no longer has to be an exotic rich man’s import.

It can be a normal commercial choice for:

- construction companies;
- rural users;
- Hokkaido farms;
- forestry;
- American subsidiaries;
- recreation;
- and buyers attracted to its image.

A Pinto-family compact—or its later successor, depending on which model names remain canon—can penetrate much farther into ordinary urban use.

It is still competing with better-localized Japanese cars.

But it may be priced as a middle-class alternative rather than a luxury curiosity.

In Germany and Britain, American pickups and large cars are easier to accommodate. In Italy and Japan, American compacts, vans, and specialty models do better than the largest domestic American vehicles.

## Other successful exports

The strongest American export categories would probably include:

- personal computers;
- business software;
- entertainment;
- medical equipment;
- commercial aerospace services;
- industrial electronics;
- power tools;
- agricultural machinery;
- specialty vehicles;
- communications equipment;
- and selected household appliances.

Not every American product succeeds.

Many are too large, inefficient, poorly localized, or unsuited to foreign infrastructure.

The important change is that American manufacturers now expect foreign sales to be a normal part of the product plan.

They design export versions from the beginning.

---

# The panic helps create the demand

The “American century” anxiety should itself increase American sales.

Foreign media depicts American:

- computers;
- private spaceplanes;
- corporate towers;
- cars;
- advertising;
- software;
- and financial markets

as the material culture of the future.

That image is intended partly as a warning.

For many consumers, especially young ones, it functions as advertising.

A Japanese programme warning that Tokyo may one day be covered in American corporate signs makes those signs culturally recognizable.

A German drama about engineers leaving for California gives California greater prestige.

A British satire about London becoming New York’s branch office helps make American products familiar rather than foreign.

The feared culture acquires glamour because it is presented as powerful enough to be feared.

That is the inversion:

> Governments worry that American products signify dependence.  
> Consumers buy some of them because they signify arrival in the future.

---

# A plausible chronology

| Period | Development |
|---|---|
| **1985–1986** | Interlink and Concord establish foreign licensing, localization, distribution, and technical-support offices |
| **1987** | Reciprocal Commerce opens the main export window; Bridge compatibility becomes commercially valuable outside America |
| **1988–1989** | Concord becomes a visible premium global brand; foreign manufacturers add Bridge environments and American-compatible commercial lines |
| **1989–1990** | American-century anxiety peaks; American computers, software, cars, aerospace services, and consumer goods become future-coded products |
| **1990** | Ownership crisis closes capital integration but leaves product imports, installed systems, and software contracts intact |
| **1991–1994** | Weak American demand and a cheaper dollar push surviving firms toward exports; Bridge becomes the leading cross-bloc commercial application layer |
| **Mid-1990s** | National machines increasingly advertise native identity plus Bridge compatibility; Concord retains a smaller but lucrative international ecosystem |
| **Late 1990s** | Foreign software firms routinely plan native, Bridge, and sometimes Concord editions; American commercial interfaces become part of global computing even though networks remain politically divided |

# The lasting settlement

This direction should not make Bridge the world’s only operating environment or Concord the world’s dominant computer company.

The more interesting result is that neither company has to dominate numerically to change everyone else’s decisions.

Bridge becomes the platform a foreign software company supports because it wants international customers.

Concord becomes the machine a foreign hardware or media company supports because its users are affluent, influential, and willing to spend.

German, Japanese, British, and Latin systems remain strong enough to prevent complete American standardization. But they increasingly define their own products partly in relation to American compatibility:

- native;
- Bridge-compatible;
- Concord-certified;
- or able to exchange with both.

That is the real American computing victory.

The American capital market promises to unify the world and collapses.

American software settles for being useful everywhere and succeeds.
