You’re right. The previous model treated the Siberian middle as though violence were an early emergency that gradually gave way to an imperfect regional order. That is too orderly.

The better governing premise is:

> **The Siberian middle remains a system of armed successor states, disputed cities, refugee populations, military economies, smuggling corridors, and intermittent regional wars from the late 1940s into the 1970s.**

These are not merely states that disagree over which government ought to reunify Russia. They repeatedly attempt to alter borders, overthrow neighboring regimes, seize rail junctions, recover refugee districts, and sabotage one another’s economies. What begins changing in the 1970s is not mutual trust. It is the recognition that none of them can win cheaply enough to justify another major campaign.

I’ll standardize the dictation form **Ikirsk** as **Irkutsk**.

## The Siberian middle is a war system

The earlier formulation that these are “successor bureaucracies with armies” remains useful. They inherit party committees, military districts, rail administrations, evacuated factories, police organizations, and technical cadres rather than collapsing immediately into one-man bandit kingdoms. But those bureaucracies become the machinery through which regional wars are fought.

The existing material already establishes the basic social pressure: northern Kazakh cities and rail corridors become heavily Russian, the countryside remains Kazakh, Central Asian administrations remain divided between Russian-Soviet urban institutions and native rural populations, black markets are enormous, and ethnic resentment grows. fileciteturn12file1 It also establishes that the wider frontier contains Russian successor governments, railway authorities, military districts, refugee administrations, local strongmen, and competing foreign missions, without either Germany or Japan claiming the whole region. fileciteturn12file11

The correction is that these authorities don’t merely coexist awkwardly. They fight.

Not every year produces a declared interstate war. The more characteristic pattern is:

- three years of fighting;
- a ceasefire without a peace treaty;
- several years of raids and assassination;
- a customs crisis;
- support for an uprising across the border;
- a limited offensive around one railway;
- another ceasefire imposed by exhaustion.

This makes the region violent without requiring a continuous thirty-year front line.

# Irkutsk as the permanent threat to Far Eastern Russia

Irkutsk should become Mikhail’s principal military concern.

Manchukuo is the more powerful industrial neighbor, but its conflict with the Russian Far Eastern State is contained inside the Japanese imperial system. Tokyo can arbitrate tariffs, rail rights, maps, commercial privileges, and military deployments.

Irkutsk is different. It stands outside the Japanese sphere, rejects the Chita monarchy’s legitimacy, and is organized around the belief that the Russian Far East remains occupied Russian territory.

## The political character of Irkutsk

The formal name can remain open, but the state itself should probably be the strongest Soviet-restorationist regime in Siberia.

A working description would be:

> **The Irkutsk Soviet State is a militarized successor government claiming continuity with the lawful Soviet state and regarding Far Eastern Russia as a Japanese puppet administration.**

It doesn’t need to preserve every aspect of pre-collapse Soviet ideology unchanged. Over time, its Sovietism would become narrower, more Russian, more military, and more centered on the Baikal frontier. It still uses party language, red symbols, state ownership, security organs, and the claim that the Union survives. Functionally, however, it is an Irkutsk-centered fortress state.

Its legitimacy rests on four claims:

1. it never surrendered to Germany or Japan;
2. it retains Red Army and Soviet administrative continuity;
3. Mikhail accepted a foreign crown and therefore forfeited Russian legitimacy;
4. the eastern territories will eventually be “liberated,” even if that liberation cannot presently be carried out.

## Why Irkutsk is dangerous but cannot win

Irkutsk doesn’t need the strength to conquer Far Eastern Russia in order to dominate Chita’s defense planning.

It can maintain:

- fortified forces west of Lake Baikal;
- raiding units around the northern and southern approaches to the lake;
- intelligence networks inside Buryatia and Chita;
- exile groups claiming to represent “occupied” eastern districts;
- railway saboteurs;
- propaganda broadcasts;
- support for republican, Soviet, or anti-Japanese underground cells;
- seasonal incursions over frozen water and mountain routes.

The frontier is long enough and difficult enough that Chita can never seal it completely.

But Irkutsk cannot sustain a successful general invasion.

A major eastward campaign would depend upon a small number of railway and road corridors around Lake Baikal. Far Eastern forces could fall back toward Chita while Japan supplied them by rail and air. Irkutsk would then be exposed to Japanese reconnaissance, bombing, long-range artillery, and intervention forces arriving through Manchukuo and the Far Eastern transport network.

So Irkutsk’s military logic is:

> **Do enough damage to keep the frontier unsettled, but never create an emergency large enough to make Tokyo destroy the Irkutsk state’s offensive capacity.**

This produces an unstable escalation ladder.

### Below the Japanese threshold

Irkutsk can probably get away with:

- patrol clashes;
- covert border crossings;
- support for sabotage;
- assassination of Far Eastern officials;
- brief occupations of remote posts;
- attacks followed by immediate withdrawal;
- deniable volunteers;
- propaganda and intelligence operations.

Japan complains, rearms Chita, and sends advisers, but leaves the fighting primarily to Far Eastern Russia.

### At the threshold

A larger raid that destroys a railway station, overruns a town, or kills Japanese personnel could bring:

- Japanese aircraft over the border;
- strikes on staging camps;
- temporary seizure of commanding terrain;
- destruction of bridges and supply depots;
- direct Japanese reinforcement of Far Eastern divisions.

### Beyond the threshold

An actual Irkutsk invasion aimed at Chita or the destruction of the monarchy would trigger a disproportionate response.

Japan would not necessarily annex Irkutsk. It would probably destroy the field army, railway yards, airfields, ammunition plants, command centers, and bridge network necessary for another offensive, then withdraw behind the recognized frontier.

That is more useful than occupation. Tokyo does not want to inherit Irkutsk’s population or become responsible for governing western Baikal. It wants Irkutsk punished badly enough that the lesson survives for another decade.

## Mikhail’s military identity

This also helps distinguish Mikhail from a passive ornamental monarch.

His military problem is not preparing to defeat Manchukuo in a conventional war. That war isn’t politically possible without first breaking with Japan.

His problem is maintaining a frontier army capable of absorbing Irkutsk’s harassment without calling for Japanese rescue every time a patrol disappears.

That means Far Eastern military prestige concentrates around:

- border infantry;
- mountain and forest units;
- railway troops;
- aviation;
- signals;
- winter patrol;
- reconnaissance;
- counter-sabotage;
- rapid reinforcement.

The crown army’s mythology would be built around defending Russian homes from men who insist they are liberating them.

# The Kazakh–Russian conflict

Kazakhstan should produce the largest demographic war in the region.

The central issue is exactly as you described it. The Russians arrive as refugees and emergency administrators. They take control of cities, factories, railways, ministries, police forces, and military commands because they possess the technical personnel and inherited Soviet institutions.

Initially, all of this can be justified as temporary.

The Russian officials say:

- the war isn’t over;
- the refugees will return west;
- the Union will be restored;
- the industries must remain under experienced management;
- political reorganization must wait until survival is assured.

By the early or middle 1950s, the Kazakh conclusion is that none of those things is going to happen.

The Russians are staying. Their children are entering schools locally. Their officers are buying homes. Their ministries are no longer evacuation offices but a permanent governing class. The Kazakh republic is being transformed into a Russian-administered refuge state in which Kazakhs remain numerous but cease to be the state-bearing people.

The earlier setting material already points directly toward this conflict: Russian and Slavic refugees dominate northern cities, industrial towns, military settlements, and major rail corridors while Kazakh life remains stronger through much of the countryside. fileciteturn12file1

## The opening political crisis

The conflict probably begins with Kazakh attempts to recover the state before it begins with mass expulsion.

A Kazakh nationalist government or coalition demands:

- Kazakh control of the interior ministry;
- nationalization of refugee military formations into a Kazakh army;
- Kazakh-language administration outside designated Russian districts;
- removal of temporary Russian emergency officials;
- redistribution of land and housing;
- limits on further Russian immigration;
- recognition that Kazakhstan is sovereign rather than a holding territory for a future Russia.

Russian city councils, factory ministries, railway commands, and military officers refuse.

Their counterargument is that the Kazakh government cannot safely run the industrial and military system, and that Russian populations require protection against nationalist retaliation.

At that point both sides can plausibly claim self-defense.

## The war

I would place the principal conflict roughly between **1954 and 1963**, with irregular violence continuing afterward.

It would not be one clean front between two national armies. It would contain several overlapping struggles:

- Kazakh rural forces against Russian-held cities;
- Russian railway and industrial militias against Kazakh ministries;
- former Red Army formations splitting along political and ethnic lines;
- Kazakh units attempting to isolate Russian urban enclaves;
- Russian forces seizing food and rail corridors;
- reprisals against villages accused of assisting the other side;
- forced removals from strategically exposed districts;
- rival authorities recruiting Cossacks, deported minorities, and local clans;
- refugee columns moving north, east, and south.

The principal violence is likely to occur around the rail-industrial chain rather than across every part of the steppe.

Petropavlovsk, Pavlodar, Akmolinsk, Karaganda, Semipalatinsk, and Ust-Kamenogorsk have different balances of population, industry, military importance, and access to Russian successor states. That makes the war geographically uneven. Some cities may become Russian enclaves. Others are taken by Kazakh forces after sieges or negotiated evacuations. Still others retain Russian technical populations under a Kazakh political government.

## The likely result

Neither complete Russian victory nor complete removal of every Russian is plausible.

The Kazakh state should achieve its main political objective:

> **Kazakhstan becomes recognizably Kazakh-governed rather than a Russian evacuation administration operating under a Kazakh name.**

But the cost is enormous.

The settlement could leave:

- a Kazakh-controlled central and southern state;
- several heavily Russian northern districts lost, autonomous, or tied economically to Omsk;
- a reduced Russian technical population retained in major industrial cities;
- hundreds of thousands or potentially millions of displaced people over the course of the war and its aftermath;
- permanent property claims and stories of expulsion;
- a militarized northern frontier;
- Kazakh suspicion of every Russian successor government;
- Russian successor propaganda portraying Kazakhstan as the destroyer of refugee communities.

The Russian refugees don’t all return to one Russia. They disperse.

Some go to Omsk and Novosibirsk. Others reach Krasnoyarsk, Irkutsk, Magnitogorsk, Chelyabinsk, Tashkent, or Far Eastern Russia. Officers and technicians may be deliberately recruited by whichever successor state can promise housing, citizenship, and command.

This refugee wave strengthens the Russian successor states while making them more revanchist.

The war therefore prevents unification in two ways. It physically divides the region, and it produces several populations convinced that they have territorial claims against their neighbors.

# Omsk and Novosibirsk

The Omsk–Novosibirsk arrangement should remain, but it should arise through conflict rather than administrative convenience.

Omsk and Novosibirsk possess complementary strengths:

- Omsk has military authority, western defensive prestige, and an older claim to all-Russian government.
- Novosibirsk has industry, planning offices, scientific and technical cadres, transport administration, and a larger civilian-production base.

Neither trusts the other.

## The unification war

The two could fight a limited **Western Siberian War** during the late 1940s or early 1950s.

Omsk attempts to subordinate Novosibirsk under military emergency authority. Novosibirsk resists through factory militias, railway control, and alliances with nearby regional commands.

Neither can win cleanly.

Omsk can threaten the city but cannot run the industrial economy without Novosibirsk’s administrators. Novosibirsk can stop trains and manufacture weapons but cannot defend the whole western frontier without Omsk’s army.

The eventual union is therefore an armed compromise:

- Omsk becomes the military and ceremonial capital.
- Novosibirsk becomes the industrial, financial, and planning capital.
- The army swears to the federal state but retains an Omsk command culture.
- Economic ministries remain concentrated in Novosibirsk.
- Each city maintains its own security services and political clients.
- Constitutional rules prevent either from moving every central institution onto its own territory.

They are unified enough to fight outsiders and divided enough that every succession threatens an internal crisis.

That is a much stronger tone than a cooperative dual-capital federation.

# A working regional war sequence

I would not fix all of these dates as canon yet, but the broad sequence could be:

## 1946–1951: the Railway Wars

The initial successor governments fight over:

- rolling stock;
- locomotives;
- bridges;
- grain trains;
- evacuated factories;
- ammunition depots;
- telegraph stations;
- fuel;
- refugee settlements.

These are short, chaotic wars involving military districts, railway guards, local Soviets, commanders, and provincial governments.

The main result is that every major state learns to fortify railway junctions and keep strategic rolling stock under armed guard.

## 1949–1954: the Omsk–Novosibirsk War

The principal western Russian centers struggle over which one commands the Siberian state. They end in a tense dual union because neither can eliminate the other.

## 1954–1963: the Kazakh–Russian War

Kazakh national forces attempt to recover political control and force out Russian emergency administrations. The conflict produces expulsions, enclaves, refugee movements, and a permanent frontier.

## 1957–1968: the Yenisei conflicts

The Omsk–Novosibirsk state and Krasnoyarsk-centered authorities fight intermittently over rail access, food, mining districts, and the Yenisei corridor.

This need not be one declared war. There could be two or three limited campaigns separated by ceasefires.

## Mid-1950s through early 1970s: the Baikal frontier conflict

Irkutsk and Far Eastern Russia fight raids, sabotage campaigns, intelligence wars, border actions, and several larger clashes.

One episode probably approaches the Japanese intervention threshold and ends with a severe Japanese punitive operation against Irkutsk’s military infrastructure.

## 1960s through early 1970s: southern and western frontier wars

Magnitogorsk, Chelyabinsk, Altai commands, Kazakh remnants, Tashkent authorities, and smaller military states continue fighting over mines, industrial towns, water, pasture, and rail links.

By the middle 1970s, the number of major offensives begins declining. But this is because the participants have been exhausted and their borders militarized, not because someone has created a cooperative Siberian order.

# The black economy

The Siberian middle should not possess a tidy shared transit organization. Official interstate trade exists, but the unofficial economy is often more reliable.

The region’s actual circulatory system is made of:

- bribed railway officials;
- falsified cargo documents;
- diverted military trains;
- river smugglers;
- winter-road convoys;
- black-market pilots;
- refugee guides;
- arms brokers;
- concession companies;
- customs officers who are paid by both sides;
- state security organizations running supposedly criminal operations.

The most valuable goods aren’t always luxury goods. They are the items required to keep a state operating:

- locomotive bearings;
- fuel injectors;
- radio tubes;
- antibiotics;
- machine tools;
- copper wire;
- tires;
- ammunition;
- replacement barrels;
- aviation fuel;
- spare electrical equipment;
- forged identity papers.

A government may publicly execute smugglers while using the same network to obtain parts it cannot import legally.

## State-sponsored criminality

The distinction between state trade and smuggling becomes deliberately unclear.

An Irkutsk intelligence officer funds smugglers moving rifles into Buryatia.

A Novosibirsk ministry buys stolen Japanese machine tools through three intermediaries.

A Kazakh border commander sells confiscated Russian ammunition to another Russian state.

A Far Eastern customs official seizes a train as contraband, then its cargo appears in army depots two months later.

This produces a region where almost every serious merchant has political protection and almost every intelligence service has commercial assets.

The black market is not a symptom sitting outside the political order. It is one of the ways the political order functions.

# Kalashnikov and the AK-47

Kalashnikov should remain in the setting, and **Novosibirsk is the strongest destination**.

Historically, Mikhail Kalashnikov was born in the Altai region, was seriously wounded in 1941, and began developing automatic weapons during the war. His work eventually produced the design selected in 1947. He was sent to Izhevsk only later, in 1948, to prepare documentation and pilot production. That means the rifle’s development was far enough advanced to survive the setting’s Soviet collapse, while its final production center was not yet inevitable. citeturn334349search0turn334349search3

## Why Novosibirsk works better than Irkutsk

Putting Kalashnikov in Irkutsk would make the rifle an especially strong symbol of the Soviet-restorationist state. That is possible, but it would make its broad spread across rival successor states somewhat harder.

Novosibirsk gives us more:

- it lies close to his Altai origins;
- it possesses a larger technical and industrial environment;
- it is the civilian-industrial half of the Omsk–Novosibirsk state;
- it has reason to produce a standardized rifle for a large army;
- its position on the Siberian rail system makes export, theft, copying, and capture easier.

So the likely alternate sequence is:

1. Kalashnikov and part of the design group are moved east as the Soviet state contracts.
2. The collapsing central armaments administration establishes a replacement proving and design office around Novosibirsk.
3. The 1947 design competition survives in reduced form.
4. The Omsk–Novosibirsk government adopts the **AK-47** as its new standard automatic rifle.
5. Initial manufacture begins in Novosibirsk and one or more associated machine plants.
6. Irkutsk, Krasnoyarsk, Kazakh forces, and independent arsenals later copy or modify it.

## It isn’t instantly easy to manufacture

We should qualify “everyone can make them.”

The design is rugged and relatively tolerant in service, but early production still requires serious metallurgy, machining, heat treatment, gauges, ammunition production, and quality control. Historically, the original stamped-receiver manufacturing process proved imperfect enough that a milled receiver was substituted by 1951. citeturn399362search1

That actually helps the setting.

The earliest Siberian AKs would probably be:

- produced in modest numbers;
- relatively heavy;
- made with milled receivers;
- concentrated in frontline and guard formations;
- copied imperfectly by lesser arsenals.

By the 1960s, improved stamping methods spread through the region. At that point, simplified derivatives become common enough that Krasnoyarsk, Irkutsk, Kazakhstan, Magnitogorsk, and smaller governments can manufacture their own versions.

So not every village blacksmith can build an AK. But almost every surviving industrial state with tractor works, rail shops, machine-tool plants, and an ammunition factory can eventually produce a recognizable derivative.

## The name without the celebrity

Your cultural point works extremely well.

Inside the Omsk–Novosibirsk state, Kalashnikov becomes a highly regarded engineer:

- state awards;
- factory institutes bearing his name;
- technical-school lectures;
- portraits in armaments plants;
- public appearances with soldiers and apprentices.

Outside that state, the weapon spreads more effectively than his biography does.

A fighter in Magnitogorsk may know:

- the rifle is marked `AK-47`;
- it uses the common 7.62 mm intermediate cartridge;
- it takes a curved thirty-round magazine;
- it was developed somewhere around Novosibirsk;
- it is reliable in mud, cold, and poor maintenance.

He may not know that `AK` means *Avtomat Kalashnikova*. He may interpret it as a factory code, an army designation, or simply the name of the weapon family.

That absence of universal Soviet propaganda prevents Kalashnikov from becoming one of the world’s best-known Russian surnames. The gun is famous. The man is regionally famous.

## A Siberian weapons family

By the 1960s, “AK” becomes less a single rifle than a family of regional copies:

- the original Novosibirsk AK-47;
- an Irkutsk simplified military model;
- a Krasnoyarsk export or militia model;
- Kazakh-produced rifles assembled from captured machinery;
- crude black-market rebuilds;
- folding-stock cavalry and vehicle variants;
- squad automatic derivatives;
- rifles rechambered experimentally where ammunition is scarce.

Quality varies considerably.

A Novosibirsk state rifle may be carefully gauged and proofed. A frontier copy may accept the same magazine but have rougher sights, weaker finish, inconsistent heat treatment, and parts that aren’t fully interchangeable.

This gives the Siberian middle a shared visual weapon without giving it a shared political system.

# Far Eastern Russia and Japanese equipment

Far Eastern Russia should not standardize upon the AK.

Its early forces inherit Mosin-Nagants, Soviet machine guns, Japanese wartime weapons, and whatever local arsenals contain. But Japanese assistance gradually replaces that mixture.

The established Japanese sequence gives the sphere the 7.7×58 mm Type 7 self-loading rifle in 1947, followed by the 6.5×45 mm Type 16 automatic rifle in 1956 and the Type 24 automatic rifle in 1964. fileciteturn13file0

That produces a plausible Far Eastern sequence:

**Late 1940s**

- Mosin-Nagants and Soviet weapons remain widespread.
- Japanese Type 99 and Type 7 rifles equip Japanese-supported units.
- Ammunition supply is confused.

**Late 1950s**

- The crown army begins standardizing frontline infantry on the Japanese 6.5×45 mm Type 16.
- Older 7.7 mm Japanese rifles move to police, training, and reserve units.
- Soviet rifles remain in storage and local auxiliary service.

**1960s onward**

- Type 24 rifles and other Japanese-pattern weapons become normal.
- Manchukuo or Far Eastern arsenals may assemble simplified licensed versions.
- Soviet-caliber equipment remains in frontier depots because captured Irkutsk weapons are common.

## AKs on the Baikal frontier

AK-47s would still appear constantly along the border.

They are used by:

- Irkutsk raiders;
- infiltrators;
- smugglers;
- captured auxiliary units;
- Far Eastern intelligence services operating across the frontier;
- irregular Buryat or Russian groups;
- local police who obtained them before standardization.

But the crown army doesn’t adopt them widely because 7.62×39 mm ammunition creates another supply chain alongside Japanese 6.5×45 mm and the older reserve cartridges.

A Far Eastern patrol could therefore recognize the sound and silhouette of an AK immediately while not issuing one itself.

The weapon becomes associated locally with the dangerous western frontier:

> Japanese-pattern rifles belong to the crown army. AKs belong to Irkutsk, smugglers, rebels, and the lands beyond the lake.

# Why the wars finally cool

The fighting should persist into the 1970s. After that, several pressures begin reducing its frequency.

Not reconciliation—cost.

By then:

- the borders have trenches, mines, fortified stations, and permanent garrisons;
- each state has lost a generation of men;
- the populations expelled during earlier wars are no longer immediately across the border waiting to return;
- the railway junctions most worth seizing have become difficult to take intact;
- outside powers can rapidly supply threatened clients;
- states have developed industries and cities that would be destroyed by renewed war;
- younger officials’ careers depend on administering existing territory rather than conquering a theoretical Russia.

The result is **armed normalization**.

Countries begin signing narrow agreements on:

- prisoner exchange;
- border incidents;
- missing civilians;
- railway passage;
- disease control;
- flood warnings;
- return of stolen rolling stock.

But smuggling, intelligence warfare, border shooting, and political assassination continue.

Irkutsk remains the principal exception. It may reduce conventional raids after one severe Japanese punishment, but it never renounces the claim that Far Eastern Russia is occupied territory.

By 1985, the Tehran Concord’s rule that neither Germany nor Japan will annex the Siberian middle or recognize one claimant as ruler of all Russia gives the external powers a reason to restrain major escalation. It does not turn the successor states into a community. fileciteturn11file3

## Revised working conclusion

The Siberian middle should be established as:

> **A belt of regional military states whose governments inherit Soviet institutions but lose any accepted national center. From 1947 through the early 1970s, they fight repeated limited wars over railways, industrial cities, refugee districts, food, borders, and competing claims to Russia. Omsk and Novosibirsk unify only after failing to defeat one another, preserving a divided military-industrial dual state.**

> **Irkutsk becomes the principal Soviet-restorationist frontier state and the permanent military threat to Mikhail’s Far Eastern monarchy. It can raid, sabotage, and destabilize the Baikal border but cannot invade successfully without provoking a destructive Japanese intervention.**

> **Kazakhstan undergoes the region’s largest demographic war when Kazakh national forces attempt to remove the supposedly temporary Russian emergency establishment that has taken control of the cities, railways, ministries, and army. Kazakhstan survives as a Kazakh state, but northern territorial disputes, Russian enclaves, expulsions, and refugee movements harden the surrounding Russian successor governments.**

> **Kalashnikov’s rifle is completed and adopted around Novosibirsk as the AK-47. It becomes the characteristic weapon of the Siberian successor wars and is copied throughout the region, while Kalashnikov himself remains principally a Novosibirsk state hero rather than a universally known global figure. Far Eastern Russia instead standardizes on Japanese-pattern rifles, leaving the AK as the familiar weapon of Irkutsk raiders, smugglers, and captured frontier arsenals.**

> **After the 1970s, the region becomes less openly warlike but not peaceful. Borders are accepted because changing them has proved prohibitively expensive. The black market remains the most reliable form of regional integration, and nearly every state continues to describe its own foreign dependence as legitimate assistance while condemning every rival as a puppet.**

The core tone is therefore not failed cooperation. It is **exhausted hostility**: a region that eventually stops trying to conquer itself, but never becomes safe enough to forget why every railway station has soldiers.

# Weltnetz wins the network layer, not the whole computing world

This direction resolves one of the major questions intentionally left open after 1985: which system becomes the common interchange layer among the American Data Network, Weltnetz, the Japanese imperial networks, Commonwealth packet services, and the Latin public systems. Those networks already exist separately and exchange traffic through gateways by 1985. fileciteturn64file0 The new conclusion would be:

> **Weltnetz becomes the common global internetwork. Japan shapes much of its practical form, Bridge makes it commercially unavoidable, and national services remain politically separate above it.**

So Germany wins the protocol and infrastructure contest without necessarily winning:

- hardware;
- operating systems;
- software;
- search;
- media;
- or consumer computing.

The mature global system is German at the base, partly Japanese in its handling of text and mobile communication, heavily American in commercial software, British in translation and gateway services, and nationally fragmented at the level of content.

That is a much more interesting victory than Germany simply building the biggest network.

I’ll retain the canonical spelling **Weltnetz**. “Veltnets” can remain a common dictation or foreign pronunciation, but the German name is singular: *das Weltnetz*.

---

# The five independent beginnings

The blocs should develop their networking systems at roughly the same time for different reasons. Packet switching is not one miraculous American invention copied by everyone else. It is the increasingly obvious answer to sharing expensive computers and unreliable long-distance communications.

## The United States: the American Data Network

The **American Data Network**, or ADN, begins closest to the historical American pattern.

Its first users are:

- military research establishments;
- universities;
- aerospace contractors;
- major computer manufacturers;
- and government laboratories.

Its governing assumptions are decentralization, survivability, general-purpose computers, and relatively open technical documentation. By the early 1980s it has expanded into banks, government records, electronic newspapers, contractors, and local dial-up boards. It also carries software, games, pamphlets, rumors, and political material beyond broadcast control. fileciteturn63file2

The ADN’s strength is continental speed and openness.

Its weakness is that it grows as a collection of American institutional networks rather than as an international administrative architecture. Foreign traffic passes through translation gateways. Names, character sets, billing systems, authentication, and commercial access are added unevenly.

It is excellent at connecting universities in California and Massachusetts.

It is much less prepared to authenticate a provincial office in Manchukuo, route a commercial message through several national clearing systems, display Japanese vertical text, and bill a customer in the Philippines without bespoke arrangements.

## Germany: the imperial administrative network

The German precursor grows from three systems that already exist by the later 1960s:

- military and aerospace command links;
- the automated rail, commodity, and industrial networks of the Reich;
- and colonial administrative systems such as MOSAIK.

The first German system is therefore not called Weltnetz. A working institutional name might be **Fernrechnerverbund**, the Remote Computer Federation, or **Reichsdatenverbund**, the Reich Data Federation.

Its purpose is not public communication. It connects:

- ministries;
- banks;
- rail authorities;
- commodity boards;
- major industrial combines;
- Raumhafen control;
- Eastern administrative centers;
- and eventually Mittelafrika.

Germany is trying to govern an empire whose important offices are separated by thousands of kilometers. Kongostadt, Moscow, Kiev, Hamburg, Kribi, and Berlin all need access to the same records without relying upon mail, telex, and manually reconciled ledgers.

Falkenberg’s later achievement is not inventing every component. It is recognizing that the imperial administrative network can become a general commercial system. His established objective is to make distance an engineering problem and to connect firms, banks, universities, clients, and satellites while preserving heterogeneous local machines. fileciteturn65file1

## Britain: the Commonwealth Packet Service

Britain develops the broadest early information-service culture. Its networking grows from:

- time-sharing;
- packet switching;
- public data services;
- videotex;
- university computing;
- shipping and insurance;
- Commonwealth communications;
- and translation among incompatible systems.

A working name would be the **Commonwealth Packet Service**, or CPS.

The CPS is less ideologically open than the American network but more service-oriented. A university, port authority, bank, government department, or school system purchases access to a managed information service. Britain becomes especially good at connecting unlike machines because the Commonwealth itself contains so many different administrations, currencies, industries, and levels of development.

Its weakness is physical reach. Britain can connect the Commonwealth’s principal cities and ports, but it does not possess Germany’s satellite-launch volume or Japan’s consumer-electronics scale.

## Japan: the Imperial Information Network

Japan’s network grows from:

- factory control;
- bank and trading-company transactions;
- shipping;
- imperial logistics;
- electronic text;
- paging;
- household electronics;
- and the need to administer a multilingual maritime sphere.

A working official name before convergence might be **Teikoku Jōhōmō**—帝国情報網, the Imperial Information Network.

Japan’s system is less open to arbitrary independent computers than the ADN. It is very good at controlled transactions:

- a shipment;
- a bank instruction;
- a factory order;
- a railway reservation;
- a pager message;
- a household-service request;
- or a transaction between associated states.

Japan is also forced to solve text and presentation questions earlier than the other blocs. Its systems must handle kana, ideographs, vertical display, complex line breaking, and multiple scripts. Japan consequently leads the universal-character project that produces UNICODE 80 in 1980. fileciteturn64file15

## The Latin system

The Latin bloc’s network grows somewhat later from:

- Olivetti business machines;
- Italian state corporations;
- banking and Scudo clearing;
- ports and shipping;
- Occitan scientific computing;
- Spanish and Portuguese telecommunications;
- and public administrative services.

A suitable collective name would be **Rete Pubblica Latina**, or **Rete Latina**. Spanish and Portuguese institutions would use local translations without treating the Italian wording as politically sovereign.

The Latin system is particularly good at:

- structured forms;
- professional databases;
- public-service terminals;
- commercial logic;
- legal and accounting records;
- and multilingual document exchange.

It is slower to reach ordinary households, but its public systems are relatively coherent.

---

# Why Weltnetz is technically different

Falkenberg’s salesmanship emphasizes satellites. But he knows that most dense traffic will still travel through cable, microwave, fiber, and local packet networks. That distinction is already part of his established characterization. fileciteturn63file11

Weltnetz is therefore **satellite-centered**, not satellite-only.

The satellite system does three things.

First, it guarantees that every major regional network can reach the common backbone without waiting for a terrestrial line through friendly territory.

Second, it provides fallback routes when cables are cut, states close borders, or local infrastructure fails.

Third, it forces the protocols to cope with delay, limited bandwidth, intermittent contact, and transmission errors from the beginning.

Dense traffic between Berlin and Hamburg stays on terrestrial lines. A remote mine in Kaukasien, a ship in the Indian Ocean, an office in Kongostadt, or a station in Siberia may reach the same network through a satellite gateway.

## The satellite architecture

The physical system would probably contain three layers:

| Layer | Principal use |
|---|---|
| Geostationary satellites | Large regional trunks, television/data broadcast, stable commercial links |
| Highly elliptical and polar satellites | Northern Germany’s Finnish, Arctic, and Russian systems |
| Lower-orbit packet relays | Remote store-and-forward service, mobile traffic, ships, isolated colonial districts |

Germany’s lead in launch capacity lets it deploy this infrastructure sooner and more consistently than the other blocs.

Japan later supplies many of the compact terminals, switching components, household devices, and mobile receivers using it.

---

# Compactness and redundancy

There is an apparent contradiction between making packets compact and adding redundancy. The architecture can reconcile them by putting each kind of redundancy in the layer where it is useful.

Weltnetz uses:

- a short fixed packet header;
- optional extension fields rather than one enormous universal header;
- compact local character encodings mapped to UNICODE identities;
- segmentation of large messages into small recoverable blocks;
- sequence numbers and checksums;
- hop-by-hop repair on unreliable satellite links;
- end-to-end validation at the application level;
- store-and-forward queues when a route is temporarily unavailable;
- and duplicate transmission only for priority traffic.

A routine commercial message is not sent three times over three satellites.

An emergency state order, bank-clearing instruction, or orbital command may be.

The system’s early engineering principle might be:

> **As little as necessary in every packet; enough in every message to survive the route.**

This makes Weltnetz better suited than the ADN to variable-quality international infrastructure.

## Local caching

Satellite delay makes constant interactive communication awkward, especially through geostationary relays.

Weltnetz compensates through:

- local mirrors;
- cached directories;
- regional document stores;
- queued mail;
- replicated public records;
- and incremental updates rather than full retransmission.

A user in Mittelafrika does not retrieve every German government document directly from Berlin each time. A regional gateway holds the current authorized copy and receives changes as they occur.

This is one reason the system can scale to hundreds of thousands and later millions of simultaneous users without requiring every interaction to cross half the world.

---

# Identity is built into the network

Weltnetz is not born from an American culture of anonymous university experimentation.

Its basic architecture assumes that:

- machines are registered;
- institutional gateways are certified;
- subscribers possess identities;
- traffic can be billed;
- and transactions can be attributed.

The existing working treatment already states that users and machines are identified, authenticated, and logged. fileciteturn63file12

A likely identity model would distinguish:

- **Rechnerkennung** — machine identity;
- **Teilnehmerkennung** — subscriber identity;
- **Dienstkennung** — service identity;
- **Netzstelle** — registered network location.

Public pseudonyms can still exist.

A bulletin-board user may appear as “MoonRider42,” but the service provider knows which subscriber account connected. Anonymous speech is therefore a social or legal permission granted above the network, not a technical default.

This fits several blocs for different reasons:

- Germany wants administrative legibility.
- Japan wants reliable transactions and household billing.
- Britain wants accountable public services.
- The Latin bloc wants legal and professional identity.
- American corporations want payment, credit, advertising, and customer records.

American hobbyists dislike it, but commercial America finds it useful.

---

# The German–Japanese convergence

The Tehran Concord does not need to contain a complete computer treaty. But its 1986 implementation instruments provide the political umbrella under which the two technical systems begin converging. Germany and Japan are already cooperating through the Raumhafen modules and selected technical exchanges by then. fileciteturn63file17

The resulting system remains recognizably Weltnetz because Germany contributes:

- the packet architecture;
- satellite backbone;
- global addressing hierarchy;
- administrative identity model;
- and principal internetwork gateways.

Japan contributes several things that prevent Weltnetz from becoming merely a German imperial network.

## UNICODE 80 becomes native

Germany had been slow to adopt UNICODE 80 generally. Weltnetz forces the change.

The common network does not merely allow UNICODE text as an optional payload. Its directory, message, page, and service-description layers use UNICODE identities natively.

Compact regional encodings remain permitted on local links, but gateways must be able to map them into the common character space.

This is a major Japanese victory inside a German system.

## Japanese layout rules

Japan contributes practical standards for:

- character-cell negotiation;
- horizontal and vertical text;
- alternate writing directions;
- page segmentation;
- line-breaking metadata;
- device capability descriptions;
- and compact graphic symbols.

A German terminal can ignore vertical Japanese display.

It cannot corrupt the underlying document by assuming horizontal Latin text is the only legitimate form.

## Paging and delayed delivery

Japan’s experience with paging, factory messages, household electronics, and intermittent mobile terminals shapes the message layer.

Weltnetz therefore treats delayed delivery as normal rather than exceptional.

A message can be addressed to:

- a person;
- household;
- machine;
- office;
- ship;
- or mobile terminal

and held until that recipient next reaches a gateway.

That becomes valuable far beyond Japan.

## The Japanese name

Inside the Japanese sphere, the common system would probably be called:

> **世界情報網 — Sekai Jōhōmō**, the World Information Network

In ordinary speech this may shorten to **Sekaimō**, “world net.”

It is not a separate network by the later 1980s. It is the Japanese presentation, administrative namespace, and service environment built over the same underlying protocol family.

German engineers say Weltnetz.

Japanese users say Sekaimō.

The programmer joke becomes:

> “It’s the same net. The question is whether the manual prints it in Latin letters or katakana.”

There are real differences in menus, directories, state control, search, and services. There is no longer a fundamental difference in packet transport.

---

# Bridge is the decisive commercial conversion

The German–Japanese agreement makes Weltnetz large.

Bridge makes it global.

Martin Keene’s entire project is to make applications portable through stable interfaces, device abstraction, and translators. Bridge/16 already creates America’s largest compatible computer ecosystem in 1981, and Keene has already licensed tools into German systems despite the Munich controversy. fileciteturn65file1

By 1987 or 1988, Interlink faces a simple commercial problem.

Bridge software can run across many kinds of American-compatible hardware. But Bridge applications still encounter several mutually incompatible international networks.

A German–Japanese network covering:

- continental Europe;
- the German empire;
- Japan;
- Korea;
- Manchukuo;
- Southeast Asia;
- the Philippines;
- and associated states

is too large to treat as a foreign curiosity.

## Bridge/WN

Interlink therefore produces a **Bridge/WN** networking environment.

It provides:

- Weltnetz addressing;
- subscriber authentication;
- message and file transfer;
- directory lookup;
- Seitenplan display;
- UNICODE 80 conversion;
- and translation between Bridge files and Weltnetz services.

Keene does not adopt it because he favors Germany politically. He adopts it because his customers want access to the largest reachable commercial network.

His likely defense is:

> A general-purpose operating environment does not acquire a foreign policy merely because a packet crosses a border.

That is entirely consistent with his established personality. fileciteturn65file1

## Concord follows

Concord initially resists.

Mercer dislikes surrendering control of the network experience to a foreign standard. Concord attempts a proprietary gateway and curated international service.

But Concord’s foreign customers want:

- Weltnetz mail;
- German and Japanese commercial directories;
- international publishing;
- satellite services;
- and access to Bridge-compatible partners.

By 1989, Concord introduces a certified Weltnetz environment.

It retains a polished Concord interface, parental and institutional controls, proprietary publishing, and its own content stores. Beneath that presentation, the machine speaks Weltnetz.

The commercial effect is enormous.

Once Bridge and Concord both support Weltnetz, American software firms no longer need the ADN to reach ordinary foreign customers.

---

# What happens to the American Data Network

The ADN does not physically vanish.

Its terrestrial cables, packet switches, university links, bank circuits, and government infrastructure remain valuable. The change is that its civilian portions increasingly carry Weltnetz traffic.

The distinction is similar to a railway adopting a common gauge. The tracks remain American. The vehicles and interchange rules become international.

## Civilian migration

American commercial providers prefer Weltnetz because it gives them:

- German and Japanese customers;
- foreign satellite access;
- UNICODE support;
- standardized international identity;
- Bridge integration;
- and predictable billing across national gateways.

The Reagan boom accelerates this migration. Companies want one international system, not a chain of bespoke gateway contracts.

The 1990 crash completes it.

Washington no longer wants to subsidize a parallel civilian protocol merely to preserve national pride. American firms need export revenue, and Weltnetz is where their foreign customers are.

## Strategic survival

The original ADN core becomes progressively restricted to:

- defense;
- intelligence;
- aerospace command;
- emergency government;
- strategic industrial coordination;
- and protected financial settlement.

A likely later name would be the **Strategic Data Network**, although it remains descended from the ADN.

This network is faster within the United States, more heavily encrypted, and more isolated from foreign gateways.

So the irony is exact:

> America creates the decentralized packet network that could have become the world standard. Its surviving pure form becomes a military and government network, close to the environment from which it originally emerged.

Civilian America joins Weltnetz instead.

---

# Britain and the Latin bloc do not disappear

Weltnetz dominance does not mean the CPS and Rete Latina are dismantled.

They become national and bloc-level carrier systems underneath or beside the common internetworking layer.

## Britain

The Commonwealth Packet Service retains:

- Commonwealth subscriber accounts;
- educational services;
- public records;
- banking;
- translation;
- shipping and insurance networks;
- and British legal jurisdiction.

Its gateways speak Weltnetz.

Britain becomes one of the major providers of translation, caching, and protocol-conversion services, particularly during the transition.

## The Latin bloc

Rete Latina keeps:

- Scudo settlement;
- public administrative terminals;
- professional databases;
- Latin corporate services;
- and national-language interfaces.

It adopts Weltnetz transport because Latin firms want access to Germany, Japan, Britain, and American Bridge software.

The Latin states still control which services are licensed and which foreign systems may index domestic content.

The common network therefore connects national networks without dissolving them.

---

# Search remains national

This is one of the strongest parts of the proposed model.

A search engine is not the network.

Weltnetz can define:

- addresses;
- documents;
- links;
- identity;
- transfer;
- and presentation

without defining one universal index of everything published.

Each bloc consequently develops its own major search and directory services.

A German engine emphasizes:

- registered publishers;
- official directories;
- certified commercial data;
- German-language relevance;
- and state-authorized access.

A Japanese service emphasizes:

- Japanese language;
- vertical text;
- household and commercial services;
- domestic publishers;
- and the Co-Prosperity information sphere.

An American search company emphasizes:

- commercial pages;
- advertising;
- independent publishing;
- and Bridge software services.

Britain emphasizes:

- reference;
- public information;
- libraries;
- Commonwealth records;
- and multilingual gateways.

The Latin system emphasizes professional, cultural, legal, commercial, and state directories.

Foreign search services are reachable, but they are not necessarily useful.

A German search engine may not possess permission to crawl most Japanese services. An American engine may not understand the ranking and directory metadata used by the Latin public networks. National gateways may charge for bulk indexing or prohibit it.

Thus there is no Google-equivalent used by nearly everyone.

There are several Yandex-like national systems operating over one shared technical network.

That preserves political and cultural borders after protocol convergence.

---

# The Weltnetz document system

The HTML equivalent should not simply be Rechenplan placed inside angle brackets.

Rechenplan is too formal, heavy, and strategically certified. Kurzplan is accessible but too much of a small-computer programming language.

The better result is a new declarative language drawing from both:

> **Seitenplan** — Page Plan

A first international edition might appear as **Seitenplan 88**.

## Its ancestry

Rechenplan contributes:

- explicit structure;
- typed data;
- validation;
- reproducibility;
- and separation between content and operation.

Kurzplan contributes:

- compact syntax;
- easy authoring;
- limited-memory implementations;
- and suitability for home and office machines.

Japan contributes:

- script independence;
- vertical and horizontal layout;
- page segmentation;
- device-description rules;
- and UNICODE 80.

Britain contributes:

- gateway translation;
- document libraries;
- and device-independent service presentation.

The Latin system contributes:

- structured forms;
- database queries;
- and declarative logic.

It remains called Seitenplan because the German commission publishes and controls the normative standard.

## Basic terminology

The standard vocabulary might include:

| German term | Function |
|---|---|
| **Seite** | Page or document |
| **Fenster** | Independent display region or updating pane |
| **Verweis** | Link or reference |
| **Bild** | Image |
| **Tabelle** | Table |
| **Formular** | Interactive form |
| **Dienst** | Network service |
| **Netzstelle** | Site or registered network location |
| **Kennung** | Identity or identifier |
| **Knoten** | Node |
| **Abruf** | Request or retrieval |

A minimal document might contain tags resembling:

`<SEITE>`, `<FENSTER>`, `<BILD>`, and `<VERWEIS>`.

The exact textual syntax can vary by authoring language because the transmitted form is tokenized. Japanese tools may display localized keywords while emitting the same underlying structural codes.

But the canonical names in standards manuals remain German.

## How much German enters ordinary language?

Programmers across the world routinely know the German words.

An American developer may say:

- “put it in a Fenster”;
- “the Verweis is broken”;
- or “publish the Seite to the Netzstelle.”

Ordinary American users may continue saying “page,” “window,” and “link” for years.

The German terms spread unevenly from technical language into popular language, much as computer terminology in our world often moves from standards manuals into ordinary speech.

Japan transliterates some of them into katakana. Latin developers often use local cognates in user interfaces while retaining German names in specifications.

---

# Dynamic services are more controlled than the historical web

Germany would be wary of arbitrary code downloaded from an unknown publisher and executed automatically on a private machine.

Early Seitenplan is therefore primarily declarative.

Interactive functions work through:

- server-side services;
- submitted forms;
- signed modules;
- or locally installed Bridge and Concord applications.

A later scripting system could develop from Kurzplan, perhaps called **Netzfolge**, but executable modules would carry publisher identities and signatures.

This produces a network that is:

- less anonymous;
- less technically chaotic;
- easier to bill;
- easier to censor;
- safer against some forms of malware;
- and more vulnerable to institutional surveillance.

American commercial pressure gradually opens it, but the identified foundation remains.

That fits the later corporate American order extremely well. A corporation does not merely know which advertisement appeared on a page. The provider can connect the page request to a subscriber, machine, employer, payment account, and service history.

---

# Why Weltnetz wins without universal political trust

Every bloc can tell itself it has not surrendered.

Germany says it supplies the world standard.

Japan says the standard would be unusable without Japanese characters, terminals, paging, and electronics.

America says Bridge and Concord turned a bureaucratic German network into a real commercial market.

Britain says the system depends upon Commonwealth gateways and translation.

The Latin bloc says it preserved its public services and professional databases.

All of those claims are partly true.

The adoption is possible because Weltnetz is not presented as a German social network, newspaper, search engine, or software monopoly.

It is presented as plumbing.

By the time governments recognize that plumbing carries political influence, removing it would disconnect their own firms, universities, exporters, banks, and consumers.

The system’s real achievement is that every bloc can use it while believing the important part remains national.

---

# Working chronology

| Date | Development |
|---|---|
| **1966–1970** | American, German, British, Japanese, and Latin packet-network experiments emerge independently |
| **Early 1970s** | ADN links American research institutions; German administrative networks connect rail, industry, aerospace, and MOSAIK; Japanese factory and transaction networks expand; Britain develops packet services; Latin public networks begin |
| **1975–1980** | National networks add public terminals, electronic mail, databases, videotex, paging, and commercial gateways |
| **1979** | Falkenberg’s “Computing Without Distance” lecture proposes a satellite-centered world federation |
| **1980** | UNICODE 80 creates the common abstract character system |
| **1981** | Germany begins the formal Weltnetz study |
| **1982** | Falkenberg receives a special network commission; civilian German language competition is liberalized |
| **1983–1985** | German terrestrial and satellite gateways are tested across the Reich and partner states |
| **1985** | The world still contains several gatewayed internetworks rather than one Internet |
| **1986** | Tehran implementation opens formal German–Japanese network cooperation |
| **1986–1988** | Weltnetz incorporates Japanese character, layout, paging, and delayed-delivery rules; Sekai Jōhōmō becomes the Japanese presentation of the common system |
| **1988** | Interlink releases Bridge/WN, giving the American compatible market direct Weltnetz access |
| **1989** | Concord adds certified Weltnetz support; Seitenplan 88 spreads as the common document format |
| **1990–1992** | The American crash and export dependence accelerate civilian migration from ADN protocols to Weltnetz |
| **Early 1990s** | Britain and the Latin bloc adopt Weltnetz as their external internetworking layer while retaining national services |
| **Mid-1990s** | Weltnetz becomes the default global commercial and civilian protocol family |
| **Late 1990s onward** | National search engines, portals, identity regimes, and content controls remain distinct over a common German-led network |

# The final synthesis

The mature system is not a German version of our Internet in which everyone visits the same websites through one search engine.

It is closer to a shared global railway gauge.

The tracks, stations, operators, laws, timetables, and destinations remain national. But a compatible vehicle can cross from one system into another without being rebuilt at every frontier.

The defining division is:

- **Weltnetz controls how systems find and communicate with one another.**
- **National networks control what their users normally see.**
- **Bridge and Concord control much of the commercial software reaching those users.**
- **Search remains divided by language, law, and political bloc.**

The clean cultural formula would be:

> **Germany builds the road.  
> Japan teaches it to carry the world’s writing.  
> America fills it with software.  
> Every government builds its own signs and checkpoints.**
