## The Co-Prosperity Sphere as an association of national states

This establishes the constitutional core of the Sphere more clearly than a formal charter alone could.

> **The Co-Prosperity Sphere has common leadership, defense, markets, and standards. It does not have a common people.**

There is no Sphere citizenship, no general right of movement, no common electorate, and no presumption that long residence turns one nationality into another. Japan leads a collection of enduring national communities rather than slowly absorbing them into one imperial population.

That also clarifies the Japanese doctrine of guardianship. Japan does not claim that every Asian nation should eventually become Japanese. It claims that each nation should remain itself while performing its proper office within a Japanese-led order.

The existing Japanese political material already points toward this arrangement: associated governments increasingly demand consultation, while Japanese factions debate how to lead rather than whether Japan should lead. The emperor’s authority remains specifically Japanese, even as the imperial household becomes the ceremonial patron of concord among the associated states. fileciteturn21file3 fileciteturn21file6

# I. Nationality is permanent

The normal rule throughout the Sphere is **hereditary national membership**, not naturalization through residence.

A Chinese man remains Chinese in Japan. A Japanese family living in Manchukuo remains Japanese. A Korean engineer in Manila remains Korean. Their children normally inherit the nationality of their family rather than the territory in which they happen to be born.

Residence changes where a person lives. It does not ordinarily change who he is.

## No general naturalization

Most member states either prohibit naturalization outright or make it so exceptional that it has little practical importance.

A foreign resident may receive:

- permission to reside;
- permission to work;
- a corporate or professional sponsorship;
- local tax registration;
- access to particular schools and clinics;
- renewable or permanent domicile;
- protection under bilateral treaty law.

He does not ordinarily receive:

- voting rights;
- eligibility for public office;
- military command;
- unrestricted landholding;
- national welfare rights identical to citizens;
- a passport from the host state;
- citizenship for children born there.

A man may live in the same country for forty years and remain legally foreign.

This is not regarded as an unfortunate transitional condition. It is the intended order.

## Birth does not create local citizenship

The system rejects unrestricted *jus soli*.

A Korean child born in Japan remains Korean. A Japanese child born in Manila remains Japanese. A Chinese family living around a Mantetsu concession in Mongolia does not become Mongolian merely because its children are born there.

This prevents company migration and imperial labor movement from quietly changing the political nation.

It also means that the Sphere can move technicians, merchants, clerks, dockworkers, and specialists without promising that the host society must eventually absorb them.

## Renunciation is difficult as well

The logic probably runs in both directions. Nationality cannot easily be acquired, but neither can it be discarded simply for convenience.

A Japanese businessman cannot evade Japanese military or tax obligations merely by declaring himself Manchukuoan. A Filipino cannot abandon Philippine jurisdiction because a Japanese corporation offers him a better legal category.

This makes nationality a public inheritance rather than a private consumer choice.

# II. Residence and labor movement

The Sphere has no free movement comparable to a supranational common market.

Movement is permitted because a particular person is useful, because a firm sponsors him, because a treaty provides for it, or because a government has accepted a defined labor program.

The usual system would involve three separate documents:

1. a passport or national identity document issued by the home state;
2. a Sphere travel endorsement or entry visa;
3. a work, study, or residence permit issued by the host state.

A Mantetsu engineer may hold long-term residence rights in three countries without becoming a citizen of any of them except his own.

## Company-sponsored migration

Large firms become the principal instruments of mobility.

A Japanese company wishing to transfer a Korean machinist to Osaka, a Chinese accountant to Singapore, or a Mongolian surveyor to Manchukuo accepts responsibility for:

- employment;
- housing;
- medical provision;
- good conduct;
- return transport;
- taxation;
- notification of local authorities.

The worker’s right to remain may initially depend upon the sponsoring employer. This gives Japanese corporations enormous leverage over expatriate personnel.

By the 1970s, professional residents may receive permits independent of one employer, but political membership remains unavailable.

## Permanent foreign communities

Some residents become effectively permanent despite never becoming citizens.

Japan proper might contain second- and third-generation Korean, Chinese, Taiwanese, Filipino, or Manchukuoan communities whose members:

- speak Japanese as their first language;
- attended Japanese schools;
- work in Japanese firms;
- have never lived in their formal homeland;
- remain legally foreign.

That creates a real social contradiction. The official answer is that culture and nationality are not identical: a man may participate fully in Japanese economic and social life while remaining a member of another national people.

The lived result is more difficult. Some families will experience this as orderly preservation of identity. Others will experience it as being born in a country that permanently refuses to accept them.

This is particularly important for Korea. Cultural Japanization does not automatically produce Japanese citizenship. Korea can become deeply assimilated in language, schooling, names, employment, and military practice while Koreans remain a legally separate population. The result is not civic incorporation but **assimilation without absorption**. The existing canon’s description of highly Japanized urban Korea should therefore be read in that light. fileciteturn21file11

# III. The two naturalizing exceptions

## Vladivostok

Vladivostok is the clearest full-state exception.

Its identity is not based upon one ancestral nation. It exists as a Japanese-protected maritime polity containing Japanese, Russians, Koreans, Manchus, Chinese, mixed families, and foreign commercial communities.

Its citizenship is therefore civic and selective.

A foreign applicant normally requires:

- a needed skill, profession, investment, or commercial activity;
- lawful sponsored entry;
- five years of continuous residence;
- tax and employment records;
- competence in Japanese, the legal language;
- a clean security record;
- evidence of permanent commitment to the city.

Naturalization is possible because Vladivostok needs people who will belong to the protectorate rather than remain indefinitely attached to competing neighboring states.

This also prevents every resident from being politically claimed by Chita, Manchukuo, Korea, China, or Japan.

A naturalized Russian-speaking citizen of Vladivostok is no longer merely a Russian temporarily living under Japanese authority. He is a member of the city-state.

## Singapore

Singapore reaches a similar result from a different direction.

Vladivostok naturalizes specialists to create a strategically loyal maritime society. Singapore naturalizes residents because a commercial city-state cannot function if most of its merchants, dockworkers, clerks, financiers, and families remain permanent foreigners with no stake in municipal government.

Singaporean citizenship would likely be based upon:

- sustained residence;
- taxation;
- employment or business;
- public order;
- family establishment;
- some proficiency in one or more recognized civic languages;
- an oath to the city and its charter.

It is less ethnically defined than surrounding Malaya and more openly mercantile than Vladivostok. Chinese, Malay, Indian, Japanese, Eurasian, and other residents can become Singaporean without ceasing to possess cultural ancestry.

Singapore may therefore operate almost like a corporate-commercial precinct enlarged into a sovereign city. Citizenship means membership in the port’s civic order, not admission into a single ancestral nation.

These two exceptions don’t undermine the general rule. They demonstrate why the rule exists. Naturalization appears where the state itself is built around a city and function rather than an inherited national people.

# IV. There is no supranational emperor

The emperor is **Emperor of Japan**, not emperor, regent, caliph, or president of the Co-Prosperity Sphere.

State Shinto remains a Japanese institution. It is not imposed upon:

- Filipino Catholics;
- Mongolian or Tibetan Buddhists;
- Uyghur Muslims;
- Russian Orthodox Christians;
- Thai or Burmese Buddhists;
- Chinese Confucian, Buddhist, Daoist, or popular religious communities.

Associated rulers and governments may honor the Japanese emperor as the sovereign of the presiding power, treaty guarantor, or ceremonial patron of concord. They do not become his domestic subjects.

Akihito’s later public diplomacy can therefore make him the symbolic figure of the multinational order without changing his legal title. Visits to associated states, religious authorities, technical institutions, and disaster memorials express Japanese responsibility rather than a universal imperial cult. That distinction was already implicit in the existing account of the monarchy’s later role. fileciteturn21file3

# V. Three political levels

The Sphere has three practical levels, although its public language avoids describing them too bluntly.

## 1. Japan: the presiding power

Japan possesses the reserve authority of the system.

It controls or leads:

- common defense;
- naval security;
- strategic aviation;
- inter-Sphere military planning;
- the highest industrial and technological standards;
- currency and clearing coordination;
- great-power diplomacy;
- admission of new members;
- final arbitration of existential disputes.

When Japan makes a genuine determination on a matter affecting the survival of the Sphere, the other members understand that they are expected to comply.

But Japan’s authority is strongest precisely because it is rarely expressed as a command.

The Japanese government normally seeks:

- bilateral agreement;
- conference consensus;
- ministerial negotiation;
- financial inducement;
- corporate implementation;
- quiet pressure through advisers;
- a request from the affected government.

A Japanese directive is held in reserve for circumstances where ordinary consultation has failed or an emergency leaves no time for it.

## 2. The principal associated powers

Four states possess enough weight to alter the direction of the Sphere:

- **Manchukuo**;
- **National China**;
- **Siam**;
- **the Philippines**.

Their influence comes from different sources.

### Manchukuo

Manchukuo controls the northern heavy-industrial center, continental military production, Mantetsu’s original base, and a major share of the northeast Asian economy.

It cannot easily be ignored without disrupting the machinery of the Sphere.

### National China

China’s practical military authority is limited, but its population, market, civilizational prestige, and cultural importance make its participation politically necessary.

China’s engagement varies. Sometimes Nanjing insists upon acting as one of the great voices of Asia. At other times it is content to preserve its protected internal civilization and leave strategic management to Japan.

Japan and the other principal states accommodate Chinese participation when China demands it, but China does not possess an overseeing or permanent directing authority.

### Siam

Siam is the senior old ally rather than a state created by Japanese victory.

Its monarchy, army, diplomatic establishment, and independent history give it a capacity to say no that many other members lack. Japanese authority works particularly well with Siam because Tokyo rarely humiliates Bangkok by exercising it openly.

### The Philippines

The Philippines is the showcase of negotiated association and possesses growing influence in maritime policy, Catholic and Southeast Asian affairs, merchant shipping, and the political definition of associated sovereignty.

Its independence settlement made Japanese promises of partnership harder to treat as mere propaganda. Earlier Japanese development planning already treats Manila as the visible proof that association can produce genuine national institutions rather than permanent occupation. fileciteturn21file0

These four do not govern the Sphere alongside Japan as equals. They are the states Japan must seriously consult when it wants the Sphere to act as a coherent whole.

## 3. Protected and functionally dependent members

The remaining states possess domestic government but limited ability to redirect the wider system.

These include, in varying forms:

- United Mongolia;
- the Indochinese states;
- Burma;
- the Indonesian states;
- Xinjiang;
- Tibet;
- Far Eastern Russia;
- Vladivostok;
- some Malayan and Pacific arrangements.

Their participation rests on a clearer bargain:

> Japan constrains their diplomacy and strategic military freedom. In return, Japan guarantees that neither an outside power nor another member of the Sphere will destroy them.

For Xinjiang, this means protection from the Central Asian and Soviet successor frontier.

For Tibet and Burma, it means insulation from the Indian wars.

For Far Eastern Russia, it means protection against Irkutsk and against partition by Manchukuo.

For the Indonesian states, it means protection of islands, sea lanes, and governments that could not defend themselves independently.

These states may not possess unrestricted authority to form alliances, admit foreign bases, or negotiate major strategic treaties. They can still conduct ordinary commerce, consular relations, cultural agreements, and local border arrangements within Japanese-approved limits.

They aren’t provinces of Japan. But they are not fully free actors in international politics either.

# VI. The Indian associate outside the Sphere

I’m reading the dictation form “Agha government” as **Azad Hind**.

The distinction you’ve drawn is useful:

> Azad Hind is associated with Japan, not admitted as a member of the Co-Prosperity Sphere.

Japan may provide:

- financial support;
- weapons;
- advisers;
- intelligence;
- political recognition;
- development assistance;
- security guarantees.

But Azad Hind remains part of the unsettled Indian order. Admitting it to the Sphere would imply that Japan has accepted a particular settlement of India and may owe it full collective defense.

That is a larger commitment than Tokyo wants to undertake.

It also leaves room for Hyderabad’s later, separate movement into Japanese association after the Tehran settlement without making Azad Hind the recognized government of all India. The existing canon already distinguishes Hyderabad’s post-1986 association from Azad Hind as a separate institution. fileciteturn21file11

# VII. Authority works because Japan does not exhaust it

This is the most important part of the system.

Japan possesses something close to **reserve suzerainty**, but it governs through restraint.

A ruler who issues commands every week soon discovers how many of them can be evaded. A ruler who speaks only when the question is grave can make the act of speaking itself decisive.

Japan’s statesmen understand that their authority rests on several conditions:

- members believe Japan ordinarily respects their domestic government;
- Japan provides real external security;
- economic integration produces visible benefits;
- disputes with Japan can normally be negotiated;
- Japanese bases rest on treaties rather than naked seizure;
- associated governments retain public dignity;
- Japan does not casually force one member to sacrifice itself for another.

Therefore, the Japanese bases in Xinjiang, Tibet, Burma, or Indonesia are negotiated directly with the affected government. They are not imposed through an abstract right of the Sphere headquarters to place troops anywhere it chooses.

Legally, Japan might possess or claim such a right in an existential emergency. Politically, exercising it in ordinary circumstances would destroy the doctrine of association.

The system can therefore be described as:

> **Japanese supremacy in reserve, national sovereignty in ordinary practice.**

# VIII. How common decisions are made

The Sphere should not possess a powerful supranational executive comparable to a federal cabinet.

Its common institutions are better understood as a **conference system**.

There would likely be:

- periodic heads-of-government conferences;
- a permanent council of ambassadors or resident ministers;
- defense, finance, shipping, standards, health, and development boards;
- Japanese-chaired secretariats;
- bilateral commissions beneath the common framework.

Japan chairs. The principal associated powers receive the strongest voices. The smaller states attend, petition, negotiate, and sometimes form groups around a common concern.

But a Sphere resolution does not automatically become domestic law.

Each government implements it through:

- national legislation;
- executive decree;
- a bilateral protocol;
- a concession agreement;
- a military-access treaty;
- a corporate contract.

This preserves the legal fiction—and often the real practice—that each state remains self-governing.

## Consensus rather than voting

Formal majority voting would expose the inequality of the arrangement.

If every state had one equal vote, Japan could theoretically be defeated by its own clients. If votes were weighted by power, Japanese dominance would become embarrassingly explicit.

The normal method is therefore consensus under Japanese chairmanship.

Japan determines when sufficient agreement exists. The principal states can delay, qualify, or reshape a decision. Smaller states can win exemptions or compensation, but seldom overturn the broad direction once Japan and the principal associates agree.

# IX. Duties rather than equal capacities

The Sphere’s public doctrine does not say that every member is equal in power or identical in function.

It says that each holds a **proper duty** within a common order.

Japan’s duties include:

- common defense;
- naval power;
- strategic technology;
- arbitration;
- maintaining the external balance.

Manchukuo’s duties emphasize:

- continental heavy industry;
- machinery;
- rail;
- armaments;
- northern production.

China claims:

- civilizational culture;
- scholarship;
- the vast central market;
- agricultural and demographic depth.

The Philippines and Singapore contribute:

- maritime services;
- shipping;
- ports;
- commerce;
- communications;
- financial and cultural links beyond the Japanese language world.

The resource states contribute:

- oil;
- rubber;
- tin;
- food;
- minerals;
- tropical commodities.

The frontier states contribute:

- territory;
- surveillance;
- bases;
- local armies;
- insulation from the disorder outside the Japanese system.

This doctrine permits hierarchy while denying that hierarchy means one people is simply worthless compared with another.

It also allows Japanese leaders sincerely to argue that Japan’s leadership duty does not make Japan morally “more important.” Japan carries the heaviest military and organizational burden because that is its office.

The obvious objection is that Japan has assigned itself the office that also gives it control over everyone else.

Japanese doctrine answers that leadership remains legitimate only while Japan continues providing the service that justifies it.

# X. The system’s central tensions

## Permanent residents who can never belong

The lack of naturalization will create large populations whose legal nationality no longer matches their lived homeland.

This problem will grow rather than disappear, especially in Japan, Korea, Manchukuo, Singapore’s surroundings, and the great corporate cities.

The system will eventually require decisions concerning:

- children whose ancestral country they have never visited;
- mixed marriages;
- military service;
- pensions;
- inheritance;
- deportation after criminal conviction;
- access to universities;
- ownership of homes and firms.

It can preserve distinct nations, but it can also trap people permanently between them.

## Japanese expatriate privilege

A Japanese citizen residing in a smaller member state remains Japanese and may benefit from corporate influence, treaty courts, superior schools, or Japanese consular intervention.

Even without formal extraterritoriality, local populations may conclude that Japanese residents are foreigners who possess more influence than citizens.

That could undermine the claim that fixed nationality protects every host nation equally.

## Corporate empires without political membership

A Chinese or Korean man may work for Mantetsu across three countries, speak Japanese professionally, receive company housing and a pension, and still have no political standing in the community where he spends most of his life.

The corporation becomes more portable than citizenship.

This strengthens the Japanese-centered economy while weakening the connection between residence, labor, and political membership.

## The principal associates will demand conventions

Japan can manage the early Sphere through personality, bilateral treaties, and inherited wartime authority. A mature system will require clearer conventions.

The Philippines and Siam will want assurances that Japanese reserve power cannot be used arbitrarily. Manchukuo will want recognition of its industrial importance. China will periodically demand ceremonies and institutions reflecting its civilizational status.

Japan may resist codifying exact limits because ambiguity favors the stronger power. But excessive ambiguity risks making every crisis a test of the entire system.

## Functional assignments can become ceilings

A state told that its duty is to supply oil or guard a frontier may eventually conclude that “proper duty” is merely a polite term for permanent subordination.

Japan’s broader development doctrine partly answers this by allowing associated states to move upward in manufacturing, infrastructure, and technical capacity. The established prosperity program already assumes that the associated economies gain real productive development rather than remaining indefinitely frozen as raw-material appendages. fileciteturn21file1

But Japan will still control how far and how quickly they move.

# Canon formulation

The institutional settlement can now be stated as follows:

> **The Greater East Asian Co-Prosperity Sphere is an association of sovereign and protected national states under Japanese headship. It possesses no common citizenship and does not treat residence as a normal path to naturalization. Nationality is ordinarily inherited through the family and remains permanent despite foreign residence. Treaty residents may work, own limited property, raise families, and obtain permanent domicile abroad without voting or becoming members of the host nation. Their children inherit the family nationality rather than citizenship by birthplace.**

> **Vladivostok and Singapore are the principal exceptions. Both are cosmopolitan maritime city-states whose political communities cannot be defined through one ancestral people. Vladivostok offers selective naturalization, normally after five years, to skilled or economically useful permanent residents. Singapore operates a broader commercial-civic system based upon residence, taxation, family establishment, and contribution to the port community.**

> **The emperor remains Emperor of Japan and holds no universal throne over the Sphere. State Shinto is not imposed outside Japan. The common order is headed politically by Japan through treaty leadership, defense guarantees, financial coordination, strategic standards, and reserve authority rather than through direct annexation.**

> **Three practical levels emerge. Japan is the presiding power. Manchukuo, National China, Siam, and the Philippines are the principal associated powers whose interests substantially shape common policy. The remaining protected and dependent states retain domestic government but possess limited strategic diplomacy and little ability to redirect the Sphere as a whole.**

> **Japanese authority is technically extensive but ordinarily restrained. Bases, concessions, and military arrangements are negotiated bilaterally rather than issued as routine Sphere decrees. Common action proceeds through conference consensus, Japanese chairmanship, and national implementation. When Japan rarely makes an explicit determination on an existential question, the other members normally comply because Tokyo has not exhausted its authority through continual interference.**

The governing paradox is now very clear:

> **Japan remains obeyed because it usually negotiates when it could command.**

That is not merely politeness. It is the constitutional discipline that prevents Japanese leadership from revealing itself too openly as dominion.

But this is one of those few mandates that come down through the Co-Prosperity Sphere as something that is effectively mandated by Japan. This is a mandate that had some disagreements between the different states as far as what they wanted to do, how they wanted to implement it, some negotiation, some argument, and ultimately a stalemate, which Japan broke. This also was an instance in the Co-Prosperity Sphere where the sphere itself kind of had a mixed reaction. There was a stalemate among the principal powers, and on top of it, there was, this is a mandate that helps the average person, not just the national organization as a whole. Yes. This supersedes my previous formulation of Korea as “assimilated without absorption.” The correct model is almost the reverse:

> **Korea is legally absorbed into Japan and culturally assimilated over time.**

A Korean born in Keijō is a Japanese citizen. He may move to Nagasaki, Tokyo, Formosa, or another integral imperial territory without immigrating into a foreign country. His Korean ancestry may remain socially visible, but it is not a separate nationality under law. This fits the existing cultural endpoint, where Korean performers become Japanese national celebrities and Korean identity increasingly functions as a regional or ancestral distinction rather than citizenship in a separate country. fileciteturn22file8

## The integral Japanese nationality

The Co-Prosperity order now has to distinguish two things clearly.

### Integral Japan

These territories belong directly to the Japanese Empire:

- the home islands;
- Korea or Chōsen;
- Formosa;
- Karafuto;
- the older incorporated Micronesian territories;
- any other territory later fixed as an integral imperial province.

Their inhabitants possess **Japanese nationality**. There is no Korean, Formosan, or Micronesian citizenship alongside it.

A Korean may still be ethnically Korean. A Formosan family may retain a Taiwanese, Hoklo, Hakka, or indigenous identity. A Micronesian community may retain its language and local customs. But legally, these are regional or ancestral identities within the Japanese nation.

This means they possess the ordinary right to live throughout Japan. There is no work permit separating a Korean in Fusan from a Korean in Osaka. There may be prejudice, regional stereotypes, differences in education, and unequal access to elite institutions, but not foreign-resident status.

The tragedy is therefore not that Koreans remain foreigners despite assimilation. It is that the state can point to their full citizenship as evidence that no separate Korean nation is required.

### Associated national states

Filipinos, Chinese, Manchurians, Mongolians, Russians, Siamese, Vietnamese, Laotians, and the other associated peoples remain citizens of their own states.

A Filipino born in Yokohama remains Filipino. A Chinese family living for three generations in Singapore remains Chinese unless Singapore’s exceptional naturalization law applies. Residence, language, and culture do not alter the inherited legal nationality.

That gives the system a sharp boundary:

> **Korean is an ethnicity within Japan. Filipino is a foreign nationality allied to Japan.**

The later cultural-preservation doctrine does not erase that distinction.

## The Korean term

The modern term you are probably reaching for is **Zainichi Korean**. But the exact real-world meaning would not transfer cleanly.

In our history, *Zainichi* Korean identity developed around Koreans living in Japan who became legally foreign after the Japanese Empire collapsed. In this setting, the empire does not collapse, Korea remains part of Japan, and Koreans retain Japanese citizenship.

So *Zainichi* might survive colloquially for peninsula-origin families living in the home islands, but it would not denote a foreign legal community. A more precise official expression would probably be something like:

- **Chōsen-kei Nihonjin** — Japanese of Korean descent;
- **Chōsen-shusshin** — originating from Korea;
- or an ordinary regional label comparable to describing someone as being from Kyūshū or Hokkaidō.

The exact popular term should remain open until we examine Korean society in detail. The important point is that it names ancestry or regional origin, not another nationality.

# The National Home and Return Mandate

The early 1980s mandate provides a strong example of Japan using its reserve authority for a rare, system-wide determination.

A suitable working English title would be:

> **The National Home and Return Mandate**

Its official rhetoric probably avoids an abstract universal “right.” Instead, it establishes three guarantees:

1. every national state must recognize its inherited citizens abroad;
2. those citizens must be admitted if they choose permanent return;
3. the Sphere will assist with the material cost of returning and resettling them.

A Filipino living in Singapore does not become Filipino through the mandate. He was already Filipino. What changes is that Manila can no longer treat him as an inconvenient expatriate and refuse to receive him.

The mandate converts inherited nationality into an enforceable **right of national admission**.

## Why it becomes necessary

The original system assumes foreign residence is temporary or professionally limited. By the 1970s, that assumption no longer works.

The Sphere contains:

- second- and third-generation Filipino families in Singapore;
- Chinese families in Manchukuo and Mongolia;
- Manchurian families in Japanese industrial cities;
- Japanese commercial families living abroad for decades;
- Russians employed throughout the northern corporate network;
- mixed-nationality households;
- children whose legal country is a place they have never seen.

The Sphere refuses common citizenship and largely refuses naturalization. Without a return mechanism, it creates hereditary foreign populations with nowhere they are unambiguously entitled to settle.

That contradicts the emerging Japanese claim that the Sphere protects national cultures rather than dissolving them.

The mandate is the institutional answer:

> **A nation that insists a man remains one of its people cannot refuse to take him home.**

## How the return program works

The mandate would require more than permission at the border. Otherwise it would be ceremonial.

A common Sphere fund—financed disproportionately by Japan, major corporations, and the richer associated states—would cover some combination of:

- transport for the returnee and his household;
- shipment of ordinary personal property;
- temporary housing;
- several months of subsistence;
- language and cultural-acclimation courses;
- translation of qualifications and employment records;
- transfer of pensions and company savings;
- school placement for children;
- job-matching and settlement assistance.

The home state must recognize the person’s nationality papers and cannot impose a normal immigration quota upon him.

It can still exclude or delay:

- convicted serious criminals;
- active enemy agents;
- persons under lawful military or tax obligations;
- disputed claimants whose paternal identity cannot be established.

But those become reviewable exceptions rather than excuses to refuse a politically inconvenient diaspora.

## The returnee is legally native and culturally foreign

This produces a new social category throughout the Sphere.

A returning man may possess:

- citizenship by birth;
- an ancestral surname;
- a father and grandfather legally belonging to the nation;
- no command of the national language;
- foreign manners;
- foreign professional habits;
- a foreign spouse;
- children who understand the ancestral country only through stories.

The local population then divides over what he is.

One position says:

> “He possesses our passport, but he isn’t really one of us.”

The other says:

> “He could have remained abroad. Choosing to return proves that he wishes to become one of us in practice.”

Both attitudes can exist within the same family.

### The Philippines

**Balikbayan** is the natural Filipino popular term. In this timeline it would broaden beyond a temporary overseas visitor and come to include the foreign-raised Filipino who permanently returns under the mandate.

There would be several recognizable types:

- the Japanese-speaking balikbayan;
- the Singaporean Chinese-cultured balikbayan;
- the Manchukuoan industrial returnee;
- the second-generation child who speaks English or Japanese better than Tagalog or his family’s regional language.

The government praises them as recovered sons and daughters of the nation. Local Filipinos sometimes regard them as privileged foreigners arriving with subsidies and better qualifications.

### China

China would probably revive or broaden a term equivalent to **returned overseas Chinese**. The examination state might create accelerated language, classics, and civic courses for returnees whose legal nationality is Chinese but whose cultural formation is Japanese, Manchurian, or Southeast Asian.

### Far Eastern Russia

The crown would treat returnees as recovered Russian households but expect Orthodox, linguistic, and civic acclimation. A Russian-national family returning from Vladivostok or Manchukuo might be legally welcomed while culturally regarded as Japanized.

Each country develops its own term because each country understands the problem differently.

# Patrilineal nationality

The most contentious part of the mandate is the rule that nationality follows the father.

The system recognizes only one legal nationality. It does not recognize a permanent “half-Chinese, half-Manchurian” category.

The rule is simple:

- Japanese father and Filipino mother: **Japanese child**;
- Filipino father and Japanese mother: **Filipino child**;
- Chinese father and Manchurian mother: **Chinese child**;
- Russian father and Mongolian mother: **Russian child**;
- Siamese father and Vietnamese mother: **Siamese child**.

This applies regardless of:

- birthplace;
- language;
- appearance;
- mother’s residence;
- which culture predominates in the home.

A Japanese-Filipino child who looks more Filipino remains Japanese if his father is Japanese. A Chinese-Manchurian child raised entirely in Manchukuo remains Chinese if his father is Chinese.

The legal purpose is to prevent three problems:

1. competing claims by two states;
2. stateless or permanently ambiguous children;
3. the gradual creation of a supranational mixed population outside all national orders.

The result is administratively clear and socially rough.

## No legal “half” category

The law does not mean mixed ancestry disappears. It means the state refuses to make mixed ancestry a nationality.

People will still notice:

- physical appearance;
- maternal language;
- religion;
- accent;
- food;
- family customs;
- maternal relatives;
- where the child was raised.

Colloquial expressions equivalent to “half,” “mixed,” or “mother-side Filipino” will still exist. Some are neutral, some affectionate, and some insulting.

But the passport, military record, school registry, and return entitlement contain one nationality.

This creates a useful formal-versus-functional distinction:

> **The law answers what state claims the person. It cannot completely answer which culture formed him.**

## Marriage probably does not alter the wife’s nationality

The most coherent extension—though this specific detail remains an inference rather than a stated decision—is that marriage does not automatically transfer the wife’s nationality.

A Filipino woman marrying a Japanese man remains Filipino but receives spousal residence in Japan. Their children are Japanese.

A Japanese woman marrying a Filipino man remains Japanese but receives residence in the Philippines. Their children are Filipino.

This prevents marriage from becoming an automatic naturalization mechanism. It also produces households containing two nationalities without creating dual-national children.

Widowhood, divorce, custody, and return migration then become politically sensitive. A Filipino widow in Japan may possess a right to return to the Philippines, while her Japanese children remain Japanese and cannot simply be reclassified as Filipino. The mandate would need family-unity residence rules to prevent nationality law from casually separating households.

That can be resolved without changing the descent rule:

- spouses receive durable residence with the husband’s country;
- widows retain residence while raising minor children;
- families may accompany a returning father even when the wife retains a different nationality;
- children remain attached to the father’s national state.

# Korea under the mandate

Koreans are not eligible to “return to Korea” as foreign nationals because Korea is not a separate state. They already live within their national country: Japan.

A Korean family in Tokyo can move to Keijō, but that is internal migration rather than repatriation.

This creates one of the deepest contradictions in Japan’s preservation doctrine.

Japan tells a foreign-raised Filipino:

> “You remain Filipino and must be allowed to return to the Philippines.”

It tells a Korean:

> “You are Japanese; Korea is one of Japan’s historic regions.”

The Korean preservation movement can therefore receive:

- Korean-language schools;
- heritage broadcasting;
- Hangul publishing;
- grants for archives and folk traditions;
- incentives for families to settle in northern or rural Korean districts;
- protection for churches and regional customs.

But it cannot receive recognition of Korean nationality without reopening the constitutional incorporation of the peninsula.

Japan’s answer is that cultural preservation does not require political separation. Critics answer that Japan protects every culture more readily when that culture possesses a foreign state.

The same problem applies, in different forms, to Formosan indigenous peoples and Micronesian island cultures. They may receive cultural protection as peoples within Japan. They do not receive national return to independent homelands that the imperial constitution does not recognize.

# Why Japan breaks the stalemate

This is precisely the kind of question for which Japan claims its reserve headship exists.

The principal associated states would divide.

Some would object that:

- Japan is dictating citizenship practice;
- states must control admission to their own territory;
- returnees may burden housing and employment systems;
- foreign-raised nationals could become politically disruptive;
- mixed families make paternal classification too crude.

Others would support it because:

- it protects ordinary people rather than corporations;
- it reinforces distinct national identities;
- it prevents expatriate populations from becoming stateless;
- it gives substantive meaning to the anti-assimilation doctrine;
- it requires Japan to finance part of the consequences of imperial labor movement.

Consensus fails.

Japan then determines that the mandate will take effect.

This is controversial, but it is also politically defensible in a way that an arbitrary military decree would not be. Tokyo can argue:

> The Sphere has insisted that nationality is permanent. It must therefore guarantee that permanent nationality has a home.

Some governments call this an overreach. Others call it the exact purpose of Japanese headship. Most eventually accept it because the mandate is narrow, rule-bound, and visibly benefits families.

The episode therefore strengthens and tests the reserve-power principle at the same time.

Japan’s authority survives because it does not say:

> “We may decide anything.”

It says:

> “When the common order reaches a contradiction that the members cannot resolve, Japan must give the final determination.”

# Revised canon formulation

> **Korea is an integral territory of the Japanese Empire. Koreans possess Japanese nationality and citizenship, not a separate Korean nationality. They may reside and work throughout Japan without immigration status. Korean identity survives as an ethnic, regional, familial, and cultural distinction inside the Japanese nation. Formosa, Karafuto, and the incorporated Micronesian territories follow the same governing principle, although their local cultures and degrees of assimilation differ.**

> **The Co-Prosperity Sphere otherwise rejects common citizenship and broad naturalization. Nationality is inherited rather than acquired by residence, and birth in a foreign member state does not confer local citizenship. In mixed-nationality marriages, children receive the father’s nationality. The legal order recognizes one nationality rather than dual or half-national status, even where mixed ancestry and cultural hybridity remain socially visible.**

> **In the early 1980s, Japan resolves a dispute among the principal associated states by issuing the National Home and Return Mandate. Every member state must admit citizens of its nationality who have been born or raised abroad and choose permanent return. A common fund assists transport, housing, credential conversion, education, and resettlement. The mandate does not naturalize foreigners; it makes inherited citizenship materially usable by guaranteeing access to the citizen’s national home.**

> **Returned citizens often remain culturally foreign. Each society develops its own vocabulary and arguments concerning them. In the Philippines, the returning foreign-raised Filipino is commonly understood as a form of balikbayan: legally Filipino, but expected to prove through language, conduct, and participation that he can become Filipino in culture as well.**

The central distinction is now sharper:

> **The Sphere protects separate nations outside Japan, but it protects regional cultures inside Japan. Korea’s tragedy is that it belongs to the second category.**

# The wartime territorial settlement

## Thailand rather than Siam

The formal name should probably remain **the Kingdom of Thailand**.

The wartime renaming from Siam to Thailand is validated by victory, territorial expansion, and the survival of the nationalist military establishment. “Siam” would remain common in older diplomatic language, royal circles, foreign journalism, and discussions of the wider historical kingdom. But official documents, maps, ministries, and treaties normally say Thailand.

This creates an intentional contradiction. Thailand presents itself as the national kingdom of the Thai people while ruling substantial Lao, Khmer, Malay, and other subject populations. Critics inside the Sphere can therefore argue that Thailand has become an empire in function while preserving the constitutional title of a kingdom.

## The Cambodian province is Battambang

The name you were trying to recall is almost certainly **Battambang**.

The historical 1941 settlement transferred all of Battambang and portions of Siem Reap, Stung Treng, and Pursat to Thailand. Thailand also acquired Lao territories including Sayaboury and Champasak. Angkor itself was excluded from the Thai acquisition. citeturn482775search1turn482775search14

For this setting, I would narrow that somewhat into a durable but manageable settlement:

- Thailand permanently retains **Battambang and the Sisophon corridor**.
- Thailand also keeps **Sayaboury** and perhaps limited west-bank Lao districts.
- **Angkor and the central Siem Reap region remain Cambodian**.
- Most of Stung Treng and Pursat remain with Cambodia.
- Laos retains enough of Champasak to remain territorially coherent.

That gives Cambodia one unmistakable national wound without reducing it to an obviously mutilated nonstate. It also avoids placing Angkor under Thai authority, which would turn the issue from a painful territorial dispute into the central question of Cambodian national existence.

Thailand administers Battambang as an ordinary Thai province, probably under a Thai form such as **Phra Tabong**. By the second generation, the territory contains Thai officials, settlers, schools, military families, and infrastructure that make simple retrocession increasingly difficult.

Cambodia never recognizes the arrangement emotionally, even after recognizing it legally.

# The three post-French states

Japan already created the outlines of the necessary political order during the historical March 1945 coup, when it displaced French authority and sponsored the Empire of Vietnam, the Kingdom of Kampuchea, and the Kingdom of Luang Prabang. In this timeline Japan wins, so those emergency governments become the foundations of enduring states rather than collapsing within months. citeturn372210search3

France does not return as sovereign. That is the decisive difference from real history.

French administrators, engineers, businessmen, teachers, missionaries, physicians, and plantation personnel may remain under contract or private residence. French law and language survive for a generation in courts, medicine, higher education, and commercial practice. But there is no restored French Union and therefore no First Indochina War against returning French rule.

The political question becomes how to replace French administration without destroying the administrative machinery the new states need.

# I. Vietnam: the dominant Indochinese state

Vietnam is the only one of the three with enough population, coastline, cities, agriculture, and educated personnel to become a substantial regional country.

It remains subordinate to Japan, but it is not as marginal as Cambodia or Laos.

The natural foundation is the **Empire of Vietnam under Bảo Đại**.

Bảo Đại gives Japan several advantages:

- dynastic continuity through the Nguyễn house;
- a Vietnamese head of state rather than a Japanese military administration;
- a court capable of reconciling northern, central, and southern elites;
- a noncommunist national symbol;

The monarchy probably becomes constitutional and administrative rather than strongly personal. Bảo Đại is useful as a sovereign and symbol, but the country is governed through ministers, provincial authorities, army officers, mandarinal families, commercial elites, and Japanese advisers.

The first government can retain **Trần Trọng Kim** and other figures associated with the 1945 independence government. Over time, younger nationalist, Catholic, Confucian, technocratic, military, and commercial factions replace the wartime generation.

Vietnam should not have one city that monopolizes every national function.

Huế is the **imperial and ceremonial capital**:

- national religious and historical ceremonies;
- classical scholarship;
- the symbolic continuity of the Vietnamese state.

### Hanoi

Hanoi is the **administrative and intellectual capital**:

- ministries and higher civil service;
- universities;
- northern military command;
- publishing;
- literary culture;
- scientific and technical institutions;
- national radio and later public television.

### Saigon

Saigon is the **commercial and popular-cultural capital**:

- banking;
- shipping;
- Japanese corporate offices;
- private publishing;
- advertising;
- film studios;
- popular music;
- commercial television;
- consumer imports.

So your Saigon instinct is correct, but it should be the principal **commercial film center**, not the country’s only media center.

A high-budget romantic drama, comedy, musical, or modern crime film is likely made in Saigon. A state historical epic may be produced through Huế court scholars and Hanoi public studios. Hanoi develops documentary, educational, literary, and prestige work. The three cities create competing ideas of what Vietnamese culture ought to be.

## Ho Chi Minh and the Viet Minh

Ho Chi Minh still exists and still matters. He founded the Viet Minh in 1941 and was positioned to lead a national revolution by 1945. citeturn372210search6turn372210search7

But the conditions that allowed him to win in real history are absent:

- Japan does not surrender.
- France does not return.
- Communist China never supplies a secure northern sanctuary.
- The Soviet Union collapses.
- Bảo Đại’s state possesses real independence in domestic law, even if strategically subordinate to Japan.
- Japan can deploy aircraft, communications, intelligence, and well-supplied local forces indefinitely.

Ho therefore remains the principal revolutionary opponent of the new Vietnamese order, but he cannot plausibly create a lasting rival state.

The best model is a serious **1945–early 1950s Viet Minh insurgency**, concentrated especially in the north and interior. Japan and the Vietnamese government answer it through four means:

1. targeted military operations against the communist command;
2. broad amnesty for ordinary nationalist and local Viet Minh adherents;
3. limited tenancy, debt, and village reforms to deny the communists their strongest grievances;
4. absorption of noncommunist nationalists into the monarchy and civil service.

Ho’s exact fate can remain open for now. He could die in a failed campaign, be captured and disappear into detention, or escape into the Chinese or Siberian frontier. What should not happen is an internationally recognized Ho government surviving into the later 1950s.

By 1960, “Viet Minh” has become the name of a defeated revolutionary generation, not the government of half the country.

## Economy

Vietnam receives more economic depth than Cambodia or Laos but not enough to become strategically independent.

It can develop:

- rice milling and export;
- rubber;
- coal and mineral extraction;
- textiles;
- food processing;
- fertilizer;
- ceramics;
- ship and railway repair;
- bicycles and motorcycles;
- simple machinery;
- consumer-goods assembly;
- later radio, television, appliance, and computer assembly.

It does not independently control:

- advanced aircraft production;
- major warship construction;
- high-end engines;
- strategic electronics;
- precision machine tools;
- nuclear technology;
- sophisticated weapons.

By the 1970s, a Vietnamese family may own a radio or television assembled in Saigon from Japanese components. The brand, internal design, standards, and most valuable parts remain Japanese. The housing, plastic casing, final assembly, packaging, advertising, and some software or programming may be Vietnamese.

Vietnam thus becomes an important **secondary manufacturing and cultural market**, but not another Manchukuo.

# II. Cambodia: the wounded monarchy

Cambodia is smaller, less industrial, and more dependent. But it has one major source of national coherence that Laos lacks: the Khmer monarchy and Angkorian inheritance.

## Sihanouk’s state

Norodom Sihanouk is already king when Japan removes French authority. Japanese planners historically worked with his monarchy while also cultivating the nationalist Son Ngoc Thanh, whose career was tied to both Thailand and Japan. citeturn482775search7turn372210search13

That gives Cambodia two major postwar currents:

- **Sihanoukian royal nationalism**, centered on the monarchy, Buddhism, territorial continuity, and gradual development;
- **Thanhite republican nationalism**, more militant, anti-French, anti-Thai, and suspicious that the court accepts too much Japanese direction.

Japan probably backs Sihanouk because the monarchy is the more stable institution. Son Ngoc Thanh and similar figures may receive ministries, parliamentary roles, or controlled opposition status, but they cannot be allowed to turn Battambang into a permanent call for war with Thailand.

Sihanouk need not follow his exact real-world career. Without the French independence struggle, he has less reason to abdicate in order to become an active party politician. He can remain an unusually political monarch, working through appointed ministries, royal councils, Buddhist institutions, provincial notables, and a limited elected chamber.

## The Battambang wound

Cambodian public life treats Battambang as:

- lost Khmer soil;
- proof that Thailand profited from Cambodia’s weakness;
- evidence that Japanese friendship has limits;
- a territory that may one day return, even when no government expects that soon.

The government is allowed to commemorate the loss but not organize armed irredentism.

School maps may show the international frontier clearly while using shaded historical maps that include Battambang within the Khmer world. Veterans’ associations, refugee families, Buddhist temples, and land claimants preserve the issue.

Thailand answers that the territory has passed repeatedly between Thai and Khmer authority and that the wartime settlement is final.

Japan’s position is blunt in practice:

> Cambodia may mourn Battambang. It may not threaten Thailand over it.

Japan refuses retrocession because Thailand is one of the principal associated powers and because reversing a victory settlement decades later would make every Sphere frontier provisional.

## Compensation rather than territory

Tokyo will attempt to compensate Cambodia materially.

Likely projects include:

- earlier development of **Kompong Som** as a Cambodian national port;
- road and rail links that do not depend entirely on Thailand or Vietnam;
- irrigation and flood-control projects;
- Angkor restoration and tourism;
- rice and rubber investment;
- Japanese scholarships;
- guaranteed access to Japanese and Singaporean markets;
- a Cambodian share in Mekong shipping.

This doesn’t erase the grievance. It makes continued membership more advantageous than confrontation.

## Cambodian internal problems

Cambodia’s mature difficulties are likely to be:

- rural indebtedness;
- court corruption;
- conflict between monarchy and republican nationalists;
- Khmer resentment of Vietnamese commercial and settler communities;
- Thai influence in the lost western districts;
- tension between Buddhist institutions and modern schooling;
- overreliance on Japanese tourism and commodity purchasing.

Japan handles these through royal patronage, limited agrarian reform, Buddhist cooperation, and controlled investment rather than mass political transformation.

Cambodia remains culturally coherent but economically fragile.

# III. Laos: the corridor monarchy

Laos is the weakest of the three states.

Its problem is not one overwhelming nationalist wound. Its problem is that it is difficult to govern as one country at all.

## The royal settlement

The Japanese-backed **Kingdom of Luang Prabang** should expand into a unified **Kingdom of Laos** after 1947.

King Sisavang Vong provides continuity, but unification requires bargains with:

- Vientiane;
- the southern house of Champasak;
- provincial governors;
- Buddhist monasteries;
- highland peoples;
- military commanders;
- Vietnamese and Chinese merchant communities.

Luang Prabang remains the royal and religious capital. Vientiane becomes the administrative capital because it is better placed for government, transport, and relations with Thailand and Vietnam.

This creates a dual-center system similar in form, though not scale, to Vietnam:

- **Luang Prabang:** crown, court, Buddhism, national ceremony;
- **Vientiane:** ministries, foreign missions, development boards, army headquarters.

## The principal Lao fear

Laos is squeezed between larger cultures.

Thailand can argue that Lao and Thai peoples belong to closely related civilizational and linguistic worlds. Vietnam has stronger administrative, commercial, and technical networks in parts of Laos. Japan supplies the outside money and security.

The Lao state therefore worries less about immediate conquest than about gradual disappearance.

Its governing doctrine emphasizes:

- the Lao monarchy;
- Theravada Buddhism;
- Lao-language schooling;
- territorial administration;
- separation from Thailand despite cultural relationship;
- limits on Vietnamese settlement and official employment.

The loss of Sayaboury reinforces this. Laos can point westward and say that excessive Thai influence has already cost it territory.

## Economy

Laos remains largely agrarian and rural.

Its principal activities are:

- timber;
- coffee and other highland crops;
- mining;
- hydropower;
- river transport;
- limited tourism;
- military and commercial transit;
- small-scale processing.

Its greatest strategic value is not what it manufactures but where it lies.

Laos connects Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia, China, and the wider Mekong basin. Roads, river ports, airfields, and later power lines turn it into a corridor state.

That makes infrastructure politically dangerous. Every railway or dam helps Laos materially while binding it more closely to a stronger neighbor or Japanese corporation.

## Internal conflict

Laos is unlikely to experience one enormous national civil war under these conditions. It is more likely to suffer repeated limited disorders:

- highland revolts;
- royal succession disputes;
- military coups or attempted coups;
- smuggling;
- border raiding;
- disputes among Luang Prabang, Vientiane, and Champasak elites;
- communist or republican remnants;
- localized resistance to taxes, road building, or resettlement.

Japan prevents regime collapse but has little interest in administering every mountain district directly.

Laos is stable on the map and uneven in practice.

# IV. The Indochinese caucus

The three states become more influential together, but they do not create an Indochinese federation.

The word **Indochina** itself gradually becomes controversial because it originated as a French colonial category. It remains useful in foreign and Japanese bureaucratic language, while the three governments prefer terms such as:

- the Three States;
- the Mekong States;
- the Indochinese Associated States;
- the Three Kingdoms Conference.

A working institutional name could be:

> **The Council of the Three Indochinese States**

Its membership is Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos. Japan attends as guarantor or chair on strategic questions but is not formally one of the three.

## What the council does

The council manages problems that cannot be solved nationally:

- Mekong navigation;
- rail and road connections;
- customs transit;
- public-health campaigns;
- river flooding;
- postal and telephone standards;
- university exchanges;
- extradition;
- broadcasting rights;
- refugee movements;
- Japanese development applications;
- joint petitions to the Sphere.

It does not possess:

- a common citizenship;
- a common army;
- an executive government;
- power to override national law;
- independent foreign policy.

Vietnam naturally tries to lead because it supplies most of the population, trained personnel, media, and commercial capacity.

Cambodia and Laos resist Vietnamese leadership because they remember French Indochina as a structure in which Vietnamese officials and workers often became the practical intermediaries of colonial authority.

Japan therefore supports the council but prevents Vietnam from controlling it. A rotating secretariat and unanimous decision rule would suit Tokyo: enough cooperation to simplify administration, not enough unity to produce a new regional power.

## Political weight

When the three act together, they can:

- demand additional consumer-industry licenses;
- request shared development funds;
- pressure Japanese broadcasters for more local programming;
- ask for greater representation on health, education, and cultural boards;
- complain about Thai trade or border practices;
- negotiate better commodity prices.

They cannot force Japan or Thailand to accept a major strategic reversal.

They are a caucus, not a directing power.

# V. Consumer life and Japanese companies

Your instinct that Japanese products dominate is correct.

By the 1960s and 1970s, an urban Vietnamese, Cambodian, or Lao household is likely to encounter Japanese brands through:

- radios;
- bicycles and motorcycles;
- sewing machines;
- fans;
- watches and clocks;
- cameras;
- kitchen goods;
- medicines;
- processed food;
- electrical appliances;
- televisions;
- recorded music;
- eventually home computers and game systems.

Chinese, Siamese, Filipino, and local products also circulate, especially food, textiles, household wares, and cheaper goods. But the high-prestige manufactured object is usually Japanese.

The crucial point is that “Japanese-made” may eventually include local assembly.

A television sold under a Japanese brand in Saigon might contain components from Japan and Formosa, be assembled in Vietnam, packaged by a Vietnamese contractor, and sold through a local department store. A radio sold in Phnom Penh may be imported complete. Laos may import almost everything except the cabinet or basic repairs.

This produces three different consumer experiences:

- **Vietnam:** growing assembly and local distribution;
- **Cambodia:** import market with some food, rubber, and textile processing;
- **Laos:** small market dependent upon Thai, Vietnamese, and Japanese routes.

# VI. Media and cultural dependence

Japanese media dominates because it possesses the money, studios, equipment, actors, animation houses, music companies, and distribution system required for expensive production.

But the three states aren’t culturally erased.

## Vietnam

Vietnam develops the only substantial local commercial media system of the three.

It produces:

- films;
- popular songs;
- historical dramas;
- theatre;
- radio serials;
- television news;
- literary adaptations;
- court and martial epics.

Vietnamese productions can circulate into Cambodia, Laos, southern China, and expatriate communities elsewhere in the Sphere.

Japanese films and television remain technically superior and better funded. Chinese historical media provides another major competitor.

## Cambodia

Cambodian media emphasizes:

- Angkorian history;
- court drama;
- Buddhist stories;
- dance;
- royal ceremonies;
- border memory;
- rural morality.

Its industry is smaller and often depends upon Japanese equipment or Vietnamese technical crews.

## Laos

Laos produces the least expensive screen media and relies most heavily on:

- radio;
- religious broadcasting;
- court ceremonies;
- music;
- regional news;
- Japanese, Thai, and Vietnamese imports.

Dubbing becomes central to all three cultures. Japanese stories are not simply shown unchanged; they are translated, renamed, localized, and interpreted through local moral expectations.

By the 1980s, a Cambodian child may grow up watching Japanese animation in Khmer, Vietnamese historical drama, Thai music programs, and locally produced Buddhist holiday broadcasts.

# VII. Language

Domestic government uses the national language:

- Vietnamese in Vietnam;
- Khmer in Cambodia;
- Lao in Laos.

Japanese is required for:

- senior corporate work;
- technical scholarships;
- military liaison;
- inter-Sphere diplomacy;
- advanced imported machinery;
- some university subjects.

French declines slowly.

It remains useful among older elites, Catholics, physicians, lawyers, architects, and families with colonial education. But it ceases to be the language of power because France no longer rules and because ambitious young men increasingly need Japanese.

By 1980, French is a prestige and historical language. Japanese is the practical imperial language.

# Development over time

## 1945–1950: separation and emergency rule

Japan removes French sovereignty and recognizes Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos separately.

Local monarchies and officials inherit administrations designed for one federation. Customs, railways, police, courts, and finances must be divided while war and insurgency continue.

Thailand’s territorial gains are confirmed.

## 1950–1960: pacification and national consolidation

Vietnam defeats the principal Viet Minh insurgency.

Cambodia stabilizes around Sihanouk but preserves the Battambang grievance.

Laos unifies through a royal-federal compromise rather than through strong central administration.

The Council of the Three States begins as a technical conference.

## 1960–1970: consumer integration

Japanese goods spread rapidly through the cities.

Vietnam develops light industry and a meaningful domestic media sector. Cambodia receives ports, roads, tourism, and commodity investment. Laos becomes a transport and power corridor.

The political regimes become less visibly provisional.

## 1970–1980: developmental dissatisfaction

The first postwar generation asks why the three states still import almost every high-value manufactured good.

Vietnam demands more manufacturing licenses. Cambodia demands better commodity prices and continued Japanese compensation for its territorial losses. Laos demands control over its dams, roads, and concessions.

Japan concedes local assembly, management positions, and cultural funding without giving up strategic technology.

## 1980–1985: cultural guardianship

Japan’s preservation doctrine encourages:

- local-language broadcasting;
- script and archive programs;
- national historical productions;
- traditional music and religious programming;
- local software interfaces;
- scholarships for cultural institutions.

The Home and Return Mandate also affects Indochinese diaspora families. A Vietnamese, Cambodian, or Lao citizen raised elsewhere in the Sphere can return under assisted settlement even when he speaks the national language poorly.

This strengthens national cultures without making the states strategically independent.

# Working conclusion

The mature Indochinese order should be:

> **Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos become separate Japanese-protected states after the destruction of French sovereignty. Vietnam retains the Nguyễn monarchy and becomes the region’s dominant demographic, commercial, and cultural state. Cambodia stabilizes beneath Sihanouk but carries a permanent grievance over Thailand’s annexation of Battambang and the western border districts. Laos survives as a weak dual-capital monarchy connecting Luang Prabang’s royal-religious authority with Vientiane’s administrative government.**

> **The three cooperate through a Council of the Indochinese States governing transport, river development, health, customs transit, and common petitions. Japan supports the council but prevents it from becoming a federation under Vietnamese leadership.**

> **Their economies remain principally agricultural, extractive, commercial, and light-industrial. Japan supplies most high-value consumer goods, advanced machinery, electronics, vehicles, and computers. Vietnam develops local assembly and a serious media industry; Cambodia and Laos remain more dependent upon imported Japanese, Vietnamese, Chinese, and Thai content.**

> **Their bargain is straightforward: Japan limits their foreign and strategic independence but protects them from conquest, internal collapse, and each other. They possess enough national culture and domestic government to regard themselves as real countries, but not enough military or industrial power to redirect the Co-Prosperity Sphere.**

The defining Indochinese image would be three trains arriving at the same Japanese-built junction: one bearing the Vietnamese imperial crest, one the Cambodian royal arms, and one the Lao elephant—different flags, different citizens, and the same Japanese signals controlling the track.
