The first correction is structural. The older British-side treatment compressed the Delhi-centered Congress successor and “Hindustan” into one state. That shorthand should now be superseded. Azad Hind faces **two rival all-Indian projects** in the north-central theater: a Congress state claiming the constitutional inheritance of India and a Hindu-nationalist Hindustan claiming Delhi and the civilizational core. fileciteturn38file0 fileciteturn37file9

The Indian Wars consequently look very different from Calcutta than they do from London.

> Britain sees the disintegration of a former imperial territory.  
> Azad Hind sees one unfinished war for Delhi.

# What historical Azad Hind gives us

Historical Azad Hind was already more than a military unit attached to Japan. The Provisional Government of Free India had a small cabinet, with Bose simultaneously serving as head of state, prime minister, and minister for war and foreign affairs. It incorporated representatives of the Indian National Army and civilian advisers drawn from the Indian Independence League’s networks across Japanese-controlled Asia. citeturn173198view0turn173198view3

It also possessed the beginnings of institutions that could mature into a real state:

- the INA as a prospective national army;
- the **Azad Hind Dal**, trained to administer liberated territory;
- the Azad Hind Bank;
- propaganda, supply, finance, and external political departments;
- the Rani of Jhansi Regiment and associated women’s organizations.

The Rani of Jhansi Regiment was intended partly for medical and support work, but Bose understood its armed public image as a major statement about the revolutionary character of the movement. citeturn173198view1turn173198view2

That means the alternate state is not created from nothing in 1948. It is an exile government, army, financial network, and diaspora movement that finally reaches Indian territory.

## The permanent provisional government

The formal state should remain the **Provisional Government of Free India**, or *Arzi Hukumat-e-Azad Hind*, long after it controls Calcutta.

That apparent oddity becomes central to its identity.

Calcutta is the:

- administrative capital;
- actual seat of government;
- main port;
- principal arsenal;
- headquarters of the National Army;
- center of Japanese diplomatic and military support.

Delhi remains the **lawful national capital**.

Azad Hind refuses to promulgate a final constitution because doing so would imply that its eastern territory is the completed country. A constituent assembly is repeatedly promised for the period after national liberation and repeatedly postponed because Delhi has not been recovered.

This creates a state that is stable in practice but permanently revolutionary in theory.

Its official maps show India as one country. Ceasefire lines are marked as military lines, not international borders. The Colombo agreements are called armistices rather than peace treaties. Calcutta is described as the temporary seat from which the nation continues its march toward Delhi.

> **The war can stop. The provisional condition cannot.**

# Bose’s political system

Azad Hind should not be a Japanese copy, a communist state, or a liberal parliamentary republic.

Its strongest model is a **national-revolutionary planning state**.

Bose had already argued for a strong central government combined with substantial cultural and governmental autonomy for minorities and provinces. That combination fits the setting unusually well: authority at the center, pluralism beneath it, and no willingness to permit religion or province to overturn national unity. citeturn865775search3

The mature system therefore rests on four principles.

## One Indian political nation

Azad Hind formally rejects a Hindu state, a Muslim state, a Bengali state, and a Japanese client identity.

Its citizens are Indians first.

This is not liberal individualism. It is disciplined civic nationalism. Religious, linguistic, caste, and provincial identities may be protected, but they are not permitted to become rival sovereignties.

The military is the model institution because it can point to Hindu, Muslim, Sikh, Christian, Bengali, Tamil, Punjabi, and other officers serving beneath one command.

Caste discrimination is formally excluded from military and central government service. Communal political organizations are watched closely whenever they appear capable of dividing the army or state.

The gap between formal doctrine and ordinary society remains substantial, particularly in villages and religiously divided districts. But the official position is unambiguous.

## A concentrated executive

Bose initially holds extraordinary authority because the state is still at war.

He presides over:

- the Council of Ministers;
- the National Army;
- foreign relations;
- national planning;
- wartime appointments;
- provincial military administrations.

There may be consultative assemblies, provincial delegations, professional chambers, and Indian Independence League congresses. None can remove the government during the national emergency.

This does not have to mean that Bose intends permanent personal dictatorship. It means every argument for constitutional normalization can be answered with the same question:

> “Has Delhi been liberated?”

Until the answer is yes, emergency government continues.

## National planning without communism

Azad Hind favors:

- large infrastructure;
- state-directed industrialization;
- national arsenals;
- railway development;
- economic planning;
- controls on strategic trade;
- military-industrial coordination.

Private property and Indian commercial houses continue, but strategic investment is directed toward national objectives.

Japanese firms receive important concessions and supply much of the advanced machinery. They do not formally own the Azad Hind state, and Bose resists becoming another associated resource client. That creates a persistent disagreement with Japan even while the alliance remains close.

## The army as the founding estate

The original INA becomes an elite institutional caste inside the much larger **Azad Hind National Army**.

By 1955, most soldiers did not serve in the wartime INA. The force has expanded through:

- local recruitment;
- former British Indian Army personnel;
- regional militias;
- Bengali and Assamese formations;
- officers trained by Japan;
- volunteers from Indian communities elsewhere in Asia.

But original INA service remains prestigious. Wartime officers dominate the senior command, veterans receive preferential public employment, and the state’s founding story is military rather than electoral.

The Indian Independence League evolves into the state’s external political, diaspora, fundraising, and commercial network. The Azad Hind Bank becomes either the central bank outright or the institutional ancestor of one.

The Rani of Jhansi organization survives as a women’s military and national-service institution, especially in medicine, communications, logistics, civil defense, and officer training. It does not necessarily produce universal female combat service, but it gives the state a conspicuous female patriotic tradition absent in most neighboring regimes.

# Calcutta and Delhi

Delhi’s status should be even more politically important than the Bonn–Berlin comparison.

Bonn was a temporary capital accepted by a state that could function without constantly fighting toward Berlin. Azad Hind continues defining itself by the march toward Delhi.

**Calcutta is where the government works. Delhi is why the government exists.**

The national slogan *Chalo Delhi* therefore survives after the state acquires territory. It appears on:

- military monuments;
- currency;
- school walls;
- veterans’ halls;
- railway stations;
- annual national ceremonies;
- the seals of the provisional government.

Every government building in Calcutta is implicitly temporary, even after standing for fifty years.

That affects architecture as well. Calcutta receives monumental ministries and parade avenues, but the state avoids describing them as the final national capitol. The great permanent parliamentary complex is always supposed to be built in Delhi after victory.

# Azad Hind’s eastern consolidation, 1948–1952

The existing canon places Azad Hind around Calcutta, Bengal, Orissa, and the corridors toward Assam and Burma. fileciteturn37file9 The new material makes that position more coherent if Azad Hind’s first war is not westward conquest but **eastern consolidation**.

It has three immediate problems.

## Eastern Bengal

The Bengali Muslim population around Dacca cannot simply be treated as a conquered provincial population.

The most plausible settlement is an **autonomous East Bengal administration within the Azad Hind defense and political system**.

Dacca receives:

- a locally elected or corporative government;
- Bengali as its principal public language;
- Muslim religious and family-law protections;
- its own police and territorial formations;
- control over ordinary land and education policy.

Calcutta retains:

- foreign affairs;
- heavy military command;
- interstate rail and river transport;
- currency;
- national planning;
- final constitutional authority.

This does not eliminate Bengali Muslim separatism. It gives those who fear Hindu domination a reason to choose Bose’s officially noncommunal state over Hindustan or a collapsing independent Dacca regime.

The later word **Bangladesh** can emerge as the cultural and common name of this eastern constituent territory, even while Azad Hind insists that it remains part of Free India.

## Assam

Azad Hind can secure the Assam corridor without uniformly governing every hill people.

Its practical control follows:

- railways;
- river routes;
- tea districts;
- oil fields;
- larger towns;
- military roads;
- airfields.

Hill districts retain local chiefs, councils, or emergency administrations. Some remain insurgent.

Armor is useful in the valleys and along improved roads. It cannot solve upland resistance. The state controls the corridor more completely than it controls the country through which the corridor passes.

## Orissa and the western approaches

Orissa is easier to integrate politically but remains economically poor and administratively uneven. Its ports, mines, workshops, and road routes become essential to the Azad Hind war economy.

By 1952, Calcutta has secured a workable territorial system:

> Bengal supplies population and administration; Orissa supplies depth and resources; Assam supplies the eastern corridor; Japan supplies the modern war matériel.

# The northern Indian claimants

The cleanest map contains **four major political traditions**, plus the surviving communist state and the regional powers outside the central contest.

| State | Working political center | Governing claim |
|---|---|---|
| **Azad Hind** | Calcutta; Delhi claimed | Armed national liberation and revolutionary unity |
| **Congress India** | Allahabad or Lucknow | Constitutional, secular continuity of the Indian national movement |
| **Hindustan** | Delhi | Hindu national state and control of the civilizational capital |
| **Princely systems** | Rajputana, Hyderabad, central courts | Dynastic legitimacy, local order, and resistance to mass revolutionary states |
| **Telangana People’s Republic** | Telangana interior | Agrarian communist revolution |

The Congress–Hindustan split should explicitly supersede the earlier fused “Indian Union/Hindustan” model.

## Congress India

The Congress state is formally likely to call itself the **Republic or Union of India**. “Congress India” is the name foreigners and rivals use to distinguish it from the other claimants.

It inherits:

- much of the Congress political organization;
- portions of the old civil service;
- railway and legal administrators;
- provincial politicians;
- sections of the British-trained army;
- the strongest international claim to constitutional continuity.

Jawaharlal Nehru makes much more sense as its executive leader than Gandhi. Historically, Gandhi exerted decisive moral influence within Congress and favored Nehru for national leadership, but Gandhi himself was not suited to operating a militarized emergency government. Congress also remained politically distinct from the Communist Party, despite Nehru’s planning and socialist sympathies. citeturn400091search1turn400091search3

Gandhi’s best role is as:

- moral father of Congress India;
- itinerant peace advocate;
- critic of militarization and communal reprisals;
- a man whom the government invokes and frequently ignores.

His precise survival or assassination can remain open. Either route creates a useful problem. A living Gandhi embarrasses the war government. A dead Gandhi becomes its nearly uncontestable martyr.

Congress India is secular and constitutional in theory, but war forces it toward:

- emergency decrees;
- military governors;
- requisition;
- censorship;
- postponement of elections;
- deals with local commanders.

It considers Azad Hind courageous but illegitimate: an Indian nationalist movement that permitted Japanese power to determine the route to independence.

## Hindustan

Hindustan should be a separate Hindu-majoritarian national state centered upon Delhi and the western Hindi-speaking belt.

Its political ancestry comes from some combination of:

- the Hindu Mahasabha;
- RSS networks;
- military officers;
- refugee organizations;
- conservative urban elites;
- princes seeking protection against Congress and communism.

Syama Prasad Mookerjee is a plausible early civilian leader or constitutional architect. Historically, he represented a distinct Hindu nationalist and strong-central-state current rather than Congress continuity. citeturn259933view4

Hindustan’s possession of Delhi creates the sharpest Azad Hind grievance.

From Calcutta’s perspective, Delhi is occupied not by a foreign European power but by a sectarian Indian government that has reduced India to a Hindu nation. Azad Hind regards this as a betrayal of the multireligious army and political nation for which Bose claims to fight.

Hindustan in turn depicts Bose’s system as a Japanese-supported military state using abstract national unity to conceal Bengali and foreign domination.

## The princely systems

These should remain plural rather than becoming one coherent state.

The major components include:

- Rajputana leagues;
- a reduced Hyderabad;
- central Indian princely federations;
- smaller neutral courts;
- fortified dynastic territories.

Some are traditional monarchies. Others are military governments operating under a prince’s name. Their armies use whatever weapons can be bought.

They survive because the mass claimant states are often too exhausted to conquer them and because the princes can bargain with Britain, Germany, Japan, and neighboring Indian governments.

## The communist state

Communism should not be assigned to Congress India.

The strongest independent communist state is a **Telangana People’s Republic** or wider **People’s Republic of the Deccan**.

The historical Telangana armed rebellion began in 1946 and continued into the early 1950s under Communist Party leadership. In the alternate collapse of central authority, it has a far better opportunity to seize and retain territory rather than being suppressed by a consolidated Indian government. citeturn496995search0turn496995search6

It survives because it possesses:

- an agrarian base;
- committed cadres;
- armed village organizations;
- difficult territory;
- access to the black arms market;
- enemies too divided to concentrate against it.

It is one of the last openly communist states in the wider world, but it has no Moscow capable of sustaining it. Its communism consequently becomes more agrarian, militarized, locally self-reliant, and doctrinally defensive.

It fights Hyderabad, Congress India, local landholders, and sometimes other communist factions. It is not Azad Hind’s principal opponent because geography keeps their main armies apart.

# Azad Hind’s armored advantage

The armor does not make Azad Hind invincible. It gives it something most Indian successors initially lack: **a coherent armored system rather than a collection of individual tanks**.

The characteristic early fleet contains:

- Type 3 Chi-Nu medium tanks as older support and second-line vehicles;
- Type 4 Chi-To tanks as the principal modern medium;
- Type 5 Chi-Ri tanks in small numbers as heavy-medium, command, and breakthrough vehicles.

The established land reference fixes the Chi-To and Chi-Ri as Japanese 75 mm vehicles, with the Chi-Ri notably heavier and always more limited. fileciteturn38file1

Some of the transferred vehicles are veterans of the Eastern Siberian campaigns. Their Japanese tactical marks are painted over but not always completely removed. Azad Hind regiments preserve small Siberian badges or plaques as battle honors.

These tanks become known informally as the **Siberians**.

## Scale

A reasonable high-water working estimate is **roughly 120–180 serviceable tanks** in the main Azad Hind army by 1954–55.

That might support:

- two small armored brigades or groups;
- several independent armored battalions;
- training, reserve, and replacement pools.

The number matters less than the relationship.

Azad Hind can concentrate fifty or sixty functioning tanks at a chosen point. Many rivals may own comparable numbers on paper but cannot bring them together with fuel, ammunition, radios, recovery vehicles, trained crews, and infantry support.

## What the tanks permit

In Assam, they secure roads, railheads, oil districts, and towns.

Across Bihar and the Ganges Plain, they permit:

- breakthrough of militia positions;
- rapid seizure of railway junctions;
- overrunning lightly armed infantry;
- exploitation before defenders can rebuild a front;
- mobile support for Japanese-trained infantry.

The Chi-Ri is especially intimidating in a theater where many enemy units possess no reliable antitank gun beyond mines, field artillery, or improvised close assault.

## What they require

The armored advantage depends upon:

- Japanese 75 mm ammunition;
- specialized spares;
- diesel and lubricants;
- rail transport;
- bridges and ferries;
- recovery vehicles;
- Japanese-trained mechanics;
- functioning radios;
- a steady flow of artillery ammunition supporting the tanks.

The fleet is coherent, which makes it powerful.

It is also coherent around a foreign supply chain, which makes it brittle.

# The 1952–1956 Ganges campaigns

The existing timeline already identifies 1952–56 as the proxy high tide of the Indian Wars. fileciteturn36file2 From Azad Hind’s perspective, this is the **Delhi Campaign**, even though the army never reaches Delhi.

## 1952: the armies finally meet

Until 1952, Azad Hind and Congress India are primarily consolidating their own territories.

Azad Hind pacifies or bargains with:

- eastern Bengal;
- Assamese districts;
- Orissan authorities;
- communist cells;
- local militias;
- former British units.

Congress India is doing much the same in the middle Ganges basin.

Once their rear areas become sufficiently stable, they encounter one another as organized states rather than irregular coalitions.

## 1953–1954: Japanese matériel decides the tempo

Azad Hind possesses the better integrated army.

Japanese support supplies:

- tank and artillery ammunition;
- radios;
- trucks;
- engineers;
- aircraft parts;
- medical equipment;
- advisers;
- replacement weapons.

Congress India possesses larger local manpower and parts of the inherited Indian administrative system, but its army remains materially mixed.

Azad Hind pushes west through Bihar and along the Ganges routes. Its offensives are not effortless, but Congress repeatedly has to abandon positions before armored penetration or encirclement.

By 1954, foreign observers begin treating Azad Hind as the likely northern victor.

## 1955: the high-water mark

Azad Hind approaches the central Ganges position and threatens the Congress wartime capital around Allahabad or Lucknow.

Its propaganda claims that the next campaign will open the road to Delhi.

Then the Burmese Federal Crisis breaks the supply route.

# The Burma–Assam lifeline

The supply system is better understood as the **Burma–Assam corridor** rather than only the historical Burma Road.

Japanese matériel travels through a connected system:

> Japanese and imperial ports → Rangoon or Moulmein → Burmese rail and road depots → western Burma and the Chindwin crossings → Imphal/Assam routes → Bengal railways → the Azad Hind front.

A direct maritime route into Calcutta remains possible. It is less attractive because of:

- hostile submarines and naval raiders;
- mines;
- the vulnerability of the Bay of Bengal route;
- damaged or congested port facilities;
- the difficulty of protecting a regular high-volume ammunition service;
- the greater cost compared with a secure inland system.

The inland route had been selected because it was predictable.

When Burma fragments, predictability disappears.

The crisis does not cause Japanese officers to confiscate Azad Hind equipment and hand it to Burma. It breaks the road, rail, depot, and convoy network through which consumable war matériel reaches India.

Some shipments continue during 1955. Others sit in Burmese depots, are diverted around fighting, seized by local forces, or simply cannot move.

The effect takes months to reach the front.

That delay explains why Azad Hind continues winning for much of 1955.

# The ammunition crisis of 1956

By early 1956, the shortage reaches the battlefield.

The problem appears in a sequence.

First, artillery fire is rationed.

Then tank crews are issued fewer high-explosive rounds.

Then infantry units receive reduced machine-gun and mortar allocations.

Finally, formations begin drawing down the defensive caches near Bengal that were never intended to sustain an offensive hundreds of kilometers farther west.

The Japanese advisers are not calm observers. Many have spent years building this army and believe it is within one campaigning season of breaking Congress India.

They understand that replacement tanks arriving without shells are almost irrelevant.

## The final offensive

Azad Hind nevertheless attacks.

Politically, retreating without one last attempt is unacceptable. Bose’s government has already announced the approach to Delhi. Congress appears weakened. Commanders believe one concentrated blow might destroy it before the ammunition account becomes decisive.

The offensive is tactically unsound for exactly that reason.

Artillery preparation is too short. Tanks are required to advance while conserving rounds. Infantry cannot maintain suppressive fire. Units that seize positions cannot repel repeated counterattacks. Broken vehicles are abandoned because recovery fuel and spare parts are also scarce.

The Azad Hind army may achieve an initial penetration. It cannot exploit it.

Congress India counterattacks with shorter supply lines, locally available British-pattern ammunition, and increasing quantities of Russian-derived equipment.

Azad Hind falls back toward older positions where prepared depots still contain ammunition—probably eastern Bihar, the Chota Nagpur approaches, and ultimately the stronger defensive system protecting Bengal and Calcutta.

It is not destroyed.

It loses the war of movement.

## The two national interpretations

Azad Hind teaches:

> “Congress did not defeat us. Burma emptied our guns.”

Congress India teaches:

> “A foreign-supplied army collapsed when its foreign supply stopped.”

Both explanations contain truth.

A powerful Azad Hind phrase might be:

> **“Delhi was lost at Rangoon.”**

That sentence becomes the foundation of its permanent hostility toward Burma.

# The Indian arms market

Congress India, Hindustan, the princely states, and the communist territories do not begin with one coherent weapons system.

They inherit and purchase mixtures of:

- old British equipment;
- abandoned colonial depots;
- Russian and Soviet vehicles;
- American commercial weapons;
- captured Japanese matériel;
- local copies;
- weapons sold by private brokers.

A single brigade may operate four or five equipment families.

That is tactically inefficient. It requires different:

- ammunition;
- engines;
- tracks;
- radios;
- lubricants;
- tools;
- training manuals.

But it has one strategic advantage over Azad Hind: there is no single pipeline whose interruption silences the whole army.

Small arms and ammunition can move through mountain and caravan routes. Tanks and heavy artillery require railways, roads, river transport, or maritime shipment. They arrive through combinations of Central Asian successor states, Afghanistan, Persia, the Indus system, captured British ports, and private shipping.

Arms brokers become some of the richest men in the Indian Wars. They sell not merely weapons but complete logistical packages—when they possess them. More often they sell twenty tanks and enough spare parts to keep twelve running.

## Why Russian armor becomes dominant

Russian equipment has several advantages in this environment:

- large surviving wartime stocks;
- many desperate successor states willing to sell;
- rugged diesel vehicles;
- relatively simple repair requirements;
- large pools of displaced mechanics and former soldiers;
- prices lower than current Japanese or German systems.

T-34/85s become especially common. SU-series assault guns and tank destroyers appear in smaller quantities. Heavy tanks exist as prestige assets but are difficult to move and sustain.

This gives the Indian Wars a visual military identity different from the political alignments.

A Congress unit may be politically anti-communist and still fight in Russian tanks. A prince may receive British rifles, Russian artillery, German radios, and Japanese trucks from the same broker.

Equipment origin does not reliably indicate political loyalty.

# Who develops the Indian T-55 equivalent?

The strongest choice is **Congress India**.

Not because it is communist or pro-Russian. It is neither. It develops the vehicle because it is the state most traumatized by Japanese armored superiority and most capable of combining the inherited Indian administrative system with a national industrial program.

Congress India possesses several advantages:

- surviving ordnance officials;
- railway workshops;
- a large recruitment base;
- planning institutions;
- captured and purchased Russian tanks;
- access to Russian manuals, parts, engineers, and manufacturing knowledge;
- a political need to prove that it can defend India without Britain or Japan.

The real T-54/T-55 family represented the first mature postwar Soviet tank generation, combining a comparatively compact vehicle with a powerful gun, diesel mobility, and mass producibility. citeturn671782search10 The alternate Indian vehicle should occupy that role without being a literal copied T-55.

## The Congress universal tank

A plausible early-1960s Congress design would have:

- a combat weight around 36–39 tonnes;
- a four-man crew;
- a 100 mm rifled gun;
- a low turret and hull;
- a compact diesel;
- torsion-bar suspension;
- relatively simple optical fire control;
- armor sufficient against common wartime guns;
- emphasis on production and repair rather than electronic sophistication.

Its ancestry would be visible in the T-34 and scattered T-44/T-54 developmental knowledge, but the final vehicle would be Indian.

The formal name should be left open. A working service title such as **National Tank Model 62** and a patriotic name such as **Vijaya** would both be plausible, but this need not be fixed yet.

It becomes the characteristic armored vehicle of the Congress state during the 1960s and later spreads through:

- export;
- capture;
- licensed copies;
- black-market parts;
- successor designs in Hindustan and other Indian states.

Hindustan may eventually develop a simpler rival or local modification. Telangana keeps older Russian-derived vehicles running but lacks the industrial scale to originate the principal postwar tank.

This gives the T-55 concept a recognizable but transformed history:

> It is not the universal tank of a surviving Soviet Union. It is the tank with which Congress India proves that it survived Azad Hind.

# Azad Hind after the defeat

The 1956 reversal permanently changes the state.

Its first conclusion is not that armored warfare failed. Its conclusion is that **foreign ammunition dependency failed**.

The government establishes an emergency industrial program for:

- rifle and machine-gun cartridges;
- mortar bombs;
- artillery shells;
- tank ammunition;
- propellant;
- primers;
- shell casings;
- spare barrels;
- tracks and engine parts.

The initial goal is not to manufacture an entire modern Japanese tank. It is to ensure that an existing tank can continue firing after the Burma route closes.

Japan eventually tolerates and assists part of this program. Japanese military advisers were themselves humiliated by the 1956 shortage, and a reliable allied arsenal is strategically useful. Japanese companies still retain control over newer vehicles, advanced optics, engines, and designs.

Azad Hind consequently becomes less materially dependent without becoming industrially equal to Japan.

## The political consequence

The defeat strengthens rather than weakens the permanent provisional government.

Bose and his successors can argue:

- national unity remains incomplete;
- Congress and Hindustan still occupy Indian territory;
- Delhi remains unliberated;
- the armistice is not peace;
- demobilization would surrender the national mission.

The army remains central. Elections or consultative institutions may widen, but the founding executive order survives.

The state’s national calendar contains three foundational moments:

1. the proclamation of Azad Hind in 1943;
2. the entry of the government into Calcutta;
3. the interrupted Delhi campaign of 1956.

The third is commemorated not as simple defeat but as the year India was denied reunification by Burmese disorder.

# Working canon

> **Azad Hind develops from the historical Provisional Government of Free India, the INA, the Indian Independence League, the Azad Hind Dal, the Azad Hind Bank, and the Rani of Jhansi organization. It enters India as an already existing revolutionary government rather than being invented by Japan after the Breaking of the Raj.**

> **Calcutta becomes its permanent administrative capital, but Delhi remains the lawful and promised national capital. Azad Hind refuses to promulgate a final constitutional settlement while Delhi remains outside its control, producing a stable state that continues formally to describe itself as provisional.**

> **Bose’s state is pan-Indian, secular in national law, militarized, centrally planned, and culturally federal beneath a strong executive. It rejects Hindu, Muslim, Bengali, communist, and princely claims to divide the Indian political nation.**

> **The Congress successor and Hindustan are separate states. Congress India is a Nehru-led secular constitutional claimant centered in the middle Ganges system. Hindustan is a Delhi-centered Hindu-majoritarian state. The Telangana People’s Republic becomes the strongest surviving communist territorial state, while Rajputana, Hyderabad, and other princely systems remain separate.**

> **Azad Hind’s early military superiority depends upon a coherent Japanese supply system and a concentrated armored force built around Chi-Nu, Chi-To, and limited Chi-Ri tanks, including veterans of the Eastern Siberian campaigns. The system is more effective than the mixed arsenals of its rivals while supplies flow.**

> **The Burmese Federal Crisis of 1955 breaks the Burma–Assam ammunition corridor. Azad Hind continues advancing until accumulated stocks run down in 1956, launches an ill-advised final offensive, and is driven back toward its eastern depots by Congress India. The state blames Burma rather than accusing Japan of deliberate betrayal.**

> **Congress India later develops the first major indigenous postwar Indian universal tank from Russian-derived equipment, captured technical knowledge, and its own ordnance institutions. This vehicle occupies the historical technological position of the T-55 while possessing an Indian national origin.**

From Azad Hind’s perspective, the Indian Wars are not the story of an empire collapsing into many countries.

They are the story of a national army that came out of exile, reached Indian soil, came close enough to imagine Delhi—and then heard its guns fall silent because the road behind it had disappeared.

This is the point where in which the Indian successor, North Indian successor states finally start investing significantly into their economy beyond the mere military perspective. Because at this point, all of the different powers do not expect that they're going to win the war soon. Instead, it's an expectation that they're going to have to fight for a very long time. And so food production, mineral production, everything is made with the expectation that a war will kick off any day now, but these things are necessary. They can't run with austerity forever. This also creates a very kind of unique culture in North India that ironically all four or five, if you want to count the princely states, cultures kind of converge on. And that is the concept of a militarized civilian populace. Gun ownership among civilians is basically expected. It's almost a Switzerland kind of legal expectation. It's not always a legal expectation, but many of these states agree on the concept and kind of enforce a conscription policy and the general armament of their populations. Because the concern is if we don't have an armed population and the other, and an enemy power comes into our region, they bypass the military or something, we don't have a guerrilla force to fight them. This ends up being vindicated during parts of the latter part of the war, where guerrilla forces were actually part of the reason that one or another nation state didn't fully push through a region. Ultimately though, it more interestingly creates a system where a lot of civilian goods are dual purpose. They have a civilian purpose and a military purpose. If there is a radio produced locally, for example, in Congress India or Hindustan, it is also the same radio that is used by the military, if used for civilian purposes, but it has the means to be used for military purposes due to range or power settings, etc. Firearms are also part of Northern Indian culture very rapidly, as the expectation is any day now you're going to be called up to serve as we fight the various neighbors. It also creates a very paranoid locally diplomatic society. Every single one of the states thinks the other states are out to get them. And even if that isn't actually the case, which it is, authorly, it doesn't make the politics any easier. Diplomacy between Northern Indian states is effectively killed by the second Northern Indian War. And all of the conflicts that precede or succeed that just further cement the North Indian impression that war is inevitable and that everyone else is out to get them. It is a pretty exhausting and kind of dystopic approach, and the setting doesn't really shy away from that. North India is genuinely, by most modern sense, and even in setting senses, a dystopia. The government is very much overbearing. The concern about dying in battle is something that everybody kind of expects is probably going to happen. The threat of treason genuinely causes effectively witch hunts. If someone is accused of being a communist, that could be something that is treated as a death sentence in some states. So too if someone says that they are a fascist or something else. Any kind of contradiction with whatever the direction of the established government is can be treated as a treasonous directive, which very much routinely leads to political executions and repression on a level that is really only capable in a militarized society. But it keeps going because it genuinely is a threat. There is the understanding that the neighbor powers, if they sense any weakness, will come in and invade. Interestingly though, most of the powers do kind of, they do genuinely try to exploit each other's weaknesses, but none of them are actually capable of taking out the other powers. Azad Hind never comes close to its high watermark in 1955, 1956. It never has enough power to finally overwhelm the defenses that have been built up. And ultimately, the battle and the war in Northern India have built up such defenses and such overlapping fields of fire and deep entrenchments, bunker networks, such that it genuinely would be a very bloody assault for anyone to attack anyone else. An actual full-out assault is something that kind of isn't possible, not without a serious change in the internal state in whichever state they're looking at. Air power is one of those things that also becomes a very interesting deal. As Azad Hind gets Japanese jets, the other states get usually purchases of a variety of other states. Hyderabad gets German jets, but Then, oftentimes, sell those jets to some one or another of the powers adjacent to them. They typically don't sell them to the communists. The communists typically get their jets from somebody else. But it creates a particularly interesting scenario where arms dealers kind of get a little bit more leeway than you would really expect in the setting, because they are principally the only way that new technology gets into the region. You want a fancy new German, American, French, well, opposite, or American jet, you're going through an arms dealer. You are not going to that country directly because very few countries take your money. You don't actually have money, for all intents and purposes, as far as most states are concerned. You have local resources, which can sometimes be useful but are hard to get in and out of the country. Thus, northern India becomes kind of an arms dealer's paradise. Now, eventually, probably near the 70s or 80s, Hyderabad, or Congress India and Hindustan, probably both begin to develop their own jets, fighter jets and the likes, their own aircraft production, independent of having to import stuff. Enough years of investigating assets brought into the region eventually give them a pretty good understanding of what they need in order to get these things running themselves. And as soon as domestic production starts to kick in, some of these states do genuinely think, hey, we've got a shot at overwhelming the other powers. Now, I will also note that one of the other assets that are brought in that these arms dealers are anti-air assets. So just because you have your own jets that you can attach bombs to and drop them on things, does not mean that the enemy does not have an anti-air missile or an anti-air gun platform that can shoot your jet down. Azad Hind kind of gets the better end of the tech deal, but it also has a manpower problem. As the years go through, Azad Hind has to kind of manage its own internal situation, which is anything but easy and simple. Thus, while yes, it is getting more equipment than most other states via their Japanese connections, they're also oftentimes having to use that equipment to manage their own internal multinational state. It's not perpetually a problem, but it is often enough of a problem that Azad Hind doesn't really feel confident that they can simply overwhelm and overpower their opponents. They do, though, typically have air superiority or at least air supremacy in most combat situations. But as is a turn of phrase that becomes pretty common in Azad Hind military circles, just because you own the air does not mean that you have cleared out the ground. That is, just because you can technically bomb the enemy does not mean that bombing the enemy gets rid of him. Because the bunker networks and the underground defensive structures that have been built up and are predominant throughout much of the region have rendered much of the northern part of the subcontinent kind of a military nightmare to attack into.

This gives northern India a much clearer post-Colombo development. The **Colombo Armistice System** ends the broadest phase of the British Indian Wars, but it does not create confidence that the borders will survive. The existing canon already defines Colombo as a patchwork freezing ceasefire lines, transit, ports, minority questions, and foreign intervention without resolving the concept of India. fileciteturn40file0

The new development is that northern India passes through four stages:

> **retreat and fortification → armed armistice → renewed general war → permanent militarized coexistence**

The 1963–65 conflict is therefore neither a contradiction of Colombo nor merely another border incident. It is the last serious attempt by the northern claimants to prove that the map can still be decided through one general campaign.

# The first armed armistice, 1957–1960

Congress India’s 1956 counteroffensive does not destroy Azad Hind. It pushes Azad Hind back into positions that had already been prepared as fallback defenses during the Delhi Campaign.

That matters because Congress reaches the end of its logistical strength just as Azad Hind reaches the beginning of its strongest defensive ground.

Congress has three reasons not to continue.

First, its supply lines now run eastward through territory damaged by several years of fighting.

Second, Azad Hind is defending closer to Bengal, Calcutta, and its established ammunition depots.

Third, Congress cannot strip its western front. Hindustan still controls Delhi and represents a separate all-Indian claimant, not merely a rival faction inside Congress India.

Congress therefore halts, reorganizes, and begins entrenching its newly recovered ground.

Azad Hind does the same.

## The eastern fortified belt

The resulting frontier should not be one continuous line of enormous concrete forts. India has neither the time nor the undamaged industrial capacity to build a literal copy of the French Maginot Line by 1960.

Instead, it becomes a fortified **belt** with three layers.

### The security strip

The forward zone contains:

- wire;
- minefields;
- patrol tracks;
- observation posts;
- demolished bridges;
- cleared fields of fire;
- abandoned or relocated villages;
- small infantry bunkers.

This is where most later border incidents occur.

### The main defensive zone

Behind it are:

- entrenched towns;
- reinforced railway stations;
- river and canal strongpoints;
- concrete artillery shelters;
- anti-tank ditches;
- buried command posts;
- protected ammunition stores;
- prepared infantry positions.

The strongest sectors appear around transport routes and river crossings rather than forming one perfect wall.

### The operational rear

Farther back sit:

- reserve camps;
- rail loops;
- repair workshops;
- alternate bridges;
- field hospitals;
- hardened airfields;
- dispersed fuel and ammunition depots.

The practical objective is not to make penetration physically impossible. It is to ensure that any penetration arrives exhausted, disorganized, and exposed to counterattack before it reaches the Bengal heartland or the Congress interior.

## Indian geography changes the fortifications

Drainage matters nearly as much as concrete.

A bunker that cannot survive the monsoon is not a bunker. Roads become impassable, trenches flood, and rivers change character across the year. Both armies therefore militarize:

- canals;
- embankments;
- irrigation works;
- rail causeways;
- reservoirs;
- seasonal floodplains.

In some sectors, the defensive plan deliberately allows low ground to flood during mobilization. In others, roads and raised railway beds become the only usable approaches and are covered by artillery.

This makes the frontier resemble both the Maginot Line and the First World War’s Zone Rouge, but without the same level of chemical contamination. Its scars are instead:

- unexploded shells;
- mines;
- collapsed tunnels;
- abandoned farms;
- military forests;
- villages rebuilt several kilometers from their original sites;
- roads that end at checkpoints and concrete barriers.

By 1970, children are growing up in towns where the nearest hill is officially an artillery observation area and the old family fields lie inside a restricted defense zone.

# Congress India’s defensive problem

Congress India is the principal pivot of the northern system because it faces threats in several directions.

To the east is Azad Hind.

To the west is Hindustan, holding Delhi and claiming the political and civilizational center.

To the south are princely systems, communist districts, Hyderabad’s sphere, and unstable frontier authorities.

Congress possesses the largest useful population base among the northern claimants, but it cannot concentrate that population on one front.

That explains why its defensive policy is not timidity. It is the only strategy that allows Congress India to survive.

> **Congress trades the possibility of victory for the probability of continued existence.**

Its field army becomes centered on:

- fortified infantry;
- large reserve formations;
- artillery;
- engineers;
- railway troops;
- mobile armored counterattack groups.

Congress does not expect the frontline infantry to defeat every attack. It expects them to hold long enough for reserves to move behind the defensive belt and strike the penetrating force.

This doctrine ultimately saves the state in 1963–65. An offensively oriented Congress army would disperse itself against Azad Hind and Hindustan, exhaust its ammunition, and expose the interior. A defensive Congress army can lose towns without losing the country.

# The Second Preparatory War

The period from approximately 1959 or 1960 through early 1963 could become known as the **Second Preparatory War**.

It is not technically a war. The name reflects what governments and civilians experience.

Every state:

- calls up reservists;
- extends trenches;
- purchases aircraft;
- digs new depots;
- trains militias;
- expands arsenals;
- reinforces bridges;
- accuses its neighbors of preparing an attack.

Each buildup is defensible in isolation.

Together, they form a mobilization cascade.

Congress sees Hindustan strengthening the Delhi approaches and assumes an offensive is imminent.

Hindustan sees Congress moving divisions west and assumes Congress intends to recover Delhi.

Azad Hind sees Congress shifting formations away from the eastern front and concludes that the temporary opportunity it has awaited may finally have arrived.

The Telangana People’s Republic sees the larger powers distracted and expands its protected zones.

Princely armies prepare to seize disputed towns before one of the mass states reaches them first.

No one needs to plan a general war. Everyone merely acts against the war he expects someone else to begin.

# The Northern Indian War, 1963–1965

The neutral international name should probably be the **Northern Indian War**.

Historians who emphasize continuity may classify it as the final major campaign of the British Indian Wars. Historians who emphasize the Colombo interlude treat it as a separate war because:

- Britain is no longer the central external participant;
- the stable southern states largely remain outside it;
- the principal combatants are now established northern governments;
- the objectives concern post-Colombo borders rather than the immediate succession to the Raj.

Both classifications remain reasonable.

## The opening

The exact first incident can remain open. Structurally, a mobilization cascade is stronger than one accidental gunshot.

A likely sequence is:

1. Hindustan begins a major frontier concentration against Congress India.
2. Congress transfers reserves westward.
3. Azad Hind interprets the transfer as the opening for a limited line-breaking campaign.
4. The Telangana forces and several princely states exploit the general mobilization.
5. Local attacks merge into a northern general war.

The sides do not form two clean coalitions.

Azad Hind and Hindustan both fight Congress, but they are not allies. Each claims Delhi and all India. Neither wants the other to become strong enough to defeat Congress outright.

The Telangana People’s Republic fights whichever neighboring authority threatens its territory, while also sponsoring agrarian revolt behind several fronts.

The princes sometimes cooperate against a mass state and sometimes fight one another over the same road or district.

The result is not one front. It is a network of connected wars.

# Azad Hind’s 1963 campaign

Azad Hind no longer expects to reach Delhi in one operation.

Its objectives are narrower:

- break selected Congress fortifications;
- recover towns lost in 1956;
- straighten the frontier;
- seize useful railway junctions;
- demonstrate that the Delhi mission remains alive;
- prevent Congress from becoming permanently stronger.

This limited objective is more rational than the final 1956 offensive. But it still encounters a much harder battlefield.

Congress has spent six years preparing the exact ground Azad Hind must cross.

## The new Japanese tanks

Azad Hind receives a limited number of Japan’s postwar **Type 16 Shu-Ha** main battle tanks before the war.

The Type 16 entered Japanese service in 1956 as a 36-tonne, four-man vehicle with a 90 mm gun, compact diesel, good mobility, optical rangefinding, and protection against common medium-caliber weapons. The 1962 *Kai* improves stabilization, power, and the final drive. fileciteturn40file1

It is a better integrated machine than most of the vehicles fielded by the Indian successors.

That does not mean an Azad Hind Type 16 formation performs like a Japanese armored formation.

The difference lies in:

- crew training;
- recovery;
- maintenance;
- infantry cooperation;
- engineer support;
- artillery timing;
- radio discipline;
- command experience.

Azad Hind receives the tank faster than it can reproduce the Japanese institution built around the tank.

A Japanese crew has spent years moving through a common gunnery, maintenance, and maneuver system. An Azad Hind crew may have trained for months, then been assigned to a newly formed regiment containing officers accustomed to Chi-To, Chi-Ri, or Chi-Ru tanks.

The machine is advanced. The formation is immature.

## The National Tank Model 62 Vijaya

Congress India’s **National Tank Model 62**, commonly called **Vijaya**, gives the Type 16 a genuine regional opponent.

The Vijaya should not be more technologically refined than the Japanese tank. Its advantage is that Congress designed it around what Congress can maintain.

A working technical profile would be:

- roughly 37–39 tonnes;
- four-man crew;
- 100 mm rifled gun;
- compact diesel;
- low silhouette;
- conventional torsion-bar suspension;
- simple optical sighting;
- strong frontal steel protection;
- limited night capability;
- components designed around Congress workshops and railway transport.

Its Russian inheritance is visible, but it is not a Soviet vehicle carrying an Indian name. Congress engineers have studied T-34-series vehicles, fragments of later Russian projects, captured documentation, and whatever foreign specialists can be hired. They then redesign the result around Indian production.

The Vijaya is less comfortable, less refined, and probably less reliable in its first production series than the Type 16.

But Congress crews know its controls. Congress depots stock its parts. Congress ammunition plants manufacture its rounds. Its mechanics have followed the project from prototype to service vehicle.

In a prepared defensive position, that relationship matters more than the difference between the two specification sheets.

## Why Azad Hind loses so many tanks

The principal Azad Hind armored losses come from the entire defensive system rather than from Vijaya tanks alone.

Type 16s are lost to:

- mines;
- anti-tank ditches;
- artillery;
- recoilless weapons;
- close infantry attacks;
- damaged bridges;
- mechanical failures beyond recovery;
- counterattacks by Vijaya units once Azad Hind has entered a prepared pocket.

Some Japanese tanks are abandoned almost intact because the recovery vehicles cannot reach them.

Others are destroyed after infantry support falls behind in trench and village fighting.

Azad Hind may win several direct tank engagements. It still loses the larger armored contest because Congress forces it to fight at the place and tempo Congress selected.

The lesson is not that Japanese armor is overrated.

It is:

> **A Japanese tank with an Indian crew is not a Japanese armored division.**

# The Azad Hind Armoured School

The war leads directly to a dedicated national tank school, probably established in the Calcutta–Kharagpur industrial and railway corridor.

Its curriculum is broader than gunnery.

It covers:

- crew coordination;
- radio procedure;
- infantry–tank cooperation;
- minefield breaching;
- artillery liaison;
- field maintenance;
- recovery under fire;
- night movement;
- railway loading;
- command of mixed Japanese tank fleets.

Japanese advisers are retained, but the school’s purpose is to create an Azad Hind armored doctrine rather than teach translated Japanese drills indefinitely.

This is one of the war’s clearest institutional gains. Azad Hind fails to break Congress but stops treating imported equipment as a substitute for organization.

# Congress holds because it does not chase

Congress India loses some forward towns and fortified positions.

Its leaders resist the demand for a general counteroffensive.

Instead, they:

- seal penetrations;
- counterattack exposed spearheads;
- restore rail connections;
- trade ground where necessary;
- keep major reserves behind the line;
- refuse to pursue withdrawing Azad Hind forces too far.

That restraint is politically difficult. Newspapers accuse generals of cowardice. Refugees demand recovery of their districts. Congress politicians argue that Azad Hind has been weakened and should be destroyed.

The army answers that the western front with Hindustan remains active.

Congress survives because it understands that every victorious pursuit in the east is a possible defeat outside Delhi.

# The air war

Azad Hind usually possesses the strongest air arm in an individual northern campaign.

Japan supplies:

- jet fighters;
- reconnaissance aircraft;
- radios;
- maintenance support;
- training;
- munitions;
- radar assistance.

That often gives Azad Hind **local air superiority**, particularly during a prepared offensive.

It does not automatically give permanent air supremacy over all northern India.

Congress, Hindustan, Hyderabad, and the princely states acquire aircraft through brokers, re-export arrangements, and captured stocks. Their fleets are less coherent, but they are difficult to eliminate because aircraft and airfields are dispersed across a very large region.

## The arms-dealer air forces

One air force might contain:

- former British jets;
- Russian-derived fighters;
- German or Occitan aircraft re-exported through Hyderabad;
- Japanese aircraft captured or purchased secondhand;
- locally rebuilt trainers converted for attack.

This is a maintenance disaster. It is also surprisingly resilient.

Destroying the supply for one type does not ground the whole air force.

Hyderabad becomes particularly important as a technical and commercial broker. German aircraft delivered to Hyderabad may later appear in neighboring service through:

- resale;
- debt settlement;
- political sponsorship;
- spare-parts agreements;
- transfers disguised as private contracts.

The communist state normally receives fewer Western or German types, but can acquire older Russian aircraft and specialists through the Central Asian arms market.

## Air defense

The same dealers who sell fighters also sell:

- radar;
- anti-aircraft cannon;
- searchlights;
- rangefinders;
- early guided missiles;
- communications gear;
- foreign technicians.

This makes the northern air war increasingly expensive.

Azad Hind can still dominate exposed troops, bridges, rail yards, and moving columns. But low-altitude attacks against prepared defensive zones encounter dense gunfire, concealed batteries, and eventually missile sites.

Aircraft force armies to:

- disperse;
- camouflage;
- move at night;
- bury supplies;
- build alternate bridges;
- maintain false positions.

They do not force infantry out of deep prepared defenses.

The Azad Hind military saying therefore fits perfectly:

> **Owning the air does not clear the ground.**

Aircraft can close the bunker entrance, destroy the road above it, and prevent reserves from moving in daylight. Infantry and engineers still have to enter the position.

# The end of the 1963–65 war

By 1965, no principal power is close to collapse.

Azad Hind has gained combat experience and perhaps a small amount of territory, but has not broken the Congress position.

Congress has demonstrated that its defensive state can survive simultaneous pressure, but it has not recovered Delhi or destroyed Azad Hind.

Hindustan remains in Delhi and preserves its separate national claim.

The Telangana People’s Republic survives another campaign and confirms that no neighboring state can eliminate it cheaply.

The princely systems retain their fortified cores.

The war ends through another set of armistice protocols rather than one conclusive peace.

The lines shift locally. The political map does not.

That is the real turning point.

Before 1965, governments still believe one general campaign might settle northern India.

After 1965, they believe the war may last for generations.

# From emergency austerity to permanent war economy

This changes economic policy.

Before 1965, each state tries to survive until the next decisive campaign. Civilian development can be postponed because victory is supposedly close.

After 1965, victory is not close. A country cannot live under temporary austerity for another twenty years.

The successor states therefore begin building civilian economies, but they build them for permanent mobilization.

The priorities are:

- food;
- fertilizer;
- irrigation;
- coal;
- steel;
- cement;
- rail repair;
- electrical power;
- radios;
- medicine;
- trucks;
- machine tools;
- chemicals.

These are civilian industries and military industries simultaneously.

A fertilizer plant increases harvests and provides chemical-industrial capacity.

A radio factory serves households and produces reserve communications equipment.

A tractor workshop supports farmers and repairs military prime movers.

A truck designed for commercial use includes standard military towing and communications fittings.

A village school doubles as a reserve muster center and emergency clinic.

This is not ordinary consumer development. It is **defense developmentalism**.

The state allows civilian life to improve because a better-fed, technically capable, industrially trained population is also a stronger reserve army.

# The militarized household

Northern India’s reserve culture resembles Switzerland only in one narrow sense: weapons and military obligations are widely distributed through the civilian population.

The political atmosphere is entirely different.

Depending on the state, an adult man may be required or expected to keep:

- a service rifle;
- sealed ammunition;
- a gas mask;
- a field kit;
- mobilization papers;
- a radio or civil-defense receiver.

Annual reserve training becomes normal.

Some states retain weapons in local depots rather than homes. Others deliberately distribute them because the founding wars proved that isolated towns and villages might have to resist without regular troops.

The late campaigns repeatedly vindicate the concept. Guerrillas and territorial units slow breakthroughs, destroy bridges, and deny easy occupation.

They also make political violence more dangerous.

A society containing millions of trained reservists and widely available rifles experiences:

- family feuds turning lethal;
- partisan militias;
- armed political marches;
- assassinations;
- communal defense organizations;
- nervous police checkpoints.

Governments accept the danger because they fear an unarmed population more.

# Five versions of the fortress society

The principal northern states converge on militarization, but they explain it differently.

## Azad Hind

Azad Hind presents mobilization as the unfinished national liberation of India.

Military service is tied to:

- the INA inheritance;
- the march to Delhi;
- unity across religion and province;
- sacrifice against partition;
- loyalty to the provisional state.

Its strongest technical advantages remain Japanese aircraft, electronics, and newer weapons.

Its limitation is manpower and internal administration. Forces needed against Congress cannot always be detached from:

- eastern Bengal;
- Assam;
- hill districts;
- communal crises;
- internal insurgencies.

Azad Hind usually has the best equipment available at the point of contact. It does not always have enough reliable formations to exploit that equipment.

## Congress India

Congress India presents itself as the constitutional state forced into emergency rule by enemies on every frontier.

It maintains:

- assemblies;
- courts;
- civil ministries;
- Congress political institutions;
- a language of secular constitutional legitimacy.

But the permanent emergency gives the army, security services, and fortress administration enormous influence.

The government claims that constitutional normality will return when the other claimants abandon force.

The other claimants never do.

Congress consequently becomes a republic whose temporary emergency has no credible ending date.

## Hindustan

Hindustan’s militarization is more openly national and religious.

Delhi is not merely its capital. It is the proof that Hindustan possesses the center of Indian civilization.

Military defense becomes connected to:

- sacred geography;
- refugee memory;
- Hindu national survival;
- defense against communists, Congress secularism, and Japanese-supported Azad Hind.

Hindustan relies heavily on mass organizations, militias, ideological schools, and security investigations.

It can accuse an opponent of being:

- a communist;
- a Japanese agent;
- a Congress conspirator;
- a communal traitor;
- an enemy of the national religion.

The terminology changes by faction. The political consequence is similar.

## The Telangana People’s Republic

The TPR operates through a party-army and armed village system.

Its defenses emphasize:

- tunnels;
- dispersed stores;
- village militias;
- concealed workshops;
- political commissars;
- agrarian networks;
- intelligence among the rural population.

It is less capable of conventional mechanized war than the three large northern claimants.

It is extremely difficult to conquer.

Its security system is also severe. Landlord agents, revisionists, foreign spies, and factional enemies can all become categories for political execution.

## The princely fortress states

Hyderabad, Rajputana authorities, and smaller princely systems organize defense around:

- royal guards;
- fortified cities;
- hired specialists;
- dynastic officer corps;
- foreign equipment;
- negotiated neutrality;
- control of roads and water.

Their governments are smaller, but some possess concentrated wealth and technical institutions.

Hyderabad in particular can become a major aviation, repair, and arms-broker center despite lacking the population to dominate India.

The princes survive not because they could defeat every claimant, but because attacking them would expose the attacker to several other enemies.

# Treason as an ordinary political category

Northern India’s repression works because the threat is not imaginary.

Every state genuinely maintains:

- spies;
- agents;
- funded opposition groups;
- military contacts;
- border militias;
- propaganda networks.

That gives security governments a real foundation.

It also gives them an unlimited excuse.

A politician can be arrested because he actually met an enemy agent. Another can be arrested because his economic program threatens the ruling party and the charge of foreign contact is convenient.

A village can contain a real communist cell. A neighboring village can be accused of communism because a local official wants its land.

The line between counterintelligence and political persecution becomes difficult to observe from outside and sometimes impossible to observe from inside.

The result is not constant indiscriminate terror everywhere. It is more administratively durable:

> **Every citizen knows that treason exists, and no citizen can be completely certain where the state has decided treason begins.**

# Arms dealers as bankers

Northern India becomes an arms dealer’s paradise because the successor governments often lack currencies trusted beyond their own borders.

A broker may accept payment in:

- tea;
- jute;
- coal;
- ore;
- gemstones;
- future customs receipts;
- railway priority;
- mining concessions;
- warehouse certificates;
- state-backed delivery contracts.

The arms dealer therefore becomes a quasi-banker.

He does not merely sell twenty tanks. He finances the purchase, hires mechanics, arranges rail shipment, obtains ammunition from a third country, and accepts repayment from future exports.

That is why the dealer can become richer than the government purchasing from him.

It also explains why formations develop four or five equipment trees. A government does not choose an ideal standardized force. It buys whatever complete package can reach the front before the next war.

## The logistical consequence

Mixed equipment creates specialist enclaves.

One depot understands German aircraft.

Another understands Russian tanks.

A third repairs Japanese radios.

An artillery regiment may possess guns in three calibers and depend upon a commercial broker to locate ammunition.

The resulting armies are less efficient than their parade inventories suggest. But they are also difficult to cripple through one embargo.

# Domestic aircraft production

By the 1970s and 1980s, Congress India and Hindustan can plausibly develop their own combat aircraft, but the process should be gradual.

Studying imported aircraft alone is not enough. They need:

- machine tools;
- aluminum and high-temperature alloys;
- precision bearings;
- turbine metallurgy;
- instrumentation;
- wind-tunnel work;
- trained engineers;
- quality control;
- large repair depots.

The likely progression is:

1. **Depot overhaul:** rebuilding imported aircraft.
2. **Component substitution:** manufacturing simple spares and airframe pieces.
3. **Local assembly:** assembling a foreign or derivative aircraft from imported engines and systems.
4. **National airframe:** designing a local aircraft around a foreign engine.
5. **Independent engine and weapons production:** the final and most difficult stage.

So a 1970s “indigenous” Congress fighter may possess:

- an Indian-designed airframe;
- Congress-built structure;
- a locally assembled but foreign-derived engine;
- imported radar;
- brokered missiles.

That still represents an enormous national achievement.

Congress India is the likely first northern state to reach this stage because the Vijaya program has already built a culture of national ordnance development.

Hindustan follows with a simpler interceptor or fighter-bomber intended for rapid production and defense of Delhi.

Hyderabad becomes a major assembly, repair, and re-export center using German or other European systems.

Azad Hind continues receiving the best organized Japanese assistance, but that assistance can slow its domestic independence. Calcutta often finds it cheaper and faster to obtain another Japanese system than to fund a complete national replacement.

# Air superiority without victory

The mature northern battlefield therefore reaches an odd balance.

Azad Hind often has the better aircraft.

Congress often has the stronger fortifications and larger defensive manpower reserve.

Hindustan possesses the political advantage of Delhi and its own growing arms system.

The TPR is weakest in the air but hardest to eradicate on the ground.

The princes possess isolated pockets of very advanced equipment without the depth for prolonged general war.

No side can convert its strongest advantage into complete victory.

Aircraft cannot clear the bunkers.

Tanks cannot cross the fortified belt without infantry and engineers.

Infantry cannot advance without artillery.

Artillery cannot fire indefinitely without industrial ammunition production.

Industrial production cannot be concentrated without becoming an air target.

Every answer creates another dependency.

# The post-1965 long war

After 1965, major offensives still occur, but their objectives become limited.

A state may attempt to:

- seize a town;
- move the frontier to a river;
- capture a railway junction;
- destroy an enemy salient;
- test a new weapon;
- support an internal revolt;
- improve its bargaining position.

It no longer announces that one operation will settle India.

The permanent defensive systems make a general conquest prohibitively costly unless one state first collapses internally.

That becomes the governing strategic assumption:

> **You do not defeat the neighboring state at the frontier. You wait for its politics, economy, or national structure to break, then move before the others do.**

This makes diplomacy almost impossible.

An economic crisis is interpreted as preparation for war.

A political reform is interpreted as weakness.

A troop reduction is interpreted as deception.

A peace proposal is interpreted as an attempt to divide the opposition.

Every state knows the others are waiting for an opening because every state is doing the same thing.

# Working canon

> **The Colombo Armistice System begins freezing the broad Indian Wars from 1956 onward, but northern India remains on a continuous war footing. Between 1957 and approximately 1960, Congress India and Azad Hind fortify the positions reached after the failed Azad Hind Delhi Campaign and the Congress counteroffensive. The resulting eastern frontier becomes a layered belt of minefields, fortified towns, river and canal obstacles, underground positions, artillery shelters, depots, reserve camps, and hardened airfields.**

> **Congress India remains caught between Azad Hind in the east, Hindustan and Delhi in the west, and princely or communist pressures to the south. Its defensive orientation allows it to man several fronts and prevents it from exhausting itself in an offensive campaign.**

> **The Second Preparatory War of approximately 1960–63 is a period of escalating mobilization rather than continuous general combat. Every northern state assumes another is preparing to attack, producing a self-reinforcing buildup. A mobilization cascade in 1963 expands into the Northern Indian War.**

> **Azad Hind employs limited numbers of Type 16 Shu-Ha tanks and maintains the strongest Japanese-supported air arm. Congress India debuts the Russian-influenced National Tank Model 62 Vijaya. The Japanese tank is technically more refined, but Congress crews, maintenance, local ammunition, and prepared defensive ground allow the Vijaya to compete effectively. Heavy Azad Hind losses lead to the establishment of a national armored-warfare school and a doctrine emphasizing combined arms rather than equipment alone.**

> **The 1963–65 war ends without a decisive territorial settlement. Congress loses some local positions but preserves the state. Azad Hind fails to break the defensive belt. Hindustan retains Delhi. The TPR and principal states survive. After 1965, no major government expects one final general offensive to reunify India.**

> **Northern India consequently develops a permanent mobilization economy and armed reserve society. Civilian industries are designed for dual use; household or local-depot weapons become common; conscription and reserve service shape education and employment; and actual foreign subversion makes political witch hunts and security repression easier to justify.**

> **Arms dealers become financiers as well as merchants, exchanging weapons, expertise, and credit for commodities, concessions, and future state revenue. The resulting mixed arsenals gradually produce indigenous tank, aircraft, ammunition, and repair industries during the 1970s and 1980s.**

The defining feature of northern India after 1965 is not that everyone believes peace is impossible.

It is that everyone believes peace would be possible **if the other states could first be made incapable of breaking it**.
