# 11. South Africa, Rhodesia, Portuguese Africa and Mittelafrika gradually develop a regional modus vivendi

I agree with this direction.

They do not become ideological allies.

They recognize that they inhabit a common strategic geography and, by the 1980s and 1990s, each has learned that permanently destabilizing its neighbors creates refugee, insurgency and trade problems for itself.

So you start getting practical agreements among:

- South Africa;
- Rhodesia;
- Portuguese Angola;
- Portuguese Mozambique;
- German Mittelafrika.

These can cover:

- railway transit;
- river and port movements;
- anti-smuggling operations;
- disease control;
- refugee return;
- extradition;
- aviation corridors;
- hydrographic data;
- border pursuit rules;
- veterinary disease;
- mining transport;
- and eventually regional electrical grids.

Pretoria and Salisbury still distrust German racial ideology and German strategic ambitions.

Kongostadt still sees the British-derived settler states as foreign competitors.

Portugal maintains its Latin allegiance.

But everybody has reached the stage of:

> “We are still neighbors tomorrow.”

And because the wider great-power system is itself learning this lesson after Tehran and Verona, African practical détente fits the global direction rather nicely.

Britain's chagrin is that this means its African partners develop **foreign relationships London did not mediate**.

That is the price of telling them to govern themselves.

---

# 12. The population-policy borrowing is plausible, but it should remain politically radioactive

Mittelafrika's established policy provides a model that African settler governments could borrow: contraception is illegal for Germans but freely and formally voluntarily supplied to subject populations, alongside small-family incentives; punitive sterilization is a separate and restricted criminal punishment. fileciteturn11file1

South Africa and Rhodesia can absolutely look at the German statistics and conclude that fertility policy is cheaper and less destabilizing than mass expulsion.

But I would not make London simply regard this as uninteresting.

The workable distinction is:

**Pretoria regards it as population administration.**

**London regards it as something it does not want documented in a Cabinet paper.**

The South African version might include:

- free contraceptive clinics in black administrative districts;
- aggressive family-planning advertising;
- cash or housing advantages for smaller black families;
- white pronatalist tax and housing policy;
- legal or medical restrictions upon contraceptive provision to whites;
- and state rhetoric that treats falling African fertility as evidence of “development.”

Formally voluntary.

Clearly racially asymmetrical.

And surrounded by a political order in which the state controls housing, employment and movement enough that critics can reasonably argue that the distinction between encouragement and coercion is not clean.

Rhodesia probably copies a cheaper, less bureaucratic version.

Kenya is more complicated. If it remains more directly Crown-linked, London would have more power to prevent an openly racial law. Its local administration might instead use ostensibly nonracial regional family-planning programs whose practical targeting is obvious.

The key is that **these policies cannot become respectable British public doctrine**.

If a government minister stands at the dispatch box and says, “Yes, we support reducing black fertility while raising white fertility,” that is still a major political crisis.

The system works because ministers can say:

- fertility policy is devolved;
- contraceptive use is voluntary;
- no British funds compel acceptance;
- local governments operate their own health systems;
- and Britain does not dictate private family decisions.

Everybody paying attention understands that this is evasive.

But evasion has been part of the African settlement since the Salisbury Understanding.

---

# 13. “Don't ask” becomes an actual late-Commonwealth political culture

Your hypothetical exchange is exactly the right flavor.

A Mittelafrika report reaches Pretoria describing some unpleasant but effective population-control or security measure.

A British official asks whether the Rhodesians have adopted anything comparable.

The Rhodesian representative says:

> “No comparable regulation exists.”

Technically true.

The British official notices he did not say **practice**.

He does not ask again.

The government does not want ignorance in the literal sense. Intelligence services still know what is happening. What ministers want is **distance from actionable responsibility**.

This produces an important formal-functional distinction:

- London is strategically responsible for the Commonwealth.
- Local governments are domestically sovereign enough to be blamed for their own internal policy.
- British intelligence knows more than ministers publicly acknowledge.
- Parliament can demand an inquiry.
- The government can truthfully answer that it did not issue the offending order.

That is the late Siege Commonwealth's constitutional trick.

---

# 14. It also explains why apartheid survives much longer

Not because space magically makes racial politics disappear.

Rather, every historical pressure pushing London toward confrontation has weakened:

- Britain never experiences the same decolonization consensus.
- South Africa is strategically more valuable.
- Rhodesia does not undergo the same regional isolation.
- Portugal retains Angola and Mozambique.
- German Mittelafrika provides a much harsher comparator.
- there is no Soviet bloc financing the same liberation movements;
- and Britain's central national project after 1990 is elsewhere.

Then add space itself:

South African stations, industry and minerals are now helping Britain reach other planets.

So the British establishment's practical question becomes:

> Why create a Commonwealth constitutional crisis over Pretoria now, when Pretoria is stable, useful, loyal in foreign policy and participating in the largest national project of the age?

That does not eliminate dissent. Labour backbenchers, churches, missionaries, African politicians, universities and newspapers still attack the system.

It means none of them can easily make **breaking with South Africa** the governing priority.

Apartheid can therefore survive into the 2000s, though it probably evolves administratively rather than remaining frozen in its 1950s form.

---

# 15. This changes the whole emotional meaning of 1990s Britain

The country that entered the postwar era obsessed with what it had lost becomes increasingly obsessed with what it can still reach.

That is a profound cultural transition.

The British child of 1955 sees maps of:

- Gibraltar;
- Malta;
- Africa;
- the Cape;
- the Commonwealth sea routes.

The British child of 1995 sees maps of:

- Earth orbit;
- Resolution;
- Serenity;
- Mars;
- Valles Marineris;
- planetary transfer windows.

The old imperial reflex does not disappear. It changes scale.

That is where your “Scramble for the Solar System” analogy becomes useful, provided we keep the obvious distinction that there are no indigenous societies being conquered.

Britain approaches extraterrestrial territorial questions with an inherited vocabulary of:

- occupation;
- station rights;
- survey;
- prior use;
- flags;
- permanent settlement;
- navigation;
- charter;
- and Commonwealth jurisdiction.

So when the British land in western Valles Marineris, London absolutely does not regard the settlement as a temporary scientific camp that Japan may later absorb into an eastern Valles administrative zone.

The British answer is:

> We landed here. We maintain it. It is inhabited. The Crown's jurisdiction follows its people.

Germany says something similar at Olympus.

America's corporations say something stranger about property and charter rights.

Japan talks about administered development zones.

The Latin bloc talks about stations and exploration claims.

And now the nineteenth-century diplomatic habits begin reappearing **on maps of Mars**.

---

## The clean 1986–2000 British synthesis

Britain finishes the Falklands War having finally proved that the post-1947 Commonwealth can defend itself.

Ashcombe then turns that victory into institutional reconstruction and builds a proper Commonwealth space infrastructure. His caution is initially popular because the country has just endured a war.

By the early 1990s, however, Stella Maris, German Mars preparations and Japanese expansion make caution feel like decline.

Calder—or a new character occupying essentially Calder's political space—turns this into a mass political project. Britain stops asking whether it can afford to remain in the space race and starts treating space access the same way earlier governments treated the Royal Navy: **a first-order attribute of great-power sovereignty**.

By 2000, Britain has:

- one of the world's major orbital stations;
- independent high-cadence crew and cargo capacity;
- a permanent and expanding Mare Serenitatis settlement;
- an independent human Mars landing and small western Valles outpost;
- planetary orbiters across the inner solar system;
- a global/deep-space Commonwealth communications network;
- and an aerospace-industrial complex distributed across several continents.

At the same time, London governs its terrestrial periphery less directly than ever. Pretoria, Salisbury and increasingly the East African governments receive extraordinary domestic discretion as long as they remain strategically loyal.

So Britain's transformation is not really from **empire to post-empire**.

It is from a **territorial Siege Commonwealth** into an increasingly **infrastructural Commonwealth**, whose center of political imagination is moving upward and outward even while the older racial and colonial arrangements on Earth remain unresolved beneath it.

Yes. And the fortunate part is that the **actual lunar geometry of 1 January 2000 makes the idea better**, provided we do not insist that everyone sees it at midnight.

On 1 January 2000 the Moon was a **waning crescent, about 20–21% illuminated**, with new Moon not occurring until 6 January. That means roughly four-fifths of the Earth-facing disk was on the lunar night side. citeturn652983search0turn652983search2 The natural crescent would therefore frame a largely dark disk faintly visible by earthshine, which is a real and significant illumination source on the lunar night side. citeturn426835academia51

So the iconic image can genuinely be:

> **a thin natural crescent, the ghostly earthlit disk behind it, and unmistakably artificial points of light arranged across the Moon.**

That is considerably stronger than trying to alter the appearance of a full Moon.

## The first problem: it cannot really be a midnight event

A waning crescent is principally a **predawn** object. NASA's general phase description places the waning crescent near the Sun in the sky; by this stage it rises during the latter part of the night and remains visible into morning. citeturn426835search1

So when London celebrates midnight on 31 December, the Moon is not conveniently sitting over Parliament waiting to be illuminated. The same problem occurs with different timing around the world.

I would therefore make the event a **rolling 30–36-hour international ceremony**, beginning as 1 January reaches the western Pacific and continuing until the date has passed through the Americas.

The television ceremonies still occur at midnight. Lunar feeds show the stations preparing and the lights switching on. But the thing people remember personally is going outside **before dawn on 1 January** in whichever part of the world they inhabit.

That actually gives the event a wonderful accidental name. Newspapers can call it something like **the Millennium Dawn**, even if its technical title is much drier.

There will inevitably be calendar pedants pointing out that the mathematical third millennium begins in 2001. Nobody organizing the largest public spectacle in human history particularly cares.

## Giant reflective sheets alone will not quite solve it

Your reflective-sheet instinct is directionally useful, but it has two problems.

First, the Moon subtends only about **30 arcminutes** in Earth's sky. citeturn744405search1 Normal 20/20 vision resolves detail of roughly one arcminute under good conditions. citeturn631170search0turn631170search1 At lunar distance, one arcminute corresponds to roughly **110 kilometres**.

So if we wanted someone standing in Montana or Kent to resolve an actual cross painted on the Moon, the major parts of that cross need to be separated by something like a hundred kilometres, and the complete symbol probably needs to span several hundred.

A reflective sheet twenty kilometres across is enormous engineering from the lunar perspective and still merely a bright unresolved speck from Earth.

Second, on 1 January most of the useful display area is on the **night side**. A mirror lying on Mare Serenitatis has no direct sunlight to reflect toward Earth if its local Sun is below the horizon. Earthshine is much weaker than sunlight.

So I would keep reflective sheets as a secondary element, especially for telescopic photographs after the local lunar sunrise, but **not make them the principal mechanism of the Millennium display**.

The principal mechanism should be active optical beacons.

# The Millennium Beacon System

By the late 1990s, the lunar powers already possess most of the technologies required:

- megawatt-class electrical systems;
- nuclear reactors;
- hydrogen and oxygen production;
- precision Earth tracking;
- optical communications;
- remote construction vehicles;
- automated navigation;
- and outlying mining, communications and survey stations.

The Five Powers agree in roughly 1996–97 to install a temporary **Earth-facing optical beacon network**.

These are not floodlights.

Each is essentially an enormous steerable optical transmitter: a bank of high-intensity visible lasers or similarly collimated light sources, large tracking optics, thermal radiators, and a power package. The beam is deliberately spread enough that it illuminates the entire disk of Earth, or a very large terrestrial region, rather than attempting the pencil-thin beam used for communications.

The energy requirement is surprisingly manageable.

A zero-magnitude visible astronomical source corresponds to an irradiance on the order of a few billionths of a watt per square metre. citeturn426835search0turn426835search3 If a lunar beacon spreads its output across roughly the apparent diameter of Earth as seen from the Moon, an order-of-magnitude calculation gives **about 0.4 MW of visible output for a zero-magnitude source**, approximately **1 MW for magnitude –1**, and a few megawatts for something approaching Jupiter/Venus-like brilliance.

Allow for atmospheric losses, imperfect optics, safety margins and nonideal wavelengths, and I would design the beacons around something like:

> **1–5 MW optical peak output, perhaps 5–20 MW electrical input, operating in short synchronized bursts rather than continuously.**

That is substantial machinery.

It is not absurd machinery for the year-2000 Moon in this setting.

A remote display unit does not even need its own permanent reactor. It can be supplied beforehand with hydrogen and oxygen and run a large fuel-cell or turbine-generator installation for several minutes at a time. The show only needs perhaps ten minutes of full brightness every hour during the viewing window.

Afterward, many units can be converted into navigation, communications, survey or emergency beacons.

So this is a spectacular waste of money—but not completely useless infrastructure.

## The trick that makes symbols possible

The individual light does **not** have to be 110 kilometres across.

Stars are visible even though their apparent disks cannot be resolved.

What needs to be separated by roughly an arcminute is the **spacing between the lights**.

That means a five-point cross can consist of five relatively compact beacon stations arranged perhaps 120–150 kilometres apart. The complete pattern spans three or four hundred kilometres, but each luminous source may occupy only a few tens of metres of actual machinery.

This is the conceptual breakthrough.

You don't build a 400-kilometre illuminated cross.

You put five artificial stars on the Moon in the shape of a cross.

With binoculars, it is unmistakable.

With good naked-eye vision under a dark sky, the brightest and most widely separated nodes can be distinguished.

Through the observatories and television optics available in 2000, the pattern is brilliant.

That gives us three simultaneous versions of the event:

| Observer | What they see |
|---|---|
| Naked eye | Several impossible star-like lights embedded in the dark face of the Moon |
| Binoculars / small telescope | Distinct geometric clusters and national motifs |
| Television / observatory telescope | The complete planned beacon patterns, base lighting, reflective panels and surface installations |

That is much more believable than demanding that every person resolve a giant national emblem unaided.

# The national displays

I would make this explicitly cooperative without eliminating national rivalry.

Each power receives a designated display zone, chosen according to existing infrastructure and Earth visibility rather than simply wherever its main base happens to sit.

That solves two geographic problems.

**Mondhafen Süd is too close to the lunar south pole** for a complicated symbol to present cleanly toward Earth. Features are heavily foreshortened there.

Likewise, if **Our Lady of the Moon** is eventually placed sufficiently close to the lunar limb to obtain its periodic Earthrise behind the altar, a large nearby cross would also be badly foreshortened.

So the lights do not all sit immediately outside the front door of the corresponding settlement. The German and Latin systems place some ceremonial beacons hundreds of kilometres toward the visible near side, linked administratively and by transport to their bases.

The patterns themselves can be unapologetically national because the cooperation lies in everyone agreeing to perform them together.

The Latin bloc's is the easiest: a **Latin cross of five or perhaps nine brilliant points**.

America can use a **five-pointed star**, probably outlined with ten beacon nodes.

Japan can create a **circle or sun**, using perhaps eight or twelve points.

Britain/Commonwealth could use a stylized **crown or compass star**, rather than attempting the absurd complexity of a Union Jack at lunar scale.

And Germany can indeed make a **swastika**. But this is probably a thirteen- or seventeen-beacon pattern intended primarily to resolve through binoculars and television rather than unaided vision. Its ground coordinates are deliberately distorted—an **anamorphic layout**—so that foreshortening makes the symbol look geometrically correct from Earth.

That last point feels very German in this setting: the physical arrangement on the lunar surface looks strangely distorted if you stand beside it, because it was designed to be viewed from 384,000 kilometres away.

## Mare Serenitatis becomes Britain's showcase

Britain has the best location for the visual spectacle.

Mare Serenitatis—the Sea of Serenity—is one of the large dark basaltic maria on the near side, and it gives the Commonwealth a broad, comparatively uncluttered dark background. citeturn744405image0

So I would preserve your reflective-sheet idea **here**, but in a supporting role.

During 1998–99, Commonwealth surface vehicles unroll large fields of metallized film around selected parts of the Serenity complex. Some serve thermal, radio, communications or solar-engineering purposes after the celebration; others are frankly ceremonial.

They do not make Britain naked-eye visible on the night side.

Instead:

- active beacons provide the Earth-visible lights;
- the sheets make the entire British complex extraordinarily conspicuous through telescopes when illuminated;
- and as lunar morning eventually reaches Serenity, the Commonwealth site becomes a bright artificial patch against the naturally dark basalt.

For several days after the initial ceremony, telescopic photographs continue changing as sunlight advances across the beacon fields and reflective installations.

So the spectacle has an afterlife rather than lasting ten minutes.

# The cooperative finale is what makes the event memorable

The individual national displays are impressive.

But if you want the genuinely wholesome setting-defining image, I would **not** make the final image merely five competing national logos.

Instead the ceremony happens in three movements.

First, each cluster illuminates independently as its national broadcast introduces the crews and workers who built it.

Then all five national patterns illuminate simultaneously.

And finally the colors or distinctive flashing patterns disappear and **every beacon turns the same white**.

For several minutes, there are simply dozens of human-made points scattered across the dark face of the Moon.

No slogan.

No attempt to draw an Earth-sized word.

Just the obvious fact:

**people live there.**

That is the image.

A natural crescent hangs on one side. Earthshine reveals the dim outline of the rest of the Moon. And inside that darkness are artificial lights belonging to several civilizations that spent much of the previous half-century preparing to fight one another and nevertheless cooperated long enough to do this one ridiculous, magnificent thing.

The photograph in every 2000 retrospective is not necessarily taken by somebody standing outside without magnification. It is a high-resolution observatory photograph deliberately exposed so that the earthlit lunar surface is visible without blowing out the beacon points.

But people on Earth **did see the lights themselves**.

That's important.

A father wakes his children at four in the morning. Someone brings binoculars into the street. Television stations tell viewers exactly where to look. Astronomical societies put telescopes in public squares. In parts of the world with clear skies, people can pick several individual lights out unaided.

For the first time, an ordinary person can look at another celestial body and see something on it that unquestionably was put there by human beings.

That is the emotional core.

## I would canonize the event roughly this way

The **Millennium Lunar Illumination** is agreed among the five great space systems during the late 1990s and operates across the transition from 31 December 1999 to 1 January 2000. Because the Moon is a roughly 20-percent-illuminated waning crescent on 1 January, the principal public observing periods occur before local dawn rather than at midnight. The display therefore runs on a rolling global schedule long enough for the Moon to become visible from each major inhabited region. citeturn652983search0turn426835search1

Its principal display units are high-power, Earth-tracking optical beacons positioned at lunar bases, mines, relay sites and temporary ceremonial stations. Individual beacons are bright enough to appear as unresolved artificial stars; groups are separated by hundreds of kilometres so that binoculars and small telescopes resolve crosses, stars, circles and national emblems. The complete patterns are several hundred kilometres across because normal human visual resolution is about one arcminute while the whole Moon is only about thirty arcminutes wide. citeturn631170search1turn744405search1

The national displays culminate in a synchronized white-light sequence in which all sites remain illuminated together. The resulting image—a waning crescent surrounding an earthlit lunar disk marked by dozens of artificial lights—becomes the defining public image of the turn of the century.

And I think the fact that **1 January 2000 accidentally gives us a waning crescent rather than a full Moon is a gift to the setting**. A full Moon would make the lights technically harder to distinguish and visually less dramatic. The actual sky gives you almost exactly the background you would choose if you were designing the photograph yourself.

# The largest new issue created by this chat: who owns space?

This is now unavoidable.

Up through 1985, orbital law can concentrate on:

- registration;
- rescue;
- debris;
- approach notification;
- station safety;
- military inspection;
- and protection of life support.

But by 2000 we have something qualitatively different.

There are now:

- permanent lunar settlements;
- industrial mines;
- propellant facilities;
- corporate American installations;
- national British, German and Japanese bases;
- Latin facilities;
- a German settlement on Mars;
- an American settlement on the other side of Olympus;
- a British presence in Valles Marineris;
- Japanese preparations elsewhere;
- and actual extraterrestrial construction using local resources.

Someone has to answer:

> Does planting a flag claim land?

And I think the answer should probably be **no—but continuous occupation creates a protected jurisdictional zone**.

That gives us a plausible middle course between two impossible extremes.

The powers are not going to accept:

> “Germany landed near Olympus first, therefore Germany owns Olympus Mons.”

But neither are they going to accept:

> “A British expedition may build a laboratory fifty metres outside the German airlock because celestial bodies cannot be claimed.”

The mature rule probably becomes something resembling:

**No sovereignty through symbolic discovery. Real jurisdiction through actual occupation and continuing use.**

That would naturally generate categories such as:

- settlement zones;
- safety zones;
- mining concessions;
- transport corridors;
- scientific preserves;
- navigation facilities;
- temporary exploration claims;
- abandonment rules;
- and perhaps an upper limit on territorial exclusion unsupported by actual infrastructure.

This would explain your “Scramble for the Solar System” without turning every landing into absurd continent-sized paper sovereignty.

And it immediately creates future conflicts.

Suppose an American mining company starts excavating sixty kilometres from a German Martian water-processing installation.

Is sixty kilometres close?

Mars is enormous.

The Germans may say yes because the aquifer or transport route is part of their settlement's economic hinterland.

The Americans may say:

> “Then use it. You don't get three million square kilometres because you put a pipe in one valley.”

That is exactly the kind of dispute the twenty-first-century Concert will need to solve.

I think **this may be the single most important conceptual subject remaining before we go past 2000.**

- whether there is another conclave before 2000;
- how Rome responds to mature Ordensglaube;
- what Rome does about the Second Cristiada settlement and possible Mexican monarchy;
- and especially how ecclesiastical jurisdiction follows Catholics into orbit and onto the Moon.

The first permanent Catholic priest on the Moon is not merely a flavor detail.

Rome has to decide whether Our Lady of the Moon is:

- a parish of some terrestrial diocese;
- under a military or personal ordinariate;
- under an apostolic administration for extraterrestrial missions;
- or the beginning of an entirely new territorial jurisdiction.

Then Mars happens.

And Ceres.

By 2010, the Church needs canon law for clergy who may be **months or years beyond the practical reach of their bishop**.

That is extremely AltWWII and worth developing.

---

# Africa needs one consolidation pass

I would not attempt to map every African government before 2000, but what you established in the previous turn needs to be made coherent.

The existing Commonwealth canon already gives South Africa enormous leverage over Britain because the Cape route is indispensable, and London's willingness to confront apartheid is correspondingly limited. fileciteturn15file1

Your new development takes that further:

Britain's strategic attention moves toward space while South Africa, Rhodesia and other African Commonwealth governments gain even more domestic discretion. At the same time they develop increasingly practical relationships with Portuguese Angola and Mozambique and German Mittelafrika.

That requires us to decide the broad 2000 condition of:

**South Africa:** apartheid preserved, modified, or reorganized into what mature form?

**Rhodesia:** still a white settler state, presumably closely integrated economically with South Africa, but exactly what is its constitutional status?

**Kenya/East Africa:** much less clear because London's direct constitutional leverage is greater.

**Portuguese Africa:** what became of the 1970s insurgent/criminal wars we developed?

**Mittelafrika:** what does post-Häuptlingskrieg German Africa look like after another twenty years of the Mosaic Order?

And then the demographic-policy diffusion you just suggested needs careful definition.

That is not merely flavor. If South Africa and Rhodesia deliberately adopt racially differential fertility policy after watching Mittelafrika, that will affect population balance enormously by 2000–2020.

So I would settle it before doing serious twenty-first-century African demography.

---

# What we do **not** need to settle before 2000

This is equally important, because otherwise we'll never cross the date.

The pending ledger still contains a large number of real questions that I would deliberately leave behind for later.

The exact East Indian constitutions, Manchukuo–Far East Amur settlement, Mongolian house law, Pacific incorporation dates, Indian design-bureau allocations and Burmese war names are all still open. fileciteturn15file0 They matter if we zoom into those regions. They do **not** prevent us from understanding the global order in 2000.

Likewise, we can safely postpone:

- the exact 1947 corporate geography of Renault, Peugeot and Citroën;
- the final blocked-property settlement for every American-owned German firm;
- the Congo patrol-craft registry;
- precise Frontier spacecraft masses;
- Formula One's 1952 scoring;
- Japanese home-video format names;
- exact gold parities;
- and the creators of the 1975 hobbyist computer.

Those are reference-work debts, not chronological blockers.

Even the exact specifications of the 1990s German Mars ship can remain working. We have now established its **architecture and mission logic**, which is what later history needs.

---

# One thing I would explicitly mark as resolved from this chat

The nuclear question is closed.

The Setting Bible currently states only that nuclear weapons never become a wartime technology and that the age develops around peaceful nuclear power. fileciteturn14file15

We have now carried that much further:

**No great power produces an operational nuclear weapon through the 1990s or 2000s.**

All understand the physics.

Germany comes closest to a weapons-development capability.

None constructs the dedicated military fissile-material and weapon-production establishment.

The absence survives because there is no first-mover arms-race trigger, no compelling military mission worth the cost, and a powerful cultural and political taboo around deliberately crossing the atomic-weapons threshold.

That no longer needs reopening unless we intentionally decide centuries later that somebody breaks the equilibrium.

Similarly, the **Five-Power Concert logic** is now sufficiently developed to carry forward. We know why there is no Third World War: not MAD, but an increasingly unfavorable relationship between the achievable military objective and the political cost of winning and governing the peace.

---

# My recommended remainder of this chat

I think we need **four substantial discussions**, followed by one synthesis.

First, finish **Britain 1986–2000** and decide whether Calder is the British space politician, when he comes to power, and the exact milestones of Resolution, Serenity and Mars.

Second, do **“The Five Powers in 2000”**: Germany, America, Japan, Britain and the Latin bloc—heads of state/government, principal institutions, immediate objectives, and unresolved internal succession problems.

Third, build the **extraterrestrial legal order**, probably from the late 1980s through the 1990s, culminating in whatever treaty framework governs Moon/Mars settlement and claims by the time of the Millennium Illumination.

Fourth, do **Rome and Africa to 2000**, probably as separate discussions: papal succession/off-world Church organization, then the mature African Commonwealth/Mittelafrika/Portuguese system.

Then we produce a **1 January 2000 world snapshot**.

And I think that's the point at which we should stop looking backward.

Because once those are fixed, we genuinely have enough. Everything else can be developed when the twenty-first-century story actually runs into it.

And the opening image for that new period is now settled: before dawn on 1 January 2000, people look up at the waning crescent, see the earthlit disk behind it, and scattered across the darkness are lights that unquestionably were not put there by God or nature, but by men.

At that point, the setting has earned the right to call what follows **the Space Age**.

Yes. I think this is better than making Calder alone the political father of Britain's space surge.

The clean model is that **Ashcombe builds the machinery, but two younger rival leaders turn it into a national mission**. One comes from Labour and insists that the Space Age must materially benefit ordinary British and Commonwealth families. The other comes from the governing right and insists that Britain must enter space as a sovereign civilization rather than become a passenger in German, American, Japanese, or Latin systems.

That gives the 1990s British space program something much more durable than one charismatic prime minister: **the electorate can change governments without changing the destination**.

Ashcombe's established Resolution Compact already gives them the institutional foundation—British control and design, Canadian avionics/life sciences, Australian launch and tracking, South African astronomy, and wider Commonwealth participation. fileciteturn14file0turn14file7 Calder is also already established as supporting space while demanding concrete civilian returns. fileciteturn14file2

## The new character

I would create **Edward James Mallory**, born in 1948.

The surname has an obvious British exploratory resonance without requiring him to be related to George Mallory. In-setting journalists would certainly make the comparison anyway.

Mallory comes out of the **Crown-and-Commonwealth wing of the National Liberal–Constitutional Union**, but he is distinctly different from Matthew Halden.

Halden is defensive. His instinct is:

> What must Britain retain so that nobody can subordinate us?

Mallory's instinct is:

> What should Britain build now that survival has been secured?

That difference is enough to produce an entirely new political generation.

### Edward Mallory

**Background:** Born in Birmingham in 1948 to a middle-class industrial family. His father is probably associated with machine tools, engines, or electrical manufacture rather than aristocratic politics. Mallory studies history and law rather than engineering, serves briefly in some Commonwealth administrative or naval-reserve capacity, then enters Parliament during the 1970s.

That is useful because we do **not** need another engineer. Ashcombe already occupies that niche.

Mallory understands enough technical material to work with experts, but his real gift is explaining why the machinery matters.

He comes into prominence during the Falklands era as one of the younger politicians arguing that Britain's problem is not insufficient courage but a failure to think in generations:

- merchant fleet;
- naval reserve;
- technical schools;
- families;
- industrial capacity;
- Commonwealth settlement;
- and eventually space.

Politically he is:

- monarchist;
- strongly Commonwealth-oriented;
- socially conservative;
- pronatalist;
- economically nationalist without being anti-market;
- skeptical of unrestricted foreign ownership;
- friendly toward employee property and small enterprise;
- hostile to the idea that finance should decide whether strategic industries continue to exist;
- and extremely interested in technology as an instrument of national continuity.

So he is much closer in temperament to the **National Renewal** tradition we developed in America than either Rooke or Ashcombe, without simply being a British copy of it.

His shorthand doctrine might eventually be called **National Development Conservatism** or simply the **Development Right**.

And his principal political argument becomes:

> Britain did not survive 1947, rebuild the Commonwealth, and fight its way through the South Atlantic merely to arrive at the threshold of another world and ask somebody else for a ticket.

That is the politician who can turn space into mass politics.

---

# Why Mallory does not replace Halden

This matters because we already have a right-wing cast.

Sir Julian Rooke represents the **market right**. His solution to almost everything is freer capital, asset sales, investment and closer American commercial ties. fileciteturn14file1

Matthew Halden represents the **defensive Commonwealth right**: military reserves, immigration control, Crown, bases, strategic ownership and suspicion of dependency. fileciteturn14file1

Mallory becomes the third position:

> **The expansionist developmental right.**

He agrees with Halden that Britain must remain sovereign.

But Halden thinks principally in terms of preserving what Britain possesses.

Mallory thinks preservation without expansion eventually becomes managed decline.

That is his central objection:

> “You cannot preserve a civilization indefinitely by placing it in storage.”

And unlike Rooke, he does not think the market will automatically decide Britain's strategic future correctly.

If a lunar reactor, heavy launcher or Mars expedition will not pay a commercial return for twenty years, Mallory regards that as an argument for state direction, not cancellation.

So during the 1990s Mallory gradually eats Halden's younger constituency while also attracting industrial voters who otherwise might vote Labour.

---

# Calder and Mallory should genuinely like each other—up to a point

Not personally intimate. Not secretly the same politician.

But they respect one another.

That matters.

Calder's fear is that Mallory's space program could become:

- flags;
- military contracts;
- prestige crews;
- huge aerospace companies;
- and beautiful photographs,

while Leeds, Glasgow or Newcastle is told there is no money for apprenticeships, housing or hospitals.

Mallory's fear is that Calder could reduce space to:

- weather satellites;
- telecommunications;
- scientific grants;
- employment policy;
- and carefully costed social returns,

until Britain possesses a respectable research program but never actually goes anywhere.

Each thinks the other is missing half the point.

And each is correct.

Their argument becomes one of the defining political exchanges of the 1990s.

### Mallory's formulation

> “A nation does not go to Mars because Mars improves the quarterly accounts.”

### Calder's answer

> “No. But the men who build the ship still have to go home on Friday.”

That is the British space consensus in two sentences.

---

# Ashcombe's tragedy is exactly what you described

Ashcombe does almost everything required to make the later achievement possible.

He:

- preserves aerospace firms;
- stabilizes Commonwealth procurement;
- expands Cape York;
- creates the Resolution Compact;
- funds deep-space tracking;
- protects strategic ownership;
- restores technical education;
- creates the legal framework for Commonwealth work-sharing;
- and refuses to let Resolution become an American auxiliary station. fileciteturn14file0turn14file11

But he does not give the famous speech.

He does not order the Mars expedition.

He does not preside over the first British lunar settlement.

And because he is Ashcombe, he probably isn't even particularly bitter about that.

A journalist eventually asks whether he minds that Calder and Mallory receive credit for the British Space Age.

Ashcombe answers something painfully characteristic, perhaps:

> “They could hardly have launched it if we hadn't built it.”

Not resentful.

Just factual.

Historians later rehabilitate him enormously. Popular memory remembers **Calder and Mallory**. Aerospace historians call Ashcombe the indispensable predecessor.

---

# The political sequence

I think the cleanest chronology is not a different government every two years. British parliamentary politics still needs enough continuity to accomplish anything.

Something like this gives us the alternating leadership you want without becoming chaotic.

### 1988–1992 — Ashcombe

Ashcombe wins the Peace Election and establishes the infrastructure.

Space policy is serious but deliberately restrained:

- continuous Resolution occupation;
- Commonwealth technical integration;
- launch expansion;
- lunar reconnaissance;
- deep-space communications.

Mallory rises within the governing party and increasingly attacks the government's lack of ambition.

Calder supports much of Ashcombe's infrastructure policy from opposition while arguing for stronger regional-industrial benefits.

Then comes Stella Maris and the German Mars effort.

Ashcombe's caution stops feeling reassuring.

### 1992 — Calder narrowly wins

I think Labour winning around **1992** works very well.

Not because Ashcombe has catastrophically failed.

The electorate simply thinks the rebuilding phase is finished.

Calder campaigns on something resembling:

> **“Build Britain Into the Future.”**

He does not dismantle Ashcombe's system.

Instead he expands:

- technical colleges;
- apprenticeship guarantees;
- regional aerospace plants;
- public research;
- medical and life-support science;
- civilian satellite services;
- worker participation in aerospace firms;
- and the early Serenity program.

But Calder remains cautious about the sheer prestige cost of racing Germany to Mars.

Mallory becomes his principal parliamentary critic.

### 1993 — the German landing changes everything

This is the political earthquake.

Germany has not merely sent a probe.

There are Germans living on Mars.

Mallory's position suddenly looks prophetic.

He begins arguing for an independent British landing **before 2000**.

Calder initially resists the deadline while accepting the objective.

That creates the compromise.

---

# The Greenwich Compact

I think this deserves a named cross-party agreement.

**The Greenwich Compact of 1993 or 1994** works extremely well.

Not a constitutional treaty.

A public political settlement negotiated between Calder's Labour government and Mallory's opposition faction, with Ashcombe quietly assisting because he understands the technical dependencies better than either.

Its significance is that the two plausible governments agree on several things that **will not be reopened at every election**.

The Compact commits Britain and participating Commonwealth governments to six enduring objectives:

1. maintain independent crewed access to orbit;
2. expand Resolution into a full permanent station;
3. establish permanent Commonwealth occupation of the Moon;
4. conduct an independent crewed Mars expedition before the end of the century;
5. maintain independent deep-space communications and navigation;
6. preserve domestic/Commonwealth control of the strategic industrial capacity required to do all five.

Parliament cannot legally bind every future Parliament forever.

So they make reversal practically difficult instead.

They create:

- ten- and fifteen-year contracts;
- Commonwealth treaty commitments;
- jointly funded Australian and Canadian facilities;
- launch-site capital investment;
- long-lead vehicle production;
- a permanent Commonwealth Space Authority;
- and statutory reporting requirements forcing any government that cancels a major objective to explain itself publicly.

The **Compact is political**.

The subsequent legislation and Commonwealth agreements make it material.

That is exactly why it survives.

---

# What each side gets

The agreement succeeds because Calder and Mallory are not agreeing for the same reason.

### Mallory gets

- the Mars deadline;
- permanent lunar occupation;
- heavy launch investment;
- strategic ownership rules;
- explicit settlement as a long-term objective;
- and recognition of space as a pillar of great-power sovereignty.

### Calder gets

- regional distribution of aerospace industry;
- apprenticeship quotas;
- civilian satellite guarantees;
- public research access;
- medical and agricultural applications;
- worker pension participation in some program investment;
- strict crew safety oversight;
- and a rule that Commonwealth settlements cannot simply become private company towns beyond ordinary labor law.

And Calder insists that the enormous expenditure must produce technologies useful on Earth:

- water recycling;
- remote medicine;
- power systems;
- communications;
- automation;
- materials;
- and agricultural control.

So neither side can accuse the other of surrendering.

Mallory gets Britain to Mars.

Calder makes sure Britain doesn't arrive there by hollowing out Britain itself.

---

# 1996 — Mallory takes office

This is where I would flip government again.

Calder's first term is respectable. Britain is growing. The space buildup is advancing.

But the right reorganizes around Mallory rather than returning to Rooke.

Mallory wins the **1996 election** on a program that is not a repudiation of Calder.

That is important.

He says, essentially:

> Labour proved that national development can serve the British worker. We intend to prove that the British worker can build a civilization.

He keeps Calder's:

- technical colleges;
- worker protections;
- regional aerospace investment;
- and parts of the social settlement.

He accelerates:

- lunar construction;
- heavy lift;
- Mars hardware;
- orbital defense;
- and settlement planning.

This also means British politics has escaped the old market-vs-nationalization binary.

Both major parties have accepted a mixed developmental state.

Their argument is now **what national development is for**.

---

# The Mars landing becomes a joint achievement

Mallory can be Prime Minister when Britain lands on Mars around 1998.

That gives him the famous moment.

But he should publicly include Calder.

Perhaps Calder is invited to the mission-control gallery.

Mallory's speech explicitly credits:

- Thatcher for preserving capacity;
- Ashcombe for building the Commonwealth system;
- Calder for passing the funding and training settlement;
- and the Commonwealth partners who actually built the mission.

That reinforces the healthier aspect you want in this setting.

These men disagree genuinely and sometimes viciously.

But neither wants Britain to fail merely because the other party happens to be governing.

The Mars landing therefore does not produce:

> “Mallory won.”

It produces:

> **“Britain did it.”**

---

# And then perhaps Calder returns

If we want genuine flip-flopping, Calder could plausibly return in **2000 or 2001**, particularly once the Mars prestige mission is accomplished and voters turn back toward domestic questions.

That would establish the mature rhythm:

- Calder governments emphasize settlement quality, public services, scientific return and Commonwealth labor standards.
- Mallory governments emphasize expansion, new destinations, strategic autonomy and settlement numbers.

Neither cancels the other's spacecraft.

That is the key.

By the 2000s, Britain can change governments without the launch schedule becoming existentially partisan.

---

## The two men become a political pairing

Foreign observers probably misunderstand them.

German analysts may initially talk about a Calder “left” and Mallory “right” as though one is pro-space and one anti-space.

That stops working very quickly.

Both want:

- Resolution;
- Serenity;
- Mars;
- Commonwealth launch independence;
- nuclear power;
- technical education;
- and a permanent British/Commonwealth presence beyond Earth.

They disagree over:

- ownership;
- labor;
- military emphasis;
- settlement governance;
- welfare;
- private profit;
- and how much money can be spent how quickly.

That makes them much more interesting.

By the late 1990s newspapers might describe the space consensus as the **Calder–Mallory Settlement**, even though both men dislike the implication that their politics are interchangeable.

Ashcombe, characteristically, would probably point out that the settlement rests on the Resolution Compact he negotiated years earlier.

And he would be correct. fileciteturn14file2turn14file11

## I think this is the British generational succession we were missing

**Thatcher** proves Britain can still fight.

**Ashcombe** proves Britain can build a sustainable postwar system.

**Calder** insists that technological greatness must carry ordinary society with it.

**Mallory** insists that a civilization which has recovered has an obligation to go somewhere.

And the combination of Calder and Mallory is why Britain catches up.

Not because one brilliant leader drags an unwilling country into space.

Because by the middle 1990s **both viable governments have concluded that remaining one of the Five Powers now requires being one of the Five space powers**.

That is a much more durable explanation for why Britain can still be building aggressively on Mare Serenitatis in 2010 even after several changes of government. memcite

## The closest real-world analogy

The F# analogy is actually stronger than merely “Felix likes F# syntax.”

Historically, early F# was conceived as a pragmatic marriage between strongly typed functional programming—initially especially OCaml—and the broader .NET environment. It was not intended to replace every imperative or object-oriented language; the point was to make functional programming operate naturally inside a large existing software ecosystem. citeturn428583search24

That should be Felix's breakthrough.

He does **not** want to overthrow:

- Rechenplan;
- Werkcode;
- Klasse;
- Bridge;
- Zivil-Planform;
- or Weltnetz.

He wants the functional language to be able to use all of them.

That makes his project fundamentally different from Folge 81.

---

# What Felix dislikes about Folge

Folge is intellectually elegant but by the late 1990s probably has a reputation somewhat like:

> “A wonderful language used by mathematicians, compiler people, university researchers, and three companies in Munich that nobody else understands.”

That is exaggerated, but not entirely unfair.

Its problems would probably be practical rather than theoretical:

- weak tooling compared with mainstream German commercial environments;
- relatively small library ecosystem;
- awkward access to Klasse/object libraries;
- awkward calls into Werkcode system APIs;
- limited graphical/application-development tooling;
- fragmented implementations;
- different university dialects;
- and a tendency among its strongest advocates to regard pragmatic impurity as regrettable.

Felix **likes** functional programming but finds functional purism irritating.

That is probably the character distinction worth emphasizing.

He sees no contradiction in writing mostly immutable functional code and then saying:

> “This window is an object. Call the object.”

Or:

> “The network service is stateful. Stop pretending it isn't.”

Or:

> “If the hardware register needs to be mutated, then mutate it—but put the mutation somewhere I can see.”

That's essentially the sensibility that makes an F#-like language plausible.

---

# The existing German architecture gives him his equivalent of .NET

Germany has something enormously useful that our F# did not have to invent: **Planform**.

Rechenplan already compiles through typed Planform into machine-specific code, and by 1982 **Zivil-Planform** serves as a common interoperability target for civilian languages. Programs written in Folge or Lehrplan can already call common disk, printer and service interfaces. fileciteturn17file4turn17file14

So Felix's insight around 2001–03 could be:

> **Stop treating Planform merely as an intermediate code format. Treat it as the common software environment.**

That is the wrench.

Falkenberg loves the idea in principle because Falkenberg's whole philosophy is heterogeneous machines communicating through common interfaces. Weltnetz itself was built around the principle that everyone need not use Rechenplan. fileciteturn17file1turn17file11

But the traditional computing authorities hear something much more threatening.

If Felix is right, then Rechenplan is no longer the language around which everything else orbits.

It becomes **one language targeting a common German execution ecosystem**.

That is a subtle but profound change in hierarchy.

---

# Felix's language should therefore be functional-first, not functional-only

The authorial F# model suggests a fairly clear design philosophy.

Its core would probably include:

- ML-style type inference;
- first-class functions;
- immutable bindings by default;
- algebraic data types;
- exhaustive pattern matching;
- tuples and records;
- parametric polymorphism;
- modules and namespaces;
- pipelines/composition;
- concise anonymous functions;
- lists, sequences, maps and sets;
- and strong compile-time checking.

Pattern matching and inferred types are central parts of the real F# style as well. citeturn428583search1turn428583search2turn428583search6

But Felix adds pragmatic features aggressively.

### Objects are allowed

The language can instantiate and call **Klasse** objects and imported Bridge objects.

Felix refuses the argument that object orientation is ideologically impure functional programming.

His answer is basically:

> Objects exist. Libraries exist. We are writing programs, not theology.

### Mutation is explicit but permitted

Mutable values exist, but they are visibly marked.

The language encourages immutability without pretending every application can be pure.

### Exceptions and system calls exist

Again, controlled and typed where practical.

### Foreign libraries are first-class

This becomes one of its killer features.

A Felix-language program can call:

- Rechenplan scientific libraries;
- Klasse graphical libraries;
- Werkcode system libraries;
- Nachricht network services;
- Bridge compatibility libraries;
- and eventually Japanese or Latin packages through wrappers.

The **interop story** is what turns an interesting language into a useful one.

# Lisp influences it differently from ML

I would not give Felix unrestricted Lisp-style macros. German certification culture would despise invisible source transformation, and it would make the language much less F#-like anyway.

Instead, Felix takes three things from Lisp.

### Interactive development

He loves the REPL.

That may actually be one of his strongest personal preferences.

German computing traditionally inherits a fairly heavy:

> write → compile → certify → run

culture from Rechenplan and the *Programmbuch*. fileciteturn16file4turn17file13

Felix enjoys being able to type an expression and immediately see what happens.

Older German engineers regard this as suspiciously informal.

He regards it as **thinking with the machine**.

### Symbolic manipulation

Lisp convinces him that programs can manipulate structured representations of programs and data.

He therefore adds something resembling **typed quotations** rather than raw macros.

Code can be represented, inspected and transformed, but the compiler retains enough type information that tools can reason about what happened.

That later becomes extremely valuable for:

- query builders;
- distributed computation;
- symbolic mathematics;
- validation;
- and eventually machine-learning systems.

### Small composable functions

More cultural than syntactic.

He becomes deeply attached to the idea that complex behavior should emerge from combining small independently understandable functions.

That is almost the philosophical opposite of giant administrative Rechenplan programs.

---

# There should be one distinctly German contribution

Otherwise we're merely recreating F# under another name.

I think the best one is **units of measure and dimensional types as a first-class language feature**.

Real F# has strong units-of-measure support, but in AltWWII this could arise independently from German:

- aerospace;
- nuclear engineering;
- machine tools;
- chemical processes;
- logistics;
- and certification culture.

Felix can ask a brutally German question:

> Why does the language know that a string cannot be added to an integer but not that metres cannot be added to kilograms?

So the type system can understand things like:

- metres;
- seconds;
- newtons;
- kilograms;
- Reichsmarks;
- kilowatt-hours;
- orbital velocities;
- pressure;
- fuel flow;
- and user-defined dimensions.

This is the feature that makes older engineering authorities begrudgingly take his project seriously.

They're still dubious about all the functional cleverness.

Then someone shows them that a dimensional mismatch which would have survived ordinary testing fails at compile time.

Now they pay attention.

---

# The language project's phases

Your instinct that it should develop slowly is right.

Felix is only twenty-one in 2000. He shouldn't walk into the Reich computing establishment and reinvent German software in twelve months.

## 2000–2002: private fascination

Felix spends time with:

- ML;
- Folge;
- Lisp systems;
- British functional research;
- American software tools;
- and imported documentation.

He writes increasingly elaborate private libraries and compiler experiments.

At first, even Falkenberg treats this as:

> Felix has found his hobby.

This is somewhat amusing within the family because Alexander is talking about Mars and religious civilization, Konrad is talking military exercises and motorsport, Sophie is appearing in films—and Felix is intensely explaining pattern matching over dinner.

Katharina probably understands approximately none of it but is happy he's enthusiastic.

Wolfgang understands enough to recognize that his son is taking it seriously.

## 2002–2004: the compiler project

Felix begins writing or sponsoring a proper compiler.

He does not work alone. That would be implausible and wrong for his character.

He gathers:

- a couple of Folge compiler researchers;
- Planform engineers;
- one Klasse interoperability specialist;
- a Bridge expert;
- and eventually a small state/university team.

His role is closer to:

- principal language designer;
- technical patron;
- specification editor;
- and extremely active programmer.

The first versions are genuinely rough.

## 2004–2006: the “prince's language”

This is when outsiders notice.

German programmers give it a mildly mocking nickname:

> **Prinzensprache** — “the prince's language.”

The criticism is obvious:

> Of course his hobby gets a compiler team. His surname is Hitler.

And there is truth in that.

A twenty-five-year-old engineer without Felix's family would have to fight considerably harder for those resources.

Felix himself is uncomfortable with this criticism precisely because he knows it's partly valid.

So he makes a politically clever decision:

**publish the language specification openly inside the German civilian software system.**

Not necessarily completely open-source in our modern legal sense, but:

- documented;
- independently implementable;
- available to universities;
- not reserved for the Führer household;
- and not licensed exclusively to one favored corporation.

Now the language has to survive on whether programmers actually want to use it.

That gives it legitimacy.

---

# Where the institutional fight occurs

There are really four camps.

## Rechenplan establishment

Their objection:

> We already possess a validated, standardized, portable national programming system. Why are we creating another strategic language?

Felix's answer:

> I'm not proposing it for reactor control or weapons.

At least initially.

## Folge community

Ironically, these may be his most personally annoyed opponents.

Their reaction is:

> You took our language, added objects and commercial libraries, simplified some of the theory, and now everybody calls it revolutionary because you're Hitler's son.

Again, not entirely unfair.

This gives Felix some great technical arguments with serious academics who think he has vulgarized their work.

## Commercial software houses

They initially love the syntax but ask the only question that matters:

> Where are the libraries?

Once interoperability works, they become his strongest constituency.

A concise functional language with access to existing German and Bridge APIs is suddenly useful for:

- finance;
- scientific software;
- network services;
- data processing;
- simulation;
- and server applications.

## Falkenberg's network establishment

Falkenberg is supportive but keeps pushing Felix toward distributed computing.

Felix keeps answering:

> Not everything is a network problem, Matthias.

That can become a running joke between them.

Falkenberg wants the language to become the natural language of Weltnetz services.

Felix wants it to be useful **even when the machine isn't connected to anything**.

That distinction preserves their established relationship beautifully.

---

# The mid-2000s breakthrough

I would avoid having it suddenly become Germany's dominant language.

A better success is that around **2006–08** one important project adopts it.

Possibilities include:

- a Weltnetz search/indexing system;
- financial analysis;
- Raumhafen logistics;
- scientific modeling;
- compiler infrastructure;
- a large statistical system;
- or planetary mission planning.

My favorite would be **Raumhafen/Mars logistical planning**, partly because that reconnects Felix to his family's space project without making him an aerospace engineer.

The software problem involves:

- heterogeneous cargo types;
- schedules;
- orbital windows;
- resource constraints;
- failures;
- alternative routing;
- and lots of immutable planning states.

Functional programming is extremely well suited to that kind of transformation-heavy domain.

The program succeeds.

Suddenly the language stops being:

> Felix Hitler's interesting hobby.

and becomes:

> That language they used for the Mars logistics system.

That's the point at which universities start teaching it seriously.

---

# Its 2010 position

By the early 2010s, I would give it a strong but bounded niche.

It becomes especially common in:

- scientific computing;
- financial systems;
- network services;
- compiler work;
- data transformation;
- aerospace planning;
- statistics;
- symbolic systems;
- and increasingly machine learning.

It does **not** replace:

- Werkcode for kernels/drivers;
- Rechenplan for certified strategic systems;
- mainstream object languages for huge commercial GUI ecosystems;
- Kurzplan descendants for education;
- or Bridge-family languages internationally.

That is much more believable.

Its reputation becomes roughly:

> **The language German programmers love once they understand why anybody would want it.**

Which feels extremely appropriate for Felix.

---

# Naming

I would not decide the final name yet, but I think there are three particularly good directions.

### **Folgewerk**

My favorite at the moment.

It acknowledges that Felix did not invent German functional programming from nothing.

**Folge** supplies the intellectual ancestry.

**Werk** communicates that this is the practical, production-oriented version.

It also subtly answers the criticism:

> Folge is theory. Folgewerk builds things.

The Folge academics would probably hate that implication.

Excellent.

### **Funktionsplan**

Very German and immediately legible, but perhaps too bureaucratic and too obviously derivative of Rechenplan.

It sounds like something a ministry committee would name, not something Felix loves.

### **Formwerk**

More independent and elegant.

“Form” catches types, structure and transformations; “Werk” catches practical construction.

It also avoids explicitly subordinating the project either to Folge or Rechenplan.

I could imagine **Formwerk** being Felix's preferred name while journalists continue calling it *Prinzensprache* for years.

My slight preference is **Formwerk** if you want it ultimately to stand on its own, and **Folgewerk** if you want the lineage and academic controversy to remain obvious.

---

## The larger reason this works for Felix

This is exactly the kind of project he should have.

Alexander's interests naturally become monumental.

Konrad's are physical and public.

Felix cares about something that most people cannot even see.

There is a charming family absurdity to Wolfgang asking his adult sons what they are doing:

- Alexander is discussing religion, Mars and succession.
- Konrad is reorganizing some military or sporting institution.
- Felix says he has spent six months redesigning the type inference rules in his compiler.

And Felix may be **equally serious** about his answer.

The irony is that his apparently esoteric hobby can end up having enormous long-term consequences. Germany already established the principle under Falkenberg that it should **certify uses rather than ideas**, allowing a diverse civilian language ecology beneath Rechenplan's strategic dominance. fileciteturn16file8turn17file11 Felix becomes the next generation's test of whether that promise was genuine.

His project asks:

> Did Germany really mean that programmers could invent new ways of thinking?

Or did it only mean:

> You may experiment until the Führer's son invents something the old establishment finds inconvenient?

That is a very good computing conflict for the early twenty-first century—and it lets Felix matter politically through something he authentically loves rather than giving him an artificial succession ambition.

The medical evidence gives us considerably more freedom than I expected. **Parkinson’s is not normally inherited strongly from father to son**, and Adolf Hitler’s own condition cannot safely be treated as proof of a hereditary form.

There is also one small canon-date issue first: the current Setting Bible has Adolf Hitler dying on **12 February 1962**, not 1960. fileciteturn19file0 That actually works well for this question, because Wolfgang has direct adolescent memories of watching his father's physical decline before the succession.

### What we actually know about Hitler

The retrospective case that Hitler suffered from **parkinsonism** is fairly strong. Medical reviews point to progressive resting tremor, stooped posture, bradykinesia, smaller handwriting, reduced facial expression and gait problems during his final years. What remains disputed is the cause: some authors have considered ordinary idiopathic Parkinson's disease, while others have proposed post-encephalitic parkinsonism and other explanations. There was no neurological autopsy capable of settling the question. citeturn258408search0turn258408search1turn258408search2

So for AltWWII I would actually preserve the wording:

> **Adolf Hitler suffered from progressive parkinsonism, probably Parkinson's disease, but the exact etiology was never conclusively established.**

That is both historically defensible and useful for the setting.

The methamphetamine point is even less certain. There is evidence in modern populations that serious methamphetamine/amphetamine abuse is associated with an increased later risk of Parkinson's disease—for example, one large cohort found an elevated hazard compared with controls. citeturn725508search0turn725508search1 But that does **not** establish that Morell's drug treatment caused Hitler's parkinsonism, much less that it would somehow make the condition hereditary.

So Wolfgang does not inherit his father's drug exposure.

## Parkinson's inheritance is fairly weak in most families

The overwhelming majority of Parkinson's disease is not a simple Mendelian hereditary disorder. The Parkinson's Foundation currently estimates that roughly **10–15% of cases have a known genetic link**, while most people with Parkinson's do not have a known disease-causing inherited variant. Their simplified family-risk estimate is about **2% for someone with an affected relative versus about 1% without one**. citeturn754198search0turn754198search5

There are rare exceptions. Variants in genes such as **LRRK2** can behave in an autosomal-dominant fashion. If Adolf possessed such a variant, Wolfgang could have a 50% chance of inheriting the **variant**. But even then, penetrance can be incomplete: carrying the variant does not guarantee disease. And crucially, it is **not male-line inheritance**. Daughters could inherit it just as sons could. citeturn752890search12

Nothing about Hitler's known family history forces us to posit such a mutation.

So the medically conservative authorial conclusion is:

> **Wolfgang is at somewhat elevated risk if Adolf truly had idiopathic Parkinson's disease, but he is nowhere near genetically doomed to develop it.**

## Wolfgang's age actually gives us a very natural window

Born in late 1947, Wolfgang is approximately:

- **52 in 2000**
- **62 in 2010**
- **67 in 2015**
- **72 in 2020**

The average onset of Parkinson's is in the **early-to-mid 60s**; onset before 50 is considered early-onset and represents only a minority of cases. citeturn754198search3turn752890search7

So there is no medical reason Wolfgang should be visibly dying in 2000. At fifty-two, Parkinson's would actually be somewhat early.

But **the early 2010s are almost perfect** if we want him to develop ordinary Parkinson's without invoking an unusual hereditary syndrome.

And diagnosis would not mean rapid death. Modern Parkinson's patients can live many years after onset; published cohorts give median survivals on the order of roughly 15–18 years for many patients, although prognosis varies enormously with onset age, cognition and other illnesses. citeturn752890search1turn752890search8

A Wolfgang diagnosed at sixty-two could quite plausibly still be alive at seventy-two.

## I think the strongest character route is to give him Parkinson's—but not because he “inherited Hitler's disease”

I would make it a **supported authorial coincidence rather than genetic destiny**.

Something like this:

Around **2008–2010**, Wolfgang begins showing symptoms subtle enough that only Katharina and his physicians notice them at first. Perhaps reduced arm swing, stiffness after long meetings, slightly smaller handwriting, or a faint unilateral resting tremor.

This has an immediate emotional significance because Wolfgang remembers his father.

He knows what everybody else in the room is thinking before anybody says it.

By around **2010–2012**, specialists diagnose probable idiopathic Parkinson's disease.

Treatment works reasonably well. Levodopa, physical therapy, carefully managed exercise and potentially later deep-brain stimulation give him years of useful function. He remains mentally capable of governing.

The political problem is not:

> Wolfgang is incapable.

It is:

> **Wolfgang knows this is progressive.**

And that lets us create one of the strongest contrasts between father and son in the whole German story.

Adolf's decline became hidden, increasingly debilitating, and entangled with a state whose institutions depended upon pretending the Führer remained physically and intellectually inexhaustible. The existing German branch already has teenage Wolfgang watching his father's tremor, slowness, exhaustion and increasing difficulty while the household conceals how serious the decline has become. fileciteturn18file3

Wolfgang can decide:

> **I am not doing that to my children or to the Reich.**

He does not wait until he is bedridden.

He begins preparing the succession while everyone can still see that **he** is the person making the decision.

That is a much stronger voluntary handoff than having him simply die.

### The likely chronology I would favor

I would provisionally aim for:

**2009–2010:** first symptoms.

**2011:** private diagnosis.

**2012–2014:** symptoms become publicly noticeable despite treatment; Wolfgang begins formal succession preparations.

**2014–2016:** voluntary transfer of the Führership to Alexander, with the full institutional confirmation mechanism.

Wolfgang then remains alive as an elder statesman and family patriarch.

He might easily survive into the **early or middle 2020s**. Parkinson's slowly restricts his mobility and stamina, but he remains politically and personally relevant for years after retirement.

That gives Alexander a tremendous advantage compared with Wolfgang's own accession: **his father is still there to advise him**.

It also creates a very good relationship with Konrad's eventual refusal to challenge Alexander. Wolfgang can know about the administrative concern surrounding Alexander's SS sympathies while still deliberately choosing him.

## It also produces a powerful public moment

Eventually the tremor becomes visible.

Everybody knows what it resembles.

The foreign press immediately runs archival images of Adolf in his last years alongside footage of Wolfgang.

The regime cannot prevent the comparison.

But Wolfgang can destroy the comparison politically by handling it differently.

Instead of disappearing from view and pretending nothing is wrong, he can eventually make a controlled public statement along the lines of:

> He has Parkinson's disease. His physicians believe he can continue his duties for the present. The illness is neither shameful nor secret. And because the Führership exists to serve Germany rather than to provide employment until death, the succession will be settled before illness settles it for them.

That would be an extraordinary moment in the political evolution of the Reich.

It also reinforces something already embedded in the succession system: **Göring voluntarily gave the office to Wolfgang in 1965.** fileciteturn18file9 Wolfgang would therefore be following Göring's precedent rather than his father's.

That creates a surprisingly durable constitutional custom:

> The Führer may designate and transfer authority while still living.

And that may be much more important to the long-term stability of the pseudo-dynasty than whatever genetics gave Wolfgang the tremor in the first place.

So my recommendation is: **do not treat Parkinson's as a strongly inherited Hitler-family disease. But giving Wolfgang ordinary late-onset Parkinson's around age 61–64 is medically plausible and narratively excellent, because it gives him the chance to confront the same decline he watched in his father and deliberately choose a different ending.**
