# Aviation needs the same “experimental versus operational” distinction

The Me 262 first flew under jet power in July 1942 historically; the Smithsonian and Deutsches Museum both place the decisive all-jet flight in that window. citeturn911572search0turn911572search2

Your divergence does **not** require moving that flight.

It changes what happens afterward.

### The experimental night interception is plausible, but I would not put radar aboard the first one

Early airborne interception radar is bulky, crew-intensive equipment. Trying to turn the first single-seat Me 262 prototype into a complete radar night fighter immediately after its first jet flights is the sort of thing that makes the development program less believable.

The cleaner sequence is **ground-controlled night interception first**.

During the winter of 1942–43, one or two jet prototypes are temporarily placed with a night-fighter evaluation detachment. Ground radar and Himmelbett controllers vector the jet toward a bomber stream.

The Me 262 has awful endurance for this mission at the moment. Its engines are experimental. It lacks onboard radar. It may get only one interception opportunity.

But one opportunity is enough.

Imagine a Lancaster crew reporting that an aircraft came through the formation at a speed unlike any Bf 110 or Ju 88 they'd encountered. A gunner sees no propeller discs. Another crew reports the peculiar sound. British radar plots show an implausibly fast interceptor.

One report gets dismissed.

Three become an intelligence problem.

German aerial experimentation has now **revealed the existence of a jet fighter without revealing that the thing is nowhere near squadron readiness**.

That's perfect.

### Then the dedicated night-fighter Me 262 becomes a 1943 development branch

Once the experiment works, the Luftwaffe funds a proper two-seat or radar-equipped night derivative much earlier.

Not mass production.

A development aircraft.

That means when the Me 262 program gets its major 1943 production commitment, the requirement already includes **day interceptor and night interceptor branches**.

The home-defense problem in this timeline is British night bombing, so this makes much more sense than allowing the night fighter to remain an afterthought.

The Me 262 can therefore have the unusual historical distinction you're looking for:

**Germany uses a jet in combat first, experimentally.**

**Britain may officially field a jet squadron first.**

**Germany then fields the more capable first major operational jet fighter force.**

That is exactly the sort of thing historians argue about for eighty years.

## Britain does not need to invent jets after the encounter—it needs to reprioritize them

This is the main correction I'd make.

Britain already had a real jet effort before 1943. Whittle's work and the Gloster development path existed, and historically the Meteor first flew on 5 March 1943. The Vampire project was also underway and its prototype flew later that year. citeturn499535search0

So in our setting, I wouldn't say Britain had **abandoned jet propulsion entirely**.

I would say the wartime emergency had pushed it into a low-priority experimental category.

Immediate production of Spitfires, night fighters, radar, bombers, engines, naval aircraft, and replacement equipment matters more than an immature jet fighter whose engines are not yet trustworthy.

Then RAF crews encounter the Me 262.

The Air Ministry's conclusion becomes:

> The Germans are not merely experimenting with engines. They are already evaluating a jet as a combat interceptor.

That changes priority.

Meteor goes from *promising future fighter* to **emergency national air-defense program**.

Historically the Meteor prototype flew in March 1943 and the program had enough developmental basis that accelerating limited service by several months is much easier than inventing a jet from scratch. citeturn499535search0

I would therefore consider:

**early 1943:** Meteor prototypes fly.

**late 1943:** first limited operational RAF jet detachment.

**1944:** real squadron deployment.

That easily gives Britain substantial jet forces by the Second Battle of Britain.

### German piston development doesn't stop

The Bf 109 and Fw 190 continue recognizable historical evolution because production improvements, better engines, armament changes, and field modifications are still useful.

What Me 262 priority probably kills or slows is **the next speculative piston generation**, not ordinary Bf 109G or Fw 190A/F development.

Germany isn't going to shut down the fighters protecting its army because a jet prototype is promising.

It is going to redirect the most talented forward-looking engineers, test capacity, scarce high-temperature materials, and political attention away from increasingly elaborate clean-sheet piston projects.

That is a much more natural tradeoff.

## Graf Zeppelin gives Germany a small but real naval-aircraft branch

Bf 109T should absolutely survive if Graf Zeppelin survives as an active construction program.

The aircraft doesn't have to be a front-line 1943 naval fighter yet. It becomes the **carrier-training and doctrine-development aircraft**.

A small Träger unit practices arrestor approaches on shore, deck-handling procedures, corrosion control, naval radio procedure, and the peculiar logistics of an aircraft whose airfield moves.

That is useful even while the ship itself remains incomplete.

And I like introducing Focke-Wulf competition.

The Fw 190 has two attributes that would make the Kriegsmarine interested immediately: its wide-track landing gear is much friendlier to deck operations than the Bf 109's narrow gear, and its radial engine is attractive for maritime robustness.

So during 1942–43 the Kriegsmarine can sponsor a **navalized Fw 190 study**, probably initially aimed at fighter-bomber, reconnaissance, and anti-shipping work rather than instantly replacing the Bf 109T.

That creates a real procurement contest:

Messerschmitt argues that Bf 109T already exists and wastes less time.

Focke-Wulf argues that its aircraft is better suited to repeated hard carrier landings and carries useful strike weight.

The carrier isn't ready yet, so Germany has time to test both.

Again: denser portfolio.

---

## Guided anti-shipping weapons get more, not less, relevant

Germany still has every reason to keep Hs 293 and Fritz X development moving.

The historical Hs 293 reached combat use in August 1943, and Fritz X followed in the same period. citeturn499535search4 The absence of American pressure doesn't remove their purpose because Britain remains a major naval opponent.

If anything, Malta and Torch make the argument clearer:

> A bomber does not need to penetrate the fleet's entire AA envelope if it can release a guided weapon outside the most dangerous part of it.

So I would keep roughly the historical **maturity date**, but give Germany a larger evaluation and production base afterward.

The difference is not “Fritz X in 1942.”

The difference is that after it works in 1943, no collapsing strategic situation prevents a sustained family of guided anti-ship weapons from developing.

Italy then becomes a logical technical partner rather than a future victim.

# Peenemünde: one naming correction, then I agree with the direction

The A4 successful-flight anchor on **3 October 1942** should remain. NASA identifies October 1942 as the first successful launch, with historical sources specifically recording the 3 October test. citeturn911572search1turn911572search12

But the Aggregat numbers are not a simple chronological staircase.

**A5 actually precedes A4 as a smaller development/test vehicle.**

So the richer alternate program should not be:

A4 → A5 → A6.

It should be more like:

A5 continues as a guidance/recovery/reentry test platform while A4 matures; then A6, A7, A8, A9, and A10 studies branch into different propulsion, winged, long-range, and booster problems.

This is actually better for what you want.

Germany has enough resources that some projects historically left as paper or very limited experiments can reach hardware.

I would still prevent it from becoming “Germany has an ICBM in 1944.”

The plausible acceleration is:

**1943:** funded A4 improvement, high-altitude scientific payload work, winged and long-range studies.

**1944:** experimental winged A4-derived vehicles and larger-engine/propellant work.

**1945:** A9-type high-speed winged upper-stage prototypes become genuine flight hardware; A10-scale booster work reaches major static and structural tests.

**1946–47:** increasingly explicit military-space crossover—high-altitude instrumentation, recoverable payloads, guidance experiments, staging demonstrations.

That gives Raumbote I a much richer ancestry.

The rocket program after 1947 isn't “we found the V-2 and decided to go to space.”

It's an institution that has already been thinking about **staging, recovery, wings, high-altitude research, long-range guidance, and larger boosters for years**.

# Britain: don't slim Cromwell by 20 percent—Cromwell is already the slim answer

This is the biggest equipment correction on the British side.

Cromwell was not really a heavy tank. The Tank Museum gives the historical Cromwell IV at about **27.5 tons** and emphasizes its high speed; it was already built around mobility and the powerful Meteor engine. citeturn868343search1

Dropping another twenty percent puts it around 22 tonnes.

At that point you are trying to keep a useful turret, crew, ammunition, Meteor engine, fuel, cross-country suspension, and meaningful armor inside what is becoming light-tank weight.

I don't think we need to do that.

Your British logistical logic works better if it manifests as **strict refusal to let Cromwell grow heavier**.

In our setting, every ton matters because Britain expects to ship its army across the Commonwealth.

So the alternate Cromwell requirement stresses:

shipping dimensions;

bridge loading;

 landing-craft compatibility;

engine accessibility;

dust filtration;

cooling;

long-range road reliability;

low track and suspension wear;

and high power-to-weight ratio.

Historical Cromwell already gives us the right starting architecture. Its development suffered faults that historically took nearly two years to resolve before combat service; Britain under this pressure has a good reason to devote more effort to solving those reliability problems early. citeturn868343search1

So instead of making the tank radically lighter, I'd make it **earlier, better debugged, and prevented from suffering armor creep**.

Perhaps 25–27 tonnes becomes the target range.

That is already a superb expeditionary weight compared with Panther or Tiger.

### Torch gets a few Cromwells

That also fits your earlier campaign.

Not hundreds.

A pilot regiment or even a couple of squadrons can go to Algeria because the Army urgently wants operational data.

Some are lost.

One or more eventually reach Italian hands after the capitulation.

And what Italian engineers find interesting may not even be the armor.

It's the **Meteor engine, transmission, cooling, filters, track arrangement, engine access, and the fact that the British got this performance from a tank substantially lighter than P40's German competitors**.

That absolutely influences Italian post-Torch design.

### Comet should accelerate, but I would distinguish prototype from service

The historical Comet requirement appeared in 1943; its prototype was running by February 1944, and deliveries began later that year. It was extensively redesigned from Cromwell—only around forty percent of parts remained unchanged according to the Tank Museum. citeturn868343search0

So full operational Comet units in autumn 1943 feels too fast.

But we can move the entire process forward.

Torch gives Britain two shocks simultaneously: the P40 is better than expected, and intelligence from the east keeps reporting increasingly powerful German guns and heavy tanks.

So instead:

**spring 1943:** accelerated next-cruiser requirement.

**autumn 1943:** first A34/Comet prototype.

**December 1943:** troop-trial vehicles.

**early 1944:** first operational formation.

That's roughly a year ahead in actual combat availability without pretending a substantially revised tank goes from drawing board to mature battalion in six months.

And British doctrine remains distinctive.

It doesn't answer Panther with “build a British Panther.”

It answers:

> Make the cruiser lethal enough to survive the expeditionary battlefield without turning it into a forty-five-ton shipping problem.

That is exactly the path that later makes Centurion interesting.

---

# Italy: 1943 should be its “Serie 5” moment

I agree on retaining all three major high-performance piston fighters rather than rationalizing them away prematurely.

C.205, G.55, and Re.2005 all reach the setting because Italy still has competing design houses and no armistice terminates their development.

But Italy's constraint is engines and production scale.

So they remain a **small modern spearhead inside a larger older air force** during 1943.

That is actually visually and institutionally useful. One squadron may have genuinely first-rate new fighters while the formation beside it is still flying C.202s.

The Regia Aeronautica learns which airframe is easiest to manufacture, which has the best altitude performance, which is easiest to maintain in North Africa, and which offers the best naval-development potential.

Then 1944–45 can rationalize the survivors.

Again: first broaden, then select.

---

# Japan needs to diverge in a different direction

I agree strongly that importing Panzergrenadier doctrine into Japan would be wrong.

The Japanese strategic problem is not Germany's.

Germany has enormous continental fronts where armored formations need infantry capable of fighting **with the tanks**.

Japan is fighting across China and maritime Asia where roads, bridges, shipping capacity, mountains, jungle, rice country, and huge infantry requirements all punish heavy mechanization.

So Japanese tracked carriers remain **battle taxis**.

They bring infantry through dangerous approaches.

They drop them.

Then the infantry fights primarily dismounted.

That should remain a very visible doctrinal difference between the two Axis armies even after decades of technical exchange.

### The 1942–43 Japanese tank question should be split in two

The **actual China requirement** asks for reliability, useful HE, good cross-country performance, infantry support, communications, and enough armor to defeat Chinese antitank weapons.

The **Soviet contingency requirement** asks a much nastier question:

> What if we eventually have to fight the tanks Germany keeps reporting?

That is where the dog-eared Strike North file starts influencing R&D before it influences strategy.

I would keep the improved 47 mm medium family as the principal production equipment of 1942–43.

Meanwhile, a 75 mm gun/tank program receives growing support. The justification isn't exclusively tank-versus-tank fighting; a 75 mm weapon is also extremely useful against Chinese fortified positions and fieldworks.

So Japan can begin building the **Chi-He/Chi-Nu-type transition** sooner and in somewhat more serious numbers without pretending China suddenly contains Soviet tank armies.

The heavier Chi-To/Chi-Ri direction is then the Soviet contingency family: larger gun, improved suspension, stronger frontal protection, and enough growth margin for a northern continental war.

It stays secondary until Berlin's victories make Strike North look genuinely plausible.

And Japanese procurement continues emphasizing trucks, artillery tractors, bridging, engineers, radios, transport aircraft, and compact armored vehicles, because those provide more benefit in China than trying to create a Japanese Panzer division.

The same principle should govern Japanese aircraft: they keep developing serious fighters and carrier aircraft, but range, reliability, naval endurance, and China-ground-support needs shape them differently from German interception requirements. Japan's technical establishment was already watching German jet work; Smithsonian records note that Japanese representatives were aware of Me 262 testing during the war. citeturn911572search5

We can do the dedicated Japanese 1942–45 equipment pass separately rather than casually inheriting the old reference tree.

---

# The Soviet contrast should not be technological stupidity; it should be forced simplification

This is important.

The Soviet arsenal should not literally become more primitive every year in the sense that engineers forget how to build things.

It becomes **narrower**.

Germany's advantage after 1942 is that more projects can remain alive.

The Soviet advantage is increasingly that it knows exactly which projects it cannot afford.

So Soviet production concentrates brutally around things that can be made in enormous numbers from existing tooling:

T-34 family;

simple assault guns;

ZiS-type field and antitank guns;

Mosin rifles;

PPSh/PPS submachine guns;

reliable machine guns;

simple trucks where possible;

and enormous repair/cannibalization systems.

Advanced heavy tanks, new turrets, improved optics, and more powerful antitank systems still appear when the German threat demands them.

But every new system now has to answer:

**Which factory stops making something else?**

And the deeper problem is not necessarily the tank factories.

It is trucks.

Locomotives.

Rail stock.

Copper.

Radios.

Food.

High-quality fuel.

Machine tools.

Skilled workers.

The German force therefore becomes more **technically differentiated** with time.

The Soviet force becomes more **industrially monastic**.

By 1946 a German Panzergrenadier platoon may look startlingly modern.

A Soviet rifle regiment may still contain equipment whose basic pattern would have been completely familiar in 1942—not because the Soviets are incompetent, but because it is the equipment their collapsing industrial geography can still make, repair, and feed.

That is a much stronger contrast.

---

## The underlying German economic rule

And finally, I agree that we should not import historical **Totaler Krieg** mechanically.

The current wiki already characterizes Germany's later strength as technical ambition, mechanization, standardization, and a persistent military-industrial floor rather than simply one permanently maximized wartime command economy. citeturn515561view0

Historically, the famous *Totaler Krieg* political moment belongs to 1943; this Germany has no Stalingrad catastrophe, no American ground war, and nothing resembling the historical combined Anglo-American strategic bombing campaign.

That means German propaganda can genuinely boast that it has **not sacrificed ordinary national life in the manner Britain and the Soviet Union have**.

But we shouldn't translate that into free resources.

The eastern war still consumes extraordinary quantities of steel, fuel, locomotives, ammunition, tires, manpower, machine tools, and rail capacity.

The difference is that German factories remain standing, engineering departments remain together, and there is no western land campaign consuming another massive field army.

So I would use one governing rule throughout the equipment rewrite:

> **Additional German resources buy parallel development, longer testing, better maintenance infrastructure, and more second-generation designs before they buy universal mass issue.**

That is how we get a recognizably strange 1943–45 arsenal without turning the setting into Wehraboo science fiction.

By 1945, the photograph should indeed look wrong to someone expecting our Second World War: maintainability-focused Panzer Vs accompanied by purpose-built recovery vehicles; old but ubiquitous MG42s beside StG44s and emerging StG45As; roofed Kätzchen prototypes appearing beside endless Sd.Kfz.251s; dot-pattern Panzergrenadiers; experimental jets and guided weapons; multiple rocket development vehicles beyond A4.

But each of those things has a traceable **1942 problem that created it**.

That's the equipment history we should build.

Yes. I think **Italy as the third power to put a turbojet combat aircraft into service is quite plausible**, and the argument gets stronger once we distinguish several different “firsts.” The one correction is that the Caproni Campini N.1 itself was much less capable than its reputation might suggest. It was historically important, but it was a **motorjet**—a piston engine mechanically drove the compressor—and its performance was not exceptional compared with contemporary piston fighters. Italy's real advantage is not that the N.1 can be turned directly into a better fighter. It is that Italy already possesses an institutional nucleus of engineers, flight-test experience, ducted reaction propulsion, combustion work, and political interest in jet flight before anybody has to persuade Rome that the entire idea is real. citeturn714529search0turn612634search24

That gives us a very good alternate jet race.

## The “who was first?” argument should become genuinely messy

I would deliberately avoid a single clean ranking, because there are at least four defensible criteria:

| Criterion | Likely setting result |
|---|---|
| First Italian reaction-powered aircraft | **Italy — Campini-Caproni**, 1940 |
| First true turbojet aircraft among the eventual combatants | **Germany**, from the prewar Heinkel work |
| First turbojet used against an enemy | **Germany**, via experimental Me 262 interception |
| First formally operational jet fighter squadron | **Potentially Britain**, depending on the exact dates we set |
| Third country to deploy a true turbojet combat aircraft | **Italy** |
| Fourth | **Japan or the United States**, depending on what we mean by deployment |

That gives historians something to fight about for decades.

The RAF historically declared No. 616 Squadron operational with Meteors in 1944, while the first historical Me 262 jet combat occurred in July 1944. citeturn470299search0turn623287search24 In our setting, because the Germans conduct an earlier **experimental combat interception** while Britain responds by accelerating Meteor into an actual organized service unit, you can get the wonderful technicality:

> **Germany was first to fight with a jet. Britain was first to field jets as an operational fighter unit.**

Both statements are true depending upon the definition.

Then Italy becomes the **unambiguous third belligerent to field a true turbojet combat type**.

## But the Italian jet should not really descend mechanically from the Campini N.1

This is the most important technical distinction.

Campini's machine gives Italy experience with reaction propulsion, but it does not solve the difficult part of a true turbojet: a gas turbine driving its own compressor at extremely high rotational speed and temperature.

So Italy needs **German engine technology**.

That is completely plausible in this setting. Germany and Italy are allies, Italy has just won Malta and is carrying an increasing share of the Mediterranean war, and Germany is not desperately hoarding every experimental engine against an Anglo-American invasion. There is a strong strategic reason to make the Italian air force more capable.

I would make the sequence something like this.

### 1942 — Campini gets a second life

The Me 262's July 1942 jet-powered flight changes how the Regia Aeronautica interprets its own earlier experiment. Historically, Campini's approach was rapidly becoming a dead end as true turbojets proved superior. In this timeline, the Air Ministry does **not** respond by doubling down on the motorjet. Instead it says:

> Campini was right about reaction propulsion and wrong about the engine architecture.

That is an enormously healthier institutional response.

Campini and the surviving N.1 engineering organization become a **reaction-propulsion research office** rather than being expected to provide the actual production engine.

They work on:

- intakes and airflow;
- combustion;
- jet-pipe geometry;
- high-speed airframe integration;
- thermal protection;
- controls;
- test instrumentation;
- and eventual afterburning research.

The Germans supply the missing knowledge about compressors, turbines, and practical turbojets.

### 1943 — Germany transfers an engine package

This is where I would make a fairly explicit Axis technology-sharing deal.

Italy receives perhaps:

- one or more Jumo 004 development engines;
- drawings and manufacturing information;
- Junkers technical advisers;
- metallurgy data;
- test instrumentation;
- and eventually permission for licensed manufacture.

Italy doesn't immediately manufacture a perfect 004 domestically. The metallurgy and precision-manufacturing problem is real.

So the **first Italian turbojet prototypes use German-built engines**.

Fiat, Isotta Fraschini, or another Italian engine concern simultaneously begins localization.

That is the key shortcut.

Italy does not have to reproduce Whittle or von Ohain independently from first principles. It is starting from a working engine sitting on a test stand.

## Then I would not make the Italian production fighter a modified N.1

The N.1 is too compromised by its original propulsion arrangement.

Instead, let the N.1 supply **people and institutional ancestry** while Italy's excellent fighter designers supply the airframe.

There are several possible branches.

A Caproni-led design has the strongest propaganda continuity: *the firm that put Italy into reaction flight now produces its first true jet fighter.*

A Reggiane-derived design has the strongest aerodynamics argument, because Reggiane is simultaneously producing the extremely refined Re.2005 piston fighter; the Italian Air Force records the Re.2005 at over 628 km/h. citeturn612634search11

Or, probably best, make it a **joint Caproni-Reggiane program**: Campini's propulsion/test organization, Reggiane's fighter airframe group, and a German-supplied or licensed engine.

That gives Italy a fighter that is unmistakably Italian rather than a license-built miniature Me 262.

### I would make it single-engined

This is where Italy can use its constraints creatively.

Germany builds a relatively large, heavy twin-engine Me 262 because it wants tremendous speed, heavy armament, and enough thrust for a substantial interceptor.

Italy does not need to copy that.

It wants something it can actually afford to manufacture.

So its first jet fighter could be a **small, light, single-engine interceptor** around one Jumo-derived turbojet. That necessarily gives up some performance and payload compared with the Me 262, but it also halves the jet-engine requirement per aircraft.

That matters enormously for Italy.

You could end up with something visually halfway between the elegant late-war Reggiane fighters and the first generation of postwar single-engine jets: relatively straight or modestly swept wings, nose or side intake, one engine, two cannon, short endurance, excellent speed compared with contemporary Italian piston fighters, but no pretense of being a long-range escort.

That feels much more Italian than “Me 262 with roundels.”

## A reasonable Italian timeline

I'd currently aim for:

**Late 1942:** true-turbojet Italian program formally authorized.

**Early 1943:** German engine and technical package arrives; Italian static testing begins.

**Late 1943:** first Italian true-turbojet prototype flies.

**Early–mid 1944:** service-test aircraft.

**Late 1944:** first small operational jet fighter unit.

**1945:** meaningful—but still limited—jet fighter strength.

That places Italy comfortably third without giving it hundreds of jets.

And because Italian industry remains the limiting factor, its jet force might be something like **dozens**, while C.205s, G.55s, and Re.2005s still constitute the modern piston core.

The jet is the spearhead, not the whole Regia Aeronautica.

---

# The Me 262 itself is also worth recalibrating

Your broader understanding is right, but I think you're conflating **Bodenplatte** with some of the Me 262's early interception problems.

Operation Bodenplatte on 1 January 1945 was principally the great Luftwaffe attack on Allied airfields. It was not the defining Me 262-versus-heavy-bomber interception battle. Me 262s did participate in the broader period and some jet units flew ground-attack operations, but the famous bomber interceptions belong to other engagements. citeturn206175search1turn206175search13

The more important point is that the Me 262 was **not simply a bad fighter that happened to be fast**.

At speed, it was an extremely dangerous interceptor. The RAF's own historical study notes both its high level-flight performance and that it could have a fine turn of speed when its engines behaved. The serious weaknesses were engine reliability, slow throttle response, poor acceleration at low speed, long-runway requirements, and vulnerability during takeoff, landing, and the initial climb. Allied piston fighters learned to exploit those phases. citeturn433044view1turn433044view0

So a good conceptual distinction is:

> **The Me 262 is bad at fighting like a Spitfire. It is very good at refusing to fight like a Spitfire.**

If it gets drawn into a low-speed turning fight, the piston fighter has opportunities.

If it makes a high-speed firing pass through a bomber formation and uses its speed to disengage, the conventional fighter has a much more difficult problem.

That is why the German night-interceptor experiment we established is so frightening to Britain. A bomber does not need the Me 262 to win a prolonged dogfight. It needs the jet to be vectored into position, make one brutally fast firing pass, and disappear.

## Also: I think you mean advanced piston fighters rather than turboprops

Actual **turboprops are not yet the mature alternative in 1943–44**. The RAF Museum dates the Rolls-Royce Trent turboprop's first flight in a modified Meteor to 1945. citeturn801841search0

What the early jets are competing against during most of this period are superb **late piston fighters**: Spitfires, Fw 190s, Bf 109s, Tempests, Reggianes, and so forth.

And those aircraft retain very real advantages:

- mature engines;
- better low-speed throttle response;
- longer endurance in many missions;
- easier field maintenance;
- better low-speed handling;
- and enormous existing production/training infrastructure.

So the jet does not instantly obsolete the piston fighter in 1943.

It establishes where high-performance interception is going.

---

# America is the strange case, because it already has a jet

This makes the ranking much more interesting than simply asking whether America can bootstrap jet technology.

It **doesn't need to**.

The XP-59 Airacomet first flew in the United States on 1 October 1942. The American engine itself derived from British Whittle technology. The U.S. Air Force Museum describes the P-59 as America's first jet, notes that the design's performance was disappointing, and that it never saw combat. citeturn504962search0turn504962search10

That program is also particularly likely to survive our divergence because its origins precede Pearl Harbor. It is not fundamentally a product of America's later total mobilization.

So I would actually keep:

**1942: American XP-59 flies.**

This creates another delicious historiographical complication.

An American historian can say:

> “Italy wasn't the third jet power. We had a true turbojet flying in 1942.”

The Italian response is:

> “Your prototype never fought anybody.”

And both can be right.

### The difference is what America does next

Historically the XP-59 was disappointing, while Lockheed produced the much more capable XP-80 remarkably quickly; its first flight came in January 1944. citeturn504962search1turn623287search5

In this setting America has **much less operational pressure**.

It is not sending fighter groups to Europe.

German jets are not intercepting American bomber streams.

The Pacific is not consuming American aircraft.

So I would expect the P-59 program to remain essentially an **experimental and conversion school**.

Perhaps ten or twenty rather than fifty production-type machines are eventually built.

The Air Corps learns jets.

GE learns turbine engines.

Bell learns jet airframes.

The Navy tests one.

But no one can point to a mission requiring an emergency jet fighter.

Then reports arrive that:

- Germany is using jets operationally;
- Britain is forming a jet squadron;
- Italy has a genuine turbojet fighter program;
- Japan is beginning one.

That is when America funds the equivalent of the P-80 in earnest.

American industrial capacity means it can close the gap frighteningly quickly once Washington decides it matters.

So I would put the United States around **1944 prototype / 1945–46 operational-service territory**, rather than having it asleep until the 1950s.

---

# Japan is nevertheless my preferred fourth **combat** jet power

This is where I agree with your instinct.

Historically, Japan's Kikka program began only in September 1944 after Japanese officials had observed the Me 262. The Smithsonian specifically notes that the Japanese air attaché had witnessed Me 262 trials, while the Kikka's indigenous Ne-20 engine was heavily influenced by the German BMW 003. citeturn623287search14turn623287search32

Our Japan has almost every reason to start that process earlier.

There is no Marianas catastrophe forcing desperation, but there also isn't:

- a devastated aviation industry;
- American bombing of the home islands;
- catastrophic fuel collapse;
- destroyed shipping;
- or the same difficulty simply keeping advanced programs alive.

And, more importantly, its liaison officer is seeing the Me 262 **actually demonstrate combat potential earlier**.

So Tokyo doesn't wait until September 1944 to say, “perhaps we should investigate this.”

It opens the folder in **1942–43**.

### The Kikka should still look like the Kikka

I agree strongly on this.

Its historical resemblance to the Me 262 has a real causal origin, not merely visual coincidence. Japanese officials had observed the German machine, and the Naval Staff explicitly asked Nakajima for a twin-jet aircraft inspired by it. citeturn623287search7turn623287search14

So preserving a Kikka-like machine in our setting actually makes **more** sense, not less.

The divergence is the calendar.

Perhaps:

**late 1942:** Japanese technical mission reports Me 262 progress.

**1943:** Naval Air Technical Arsenal and Nakajima receive a formal jet requirement.

**1943–44:** German engine information and perhaps an actual BMW/Jumo example arrive by submarine exchange.

**mid/late 1944:** Kikka-equivalent prototype flies.

**1945:** first operational Japanese jet units.

Because Japan is actively fighting China and still confronting Britain, it has somewhere to use the aircraft.

Thus Japan can beat America to **combat employment**, even if America flew a jet prototype years earlier.

---

## So I would make the canonical order something like this

The cleanest version is to define **combat jet power**, not first experimental jet flight:

**Germany — first combat use**, initially experimental.

**Britain — essentially simultaneous first operational deployment**, depending on the criterion.

**Italy — third combat jet power**, with an indigenous airframe around German-assisted true turbojet propulsion.

**Japan — fourth combat jet power**, via an earlier and better-supported Kikka program.

**United States — fifth to operational combat readiness**, despite having flown the XP-59 back in 1942.

And Russia is far behind because it has exactly the wrong wartime circumstances for nurturing an immature, resource-hungry new propulsion technology.

I particularly like what this says about the setting. Jet aviation does **not** emerge as “Germany invents it and everybody copies Germany.”

Instead, by 1945 there are already three distinct schools.

Germany sees the jet principally as the future of **interception and high-speed combat**.

Britain sees it as a **defensive technological necessity** created by the German threat.

Italy sees it as a way for a smaller aviation industry to regain **qualitative parity through concentrated high-performance units**, building upon an indigenous reaction-flight tradition but borrowing the missing turbine technology.

Japan sees it through the lens of **German technical observation filtered through Japanese naval-aircraft requirements**.

America, meanwhile, has perhaps the strangest position of all: it can quite legitimately say that it had a true turbojet aircraft flying before several countries that nevertheless **beat it into actual jet warfare**.

That feels exactly like the sort of technological history this setting should produce once the familiar 1942–45 development sequence starts genuinely diverging.

Before we get on to looking directly at the Japanese aircraft lineage and seeing how things change, I actually want to address first the Russians. Because the Russians have possibly the worst possible time of things when it comes to the aviation side of things. For one, the Russians are short on aluminum and the materials necessary for modern aircraft engines. They may actually have the factories. They don't actually have the material that needs to go into those factories, which is the problem. This is a big issue for the Russians. They may enter the war with plenty of Yak-1s. They probably do pretty well with it. And over time, it probably does eventually get upgraded into something resembling the Yak-7. And possibly, maybe, just if we really give them a push, into something like the Yak-9. Or even, well, I don't know if it would make sense for them to get all the way to like the Yak-3. Well, I might have the order of things. The Yak-3 seems like, no, that's an earlier version. The 9U was what I was thinking of. There is a 9P, which is much later in the war. Because that was, you know, the Russian aircraft industry during the war had quite the development cycle, including the Yakovlev, MiG, Lagg, Il, and DB programs. The DB eventually going into the Pe-2, Yer-2. The Pe-8 was their bomber for a serious amount of time until eventually the Tu-2 came online. That was late war, if I remember correctly. Thing is, like, the Il, like the Il-2, is probably still going to show up. Because for the most part, when Operation Barbarossa began in July of '41, the Il-2 was already, I mean, it was freshly on the, being produced, but it was already being produced. So a decent number of them probably exist. But the idea that something like an Il-10 would eventually develop is probably aggressive. Because the problem is, the Soviets don't have the resources they need to make these. And that includes the metallurgy. Like, the rare earth minerals, metals they need to incorporate in for the engine production. Couple that with the aluminum. Fundamentally, they're working at a problem. I wouldn't say that the entire Soviet Air Force reverts to the I-15 or the Po-2 or other, you know, canvas aircraft. That would be, for the Soviets, it would be suicidal to do that. They might actually end up employing several I-15s as kind of a reconnaissance aircraft and kind of a stopgap aircraft for reconnaissance. But Lord knows they would not be so foolish as to actually send something like that into combat. As even an MG-42 mounted on the top of a tank hull can probably knock that out of the air, and it would be a very bad day for the pilot. So, fundamentally, this requires a different calculus for how to approach things. My thought process is that for the most part, the Soviet aviation struggles. But by 1943 to '44, they've gone from air parity to very much just trying to disrupt operations in random spots, or in, not random, in important spots. And by 1945, the Soviet air arm is probably in about the equivalent position that the German air arm was in 1945. That is, not doing well, to put it gently.

I think the Soviet aviation problem should be written as **progressive narrowing, not technological reversion**. They still know how to design good aircraft; what disappears is their ability to keep several modern fighter, attack, bomber, engine, and fuel programs healthy at the same time. The exact winners therefore depend heavily on which designs can be built from wood/steel, share engines already in mass production, and avoid demanding scarce aluminum and high-grade alloying metals.

## Turn 876 — Assistant

- Timestamp: 2026-08-11T08:49:09.781Z
- Message ID: `a6da9f09-1317-4152-8410-9d05bb70453f`
- Source: ChatGPT shared conversation `Japanese Offensive 1942`
- Parallel branch: https://chatgpt.com/share/6a7d03c0-c468-83e8-acb6-3323c22c7d6a
- Relationship: parallel specialist continuation imported after the master project record through Turn 777

Yes. I think the Soviet aviation story should become one of the clearest examples of the two economies moving in opposite directions.

Germany increasingly has the luxury of asking, *what new capability should we add?* The Soviet aviation industry increasingly asks, *which capability can we still afford to preserve?*

And there is one terminology correction that helps sharpen the problem: I wouldn't describe the principal shortage as “rare earths.” For 1940s aircraft the critical issues are **aluminum/duralumin, high-grade alloying metals and steels, bearings, machine tools, rubber, and aviation fuel—especially the better fuel fractions needed to extract high performance from increasingly stressed engines**. Historical American aid included precisely things like aluminum, special alloys, bearings, machine tools, petroleum products, aircraft, and tens of thousands of vehicles because these were bottlenecks the Soviet war economy could not cheaply solve by making more tanks. citeturn640296search8turn640296search18

In our setting, that external relief is dramatically smaller. That doesn't mean Soviet factories become incapable of manufacturing aircraft. It means the **design freedom available to those factories steadily shrinks**.

## The historical Soviets already show us the first half of the answer

They were already substituting wood for aluminum during the real war.

A September 1942 State Defense Committee order explicitly instructed Il-2 factories to alter the design to reduce duralumin consumption, including wooden-wing and wooden-fuselage structures. citeturn188011search2turn188011search4 The Il-2 itself was particularly suited to this sort of brutal wartime production: armored steel formed the forward structural shell while wood and mixed construction could be used elsewhere. citeturn668420search3turn668420search9

So our divergence doesn't require inventing “wooden Soviet airplanes.”

It intensifies a decision the Soviet industry was **already making**.

The difference is that historically the material situation eventually improves enough for Soviet designers to move back toward more light alloy. In our setting, it doesn't.

That's especially important for Yakovlev.

A U.S. Air Force historical study notes that the early Yak family was heavily shaped by shortages of duralumin and other alloys. The Yak-7 remained comparatively rugged, while the historical Yak-9 emerged when improved availability of light alloys allowed metal wing spars and a lighter structure. The same study places the lightweight Yak-3 as another later branch of the basic Yak lineage. citeturn668420search24

That gives us a natural alternate fork.

## The Yak numbering is misleading

You were remembering the sequence partly backward because Soviet designation numbers don't map neatly onto chronology.

The broad family relationship is:

**Yak-1 → two important development branches.**

One branch goes through the more rugged **Yak-7** and then into the **Yak-9**.

The other pursues a smaller, lighter refinement of the Yak-1 concept and eventually produces the **Yak-3**.

So the first Yak-9 historically appears *before* the production Yak-3 even though nine is a larger number than three. citeturn668420search24

And this matters enormously for AltWWII because the two branches respond differently to scarcity.

### Yak-1: absolutely survives

There is no reason to erase it.

It is already in production when our divergence becomes serious. It is sufficiently modern to be useful. The plants, tooling, engines, trained workers, and repair knowledge exist.

The Soviet solution in 1941–42 is therefore not to replace Yak-1 prematurely but to **simplify and stabilize it**.

The VVS would accept small performance sacrifices if that allows higher availability, longer engine life, fewer difficult fittings, and more wood substitution.

So Yak-1 stays important longer than historically.

### Yak-7: probably becomes much more important

This is, I think, the big alternate winner.

The Yak-7's virtues in this situation are not glamour. They're **ruggedness, internal volume, development maturity, and the fact that the industry already knows how to build it with substantial wooden construction**. The Air Force study specifically describes the Yak-7 as the rugged branch of the family before the lighter-alloy Yak-9 development. citeturn668420search24

So rather than being predominantly a stepping stone to enormous Yak-9 production, the Yak-7 becomes a **long-lived Soviet standard fighter**.

You would see successive Yak-7 improvements:

better radios where available;

better canopy visibility;

armament refinements;

simplified fittings;

improved engine installation;

winterization;

local reinforcement of failure points;

and eventually some aerodynamic cleanup.

But the fundamental airframe stays familiar because replacing its tooling costs resources.

### Yak-9 still exists—but it loses its historical mass-production role

I would **not erase Yak-9**.

The prototype logic is too straightforward, and the Soviet aviation establishment still has enough aluminum for priority aircraft.

What changes is scale.

Historically, the Yak-9 took advantage of increased light-alloy availability to replace heavier wooden structural members, reducing weight and allowing more fuel, weapons, or equipment. citeturn668420search24turn188011search36

Our Soviets look at that aircraft and say:

> Excellent. Which regiments deserve it?

Rather than:

> Excellent. Convert the fighter industry to it.

So Yak-9 becomes an **elite/prioritized fighter family**.

Guards regiments.

Defense of Moscow.

Critical offensive concentrations.

Perhaps Leningrad/Volkhov.

Experienced pilots whose survival makes the expensive airframe worthwhile.

That is an interesting reversal from historical Soviet practice. The same aircraft that historically became extraordinarily numerous becomes visibly prestigious in this timeline because its materials are expensive.

And as shortages worsen, later Yak-9 variants proliferate **on drawing boards faster than they proliferate in squadrons**.

The Yak-9U is exactly where I would draw the line.

Could it be designed? Absolutely.

Could prototypes fly? Probably.

Could a few elite units receive it? Possibly.

Does late-war Soviet aviation turn into thousands of Yak-9Us and then Yak-9Ps?

No.

The **Yak-9P in particular belongs after the war historically anyway**, so I would not drag it into this deteriorating wartime economy.

## Oddly, the Yak-3 may survive better than you initially thought

Not because it is numbered three.

Because its philosophy is useful.

The Yak-3 is essentially an attempt to make a **small, light, exceptionally agile short-range fighter** from the mature Yak family rather than continually adding range and equipment. Historical analysis describes it as smaller and lighter than the Yak-9. citeturn361290search37

That is exactly the kind of aircraft a resource-starved Soviet Union might still want.

It doesn't need tremendous strategic range if its mission is:

> Defend this army concentration for the next three days.

or:

> Keep German reconnaissance away from this railway junction.

The difficulty is that a good lightweight fighter still requires valuable engine capacity and some scarce structural materials.

So I would make **Yak-3 a small high-performance 1944 program**, not a mass replacement.

Perhaps this becomes the characteristic aircraft of the surviving Soviet fighter elite.

It is light.

It is short-ranged.

It is fast at the altitudes where much Eastern Front fighting occurs.

And it is produced in quantities that the VVS can afford to put into the places where local air superiority genuinely matters.

That gives late Soviet aviation a very different appearance from historical 1944.

Not endless standardized modern fighters.

A large middle tier of older Yak-7/Yak-1 derivatives with **small islands of extremely dangerous Yak-3/Yak-9 units**.

---

# Lavochkin may actually be even more important

This is where I would avoid making the Soviet fighter force synonymous with Yakovlev.

The LaGG-3's famous weakness—too much weight for the available engine—is almost perversely useful to us because its wooden structure exists specifically in the Soviet world of strategic-material shortages.

Then the **La-5** gives the design a second life by mating that basic airframe concept to the Shvetsov radial engine. Soviet air-power studies already list the La-5 alongside Yak-9 as one of the major new fighters appearing in 1942. citeturn668420search26

So I would make the Soviet fighter system increasingly **two-family**:

**Yak-7-derived inline fighters** where Klimov engines and Yak tooling dominate.

**La-5-derived radial fighters** where Shvetsov engines and Lavochkin tooling dominate.

That is industrially attractive because one catastrophic engine bottleneck doesn't stop the entire fighter force.

The LaGG-3 doesn't disappear immediately.

Factories keep producing it until La-5 conversion can actually be accomplished.

Then La-5 becomes one of the most important Soviet aircraft of the middle war.

The later **La-5F/FN-type improvement path** probably continues because improving an existing fighter's engine installation, weight, visibility, and aerodynamics is much cheaper than building a whole new production ecosystem.

The La-7 is harder.

I would allow it to exist as a **1944–45 limited refinement**, but again not at historical scale. The closer an aircraft gets to requiring extensive light-alloy substitution and high-performance engine manufacturing, the more it competes directly with every other elite program.

So by 1945 a German pilot might distinguish Soviet fighters roughly as:

> The ordinary Yak.

> The radial Lavochkin.

> And the handful of new ones you do not chase casually.

That feels right.

---

# The MiG line probably gets sacrificed

MiG-3 is where the Soviet procurement state makes a brutal decision.

Its original purpose—high-altitude interception—doesn't align particularly well with the dominant conditions of the Eastern Front, while its engine family competes for resources desperately needed elsewhere.

In our setting that calculus becomes even harsher.

So rather than trying to keep **Yakovlev + Lavochkin + MiG** all healthy as fighter families, the Soviet state effectively shuts down the MiG piston-fighter branch.

The engineers do not disappear.

Some get reassigned.

Some continue theoretical work.

But there is no reason to spend scarce engines, aluminum, tooling, and pilots preserving a third frontline fighter ecosystem when Yak and Lavochkin already cover the immediate need.

That is the general Soviet pattern:

**not technological backwardness; institutional amputation.**

---

# Il-2 becomes almost untouchable

This aircraft may actually survive the industrial collapse better than almost anything else.

It is already being manufactured.

Its battlefield utility is obvious.

Its mixed wood/metal construction can be adjusted around material shortages.

And the Red Army desperately needs aircraft that attack German mobile formations because Soviet ground forces increasingly struggle to generate their own long-range operational mobility.

The National Air and Space Museum describes the Il-2 as one of the defining Soviet battlefield aircraft and emphasizes how production-friendly its mixed construction was. citeturn668420search3turn668420search9

So I think Il-2 gets something approaching **protected-resource status**.

If aluminum arrives, fighters and engines argue over it.

If armor plate arrives, Il-2 has a much stronger claim.

If AM-38-family engine production is threatened, some other aviation program gets cut first.

The two-seat development absolutely survives because combat experience creates the requirement.

Armament changes survive.

Improved radios survive selectively.

Simplified wooden structures survive.

What doesn't necessarily survive is the historical instinct to eventually replace it with the **Il-10**.

### Il-10 becomes a classic Soviet “excellent prototype we cannot afford”

This seems like the perfect role.

Ilyushin absolutely designs the next attack aircraft.

The VVS tests it.

Pilots like it.

It fixes multiple Il-2 compromises.

And the procurement authorities look at the factories and say:

> Converting production will reduce output for months.

That can kill it.

So perhaps a handful of Il-10 prototypes and preproduction aircraft appear in 1944–45.

Maybe one small service-test regiment gets them.

But the ordinary Soviet attack pilot in 1945 is still flying an **increasingly refined Il-2**, because that's what the Soviet Union can continue manufacturing by the thousands—or whatever diminished version of “thousands” the late-war economy permits.

That is more poignant than simply deleting Il-10.

They know what the next aircraft should be.

They just cannot afford the transition.

---

# The bomber families shrink much more severely

And there are a couple of lineage corrections here.

The **DB-3 develops into the Il-4**. It doesn't develop into Pe-2.

Pe-2 is a separate Petlyakov design lineage.

Yer-2 is another separate design lineage.

Pe-8 is the Soviet four-engine heavy bomber, but it never exists in enormous numbers even historically.

Tu-2 is another independent Tupolev twin-engine bomber program.

So the Soviet bomber portfolio is already fragmented before our alternate shortages begin.

That is exactly the sort of thing the wartime procurement state starts killing.

### Pe-2 survives

It already has production infrastructure.

It fills tactical/light-medium bombing and reconnaissance missions.

And the Soviet Army genuinely needs those missions.

But production loses priority relative to fighters and Il-2s as the war deteriorates.

So Pe-2 becomes a valuable aircraft that commanders constantly complain they don't have enough of.

### Il-4 survives at reduced scale

Long-range bombing does not disappear, but it becomes increasingly difficult to justify.

Long-range aircraft consume:

more engine hours;

more fuel;

more trained crew;

more navigation equipment;

and more strategic materials per useful tactical sortie.

The Soviet Union still needs maritime patrol, long-range reconnaissance, occasional strategic strikes, and deep night operations.

It does not need enormous bomber fleets while German tanks are fifty kilometers from a critical railway.

So Il-4 production and operations continue, but in a subordinate role.

### Pe-8 becomes essentially an irreplaceable strategic curiosity

Whatever aircraft already exist continue flying selectively.

They become useful for extraordinary long-range missions, prestige bombing, diplomatic transport, and special tasks.

But there is no large Soviet heavy-bomber future during this war.

The state cannot afford one.

### Tu-2 is another victim of timing

This is where I would be slightly less pessimistic than with Il-10.

Tu-2 is a very useful aircraft, and a relatively efficient twin-engine bomber is exactly what Soviet aviation would eventually like to replace older bombers with.

So I would allow the program to survive.

But it never receives the historical opportunity for comfortable large-scale expansion.

Something like:

**1942–43:** prototypes and initial production.

**1943:** production repeatedly threatened as fighter and attack requirements take precedence.

**1944:** one or two priority formations obtain meaningful numbers.

**1945:** recognized as the best future Soviet tactical bomber, but still not numerous enough to replace Pe-2.

That gives the VVS a future it can see but cannot fully realize.

---

# The really catastrophic Soviet aviation shortage is probably not airframes

It is **engines, fuel, spares, and pilots**.

This is where the 1944–45 collapse becomes much stronger.

You can build a wooden wing.

You cannot substitute pine for a high-performance crankshaft.

You cannot replace worn bearings with plywood.

And an engine designed for higher boost cannot simply keep increasing power indefinitely on whatever fuel the state happens to have.

Historical American wartime documents emphasize that aviation gasoline, aluminum, specialized industrial products, tools, and other materials were specifically part of the Allied support system because they allowed allied factories to produce more war equipment. citeturn640296search0turn640296search8

That external cushion is largely absent here.

So Soviet engine development begins hitting a wall.

The designers can create improved engines on a bench.

The question becomes whether they can manufacture them with acceptable life.

That means the VVS gradually starts accepting **lower overhaul intervals and derated performance**.

This is one of the nastier consequences I'd introduce.

A new engine may be rated at X horsepower.

Frontline units are told not to use full emergency boost except under direct attack because engine life becomes appalling.

A Guards unit gets the best production lots.

A second-line regiment gets engines that failed tighter inspection thresholds but are still usable at lower settings.

Cannibalization expands.

A damaged fighter can become an engine donor before anyone bothers repairing its wings.

By 1945 the Soviet aircraft parks may actually contain **more airplanes than the VVS can keep operational**.

That is very similar to the historical late-war German problem you're comparing it to—but reached through different causes.

## And fuel is probably the final killer

This is where air-force strength stops meaning “number of airframes.”

Suppose the Soviets have 500 fighters assigned to a major sector.

Perhaps 380 are mechanically operational.

Perhaps only 250 have enough fuel allocation for meaningful sustained operations.

Perhaps Stavka concentrates enough fuel to fly 450 of them for three days during a major crisis.

Then sortie rates collapse afterward.

That gives Soviet air power a distinctive late-war operating method:

> **concentrate, strike, disappear.**

Not because the airplanes literally vanish.

Because the fuel reserve does.

---

# So by 1943 the Soviets stop trying to contest the entire front

I think this is the doctrinal turning point you were reaching for.

In 1941–42, the VVS still thinks in terms of rebuilding broad air parity.

By 1943, that goal starts becoming unrealistic.

The new doctrine is **local air concentration around an operation**.

If Stavka plans to relieve Voronezh, aircraft are stripped from quieter sectors.

Yak-9s and the best pilots arrive.

La-5 regiments arrive.

Il-2 units arrive.

Fuel arrives by train.

For several days, the Luftwaffe can encounter a genuinely dangerous Soviet air force.

The offensive ends.

Those formations disappear elsewhere or stop flying at the same intensity.

Germany therefore never gets a perfectly empty sky.

It gets something strategically more useful:

**the ability to assume air superiority unless Soviet headquarters has deliberately chosen that particular location as one of the places where it cannot.**

That's an enormous advantage without giving the Luftwaffe omnipotence.

## 1944 becomes the year of defended islands

By 1944 I would divide Soviet aviation into priority zones.

Moscow.

The Leningrad–Volkhov supply complex.

Major surviving industrial concentrations.

Critical railway intersections.

Whatever major offensive or counteroffensive Stavka has temporarily prioritized.

Perhaps the Caucasus oil/remnant infrastructure.

Everywhere else receives thinner fighter cover and increasingly relies upon:

anti-aircraft artillery;

camouflage;

dispersal;

night movement;

and the fact that Germany cannot put aircraft above every kilometer of a continental front either.

That last point is important.

The Luftwaffe can be dominant and still have finite aircraft.

A German corps conducting some secondary operation may receive poor air support simply because the main German concentration is 400 kilometers away.

That gives Soviet units space to survive.

---

# By 1945, I agree: the VVS should resemble the historical 1945 Luftwaffe in operational condition

But I would make the resemblance deliberately superficial.

Historical late-war Germany had plenty of advanced aircraft designs but catastrophic problems with:

fuel;

trained pilots;

airfields;

maintenance;

spares;

disrupted production;

and overwhelming enemy numerical superiority.

Our late Soviet aviation has:

aircraft designs it knows are falling behind;

chronic aluminum and alloy scarcity;

inadequate high-performance engine production;

fuel rationing;

loss of training hours;

shortages of radios and instruments;

transport collapse;

difficulty supplying forward airfields;

and an enemy whose industrial and technical base is getting healthier rather than being bombed apart.

So by 1945 an elite Soviet fighter regiment might still be **very dangerous**.

It has veteran pilots.

A handful of Yak-3s or improved Yak-9s.

Ground controllers.

Good local airfields.

Fuel because Stavka has declared the sector critical.

A German pilot cannot casually ignore it.

But forty kilometers away there might be a regiment flying tired Yak-7 derivatives whose pilots received insufficient training, with half its nominal inventory awaiting engines.

That's the late-war VVS.

### And this suggests a useful aircraft hierarchy by 1945

I would make the surviving frontline portfolio surprisingly narrow:

**Yak-7 late derivatives** — ordinary, rugged inline fighter; increasingly outdated but everywhere.

**La-5 late derivatives** — ordinary radial counterpart; probably the second major fighter backbone.

**Yak-3** — scarce lightweight elite fighter.

**Yak-9** — scarce/priority multirole fighter family rather than historical mass standard; improved variants particularly rare.

**La-7-type development** — similarly scarce elite radial fighter.

**Il-2** — still overwhelmingly the standard attack aircraft.

**Pe-2** — standard tactical bomber/reconnaissance type because the replacement never fully arrives.

**Tu-2** — limited modern bomber units.

**Il-4** — declining long-range/night role.

**Po-2** — everywhere behind the front.

And then an increasingly bizarre reserve collection of anything that still flies.

That last category includes I-16s and I-153s, but your instinct is right: **they are not sent up at noon to duel Fw 190s because Moscow has collectively lost its mind.**

They fly:

training;

liaison;

night harassment;

rear-area interception against slow targets;

local reconnaissance;

artillery spotting where survivable;

and emergency ground attack.

The Po-2 is actually much more useful than an I-15-family fighter for many of those tasks because it is cheap, slow, short-field capable, and can operate at night.

An obsolete airplane isn't useless.

It simply needs a mission in which being obsolete doesn't immediately kill the crew.

---

## So I'd currently give the Soviet air war this progression

| Period | VVS condition | Characteristic aircraft |
|---|---|---|
| **1941–42** | Recovering from losses; still contests the Luftwaffe broadly where possible | Yak-1, Yak-7, LaGG-3, MiG-3 fading, Il-2, Pe-2, Il-4 |
| **1943** | Last period of something resembling broad competitive strength; begins deliberate local concentration | Yak-7, La-5, limited Yak-9, Il-2, Pe-2 |
| **1944** | Strategic-material shortages bite hard; new types become elite rather than mass replacements | Late Yak-7/La-5, limited Yak-3/Yak-9/La-7-type, Il-2, Pe-2, limited Tu-2 |
| **1945** | No longer contests the whole theater; creates temporary local air parity around critical sectors | Older backbone plus small modern elite, increasingly poor sortie generation |
| **final war period** | Airframes outnumber sustainable sorties; fuel, engines, pilots, transport, and spare parts dictate operations | Whatever can still be kept flying |

That meshes very well with the setting's larger Soviet collapse. The current wiki establishes that the German–Soviet war ends only after the western Soviet strategic system finally breaks and the Soviet state evacuates what it can beyond the Urals rather than because every Red Army formation simply ceases to exist. citeturn886733view0turn719742view1

The air force should mirror that.

It doesn't disappear.

It becomes **incapable of being everywhere that it needs to be**.

And that is probably the most important difference from our timeline. Historically, Soviet aviation grows progressively stronger as the war goes on. Here, its high-water mark probably comes around **1942–43**. Afterward the engineering bureaus continue producing intelligent answers to German development, but the economy becomes progressively less capable of converting those answers into thousands of serviceable aircraft with trained pilots, fresh engines, full tanks, radios, spare parts, and enough fuel to fly tomorrow.

That gives us the reverse developmental picture you wanted without making Soviet engineers stupid or reducing the VVS to canvas biplanes.

One of the intentions is that the Soviet Union in the setting is very much fighting well past where any reasonable party would argue they've already lost and might as well cut their losses. That is, the Soviet Union is intentionally being set up to be a tragic and heroic, not in a moral sense, but in a narrative sense. They are fighting against all odds. They are fighting an enemy which outmatches them in most things by the end. Well, actually, by the end, outmatches them in everything, save perhaps manpower. The intent is when we write narratives for the Soviet Union or from the Soviet perspective, they're not so much narratives about grand leaders fighting an obvious bad guy, but rather almost tragedies of men who oftentimes go into a battle with an expectation that any victory is going to cost, but still being willing to go into the fight. Nobody in the Soviet Union expects, especially by 1943, that they are going to take Kiev or Moscow, and certainly not Berlin. Rather, there needs to be a different target. The most politically extreme, like the NKVD, might potentially argue, yeah, we are eventually going to take Berlin. But by 1943, almost nobody in the actual military establishment of the Soviet Union believes this. And the expectation is instead, we are simply going to survive. And there is a certain level of, because of how the population is distributed, the threat of being pushed beyond the Urals is actually something that the Russians are concerned about. In fact, one of the things that I think should actually happen, especially because the Soviets aren't really getting a lot of Lend-Lease, is the Soviet experiments with whether or not they can set up agriculture in Kazakhstan and the Soviet experiments with agricultural development in Siberia, especially Southern Siberia, begin getting accelerated rapidly. Probably by 1942, those concepts of, hey, maybe we can do this as a way to supplement our food problem, becomes an actual thing. And it should be successful enough that by 1947, they aren't literally all dying from starvation in spite of a lack of serious Lend-Lease from the United States. Although all dying from starvation is already an exaggeration. One of the other things to look at is because of the steel production that they do still have, I'm curious what heavy tanks or variant tank variants are likely to still see production. Are we likely to see the T-34-85? Are we likely to see the KV-1 and eventually KV-2? Are we likely to see in 1946 something to the effect of an IS? Or fundamentally, do those things require that the Soviets be doing well enough that they can supply the factories and kind of counter the direction that we're trying to take the Soviets?

I think the tank question actually cuts in the Soviet Union’s favor more than the aircraft question did. **A deteriorating Soviet economy can still produce better T-34s and even limited heavy tanks, because those programs ride existing steel, gun, and tank-factory ecosystems much more directly than an advanced aviation program rides scarce aluminum, fuel, and engine metallurgy.** The question is therefore less “do the designs exist?” and more “which designs become mass standards, and which become scarce Guards-level equipment?”

## Turn 879 — Assistant

- Timestamp: 2026-08-11T15:52:47.785Z
- Message ID: `86253881-4a78-4ef5-81a0-e359969dc1e2`
