## Turn 966 — Assistant

- Timestamp: 2026-08-13T03:57:59.695Z
- Message ID: `5ad1eb07-230b-4612-ad74-5e296a0380f5`
- Source: ChatGPT shared conversation `British Armor Development`
- Parallel branch: https://chatgpt.com/share/6a7d697a-3074-83e8-aef9-5fec24bc7cbd
- Relationship: parallel specialist continuation imported after the master project record through Turn 777

Yes. I think the Italian branch becomes much more convincing if we stop asking, “How does Italy build its own Panther?” and instead ask:

> **What does a competent Italian armored industry, with less industrial depth than Germany but six more years of uninterrupted wartime learning, actually optimize for?**

And I think your answer—**mobility, useful firepower, and refusing unnecessary weight**—is the right institutional direction.

The existing armaments reference is already pointing toward an uninterrupted P40 → P43 lineage, but it jumps directly from a 1943 P40 to a very clean 1948 90 mm P43. Our earlier transcript explicitly treated that as provisional and said the weight, gun, engine, armor and intermediate vehicles should be rebuilt from the wartime development history. fileciteturn9file1 fileciteturn9file0

There are several things I would change immediately.

## First: the Italian designation actually solves part of the P43 question

And a minor language correction: **modello is Italian**. French would be *modèle*.

The familiar Italian system behind designations like **M13/40, M14/41, M15/42 and P26/40** combines the vehicle class, nominal weight, and model/design year. So the P40's fuller designation is **P26/40**: *Pesante*, roughly 26 tonnes, 1940.

That means we don't really have to force the next vehicle to be literally **P43** as though “43” were its generation number.

If the next heavy tank project begins in 1943 and ends up around 34–36 tonnes, something like:

**P35/43**

would actually be a very natural formal designation.

People can still shorten it conversationally to “the P43 project,” especially while we're worldbuilding it, and the later **Leone** name from the reference can remain provisional rather than controlling the wartime nomenclature.

That is actually helpful, because it lets the weight emerge from engineering rather than requiring the tank to weigh whatever its name seems to imply.

---

# The P40 is better positioned than it first appears

There is one historical specification issue worth flagging.

The present Italian Army page gives the historical P40 as **26 tonnes, 420 CV and 40 km/h**, with the 75/34. It also confirms the broad historical development sequence: designed in 1940, first prototype in early 1942 with the short 75/18, then substantially redesigned before receiving the 75/34. citeturn144022search0turn224187search0

Your **330 hp** figure isn't useless to us, though. In fact, I think it gives us a better alternate development path:

**P26/40 early production:** roughly 330 hp diesel.

**P26/40 mature production:** improved 400–420 hp powerplant as Fiat-SPA gets the intended engine into reliable series manufacture.

That gives the P40 another thing to improve during 1943–44 besides the gun.

And because our P40 has already diverged toward a **welded hull**, we're no longer obliged to reproduce every real production detail anyway. The transcript has already established that welded construction as part of the Italian learning process. fileciteturn9file3

So I would view the 1943 P40 as approximately:

- 26 tonnes;
- 75/34;
- 50 mm sloped frontal hull armor;
- roughly 45 mm sides;
- 40 mm rear;
- four-man crew;
- early 330 hp engine, improving toward roughly 400–420 hp;
- about 40 km/h maximum road speed.

That's actually a decent tank.

Not Panther-class.

But absolutely credible against the British armor Italy is fighting when it enters service.

---

# And yes: the P40 can probably accept a longer 75

I think you're worrying slightly too much about the **barrel length itself**.

The difficult part isn't that an L/48 barrel projects farther forward. Designers can compensate for that through trunnion position, equilibrators, turret balance and recoil layout.

The real problems are behind the armor:

- larger breech;
- longer and/or higher-pressure cartridge;
- greater recoil energy;
- recoil-cylinder dimensions;
- stronger mounting;
- ammunition rack dimensions;
- loader working room;
- turret-ring loading;
- and balance.

So putting a KwK 40-class weapon into a reworked P40 turret is **plausible**.

Putting a KwK 42-class L/70 into it is where I think we cross into “technically imaginable, operationally foolish.”

That's a much larger weapon system.

And here's the particularly useful Italian fact: Italy doesn't actually need to go directly from **75/34 → copy German KwK 40 → copy German KwK 42**.

Italy already possesses its own **75/46 high-velocity artillery lineage**. The Italian Army records the 75/46 as an established antiaircraft weapon, and Italy historically pursued increasingly powerful 75 mm semoventi as well. citeturn646529search24turn144022search4

So I would make the German licensing agreement work more intelligently.

Germany doesn't merely hand Ansaldo a complete KwK 40 and say, “Here, manufacture this forever.”

It gives Italy access to:

- the chamber and ammunition technology;
- high-pressure cartridge design;
- AP projectile work;
- recoil-system data;
- barrel-production tolerances;
- breech design;
- perhaps the muzzle-brake arrangement.

Ansaldo and OTO then combine that with their own 75 mm work.

The result becomes an **Italian long 75**, probably in the **75/46–75/50 class**.

That is much more interesting.

## The P40 gun progression could therefore be

**P26/40 Serie I, 1943:** 75/34.

**P26/40 improved production, 1944:** Italian 75/46 or 75/48 tank gun, heavily informed by the licensed KwK 40.

And I would keep a muzzle brake.

The fact that the 75/34 didn't need one doesn't mean the longer, higher-pressure weapon wouldn't benefit from it. If Ansaldo deliberately deletes the brake, it has to absorb the recoil somewhere else—longer recoil stroke, larger cylinders, stronger mounting—which is exactly what it doesn't want in a cramped existing turret.

It doesn't necessarily need to look like the German double-baffle brake. An Italian brake can be smaller and visually distinctive.

So the late P40 becomes something like the Italian Panzer IV equivalent in **combat capability**, without becoming a Panzer IV copy.

That's exactly what we want.

---

# I would not put the KwK 42 in the P40

This is where Germany's license becomes educational rather than literal.

Italy gets examples/drawings of the 75 mm KwK 42 and says:

> Wonderful gun. We need the next tank.

Because the Panther gun's problem isn't simply its barrel sticking out a long way.

It's the whole installation.

Large high-pressure ammunition, large breech, recoil system, turret volume, substantial mounting and a long barrel all impose costs. Trying to fit that into P26/40 would effectively turn “upgrade P40” into “redesign the entire turret and much of the hull.”

At that point you have already designed P43 badly.

So the **KwK 42 becomes the benchmark**, not the Italian production answer.

That distinction should recur throughout the Italian-German technical relationship:

> Germany frequently shows Italy the maximum-performance solution. Italy asks how much of that performance it actually needs to pay for.

That's a very believable national design culture.

---

# And I think the German 88 is actually the wrong direction for Italy

This is probably the largest thing I would change from the initial thought.

Italy already has a **90 mm gun family**.

The 90/53 existed historically and was one of the more capable Italian heavy weapons; the Italian Army's own retrospective specifically identifies the 90/53 semovente family among the few Italian armored weapons capable of standing up well against enemy armor. citeturn144022search4

So if Germany says:

> “Would you like to license the 8.8 cm KwK 43?”

the Italian ordnance establishment should seriously ask:

> Why?

They already possess:

- 90 mm tooling;
- 90 mm projectiles;
- ammunition experience;
- barrel-making knowledge;
- crews and artillery institutions familiar with the caliber.

The 88 mm L/71 can still teach them things.

But adopting it wholesale means adding **another ammunition family** to obtain something Italy can plausibly achieve by developing its own 90.

The more Italian answer is:

> **Use German long-88 work to improve the Italian 90.**

That might mean borrowing:

- AP projectile geometry;
- propellant formulation;
- cartridge construction;
- breech and recoil concepts;
- manufacturing tolerances;
- barrel metallurgy.

Then OTO/Ansaldo produces a **tank-optimized 90 mm**, probably somewhat shorter and more manageable than simply shoving the complete 90/53 antiaircraft weapon into a turret.

Something like a **90/47–90/50** strikes me as a very plausible eventual result.

And now the old armaments reference's 90 mm P43 starts making sense again. fileciteturn9file5

Not because Italy randomly jumps from 75/34 to 90 mm in 1948.

Because it spends 1943–47 systematically solving the installation problem.

---

# The P40 armor problem is also less catastrophic than it sounds

You don't actually have to turn the P40 into an 80 mm tank.

That is precisely the kind of weight creep Italy should learn to avoid.

If a field workshop puts **20–30 mm applique** over only the most important frontal areas, that doesn't add five or ten tonnes.

Thirty millimeters of steel weighs about **235 kg per square meter**. Even five square meters is only about 1.2 tonnes before brackets and structural reinforcement.

So something like:

**P40 base:** 26 t.

**P40 with serious frontal applique:** perhaps 27–28 t.

is perfectly plausible.

The problems are less:

> “The engine can no longer move it.”

and more:

- front suspension wear;
- steering load;
- brake wear;
- nose-heavy weight distribution;
- reduced acceleration;
- track life;
- recovery;
- transmission stress.

That's where crews start complaining.

And because the P40 already has **sloped frontal armor**, 50 mm isn't directly equivalent to 50 mm vertical plate anyway.

So I wouldn't have Ansaldo try to create:

> P40 + 30 mm everywhere = Panther.

I would have wartime workshops experiment with 15–25 mm plates over particular frontal zones, perhaps standardized later as a factory kit.

Then Ansaldo's conclusion is:

> **This buys useful life for P40. It does not solve the next-tank problem.**

That's what launches the successor.

---

# The successor should combine two Italian design lines

And this is where the **Carro Celere Sahariano** becomes extremely useful.

Historically Italy already investigated a purpose-built fast desert tank rather than only producing M-series vehicles. In our timeline that project becomes a dead end.

In AltWWII, the strategic circumstance which gave birth to it **never disappears**.

Italy keeps fighting in North Africa.

So I would make the P43 project essentially the marriage of:

**P40:** armor, welded construction, larger gun, conventional main battle role.

and

**Sahariano:** mobility, lower profile, high-speed desert running, suspension development.

Then add:

**German technical exchange:** high-pressure guns, optics, transmissions, armor data.

and:

**British captured matériel after Torch:** ergonomics, radios, recovery arrangements, ammunition handling, reliability practice.

That produces a genuinely Italian tank rather than a miniature Panther.

---

# The first P43 should probably be a 35-tonne 75 mm tank

I would provisionally target something like this for the first production successor.

### P35/43 — working first-generation specification

| Characteristic | Working target |
|---|---:|
| Combat weight | **34–36 t** |
| Crew | **4** |
| Main gun | **75 mm L/48–50 Italian high-velocity gun** |
| Upper frontal armor | **80 mm, strongly sloped** |
| Side armor | **45–50 mm** |
| Rear | **35–40 mm** |
| Turret front | **90–100 mm** |
| Engine | **500–550 hp** Fiat-SPA |
| Road speed | **48–52 km/h** |
| Design emphasis | Mobility, low silhouette, first-shot fighting |

And importantly, **four crew can work very well** if Italy finally does something Germany doesn't:

delete the bow machine-gunner/radio-operator position.

Then you have:

- driver in hull;
- commander;
- gunner;
- loader in a proper three-man turret.

That is a much better arrangement than making the commander double as gunner, while still keeping the vehicle compact.

Italy shouldn't automatically add a fifth man merely because Panther has five.

Again:

> Don't pay for volume unless it earns something.

That's a perfectly coherent Italian design maxim.

## Would 80 mm frontal armor make it 45 tonnes?

Not necessarily.

The Panther is enormous by comparison with what Italy needs.

Its weight comes from an entire package: hull dimensions, wide tracks, suspension, enormous turret ring, gun installation, extensive armor area, large fuel load, powertrain, five crew, ammunition and so on.

A compact Italian vehicle can put **80 mm on the frontal arc** without reproducing Panther's total protected surface.

But I'd strongly resist giving the P35/43:

- 80 mm everywhere;
- Panther turret armor everywhere;
- Panther gun;
- Panther speed;
- Panther range;

at 35 tonnes.

That would indeed be fantasy.

The Italian trick is **protection distribution**.

The front is frightening.

The sides remain in the 45–50 mm class.

The rear remains lighter.

The roof and belly remain modest.

And the vehicle is smaller.

That's how you get a roughly mid-30-ton tank that is difficult to kill head-on without pretending Italy has discovered weightless steel.

---

# And this is where the “Italian Panther” nickname becomes misleading in a useful way

Soldiers might absolutely call it:

**la Pantera italiana**, the Italian Panther.

But armor historians later should complain about that description.

Because the P35/43 isn't really Italy trying to duplicate Panther.

The shared attributes are:

- sloped armor;
- high-velocity 75;
- much stronger frontal protection than the P40;
- significantly improved mobility.

The philosophy is different.

Panther is a very powerful medium tank that becomes physically large because Germany is willing to spend weight to achieve its required combat performance.

The Italian tank says:

> **What is the smallest vehicle that gives us enough of those qualities to win our theater?**

That's closer to the later Italian instinct you're trying to establish.

And it creates a wonderful distinction once Panther V Ausf. D/E and Panzer IX appear.

Italy doesn't chase them.

The Germans say:

> “Our next tank needs more.”

The Italians say:

> “Our next tank needs to get to the right place first.”

---

# But mobility needs a precise meaning

I would refine one part of the doctrine.

The Italians probably don't conclude:

> “If the tank is driving fast enough, the enemy can't hit it.”

A forty-ton tank crossing open desert at 45 km/h remains quite hittable, and 1940s tanks generally want to slow or halt for accurate fire.

The actual Italian doctrine should be:

> **Mobility determines who chooses the engagement.**

That means five things:

**Acceleration.** Get out of a firing position quickly.

**Reverse speed.** Fire from cover and disappear rather than turning the whole tank around.

**Sustained cruising speed.** A tank that can theoretically do 55 km/h but overheats after ten minutes isn't mobile.

**Cross-country control.** Steering, suspension travel, track width and ground pressure matter more than brochure road speed.

**Operational range and maintenance.** A fast tank sitting beside the road with a broken final drive is not mobile.

So by 1945, Italian tank doctrine can crystallize around:

> **See first. Fire first. Move before the reply.**

Britain reaches a related conclusion from its fight against increasingly lethal German guns.

Italy reaches it from years of desert maneuver warfare.

That gives both armies similar tactical conclusions for completely different institutional reasons.

---

# Then Centurion forces the 90 mm question

This is where the war itself drives the P43 family forward.

A 75/48–50 P35/43 is quite respectable against:

- Cromwell;
- Sherman;
- Churchill side aspects;
- earlier British cruiser tanks.

It can fight Comet.

But as **Centurion Mk I and Mk II** begin appearing in Egypt, the comfortable margin disappears.

Now Italy faces exactly the problem Britain had with Panther:

> The gun still works, but we don't like how conditional the engagement is becoming.

Italy has two options.

One is Germany's answer:

> More velocity. Build an enormous long 75.

The other is:

> Bigger projectile.

I think Italy chooses the second.

So around 1945–46, the P43 chassis receives the **tankized 90 mm**.

Not necessarily the full 90/53 installation.

Maybe something like **90/47 or 90/50**.

Now the tank probably gains another couple of tonnes:

- larger turret/breech;
- larger ammunition;
- reduced carried rounds;
- reinforced suspension;
- perhaps another engine revision.

Something in the **37–39 tonne** range would make sense.

With perhaps **550–600 hp**, it can remain a roughly 47–50 km/h vehicle rather than becoming a slow heavy.

And **this**, not the first 75 mm P43, may be what develops into the old reference's “P43 Leone.”

That lets us preserve the destination while improving the genealogy.

---

# Semoventi should remain half the Italian armored story

This is important because Italy's historical armored strength wasn't only turreted tanks.

The Italian Army's own retrospective emphasizes that its more successful wartime armored weapons included the semoventi with **75/18, 75/34, 90/53 and 105/25**. citeturn144022search4

That shouldn't disappear once P40 arrives.

Quite the opposite.

Italy has limited turret-manufacturing capacity and increasingly large guns.

A semovente is an obvious answer.

So alongside the P40/P43 line I would expect:

**M43 75/34:** continued useful gun/assault vehicle.

**M43 105/25:** direct-fire infantry support and assault gun.

**75/46 high-velocity Semovente:** increasingly serious tank destroyer.

Then eventually:

**P40/P43-based heavy Semovente:** 90 mm antitank weapon in a better-protected, lower installation.

This matters enormously when fighting Centurion.

Italy doesn't require every Italian tank to carry the weapon capable of defeating every Centurion frontally.

A P43 formation can contain:

- ordinary 75 mm gun tanks;
- 90 mm gun tanks;
- 90 mm Semoventi;
- reconnaissance vehicles;
- mobile artillery;
- German Panthers in support.

That is a much more sophisticated armored force than:

> “Italy finally built a good tank.”

---

# And this solves the DAK problem

The German contribution can remain extremely important without turning Italian victory into German victory.

By 1945–46 the DAK possesses terrifying equipment because increasingly good German tanks are cascading down from the East.

But the DAK is **not the bulk of the army that has fought its way from Libya into Egypt and eventually Sinai**.

Italian formations provide the continuity:

- infantry;
- artillery;
- engineers;
- logistics;
- the majority of local command infrastructure;
- most of the theater's long-term garrison burden;
- a substantial share of the armor;
- Semoventi;
- P40s;
- eventually P43-family vehicles.

German armor often provides the **highest-end antitank edge**.

That is different from providing the entire victory.

And it creates a perfectly believable postwar historiographical argument.

German memoir:

> “The British Centurions could only be contained once the new Panthers reached Africa.”

Italian reply:

> “And who was holding Egypt, supplying the front, operating the artillery, and fighting the British for the five years before your Panthers arrived?”

Both statements can contain truth.

But the strategic answer is the one you've established:

> **Italy wins North Africa with German assistance. Germany does not win North Africa while Italy watches.**

---

## So my working Italian wartime armored progression would be

| Date | Vehicle | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **1941–42** | M13/40, M14/41, M15/42; 75/18 Semoventi | Existing force; severe automotive, gun, radio and support shortcomings exposed |
| **1942** | Sahariano development; P40 redesign | Two solutions emerge: speed and a larger armored gun tank |
| **1943** | **P26/40 Serie I** | Welded 26 t tank, 75/34, early engine; first credible Italian mainline heavy/medium |
| **1944** | **P26/40 improved/long-75 production** | Italianized 75/46–48 influenced by KwK 40; engine and protection improvements |
| **1943–44 development** | **P35/43 project** | Combines P40 protection/firepower with fast-desert automotive lessons |
| **1945** | **P35/43 75 mm** | ~35 t, 80 mm frontal arc, 75/48–50, ~500–550 hp, high mobility |
| **1945–46** | Heavy Semovente development | 75/46 and 90 mm antitank vehicles supplement turret tanks |
| **1946–47** | **P43-family 90 mm variant** | ~38 t, tankized 90 mm gun, improved powerpack; direct response to late British heavy armor |
| **1947** | Mature late-war family | P40 remains in second-line use while 75 and 90 mm P43 variants equip priority formations |

That is the Italian development culture I would carry forward:

> **Germany standardizes because its equipment ecosystem has become too large. Britain universalizes because it cannot keep building a different tank for every battlefield problem. Italy optimizes because it cannot afford to buy performance with forty or fifty tonnes every time the enemy improves.**

And that gives us a very natural line into the postwar Italian tank tradition. The later OF-40-like emphasis on **mobility, moderate mass, good gun performance, ease of export and relatively straightforward maintenance** no longer appears from nowhere. It becomes the mature expression of lessons Ansaldo, Fiat and OTO began learning in Egypt in 1942–47. memcite

- Timestamp: 2026-08-13T04:19:58.520Z

I think the Latin bloc now has a very strong colonization model, and it is different from America or Germany without requiring some exotic institutional gimmick.

The central distinction is this:

> **The great explorer opens the road. The settler makes the road part of civilization.**

That fits the cultural prestige of Columbus, Magellan, Vespucci and the Portuguese navigators, while also explaining why the exploration fleet is not the colony. A long-range Latin survey vessel can be glamorous precisely because it goes somewhere nobody expects to live yet. A lunar town, Martian settlement, or Ceres colony is doing something different: planting households, parishes, workshops and permanent civic life.

And the institutional foundation is already canon. The 1965 Latin Space Convention established a joint program and made Latin the common legal, technical, diplomatic, naval and aerospace language without replacing Italian, Spanish, Portuguese or Occitan. fileciteturn12file0 The existing division of labor also already gives Italy system integration and finance, Spain mass production and shipping, Occitania advanced avionics and electronics, and Portugal the Atlantic tracking and workshop role. fileciteturn12file2 So post-1985 colonization is really the maturation of a system we've already built.

## The Latin space agency should actually be Latin

I would provisionally Latinize the existing **Latin Space Community** as:

**Communitas Astronautica Latina — CAL**

Literally, the Latin Astronautical Community.

I like *Communitas* because this is not the Italian Imperial Space Ministry with some Spanish subcontractors. The whole political purpose is that Italy leads without formally swallowing Spain, Portugal or Occitania. A deliberately neutral common language is part of how that works.

And CAL probably does become much more consequential than a conventional space agency. By the 1990s it would coordinate common transport architecture, technical standards, shared settlements, deep-space navigation, rescue, settlement grants and the legal framework governing genuinely multinational Latin colonies. National space offices and national firms still exist underneath it.

So an Italian Mars base can remain Italian. A Spanish mission can remain Spanish. But the first settlement on Ceres can be **Latin**, in the political rather than merely geographic sense.

That is a useful distinction.

## The Moon should have an official base name and a famous church name

I agree completely with the correction to **Sancta Maria Lunae**.

That should not really be the administrative name of the entire lunar settlement.

It is the church.

Early documents might have some dreary designation along the lines of *Statio Lunaris Prima* until we decide the actual geography and naming convention. Engineers, customs authorities and CAL bureaucrats use that name.

But everybody else says:

> "Sancta Maria."

Because that's where **Sancta Maria Lunae**, Our Lady of the Moon, stands.

And eventually that popular usage may become so entrenched that even people who know perfectly well that the church and settlement have separate names use *Sancta Maria Lunae* for the whole place in ordinary speech.

That happens to places on Earth all the time. The landmark wins.

The ecclesiastical development is also quite plausible. Rome doesn't need to pretend that a few thousand lunar Catholics satisfy some magic population threshold for an ordinary Earth diocese. Current canon law already allows territorial prelatures, apostolic vicariates, apostolic prefectures and similar particular churches for special circumstances; it does not establish a simple minimum-population rule for creating them. citeturn554190search0

So the likely progression is not:

**chapel → suddenly bishop because Moon.**

It is more like:

**chaplaincy → permanent parish/church → special lunar apostolic jurisdiction → territorial prelature or vicariate → eventual Diocese of Luna once the Church judges a bishop useful.**

Then **Sancta Maria Lunae becomes the cathedral because the bishop's chair is placed there**.

And distance is a perfectly good reason for Rome to move earlier than population alone would suggest. An Earth bishop who needs days or weeks of travel, launch clearance and an interplanetary transport schedule to visit a parish is not exercising ordinary pastoral proximity.

There is also a wonderful Catholic consequence hidden inside this. If Rome ultimately defines the bishop's territory as **the Moon**, his ecclesiastical map need not follow the German, American, British, Japanese and Latin political claims at all. A Catholic in a German lunar settlement and a Catholic in a Spanish mission may theoretically answer to the same lunar ordinary.

That fits the Council of Christ the King's emphasis on the Church not becoming the possession of national states rather nicely.

## Latin signage becomes far more important than decoration

Your signage idea works, but the signs themselves aren't enough to create a new language.

What creates the new language is that the signs are part of a whole environment in which **Latin is the only language everybody is expected to possess**.

That was already where the pre-colonization program was moving. Earlier work established Latin as the language of Community specifications, interfaces, multinational mission coordination and potentially the common crew language of *Aquila*, while national teams continued using their own languages internally. fileciteturn12file17

Settlement takes that existing high-register language and forces it downward into ordinary life.

An Italian engineer and a Spanish machinist discuss the reactor in Latin because neither wants to conduct technical work in the other's vernacular.

The municipal office publishes its ordinances in Latin.

A Portuguese family fills out its housing forms in Latin.

The Occitan schoolteacher teaches children from four national backgrounds.

The hospital has Italian, Spanish and Portuguese staff.

The grocery clerk has no reason to print four versions of every aisle marker.

The priest already celebrates a Latin Roman Rite.

The result is that **Latin stops being the language you switch into for official business and becomes the language in which the settlement itself exists**.

I would still make safety signage redundant at first. You don't want somebody misunderstanding an oxygen emergency because Rome wanted elegant linguistic neutrality. Critical warnings can use standardized symbols, Latin and appropriate vernacular translations. Ordinary wayfinding, room names, public administration and technical labels can become Latin much more aggressively.

And the Community would need a huge Neo-Latin vocabulary. It isn't going to rely on Cicero having thoughtfully supplied a word for an airlock controller.

So CAL probably has a permanent terminology commission producing standardized modern Latin for:

laboratories, workshops, pressure locks, reactors, life-support systems, computer networks, radiation shelters, transport platforms, mining equipment and every other mundane thing that turns space from an expedition into a town.

That commission becomes much more culturally important than anyone expected in 1965.

## But I wouldn't call the resulting speech a pidgin—at least not initially

The likely development is stranger and, I think, more interesting.

Italian, Spanish, Portuguese and Occitan speakers already possess related Romance languages. The educated and space-going population has learned institutional Latin. Their shared language therefore isn't being improvised from nothing between mutually unintelligible peoples.

What develops is more like a **spoken Neo-Latin koiné**.

The first generation tries to speak reasonably correct Community Latin. But ordinary speech immediately begins simplifying it.

Word order becomes more fixed. Prepositions do more work. Some case distinctions get sloppier. Vocabulary gets borrowed from Italian, Spanish, Portuguese and Occitan. Pronunciation remains largely ecclesiastical in formal contexts but acquires national and then colonial accents. Technical nouns remain unusually conservative because they're printed on every panel and manual.

Nobody sat down and designed "Lunar Latin."

People simply start speaking bad formal Latin quickly enough that their children eventually speak very good bad formal Latin.

And then something important happens.

### The children nativize it

Suppose an Italian man and Portuguese woman raise a child on the Moon. They know each other's languages imperfectly. Both speak Latin fluently because they work there. Their neighbors are Spanish. The children's school is multinational. Their best friend has an Occitan mother and Italian father.

What language do the children use when playing?

Probably Latin.

Once children begin using it with one another when no teacher is present, the entire linguistic situation changes.

The settlement no longer merely **uses Latin**.

It possesses **Latin native speakers**.

I think **2000 is somewhat early for widespread loss of the national languages**, though. A man born in Spain and moved to the Moon in 1992 is not forgetting Spanish in eight years. His children probably speak Spanish at home and Latin with friends.

But by the **2010s and 2020s**, especially in mixed households, what you described becomes plausible.

A Moon-born young adult arrives in Barcelona and speaks excellent Latin, fluent colonial colloquial Latin, perhaps decent Italian because his father was Italian, and embarrassingly poor Spanish despite having a Spanish grandmother.

Someone asks:

> "You're from the Latin Community. How do you not speak Spanish?"

And his answer is essentially:

> "Because I'm from the Moon."

That is exactly the sort of cultural surprise that tells everyone the colonies have stopped being extensions of Earth and started becoming societies.

There will probably eventually be names such as **Latinum Lunare** for Lunar Latin, although I wouldn't standardize those yet.

## Importantly, this happens mainly in common settlements

An Italian Mars base should not mysteriously stop speaking Italian.

A Spanish mission should be largely Spanish-speaking.

A Portuguese navigation depot will remain Portuguese-heavy.

An Occitan scientific installation will have a strong Occitan vernacular life.

Latin becomes socially dominant where **no national population has enough numerical or political weight to establish its own language as the obvious default**.

That means the jointly administered lunar settlement is an excellent birthplace for spoken Latin.

The first Ceres settlement may be even better.

Ceres is far enough away, expensive enough, and inherently multinational enough that no one member is likely to finance the entire permanent settlement alone. If the founding families are deliberately Italian, Spanish, Portuguese and Occitan, **Ceres could ultimately become the most linguistically Latin place in the Solar System**.

The irony is wonderful.

Rome preserves Latin through the Church.

The Latin Community revives it as administrative neutrality.

And Ceres turns it back into somebody's mother tongue.

Nobody planned the final step.

## The colonization motive isn't really overpopulation

I would qualify this part slightly, because it makes the system stronger.

The Latin countries do not need to be suffering a Malthusian population crisis before space settlement makes sense. A permanent lunar colony of ten thousand people is demographically invisible against Italy, Spain, Portugal and Occitania.

What they need is a **large reservoir of young families for whom emigration offers something materially and culturally attractive**.

And your demographic assumptions make that very plausible.

I would not derive elevated fertility mechanically from "they are Catholic." Urbanization, housing, marriage ages, economic insecurity and ordinary human preference still matter. But in this setting the core Latin states preserve strong Catholic family culture, do not normalize contraception as our Western Europe did, have no equivalent population-bomb political consensus, and have governments materially interested in household formation.

So they don't need seven-child SS demographics.

A population that spends decades around replacement or modestly above it, with substantial regional pockets of genuinely large families, is enough to provide a continuous stream of settlers.

More importantly, those families face a terrestrial problem.

Italy has some African settlement opportunities, but North Africa already has inhabitants and significant political limits.

Portugal possesses Angola and Mozambique, but neither is an unlimited empty settler frontier—and their security crises make mass family emigration less attractive.

Spain does not have an obvious giant demographic frontier.

Occitania essentially has none.

Space suddenly offers a different proposition:

> **You can establish a new household somewhere without taking somebody else's farm to do it.**

That is incredibly powerful in a Catholic-bloc context.

For the second or third son of a large rural family, the Moon can eventually offer the thing his father's village cannot: property, work, marriage prospects and room to establish a household of his own.

For a young urban couple, CAL can offer subsidized passage, guaranteed housing, employment and unusually generous family provisions.

For a craftsman, there are workshops.

For a religious order, there are schools and hospitals to found.

For a priest, there are souls without enough clergy.

For a town government, there is literally a town to create.

So the Latin colonization pitch is not chiefly:

> "We need bodies for the imperial machine."

Nor:

> "Your corporation can own a planet."

It is:

> **"Come found something."**

That fits the bloc beautifully.

## Spain's "missions" should absolutely survive as a specific institution

I would keep the word **mission** precisely because of the historical echo.

But the inversion matters.

There are no Martians to evangelize.

A Spanish mission is therefore a **founding nucleus**: chapel, habitation, communications, workshop, clinic, greenhouse, survey office and landing ground. Initially perhaps thirty or fifty people. Later a couple hundred. If the site succeeds, ordinary settlers grow around it and the mission becomes the center of a town.

The cross isn't there because Spain intends to convert imaginary natives.

It is there because the Spaniards brought their parish with them.

That is a far better use of the historical reference.

And it gives Spanish colonization a recognizable texture without making every Spanish settlement some parody of New Spain.

## Italy remains the bloc's heavy backbone

Italy should still have its own major Martian presence.

The joint Latin identity does not erase Italian great-power ambition. Rome will want an unmistakably Italian settlement on Mars—Italian administration, Italian streets, Italian schools, Italian parish life, Italian companies—especially if Germany, America and Japan all possess their own national colonies.

But the Italian settlement plugs into a wider Latin logistical network.

Its guidance systems might be Occitan.

Some structural modules Spanish-built.

Deep-space tracking Portuguese.

The common emergency net Latin.

A nearby CAL scientific station genuinely multinational.

So Italy gets to say:

> **Italy is on Mars.**

And the Community gets to say:

> **The Latin world is on Mars.**

Both are true.

## Ceres is where exploration turns into settlement

I think making the **first permanent settlement on Ceres Latin** is one of the best choices here.

It completes the bloc's exploratory identity.

Germany and America are initially preoccupied with Moon–Mars settlement and the infrastructure between them. Japan has its robotic-and-settlement network. The Latin program has spent decades developing a prestige culture around going farther, surveying, charting and opening routes.

So eventually one of those expeditions reaches Ceres and the obvious question becomes:

> Why are we going home?

Not because Ceres itself is immediately some fabulous paradise. It isn't.

But it is a natural operating base for the asteroid belt, scientific work, deep-space navigation, resource prospecting and later transport. A temporary exploration station becomes permanent because permanent occupation is cheaper than repeatedly rebuilding the same capability.

Then spouses arrive.

Then a priest.

Then children.

Then someone opens a bakery.

At that point the explorers have accidentally founded a colony.

And Ceres probably becomes ideologically important in a way its population does not initially justify. It is the settlement that proves the Latin people did not merely follow Germans and Americans to the obvious destinations.

They **went beyond them and stayed**.

## That gives us a clean Latin colonization formula

The Latin bloc does not need one single mechanism.

**The Community builds the road. National states plant some settlements. Joint Latin settlements occupy places no one member could efficiently hold alone. The Church supplies a transnational institution already comfortable crossing borders. Families provide continuity. And exploration supplies the cultural story that makes leaving Earth prestigious rather than merely strange.**

This also gives the bloc a surprisingly coherent spatial hierarchy by the early twenty-first century.

There is a common Latin lunar center whose church, **Sancta Maria Lunae**, becomes more famous than the base's administrative name.

There are national facilities around it.

There is an Italian Martian colony and several Spanish missions, followed eventually by Portuguese and Occitan settlements or specialist communities.

And there is a first permanent Latin settlement on Ceres, probably the place where the common Latin identity develops fastest because distance makes national compartmentalization increasingly absurd.

The deeper consequence, though, is linguistic and cultural.

America may eventually produce **American Martians**.

Germany produces **German Martians**, with that complicated metropolitan/Eastern mixture we just developed.

Japan reproduces a hierarchy of Japanese and associated national settlements.

The Latin bloc may do something none of them intended:

> **It may eventually produce Latins.**

Not Italians pretending they aren't Italian, nor Spaniards surrendering Spanish identity. The Earth-born generation remains national. But their descendants can become people for whom Italy, Spain, Portugal and Occitania are ancestral countries inside a larger civilization, while the language they actually use with their spouse, children, priest, employer and neighbor is a form of Latin that no Roman senator would recognize as proper—but would probably understand far more of than he had any right to expect.

That feels like the strongest long-run payoff of the Latin space program. memcite

The Ha-Go, I mean, does very well because the opponent doesn't really have very good anti-armor. And then 1943 starts rolling around, and then the Japanese start fielding better and better tanks. And the British and Commonwealth exports to China are fighting those better and better Japanese tanks. And eventually China falls, or at least the American attachés note that their version of China has fallen. And then the Japanese, the American attachés may not necessarily see the last generation of Japanese tanks deployed before 1947, because those tanks would be seeing combat in Siberia. But ultimately, the American experience of the Second World War would be watching everybody else make bigger and bigger tanks with more and more armor. And even the Japanese, who started out with practically paper, start, or practically paper light and medium tanks, start also making bigger and bigger tanks. And so I think the American understanding of tanks very rapidly goes from, yeah, the M4 is sufficient, to, well, the M4 cannot possibly be sufficient, because A, the British immediately started replacing our guns with their own guns and upgrading them, and B, by the end of the war, or by, actually, by 1943, M4 Shermans were being routinely taken out. So the M4 is insufficient. And so the understanding might genuinely reach the American design bureau and the American army as, we need really heavy tanks, the future is big gun and lots of armor. And then if the United States ever have to do expeditionary conflict, that's where it's arguing, well, then we need to just make sure that the expeditionary craft can handle that big of a tank, because that's the kind of tank we need. There may be a cohort, especially in the cavalry component of the U.S. Army, that argues, actually, we need to have light tanks that can, you know, exploit. And they can routinely point at German, Italian, and Japanese light tanks that do manage to exploit breakthroughs pretty well. And that the Italians themselves, especially near the end of the war, do employ lighter, mobility-focused vehicles. Just because the tanks are really big does not mean that the vehicle can't be fast. And the late war British and German tanks really demonstrate that. So America probably has a split personality as far as tank development doctrine. And I think that's actually something we should persist through 1947. After 1947, and particularly with the newest electorate, economic rationalization and budget cuts and budget discipline may lead the U.S. Army to not have as much funds for producing new stuff. So 1946 is probably the last development year where the U.S. Army has a decent budget to play with. And that could produce a particularly interesting half-measure by the end of 1946 or '47, where a tank that's in development ends up being, quote, the American post-war tank, end quote, simply because the funds kind of run out, and they get stuck with what they get stuck with. But it establishes the United States as kind of learning by watching rather than learning by doing. American tank design does technically have reports coming back from the British, but those reports increasingly start saying the M4 is insufficient. And that's about all that they can work with. Specific complaints are hard to work with. It needs a bigger gun is probably the thing they keep hearing, or it needs more armor.

Yes. I think the United States becomes much more interesting once we stop treating “neutral” as meaning **technologically idle**.

The American armored story from 1941 to 1947 should be the story of a country that has enough money, industry, proving grounds, intelligence access, and institutional anxiety to keep designing tanks, but **doesn't possess the combat feedback loop that tells everyone which ideas are actually important**. The old Land Armaments Reference got the broad post-Philippine direction right, but its 1941–56 American sequence is much too tidy and, as you said, somewhat arbitrary. It should be reopened. fileciteturn14file10

There is also already an archival precedent for exactly the T22 idea you're proposing: in the earlier German autoloader discussion, we explicitly treated the American T22 autoloading variant as an experimental vehicle that existed but never saw combat. fileciteturn14file0 So we aren't inventing this from nothing now. What we need is the institutional reason why neutral America funds it.

## America is learning the war through glass

The most useful real-world fact is that **foreign observation was already shaping American armor before Pearl Harbor**. In 1940–41, reports of heavier foreign tanks pushed the U.S. Armored Force away from its earlier light-tank emphasis and toward a greater proportion of mediums; its stated aspiration was to make the American armored division at least equal to, and preferably superior to, the German equivalent. British combat experience was also explicitly feeding into American organizational and technical thinking. citeturn146922view1turn146922view3

So removing Pearl Harbor does not produce an Army that says, “Nothing concerns us; stop designing tanks.”

It produces an Army that says:

> **We're watching the largest armored war ever fought, and we'd prefer not to discover in 1948 that everyone else learned six years of lessons while we were building the same tank.**

But this has a catch.

The United States gets **reports** rather than experience.

An attaché can report that a Panther has an 80 mm sloped glacis and a long high-velocity gun.

He can photograph a Tiger II.

He can talk to a British officer who says the Sherman needs more gun and protection.

He can read a report saying that the British have put a 17-pounder into an American tank because the American 75 isn't enough.

What he doesn't have is fifty American battalion maintenance reports explaining that the terrifying new enemy tank has thrown sixteen final drives this month, that one regiment can barely move half its tanks, or that a slightly less impressive vehicle generates twice as many combat-ready tank-days.

That produces what I would call the **American observer's distortion**.

America is likely to overlearn the things that are easiest for an observer to measure:

armor thickness;

gun caliber and penetration;

maximum speed;

silhouette;

headline weight.

And underlearn the things soldiers discover through owning a machine for six months:

maintenance burden;

crew exhaustion;

recovery;

ammunition handling;

parts consumption;

fuel use;

ease of servicing;

actual availability.

That is almost perfect for getting America into the doctrinal split you're describing.

## The inherited 1941 programs give us the foundation

The M3/M4 sequence already survives the divergence. The Army's own history describes the M3 as a stopgap pending a tank with a turret-mounted 75 mm gun—the vehicle that became the M4. citeturn146922view0 Our earlier transcript had already frozen the T6/M4 as a **committed program on 1 August 1941**, even though the pilot itself was not quite complete. fileciteturn12file5

The heavy T1 program also survives. Our previous chronological pass already established that the first American heavy-tank pilot is delivered in December 1941, and crucially, in this timeline that happens **without America waking up the next day in a world war**. fileciteturn13file8

I would leave one nomenclature detail open for the eventual M6 deep dive: I don't want to lock your “December 1941 T1E1” suffix until we have the period Ordnance paperwork in front of us. The important canonical point is simpler: **the T1 heavy program is already real by the POD and produces running hardware in 1941.**

That gives us three inherited schools almost immediately.

The M4 school says, “Build a reliable medium in quantity.”

The heavy-tank people say, “Europe is demonstrating that some problems require armor and gun power beyond a medium.”

And the mechanized cavalry tradition says, “If every tank becomes a fortress, who exploits the breakthrough?”

None gets decisively vindicated because none fights.

---

# T20/T22/T23 can survive very naturally as a technology program

This is, I think, how we save T22E1 without pretending the historical October 1942 rationale happens unchanged.

Instead of starting the T20 family as an urgent combat replacement for Sherman, **Ordnance begins an Advanced Medium Tank Experimental Program in 1942**.

The requirement is deliberately broad:

> What should replace M4 if foreign tank development continues at its present rate?

That wording matters.

Congress isn't authorizing five new armored divisions.

The Army isn't asking for 10,000 tanks by Christmas.

They're buying **information**.

And prototypes are cheap compared with fleet conversion. A government unwilling to spend billions replacing thousands of Shermans can still be perfectly willing to fund several one-off tanks so Ordnance can test transmissions, suspensions, turret layouts, new guns, electrical systems and automatic loading.

This also fits the real institutional character surprisingly well. The Army's official history shows Ordnance continuing independent heavy-tank development even when Army Ground Forces opposed it; only senior intervention kept the program alive. The same period saw a real dispute between officers who wanted heavier tank armament and McNair's school, which preferred the existing M4 plus separate tank destroyers. citeturn801148view0

So AltWWII America gets the same sort of bureaucratic argument **without the battlefield eventually resolving it**.

I would therefore preserve **T20, T22 and T23 as parallel experimental answers**, but make their principal purpose comparative engineering rather than immediate production competition.

T20 represents one automotive and layout solution.

T22 represents another, more conservative enough that experimental turret technology can be hung on it.

T23 becomes the electrical-drive school.

Whether we retain exactly the historical number of pilots is less important. In this setting, **one to perhaps three of each** feels more natural than 250 T23s, because there is no wartime mobilization forcing a production commitment.

And that is where T22E1 belongs.

## T22E1 becomes one of America's great “we built that in the forties?” museum pieces

The rationale for the autoloader doesn't need to be:

> We desperately require more rounds per minute in combat.

It can instead be a series of engineering questions.

Can we remove some of the loader's physical workload?

Can an automatic mechanism produce a predictable loading cycle?

Can we reduce required turret volume?

Can ammunition presentation be standardized mechanically?

Can a future larger gun remain practical without requiring an increasingly exhausted loader to manhandle increasingly heavy rounds?

And perhaps most importantly for American Ordnance:

> **What happens if we just build one and find out?**

That's an extremely plausible technology-demonstrator mentality.

I would not yet canonize the claim that T22E1 is **the world's first autoloading armored vehicle**. The “first” question gets messy once we include obscure prototypes, automatic artillery systems and different definitions of autoloading. I haven't found a sufficiently good period U.S. primary source for the exact T22E1 mechanism to make that categorical claim.

But I am comfortable making it in-setting **one of the earliest serious automatic-loading tank experiments**, and something Americans later routinely advertise as “the first American autoloading tank.”

The distinction is useful.

The vehicle works well enough to prove that the idea isn't nonsense.

It works badly enough that nobody wants to standardize it in 1943.

That is much more valuable to our setting than making it secretly perfect.

The loading mechanism can be sensitive to ammunition alignment, require awkward replenishment of its ready mechanism, complicate malfunction clearance, and consume enough turret space that its practical advantages remain debatable. Meanwhile foreign reports are already saying that **75 mm isn't the future anyway**.

So T22E1 receives the worst verdict a technology demonstrator can receive:

> Interesting. Don't build more of them.

Then it goes to Aberdeen.

And forty years later, when America is designing the autoloading M13 family, somebody inevitably drags the old T22E1 files back out. The existing reference already gives the 1985 M13 a bustle autoloader, so this becomes a delightful distant technological ancestry without requiring an unbroken T22 → M13 engineering line. fileciteturn13file16

America can have forgotten the technology twice.

---

# The Sherman becomes an export product whose customer keeps complaining about it

I think the M4 still sees **thousands** produced.

But I would no longer freeze the current reference's exact 8,000 total or 5,200 Commonwealth allocation. fileciteturn12file12 We should recalculate that after fixing exactly how many Shermans Britain wants alongside Ram, Cromwell, Comet and its other domestic programs.

The broad structure is sound.

America needs enough M4 production to:

maintain domestic armored units;

sustain its mobilization base;

fulfill British/Commonwealth purchases;

supply selected other customers;

and keep the factories capable of expansion if the United States itself suddenly enters the war.

But it never becomes the industrial ecosystem of almost fifty thousand tanks that the real Sherman became.

That means fewer specialized derivatives and much slower replacement of manufacturing tools simply because a better variant has appeared.

And British feedback produces a strange relationship.

The British may say:

> We like the automotive reliability.  
> We like the turret arrangement.  
> We like the radio fit.  
> We like being able to get parts.  
> We need a much better gun.

Then they put the 17-pounder into it.

From the American perspective, that is simultaneously embarrassing and reassuring.

Embarrassing because their principal combat customer has concluded the standard American gun is inadequate.

Reassuring because the customer keeps ordering the tank.

So Ordnance's lesson becomes:

> The basic vehicle is sound. The weapon is aging.

Not:

> Sherman itself is a failure.

And that is a much more realistic foundation for continued experimentation.

The later historical American experience confirms that the M4's deficiencies against late German armor became increasingly apparent as armor and high-velocity guns improved; the Army's own history specifically describes the 75/76 mm Sherman struggling against Panther and Tiger frontal protection. citeturn519838view2 In AltWWII, Americans learn the same lesson through **British reports and intelligence assessments rather than their own dead tank crews**.

That makes the lesson emotionally weaker but intellectually persistent.

---

# M10 probably survives more easily than almost anything else

This is another case where Pearl Harbor isn't actually the prerequisite people might assume.

The Army's tank-destroyer concept was already institutionally underway **before** U.S. entry. Marshall approved an enormous planning basis for tank-destroyer battalions in October 1941, and the 1941 Louisiana and Carolina maneuvers were already being used to test antitank concepts. citeturn215723search6

So an American self-propelled 3-inch antitank vehicle remains extremely plausible.

What changes is the scale.

I would keep the M10 as:

an American domestic antitank reserve vehicle;

a training and doctrine vehicle;

and, increasingly, an **export weapon**.

Britain is an obvious customer. A smaller British M10 pool then becomes the basis for the Achilles conversions you've already established.

Again, the feedback is wonderfully uncomfortable.

America sends Britain a 3-inch tank destroyer.

Britain says:

> Thank you. We're putting our gun in it.

By 1944 the War Department has received essentially the same message from both its exported tank and exported tank destroyer:

> **The chassis is useful. We would like more gun.**

That is going to matter.

---

# The M6 becomes the American tank that is always about to become useful

And I agree with you that the Heavy Tank M6 should survive much more substantially than the current provisional reference suggests.

The setting's old reference currently delays it to 1945 as a forty-vehicle pilot/limited-standard machine. fileciteturn14file14 I think that's too artificial now.

The first running heavy already exists in late 1941. Therefore the M6 program should be a **1942 phenomenon**, not something America mysteriously waits four years to accept.

But I would keep its production modest.

Perhaps enough to equip **one complete heavy battalion, plus school, proving-ground and replacement vehicles**. We don't need the exact total yet, but something in roughly the dozens rather than hundreds or thousands is the right category.

And its original armament makes much more sense if we view it through 1941 eyes.

A 3-inch/76.2 mm M7 is a serious gun in 1941.

The coaxial 37 mm arrangement is eccentric, but the whole vehicle belongs to an Army still figuring out what a heavy tank is supposed to do.

Then America watches 1942–43 happen.

Tiger appears.

Panther appears.

Soviet armor gets heavier.

Britain develops the 17-pounder.

The German 88 becomes increasingly famous.

Suddenly the American **heavy tank's gun does not look very heavy**.

So M6 becomes a proving chassis.

That is its enduring contribution.

Instead of asking whether to ship it across an ocean, Ordnance can use M6 to investigate:

higher-velocity 76 mm ammunition;

90 mm tank guns;

larger turret rings;

electric versus hydromechanical drive;

heavier armor arrays;

power-assisted traverse;

and eventually very large gun installations.

The American heavy school can reasonably argue:

> We have already paid for a sixty-ton-class experimental ecosystem. Use it.

And because no American soldier has died attempting to land an M6 through some miserable Mediterranean port, **the transportation objection remains abstract**.

Rail loading still matters.

Bridges still matter.

Recovery still matters.

But the institutional answer to “how do we move sixty tons overseas?” can remain:

> Then design a transporter that can move sixty tons.

That argument can survive surprisingly long when nobody has had to do it under fire.

---

# This makes T29 much easier to justify

By 1944–45, the intelligence picture reaching Washington is almost comically one-sided.

Germany has Tiger II and increasingly improved Panthers.

Britain has the 17-pounder and is moving toward Centurion.

Italy has gone from prewar small mediums toward P40 and then larger, faster, better-gunned successors.

Japan, which seemed to demonstrate in 1941 that fifteen-ton tanks were adequate, is now producing its own larger Chi-To/Chi-Ri generation.

From Washington, **every data series points upward**.

Gun caliber: upward.

Armor: upward.

Weight: upward.

Engine power: upward.

Even the traditionally light Japanese force is moving upward.

That makes a T29-class project almost inevitable as a **strategic insurance program**.

But again, not a production tank.

I would have the heavy program develop in stages.

M6 proves the 50-plus-ton automotive class.

A modified M6 or equivalent test hull investigates a much larger gun/turret installation.

Then T29/T30-type prototypes explore the 105 mm and 155 mm extremes.

The 105 mm vehicle is the serious proposal.

The 155 mm vehicle is much more of an ordnance experiment: “how large a gun can a practical tank chassis actually support?”

And because America isn't fighting, this development can be surprisingly leisurely and technically elaborate.

Nobody says:

> We need 500 next month.

Instead:

> Bring Prototype Two back after you've fixed the steering problem.

That could actually make the American experimental heavies **better engineered as prototypes** than their historical equivalents, while making them far less likely ever to enter production.

That is a very American alternate-history result.

---

# The real American split is not “heavy versus light”

I would make it a **three-way argument**, because that gives us better continuity into the Philippine War.

The first school is the **Continental Heavy School**. Its model is the Eastern Front. It says the tank's first obligation is to survive and destroy the enemy's best tank. Its ideal 1946 vehicle is perhaps 50–65 tonnes with a 90, 105, or even larger gun. Overseas transport is an engineering problem to be solved around the tank.

The second is the **Balanced Medium School**. This is where the T20/T23/T25/T26 genealogy belongs. It accepts that Sherman has reached its ceiling but argues that fifty or sixty tonnes is unnecessary. Give the Army a roughly forty-tonne tank with a 90 mm gun, sensible armor, good suspension, five crew, reliability and room for growth.

The third is the **Cavalry/Mobility School**. It looks not only at light tanks but at what German, Italian and Japanese mobile formations actually accomplish. Its argument isn't that armor is useless. It is that there is a separate requirement for a tank that can arrive first, cross more bridges, move rapidly, exploit a breakthrough, scout by fighting and be shipped without reorganizing the transport system.

And here's the important thing:

**1941–47 provides no American battlefield capable of deciding among them.**

Each faction can cherry-pick foreign evidence.

Tiger II proves the heavy people right.

Centurion proves the balanced people right.

Italian Sahariano/P43 mobility concepts prove the cavalry people right.

German Panzer IX can be cited by both the heavy and balanced schools depending upon what aspect of the tank the speaker emphasizes.

That institutional argument should remain unresolved when the war ends.

---

# The T26/Pershing-type tank is the best candidate for America's accidental postwar standard

This is the part of your proposal I like most.

By about 1944, the balanced school has the easiest political case.

A T29-class heavy is clearly expensive.

The M4 is clearly aging.

A very light cavalry tank plainly cannot be the principal battle tank.

So the T20 experimental family gradually converges toward something **T25/T26-like**:

roughly forty tonnes;

90 mm gun;

five-man crew;

substantially improved frontal protection;

torsion-bar suspension or equivalent modern running gear;

decent but not spectacular speed;

conventional manual loading;

and enough automotive maturity to be believable as something the Army could actually manufacture.

In our history, battlefield concern and institutional conflict ultimately produced the M26. The Army's official history records Ordnance pushing a more powerful 90 mm tank despite opposition from Army Ground Forces, which preferred continuing M4 production and tank destroyers. citeturn801148view0turn110007view3

In AltWWII, we can get to **approximately the same technological neighborhood for a completely different reason**:

> The War Department wants one vehicle that proves America has not fallen a generation behind the European powers.

And I would have it reach a limited-standard state in **1946**.

That's your accidental postwar tank.

Not because everybody agrees it's the perfect solution.

Because Congress then looks at the accounts.

The general war is ending.

Britain is visibly collapsing.

The Soviet Union is disappearing as a great power.

Japan is not at war with America.

Germany does not appear eager to invade North America.

And American voters start asking why the Army needs three experimental tank families.

So the 1947 appropriations knife comes down.

T29-type development falls back to proving-ground status.

The autoloader work is archived.

The experimental light programs survive at low intensity.

New heavy production authorization disappears.

And whatever forty-ton 90 mm tank managed to get standardized in 1946 becomes:

> **the tank we already have.**

Not America's great victorious tank.

Not an object of national mythology.

Just the thing sitting in the motor pools when the money stops.

That is far more interesting than the old reference's artificial “M7 Transitional Tank becomes America's 1947 standard.” fileciteturn14file11

## There is a nomenclature consequence

If that 1946 tank is literally standardized as **M26**, then the neat postwar American `M9 → M10 → M11 → M13` sequence in the current Land Reference can no longer be treated as sacred.

I think that's fine.

You have already identified that sequence as one of the parts we're rebuilding.

We have two choices later.

We can let the T26-derived vehicle remain officially **T26E3, Limited Standard** and avoid consuming an M designation—although that becomes awkward if it genuinely serves as America's principal tank for several years.

Or we can simply accept **M26** and rebuild the later American nomenclature honestly around the programs America actually creates.

My preference for the logic of the setting is the latter, but I would **not lock that yet**, because it affects everything after the Philippine War.

---

# Then the Philippine War becomes a devastating doctrinal correction

This is where the existing postwar canon suddenly becomes much stronger.

The current timeline says the 1953–56 Philippine War teaches America that transport weight is a combat characteristic, wide tracks and difficult terrain matter, and a tank that cannot be moved through the theater's ships, bridges, roads and recovery network is useless no matter how impressive it is on paper. fileciteturn10file10

That lesson becomes much more powerful if America enters the war with an armored establishment that has spent twelve years saying:

> **We'll solve transportation around the tank.**

Then it actually tries.

The 1946 “postwar tank” may be technically excellent.

It may be perfectly reliable on American training grounds.

Its 90 mm may be absurd overkill against most Filipino insurgent positions.

And commanders discover that moving it from Luzon port facilities onto weak interior bridges is a logistical project all by itself.

Meanwhile some old cavalry colonel who spent fifteen years losing procurement arguments says:

> I told you so.

That is the birth of the later American expeditionary tradition.

Not:

> Heavy tanks are bad.

Rather:

> **A tank has no combat power in a theater it cannot reach.**

The old reference's later doctrine—“Do not carry sixty tons where twenty will accomplish the mission; do not send twenty tons where only forty can survive it”—becomes a learned synthesis rather than an authorial slogan dropped from nowhere. fileciteturn11file1

---

## So I would provisionally reconstruct 1941–47 this way

| Period | American armored development | What America thinks it has learned |
|---|---|---|
| **1941** | M3 Light/Medium in service; T6/M4 committed; T1 heavy pilot; tank-destroyer establishment already forming | Germany proves armored warfare matters; heavier foreign tanks are already changing U.S. planning |
| **1942** | M4 enters limited domestic/export production; M6 receives limited-standard/proving role; **T20/T22/T23 experimental medium program begins**; M10 development continues | Don't abandon M4, but establish what its successor might require |
| **1943** | T20-family prototypes; **T22E1 automatic-loader experiment**; limited M10 exports; M6 becomes heavy-gun/powertrain testbed; British reports increasingly demand better Sherman firepower | The future probably needs more gun; experimental technologies are worth testing before committing factories |
| **1944** | 76 mm/advanced M4 work continues; T25/T26-type 90 mm medium-heavy development; T29-class heavy requirement emerges from foreign intelligence; T22E1 remains a dead-end experiment | Panther/Tiger and British 17-pdr evidence suggest 75 mm is no longer enough |
| **1945** | T26-type tank reaches mature trials; T29/T30 and M6-derived heavy-gun tests continue in tiny numbers; Sherman export production begins losing long-term rationale | Every major belligerent appears to be converging on heavier guns and armor |
| **1946** | **90 mm T26-derived vehicle selected for limited standardization**; heavy and light experiments continue but do not enter mass production | Balanced forty-ton tank appears the safest compromise between the heavy and mobility camps |
| **1947** | War ends abroad; British aid terminates; American budget retrenchment freezes most armored experimentation | The 1946 compromise becomes the postwar American tank largely because no replacement is funded |

I wouldn't lock the prototype counts, exact 1946 tank designation, or exact M4 production total yet. Those are the three places where a premature number could constrain the much more interesting institutional history.

But the underlying American character now looks very strong:

> **Germany learns tank design through fighting and standardization. Britain learns through fighting everywhere at once. Italy learns through necessity and comparison. Japan learns through radically different environments. America learns by watching all four—and therefore learns several correct lessons in the wrong proportions.**

The T22E1 is almost the perfect emblem of that American war: **technically adventurous, genuinely ahead of its time in one narrow respect, never combat tested, never adopted, and left sitting at a proving ground while American officers argue over what the war they aren't fighting is supposed to mean.** memcite

The M26 would also probably be called the Pershing because John Joseph Pershing was, you know, still an American individual of serious import. The T-34 probably does enter production in very limited numbers and probably does get a name. I don't think it ever historically got a name. But here's the thing. T-34 probably enters just enough production to outfit one heavy battalion. The M26 then enters production enough to fill out the rest of the armored division. And then the M24 gets produced in large enough numbers to be visibly, you know, useful. But the interesting aspect for us is following the design arguments and the drama behind the American procurement system. Because here's the real thing I would argue. Just because we want to get to these three designs does not mean that they get to them in a very clean manner. In fact, it probably, the development manner of these vehicles is probably going to be a mess and a very long and arduous argumentation back and forth about, well, actually, we should be using XYZ gun instead of another. I mean, at some point along the way, there might be an argument of, well, maybe we can just make a slightly longer 75 or a 76 millimeter cannon and shove that into the M4 and call it good. But ultimately, the M4 is getting lambasted so badly for bad armor by the time that the United States gets to the point of, hey, maybe we could do this, that the argument kind of falls flat on its face. Because the complaint isn't principally, oh, it has a bad gun anymore. It starts becoming, it doesn't have enough armor. So then the argument of, we'll just put a bigger gun into it, sounds short-sighted, to say the least. This is also in part the reason why I think the long 76 that we saw historically probably does not see service in the United States. It might be something that's investigated. You might see it on one or another demonstrator. But ultimately, it is not the direction the United States ends up going. It decides, okay, well, the M4 is a dead end. We're going to move on to the next idea, which could result in the T-25, correction, the medium tank T-20 project that gets developed. And here's the thing. I think the T-20 actually has quite a bit of a shot of seeing more production. And maybe even the T-25 as kind of the culmination of the development, as kind of a, yeah, this is ultimately where we wanted to be. This then is a very interesting kind of environment. T-25 gets produced in some decent numbers enough to start, you know, populating American tank forces. And then by the end of the war, with the larger Panthers or Panzer Vs that are coming out and the Centurion, the United States looks again and goes, actually, the T-25 is not sufficient. And then comes to the conclusion they want the M26. Now, I will note there is an oddity here. I am not sure why some of these vehicles are called T and others are called M. I think T is reserved for the testing, but I don't think T stands for testing. I think it stands for tank. American procurement here seems to be extremely excruciating to follow who inherited what. And there's a lot of things that have, like, well, this is an M26, and this is a T26, and those are not the same thing. One of the interesting things that I think may actually be a commentary is the American T1E1, or at least that era. It actually has frankly impressive armor. I mean, its frontal armor was 101 millimeters on the front, on both the hull and turret. It had 82 millimeters side armor all around on the turret, and 70 millimeters side armor on the hull. Like, that thing was built thick. And the fact that it's a 76 millimeter M7 cannon, I mean, it's a cannon that definitely overperforms compared to other tanks designed at the same time. Debatably speaking, the T1E1 may actually be the thing that populates American heavy formations until almost the end of the war when the Tiger II starts showing up. So by the 1945, the United States is looking around and saying, okay, the T1E1 is actually not sufficient. We need something bigger. And that really leads to the T26 evaluations, and perhaps some serious development gets thrown towards it, and ultimately the T-34 pops up as a middle ground between the T-29 and T-30 eventual targets. What this could produce is a very interesting development path in the United States. Another thing that may be interesting here is that anti-air probably is not considered as a serious concern for the United States. Not because the United States never thinks of it as a likely consideration, but rather when it comes to reports they're hearing back from the war, nobody writes about anti-air weapons. The British probably talk about things like the Skink, but the Skink is a Canadian vehicle. And the American Army, very well Army Air Corps, may very well argue, why on earth would you need an anti-air vehicle? We have anti-air vehicles, they have wings. And so the concept of an American anti-air dedicated vehicle like the T-771 or the M19 or the M42 Duster, those kind of approaches to, hey, we need an anti-air vehicle, may genuinely not actually be considered seriously. The M10 should probably see production, or it does see production because we've already set it up as this is an export variant, or an exported vehicle. That said, the American tank destroyer doctrine may end up continuing to develop as, hey, this is a thing we want to keep in mind. But ultimately, it's viewed as an anti-tank weapon. You wouldn't send an M10 GMC as a, quote, tank. It's explicitly a tank destroyer. Interestingly, that may mean that in spite of the M10 probably overperforming for the potential role, it is not actually sent to the Philippine War. Like, technically, it could go to the Philippines, and it would very much overperform there. But it never is because it's viewed as a tank destroyer. And the Philippine War, the rebels in the Philippines, do not have tanks. So why would we need a tank destroyer? Until eventually they come across a couple of Hagoes and Chi-Has, and the question suddenly is open of, hmm, we kind of should have a tank. A few M4s may be sent overseas to the Philippines as kind of a, hey, this is something. But at that point, it could also instead be T20s. Actually, that might be the interesting thing. It might be the T20 that enters, or that sees combat in the Philippines, largely against the Hagoes and Chi-Has that the Filipino nationalists have. Which provides probably an interesting kind of experience for the United States Army in that the T20 performs particularly well in the combat it's expecting. The T26 is kind of overbuilt for that kind of conflict and doesn't actually see service or see any actual warfare. But ultimately, the T20, or the T25 perhaps, ultimately demonstrates, yeah, it's not a bad vehicle. It's a bit heavy, and in certain circumstances it'd be preferable to have more. But it's not bad. Actually, the M24 might be treated as the cavalry's tank, if you will, and therefore may also see some service in the Philippine conflict, possibly. Maybe not, I'm not sure. But if it does, it could generate a pretty good reputation as, hey, this is exactly the tank we want for this kind of conflict. And so it very rapidly validates the American light tank approach, leading to things designed specifically off of the idea of we want a lighter tank, eventually leading to things like a T92 kind of design.

I think this is the right point to stop treating the American tree as “Sherman, then somehow Pershing” and instead map the **actual bureaucratic family tree**: M6/T1 heavy branch, T20→T25→T26 medium branch, M24 cavalry branch, and the T29/T30/T34 heavy branch. The three-school compromise is stronger than choosing one 1947 “winner.” It gives America a **visible armored establishment without a coherent armored doctrine**: Chaffee for cavalry, a T26/M26-family vehicle for the balanced school, and a one-battalion T34 heavy force for the continental-heavy school. ## Turn 975 — Assistant

- Timestamp: 2026-08-13T05:52:16.554Z
