- Relationship: parallel specialist continuation imported after the master project record through Turn 777

Yes. **“Menagerie” is the right word, but with an important qualification:** the Luftwaffe has a much larger *designation zoo* than it has a genuine *airframe zoo*. A Bf 109E, F, G, K, and T are not five unrelated logistical ecosystems in the way a Panther, Tiger I, Tiger II, Ferdinand, and Jagdpanther are. They share ancestry, training assumptions, manufacturing experience, and a great deal of maintenance culture even where the actual parts interchangeability becomes much less complete than the common name implies.

And that gives us a way to preserve a lot of the aircraft you like **without making German procurement completely insane**.

The attached transcript has already established two very useful principles: the Bf 109 can retain a broadly recognizable historical evolutionary path, including the surviving **Bf 109T carrier branch**, while the Me 262 gets unusually early consideration as a night interceptor because British night bombing creates a real operational requirement for it. fileciteturn7file11 Meanwhile the late-war setting itself requires Arado jet strike aircraft and a limited operational Me 264 force during the Second Battle of Britain, culminating in the White Parachutes. fileciteturn8file2

## The apparent zoo is really about eight families

| Family | The designs you're talking about | What I think happens |
|---|---|---|
| **Bf 109** | E-1/3/4 → F-1/2/4 → G series → K-4; Bf 109T | Long-lived standard day-fighter family; naval branch survives |
| **Fw 190 / Ta 152** | A-1 → A-4/5/8 → F-8 → D-9/D-12 → Ta 152C/H | Second standard fighter family; progressively takes fighter-bomber and high-performance roles |
| **Twin-engine fighter/Nachtjagd** | Bf 110 → Me 210 → Me 410; Ju 88C/G; Do 217N; He 219 | Starts badly fragmented, then rationalizes around a mass night-fighter family plus a specialist high-end machine |
| **Schlachtflugzeug** | Ju 87D; Hs 129B; Fw 190F | Ju 87 declines; Fw 190F becomes general tactical attack machine; Hs 129 retains specialist anti-armor niche |
| **Medium/tactical bomber** | He 111; Ju 88 → Ju 188; Do 217; He 177 | Aging families progressively removed; Ju line becomes principal conventional workhorse while heavy bombing separates into its own branch |
| **Long-range/maritime** | Fw 200; Me 264 | Fw 200 is inheritance; Me 264 becomes the true long-range bomber/reconnaissance system |
| **First-generation jet** | Me 262; Ar 234; He 162; Ho 229; Me 163 | Me 262 and Ar 234 are operational cores; others occupy narrower experimental or specialist roles |
| **Advanced experimental** | Do 335; BV 155; Bf 109Z; Fw 189C; Me 262 HG-II/HG-III | Some fly; some die; importantly, **not everything becomes a squadron aircraft** |

That's already much less alarming.

The real problem isn't that Germany develops a Bf 109F-4 and then a G-2. The problem comes when it simultaneously has **Bf 110s, Ju 88s, Do 217s and He 219s all solving overlapping night-fighter problems**, while another handful of factories are building specialized ground-attack machines and yet other bureaus are chasing one-off interceptors.

So I think the German aviation version of the Einheit movement should eventually become:

> **Don't standardize the Luftwaffe around one airplane. Standardize it around a limited number of airframe families, engines, weapons, radios, instruments, fittings and maintenance systems.**

Aircraft specialization is much harder to eliminate than tank specialization. A four-engine Fernbomber cannot economically be your dive bomber, naval fighter and night interceptor too.

---

# Bf 109: keep the genealogy, reduce the late-war chaos

I agree with retaining the recognizable **E → F → G → K** evolution.

The interesting alternate divergence probably isn't whether the Gustav or Kurfürst exists. It's whether Germany produces quite the same bewildering collection of overlapping late Gustav subtypes, engine fits, field kits and production standards.

The Bf 109F is our 1941 starting point. From there, increasing engine power, armor, radio equipment and armament naturally push us toward something recognizably like the G series. Nothing about our war removes that pressure.

But by 1943–45, the Einheit movement starts asking why the Luftwaffe needs G-6, G-10, G-14 and various overlapping factory and field configurations coexisting when the whole point is supposed to be standardization.

So I would preserve the **major evolutionary landmarks**, but probably make the alternate late Bf 109 family *cleaner*.

The K-series can become what it was supposed to represent in principle: **the standardized final wartime Bf 109**, rather than just another model arriving while large quantities of older Gustavs remain in chaotic parallel production.

And your **Bf 109T absolutely survives**. We've already established that directly. Because Graf Zeppelin remains an eventual operational project, old carrier airframes don't simply become irrelevant trainers. There is a small naval training and development establishment maintaining carrier procedures while everyone waits for the ship. fileciteturn7file11

That creates a very interesting later competition, because I think Focke-Wulf would almost certainly look at the 190 and say:

> Why is Messerschmitt entitled to own carrier fighters forever?

The Fw 190's wide-track undercarriage alone makes it interesting enough for the Kriegsmarine to want trials. Whether the naval Fw 190 actually wins is open; **the competition itself makes sense**.

---

# Fw 190: this is where German piston aviation probably ends up concentrating

The Fw 190 is almost ideal for our alternate German procurement culture because it begins as the disruptive alternative and gradually becomes a whole **family**.

A-series: ordinary fighter.

F-series: ground attack.

D-series: inline-engined high-performance fighter.

Ta 152: increasingly specialized ultimate piston fighter.

That isn't really four different aircraft programs. It's Kurt Tank progressively extracting different missions from one industrial lineage.

And, importantly, our war gives the **Ta 152H an excellent reason to exist** even without American B-17 and B-24 formations over Germany. Britain still has heavy bombers, long-range reconnaissance, increasingly sophisticated night bombing, and eventually a Second Battle of Britain. Germany therefore has a persistent reason to want an extremely capable high-altitude piston interceptor alongside the jets.

The C-type concept is easier still: essentially the lower-altitude/general-combat high-performance branch.

By 1945–47, I would expect the Fw/Ta family to be the Luftwaffe's mature piston-engine counterpart to the Me 262.

The 109 is the veteran incumbent.

The 190 is the family that proved it could do almost everything.

---

# The night-fighter zoo is where standardization actually has to hurt somebody

This is perhaps the strongest place to cut the historical menagerie.

Bf 110, Ju 88C/G, Do 217N, He 219, Me 410 and eventually night-fighter Me 262 development can all be made technically defensible.

They **cannot all be equally important mass-production answers**.

Our established setting makes Nachtjagd more important, not less: German civilians need to remember British bombing and blackout conditions, and we've already established the early experimental Me 262 night-interceptor episode that frightens the RAF into accelerating its own jet response. fileciteturn7file11

My preferred structure is therefore:

**Bf 110** remains the inherited early-war machine.

**Me 210** still has its painful development problems. Those problems were rooted in the aircraft, not Germany losing the war, so divergence doesn't magically cure them.

**Me 410** is the corrected Messerschmitt heavy-fighter line and becomes useful in reconnaissance, anti-shipping, long-range interception and specialized attack. One small designation correction from your dictation: the later aircraft is **Me 410**, so the maritime/heavy-cannon machine would be an Me 410 B-6 variant, not “Bf 410.”

But **Ju 88-derived Nachtjäger should probably win the mass-production contest**. Germany already needs Ju 88-family infrastructure for other purposes; it has room for radar and a second crewman; and it gives the standardization bureaucracy an obvious answer.

Then **He 219 survives as the expensive specialist**.

That is how we keep the He 219 without making the Luftwaffe maintain three equally important night-interceptor fleets. It becomes what elite Nachtjagd units want when performance matters more than production simplicity, while Ju 88-family machines equip most of the force.

The Me 262 eventually intrudes from above as the future.

---

# Ground attack can undergo an even cleaner consolidation

Here I think the historical direction fits our war almost perfectly.

The **Ju 87D** continues because it is already deeply institutionalized.

But contested Soviet airspace increasingly demonstrates that a slow dedicated dive bomber is vulnerable. That pushes more work onto the **Fw 190F**, which has the performance to defend itself better and shares its production culture with the fighter fleet.

The **Hs 129** survives for a different reason: Soviet armor.

It doesn't have to become the Luftwaffe's general attack aircraft. The B-2 and later heavy-gun experiments can exist as specialized **Panzerjäger aircraft** precisely because Germany spends this whole war running into successively nastier Soviet armored formations.

So by late war:

**Fw 190F = general Schlachtflugzeug.**

**Hs 129 = specialist anti-armor aircraft in declining numbers.**

**Ju 87 = gradually withdrawn from ordinary daylight frontline work and retained where conditions permit.**

That is rationalization rather than deletion.

---

# The bomber family is where we have to do the most actual alternate-history work

The aging **He 111** should not still be a preferred frontline bomber in 1946 simply because it can technically fly.

The Ju 88, however, is different. It is too useful. The Ju 188-style evolution makes a lot of sense because it improves an existing ecosystem rather than replacing it.

Dornier's Do 217 family can survive for a while as the heavier complement, but by the Einheit period I would expect pressure to stop treating Dornier, Junkers and Heinkel as entitled to overlapping bomber fleets indefinitely.

Then we have two genuinely different heavy-bomber problems.

The **He 177 class** is the European heavy bomber.

The **Me 264 class** is the true Fernbomber.

Those need not be duplicates.

The Me 264's canonical mission gives us its development logic almost automatically. By 1945–47 Germany needs to reach Scotland and northern Britain while also possessing a long-range reconnaissance capability, and the setting explicitly requires limited Me 264 formations to do exactly that before the White Parachute raid. fileciteturn8file2

But I think its *original alternate requirement* should come from the East.

As Soviet industry retreats farther away and German armies go farther east, the old **Uralbomber problem returns in practical form**:

> We can capture the ground beneath the enemy's industrial system faster than our ordinary bomber force can reach the industrial system that has moved away from us.

That rescues the long-range bomber requirement without requiring war with America.

Then Britain gives it its second mission.

So the Me 264 becomes something like:

**1942–43:** deep Soviet reconnaissance/Fernbomber requirement.

**1943–45:** difficult development, engine and structural refinement.

**1945:** limited operational capability.

**1946–47:** mature enough for a small strategic and reconnaissance force against Britain.

**1947:** Friedensbrot.

And crucially, **small force**. The canon already says the Me 264 formations are limited rather than thousands strong. fileciteturn6file12

That saves us from having to pretend Germany suddenly becomes the United States Eighth Air Force.

---

# Now the jets

This is where I think we can keep most of your favorites while being quite ruthless about what “exists” means.

## Me 262

This is the central German jet. Everything else orbits it.

And the current transcript has already made one change I very much want to preserve: **night fighting becomes part of Me 262 experimentation unusually early**. A test aircraft or tiny evaluation detachment intercepts British bombers, proves that a jet vectored onto a bomber stream can make an extremely fast pass, and produces the RAF intelligence shock that helps accelerate Britain's own jet program. fileciteturn7file11

That doesn't mean the first Me 262 production fleet is composed of night fighters.

It means Nachtjagd enters the requirement set early.

The Me 262 then becomes day interceptor, heavy fighter, limited fighter-bomber, reconnaissance derivative, and eventually the basis for increasingly radical high-speed research.

The Smithsonian confirms the actual Me 262 was a genuine operational jet rather than merely a paper “wonder weapon”; its real limitation was that immature jet technology and wartime conditions prevented the airframe's performance from translating into a large effective force. citeturn614151search6turn614151search17 Our Germany gets to solve some of those problems under considerably better industrial circumstances.

## Ar 234

This one is almost untouchable now.

The Second Battle of Britain canon explicitly requires **Arado jet strike aircraft attacking radar, communications, airfields, depots, factories and naval installations**. fileciteturn8file2

The question isn't whether the Ar 234 lineage exists.

It's exactly which variant becomes the mature 1946 attack/reconnaissance machine.

And that is something we should rebuild later.

## Me 163

I would keep the Komet but **shrink its institutional significance**.

Rocket-interceptor research is already far enough along around the divergence that it isn't going to evaporate. But our Germany doesn't face enormous American daylight bomber streams, so the historical pressure to mass-field a seven-minute rocket interceptor is weaker.

It therefore becomes:

experimental point-defense aircraft → tiny specialist operational establishment → technology source for rockets, high-altitude flight, pressure systems and later aerospace work.

That is actually more useful to the setting long term than pretending it becomes Germany's principal fighter.

## He 162

This one needs a rewritten purpose.

The historical emergency *Volksjäger* rationale does not fit our war.

But Germany **does** become materially exhausted, and the Einheit movement is obsessed with getting more useful combat capability from fewer strategic inputs.

So a He 162-like aircraft can be born from a different requirement:

> **Build a cheap, single-engine jet which consumes fewer engines and less strategic metal than Me 262, can be produced by secondary industry, and can serve as point-defense and conversion equipment.**

Not a teenage suicide fighter.

An economy jet.

That is much more plausible here.

Whether **He 162 or Ta 183 eventually wins that single-engine jet competition** should remain open. The provisional Aerospace Reference currently lets both survive, but that's exactly the sort of duplicate fleet this investigation ought to challenge. fileciteturn8file1

---

# Ho 229: yes, we can absolutely make this work

And this is actually easier than some of the other favorites.

Your requirement is now authorial:

> **A production or at minimum genuinely operational Horten Ho 229 family exists.**

The important thing is not to justify it through “Hitler invents stealth.”

The real Ho 229 isn't a fictional Luft '46 sketch. The surviving V3 is a genuine wartime twin-jet all-wing aircraft, and Smithsonian's preservation history says Reimar Horten began designing the jet-powered all-wing concept in **1942**. citeturn614151search0turn614151search11 So our divergence does not have to conjure the basic design philosophy from nowhere.

The alternate requirement I like is **high-speed penetration reconnaissance and strike**.

Germany has just learned from Britain that defended airspace punishes conventional bomber formations.

Then jet engines appear.

The Horten argument becomes:

> Don't put a bomber fuselage, tail and engine nacelles through the air if the whole airplane can be the wing.

Low drag gives us speed and range. Internal volume gives us fuel and stores. Jet propulsion removes propeller complications.

Radar cross-section can emerge as an interesting secondary observation later. I would explicitly **not** build 1940s doctrine around “stealth”; even the Smithsonian notes that the later stealth mythology surrounding the Ho 229 has greatly outrun what can safely be claimed about its wartime purpose. citeturn614151search20

The cost is that the Ho 229 is weird.

Stability.

Yaw control.

Landing behavior.

Wood/composite structure.

Jet-engine integration.

Pilot conversion.

Maintenance access.

Those problems give us exactly the procurement story we need.

So I would make it **small but real**: perhaps a few specialized Gruppen by the end of the war rather than replacing Me 262.

That also explains why it becomes culturally enormous despite being numerically minor.

It looks like nothing else.

It flies like the future.

And postwar German propaganda can photograph the hell out of it.

---

# The HG-II and HG-III solve a different problem

Here I would be cautious about pretending the internet's beautifully rendered “HG-III” images all represent one unambiguous completed historical configuration. I wasn't able to find sufficiently authoritative archival material to lock every modern HG-II/HG-III drawing into a specific historical prototype state, so I'd treat the exact geometry as **design-study territory**, not inherited canon.

But that's fine, because you don't need it to have been historically completed.

What you want is the concept.

And the concept fits beautifully.

Once Me 262 pilots start operating at very high speed, Messerschmitt's question changes from:

> Can we make a jet fighter?

to:

> **How much faster can this airframe go before the airframe itself becomes the limiting factor?**

That generates the **Hochgeschwindigkeit program**.

I would make the HG sequence an actual organized research family:

**HG-I:** relatively conservative aerodynamic cleanup of the Me 262.

**HG-II:** substantial swept-wing/cockpit/airframe work, still clearly an Me 262; this one can plausibly become a flying high-speed prototype.

**HG-III:** the radical machine you like, with engines brought into the wing-root/fuselage structure and a much more comprehensively redesigned aerodynamic layout.

And here is the important distinction:

> **The HG-III does not need to become the Luftwaffe's 1947 standard fighter to “exist.”**

I would actually prefer that it doesn't.

Make it a real flying prototype or preproduction research aircraft around **1946–47**.

Now it can appear in photographs. Test pilots fly it. British intelligence is obsessed with it. The public later treats it as one of the iconic last wartime jets.

But the Luftwaffe itself says:

> Excellent. Now take everything we've learned and design the next aircraft properly.

That then gives us an honest ancestor for whatever eventually replaces the Me 262 after the war. It also matches the *broad* idea already present in the provisional Aerospace Reference, where HG-III research feeds the later clean-sheet Messerschmitt generation rather than spawning endless 262 subvariants. fileciteturn8file1

I think that is the best possible fate for the HG-III.

It gets to be **real, beautiful and important** without us having to pretend it was sensible to mass-produce.

---

# And some things should lose

This is important because the authorial favorites become much more believable if we're willing to kill other programs.

The **Bf 109Z** should probably remain an experiment or paper curiosity. There are too many cleaner ways to obtain a long-range/heavy fighter.

The **Fw 189C** has little reason to beat both Hs 129 and Fw 190F.

The **BV 155** has to compete against Ta 152H for essentially the same increasingly specialized high-altitude piston niche. I would favor the Ta.

The **Do 217 night fighters** probably become transitional rather than permanent once Ju 88-family Nachtjagd dominates.

The **Do 335** is more interesting. I could justify small production because jets still have endurance, throttle-response and maintenance disadvantages. A very fast piston reconnaissance/strike aircraft can remain valuable even after Me 262 appears. But it probably never becomes a huge fleet.

And I could **not verify a genuine wartime Blohm & Voss “BV 235”** from reliable material. I suspect that particular number may be a game/what-if designation or a slip for another Blohm & Voss project, possibly the BV 238. I would leave **BV 235 uncanonized** until we identify which aircraft you have in mind.

That willingness to say “prototype only,” “small series,” or “loses the competition” is what lets us retain Ho 229 and HG-III without turning the Luftwaffe into a War Thunder tech tree.

## So the German wartime arc I see is becoming quite coherent

**1941–42:** Germany still tolerates a large competitive design culture. Bf 109 and Fw 190 compete; heavy-bomber policy is unsettled; night-defense work accelerates; Me 262 technology develops; the Me 264 requirement gains a real eastern strategic purpose.

**1943–44:** material strain makes standardization political. Fw 190 begins absorbing ground attack; Ju 88-family aircraft consolidate much twin-engine/night work; Me 410 repairs the Me 210 lineage; Me 262 becomes a serious operational project; Horten receives support as a specialized penetration concept.

**1945–47:** the Luftwaffe is technologically diverse but organizationally much cleaner. The principal fleets are descendants of Bf 109/Fw 190, Ju 88, Me 262, Ar 234 and a limited Fernbomber family. He 219, Hs 129, Ho 229, Do 335 and similar machines exist in narrower specialties. Experimental branches such as HG-III are explicitly research programs rather than excuses to create another thousand-aircraft supply chain.

That gives us something much more believable than either extreme: **Germany doesn't magically abandon its historical aviation creativity, but the Einheit culture increasingly forces each strange new airplane to answer the question, “What existing fleet are you replacing, and why can't that fleet do this job?”**

And Ho 229 gets an answer good enough to survive.

## Turn 992 — Assistant

- Timestamp: 2026-08-13T08:18:11.024Z
- Message ID: `08092d02-5e14-4917-9a0f-a4e0001da994`
- Source: ChatGPT shared conversation `WWII Air Development 1941`
- Parallel branch: https://chatgpt.com/share/6a7e5b4c-a75c-83e8-b24d-617523189a3c
- Relationship: parallel specialist continuation imported after the master project record through Turn 777

Yes. I think this is a substantially cleaner late-war Luftwaffe, and most of your cuts make the remaining exotic aircraft **more** convincing rather than less. We are no longer preserving a Luft ’46 catalogue. We are preserving a few strange programs because each has a recognizable job.

There are three technical corrections I would make before locking it: the Do 335 shouldn't die because escape is impossible; the Ho 229 can be unusually maneuverable without becoming a jet-powered biplane; and the HG-III's “fuel hog” reputation works better if we define *why* it consumes fuel rather than making aerodynamic streamlining itself somehow inefficient.

The current provisional Aerospace Reference is therefore already superseded in several places—particularly its operational He 162, its late 1948 Ho 229, and its treatment of HG-III purely as a research predecessor. fileciteturn11file13

## First, I think the cutting decisions work

| Aircraft | Revised AltWWII status by 1947 | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **He 162** | Paper/prototype evaluation; canceled | Volksjäger requirement never becomes compelling |
| **Me 163** | Small experimental/service-test program; abandoned as fighter | Valuable aerodynamic/rocket demonstrator, poor operational weapon |
| **Hs 129 B-3** | Small but real operational type | Specialist anti-tank aircraft; BK 7.5/autoloader technology matters later |
| **Do 335** | Prototype/preproduction evaluation only | Superb performance but expensive role duplication as jets mature |
| **Ho 229** | Limited but genuine operational escort/heavy fighter | Efficiency, range, speed, unusual maneuver characteristics |
| **Me 262** | Principal German jet fighter | The mass-service jet |
| **Me 262 HG-I/II** | High-speed development and limited operational derivatives | Progressive aerodynamic refinement |
| **Me 262 HG-III** | Very small early-1947 operational batch | Exceptional speed, poor operational economics; feeds Me 362 |
| **Ar 234** | Major reconnaissance/strike jet | Already required by Second Battle of Britain canon |
| **Me 264** | Small but strategically important Fernbomber/Höhenbomber family | Urals first, Britain second, Friedensbrot culmination |

That feels like an actual procurement system.

### He 162: kill it

I would go essentially all the way with you.

The **Volksjäger never becomes an operational procurement program**. Heinkel can produce a study showing that a small single-engine jet can be substantially cheaper per airframe and consume only one turbine, but the Luftwaffe response is:

> Yes, but then we have to create another airplane.

That means another production line, undercarriage, control system, cockpit installation, manuals, spare-parts chain, training program, weapons installation and maintenance syllabus. Germany isn't trying to put a minimally trained teenager into anything capable of flight. It's trying to increase the number of **effective jet-fighter sorties**.

If turbine production is the constraint, increase turbine production.

If trained pilots are the constraint, giving them a less capable airplane doesn't manufacture more pilots.

If Me 262 production is the constraint, simplify the Me 262 production system.

So the He 162 is interesting enough to reach model/prototype consideration, perhaps even one or two flying evaluation machines if we particularly like that, and then gets the most German bureaucratic death imaginable:

> *Technically satisfactory. No production requirement.*

The provisional reference's He 162C in service in 1947 is gone. fileciteturn11file1

## The Me 163 likewise gets demoted from weapon to laboratory

This fits extremely well.

Historically the Me 163 really did become an operational rocket interceptor, but the entire arrangement was extraordinarily specialized: rocket propulsion gave enormous climb and speed while providing only a very short powered portion of the mission. Smithsonian material describes it as the only tailless rocket interceptor to enter operational service and emphasizes the extreme limitations of the concept. citeturn407569search4turn407569search20

Our Luftwaffe gets enough experience to conclude:

> Fascinating aerodynamics. Fascinating rocket propulsion. Terrible fighter.

So I would allow a tiny evaluation establishment rather than necessarily making every surviving airframe purely experimental. Crews learn high-speed climb, gliding approaches, rocket handling, tailless flight and high-altitude physiology.

Then the fighter branch dies.

What survives is **knowledge**.

That matters later for aerospace far more than another thirty operational Komets ever would.

## Hs 129 B-3 stays

Agreed, and just one nomenclature correction: **Hs 129 B-3**, rather than Hs 192.

It's a perfect example of something that can be a small operational oddity while still having enormous technological significance later. Germany doesn't have to believe that hanging the 7.5 cm BK beneath an airplane is the future of close air support. It merely has to build enough of them to discover that a large cannon can be mechanically fed in an armored fighting system under severe acceleration and vibration.

That gives us the technological ancestry already carried into the Panzer X autoloader discussions without requiring the Hs 129 B-3 to be common.

---

# I would change the reason we kill the Do 335

Your conclusion works. The escape problem doesn't quite.

Dornier recognized exactly the rear-propeller problem you're describing. The Do 335 had an ejection seat and a jettisonable upper fin; the escape system was designed specifically because simply bailing out past the rear propeller would be extraordinarily dangerous. citeturn407569search0

That doesn't make the aircraft psychologically pleasant. A pilot still knows he's sitting between two engines with a propeller behind him and an escape sequence involving pyrotechnics.

But I wouldn't have test pilots reject it as essentially unsurvivable.

I'd give it a crueller procurement fate:

> **It works—and by the time it works, nobody desperately needs it.**

It is an extremely fast piston aircraft requiring two large piston engines to do jobs now being approached by the Me 262, Ar 234, Ho 229 and high-performance Fw/Ta family.

Its push-pull arrangement means two engines, long drive arrangements, unusual cooling and access requirements, a complicated rear installation, specialized escape equipment and an airframe that isn't substantially common with Germany's principal piston families.

So the Luftwaffe evaluates it, loves its speed, and asks the fatal question:

> What squadron are we replacing with this?

There isn't a good answer.

That gives us several Do 335 prototypes and perhaps A-0 preproduction machines as famous test aircraft. Production authorization never follows.

That's a much stronger way of killing it because the Do 335 loses **despite being good**.

---

# The Ho 229 is the most interesting case

I like your escort interpretation enormously. It gives the aircraft a purpose that arises from AltWWII rather than desperately rebuilding the historical *3×1000* requirement.

But I would modify two things: its construction and its dogfighting mythology.

### Don't make it purely aluminum

The Ho 229's wood isn't simply equivalent to the He 162's emergency cheap construction.

The actual V3 was already a mixed structure using plywood, other wood, ferrous alloys and aluminum alloys. Smithsonian's Horten interview archive is especially interesting here because Reimar Horten specifically discussed metal construction, bonding aluminum to wood, reinforcement and the peculiar structural demands of the H IX. citeturn531287search0turn531287search2turn531287search4

So our prosperous production Ho 229 should probably be **a much better mixed-construction airplane**, rather than an all-metal rewrite.

Its central structure can use welded high-quality steel and increasing amounts of duralumin. High-load fittings, engine mounts, landing-gear structure and wing reinforcement become metallic. The outer wing can retain carefully manufactured bonded plywood where it makes aerodynamic and structural sense.

That preserves actual Horten engineering ancestry rather than turning Gotha into Northrop.

And because Germany isn't manufacturing it in underground desperation, the woodwork can actually be *good*: controlled humidity, consistent resin, proper curing, inspected bonding and adequate material stocks.

### Its aerodynamic efficiency really can be one of its signatures

Here your instinct is sound.

The flying wing eliminates a separate fuselage and tail producing their own wetted area and drag. Horten's work was also explicitly concerned with span loading and induced drag; later NASA investigation of Horten-type spanloads found real efficiency advantages rather than treating the idea as aesthetic eccentricity. citeturn407569search6turn407569search16

That makes a long-range escort role a very natural thing for the Luftwaffe to discover:

> The strange fighter carries surprisingly little fuel for the distance it covers.

However, early turbojet fuel consumption still exists. I would not give a Jumo-004-powered Ho 229 enough range to accompany an Me 264 from Germany to Magnitogorsk and back.

Instead, its escort role operates in two ways.

Against Britain, this isn't a major problem. Forward fields in France, Belgium and the Netherlands place the entire British theater within reasonable reach.

Against the USSR, Ho 229 units deploy to **forward prepared fields** as the Germans move east. They protect Fernbomber formations through the defended portion of their penetration and recovery. The Me 264 then has the endurance to continue farther.

That is actually more interesting operationally than an escort with magically equal range. Bombers have corridors where escort coverage begins and ends.

---

# I would definitely give the Ho 229 a frightening turning reputation—but narrow the claim

This is the main place where I think we're pushing the physics too far.

There is actually a fascinating piece of supporting evidence for your intuition. In Smithsonian's archive of later interviews with Reimar Horten, he recalled reports from test pilot Erwin Ziller that the H IX V2 **could out-turn and out-climb an Me 262** during informal mock combat. But the same archive explicitly says these were impressions communicated by telephone, not precise measured comparative trials. citeturn531287search4

So we have a historical seed for exactly the reputation you want.

What I would *not* turn that into is:

> It can almost out-turn biplanes and normally beats Spitfires in one- and two-circle fights.

Being all wing does not make lift free. Turn performance still depends on wing loading, maximum lift coefficient, available thrust, structural limit, control authority, energy loss and trim. Tailless swept aircraft also pay real control penalties; NACA and later NASA work found stability, control and trim to be genuine design problems rather than automatically superior characteristics. citeturn407569search3turn407569search17

Instead, I'd give it a **regime-specific monster reputation**.

At medium-high speed, the Ho 229 has an astonishing amount of lifting area for its mass and loses relatively little energy in a broad sweeping turn. A British pilot sees a large twin-engine jet and expects something resembling an Me 262.

Then the thing banks hard and comes around **far faster than a twin-engine jet has any right to**.

That's the shock.

An early Meteor almost certainly does not want to enter that fight.

An Me 262 doesn't want to enter that fight.

A Mosquito most certainly doesn't.

And even a Spitfire pilot can get killed by assuming:

> Jet = straight-line fighter.

But as speed decays, the picture changes. The Spitfire's mature controls, propeller thrust at low speed and conventional aerodynamic layout become increasingly valuable. The Ho 229's drag rudders, yaw coordination, elevon trim and early turbojets become increasingly troublesome.

So I'd describe its combat envelope something like this:

**High-speed instantaneous turn:** exceptional for a jet and deeply surprising.

**Medium-speed sustained turn:** very good, particularly for its size.

**Low-speed turning contest:** increasingly unfavorable against the best British piston fighters.

**Roll/yaw precision and gun tracking:** more demanding than on a conventional fighter.

**Energy recovery after the pilot gets slow:** bad, because early jets don't suddenly give him piston-fighter acceleration.

That produces exactly the RAF story you're seeking:

> “Don't turn with the bloody wing.”

But it's not because a 1940s flying wing has somehow become more agile than a Gladiator.

And I particularly would **not** give it an automatic two-circle advantage. The one-circle fight—who can change direction sharply first—is where its unusual lift and geometry can be frightening. A prolonged two-circle contest makes thrust, sustained specific excess power and energy loss increasingly important.

That gives it character rather than universal superiority.

### And your gun is the MK 103

The slow-firing 30 mm cannon you're describing is the **MK 103**, rather than “MK-03.”

That also fits the provisional Aerospace Reference's intended Ho 229 armament: two 30×184B mm MK 103 cannon. fileciteturn11file14

I like retaining them.

They're disproportionately heavy for a fighter, but that's part of why the Ho 229 feels like an unusually vicious Begleitjäger. It isn't throwing an enormous volume of fire. It's firing a smaller number of very high-energy 30 mm shells from a stable gun platform.

That makes it useful against bombers, reconnaissance aircraft and even light naval targets in addition to escort work.

---

# Me 262 remains the actual German jet fighter

This distinction is important.

The Ho 229 becomes the aircraft that everybody remembers from posters.

The **Me 262 is the aircraft the Luftwaffe actually fights the jet war with**.

That is already consistent with the setting's Second Battle of Britain, where German and British jets are fighting over the southern approaches while Arado strikes attack the British air-defense and support system. fileciteturn11file0

So when someone writes a German fighter pilot memoir of 1946, the normal experience isn't:

> “I was assigned my fantastic flying wing.”

It's:

> “I converted from the 109 or 190 to the 262.”

Ho 229 pilots are the weird specialists.

That keeps the setting grounded.

---

# The HG-III works, but I'd change exactly what “fuel hog” means

This is another place where your narrative requirement is good but the simple engineering explanation fights the design.

If HG-III is aerodynamically cleaner than the ordinary Me 262, **it shouldn't inherently burn more fuel to fly the same speed with the same engines**. Less drag ordinarily works in the other direction.

So rather than saying:

> The HG-III shape is inefficient.

I'd make its reputation arise from the **mission it was designed to perform**.

The HG-III only justifies its existence when flown very fast.

Its more heavily swept wing gives worse low-speed characteristics. Its larger or uprated engines are operated at aggressive power settings. Its buried/wing-root engine installation takes away some useful internal volume and imposes intake and thermal constraints. It spends a substantial fraction of a combat sortie climbing, accelerating and then maintaining a high-speed dash.

So pilots discover a slightly perverse truth:

> At economical cruise, it isn't terribly thirsty—but at economical cruise you've turned your fantastically expensive HG-III into an ordinary fighter.

The moment you actually use the feature everyone bought it for, the fuel gauge starts moving alarmingly fast.

That is the reputation we want.

And there is a second problem I would add: **maintenance access**.

The ordinary Me 262 hangs its engines beneath the wings. That's aerodynamically inelegant but wonderfully straightforward when somebody needs to remove one.

The HG-III buries its engines into the aerodynamic body.

Great for drag.

Horrible when the engine has to come out.

That gives ground crews a reason to despise the aircraft even while pilots and propagandists love it.

### Slow acceleration also works

This makes sense so long as we phrase it correctly.

A higher maximum speed does not automatically mean proportionally greater thrust-to-weight. The HG-III can have much lower drag at high speed while having only moderately greater thrust than a normal Me 262.

So it takes time to reach the speed where its aerodynamic superiority matters.

That's a wonderful tactical weakness.

A pilot caught at 500 km/h cannot press the **FAST** button.

He has to accelerate.

The HG-III is terrifying when it begins the engagement with altitude and speed. Catch it taking off, climbing, recovering from a maneuver or running low on fuel and suddenly you've found a much more mortal airplane.

The actual Me 262 was already vulnerable in precisely the phases where its tremendous maximum speed was least accessible; engine immaturity and slow response were serious operational constraints. citeturn911695search7

### I would make early 1947 production smaller than a full Jagdgeschwader

This is my one numerical preference.

Late 1945 begins serious HG work.

1946 produces HG-I/HG-II flying development and a handful of operational evaluation machines.

Late 1946 freezes the HG-III configuration.

Early 1947 produces something like **30–40 operational HG-IIIs**, plus test and replacement aircraft.

That's enough for one genuine combat **Gruppe** during the Second Battle of Britain.

And that's more than enough for propaganda to talk as though the British sky is black with them.

The RAF intelligence estimate may initially assume hundreds.

There are actually three dozen.

That fits your statement perfectly:

> enormous propaganda effect; noticeably smaller military effect.

The ordinary Me 262 still matters far more.

And after the war, those HG-IIIs are invaluable because every hour they fly generates information for the clean-sheet **Me 362**.

---

# The Me 264 is where I think we can do something particularly good

The existing canon already requires a limited Me 264 force to strike and reconnoiter northern Britain and culminates in an Me 264 formation carrying out Friedensbrot. fileciteturn11file0 fileciteturn11file12

Your new addition—that Soviet industrial evacuation makes **Magnitogorsk culturally synonymous with the Me 264**—also solves the aircraft's original purpose beautifully.

But the high-altitude requirement changes the airplane significantly.

And here's the important point:

> **I don't think we need to turn it into a jet to get there.**

Germany already has practical high-altitude aircraft experience. The Ju 86P was a dedicated high-altitude model, and British collections explicitly identify it as such. citeturn968344search0 German captured technical archives also show how extensively wartime industry was investigating swept wings, compressors and jet propulsion rather than beginning from zero in 1945. citeturn381786search11

So the Me 264 can become a **Höhenfernbomber** through an evolutionary program.

But 14 km cannot be achieved merely by bolting on somewhat better engines.

### A true 1946 Me 264 Höhenfernbomber would need a major redesign

I would target the aircraft around **normal combat operation at roughly 12.5–13.5 km**, with a lightly loaded ceiling somewhere around **14–15 km**.

That distinction matters.

An airplane whose theoretical service ceiling is 14 km is a miserable airplane to ask to fly a bombing formation at 14 km. At its ceiling it has almost no remaining climb or maneuver capability.

We want its **working altitude** to sit where British interceptors are gasping.

That means roughly 45,000 feet becomes a desirable *raid altitude*, not merely the number in the brochure.

And to accomplish that, the Me 264 needs a new high-altitude wing, dedicated Höhenmotoren with two-stage supercharging and/or turbo-supercharging, large efficient propellers, a properly pressurized crew compartment, serious heating and demisting, revised engine cooling, high-altitude mixture and ignition control, de-icing provisions, remote or carefully sealed weapons installations and a significant reduction in bombload.

Oxygen masks alone aren't the right answer for crews spending hours around 13–14 km. The aircraft needs to become a **pressurized machine**.

The other trade is bombload.

I would not make this:

> 14 km + huge bombload + enormous range + heavy defensive guns.

Pick three and something has gone wrong.

Instead, Soviet industrial raids might carry perhaps a few tonnes at lower altitude when the target is extraordinarily distant, while the special British Höhen raids sacrifice bombload for altitude.

Something around **1–2 tonnes of bombs on the highest-altitude profile** is much easier to defend technically than insisting upon a 5-tonne strategic load.

And Friedensbrot is particularly forgiving because its decisive payload isn't explosives.

### This is a substantially different Me 264—but still recognizably one

I'd expect it to acquire:

a longer/high-aspect-ratio wing;

substantially more powerful high-altitude engines;

a redesigned pressurized forward crew capsule;

less protruding defensive armament;

remote-controlled defensive weapons if retained;

reworked fuel and oxygen/pressurization systems;

and eventually a visibly different engine-nacelle arrangement.

At that point you're looking at the Bf 109E-to-K kind of family resemblance:

clearly the same lineage;

definitely not interchangeable aircraft.

That seems perfect for the Me 264's setting identity.

The early Me 264 is the **Ural bomber**.

The mature Me 264 is the **high-altitude Fernbomber**.

And the 1947 public sees only the mature airplane and assumes it was always that good.

---

# Why high altitude works better than simply giving the Me 264 enormous speed

The genius of your mission concept isn't actually:

> Meteor cannot reach 45,000 feet.

That's slightly too categorical.

The better operational statement is:

> **The RAF can technically put certain fighters near the Me 264's altitude, but it cannot routinely generate useful interceptions there.**

That's much harder to defeat.

An interceptor whose ceiling is roughly equal to the bomber's operating altitude has almost no excess performance once it gets there. It must be in almost exactly the correct position before the bomber arrives.

The German formation meanwhile already has altitude, speed and forward momentum.

So radar detects it.

Controllers scramble fighters.

The fighters climb for ages.

And unless the geometry is good, the Me 264s pass while the interceptors are still trying to get ahead of them.

That is how the bomber gets its reputation for **impunity without actually being invulnerable**.

Some are caught.

Some suffer engine failures.

Special British high-altitude units develop tactics against them.

Jets can occasionally make zoom interceptions.

Weather and contrails betray formations.

But the kill ratio is appalling enough for Britain that the Germans regard altitude as defensive armor.

That is more convincing than drawing an absolute line at 44,999 feet saying Britain cannot cross it.

---

# I would not use the P.1107 solution yet

A jet successor absolutely makes sense.

But it solves a somewhat different problem.

Turbojets are extraordinarily attractive at altitude because they free the aircraft from the increasingly awkward problem of maintaining piston-engine power and propeller efficiency in very thin air. They also offer speed.

The price, especially with 1940s engines, is **fuel**.

And the Me 264's first defining property is strategic endurance.

So converting the Fernbomber to pure jet power to obtain altitude risks sacrificing the thing that made it useful against the Urals in the first place.

There is another problem: once you install four or six jet engines, redesign their inlets and fuel system, alter the wing, change the pressure cabin and rebuild the bomber around much higher speed, you don't really have “an Me 264 with new engines.”

You have its successor.

I haven't found sufficiently clear primary archival material to treat the popular modern P.1107 drawings and specifications as one uniquely settled historical airplane, so I would not let a modern reconstruction dictate our design. We **can** use P.1107 as the name/seed of the Messerschmitt jet-Fernbomber studies, but the AltWWII aircraft should come out of our own requirements.

And this gives us a very clean genealogy:

> **Me 264 → high-altitude piston Me 264 → P.1107 jet-Fernbomber studies → postwar German strategic jet bomber.**

Rather than:

> Me 264 suddenly becomes a jet because we need another 5,000 meters.

The piston Höhen-Me 264 gets Germany through the end of the war.

P.1107 is what the engineering staff is already sketching because they know the piston solution is approaching its ceiling.

## So I think we've just found the late-war Luftwaffe's personality

It isn't actually a wonder-weapon force.

It's a force where **a few weird aircraft have become highly specialized tools around one overwhelmingly important jet fighter**.

The Me 262 is ordinary German jet combat power.

The Ho 229 is the bizarre, long-legged escort that turns far harder than opponents initially expect.

The HG-III is the glamorous high-speed interceptor whose brochure performance conceals ugly fuel and maintenance economics.

The Ar 234 is the working reconnaissance/strike jet.

The Hs 129 B-3 is a peculiar anti-tank technological branch.

The Me 163 and Do 335 are famous dead ends.

The He 162 is a proposal the Reich is rich enough to reject.

And the Me 264 is not Germany's B-17. It is a **small strategic specialist fleet whose entire doctrine is to go farther or higher than ordinary Luftwaffe aircraft can go**.

That last distinction, in particular, makes the Second Battle of Britain work much better. Germany doesn't somehow build a gigantic strategic bomber establishment after spending the war as a tactical air power. It builds **enough Me 264s to create a problem Britain has difficulty solving**. fileciteturn11file0

---

But turning, the tightness of the turn is, as you mentioned, way tighter than a two-engine jet plane has any right to have, and is kind of the thing that it gains a reputation going forward in the setting, as evidence that a jet fighter can be very nimble. And it genuinely is, for a very long time, the most nimble jet fighter, in spite of its size and two-engine layout. Eventually, more nimble jet fighters do get developed, possibly the Japanese make one, but it takes a little bit of time for that to come to fruition. As for the Me 264, as we discussed it, I think it may be proper to end up calling it an Me 364 instead of pretending it's the same Me 264 of our timeline. Because as soon as you start changing the actual geometry of the plane by saying, okay, we're gonna make an even longer wing, we're gonna make different kinds of engines, and redesign the pressurized forward crew capsule, like, when you start describing all of the aspects about it that we're changing, it's not an Me 264 at that point. It's the next generation after that. And that's okay. We can have a very small kind of production run of an Me 364 that is produced probably in 1946. And therefore, there's enough of them present in 1947 to be serving in the Second Battle of Britain as the high-altitude bomber for hitting positions that the Schnellbombers, the Erredos, are not well equipped to break through. The Second Battle of Britain also should probably be kind of one of the thought processes with it, that the Erredos come in, they knock out the radar stations that are on the coasts of Britain. However, as they try to come in closer to knock out airfields and things like that, the Schnellbomber is ultimately running into problems because Britain has their own jet fighters. And so Schnellbombers need Schnell escorts, like the Me 262. And interestingly, the Ho 229. Problem is, the Schnellbombers cannot actually make the attack safe simply because they're going fast. So the Hohenwehran bombers, the Me 364s, as I think we're gonna end up calling them, end up being what is used to bomb British airfields that are known, and also doing high-altitude reconnaissance. High-altitude reconnaissance is typically particularly difficult, at least in Britain, because of cloud cover. But on occasion, it can be useful. And said occasion is far and few between. Typically, the 364 is used as a high-altitude bomber to drop relatively significant enough payloads to try and mess up the airfields. One possible option that I could imagine being done, especially for the bombing of airfields, would be cluster munitions. Not mines. I'm not thinking of cluster mines, but something where you drop something, a single bomb, say, on the scale of like a Fritz X kind of thing, as far as weight goes. Said bomb then gets down to a decent amount of altitude where the spread is going to be able to cover the majority of the airfield, and then it breaks apart into several smaller bomblets. The result is not one giant crater, but a whole host of craters all over the place, spread out and distributed, such that, ideally, you manage to hit a few aircraft that might possibly be on a runway, or potentially in an exposed area. But most importantly, you've just pockedmarked that runway and made it very unsafe to land on. That's the target thought process for how to make the most out of a limited bomb load. That said, I can imagine that said cluster munitions would be possible with late 1946 technology. It just might be on the edge of possible. I'm not sure if any design was ever made equivalent to what I'm describing here. But it doesn't seem to me that it would necessarily require computers or anything like that.

## Turn 996 — Assistant

- Timestamp: 2026-08-13T08:47:47.098Z
- Message ID: `6ebaa4ee-8f04-4152-a62d-36636fdfbbf3`
- Source: ChatGPT shared conversation `WWII Air Development 1941`
- Parallel branch: https://chatgpt.com/share/6a7e5b4c-a75c-83e8-b24d-617523189a3c
- Relationship: parallel specialist continuation imported after the master project record through Turn 777

Yes. With those corrections, I think the system becomes technically coherent rather than merely narratively convenient. There are still a few places where I would sharpen the wording, but the underlying aircraft roles now fit together very well.

The largest change is that I would stop describing the HG-III as having **poor acceleration** in a general sense. What you're really describing is **poor throttle response and poor low-speed recovery combined with excellent high-speed acceleration once the engines are actually producing thrust**. That distinction matters.

## The HG-III: low endurance, not intrinsically thirsty

Your revised model works, with one packaging correction.

The ordinary Me 262 carries its principal fuel tanks in the fuselage, forward and aft of the cockpit, rather than in large wing-root tanks. Contemporary pilot-handbook material describes separate forward and rear main tanks and the transfer system between auxiliary and main tanks. citeturn307069search0turn307069search24

So the HG-III shouldn't lose fuel because:

> “The engines occupy the old Me 262 wing fuel tanks.”

Instead, it loses fuel because **the entire center section has been repackaged**.

Bringing larger engines inward requires intake trunks, engine bays, stronger wing-root structure, firewalls, ducting, controls and access spaces. At the same time, the more heavily swept wing changes the carry-through structure. Messerschmitt can preserve the original Me 262's external dimensions only by taking volume away from somewhere else, and the easiest place to lose useful volume is fuel.

That gives us the result you want without cheating the underlying Me 262 layout:

> **HG-III carries perhaps 25–30 percent less usable internal fuel than a contemporary standard Me 262 despite having more powerful engines.**

I wouldn't lock an exact litre figure yet because we haven't drawn the HG-III internal arrangement. But that gives us a design target.

And then the new engines compound the problem.

A next-generation engine plausibly provides substantially more thrust than the Jumo 004. Germany was already developing the Heinkel-Hirth HeS 011 as a higher-pressure-ratio second-generation turbojet with significant growth potential. citeturn561353search3

But **more powerful does not inherently mean slower to accelerate**.

The version that works is this:

The engine has a larger rotating mass and much higher mass flow. More importantly, its fuel-control schedule is deliberately conservative because rapidly dumping fuel into an early axial compressor can produce surge, overtemperature or unstable combustion. Period NACA work on early turbojets found precisely these kinds of acceleration limitations; some engines could take a distinctly long time to move safely through portions of their operating range, especially under difficult altitude conditions. citeturn546825search20turn546825search23

So:

**Throttle response:** poor.

**Low-speed energy recovery:** poor.

**Acceleration once stabilized at high thrust:** actually quite good.

**Time needed to reach the airplane's spectacular headline speed:** long enough to matter tactically.

That's better than simply saying it accelerates slowly.

A British pilot catches one at 550 km/h and the HG-III pilot pushes the throttles forward. There is an uncomfortable interval where the German aircraft hasn't yet become the aircraft the brochure describes.

But once the engines stabilize and it gets through 750–800 km/h, the aerodynamic cleanup begins paying enormous dividends.

That's the combat personality.

And your maintenance problem is excellent. An Me 262 technician can remove a podded engine comparatively directly. On HG-III, if the design integrates the engine deeply into the wing-root structure, a serious engine change could involve removing large access panels, control runs and portions of the center/wing structure. It needn't literally require detaching the whole wing every time, but crews can absolutely joke that **“you dismantle the airplane to change the engine.”**

I would make that one of the major reasons production ends quickly.

So by early 1947:

- ordinary Me 262: reliable enough, accessible, adequate endurance;
- HG-III: much faster, shorter-legged, difficult at low speed, awful to service;
- propaganda ministry: HG-III is the future;
- fighter-command logistics officers: please give us more ordinary 262s.

That is exactly the tension we want.

---

# Ho 229: we're basically aligned now

Your revised maneuverability claim works much better.

I'd describe the Ho 229's reputation as:

> **The most maneuverable first-generation operational jet in the high- and medium-speed regime, particularly in instantaneous pitch and vertical maneuvering.**

Not universally the tightest-turning airplane in existence.

And avoiding the drag rudders absolutely becomes part of pilot technique. The control arrangement means aggressive yaw correction extracts an aerodynamic price. A skilled Ho pilot therefore learns to maneuver through coordinated bank and pitch whenever possible and use differential drag sparingly.

The vertical maneuver you're describing can happen, but I would be careful about saying:

> “It reliably does a complete loop and ends up behind whoever was following it.”

Geometry matters.

What becomes frightening is a **vertical overshoot maneuver**.

A British fighter comes in behind an Ho 229 expecting the large twin-engine jet to run.

Instead the Ho pitches violently upward into the vertical.

If the pursuer follows, he's entering the Ho's game. If he cannot match the vertical radius or bleeds too much energy, he falls behind during the maneuver.

If he doesn't follow, his closing speed may carry him underneath and ahead while the Ho rolls or pitches back down into the fight.

A complete 360-degree loop *can* put the Ho behind a committed pursuer under the right geometry. It isn't an automatic reversal button.

So RAF lore eventually becomes something like:

> **Don't follow the wing over the top.**

That is much more believable than “don't turn at all.”

And it lets us preserve exactly what you want historically: pilots initially assume that **large + twin-engine + jet = poor turning fighter**, discover they're badly wrong, and update their tactics.

The Ho's great weakness then remains energy management.

One hard turn? Frightening.

A second maneuver while still fast? Still dangerous.

A prolonged low-speed wrestling match? Now it starts wishing it were a Spitfire.

That also means it can remain the benchmark for jet maneuverability for a surprisingly long period without becoming the universally best dogfighter.

---

# Me 364 is a better name and, more importantly, a better conceptual break

I agree completely.

We've changed too many engineering fundamentals to keep pretending this is merely “Me 264 Ausf. whatever.”

The relationship should be analogous to:

> **Me 264 establishes the Fernbomber architecture. Me 364 takes that experience and builds a dedicated Höhenfernbomber around it.**

That gives both airplanes distinct cultural identities.

### Me 264

This is the **Ural bomber**.

Magnitogorsk remembers it.

Its defining characteristic is range.

It exists because Soviet heavy industry has physically retreated outside ordinary Luftwaffe bomber reach.

It isn't especially glamorous aerodynamically by 1947. It's remembered because German bombs arriving over the Urals meant the geographic sanctuary had disappeared.

### Me 364

This is the **high-altitude bomber**.

Britain remembers it.

Its defining characteristic is altitude rather than maximum range.

It is a 1945–46 development based upon everything Germany has learned from the Me 264, Ju 86 high-altitude work, high-altitude engine development, pressure cabins and the increasingly sophisticated British air-defense system.

And there's a very strong historical engineering basis for this.

The captured Ju 388L examined at Wright Field used exhaust-driven turbosuperchargers feeding engine-driven superchargers, a pressurized crew cabin, electrically heated suits, wing and tail de-icing and a heavily automated engine-management system. It was explicitly an operational German high-altitude aircraft. citeturn329841search0

So the Me 364 isn't requiring Germany to invent an unknown technical category in 1946.

We're asking them to **scale techniques they already knew** into a purpose-designed four-engine bomber.

That makes 13–14 km far less problematic.

I would set the performance target approximately like this, provisionally:

| Characteristic | Me 364 working target |
|---|---:|
| Normal raid altitude | **12,500–13,500 m** |
| Light-load/reconnaissance ceiling | **14,000–14,500 m** |
| Highest-altitude bomb load | **1,000–2,000 kg** |
| Crew | ~5–7, concentrated in pressurized compartments |
| Primary British mission | Airfield, command, logistics and industrial-area attack |
| Secondary mission | High-altitude photographic/weather reconnaissance |
| Strategic range | Less important than Me 264; still substantial |

That is aggressive but not fantastical.

And critically, **13.5 km operational altitude is much more useful than merely advertising a 13.5 km service ceiling**.

---

# The Second Battle of Britain now gets a useful vertical structure

I particularly like the division you're arriving at.

The German air campaign no longer consists of everyone trying to solve Britain through “go faster.”

It has layers.

### Ar 234: penetrate

The Arado attacks things which must be hit comparatively precisely:

- radar stations;
- communications;
- known operations rooms;
- exposed fuel installations;
- airfield facilities;
- naval installations;
- maintenance and supply sites.

Its defense is speed.

But once Britain has functioning jet interception, speed stops being sufficient by itself.

So the Ar 234 increasingly requires Me 262 and sometimes Ho 229 cover when it penetrates deeply enough for the RAF to concentrate against it.

### Me 262: defeat interception

This is the principal fighter.

It isn't merely escorting bombers. It's trying to keep the British jets occupied and prevent them from setting up clean attacks against the strike aircraft.

### Ho 229: longer-legged specialist escort

Especially valuable where range or extended patrol time matters and where the Germans expect interception by high-performance fighters.

Numerically much smaller.

### Me 364: go above the system

This isn't supposed to penetrate by being faster than British fighters.

It tries to operate where British fighters have **little excess performance left**.

Even when an RAF fighter can physically reach the altitude, that does not mean it can easily get ahead of a bomber already cruising there, maneuver into firing position and conduct repeated attacks.

So the Germans aren't making interception impossible.

They're making it geometrically difficult and operationally expensive.

That's much more believable.

---

# And yes: your cluster weapon is completely feasible by 1946

In fact, you're not really asking Germany to invent the basic technology.

Germany already had **Abwurfbehälter**, aerial dispensers which opened after release and scattered numerous smaller bombs. Contemporary Allied ordnance documentation records German containers such as the AB 250/500 families dispersing multiple submunitions. citeturn546825search36

No computer is needed.

At its simplest, the system is:

1. bomber releases dispenser;
2. mechanical/electric time fuze runs;
3. container reaches the desired part of its fall;
4. explosive/mechanical charge opens the casing;
5. aerodynamic forces separate the submunitions;
6. each submunition arms independently during descent.

That is entirely 1940s technology.

But there's one important correction to your intended effect.

## Tiny bomblets don't make good runway craters

Period American naval doctrine actually draws this distinction very clearly. Fragmentation clusters were recommended against **parked aircraft, personnel and revetments**, while heavier 500- and 1,000-pound bombs were recommended for attacking the runway itself. citeturn546825search1

That's because an SD 2-style bomblet is excellent at:

- punching holes in aircraft;
- cutting exposed personnel down;
- shredding trucks;
- damaging light buildings;
- littering a maintenance area.

It's not going to make a serious crater in a paved runway.

So what Germany needs in 1946 is not a radically new cluster bomb.

It needs a **new submunition for an existing dispenser principle**.

---

# The Me 364's anti-airfield weapon should use larger submunitions

I'd build it around perhaps **20–50 kg individual bombs**, rather than hundreds of 1–2 kg fragmentation bomblets.

The conceptual weapon could be around **500–1,000 kg total**.

For example, an approximately one-ton dispenser might carry something on the order of:

- perhaps 16–24 cratering submunitions in the 30–50 kg class;
- modest container/opening hardware;
- mechanical time fuze;
- each submunition fitted with a short-delay impact fuze.

I'm deliberately not fixing those numbers yet because we'd want to calculate actual casing, explosive fraction and desired footprint.

The bombs hit independently across an ellipse.

You don't get one enormous crater.

You get:

> crater — crater — crater — near miss — shattered edge — crater — damaged taxiway — crater.

Which is exactly your desired effect.

And notice that the bombs don't need to destroy the entire runway.

Aircraft require a **continuous usable strip**.

A handful of sufficiently awkward craters across the main landing run, especially near intersections and taxiways, can close that strip until engineers inspect, fill, compact and resurface it.

This isn't permanent destruction.

That is important.

British airfield engineers can repair bomb damage.

The German objective is **sortie suppression**.

Hit the field at 0500.

It cannot launch its intended morning complement.

Repair units go to work.

Hit it again tomorrow.

Now reserve fields, dispersed servicing, runway-repair stores, bulldozers and engineering manpower all become part of the air battle.

That's much more strategically useful than pretending one cluster bomb erases an RAF station.

---

# One dispenser should not cover “most of the airfield”

This is the other point I'd pull back slightly.

If you spread twenty bombs over an entire major airbase, they're so widely separated that most do nothing useful.

Instead, Germany wants **controlled overlapping patterns**.

Imagine six Me 364s.

Each drops one large anti-airfield dispenser.

Each dispenser creates an elongated footprint.

The bombardier's aim point isn't “RAF Biggin Hill.”

It is something more like:

> main runway / cross-runway intersection.

or:

> principal runway and maintenance-dispersal boundary.

The formation staggers the release so the six footprints overlap.

Now even mediocre high-altitude accuracy has a chance of placing enough submunitions across useful parts of the station to interrupt operations.

And that matters because high-altitude bombing accuracy remains the greatest problem in your concept.

A dispenser improves **coverage after a good release**.

It does not fix a release point that is two kilometers wrong.

So navigation, weather, wind measurement and bombing instrumentation become just as important to the Me 364 program as engines.

That gives us another excellent developmental consequence:

> **The Me 364 isn't merely driving high-altitude aircraft technology. It forces Germany to get much better at high-altitude navigation and blind bombing.**

And Britain being Britain, cloud becomes almost as important an opponent as the RAF.

---

# I would actually give Germany two Me 364 airfield weapons

Not two radically different technologies—two loads for the same dispenser family.

**Flugplatz-Sprengladung**, runway package:

Larger HE submunitions, relatively few in number, intended to crater hard surfaces and damage taxiways.

**Flugplatz-Splitterladung**, dispersal package:

Many smaller fragmentation/incendiary submunitions intended for parked aircraft, fuel bowsers, trucks, exposed maintenance personnel and lightly protected facilities.

That gives the mission planner a choice.

If reconnaissance says aircraft have been dispersed into revetments, take fragmentation loads.

If the field itself needs to stop operating, take cratering loads.

A mixed raid might have four Me 364s attacking runways and two distributing fragmentation loads over aircraft dispersal.

Again, none of this requires digital technology. The historical ingredients were already present; the alternate development lies in integrating them into a deliberate **high-altitude airfield-suppression system**. citeturn546825search36turn546825search1

## So I think the revisions lock together cleanly

The **HG-III** is not inherently wasteful with fuel. It is a short-endurance aircraft because its integrated high-speed architecture sacrifices tankage, and because exploiting its powerful engines means spending fuel rapidly. Its engines have poor throttle response rather than universally poor acceleration.

The **Ho 229** is exceptionally nimble *for an early jet*, particularly in high-speed instantaneous and vertical maneuvering. Its famous trick is forcing an unsuspecting pursuer into an overshoot or losing fight in the vertical, not magically completing a loop behind anybody who attacks it.

The **Me 264** remains the aircraft Magnitogorsk fears: the wartime long-range Fernbomber.

The **Me 364** becomes a genuinely new 1946 aircraft: a pressurized, turbosupercharged high-altitude bomber derived from Me 264 experience and built specifically to operate in the 12.5–14 km environment. German high-altitude technology already makes that engineering direction credible. citeturn329841search0

And the anti-airfield cluster weapon is not merely possible in 1946. **The dispenser is old technology by then.** What Germany invents is the purpose-designed heavier cratering submunition and the doctrine for dropping overlapping patterns from the Me 364.

That gives the Second Battle of Britain a much better character: Ar 234s and their escorts fight *through* the British air-defense system, while Me 364s try to fight *above* it, principally by disrupting the airfields from which that defense has to operate.

By 1946, Me 262s have been fighting Soviet props, and ultimately Soviet props do not stand up very well against them. This kind of encourages the Germans to keep the boom and zoom tactic as a standard for the Luftwaffe. Interestingly, this is very useful because the jet, the Me 262, is already kind of a very good boom and zoom fighter anyways. A lot of early jets were not particularly good at turn fighting. However, during the Battle of Britain, this is where the Luftwaffe really gets its first honest taste of the British jet program, a program which has actually developed. German night fighters also successfully cause enough damage and knock out enough bombers of the RAF night raids over Germany that ultimately London decides to call off the night raids.
