Yes. I think the second solution is substantially better: **the RAF's deep night offensive should ultimately be defeated by the mature German night-defense system, not by turning the Me 262 into yet another specialist fleet.** The 262 can contribute experimentally, but it doesn't need to carry the Nachtjagd story.

That also gives the Luftwaffe two very different wartime schools of air combat.

## The East teaches the Luftwaffe how to fight fast

The transcript already gives us the Soviet progression. By 1943 the VVS is abandoning any realistic attempt to contest the whole front continuously. It concentrates aircraft, fuel and its best pilots around chosen operations, fights hard for several days, and then its sortie rate falls away. By 1944–45, German air superiority is the normal condition outside those defended islands. fileciteturn12file0 The important thing is that this is **progressive narrowing, not Soviet technical stupidity**: elite Yak and Lavochkin units can remain genuinely dangerous even while the larger VVS is increasingly strangled by fuel, engines, material quality and replacements. fileciteturn12file1

That gives Germany a very good environment in which to introduce jets without pretending the Soviets are helpless targets.

I would roughly break the combat learning into four phases:

| Period | German fighter experience |
|---|---|
| **1941–42** | Bf 109/Fw 190 crews learn conventional energy fighting against dangerous Soviet piston fighters |
| **1943–44** | Luftwaffe increasingly controls when and where most air combat occurs; Soviet concentrations remain dangerous |
| **1944–45** | Me 262 begins combat deployment; jets encounter Yaks/La fighters and learn very quickly not to squander speed |
| **1945–46** | Ho 229 enters limited combat; its pilots learn unusual vertical and instantaneous-turn tactics against some of the most maneuverable Soviet fighters still operating |

So I wouldn't say jets *create* German boom-and-zoom doctrine. The Luftwaffe already understands energy fighting. What jets do is make the principle almost doctrinally non-negotiable:

> **Speed is a weapon. Don't voluntarily surrender it.**

For an Me 262 pilot, a Yak trying to lure him into a horizontal engagement is offering him a bad bargain. Make the firing pass, extend, climb, reposition, come back.

And the Soviet pilots absolutely learn how to exploit the opposite circumstance. A 262 caught slow, taking off, landing, recovering from an aggressive maneuver, or forced to turn near a defended airfield is no longer the mythical untouchable jet.

That keeps the eastern jet war useful as **real combat training**, rather than target practice.

### The Ho 229 learns a slightly different lesson

This is actually where its Soviet service becomes particularly useful.

The Me 262 pilot learns:

> Don't turn with the Yak.

The Ho 229 pilot discovers:

> I don't necessarily have to refuse the first turn.

Because the Horten retains energy unusually well when maneuvered through bank and pitch rather than aggressive drag-rudder input, it can make a frightening instantaneous or vertical maneuver. That becomes its specialty.

But the Soviet experience also teaches Ho pilots the limits. If you keep pulling until you've bled down into the Yak's speed regime, you've thrown away the reason your strange flying wing was dangerous.

So the combat doctrine becomes something like:

**Me 262:** strike, extend, reposition.

**Ho 229:** strike; exploit one violent reversal or vertical maneuver if useful; then recover energy.

That distinction gives German jet aviation two actual tactical cultures.

And I like the Soviet pilots being the people who teach the Horten force how to fight. When British pilots later encounter it, the German Ho crews aren't test pilots discovering their airplane in combat. They've already had several months of trying strange maneuvers against Yaks whose pilots are quite happy to punish a mistake.

---

# But Nachtjagd develops almost independently

This is where I think your instinct to **not** use the Me 262 is exactly right.

The transcript already has the proper origin. British night bombing causes Germany to accelerate airborne radar and night-fighter procurement in 1942, with **Bf 110 and Ju 88 conversions plus Lichtenstein radar as the immediate answer and the He 219 as the accelerated purpose-built answer.** fileciteturn13file0

And historically, that system was already capable of inflicting frightening losses despite Germany fighting under vastly worse circumstances than it does here.

The Ju 88 was well suited to night fighting because its existing airframe offered speed, handling, endurance and room for radar and crew; an RAF Museum Ju 88 R-1 preserves the nose-mounted Lichtenstein installation. citeturn553819view2 The He 219 is even more useful for our purpose: it was specifically pushed forward because British night bombing had become serious, incorporated airborne radar and later upward-firing **Schräge Musik**, and functioned inside an integrated system of ground radar, observers, radio control and onboard interception radar. citeturn180689search1

So our mature German night defense doesn't need one fantastic machine. It needs the **whole chain**:

> early warning → plotting → ground control → fighter vector → onboard radar acquisition → unseen firing position → disengagement → another interception

That's exactly the kind of systems problem Germany in this timeline has the resources to get progressively better at.

## I would make the late-war hierarchy very clear

By roughly 1944–45:

**Ju 88 night-fighter family — the workhorse.**  
This is the aircraft Germany can actually field in quantity. Good endurance matters enormously at night. It has room for the radar operator and equipment, and the basic Ju 88 industrial family is already enormous.

**He 219 — the premium specialist.**  
Faster, purpose-built, highly armed, particularly desirable against fast bombers and Mosquitoes. Smithsonian describes it as arguably the Luftwaffe's best wartime night fighter and notes that it was capable of meeting the Mosquito on much better terms than the older machines. citeturn180689search1

**Bf 110G — veteran secondary fleet.**  
Still useful where already established, increasingly displaced from the most demanding interceptions.

**Do 217N — transitional.**  
It exists, serves, and gradually loses the procurement competition.

**Me 262 Nachtjagd — experimental curiosity.**  
A few trials prove that a jet vectored onto the bomber stream can make an extremely fast interception. That can remain the event we already discussed which alarms British intelligence. But it doesn't become the backbone.

I like that because the Luftwaffe gets to say something rather sensible:

> Why put scarce Jumo turbines, jet-trained pilots and short-endurance Me 262s into a mission the Ju 88 and He 219 already perform very well?

The jet is solving the daytime/high-speed problem.

Let Nachtjagd solve Nachtjagd.

---

# The real divergence is that Germany gets to finish the night-fighter system

Historically, this was already an ugly contest.

RAF electronic warfare periodically broke pieces of the German system. **Window** was extremely effective when first used over Hamburg in July 1943; only 12 of 700 bombers were lost in that first raid because German radar was badly confused. Britain subsequently created No. 100 Group to coordinate its increasingly sophisticated radio-countermeasure campaign. citeturn983732search1

But Germany adapted too. Later radars, new control methods, emissions exploitation, free-ranging interception tactics, and weapons such as Schräge Musik kept the night defenses dangerous. RAF historical material records both the German **Wilde Sau** single-engine tactic and **Zahme Sau** system for directing night fighters into the bomber stream. citeturn180689search2

In our setting, that becomes a sustained technological duel rather than a defense system being progressively crushed underneath total Allied material superiority.

Because the things that historically killed the Luftwaffe are much weaker or absent:

- there is **no American daylight strategic-bomber offensive** forcing Germany to defend against two fundamentally different bomber wars;
- German fighter training isn't being destroyed by the same fuel collapse;
- German radar, aircraft, engine and electronics production isn't simultaneously being torn apart by the combined Anglo-American campaign;
- Nachtjagd crews have more flying hours and better continuity;
- damaged night fighters can actually be repaired and replaced;
- and Germany can sustain ground-control sites rather than watching its entire territorial system retreat eastward.

The historical RAF record makes the potential consequences quite clear. During the Battle of Berlin, Bomber Command lost **625 aircraft** across the campaign. Then, on 30/31 March 1944, the Nuremberg raid lost **95 of 795 bombers—11.9% in one night—after German night-fighter controllers correctly identified the target despite British deception.** citeturn983732search1turn553819view1 Another raid at Mailly-le-Camp in May lost 42 Lancasters, about **11.6%**, after a delay allowed German night fighters to get into the force. citeturn553819view1

And that is historical Germany while losing the wider air war.

Fractured Peace Germany can plausibly make those nights less exceptional.

---

# But I wouldn't have the RAF simply wake up one morning and cancel bombing

The stronger development is cumulative.

Say Britain goes through 1943–44 with a recognizable cycle.

A new navigation or jamming system works.

Losses fall.

Germany introduces a countermeasure.

Losses rise.

Britain changes routes.

Germany changes fighter-control practice.

A bomber countermeasure exposes another electronic signature.

The Germans exploit it.

Britain switches equipment again.

Occasionally Bomber Command achieves a very successful raid at tolerable cost. Occasionally it loses forty, sixty, perhaps ninety bombers for disappointing results.

So the strategic crisis isn't:

> “Night bombing became impossible.”

It is:

> **“We can still bomb Germany. We can no longer convince ourselves that doing so at this scale is worth what it costs.”**

That's a much more British decision.

And because this Britain is fighting alone in the western strategic air war, the arithmetic is much uglier than historically.

There isn't an American daylight force forcing Germany to maintain hundreds of fighters, pilots, flak batteries and radars against a second threat.

There isn't an American aircraft industry adding thousands of heavy bombers to the offensive.

And, increasingly importantly, there isn't a credible Soviet advance making British bombing look like one half of an inevitable military convergence on Berlin.

The transcript already establishes that the VVS progressively contracts while Britain continues bombing partly to support the Soviets and partly because bombing is one of Britain's few direct ways of striking Germany. fileciteturn13file8

By 1944–45, that justification gets harder to make.

The Soviet Union isn't marching west.

It is trying not to die.

---

# So “the RAF calls off the night raids” should mean something specific

I would canonize it as:

> **Bomber Command suspends the sustained main-force deep night offensive against Germany.**

Not:

> The RAF stops operating over Europe after sunset.

Those are radically different claims.

The Lancaster/Halifax mass raids into the Ruhr, Berlin and deep central Germany are what end.

Britain can still conduct:

- Mosquito nuisance and precision raids;
- specialist attacks where the target is considered worth extraordinary risk;
- minelaying;
- coastal and maritime operations;
- attacks on occupied France and the Low Countries;
- shorter-range interdiction;
- reconnaissance;
- leaflet and special-duty missions;
- occasional attempts to hit a uniquely valuable installation.

Indeed, historical Bomber Command did something structurally similar after the murderous end of the Battle of Berlin: the main force stopped attacking Berlin for a time while smaller Mosquito forces continued frequent raids. citeturn553819view1

So we have a historical institutional precedent for saying:

> **The strategic main force stops. The RAF does not disappear.**

That makes the eventual German offensive against Britain much more interesting too, because there are still experienced British bomber crews and aircraft around. They haven't been annihilated. The government has simply concluded that sending 700 bombers across the German night-defense belt several nights a month is no longer a rational way to spend them.

## Timing

I would currently put the break **somewhere in late 1944 or early 1945**, without locking an exact night yet.

That's late enough that Germans have lived through years of blackout, bombing and real urban destruction.

It's late enough for Lancaster culture and Britain's strategic-bombing campaign to matter deeply.

And it is early enough that Nachtjagd units can begin reallocating crews, radars and aircraft as the German strategic position shifts from primarily defending the Reich to preparing for renewed pressure against Britain.

I would prefer **cumulative collapse plus one notorious final disaster**, rather than making one raid magically decide the policy.

Perhaps the final crisis raid isn't literally our Nuremberg. We can create the alternate target later. But the shape might be:

> 600–800 aircraft dispatched; German controllers correctly identify the stream; jamming fails against the current radar fit; weather exposes the bombers; perhaps 70–90 heavy aircraft fail to return; target damage proves mediocre.

At that point the Air Staff has an argument it has been avoiding for months.

---

# This actually makes the Second Battle of Britain considerably better

Because the Luftwaffe comes into the 1945–47 campaign carrying **two different kinds of confidence**, both of which are partly justified and partly dangerous.

From Russia:

> We know how to fight an air force into local irrelevance. We have combat-seasoned jet pilots. Speed and altitude let us dictate engagements.

From the night war:

> We know how to defeat a technologically sophisticated British offensive through radar, control, electronic adaptation and attrition.

Those are real achievements.

But Britain in 1946 isn't the Soviet VVS.

That is the shock.

The first British jets aren't just individual airplanes. They're attached to the same national culture of radar warning and centralized fighter direction which came out of the First Battle of Britain. The setting already requires the RAF to survive the Second Battle by progressively moving its depth north while southeastern airfields become increasingly expendable. fileciteturn12file14

So a veteran Me 262 pilot who's spent the previous year making high-speed firing passes against Yaks encounters something quite different over Kent.

He dives.

The British fighter does not become a dot behind him quite as quickly as he's accustomed to.

More importantly, the second British fighter is already being vectored toward where his extension is taking him.

That is where Germany receives its first **honest jet-versus-jet education**.

And that gives us a lovely larger air-war progression:

**1941–42:** piston versus piston; Germany learns the Eastern air war, Britain begins the night offensive.

**1943–44:** Germany acquires broad eastern air superiority while Britain and German Nachtjagd fight an increasingly electronic war over the Reich.

**1944–45:** German jets begin acquiring combat experience against the remaining Soviet piston force; German night defenses progressively make Britain's deep bomber offensive untenable.

**1945–46:** the Soviet air threat collapses to defended pockets; Germany shifts increasing aviation attention west.

**1946–47:** the Second Battle of Britain brings everything together—Me 262 energy fighting learned in Russia, Ho 229 escort tactics learned against Yaks, Ar 234 penetration doctrine, Me 364 high-altitude bombing, German electronic warfare—and puts it against the one adversary Germany hasn't yet broken in the air: **an intact British integrated air-defense system now acquiring jets of its own.**

That is stronger than making the Me 262 solve every problem. The Luftwaffe reaches 1946 dangerous precisely because **different branches became very good at different wars**. fileciteturn14file0

---

Yes. If we let this competition run forward instead of stopping the clock in May 1945, I think the German–British night war becomes one of the most technologically advanced parts of the entire setting.

But the result isn't 1960s avionics in 1946. It is something stranger and, in some ways, more interesting: **an extremely mature analog electronic-war environment built out of vacuum tubes, magnetrons, CRT displays, mechanical plotting, radio operators, specialized crews, and increasingly elaborate deception.** By 1946–47, airborne radar is no longer exotic. Electronic countermeasures are no longer special tricks. Both have become ordinary parts of planning an operation.

And your chaff diversion idea is not merely plausible. Britain historically did almost exactly that. RAF No. 100 Group used specialized aircraft to manufacture false bomber streams with WINDOW/chaff, jamming, and carefully controlled flight patterns. One documented 1944 method used twenty-four aircraft dropping WINDOW at precisely timed intervals to produce a radar picture resembling roughly **500 aircraft**; on another operation, jamming aircraft literally generated a ghost bomber stream while the real operation went elsewhere. citeturn156434view6

So we have a very high historical floor.

The attached transcript already puts our 1942 starting point in the right place: Lichtenstein-equipped Bf 110s and Ju 88s are beginning to solve the last few kilometers of the interception while still depending heavily on German ground control, and the He 219 becomes more secure as a dedicated night-fighter project. fileciteturn17file2

## First: Wilde Sau and Zahme Sau

They have nothing to do with the later American **Wild Weasel** concept. The similarity is just the animal name.

**Wilde Sau**, literally “Wild Boar,” was the German response to the disruption of its radar-controlled night-defense system. Single-seat ordinary fighters were sent over illuminated target areas and allowed to fight visually. Fires, flares, searchlights and illuminated cloud gave the pilot enough background light to pick out bombers. It was basically saying: *if the electronic system has been confused, put a good fighter pilot over the burning city and let him hunt*. citeturn156434view0

**Zahme Sau**, “Tame Boar,” was more consequential. Instead of assigning each radar-controlled night fighter to one fixed Himmelbett interception box, controllers massed night fighters toward the bomber stream. Once inserted into it, the fighters operated much more freely, using onboard radar and their own crews to acquire individual bombers. The RAF Historical Society describes it specifically as a method of bringing freelance night fighters into contact with bombers en route to and from their target. citeturn156434view1

So the progression is conceptually:

**Himmelbett:** one controller, one fighter, one controlled interception area.

**Zahme Sau:** national radar network finds the bomber stream, controllers put a *mass* of night fighters into it, onboard systems finish the hunt.

That's already very close to what I think our 1945–46 German system naturally becomes.

## The technological race

I would currently play it approximately like this:

| Period | British move | German response | What changes operationally |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1942** | Lancaster; Gee; Pathfinding develops; bomber streams concentrate force | Freya/Würzburg/Himmelbett; Lichtenstein B/C; Bf 110/Ju 88 radar fighters; He 219 accelerated | Darkness is no longer enough to hide a bomber once a fighter has been vectored near it |
| **1943** | H2S radar navigation; Monica tail warning; WINDOW/chaff; increasingly organized jamming and deception | New radar frequencies; Würzburg anti-chaff modifications; Wilde Sau and Zahme Sau; SN-2-type AI; Schräge Musik; passive detection of British emissions begins | The contest changes from “can radar find bombers?” to “which radar and which signal can still be trusted tonight?” |
| **1944** | No. 100 Group matures: WINDOW spoof streams, MANDREL, ABC, JOSTLE, PIPERACK, bomber-support Mosquitoes, electronic deception | Flensburg homes on Monica; Naxos homes on H2S; multiband radar; dispersed fighter control; mass stream interception | Emitting becomes dangerous. A British system that helps its crew can simultaneously tell a German where the crew is |
| **1945** | Lincoln begins replacing Lancaster in high-priority units; radar-directed defensive turrets; better centimetric radar; specialized EW aircraft become normal | Improved Ju 88/He 219 families; centimetric AI accelerated; passive receivers proliferate; Reich-wide track correlation improves | Night combat becomes a systems battle involving radar, passive receivers, jammers, controllers and defensive electronics |
| **1946** | Composite spoof raids; frequency-agile or switchable jammers; better radar gun-laying; high-altitude reduced-load attacks; limited active-IR close-defense aids | Multiband GCI; cross-checking of radar and passive bearings; emission analysis; compact dish-type AI; increasingly disciplined barrier patrols | Neither side can trust a single electronic picture; classification becomes as important as detection |
| **1947** | First small jet-bomber force, Canberra-type, begins operational trials/combat | Piston Nachtjäger can no longer reliably chase it; emergency jet/all-weather interceptor requirement accelerates | Britain briefly creates a new penetration problem, but too late and in too few numbers to recreate the old mass bomber offensive |

The first four rows mostly extrapolate technologies that genuinely existed. By 1944 the historical RAF's electronic-war system was already astonishingly elaborate: specialized B-17s carried multiple MANDREL jammers, ABC or the much more powerful JOSTLE communications jammer, while other aircraft jammed German fighter radar with PIPERACK and manufactured false bomber streams with WINDOW. The Germans, meanwhile, developed Naxos to exploit H2S transmissions and Flensburg specifically to home on Monica tail-warning emissions. citeturn156434view4turn156434view6

Our divergence is that **neither technical establishment shuts down in 1945**.

---

# What does airborne radar look like by 1946?

Quite mature.

Not modern, but absolutely mature.

For comparison, historical wartime 10-cm airborne intercept radar was already remarkably capable. The American SCR-520 could detect a bomber at about 10,000 yards and a fighter around 6,000 yards; the later SCR-720/British AI Mk X generation reached about **6–10 miles** under favorable altitude conditions. These were real 1940s systems, not postwar science fiction. citeturn650511search0turn156434view4

The important limitation is what “radar-equipped fighter” means.

It still has a cathode-ray display.

It still has an operator interpreting blobs.

Ground clutter is horrible.

Altitude matters.

Weather causes trouble.

The fighter still benefits enormously from a ground controller getting it into the right piece of sky.

There is no modern pulse-Doppler look-down capability separating a moving aircraft neatly from the ground.

But by **AltWWII 1946**, I would expect a first-line German night fighter to have something roughly like:

> centimetric radar capable of reliably detecting a Lancaster/Lincoln-sized target around 8–12 miles under favorable conditions, tracking it considerably closer, giving range and angular information good enough for the operator to talk the pilot into an attack.

Occasionally you might see detection farther away. I would not advertise 20-mile fighter detection as routine.

And the ugly stag-antler arrays associated with early Lichtenstein increasingly disappear from the best machines. Centimetric radar permits more compact dish/radome arrangements.

So late He 219s and Ju 88-successor Nachtjäger begin **looking postwar** before the war has actually ended.

Not because Germany jumped twenty years.

Because it has been spending five years fighting the world's most sophisticated bomber-electronics force every night.

---

# Germany's ground network also becomes much more British-looking—but independently

One correction to your framing: Germany doesn't have to discover in 1944 that centralized radar control is a good British idea and copy it.

It already has a substantial integrated system.

**Freya** supplies early warning.

**Würzburg** provides more precise tracking.

**Himmelbett** integrates radar, controllers, searchlights, flak sectors and night fighters.

The British system is earlier and more mature as a *national fighter-defense culture*, but Kammhuber's night-defense system is already its own centralized GCI architecture by our divergence period. citeturn156434view6turn17file3

What prolonged war does is force Germany to evolve beyond the rigid early Himmelbett system.

By 1946, I imagine a **Reich-wide Nachtluftlage**—not necessarily that exact name yet—in which regional command centers combine tracks from several radar types.

One station says there are 300 aircraft.

Another wavelength says perhaps 70.

A passive station hears H2S transmitters somewhere else.

Direction-finding stations hear British VHF traffic.

Weather radar reports the chaff cloud drifting with the wind.

Now the controller can say:

> That first “bomber stream” isn't behaving like airplanes.

That is how Germany begins beating chaff.

Not by inventing a radar that simply says **CHAFF = FALSE**.

It uses **correlation**.

Real aircraft move at roughly coherent speed and heading.

Chaff progressively slows and drifts with winds.

Different wavelengths respond differently.

British jammers emit something which can themselves be direction-found.

A bomber stream has radio traffic.

Navigation radar transmissions exist.

The system compares imperfect sources.

It is basically **human sensor fusion**.

And this is where Germany's increasingly developed calculating/electromechanical infrastructure can matter. Plotting boards, teleprinters, automatic coordinate converters and mechanical intercept predictors can reduce controller workload without pretending somebody has invented AWACS software in 1946.

---

# Your fake bomber stream becomes a major RAF doctrine

And I would make it considerably more sophisticated than one aircraft dropping chaff.

Your one-aircraft idea works the first few times.

German radar sees a track.

Fighters go toward it.

The Germans discover a lone Halifax throwing metal strips out the back.

They stop falling for that.

So Britain escalates.

A mature 1945–46 **spoof stream** might have eight, twelve, perhaps twenty aircraft.

Some drop Window on a timed schedule.

Some broadcast jamming.

One or two carry active radar repeaters.

Their radio discipline resembles a bomber force.

Perhaps several H2S sets deliberately operate.

Their headings and altitude changes are designed to resemble the beginning of a real bomber concentration.

Meanwhile the actual Main Force is keeping much quieter somewhere else.

That is not speculative in principle. Historical No. 100 Group already used twenty-four aircraft to make a Window formation appear to German Würzburg radar as roughly **500 aircraft**, and RAF accounts explicitly describe “conditioning” German controllers by running a false attack one night and a similar real route the next. citeturn156434view6

That's magnificent material for this setting.

Because the Germans learn.

Then Britain knows the Germans have learned.

So Britain's job changes from:

> make false radar returns

to:

> **make a false raid behave electronically like a real raid.**

That's a much more interesting war.

---

# And emissions become ammunition

This is probably the deepest technological lesson that comes out of the whole contest.

Britain historically installs **Monica**, a rear-warning radar, because being warned that a night fighter is behind you sounds obviously useful.

Germany develops **Flensburg**, a passive receiver that homes onto Monica.

Suddenly the device warning you about the German is also broadcasting:

> **HELLO, GERMAN NIGHT FIGHTER. I AM A BRITISH BOMBER. FOLLOW THIS SIGNAL.**

When Britain discovers what Flensburg is doing, Monica is withdrawn from the bomber force. citeturn156434view4

Germany does something comparable with **Naxos**, which homes on H2S emissions; British Pathfinders are particularly attractive targets because they lead the stream. citeturn156434view4

That has enormous implications by 1946.

The question aboard a bomber is no longer:

> Do we have radar?

It's:

> **When are we allowed to turn it on?**

Radar discipline starts looking eerily like later submarine sonar doctrine.

Transmit briefly.

Search.

Turn off.

Change frequency.

Let another aircraft illuminate.

Use passive warning while somebody else transmits.

Put deliberately noisy emitters on a decoy aircraft.

That is entirely compatible with 1940s electronics.

And now your proposed infrared discipline has a direct conceptual ancestor.

---

# The bomber gunners can become considerably more dangerous

This is another place where history was already headed much farther than the popular picture suggests.

Britain historically developed **Automatic Gun Laying Turret radar—AGLT, “Village Inn”**—for Lancaster rear turrets. Imperial War Museums describes it as radar mounted beneath the rear turret that permitted automatic sighting and firing against attacking aircraft. citeturn278928search0turn278928search1

That's astonishingly relevant to what you're imagining.

So instead of going immediately to an infrared searchlight plane, I would let the late Lancaster/Lincoln defensive system evolve like this:

Rear warning tells the crew somebody is coming.

A directional radar begins tracking.

Range and angular information feeds the gun sight.

The gunner now knows roughly where to look **before he can see anything**.

At short range, an optical or infrared image-converter scope can assist final identification.

The turret can compute more of the lead/range solution mechanically.

That makes a late British bomber genuinely nasty to approach from behind.

And it creates another counter-countermeasure.

A German night fighter operator detects the bomber's defensive-radar emission.

He tells his pilot:

> Rear radar has switched on. They've seen us.

Perhaps he approaches from another quarter.

Perhaps a Schräge-Musik fighter avoids the rear hemisphere altogether.

Perhaps British crews learn to leave their defensive radars silent until another warning system gives a cue.

The **bomber itself becomes an electronic combatant** rather than merely a bomb truck surrounded by darkness.

---

# Infrared belongs in this war—but I'd keep it close-range

This is where I would preserve the flavor you're after but change the scale.

We already have German active-IR work feeding later ground systems in the setting. fileciteturn16file0 So it is completely reasonable for Britain and Germany to investigate airborne image converters.

But these aren't thermal cameras.

They don't see the heat of a fighter against the night.

They see **reflected near-infrared illumination**, or an infrared light source.

That's much less useful at long airborne ranges than radar.

An aircraft is a relatively small target.

Distances are large.

The atmosphere scatters and absorbs.

The illumination has to go out to the fighter and enough reflected IR has to come all the way back.

So I would **not** make the normal 1946 formation include an infrared searchlight bomber illuminating German fighters several miles out.

Radar is overwhelmingly better for that.

But active IR can be useful in the last few hundred meters.

So an elite late-war rear turret might eventually have:

- radar cueing and ranging;
- ordinary optical sight;
- an image-converter night sight;
- a relatively narrow IR illuminator intended for **close-range identification/aiming**, not search.

That creates precisely the counter-detection behavior you like.

A German image converter may see the British illuminator.

British crews learn not to leave it on.

Short pulse.

Acquire.

Fire.

Off.

Germany does the same thing.

By the end, both forces regard continuous IR illumination as amateur behavior.

The technology therefore produces **emission discipline**, just as radar does.

What I would *not* introduce is useful passive thermal imaging in fighter combat. British government technical material describes thermal-imaging systems as developing from the end of the Second World War onward; the practical 1946 technology here remains image-converter/active-IR territory rather than modern FLIR. citeturn492876search15

---

# Britain does climb—but that eventually makes the bomber worse at bombing

This is another excellent escalation because it contains its own failure.

German night fighters become too dangerous around normal Lancaster operating altitudes.

Bomber Command says:

> Go higher.

So selected Lancasters receive higher-altitude engines, oxygen improvements, lighter loads and other modifications.

Losses fall somewhat.

But:

bomb loads fall;

climb times increase;

formation assembly becomes harder;

crew physiology becomes more demanding;

turrets and equipment have to work in extreme cold;

winds become more important;

and bombing accuracy gets worse.

Germany responds by improving high-altitude engines and radars in Ju 88/He 219 derivatives.

Then Britain climbs another little bit.

Eventually the RAF has optimized the Lancaster into a machine that is increasingly good at **surviving the mission** while becoming less economically efficient at **delivering the bomb load**.

That's exactly when Lincoln becomes important.

The Lincoln is not speculative. Historically it first flew in June 1944, and production machines reached No. 57 Squadron in August 1945; the RAF Museum explicitly notes that it became Bomber Command's postwar mainstay but was quickly exposed by the arrival of jets. citeturn915558search0

In our timeline it is simply a wartime aircraft.

By late 1945–46, Lincoln therefore becomes the logical heavy-bomber successor to Lancaster:

more range;

better altitude;

more development room;

more electronics capacity;

same basic heavy-bomber philosophy.

And I agree completely that **Washington doesn't belong here**. Britain's later Washington was a B-29 connection. Our America doesn't have the same wartime B-29 production avalanche, and Britain has no reason to abandon its own actively evolving Lancaster/Lincoln family just so we can import that name.

Shackleton is also the wrong answer. Its lineage can eventually exist as a maritime patrol development of the Lincoln family, but turning Shackleton into a jet strategic bomber would just be designing another aircraft while pretending it isn't one.

---

# The Canberra is the final British move—and I think it is one of the best ideas in this whole sequence

This is where the technological race eventually attacks the premise of the heavy night bomber itself.

Historically, the Canberra requirement already began in **1944** as a Mosquito replacement characterized by **no defensive armament** and enough high-altitude performance to evade interception. The formal B.3/45 development specification followed in January 1946. The real prototype did not fly until May 1949, but that happened in a Britain that had demobilized from a victorious war and no longer faced an urgent German night-fighter problem. citeturn650511search7turn650511search4

That is almost tailor-made for Fractured Peace.

I would bring the causal requirement forward.

By **1943–44**, Bomber Command is already asking:

> Every turret we add makes the bomber heavier. Every jammer makes it heavier. Every radar makes it heavier. Every extra crewman makes it heavier. And German night fighters keep getting better anyway.

Then somebody revives the Mosquito argument in extreme form:

> **What if the bomber's defense is simply that the interceptor cannot get into firing position?**

No turrets.

No side gunners.

No giant defensive suite.

Two crew.

Small radar-navigation installation.

High altitude.

Jet speed.

The British don't invent the Canberra because the war ends and somebody wants a new bomber.

They invent it because **the Lancaster/Lincoln electronic fortress has reached diminishing returns**.

That's an excellent procurement history.

### I wouldn't make Canberra operational in 1946

That's just a bit too quick.

But continued existential pressure can plausibly strip years out of the historical process.

My tentative sequence would be:

**1943–44:** fast jet-bomber requirement begins earlier under Nachtjagd pressure.

**1944–45:** competing concepts; English Electric/Petter-type configuration wins.

**1945:** detailed design while Britain is still bombing Germany.

**late 1946:** prototypes flying and service trials.

**early to mid-1947:** a tiny operational evaluation unit carries out actual raids.

That is aggressive.

But unlike moving a 1955 airplane to 1946, we're pulling forward an aircraft whose historical *requirement already existed during the war* and whose real development was substantially slowed by the transition to peace. citeturn650511search7

And it creates a superb final chapter of the night war.

A Ju 88 night fighter receives a vector.

The operator acquires the target.

The pilot turns to intercept.

Then discovers that the target is simply **going away from him**.

Not because the British jammed the radar.

Not because the controller made a mistake.

He can see exactly where it is.

He cannot catch it.

The He 219 fares somewhat better depending upon geometry, but the same fundamental problem appears.

The mature German piston Nachtjagd system has finally encountered something it wasn't designed to solve.

---

# And Germany does not need to answer the Canberra before Britain loses

This is important.

Otherwise we create an endless cycle in which every weapon instantly receives a perfect counterweapon.

A few dozen Canberra-type aircraft appearing in 1947 do **not** restore Bomber Command's strategic offensive.

They have limited payload relative to hundreds of Lancasters and Lincolns.

They're expensive.

Crews are still learning them.

Navigation at high speed is difficult.

The engine supply competes with Britain's fighter requirement.

And, most importantly, Britain is now beginning to need every modern jet it can obtain for the **Second Battle of Britain**.

So the Canberra gets an almost legendary wartime reputation:

> The bomber Germany never completely solved.

But Britain never has enough of them to turn that reputation into victory.

Instead, Canberra becomes the German procurement shock that says:

> **The next Nachtjäger must be a jet.**

Not an improvised night Me 262.

A genuine all-weather jet interceptor designed from the beginning around:

radar;

a radar operator or sufficiently integrated radar presentation;

range;

altitude;

high-speed climb;

electronic counter-countermeasures;

and interception of jet bombers.

That gives us an excellent causal ancestor for the postwar German all-weather-interceptor lineage which the provisional Aerospace Reference currently places later under types like Me 501. fileciteturn17file0 The exact designation can wait.

---

# So how advanced is the night war by 1946?

I would describe it as **an early-1950s electronic-war environment trapped inside 1940s computing and display technology**.

Not literally every 1952 system appears in 1946.

Rather, the *institutional maturity* is ahead.

Radar isn't a special black box attached to a few specialist airplanes anymore.

Jamming isn't a clever mission trick.

Chaff isn't a surprise weapon.

Passive radar warning isn't exotic.

Electronic deception isn't improvised.

By 1946, both sides think in terms of:

> What is the enemy transmitting?

> Can I jam it?

> Can I home on the jammer?

> Can I make him think my twenty aircraft are five hundred?

> Can he distinguish my chaff from a real formation?

> Which radar wavelength is he expecting?

> What happens if I transmit nothing?

> If I turn my radar on, who can hear me?

That is the technological endpoint.

And it has a beautifully asymmetric result.

**Britain wins many of the individual technological rounds.** It probably remains the world's most creative offensive electronic-warfare power during this period. Historical No. 100 Group alone demonstrates how far the RAF had already gone: ghost bomber streams, communications jamming, radar jamming, Window, passive homing, and specialized fighter support were all operational by 1944–45. citeturn156434view6

**Germany wins the operational competition.**

Not because its radar is magically better.

Because in this setting it isn't simultaneously being crushed by an American daylight bomber fleet, losing its airfields, losing its fuel production, retreating across Europe, and watching its experienced Nachtjäger crews disappear faster than it can replace them.

So every British solution gets time to encounter a German countermeasure.

Window hurts terribly.

Germany recovers.

Jamming hurts.

Germany changes frequencies and control methods.

Monica warns bombers.

Germany homes on Monica.

H2S improves navigation.

Germany homes on H2S.

Spoof streams pull fighters away.

Germany learns multisensor track correlation.

Britain improves the spoof.

Germany improves the classification.

By late 1945 or 1946, the result isn't that RAF night bombing becomes impossible. It is that the **mass heavy-bomber exchange rate becomes intolerable**.

Then the Canberra appears and proves that the *next* bombing war will be different.

But Britain is running out of war before it can build that next air force.

That feels to me like exactly the right technological tragedy for Bomber Command: **it loses the mature piston night-bomber war at almost the same moment its engineers discover the aircraft that points beyond it.** fileciteturn18file0

Yes. I think this produces a coherent British late-war jet “menagerie,” but with a few corrections that actually make the development competition more interesting.

The useful inversion is that Britain isn't producing five different jets because nobody knows what they're doing. It is producing them because **five partially overlapping institutions and requirements are all trying to exploit turbine propulsion at once**: Fighter Command wants an interceptor, de Havilland wants a lighter single-engine fighter, the Fleet Air Arm needs carrier jets, Bomber Command wants a Mosquito successor, and Hawker wants its own naval/fighter answer. The provisional Aerospace Reference already has the beginnings of this—Meteor F.3 in 1944, Vampire F.1 in 1946, and Attacker FB.1 in 1947—but our discussion is now moving the Canberra and several experimental programs forward. fileciteturn19file1

## The Derwent Canberra works—but it should be the emergency Canberra, not the mature Canberra

I like your correction here.

Historically, the Canberra requirement itself is already available to us: the Air Ministry issued the Mosquito-successor requirement in **1944**, explicitly calling for no defensive armament and high-altitude performance sufficient to evade interceptors. Specification B.3/45 followed in January 1946. The actual prototype was delayed until 1949 in the postwar environment. citeturn109430view1

So continued war can absolutely accelerate the **airframe**.

The engine is the problem.

A Derwent 8 produces about **3,600 lbf**, whereas the historical Canberra B.2 ultimately used two Avon RA.3s producing about **6,500 lbf apiece**. In other words, two Derwent 8s give only about 55% of the installed thrust of the mature B.2. citeturn109567search0turn109430view1

That doesn't mean the aircraft won't fly. It means we shouldn't take the historical B.2—46,000 lb maximum takeoff weight, 6,000 lb bomb load, tip tanks, three crew—and replace the Avons with Derwents while retaining its performance.

Instead I would create precisely the aircraft you're describing:

> **Canberra B.1 — the emergency wartime Canberra.**

It remains close to the original two-seat A.1 concept. No defensive armament. No glazed bomb-aimer's nose initially. Minimal equipment except navigation/bombing radar and whatever essential countermeasures it needs. Reduced fuel relative to the later strategic-range machine. And probably only something like **1,000–1,500 kg of bombs**, with less on the highest-altitude missions.

Its job isn't to deliver Lancaster tonnage.

Its job is:

> **Get two men and enough bombs to matter through the German night-defense belt at a speed the piston Nachtjäger cannot comfortably intercept.**

I'd provisionally expect something in the broad **800–850 km/h high-altitude class**, rather than the later Avon Canberra's roughly 917 km/h. That's an engineering target rather than canon at this stage.

That is still extremely unpleasant for a Ju 88 or He 219.

And critically, it doesn't make the Canberra immune to the Me 262 or a future German jet Nachtjäger. It simply makes the entire mature *piston* night-defense establishment suddenly obsolete against this particular target.

Then the progression becomes excellent:

**1947 Canberra B.1:** 2× Derwent 8, light bomb load, limited range, emergency wartime penetrator.

**late 1947–48 Canberra development:** first Avon installations.

**postwar Canberra B.2:** substantially more powerful Avons, third crewman/bomb-aimer, greater fuel and payload—the recognizable mature Canberra.

The real Canberra B.2 used two 6,500-lbf Avon RA.3s, while the later B.5/B.6 introduced the RA.7 family, so I would also slightly change your Avon terminology: **RA.7 belongs to the later improved Canberra**, rather than being what creates the first normal production Canberra. citeturn109430view1

There is also a good procurement reason to accept the mediocre Derwent installation temporarily. Britain possesses a huge Meteor/Derwent production establishment. It can say:

> We know this engine. We can obtain it now. Build the bomber and we'll install the proper engine later.

That's very wartime.

# The Meteor should remain Britain's Me 262 equivalent

Absolutely.

But one designation correction simplifies things enormously: **there wasn't a Meteor F.6 in the historical progression**. The important sequence is F.3 → F.4 → F.8. The F.8 was the major developed form of the F.4 and used Derwent 8 engines. citeturn354916search0

So I would not invent an alternate F.6 unless we have a specific missing configuration that needs a designation.

By the Second Battle of Britain:

| Type | AltWWII 1947 status | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **Meteor F.3** | Numerous but aging | Second-line/home-defense jet, training, reserve squadrons |
| **Meteor F.4** | **Principal British frontline jet fighter** | Main opponent of Me 262 |
| **Meteor F.8** | Development/preproduction | A handful of emergency combat evaluations late in the battle |
| **Vampire F.1/F.3** | Growing operational force | Lightweight single-engine fighter |
| **Attacker F.1/FB.1** | Small Fleet Air Arm force | Naval fighter/fighter-bomber; coastal reserve |
| **Canberra B.1** | Tiny operational/service-trial force | High-speed night penetration bomber |
| **Venom precursor** | Prototype | Next-generation Vampire development |
| **Sea Hawk prototype** | Prototype/service trials | Future Fleet Air Arm fighter |

That gives you your test-field story almost perfectly with the **Meteor F.8**.

Things are going badly over southern England. Development aircraft are sitting at Boscombe Down/Farnborough/Gloster. Fighter Command asks whether some are safe enough to fight. Perhaps four or six preproduction F.8s enter an operational evaluation flight.

One survives into museum culture with a plaque along the lines of:

> *One of the first six F.8 development aircraft committed during the Second Battle of Britain.*

That feels much more grounded than somehow producing an entire new F.8 fleet in 1947.

---

# The Vampire can be much more important than it historically was by 1947

This one barely needs acceleration.

The Vampire prototype actually flew in **September 1943**, and the first historical RAF Vampire squadron existed by July 1946. Its whole engineering point was exactly the niche you're describing: the Goblin offered enough output to make a **single-engine jet fighter** practical when most early jet fighters required two engines. citeturn109430view3

So under six uninterrupted years of British war pressure, I wouldn't merely have a few Vampire F.1s.

I'd have a serious force.

The likely progression is F.1 entering service earlier than historically, followed by the **F.3 as the principal 1947 Vampire fighter**. Historically the F.3 first flew in November 1946, so pushing its production into the 1947 battle is an extremely mild alternate development. citeturn109430view3

The FB.5 can arrive at the very end or just afterward.

And I agree with calling the Vampire aesthetically Britain's counterpart to the Ho 229—the strange silhouette that immediately identifies which side built it—but functionally they're quite different.

The Ho 229 is a specialized twin-engine flying-wing escort/heavy fighter.

The Vampire's institutional argument is almost the opposite:

> **Why are we spending two jet engines on every Meteor when de Havilland can give us a perfectly useful fighter with one?**

That becomes increasingly attractive as turbine production strains under Meteor, Canberra and naval demand.

---

# A 1947 Venom prototype is more plausible than you're giving it credit for—but it should have a Ghost

This is where I would push *against* replacing the Ghost with a Goblin.

The Venom wasn't merely a differently shaped Vampire. Its defining combination was a **thinner, mildly swept wing plus the substantially more powerful Ghost engine**. BAE explicitly describes it as designed around the Ghost rather than the Vampire's Goblin. citeturn504178search1

Put a Goblin in it and you've basically created:

> Experimental thin-wing Vampire.

That isn't useless. It can exist.

But it isn't really the engineering step that creates the Venom.

More importantly, the Ghost isn't actually a technology that Britain has to conjure from 1952. De Havilland's engine company was already organized in 1944 around manufacture/development of **both Goblin and Ghost centrifugal turbojets**. citeturn903063search7

So I would rather accelerate the proper chain:

**1946:** de Havilland is already testing higher-speed Vampire wings and higher-powered engines.

**1947:** one or several experimental **Ghost-powered thin-wing Vampire/Venom prototypes** fly.

**during the Second Battle:** perhaps one prototype is briefly used for interception trials if you're attached to that anecdote.

**postwar:** this becomes the true production Venom.

I wouldn't give it the later **Ghost 103** specifically yet. Just an early wartime Ghost development engine. The engine family exists; that particular mature mark doesn't have to.

That preserves the recognizable Venom as an actual technological advance rather than a cosmetic shell running on an older engine.

---

# The Attacker needs the biggest role correction

The name is misleading.

The **Supermarine Attacker was fundamentally a naval jet fighter**, not a purpose-built close-air-support airplane. Imperial War Museums describes it directly as an “Attacker jet fighter,” and its lineage came from the Spiteful/Seafang fighter family; the Attacker retained the Spiteful-derived laminar-flow wing and landing gear. citeturn257046search1turn257046search9

So I would absolutely retain your 1947 Attacker, but for a different reason.

It is the **Fleet Air Arm's first proper production jet fighter**.

Its secondary fighter-bomber role then naturally permits:

bombs;

rockets;

anti-shipping attack;

strikes against a German landing;

close support when required.

So your Dover idea still works beautifully.

Fleet Air Arm Attacker squadrons are held at southern naval air stations and aboard whatever carriers are available. If German transports or landing craft begin moving across the Channel, the Attacker becomes one of the aircraft Britain intends to throw at them.

But that's an emergency mission for a naval fighter/fighter-bomber, not the aircraft's fundamental design purpose.

And it does **not** compete with the Canberra as a Mosquito replacement.

The Canberra requirement says:

> penetrate deep enemy airspace at night and bomb strategic/operational targets.

The Attacker requirement says:

> give the Fleet Air Arm a jet capable of fighting aircraft and carrying useful offensive stores from naval bases/carriers.

They're barely competitors aerodynamically.

They **are competitors industrially**, which is much more interesting.

They want engines.

High-temperature alloys.

Skilled technicians.

Jet pilot conversion capacity.

Airframe production space.

That is where the British jet zoo starts hurting.

---

# Sea Hawk: yes to 1947 prototype, but it isn't a twin wing-root-engine aircraft

There is a visual similarity to the HG-III, but mechanically the Sea Hawk is quite different.

The Sea Hawk has **one centrally installed Rolls-Royce Nene**, with air brought in through wing-root intakes and the exhaust divided through ducting toward the rear. It isn't a two-engine design with one turbine buried in each wing root.

Navy Wings identifies it as Hawker's first jet, a straight-wing carrier fighter/ground-attack aircraft, and notes that the **Nene 103 belongs to the later FGA.6 refinement**. citeturn856636search1

So I would not give the first prototype a Nene 103.

Give it the earlier Nene-family engine for which the aircraft was actually conceived.

And your timeline works:

**early/mid-1947:** accelerated prototype flight.

**Second Battle of Britain:** prototype/service-trial aircraft exist.

**Combat?** Perhaps one emergency sortie or a tiny evaluation flight if Britain is sufficiently desperate—but not a Sea Hawk squadron.

The Sea Hawk's real payoff comes after Lisbon, when the Navy looks at the Attacker and says:

> This got us into the jet age. Now give us a naval jet that was actually designed properly for it.

The Attacker becomes Britain's **wartime expedient**.

The Sea Hawk becomes the **postwar Fleet Air Arm jet**.

That's a much cleaner relationship.

---

# Britain really does acquire a jet menagerie

And I like the inversion because the institutional cause is different from Germany's historical late-war chaos.

Britain isn't desperately launching random *Wunderwaffen*.

Britain is still a functioning industrial state. But it has several design houses and several legitimate customers all reaching the same conclusion at once:

> **Piston aviation has run out of development room against German jets.**

Gloster says twin-engine fighter.

de Havilland says lightweight single-engine fighter.

Supermarine says naval fighter.

Hawker says better naval fighter.

English Electric says unarmed jet bomber.

Rolls-Royce says Derwent, Nene and Avon cannot all become unlimited production priorities simultaneously.

de Havilland says it also has Goblin and Ghost.

So by 1947 Britain can have a surprisingly diverse experimental and early-service jet ecosystem **without having a surprisingly diverse mature mass-production ecosystem**.

That distinction matters.

The mass war is still fought principally by **Meteor F.4 and Vampire F.1/F.3**.

Attacker is naval and scarce.

Canberra is scarce.

F.8 is coming.

Venom is developmental.

Sea Hawk is developmental.

That is a menagerie on the airshow ramp, but a much simpler force when you count actual squadrons.

---

# And yes, Germany absolutely should have moved beyond the original Jumo 004B

Here I agree with your underlying objection almost completely.

It would be strange for an industrially intact Germany to arrive in 1947 with the Luftwaffe's cutting-edge aircraft still universally powered by essentially the same early-production engine.

But I would **not call the successor “Jumo 005.”**

There is already a historical engine waiting for us: the **Heinkel-Hirth HeS 011**.

The Jumo 004B produced roughly **1,980 lbf**. The HeS 011 prototype was already a more advanced mixed/axial-compressor turbojet producing about **2,860 lbf**, and that was a wartime German development rather than a postwar invention. citeturn257304search1turn257304search9

Our divergence changes what happens to it.

Rather than:

> war ends while the HeS 011 remains an immature prototype,

we get:

> 1943–45 sustained development → reliability work → production engineering → operational engine family.

But I would still retain the **Jumo 004 lineage**.

The correct German response isn't to stop building every 004 the moment a better engine exists.

It's two-tiered.

The mature Jumo becomes the **mass engine**. Better materials, less desperation-driven substitution, improved bearings, turbine life, fuel controls and production quality make late 004-family engines much less disposable than the historical ones. The exact later designation can be settled when we deliberately construct the German engine register.

The **HeS 011 family** becomes the high-performance second-generation engine.

That means by 1946–47:

**Ordinary Me 262:** improved late Jumo 004-family engines. Cheap enough, known, maintainable, produced in enormous numbers.

**Newest Me 262 marks / experimental high-performance aircraft:** HeS 011-family engines where integration makes sense.

**HG-II/HG-III:** precisely where I'd put substantially uprated HeS 011-derived engines, because they're already expensive aircraft whose entire purpose is performance.

**Ho 229:** can migrate from early Jumo-powered machines toward a more capable later engine depending on packaging.

**Me 362:** designed from the outset around the *next* engine generation rather than being forced to accommodate an old turbine.

That also preserves one of the most important advantages of the ordinary Me 262:

> It's no longer technically the fastest thing Germany knows how to build. It's the thing Germany knows how to **build and operate in quantity**.

And that makes the HG-III relationship even better.

A 1947 HG-III isn't just “an Me 262 with swept wings.” It has newer, larger, more powerful engines buried inside a much more aggressive aerodynamic arrangement.

Consequently it is faster.

It is also shorter-legged.

Much more expensive.

More difficult to build.

Much more difficult to repair.

And if an engine needs to come out, a mechanic begins looking at the aircraft as though Messerschmitt personally insulted his family.

That's why the HG-III doesn't replace the ordinary 262.

## The interesting outcome is that Britain and Germany are optimizing in opposite directions by 1947

Germany has had several years of combat jet experience and is beginning to **rationalize**.

Its answer is:

> Me 262 for most fighter work; specialized Ho 229s and HG aircraft where their particular advantages justify the trouble.

Britain is just reaching the point at which every service understands that jets are the future, so it is temporarily **proliferating**:

> Meteor, Vampire, Attacker, Canberra, Venom development, Sea Hawk development.

That means the Second Battle of Britain catches them at different stages of the same technological process.

Germany has the more mature **jet combat institution**.

Britain has the more rapidly expanding **jet design ecosystem**.

And Britain is discovering new answers faster than Germany can comfortably dismiss them. The Canberra is perhaps the best example: Germany can dominate the piston night-bomber contest in 1946 and then, a year later, encounter a little formation of Derwent-powered bombers which doesn't carry much and doesn't range very far—but which demonstrates that the entire technical basis of that Nachtjagd victory is already becoming temporary.

That is exactly the kind of technological ending I think the Second Battle of Britain should have. Germany wins the war, but it doesn't end it having solved aviation. It ends it watching several of the problems of the **next** air war take off from British runways.

One canon point is especially useful here: the current wiki only fixes the campaign broadly as **1946–47**, says it exhausts British depth, and says the food-and-medicine load under white parachutes is locally substituted; **“Friedensbrot” is a myth Berlin creates afterward**, not necessarily the sortie’s real operational name.
