Yes. I think **Type XXV** is the cleanest designation.

The current naval reference already uses **XXIV** for the 1951 long-range postwar SSK, **XXVII** for the later coastal/export line, **XXVIII** for the 1959 *Unterseefrachter*, **XXIX** for the 1960 deep-ocean quiet boat, and **XXX–XXXIV** for the later nuclear/advanced generations. fileciteturn47file10 So XXIV, XXVIII, and XXX in particular would create unnecessary collisions. **XXV is presently empty in AltWWII's established lineage and sits exactly where a 1945–47 experimental offshoot feels like it belongs.**

I would therefore settle on:

> **Typ XXV Jagd-U-Boot**  
> unofficially **Fliegender Fisch** — “Flying Fish”  
> commonly shortened by crews and yard personnel to **der Springer** — “the Jumper.”

I would avoid **Delphin**, even though it would otherwise be almost perfect, because Germany historically already applied that name to a fast experimental midget submarine. The Imperial War Museum's wartime footage actually labels *Delphin* as a fast German experimental miniature submarine. citeturn103989search8 *Fliegender Fisch* therefore gives us the same visual idea without stepping on an existing German naval name.

And I think your breaching accident is not merely plausible. It should be the incident that **forces the design into its mature control arrangement**.

## The accident should happen because the boat is better than its controls

That's the important distinction.

The Type XXV isn't unstable rubbish.

Its problem is that its control system was designed by people accustomed to submarines operating at perhaps 10–20 knots underwater, while the new hull is suddenly doing **thirty-plus**.

Hydrodynamic control forces rise very rapidly with speed. So an elevator command that produces a respectable climb at ordinary submerged speed becomes an extraordinarily violent maneuver at 32 knots.

The early test procedure therefore makes perfect sense:

The boat is conducting a high-speed run.

It has deliberately climbed fairly close to the surface because the test staff wants to transition toward periscope depth or eventually surface.

The helmsman receives something like:

> “Bring her up gently.”

He gives what everybody aboard regards as a modest positive-plane command.

The boat responds far more strongly than expected.

The bow comes up.

The sail breaks the surface.

And because the Type XXV still has tremendous forward momentum, the entire submarine **breaches**.

Not gracefully.

For a moment perhaps most of the forward hull is physically out of the water, with spray exploding away from it, before gravity wins and the boat comes crashing back down.

The people watching from the trials vessel or shore don't see an elegant naval maneuver.

They see a **1,800- or 2,000-ton submarine unexpectedly attempt to become an aircraft**.

That is exactly the sort of event sailors will name a ship after.

### And inside, it is considerably less funny

Men who aren't braced go airborne.

Someone smashes his head into pipework.

A rating breaks an arm.

Loose equipment tears out of restraints.

Batteries, mounts, piping, shaft alignment, and hull structure immediately become matters of concern.

The chief engineer is probably convinced for several seconds that somebody has just destroyed his prototype.

Then the boat settles.

The pressure hull remains sound.

Propulsion is still responding.

No one has died.

And eventually the fear transforms into the kind of horrified laughter that produces:

> *Der fliegende Fisch.*

The Flying Fish.

By the time the boat returns to the pier, everybody at the establishment knows the story.

Within a week they're calling the prototype **der Springer**.

---

# The accident should directly create the high-speed control limiter

This makes the anecdote technologically consequential rather than merely colorful.

The investigation concludes that the controls need to behave differently according to speed.

Not fly-by-wire.

Not computers.

A mechanical/hydraulic system.

At low speed, the helmsman receives the full available plane travel because the control surfaces need large deflections to maneuver effectively.

As speed rises, a pressure/speed-linked governor progressively reduces the maximum permissible deflection.

So at 8 knots, full control input may physically move the diving planes through most of their available range.

At 30 knots, the same full helm command produces only a few degrees.

An emergency override probably exists, but it requires a deliberate action rather than simply hauling the control over.

That becomes one of the Type XXV's genuinely important inventions.

And later German submarines inherit the idea because once you're designing boats for thirty-knot submerged operation, **the control system has to know how fast the submarine is moving even if the human operator momentarily forgets**.

---

# The nickname can exist at three different levels

I wouldn't make *Fliegender Fisch* an officially assigned Kriegsmarine class name.

The paperwork remains brutally ordinary:

> **U-Boot Typ XXV**  
> *Jagd-U-Boot für hohe Unterwassergeschwindigkeit*

or whatever precise procurement language we eventually settle on.

Inside the development establishment:

> **Fliegender Fisch**

becomes common enough that it appears in letters, unofficial diagrams, workshop chalk markings, perhaps even some internal reports in quotation marks.

Among the sailors:

> **Springer**

is easier.

And different crews might say things like:

> “You're being posted to the Springer.”

rather than:

> “You're being posted to the Typ XXV Versuchsboot.”

That feels much more natural.

Interestingly, the nickname may initially be **slightly insulting**.

The test crew does not necessarily appreciate having its extremely expensive experimental Jagdboot named after the occasion on which they almost threw themselves onto the beach.

Later it becomes affectionate.

---

# The British story should remain fundamentally unresolved

I like your change here much better than Britain receiving captured technical documentation immediately after Lisbon.

Germany has absolutely no reason to say:

> Since we've made peace, here are the specifications of our most advanced submarine prototype.

Quite the reverse.

The Type XXV remains one of the highest-classification naval programs in the Reich.

So the Royal Navy gets **an encounter, not an explanation**.

And I would make it wonderfully unsatisfactory.

A convoy or support group encounters a submarine in early 1947.

The German boat makes an attack—perhaps it **damages** rather than sinks an escort, because the encounter's significance is speed rather than torpedo performance.

Contact is obtained.

The submarine runs.

The British plot begins producing increasingly strange estimates.

Twenty-four knots.

Twenty-seven.

Twenty-nine.

Perhaps briefly thirty-one or thirty-two.

Someone in the plotting team assumes there has been a ranging error.

The sonar operator insists the bearing rate is correct.

The destroyer captain pushes his own ship harder.

The target still refuses to fall behind in the way a submarine should.

Then contact is lost.

The report goes up the chain.

And the official assessment isn't:

> Germany possesses a 33-knot submarine.

It is more like:

> **Reported target speed considered unreliable. Possibility of hydrographic, plotting, or classification error cannot be excluded.**

Because the alternative is ridiculous.

The Royal Navy already knows Type XXI exists and knows Germany is experimenting with very fast underwater boats—the historical Type XXVI itself was a genuine German high-speed design project, sufficiently developed that the U.S. Navy photographed its pressure-hull model after the war. citeturn291463search2turn291463search8

But **thirty-plus knots from a battery-electric submarine** is far enough beyond what British officers expect that the natural first assumption is bad data.

And because there is only one encounter before the war ends, there is never enough operational evidence to resolve the argument.

---

# That lets the Type XXV become a genuine Royal Navy ghost story

This could be one of those things old escort sailors keep arguing about for decades.

One officer says:

> “We chased a German submarine doing thirty knots underwater.”

Another says:

> “No, you didn't.”

The first insists he saw the plot.

The second points out that the sonar solution was unstable.

A third says the Germans must have been testing one of the peroxide boats.

British postwar intelligence knows **something** unusual was being tested, but Germany never hands over the complete technical record.

So the story persists under several names.

“The Thirty-Knot U-boat.”

“The Atlantic Ghost.”

Maybe the escort group itself invents something like **the Greyhound**.

And because Germany's later submarines become extremely sophisticated, the story becomes more credible with every passing decade rather than less.

By 1965 a young Royal Navy submariner hears the story and thinks:

> Of course they had something like that.

But the men who were there remember that in 1947 it sounded impossible.

---

# The Germans remember something completely different

And this is the asymmetry I particularly like.

British institutional memory:

> **An unidentified submerged contact which apparently outran the expected performance of any German boat.**

German institutional memory:

> **That ridiculous submarine that jumped out of the Baltic.**

For Dönitz and the engineering establishment, Type XXV is not mysterious at all.

It is temperamental.

Expensive.

Short-legged at high power.

Overpowered.

Difficult to control until modified.

Not remotely ready to replace Type XXI.

But also clearly important.

The later mythology can almost reverse the contemporary reputations.

During the war:

**Type XXI** is the serious submarine.

**Type XXVI** is the dangerous experimental attack boat.

**Type XXV** is the bizarre trials machine everyone jokes about.

Twenty years later, naval historians realize that **XXV was the one whose hull geometry actually predicted the future**.

That fits the setting's existing postwar lineage particularly well. The current reference jumps from the wartime XXI/XXIII inheritance into increasingly sophisticated postwar SSKs and eventually the Type XXX nuclear *Jagd-U-Boot*. fileciteturn47file0 The Type XXV can now become the missing hydrodynamic ancestor sitting underneath that development.

So I would lock the working concept as:

> **Typ XXV Jagd-U-Boot** — experimental 1946–47 high-speed battery-electric attack submarine, about 1,600–1,700 tonnes surfaced, teardrop hull, roughly 33-knot trial submerged speed, very limited torpedo battery, and extreme emphasis on underwater maneuverability.  
>
> **Fliegender Fisch** — development-establishment nickname acquired after the prototype violently breached during a high-speed surfacing trial.  
>
> **Springer** — ordinary crew slang derived from the same incident.

And I would absolutely preserve the visual you've described: the observers watching that narrow disturbance running below the surface, expecting the submarine to gently rise into view—and then having the **entire bow erupt out of the sea** while everyone on the range collectively realizes that nobody has yet learned how to drive the thing.

Yes. I think this is the point where the German submarine lineage finally becomes internally coherent.

The current naval reference has **XXIV as the first long-range postwar diesel-electric type, XXIX as the 1960 deep-ocean quiet boat, and XXX as the first nuclear Jagd-U-Boot in 1962**. fileciteturn49file2 What it does not presently explain is *why* Type XXX suddenly has the design language of a modern nuclear attack submarine. Your Type XXV solves that.

The clean genealogy becomes:

> **Type XXI wins the wartime production argument.**  
> **Type XXVI explores extreme propulsion.**  
> **Type XXV discovers the modern submarine hull.**  
> **Type XXIV and XXIX make those lessons operationally usable.**  
> **Type XXX finally combines the XXV concept with nuclear endurance.**

That is much stronger than simply assigning numbers chronologically.

## And yes: Britain should know much less than we have been casually assuming

This is an important correction.

Lisbon is an armistice and political settlement. Germany is **not occupied**. There is no Allied technical-intelligence team walking into Kiel with clipboards, opening every filing cabinet, towing experimental boats to Portsmouth, and publishing detailed reports.

In our timeline, a huge amount of what historians know about German late-war submarine development comes precisely from Germany being defeated, occupied, and physically stripped for technical intelligence.

That doesn't happen here.

So for British naval intelligence, there should be three levels of knowledge.

| German type | British wartime knowledge | Actual German reality |
|---|---|---|
| **XXI** | Reasonably confident broad estimates | Large operational Elektroboot class |
| **XXVI** | Fragmentary reports of unusually fast special boats | Small Walter-powered Jagd-U-Boot force |
| **XXV** | One disputed “impossible” contact | Classified teardrop high-speed experimental boat |

That difference is extremely valuable.

### Britain knows Type XXI exists

This one is impossible to conceal.

Enough XXI boats are operating that escorts and patrol aircraft repeatedly encounter them. Sailors occasionally see a conning tower, Schnorchel, wake, or brief silhouette. Aircraft may obtain poor top-down views. Survivors report different handling and speed characteristics than the older VII boats.

So British intelligence can produce a perfectly respectable estimate:

- approximately this displacement class;
- six forward tubes;
- unusually high submerged speed;
- extended submerged endurance;
- sophisticated passive listening equipment;
- Schnorchel;
- probably improved batteries;
- likely improved active-sonar countermeasures.

But the intelligence sheet should contain **ranges**, not exact specifications.

Something like:

> Estimated submerged maximum: **15–19 knots**  
> Confidence: moderate.

One report says seventeen.

Another says twenty.

A captain insists the German was doing twenty-two.

The Admiralty writes seventeen or eighteen because that best fits the aggregate evidence.

And Germany never corrects them.

That fits the later setting beautifully, because the naval reference already establishes that foreign intelligence can estimate German submarine construction but remains uncertain about **readiness, configuration, and which signatures correspond to which boats** even in the mature postwar era. fileciteturn49file2

The secrecy culture has a wartime origin.

---

# Type XXVI should remain much murkier

Agreed completely.

The British can know that **something faster than XXI appears to exist** without knowing why.

A few escorts report extremely rapid underwater movement.

Signals intelligence identifies special flotillas or unusual maintenance arrangements.

Perhaps aerial reconnaissance notes unusual boats at a particular base.

Agents report that some submarines have very different machinery requirements.

But from that Britain cannot leap automatically to:

> Hydrogen-peroxide Walter turbine.

The official wartime intelligence estimate might instead say something like:

> **Experimental high-speed submarine. Propulsion unknown. Possibly advanced accumulator plant, closed-cycle diesel, turbine installation, or combination thereof.**

That is how intelligence actually works when the enemy doesn't leave the prototype sitting on your dock.

And because Type XXVI is scarce, the speed data remain contentious.

One destroyer reports 25 knots.

Another says the estimate must be wrong.

A third never sees the boat again after making contact.

So by 1947 the Royal Navy probably believes Germany possesses a **small class of unusually fast submerged attack boats**, but not:

- how many;
- exact maximum speed;
- how long they can sustain it;
- what fuel they use;
- how dangerous the propulsion plant is;
- or whether the boats represent an experimental dead end or the next German standard.

That's much better.

---

# Type XXV becomes almost mythological because Britain explains it away

This is perhaps the best part.

The British encounter is real.

The measurements are real enough.

But the conclusion sounds absurd.

A submerged object apparently moving at something around **thirty knots or more** in 1947?

The intelligence staff already has a much easier explanation available:

> **You were tracking a torpedo.**

And I think we can make the after-action report support that interpretation without making the sonar crew incompetent.

The encounter could go approximately like this.

A convoy escort gets a submarine contact.

A torpedo attack occurs.

The escort turns.

There is noise everywhere: its own machinery, other escorts maneuvering, torpedo noise, cavitation, depth charges or Squid preparation, the convoy changing course.

Then the original strong submarine contact becomes weak or intermittent.

A fast acoustic bearing appears to be moving away.

The plot says twenty-eight knots.

Then thirty.

Then perhaps thirty-two.

Afterward, analysts reconstruct it and say:

> The most probable explanation is that the original submarine contact was lost and the subsequent high-speed trace represented a torpedo, decoy, or erroneous continuation of two separate contacts.

That's reasonable.

Especially because a **30-knot torpedo is completely believable**.

A 30-knot submarine is not.

The escort crew disagrees.

The sonar rating insists:

> “It wasn't a bloody torpedo.”

But institutional history slowly wins.

By the 1950s, published Royal Navy accounts refer to the incident as a confused late-war contact against a Type XXI followed by an acoustic torpedo.

By the 1960s it is a footnote.

Old escort sailors still tell the story.

> “We chased a submarine that could do thirty knots underwater.”

Younger officers smile politely.

Then Germany opens the archive.

---

# I would make the declassification a late-1970s to early-1980s event

Not one giant dump.

A **controlled historical declassification program** makes more sense.

By then Type XXI, XXV, and XXVI are thirty years obsolete. Their exact solutions no longer reveal much about the current Type XXXIII/XXXIV boats. Germany can reveal the historical experiment while continuing to conceal the specifications of the modern fleet.

That also fits the established setting: Germany remains extremely secretive about contemporary submarine composition and capabilities even in the 1970s and 1980s. fileciteturn49file8 Revealing 1946 machinery is therefore partly harmless and partly propaganda:

> Look how far ahead German submarine engineering already was.

I could see a sequence something like this:

**c. 1976–78:** wartime Type XXI development records are partially opened. Foreign historians finally get much better information on late XXI batches, Alberich trials, sensors, and the actual thinking behind submerged operations.

**c. 1979–80:** Type XXVI documentation is released. This creates the first international “they powered it with *what?*” moment when Walter-peroxide propulsion and projected/actual sprint performance become clear.

**c. 1981–82:** the Type XXV experimental file is declassified as part of a naval-engineering historical series.

And then some Royal Navy historian has a very bad afternoon.

Because buried in the files is:

> Versuchsfahrt … 32.8 kn  
> Versuchsboot Typ XXV …

followed by photographs of **Fliegender Fisch**.

The old 1947 report comes back out of the Admiralty archive.

The bearing plot matches.

The old sonar operator, if he's still alive, gets interviewed.

And suddenly:

> “We chased a torpedo”

becomes

> “No, apparently Chief Petty Officer Harris had been right for thirty-four years.”

That is exactly the kind of historical revelation which becomes famous outside naval circles.

---

# The Germans themselves shouldn't necessarily realize how important XXV is immediately

This improves the design lineage.

In 1947, the hierarchy looks obvious.

**Type XXI** is important because it can actually be produced in useful numbers and win battles.

**Type XXVI** is exciting because its propulsion gives spectacular sprint performance.

**Type XXV** is the weird experimental boat with almost no torpedo armament that once jumped out of the water and injured half its test crew.

Nobody in 1947 necessarily says:

> This one is the future.

The war ends.

Germany now has enormous stocks of submarines.

Budgets contract.

There is no reason to put XXV into mass production.

So **Fliegender Fisch is laid up as an experimental asset**.

Perhaps it continues hydrodynamic trials for several years and then becomes a test hulk or is decommissioned.

But its reports go into the naval design archive.

And they sit there.

---

# The 1950s submarine line can remain mostly diesel-electric

That helps preserve the current naval reference rather than forcing us to rewrite everything around XXV.

The reference presently gives us:

- Type XXI — wartime ocean Elektroboot;
- Type XXIII — wartime coastal Elektroboot;
- Type XXIV — 1951 long-range ocean attack;
- Type XXVII — 1954 coastal/export;
- Type XXIX — 1960 deep-ocean quiet attack;
- Type XXX — 1962 first nuclear Jagd-U-Boot. fileciteturn49file2

I would reinterpret them like this.

### Type XXIV

Fundamentally the **mature production descendant of XXI**.

Better batteries.

Better Schnorchel.

Much better quieting.

Factory-standard anechoic treatment.

Improved passive sonar.

Improved crew habitability and endurance.

But still recognizably the practical German ocean SSK.

Germany builds many because it works.

It is not trying to make every submarine a 33-knot experimental craft.

### Type XXVII

The smaller coastal/export answer.

Again conservative.

Germany discovers there is a large market for a submarine that gives foreign navies many of the important XXI lessons without requiring German-scale infrastructure.

### Type XXIX

This becomes very interesting now.

Rather than another arbitrary diesel-electric class, XXIX is the **first production boat to consciously reintroduce Type XXV hydrodynamic thinking**.

Not necessarily the full Flying Fish geometry.

But the design staff begins asking:

> Why are we still paying so much drag for good surface behavior when this boat spends most of its operational life submerged?

So XXIX gets:

a much rounder submerged-optimized hull;

less external clutter;

more compact sail;

better machinery isolation;

more emphasis on passive detection;

and perhaps greatly improved underwater maneuvering.

Its priority is **quietness**, though, rather than XXV's spectacular sprint.

That explains the reference's existing role description: “deep-ocean quiet attack.” fileciteturn49file10

So by 1960 the old XXV files have begun influencing ordinary design.

But only partially.

---

# Then nuclear propulsion changes the question

This is the point where somebody really does pull the Fliegender Fisch drawings back out.

The setting already establishes Germany's large-scale move into nuclear power during the 1960s and specifically ties nuclear propulsion to long-endurance German submarines. fileciteturn49file8

The naval design problem becomes:

> We can now build a submarine which doesn't have to raise a Schnorchel every few days.

That makes the compromises built into the traditional diesel-electric submarine suddenly questionable.

Why optimize for surface transit?

Why preserve diesel air intakes?

Why carry an enormous battery primarily because you periodically have to become an air-breathing vessel?

Why accept a hull whose ancestry still assumes surface operation?

Someone in the design bureau says:

> Didn't we build a boat twenty years ago which assumed from the beginning that the proper state of a submarine was underwater?

Archive box comes down.

**Typ XXV.**

And I love the institutional reaction being:

> “Oh God. The flying fish.”

Because the older engineers remember it.

The younger nuclear engineers see something else.

They see:

- submerged-first hydrodynamics;
- electric-only shaft propulsion;
- large propulsion motors;
- machinery arranged around electrical power distribution;
- extremely high underwater control forces;
- speed-dependent plane limiting;
- compact weapons arrangement;
- and a design philosophy which treats surface operation as incidental.

Suddenly the weird 1946 prototype isn't weird anymore.

It is exactly the starting point they need.

---

# Type XXX should therefore be a **nuclear-electric** boat

This is where your all-electric powertrain idea becomes especially valuable.

The reactor does not literally connect wires directly to the propulsion motor.

The chain is:

> **reactor → steam generator → steam turbine → electrical generator → propulsion motor → shaft**

rather than:

> reactor → steam turbine → reduction gearing → shaft.

That costs something.

The electrical machinery is heavy.

There are conversion losses.

Large motors and generators take volume.

But Germany has a reason to accept that trade.

It gets:

much greater freedom in machinery arrangement;

no need for a giant direct mechanical shaft line from turbine to propeller;

better opportunity to acoustically isolate turbo-generators from the pressure hull;

excellent low-speed motor control;

and direct conceptual continuity with twenty years of high-powered Elektroboot expertise.

That gives German nuclear submarines a distinctive engineering character rather than merely copying whichever historical American or British SSN layout we remember.

And it means the Type XXX isn't:

> **a Type XXI with a reactor.**

It's much closer to:

> **a Type XXV enlarged enough to swallow a reactor plant, using twenty years of Type XXI/XXIV operational experience and Type XXIX quieting.**

That is the lineage I would canonize.

---

# Type XXVI contributes something different to Type XXX

I wouldn't make the nuclear boat a direct mechanical descendant of the Walter system.

The peroxide plant becomes a dead end once nuclear propulsion exists.

But XXVI contributes the **doctrine**.

Type XXVI proves the operational idea that a submarine can be a genuinely fast warship whose target is another warship.

XXV proves the hydrodynamic architecture.

XXI proves mass submerged operations.

XXIX proves mature quieting.

Nuclear power removes endurance from the speed equation.

Thus:

> **XXI → operational method**  
> **XXV → hull and electrical architecture**  
> **XXVI → high-speed Jagd-U-Boot doctrine**  
> **XXIX → quieting and deep-ocean refinement**  
> **XXX → synthesis**

That is a real family tree.

---

# And it makes the 1962 Type XXX much more frightening in context

The current reference simply says **14 Type XXX boats, introduced beginning in 1962, as Germany's first nuclear Jagd-U-Boot class**. fileciteturn49file2

Now we know what that means.

Foreign intelligence sees a much larger, bulbous German submarine which looks unlike the old XXI-derived boats.

They know it's probably nuclear.

They can estimate displacement.

They hear it occasionally.

They know it appears capable of remaining underwater for extraordinary periods.

But Germany publishes no maximum submerged speed.

No exact reactor output.

No acoustic figures.

No test-depth figure.

No sonar sensitivity.

So British and American publications say things like:

> **estimated greater than 30 knots**

or

> **probably 30–35 knots**

while naval officers privately argue whether it can do substantially better.

That's exactly the analogy you're reaching for with modern submarine specifications. The number becomes an intelligence estimate rather than something somebody looks up in Jane's with certainty.

And because Germany has kept the old wartime programs classified, foreign analysts initially assume Type XXX is the product of a **new nuclear-era hydrodynamic program**.

Then the 1981 archive release happens and everyone discovers:

> No.

> They drew the basic hull in 1945.

That is the revelation.

---

# It also makes German submarine philosophy unusually consistent

You mentioned **speed and stealth as competing priorities**, and I think that's exactly right.

Not bigger torpedo tubes.

Not progressively gigantic weapons.

The 533 mm class remains entirely capable of delivering more than enough explosive to kill surface ships. Torpedo development therefore goes into:

guidance;

homing discrimination;

range;

wire guidance;

speed;

quiet propulsion;

counter-countermeasures;

fuzing;

and eventually anti-submarine targeting.

The *platform* competition is:

> **Can they hear me?**

versus:

> **If they hear me, can they catch me?**

Different German classes choose different points on that curve.

Type XXI moves dramatically toward submerged endurance.

Type XXV says speed.

Type XXVI says even more speed, bought with dangerous machinery.

Type XXIV says practical long-range quiet patrol.

Type XXIX says quietness.

Type XXX finally says:

> Why choose?

Not perfectly—the submarine is still louder at maximum speed—but nuclear endurance means it can spend days moving fast without a battery crisis and then become very quiet when tactical conditions require it.

That explains why the mature Setting Bible can credibly describe the Kriegsmarine as centered on the **world's largest and quietest U-boat arm**, with anechoic treatments and Type XXI ancestry explicitly feeding that system. fileciteturn49file8

The Type XXV now fills in the missing part of that sentence:

**why the hulls themselves stopped looking like U-boats and started looking like modern submarines.**

And the best part is that Britain had seen it once.

They just spent thirty years telling the men who saw it that they'd chased a torpedo.

I think we are **much closer to “handoff-ready” than to “still designing the war.”** At the level of strategic outcome, major theaters, technological direction, and postwar consequences, the war is largely established. What remains is concentrated in a relatively small number of **high-leverage locks**.

My rough assessment would be:

> **The Second World War is about 85–90% established at the strategic/story level, but perhaps 70–80% ready for autonomous wiki expansion.**

The difference is mostly not missing imagination. It is **authority cleanup**. Several things we have now settled in the detailed transcripts directly supersede older lines in the Setting Timeline, Setting Bible, and armaments references. The Bible itself already establishes that later direct authorial corrections outrank earlier syntheses, so this is an expected maintenance problem rather than a canon crisis. fileciteturn59file0

I see **eight remaining jobs**, but only about five of them really need further authorial decisions from you.

| Priority | Remaining job | Why it matters before wiki handoff | How much is genuinely open? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **P0** | **Create one authoritative 1941–47 chronology** | Writers currently have mutually incompatible dates/details available | Mostly reconciliation, not new lore |
| **P0** | **Lock Torch and the Mediterranean endgame** | Torch, Egypt, Sinai and Suez affect Britain, Italy, captured technology, naval losses and Lisbon | Moderate |
| **P0** | **Lock the Soviet collapse/end of the Eastern War** | Determines when Germany can turn west, when Japan moves north, and exactly what “victory over the USSR” means | Moderate |
| **P0** | **Fix the White Parachutes → Churchill → peace sequence** | Current formal references directly contradict the decision we just made | Small but essential |
| **P1** | **Finish 1941–47 air development for Italy, Japan, USSR and USA** | German/British aviation is now unusually deep; the other four powers are still mostly endpoints | Substantial technical work, little strategic uncertainty |
| **P1** | **Finish the Atlantic from the British side and rebuild the 1947 naval ledger** | U-boat development now has a strong genealogy; RN losses/readiness and British countermeasures need to fall out of it | Moderate |
| **P1** | **Audit Japanese and American naval development** | No Pearl Harbor/Midway radically changes both construction programs; old fleet totals are suspect | Moderate |
| **P2** | **Give secondary theaters writer guardrails** | Finland, Balkans, Vichy France, partisan wars, minor fleets need boundaries, not full campaigns | Mostly delegable |

## 1. The most important thing is actually a master chronology pass

This is the single thing I would do before turning writers loose.

The current Timeline itself admits that the **exact dates and orders of battle for Torch, the Second Battle of Britain, and the White Parachutes remain unresolved**, along with the fall of the Soviet government. fileciteturn57file15

But since that file was written, we've gone considerably farther.

We now have enough information that the master chronology could probably work in **monthly resolution through 1942–43 and quarterly resolution thereafter**, with only the major operations receiving exact days.

Several contradictions need to be removed from the writer-facing source set:

**Burma:** the Timeline still says Japan takes Burma in the early southern conquests. fileciteturn59file1 The armaments transcript now establishes a substantially different course: Thailand carries most of that war, Rangoon doesn't simply collapse on the historical schedule, and Britain eventually pushes the Thai forces out in 1946 while Japan prepares but never launches the major intervention that might reverse that result. fileciteturn56file3

**Suez:** older summaries compress Italian victory into about 1945. The newer armaments discussion keeps Egypt/Sinai as one of Britain's last active fronts and has Centurion Mk I and II actually fighting there. That needs one final chronological version.

**Second Battle of Britain:** the formal files still say late 1945–47 rather vaguely and still use Me 264. fileciteturn59file0 We now have the much more specific architecture involving Ar 234, Me 262, Ho 229, HG-III, British Meteor/Vampire forces, and the **Me 364** Höhenbomber.

**White Parachutes:** the formal files call the operation *Unternehmen Friedensbrot*. We've now decided that **Friedensbrot is principally the post-hoc propaganda story**, not necessarily the actual operational codename.

**The naval ledger:** the Timeline still declares the 31 December 1947 fleet totals canon, including old British, German, Italian and Japanese numbers. fileciteturn59file1 This chat has now explicitly downgraded that reconstruction because it contains things like surviving *Bismarck* and *Hood* and other assumptions inherited from an earlier divergence model.

So before more lore, I would make a **WWII canon errata pass**.

That alone would prevent a huge fraction of bad wiki generation.

---

# 2. Torch and the Mediterranean still need one final campaign spine

Torch is close.

The detailed transcript has pushed the planning strongly toward **February 1943**, with January as an emergency possibility and March as essentially the latest acceptable window. fileciteturn57file10

I think what remains is probably one dedicated session answering:

**When exactly does it launch?**

**How large is the initial expedition?**

**Which major British/Commonwealth formations matter?**

**How long does the Algiers bridgehead survive?**

**When does Alexander capitulate?**

**Where in that campaign does the Royal Navy sink *Giulio Cesare*?**

We don't need battalion-by-battalion OOB before handoff. But we should probably know whether the Algiers Capitulation is, say, **spring 1943**, **summer 1943**, or something later.

Then comes the larger unresolved Mediterranean question:

> **What happens from the failure of Torch to the final loss of Egypt, Sinai and Suez?**

We have the strategic answer. Italy increasingly carries the war; German equipment cascades south as Russia winds down; Centurion gets combat experience; Suez becomes one of Britain's great late-war defensive struggles.

What we don't yet have is the **campaign narrative**.

That is one of the few remaining blank spaces I'd be uncomfortable telling writers simply to invent.

A writer can invent the name of a divisional action.

A writer should not decide on his own whether Cairo falls in 1944, 1945 or 1946.

---

# 3. The Soviet collapse needs a defined ending rather than just a known outcome

The beginning and middle of the eastern war are now extremely well supported.

We have German winter/logistical behavior, equipment development, Soviet production pressures, the fortified-city strategy, Soviet aviation decline, Soviet emergency battlefield promotion, and the eventual shift from coherent Red Army to increasingly localized commands.

The official chronology already fixes Stalin's overthrow in **late 1945–early 1946** and the Ural settlement in **1945–46**. fileciteturn59file1

But the actual **last six to twelve months of the Soviet war** still need knitting together.

I would want us to answer:

> When does Stalin fall relative to Moscow/Leningrad/Stalingrad becoming strategically untenable?

> Who actually authorizes negotiations?

> Is there a formal Soviet-German armistice before the Ural territorial agreement, or is the Ural settlement itself the armistice?

> How quickly do organized Red Army formations evacuate east?

> When does Germany regard the eastern war as sufficiently finished to transfer major aviation/armor resources west and south?

> When does Japan begin its northern intervention?

> How does the Pacific Fleet agreement with Japan fit into that chronology?

> When do the Baltic and Black Sea fleets meet their final fates?

This is not because the outcome is uncertain. It isn't.

It's because this is the **hinge that releases Germany's resources for 1946–47**.

Once that hinge has dates, writers can produce dozens of Eastern Front pages safely.

I don't think the mature Eastern occupation system itself is a WWII blocker. The dedicated Reichskommissariat canon already gives writers a very strong institutional model for what Germany creates after conquest. fileciteturn58file6

---

# 4. The political end of the British war must be corrected before handoff

This is small in size and huge in consequence.

The Setting Bible currently says that Churchill loses parliamentary confidence after the White Parachutes but his legally surviving ministry nevertheless negotiates the peace. fileciteturn59file0

We've now superseded that.

The working sequence is much better:

> **White Parachutes → London/Westminster demonstrations → Cabinet/coalition crisis → confidence failure → Churchill resigns → successor emergency ministry opens negotiations → Lisbon → White Parachute Election → Bevan Reconstruction Ministry.**

The only part I think still deserves an explicit yes/no is:

> **Is Clement Attlee definitely the emergency peace prime minister?**

I think he is the overwhelmingly cleanest answer, but that is a character-level decision worth making explicitly rather than letting a writer infer it.

Then we should settle one other thing:

> **When does actual firing stop?**

The White Parachutes are the last **Luftwaffe combat sortie**.

That doesn't automatically tell us whether U-boats, naval patrols and ground forces continue fighting for another three days, three weeks, or until Lisbon is signed.

A simple preliminary ceasefire date would solve a surprising number of downstream questions.

---

# 5. Aviation has one large unfinished quadrant

Germany is now very well developed.

Britain is also much better developed than it was at the start of this chat: Nachtjagd/EW race, Lancaster/Lincoln development, Meteor, Vampire, Attacker, Canberra, Sea Hawk, carrier-jet experimentation, Second Battle of Britain, and the exhaustion of Fighter Command all have strong causal histories.

But **Italy, Japan, the USSR and the United States have not received the same treatment**.

We know their destinations.

Italy is supposed to become the third true combat-jet power.

Japan probably produces a Kikka-like first jet and follows Germany/Britain/Italy.

The USSR reaches an air-power high-water around 1942–43 and then progressively loses the ability to contest the whole theater.

America remains technically capable but lacks the enormous combat-driven wartime aviation machine and probably develops the P-59/P-80-type path differently.

Those are strong premises.

What we don't have yet is the equivalent of the German answer:

> Which engines?  
> Which manufacturers win?  
> Which aircraft get canceled?  
> Which historical types survive for alternate reasons?  
> What does combat teach them?

That is probably the **largest remaining armaments task** before I would call WWII aviation done.

It doesn't require strategic decisions from you every five minutes, though. Once you've affirmed the broad destinations, most of it can be reconstructed technically.

---

# 6. The U-boat side is now ahead of the Royal Navy side

The German submarine lineage has become unusually coherent.

We now have:

**VII/IX → XXI/XXIII**, with Schnorchel and submerged operations;

**XXVI**, the rare peroxide high-speed Jagd-U-Boot;

**XXV / Fliegender Fisch**, the classified teardrop electric demonstrator;

Alberich;

GHG/passive sensing;

escort-first tactics;

Kurier-type burst communications;

the compromised naval cipher and replacement;

and the postwar genealogy into XXIV/XXIX/XXX.

That's enough for writers to make excellent German U-boat pages.

The British answer is not quite there yet.

We know the direction—HF/DF, centimetric radar, improved ASDIC/sonar, Hedgehog/Squid-type ahead-thrown weapons, support groups, escort carriers, acoustic decoys, passive listening, Schnorchel detection, increasingly specialized ASW escorts—but we deliberately stopped before playing that technical competition all the way through.

And that matters because **the outcome of that competition determines the Royal Navy's 1947 readiness ledger**.

So I would do one last Atlantic pass from the British side, then derive:

- approximate merchant losses by period;
- escort losses;
- repair backlog;
- operational versus nominal destroyer/frigate strength;
- which major escorts/classes become the wartime heroes;
- and the final RN readiness picture.

Only after that should the 1947 naval registry be regenerated.

---

# 7. We still owe Japan—and, oddly, neutral America—a naval audit

This is easy to overlook because they don't fight each other.

But precisely because they don't fight each other, their historical navies diverge enormously.

We have already caught one huge example:

> **Shinano should remain a battleship unless we establish a new reason for carrier conversion.** The historical conversion depended on the carrier catastrophe at Midway, which never happens here. fileciteturn56file13

That implies that simply importing the historical 1944–47 IJN is dangerous.

We should briefly establish:

Japan's carrier construction after Ceylon;

*Yamato/Musashi/Shinano*;

whether *Taihō* and the *Unryū* family still emerge and in what numbers;

the balance between carrier construction, escorts and merchant shipping;

Japanese submarine doctrine without an American Pacific War;

and what survives into 1947.

America has the reverse problem.

The United States never suffers Pearl Harbor and never enters full wartime mobilization. The Setting Bible explicitly says it does **not** receive historical-scale wartime industrial and aviation expansion. fileciteturn59file0

So an old registry giving America a gigantic historical-style 1947 fleet cannot simply be assumed either.

The US Navy remains large and modernizing.

But it probably does not build every Essex, Iowa, Fletcher, Gato/Balao, escort carrier and amphibious hull on the historical emergency schedule.

That audit could be comparatively short because there is little combat narrative to invent.

---

# 8. Everything else can mostly become writer territory

This is the point where I would deliberately **stop asking you questions**.

Once the items above are locked, I would allow the wiki system to infer and construct a very large amount of WWII detail so long as it labels unsupported specifics appropriately.

Writers should be free to create or reconstruct things such as:

- divisional and regimental actions inside an already-fixed campaign;
- minor operation names and codenames;
- ordinary commanders and fictional junior officers where no historical figure controls the role;
- exact minor warship losses and repair histories consistent with the locked fleet totals;
- individual squadron histories;
- local resistance and occupation incidents;
- tactical explanations for why a fixed battle went the way canon says it did;
- reasonable casualty ranges rather than fake exact totals;
- propaganda campaigns, newspaper reactions, memoir controversies and postwar historical arguments;
- minor prototype histories where the eventual equipment lineage is fixed;
- named convoys, U-boat encounters and air raids consistent with the larger Atlantic and air-war models;
- details of Finnish, Romanian, Hungarian, Bulgarian, Vichy, partisan and other secondary forces unless they change a major border or treaty outcome.

Those are **generative gaps**, not **canon gaps**.

That distinction is the threshold you're actually looking for.

## What I would *not* spend time locking

I would not try to determine the exact death toll of every campaign.

I would not build an individual history for every destroyer before the wiki starts.

I would not fix the exact ammunition load of every Torch battalion.

I would not give every Luftwaffe Gruppe a day-by-day history.

And I wouldn't completely specify every Lisbon treaty article.

Doing that before handoff would defeat the purpose of having writers.

They need **walls**, not every brick.

---

# My actual “ready for the writers” threshold

I think the WWII portion is handoff-ready when five documents or sections exist:

**1. A corrected 1941–47 master chronology.**  
No major contradictory dates.

**2. A campaign outcome matrix.**  
Eastern Front, China, Burma, Ceylon, Malta, Torch, Egypt/Suez, Atlantic, bombing war, Second Battle of Britain—each with start/end, principal actors, outcome and strategic consequence.

**3. A 1947 military snapshot.**  
Not fake precision. Approximate operational force structure and major equipment families for each great power.

**4. A supersession/errata sheet.**  
Explicitly says things like “old Burma line superseded,” “Me 264 → Me 364 for the late Höhenbomber,” “Friedensbrot is retrospective,” “Churchill does not negotiate Lisbon,” “old naval ledger provisional.”

**5. Writer-discretion rules.**  
Anything that does not alter a major campaign outcome, state border, senior political succession, major weapon lineage, or locked institutional consequence can be developed as Working Canon.

If those exist, I would be comfortable telling the wiki writers:

> **You no longer need Allen to tell you what happened in World War II. You need him only when you discover that two established facts genuinely cannot coexist.**

And that is a much narrower category.

The project documentation itself already recognizes that the broad WWII sequence is fixed and that most outstanding questions are exact dates/OOB rather than fundamental outcomes. fileciteturn57file12 After everything we've done in the armaments work since that document was written, that is even more true now.

So my recommendation for the remaining WWII work, in order, would be:

> **Torch + Suez → Soviet collapse/Japanese northern intervention → remaining four air forces → British side of the Atlantic → Japanese/US naval audit → one final chronology-and-errata pass.**

After those, I would genuinely regard the Second World War as **closed enough for autonomous expansion**, while still leaving us free to return later and spend three hours arguing about the fire-control arrangement on one Italian destroyer without changing the history of the world.

First being the J7W, rather than being a one-off prototype, I'm curious if we could potentially give it life as the shape/design of future Japanese Jets? Kikka can be locked in as the first Japanese Jet, but this much more successful, less bombed Japan may see Watanabe's design initially fit with a prop to prove capability flying between December 1944  and August '45 but rapidly seeing a jet allocated for testing. And the thing is, I think the Canard design would be a *seriously* interesting jet approach that has serious possibility going forward in setting. Especially as, coupled with the jet, it basically solves the conflict of "maneuver or speed", then comes the question of range, but I suspect a slightly elongated body could provide significant fuel volume to make the J7W3 *the* postwar Jet fighter of the Japanese, while the J7W2 (Jet engine put into a historical J7W1) features as the last element of that family to see service in combat. Thing is J7W wouldn't really have a lot of potential target, and when it comes to competing designs, yes there's the Kikka, but there's also  the R2Y2, which may be the "conventional" design that competes primarily with the J7W being more "normal" while the Kikka's life is relatively short as Japanese pilots typically don't appreciate how heavy it is (and how much differently it handles from normal Japanese aircraft). The J7W series then comes in and competes with the R2Y series for the "post-war jet" role. These are designs though and perhaps we justify the competition by moving the J7W series from being a *IJN* airframe to an *IJA* airframe (necessarily giving it an alternate Ki-# designation instead), Watanabe then isn't trying to replace the J2M series, but rather the Ki-84 series, This gives the J7W the ability to compete with a naval R2Y series in the Jet competition rather than begging the navy/army question of "why does the navy have two jet competitors and the army doesn't have one?" It could possibly also give the J7W a political defense as the Army identifies the J7W as *it's* plane protecting procurement budgets from arguments that the R2Y2 serves the same purpose. It could also invert a historical relationship where the Army's Ki planes were famous for being the faster of the Army/Navy planes while the Navy was more famous for the highly maneuverable A6M series, Well now the Army has the highly maneuverable (and unorthodox) J7W while the navy has the faster R2Y2. I'm wondering if we can make this Japanese conclusion work?

## Turn 1063 — Assistant

- Timestamp: 2026-08-14T01:15:59.614Z
- Message ID: `95438045-2ff0-4f72-9a9e-7423fa20a835`
- Source: ChatGPT shared conversation `Alternate J7W Jet Concept`
- Parallel branch: https://chatgpt.com/share/6a7eb2ea-137c-83e8-a9c8-b1fda9b3a455
- Relationship: parallel specialist continuation imported after the master project record through Turn 777

Yes. I think this works, and in fact it gives the Japanese early-jet story a much stronger institutional shape than the current extrapolated answer.

The present completion dossier says **Kikka enters limited service in late 1945 while J7W remains experimental**, largely because Japan never experiences the B-29 emergency that historically justified the Shinden. fileciteturn2file12 But that was explicitly an extrapolated answer filling a hole. Your current decision can supersede it. More importantly, the earlier transcript had already identified exactly what was required to save the Shinden: it needed a new mission and development chain rather than simply importing the historical emergency-interceptor rationale. fileciteturn2file9

And there is a rather wonderful historical fact supporting this: the Shinden wasn't merely an exotic piston fighter that somebody later imagined putting a jet into. Captain **Masaoki Tsuruno**, who led its design, envisioned turbojet propulsion as the ultimate destination of the concept from the beginning. citeturn556575search1turn460522search0

So I would change Japan's development tree.

## The first correction: make Shinden an Army program before it becomes “J7W”

There is one naming problem we can't dodge.

If this becomes an **Imperial Japanese Army Air Force** aircraft, it cannot properly be the J7W. `J7W` is intrinsically a Navy designation: `J` for land-based fighter and `W` for Watanabe/Kyushu. The old Aerospace Reference itself already codifies that difference between Navy J-codes and Army Ki-numbers. fileciteturn2file2

So I wouldn't say:

> The Navy develops J7W1, then hands J7W2 to the Army.

I'd move the divergence **upstream**.

Tsuruno's canard research exists, perhaps initially under Navy/Kugisho patronage because that's where the historical intellectual ancestry lies. But before the definitive combat aircraft receives its historical Navy identity, the **Army picks up the configuration as its next-generation fighter program**.

There's also a minor terminology correction: it isn't really “Watanabe's design.” Tsuruno led the design work; Watanabe Iron Works, soon reorganized as Kyushu Hikoki, was the manufacturer associated with it. citeturn460522search0 That actually makes our transfer easier. Tsuruno and the aerodynamic concept are one thing; which service funds Kyushu to turn it into a combat aircraft is another.

I would leave the exact **Ki-number open for the moment**. We should eventually audit the Army project sequence rather than steal a number already occupied by some obscure historical project.

For discussion, though, we can still call these **Shinden I, II and III**, with “J7W1/2/3” functioning temporarily as our familiar out-of-universe shorthand.

## Why would the Army want it?

This is where your Ki-84 replacement idea solves the problem.

The historical Shinden needed masses of B-29s to create an urgent requirement for a very fast, heavily armed point-defense interceptor. We don't have that. The current transcript already flagged this as the aircraft's central problem. fileciteturn2file9

But the **Army has a different requirement by 1943–44**.

The Ki-84 is becoming its premier conventional fighter. It's fast, powerful, maneuverable, reasonably well armed, and suitable for China. At the same time, Germany is demonstrating that the turbojet is no longer laboratory machinery. Japan is already moving its Kikka program earlier because Japanese observers encounter German jet development earlier in this war. fileciteturn2file10

So the Army's question becomes:

> **What comes after the Ki-84 when piston development stops buying us enough additional speed?**

And that is not the same question the Navy is asking.

The Navy already has carrier aviation. It has land-based attack aviation. It has Kikka. And, under your proposal, it has the **R2Y-derived line** as the more conventional high-speed jet solution.

The Army has Ki-84, Ki-100, and then… what?

That's exactly the bureaucratic opening Shinden needs.

The Army doesn't buy the canard because it needs to shoot B-29s over Tokyo. It buys it because Tsuruno is offering an airframe arrangement deliberately suited to an eventual turbine engine, and the Army wants **its own path into the post-piston fighter generation**.

That makes the program much less contrived.

## I would actually give it a three-stage development

The important thing is that **Shinden I, II and III shouldn't just be the same airplane with different engines**.

They're three stages in Japan learning what the canard arrangement is actually good for.

### 1943–44: the Army acquires the canard project

The Army sees the aerodynamic demonstrator work and funds Kyushu to develop a high-performance fighter.

The first aircraft is deliberately piston-powered because that removes the immature turbojet from the aerodynamic experiment. That's excellent engineering practice:

> First prove the airplane. Then change the propulsion system.

This machine is still recognizably the historical Shinden architecture: forward canard, rear main wing, pusher propeller, nose armament, tricycle undercarriage.

But its requirement is broader than historical J7W1. It isn't just:

> climb fast, shoot bomber, land.

It is:

> **prove that this arrangement can produce the Army's next high-speed fighter family.**

That probably means slightly less obsessive emphasis on four enormous 30 mm cannon and somewhat greater interest in fuel, handling, visibility, field service, and fighter-versus-fighter performance.

I'd absolutely keep four 30 mm as a **trial armament possibility**, because that beautifully demonstrates what the unobstructed nose permits. I just wouldn't assume the Army concludes that four 30s are the optimum everyday fighter armament.

### Late 1944–1945: Shinden I proves the concept

Your December 1944–August 1945 window works.

I would probably put the first powered prototype flight around **early 1945**, rather than December 1944, unless we later find a reason to push the program very hard. Japan isn't being bombed into urgency, so there's no reason to make the schedule miraculous.

And the piston machine should be **promising but troublesome**.

The canard works.

The visibility is excellent.

Pitch authority is impressive.

The nose is wonderfully clean for guns, sight, and eventually radar.

But the pusher arrangement creates exactly the sort of things engineers dislike:

- a long propeller shaft and associated vibration;
- cooling problems around the rear engine installation;
- propeller-clearance problems;
- awkward servicing;
- torque effects;
- unusual departure behavior;
- and a long undercarriage needed to protect the propeller.

This gives everybody a fascinating result.

The Army likes the **airplane** considerably more than it likes the **piston installation**.

And that makes the jet conversion feel inevitable rather than whimsical.

## Then Kikka gets to win the race

I would definitely keep this.

**Kikka remains the first operational Japanese turbojet aircraft.**

That is already one of the harder outcomes in the compiled development work: Japan reaches actual jet combat through the earlier German-information pipeline and becomes the fourth operational combat-jet power. fileciteturn2file10turn3file1

And I think Kikka becoming first while *not* becoming Japan's great postwar fighter is much more interesting.

Kikka is Japan's:

- first turbojet manufacturing school;
- first turbine-maintenance school;
- first jet-pilot conversion school;
- first operational experience with jet throttle management;
- first real investigation of jet fuel consumption;
- and first evidence that merely possessing jets doesn't make every aircraft good.

It wins the historical prize.

Then everybody starts noticing its compromises.

I wouldn't say pilots hate it simply because it is **heavy**. The more interesting complaint is that it *feels heavy* compared with Japanese piston fighters.

An early jet requires a different energy-management instinct. Throttle response is poor. Low-speed acceleration is poor. Approach speed is higher. A pilot accustomed to an aircraft which answers power changes immediately and can turn enormous amounts of speed into maneuver suddenly has a machine that punishes him for becoming slow.

Kikka also has the characteristic range problem of early turbojets; the historical aircraft was a relatively short-legged machine. citeturn584205search1

So pilots can respect Kikka while saying:

> “This is not the fighter I want to spend the next ten years flying.”

Perfect.

## Shinden II should be the wartime jet conversion

This is where I think your idea really comes alive.

Around **late 1945 or early 1946**, the Army takes the proven Shinden I airframe and removes almost everything that made its rear-engined piston installation unpleasant.

The propeller goes.

The shaft goes.

The rear piston cooling arrangement goes.

A turbojet goes almost exactly where the architecture had always wanted a thrust source.

Suddenly the aircraft's peculiar shape starts making much more sense.

But I would impose one technical requirement:

**Shinden II needs a larger single turbojet than the little Ne-20 class used by Kikka.**

That is another reason Kikka can fly first. Japan can produce two relatively modest turbines before it can produce one sufficiently powerful engine to make a single-engine Shinden worthwhile.

So:

> **Kikka wins because its engine requirement can be met first. Shinden II wins later because the single-engine arrangement has greater long-term potential.**

That's a very satisfying technological relationship.

And yes, I would let **Shinden II see combat in 1946–47**.

Not hundreds of them.

Perhaps enough for one operational group and another conversion/training establishment.

The northern intervention gives them something to do, although not necessarily glamorous MiG-versus-Sabre-style combat. They could conduct:

- railhead and airfield defense;
- interception of surviving Soviet reconnaissance/bomber aircraft;
- escort of high-value Japanese reconnaissance aircraft;
- rapid response between major Manchurian/Far Eastern bases;
- occasional fighter engagements against surviving Yak/Lavochkin formations;
- and attacks against important ground targets where speed makes interception difficult.

That preserves the dossier's existing point that **Ki-84 and Ki-100 still carry most of the northern air war**. fileciteturn2file13

Shinden II appears at the end of that war as a glimpse of what comes next.

That's much better than making jets commonplace in Siberia.

---

# But the canard does not solve “speed versus maneuver” for free

This is the one part of your intuition I'd narrow.

The canard can give us a fighter that has an unusually favorable **speed/manoeuvrability combination**. It cannot repeal the tradeoff.

A properly designed canard has some very useful characteristics. The forward surface can contribute positive lift rather than requiring a conventional horizontal tail to produce a balancing downforce. It can provide powerful pitch control, and a design in which the canard reaches its maximum lift before the main wing can give benign stall behavior because the nose drops before the main wing fully departs. NASA's later canard work specifically demonstrates that the configuration can offer useful stability/control and stall characteristics, while also creating its own design problems. citeturn795045search0turn795045search11

But sustained turning performance still comes from things like:

**wing loading + thrust-to-weight + induced drag + available lift + energy retention.**

And early turbojets are bad at some of those.

So I would define Shinden's reputation more carefully:

> **The Shinden is not the jet that turns like a Zero while flying like a Me 262. It is the early jet whose pilots are surprised by how little maneuverability they had to surrender in exchange for jet speed.**

That's much more believable.

And it gives Japanese aviation a distinctive technological reputation.

Germany might produce the superior high-speed interceptor.

Britain might produce the more mature integrated air-defense fighter.

Italy might produce a simple, elegant, economical jet.

Japan produces the **fighter pilot's jet**.

That is a powerful identity.

## And then Shinden III fixes the part Shinden II cannot: range

I agree with elongating it, but again I'd make the design change do several jobs rather than just saying “longer body = more gasoline.”

The Shinden III is where the family stops being:

> piston aircraft with the propeller removed and a turbine fitted

and becomes:

> **an aircraft designed from the first drawing around the turbine.**

I'd expect roughly five major changes.

First, the fuselage grows somewhat longer. That gives more internal tankage and improves longitudinal packaging.

Second, the engine installation and intakes are redesigned as one aerodynamic system rather than being adapted around spaces meant for a piston engine.

Third, fuel is spread through fuselage and wing-root cells so the center of gravity doesn't wander disastrously as tanks empty.

Fourth, the wing and canard are revised. Not necessarily a completely new planform yet, because then we're arguably outside the same family, but enough alteration to optimize transonic performance and the different weight distribution.

Fifth, landing gear and field servicing are redesigned around the lessons from Shinden II.

And the **single-engine layout** is doing quite a lot of the range work for us.

Kikka and the R2Y branch have to feed two turbines.

Shinden has one.

That does not automatically halve fuel consumption because the engine needs to be correspondingly more powerful, but it gives the designers fewer engines, less nacelle drag, fewer accessories, less maintenance, and a more compact propulsion installation.

Add:

- a larger internal fuel fraction;
- drop tanks for ferry/escort work;
- increasingly efficient turbine marks;
- and a cruise regime optimized for range;

and suddenly the Shinden III can become a genuinely useful **continental fighter** rather than another 400-kilometer interceptor.

I would make that one of the biggest reasons the Army loves it.

The Japanese Empire is enormous. An airplane that can fly very fast but has to be based directly beside everything it protects isn't necessarily what the Army wants after fighting from China into the Russian Far East.

---

# Which gives us an excellent three-way jet competition

This is probably the strongest part of your proposal.

The competition isn't really **three equal fighter designs**.

It's three answers to different questions that gradually intrude upon one another.

| Family | Service origin | What it is good at | Why it loses/wins |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Kikka** | Navy | First operational jet; strike/reconnaissance; turbine training; inexpensive technological bridge | Arrives first but has limited range, transitional handling and modest growth potential |
| **R2Y-derived jet** | Navy | High speed, powerful twin-engine performance, reconnaissance/strike growth, large sensor/weapon capacity | Conventional and fast, but larger, thirstier and more expensive |
| **Shinden** | **Army** | Single-engine air superiority, agility, lower operating burden, eventually long continental radius | Riskier aerodynamics and initially immature, but has the strongest fighter-specialist growth path |

And there is a very important bureaucratic consequence.

Suppose somebody in 1947 says:

> “The R2Y-derived aircraft is already a good jet. Why are we still paying Kyushu to build this strange Army fighter?”

The Army's answer isn't just technical.

It's:

> **Because that is a Navy airplane.**

And now an enormous procurement budget hangs on that distinction.

This is one of the rare places where Japanese Army-Navy rivalry can actually **preserve technological competition long enough to produce a better result**.

The Navy cannot simply say:

> “We have a jet. Cancel yours.”

Because the Army's response is:

> “You have a naval reconnaissance/strike-derived machine. We require a continental fighter.”

Even if the missions are becoming suspiciously similar.

And conversely, the Navy has every incentive to insist that the conventional R2Y-derived layout is safer, faster, has more volume for radar and fuel, and doesn't demand that the Empire gamble its future fighter force on Tsuruno's peculiar aerodynamics.

That is a procurement fight I can absolutely believe lasting into the early 1950s.

## The Army/Navy inversion works too

I like this as an **outcome**, although I wouldn't make it an explicit design goal.

The prewar stereotype has the Navy associated with Zero-style maneuverability while Army fighters such as the Ki-44 increasingly explore speed, climb, and interception.

Then the jet age scrambles the institutional identities.

Now the **Army** owns the elegant canard fighter whose pilots praise its pitch response and maneuverability.

The **Navy** owns the more conventional twin-engine machine whose case rests on speed, endurance at altitude, radar capacity, and reliability.

That gives Japanese aviation history a wonderful internal joke:

> each service eventually becomes famous for building the kind of airplane outsiders once associated with the other.

But it happens because their missions and technology change, not because somebody decided to invert the stereotype.

---

# The lineage I'd use

So, if we're turning your preference into the new working answer, I'd put it approximately here:

**1943** — Tsuruno's canard research attracts Army interest as a possible post-Ki-84 high-speed fighter architecture.

**1944** — Army formally takes responsibility for the combat-aircraft development, with Kyushu building it under an Army Ki project designation. From the outset, the requirement contemplates eventual turbojet propulsion.

**Early 1945** — **Shinden I** piston prototype flies. The configuration is judged aerodynamically promising; the pusher powerplant installation is judged much less satisfactory.

**Late 1945** — **Kikka enters service first**, preserving its place as Japan's first combat turbojet and Japan's initial jet school. This remains compatible with the established fourth-combat-jet-power chronology. fileciteturn3file1

**Late 1945–1946** — a sufficiently powerful Japanese single turbojet allows **Shinden II** development. Prototype testing is substantially easier because the basic airframe has already flown.

**Late 1946/1947** — Shinden II enters limited Army service and sees the last phase of wartime operations in the north.

**1946–48** — the genuinely jet-designed, stretched **Shinden III** is developed from operational experience: more fuel, redesigned intakes, cleaner fuselage, revised canard/wing relationship, improved landing gear and service access.

**c. 1948–49** — Shinden III becomes the Army's first genuinely postwar jet fighter and enters the major procurement competition against the Navy's R2Y-derived family.

Kikka progressively leaves first-line fighter work but survives for training, strike, reconnaissance, testing, and perhaps exports or associated-state service for a while.

And **Shinden III becomes the beginning of a Japanese canard design tradition**, rather than the end of one curious wartime airplane.

That last consequence may be the most valuable. The old Aerospace Reference already tried to make J7W1 → J7W2 → J7W3 into a continuing canard family, but it kept the whole thing inside the Navy and pushed the jet versions rather late. fileciteturn2file0 Your revision preserves the most interesting part of that older idea while supplying the institutional reason it was missing.

I would therefore treat this as a genuine improvement to the Japanese air-development canon: **Kikka wins the race into the jet age; Shinden wins the argument over what an Army jet fighter ought to be; R2Y keeps the argument alive by proving that the conventional answer is hardly obsolete.**

And from there, I think we have enough to start designing the actual **Shinden I/II/III specifications**—engine, weight, fuel capacity, armament, wing loading, thrust-to-weight, turn performance, range and the exact point where Shinden III has changed so much that the Army has to give its successor a new Ki-number rather than pretending it's still the same aircraft.

Kikka (we've established) flies in 1945, and then the R2Y2 starts looking for the next thing since the Ne-20 are seen as sluggish, leading to the development of the Ne-330 (I've found practically no information on what these were *supposed* to be, so I'm thinking a max thrust of 1300 kgf is *reasonable*) then the design office comes back for what the R2Y2 could look like and provides V1, V2, and V3 designs. 
V1 sees engine nacelles that emulate the Kikka (and as such give the navy a bad feeling due to previous Kikka complaints), V2 sees the engines moved to the rear of the plane with exhausts built into the root of the wing (interestingly emulating an uncanny cross between a Vampire, Venom, and Me 262 HG III (In that it retains the 2 engines of the HG III, and the wing-root intakes of all 3, but the rear mounting of the engine(s) from the Vampire and Venom)). Yes. I think **Ki-100 Shinden is clean enough to lock**, including the 1 February 1945 first flight.
