There are, however, two places where I would distinguish our alternate development from what is actually documented historically.

## Ki-100 Shinden: I would lock it

The historical Ki-100 existed because Kawasaki had Ki-61 airframes but couldn't obtain enough reliable liquid-cooled engines for them. The solution was to re-engine the airframe with a Mitsubishi radial, and the first radial Ki-100 prototype flew on **1 February 1945**. citeturn288819view0

So there is a rather elegant alternate-history rhyme here:

> **1 February 1945 — first flight of Ki-100 Shinden.**

The historical aircraft occupying that designation doesn't occur.

That does **not** necessarily mean we need to invent a long Ki-61-IV production lineage just to explain its absence. The cleaner answer is probably that the Ki-61 family remains an inline-engined fighter family for however long it remains useful. If the Ha-140/related liquid-cooled engine problem becomes manageable in this much less disrupted Japan, a Ki-61-III can continue development. If Ki-84 increasingly outclasses the basic concept, the Ki-61 may simply taper off rather than receive a fourth major model.

So:

**Canon lock:** `Ki-100 Shinden` is the Army canard fighter family, and its first prototype flies **1 February 1945**.

I'd tentatively structure the lineage as:

**Ki-100-I Shinden** — piston-powered aerodynamic and operational proof aircraft.

**Ki-100-II Shinden Kai** — first turbojet conversion and late-war combat version.

**Ki-100-III Shinden Kai Ni** — stretched, purpose-designed postwar jet rather than merely a piston airframe with the propeller removed.

That also neatly supersedes the old Aerospace Reference's Navy J7W1/J7W2/J7W3 sequence. The old reference itself distinguishes Army `Ki-` projects from Navy letter-number designations, so this is a real institutional reassignment rather than merely renaming J7W. fileciteturn2file3 And the newer transcript had already reduced that reference to a provisional destination ledger for precisely this sort of reconstruction. fileciteturn4file0

There is only one little administrative trick I would use: **the canard project can exist before it formally receives Ki-100.** Early Tsuruno/Kyushu aerodynamic work can be an Army-sponsored special fighter study during 1943–44; the Ki-100 number is allocated when the Army turns it into a formal prototype program. That keeps us from having to explain why a project conceived earlier somehow waited around specifically for the number 100.

---

# R2Y1: one correction, followed by an extremely convenient confirmation

The R2Y1 powerplant is slightly stranger than “a 24-cylinder V-12.”

The **Ha-70-01** was effectively two uprated Aichi Atsuta inverted V-12s coupled into one **24-cylinder inverted-W power unit**, producing a planned 3,400 hp and driving the enormous six-bladed propeller through a roughly four-meter shaft. citeturn970359view0

Which actually reinforces the role we're giving R2Y1.

It is already a fairly extreme experimental aircraft whose propulsion arrangement exists because Kūgishō wants an exceptionally clean, fast airframe. In our setting, with the airframe not destroyed in an American bombing raid and Japanese industry considerably healthier, it makes perfect sense that the Navy finishes the piston aircraft specifically to answer:

> **Does the Keiun airframe itself work before we commit a scarce pair of turbojets to it?**

Then comes the delightful part.

The historical **Ne-330 specification was 1,320 kgf static thrust at 7,600 rpm.** citeturn970359view1

So I wouldn't use our invented 1,300 kgf figure.

I'd lock the actual intended figure:

> **Mitsubishi Ne-330: approximately 1,320 kgf maximum static thrust.**

That's essentially exactly the engine you independently reasoned Japan needed.

Historically the first Ne-330 was completed in April 1945 and immediately lost when the Mitsubishi plant was bombed; subsequent work was scattered among facilities and never recovered before surrender. citeturn970359view2 **That failure mechanism basically disappears in our Japan.**

This gives us a very natural engine chronology:

Kikka gets the smaller Ne-20 first.

Ne-330 is already being developed independently as the next, substantially more powerful turbine.

Operational experience with Kikka then doesn't **create** Ne-330. It tells the Navy:

> “Whatever you do, get us the Ne-330.”

That's a much stronger causal sequence.

The Kikka pilot's complaint becomes evidence for a program that already exists.

---

# The R2Y2 V1/V2/V3 problem is actually useful

Here's the historical catch.

The three shapes we're accustomed to seeing as R2Y2 V1, V2 and V3 are **not equally historical designs**.

The strongest surviving evidence has Ōtsuki describing the R2Y2 with **two Ne-330s under the wings** and a very large fuel tank occupying the fuselage space vacated by the Ha-70. Another Kūgishō engineer later remembered essentially the same arrangement. The buried-engine wing-root-intake and nose-intake versions appear principally in later depictions, and their status as actual wartime designs cannot be securely established. citeturn970359view2

That's not a problem for us.

It's actually helpful because we can say explicitly:

> **In OTL, V2 and V3 never advance beyond uncertain concepts, if they existed at all. In AltWWII, the extra time, intact design bureau, functioning Ne-330 program, and observation of foreign jets cause Kūgishō to develop all three into genuine competing configurations.**

So we aren't pretending modern speculative drawings were historical blueprints.

We're taking the speculative design lineage and giving it the altered circumstances necessary to **become real**.

That is exactly the methodology we've been using elsewhere.

For in-setting terminology, I wouldn't initially call them R2Y2 V1/V2/V3. That's useful for us outside the setting, but something like **Arrangement A, B and C** during the design competition feels more natural. Only the selected aircraft becomes the formal R2Y2.

And the three arrangements produce a very good competition:

| Study | Configuration | Principal advantage | Principal liability |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A / V1** | Two underwing Ne-330 nacelles | Fastest to engineer; easy engine access; preserves huge fuselage fuel tank | Draggy/transitional appearance; repeats what pilots dislike about Kikka architecture |
| **B / V2** | Twin buried engines aft, wing-root intakes | Cleaner wing; compact frontal area; free nose; good high-speed growth potential | More ducting, heat, fire risk and miserable engine access; reduced internal fuel |
| **C / V3** | Twin buried engines aft, large nose intake with bifurcated ducts | Very clean external airflow; potentially excellent high-speed inlet | Long ducting consumes tremendous internal volume; complicated around cockpit; nose no longer free; range/maintenance penalty |

And this gives us a much better reason for **B winning than merely “B flew a little better.”**

## Arrangement A is the insurance policy

A is what an engineer shows an admiral when the admiral says:

> “I need a jet aircraft, not an aeronautical thesis.”

It's the historical configuration and therefore the easiest one to produce.

Pull the Ha-70 and shaft.

Put the giant fuel tank in the empty fuselage.

Hang two Ne-330s underneath the wing.

Do the necessary structural and systems work.

Fly.

It probably reaches prototype stage first precisely because it asks the fewest new questions.

But it suffers politically from Kikka.

Not because there's anything fundamentally wrong with podded engines. The Me 262 demonstrates rather spectacularly that podded engines can work.

The problem is that **Japanese pilots and planners mentally associate this arrangement with their transitional jet**. Kikka already has relatively modest thrust, twin nacelles, higher fuel consumption than familiar piston fighters, unfamiliar low-speed behavior, and a rather un-Japanese feeling of mass and inertia.

So when the R2Y team presents:

> “Kikka, except larger and faster,”

the Navy isn't excited.

Arrangement A may get one flying prototype precisely because it is the **control aircraft** against which the more ambitious layouts are compared.

---

# Arrangement B is where Keiun becomes its own aircraft

This is the one I think the Navy should ultimately choose.

And your visual comparison is good, with one mechanical qualification.

It would look like an uncanny meeting point among **Vampire/Venom and Me 262 HG-III**, but mechanically the HG-III is the closer analogy. Vampire and Venom use a single central engine; our R2Y2 B has **two turbines buried side by side or slightly staggered in the aft fuselage**, fed by wing-root intakes.

The point is nevertheless the same:

> get the engines out of external nacelles and make propulsion part of the airframe.

There are real penalties. The historical R2Y research specifically identifies the likely cost of buried engines: reduced central fuel volume, harder maintenance and development work associated with intake losses. citeturn970359view2

So B should be an aircraft mechanics hate before they learn how to service it.

Open a large panel.

Disconnect half a dozen lines.

Remove another panel.

Swear at Lieutenant-Commander Aburai.

Then eventually pull the turbine out sideways or downward with a purpose-built cradle.

But aerodynamically, **this is the configuration with the strongest growth potential**.

And there is one advantage I would add that becomes increasingly important after the war:

### Arrangement B leaves the nose completely free.

Initially that means:

- cannon;
- reconnaissance camera;
- gunsight;
- navigation equipment.

Later it means:

- **radar**.

That's an enormous advantage for a Navy looking toward all-weather fleet defense.

The R2Y2 design office in 1946 does not need to know precisely what a 1958 intercept radar looks like to understand that the nose is the best place for a lot of equipment they'd rather not route around an air duct.

---

# Then the Second Battle of Britain gives Arrangement B political protection

This works extremely well with what we've already established, but I would make one chronological terminology correction.

During the Second Battle of Britain, Britain has **operational Vampires**, while the proper Venom is still represented by an experimental thin-wing, Ghost-powered Vampire/Venom precursor. Germany, meanwhile, has the specialized HG-III branch demonstrating the potential of much more integrated high-speed jet installations. fileciteturn3file1 fileciteturn3file2

So the Navy doesn't literally receive a report saying:

> “The British Venom is excellent.”

Instead, Japanese observers accumulate three pieces of evidence.

The Vampire proves that an unconventional compact jet configuration can be an extremely satisfactory fighter.

The British experimental thin-wing/Ghost work shows that the configuration has substantial growth left.

The German HG-III demonstrates that burying turbines into a much more aerodynamically integrated airframe is not merely designer vanity.

And the really important distinction is:

> **Those aircraft don't cause R2Y2-B. They rescue it from cancellation.**

The engineers have already built this difficult thing.

Then procurement officials start asking why they shouldn't simply standardize the easier Arrangement A.

Reports from Britain arrive.

Suddenly the engineers can say:

> “The Germans and British are moving in exactly the direction we told you this aircraft needs to go.”

That's how foreign technical intelligence should work here—not giving Japan a blueprint, but changing which domestic engineers win an argument.

---

# Arrangement C/V3 is a superb ugly duckling

And I agree with your proposed outcome almost exactly.

The C aircraft works.

That is important.

It shouldn't be some foolish configuration everybody laughs at.

A properly made nose inlet gets clean freestream air and removes the external wing-root intake openings. There are legitimate aerodynamic reasons why a designer might be attracted to it.

But this airplane has **two engines aft of the cockpit**.

So that beautiful intake in the nose has to become a large duct that runs rearward and splits around the cockpit and other systems before feeding both turbines.

That's where the elegance on the drawing board starts getting expensive.

The aircraft loses volume to:

- inlet duct;
- splitter geometry;
- boundary-layer treatment;
- cockpit bypass;
- twin-engine feed;
- structural reinforcement around the openings.

And jet Keiun desperately needs that volume for **fuel**. Contemporary R2Y2 calculations already regarded a big central fuel tank as necessary because the Ne-330 was thirsty. citeturn970359view1turn970359view2

So I would make the R2Y2-C flight-test conclusion something like:

> **It is slightly faster in the optimum condition, but not enough faster to matter.**

Not 80 km/h.

Maybe fifteen or twenty.

Perhaps C has marginally better acceleration above some speed.

Perhaps at altitude the inlet behaves beautifully.

But its useful radius is worse.

Its mechanics prefer B, which is saying something.

Its armament installation is more annoying.

And the Navy increasingly likes B's unobstructed nose.

Therefore:

> **Arrangement C demonstrates a good aerodynamic idea attached to the wrong generation of engine and airframe.**

That's a perfect “failed” prototype.

Nobody thinks it was stupid.

They think it arrived too early.

---

# Which gets us to R2Y2 Keiun Kai

So your selection makes sense.

I'd put the sequence approximately like this:

**1944** — Ne-330 work begins alongside Japanese turbojet development. R2Y1 construction continues as the aerodynamic proof aircraft.

**1945** — Kikka flies first and remains Japan's first operational jet. Its Ne-20 installation teaches the services how different jet energy management, fuel consumption and maintenance actually are.

**1945** — R2Y1 flies as the piston development aircraft. The healthier Japanese industrial environment prevents the historical bombing-driven destruction of the program.

**Late 1945–46** — Kūgishō compares Arrangements A, B and C. A is the low-risk configuration. B and C are more ambitious attempts to create a genuinely integrated turbine airframe.

**1946** — the first Ne-330s become useful experimental engines. A probably flies first. B follows and receives the main development effort.

**1946–47** — a small B-series development batch accumulates enough hours to expose its maintenance shortcomings but also confirms its aerodynamic potential.

**1946–47 Second Battle of Britain** — reports on Vampire, the emerging Venom concept and German HG work strengthen the bureaucratic case for B.

**1947** — Arrangement B becomes the definitive **R2Y2 Keiun Kai**.

I wouldn't necessarily give it large wartime production. Japan has only a short amount of war left, and the Navy's immediate enemies aren't generating a requirement for 1,000 advanced jet fighters.

A development squadron or a handful of service-evaluation aircraft is enough.

Then R2Y2 becomes a **postwar production aircraft**.

And that is where it really starts competing with Ki-100.

---

# The Ki-100/R2Y2 rivalry is now much cleaner

Rather than two Japanese services somehow developing almost the same aircraft, they're making quite different bets.

**Ki-100 Shinden** says:

> one turbine, minimum propulsion burden, excellent maneuverability, good climb, eventually long range, fighter first.

**R2Y2 Keiun Kai** says:

> two turbines, more volume, more speed, more payload, more redundancy, better sensor growth, reconnaissance/strike/heavy-fighter ancestry.

Kikka is the first generation that teaches Japan to operate turbines.

Ki-100 becomes the **Army's fighter-pilot jet**.

R2Y2 becomes the **Navy's systems airplane**.

That's a much more durable competition than “which one has the highest top speed?”

Because both can truthfully say the other cannot replace it.

The Army looks at R2Y2's two Ne-330s and asks why the Navy needs **two engines to move one pilot**.

The Navy looks at Ki-100 and asks where the Army intends to put a second crewman, radar, cameras, navigation equipment, a meaningful bomb load and an engine redundancy margin.

Neither side is entirely wrong.

---

# And R2Y3 in 1955 can make the discarded C configuration work

I like this too, but I would make **R2Y3 considerably more than R2Y2-C with newer engines**.

Eight to ten years of jet development is too large a gap.

By 1955, the engineers who reopen the nose-intake study are no longer asking:

> “Should we build the third R2Y2 prototype?”

They're saying:

> “Arrangement C had something we never exploited. What does that idea look like with modern turbines and everything we've learned since?”

So **R2Y3 Keiun Kai Ni** can preserve:

- the central/nose inlet concept;
- aft buried engines;
- the broad R2Y aerodynamic ancestry;
- and the Navy's high-speed twin-engine philosophy.

But it should acquire:

- a thinner, probably swept wing;
- completely redesigned ducting;
- substantially more powerful and efficient engines;
- revised fuel arrangement;
- improved ejection seat/cockpit;
- much more serious electrical capacity;
- and a 1950s weapons installation.

There's also a wonderful design problem waiting for it:

**the nose intake is competing with radar.**

That's not fatal. Contemporary designers found ways to package ranging radar around nose intakes, and later centerbody/intake arrangements can carry larger antennas. But it means R2Y3 has a built-in evolutionary limitation.

That could produce a later Japanese sequence something like:

> **R2Y2:** wing-root intake — radar-friendly nose.

> **R2Y3:** nose intake — extremely good high-speed day fighter/strike aircraft.

> **eventual successor:** side intakes return because proper all-weather interception demands a large unobstructed radar nose.

Which is exactly the sort of engineering pendulum that makes an aircraft family feel real.

So I wouldn't describe C/V3 as the **loser** anymore.

I'd describe it as the design that loses **in 1947** and wins **in 1955**, once the surrounding technology changes.

---

That gives us a Japanese first-jet generation I think is substantially stronger than the existing reference:

**Kikka** wins the historical distinction of getting there first.

**Ki-100 Shinden** becomes the Army's great postwar fighter lineage, with its first flight deliberately fixed to **1 February 1945**.

**R2Y2 Keiun Kai** becomes the Navy's cleaner, faster, heavier twin-engine answer, with the wing-root-intake Arrangement B selected after a genuine three-layout competition.

And **R2Y3 Keiun Kai Ni** resurrects the discarded nose-intake idea around 1955, not because the Navy realizes it made a mistake, but because the engine, ducting and aerodynamic technology have finally caught up with what Arrangement C was trying to do.

That is exactly the sort of development history where the silhouettes are memorable **because they correspond to actual procurement arguments**, rather than because we're just keeping three cool-looking Japanese paper jets.

Yes. I think the **long peace is what makes these two lineages much more plausible**, rather than less.

The old Aerospace Reference jumps rather quickly through unrelated Japanese types because it was written before we rebuilt the development method. It already preserves Army/Navy institutional separation, but its later `A9M`, `J12`, `J13`, `J14` sequence should now be treated as provisional rather than something we have to steer back toward. fileciteturn4file0turn4file9 The more recent wartime work explicitly says that Japan's Army and Navy procurement cultures remain separate, while the setting's wider Japanese system has a narrow industrial core and chronic manpower constraints. fileciteturn4file4 citeturn275684view0

That combination—**institutional rivalry + no major war + budgets that reward reuse rather than revolutionary replacement**—is almost tailor-made for two very long aircraft design traditions.

And I think they should diverge almost exactly as you're describing.

## The Navy: Keiun becomes Japan's “big fighter” tradition

The R2Y lineage has an enormous structural advantage for surviving the generations: its defining characteristics aren't especially tied to 1946 technology.

They are:

- twin engines;
- substantial internal volume;
- long range;
- high electrical generation;
- considerable weapons capacity;
- a design bias toward speed;
- and eventually enough volume and power for serious radar and navigation equipment.

Those characteristics become **more valuable** as aviation moves from guns to radar, missiles, electronic warfare, guided strike weapons, and maritime interception.

So I wouldn't have the IJN repeatedly ask, “What replaces Keiun?”

It repeatedly asks:

> **“What does the next Keiun need?”**

That is a very different procurement culture.

And because Japan never gets its Korea or Vietnam equivalent to violently expose wrong assumptions, there isn't a combat shock that kills the lineage.

The Philippine War is close enough to cause deployments, alerts, patrols, intelligence gathering, and perhaps frightening near-contacts with American aircraft, but Japan is deliberately operating “one degree below war” rather than openly throwing the IJA and IJN into combat. The 1957 settlement in the current wiki still treats the American withdrawal as the decisive event. citeturn112414view0

So Keiun development is being validated mostly by:

**exercises → foreign observation → test ranges → fleet problems → procurement politics**

rather than combat.

That strongly favors continuity.

### The important R2Y3 qualification

I would keep the **1955 R2Y3 nose-intake aircraft** exactly as we've just established it.

But I don't think the nose intake survives indefinitely.

That's the one place where the 1955 “ugly duckling” eventually runs into the lineage's own success.

Once Keiun becomes a serious all-weather fighter, the Navy wants a large radar antenna in the nose. You *can* put radar into an intake centerbody—MiG-21-style arrangements demonstrate the basic concept—but it badly constrains antenna diameter and packaging.

So I'd have the family do something rather satisfying:

**R2Y2:** wing-root intakes.

**R2Y3:** nose intake, because the 1950s speed requirement temporarily dominates.

**next major Keiun:** goes back to lateral/wing-root intakes, because radar has become more important than the tiny aerodynamic gain that justified the nose intake.

The Navy doesn't conclude R2Y3 was a mistake. Technology has simply changed the optimization.

By the third generation, this thing can absolutely occupy the **F-4 Phantom II ecological niche**.

Not necessarily visually. Functionally.

It becomes the aircraft that can be sent out with:

- long-range radar missiles;
- short-range missiles;
- cannon;
- reconnaissance package;
- anti-ship weapons;
- conventional bombs;
- guided bombs;
- electronic warfare stores;
- drop tanks.

And because the basic aircraft is twin-engined and relatively large, every generation of better engines doesn't merely make it faster.

Sometimes the Navy says:

> We already have enough speed. Give us another tonne of fuel and weapons instead.

That's exactly the maturation I'd expect.

By the 1960s, I would seriously consider a **two-seat Keiun** becoming the principal all-weather/maritime version. The second crewman makes considerable sense before avionics automation becomes good enough to return everything to one pilot. That gives us another Phantom rhyme without merely making a Japanese Phantom copy.

One important scope distinction: **Keiun remains a land-based naval aircraft.** It doesn't need to swallow the IJN's carrier-fighter lineage. Japan's enormous maritime empire gives it hundreds of island and coastal bases where a long-range twin-engine naval fighter/strike aircraft makes tremendous sense.

So the Navy can simultaneously have:

> carrier fighter lineage + Keiun land-based heavy/multirole lineage.

That makes its huge carrier establishment much easier to reconcile.

---

# The Army: Shinden runs into a genuine aerodynamic wall

This one is even more interesting.

Ki-100-III **Shinden Kai Ni** can take the original concept surprisingly far. But eventually Tsuruno's team encounters a problem that can't be solved by putting another engine into the back.

The straight main wing is becoming the limiting component.

Sweeping it is the obvious first experiment, and I agree that **simply sweeping the Shinden wing backward shouldn't be the final answer**. That doesn't mean swept wings and canards inherently fail—they don't—but the interaction among center of pressure, canard authority, wing sweep, vortices and directional stability becomes increasingly unpleasant.

The elegant response is:

> **Don't turn the old Shinden wing into a swept wing. Replace its aerodynamic theory while preserving the Shinden layout.**

And that's where the delta arrives.

This is very well grounded technically. Saab began the Draken requirement in 1949 and selected its distinctive double-delta arrangement to achieve good behavior in both subsonic and supersonic regimes; the production aircraft ultimately reached Mach 2. citeturn180905search0turn180905search17 NASA was already experimentally studying **canard-controlled delta aircraft at Mach 2** in the 1950s, including a 70-degree delta-canard configuration and a 60-degree delta with canard controls. citeturn520968search13turn520968search14

So a victorious Japanese design establishment arriving independently at:

> **single rear engine + side intakes + double-delta main wing + swept/delta canards**

during the 1950s is entirely believable.

In fact, we don't even have to grant Japan implausibly early knowledge. The aerodynamics are contemporary.

## I think your “Draken with Shinden ancestry” visual is basically right

The main wing would sit very far aft, as it always has on Shinden.

But instead of the original straight wing, it becomes something resembling a **double delta**:

a very highly swept inner section leading into a somewhat less swept outer section.

The inner delta gives the high-speed aircraft a slender effective planform.

The outer panel helps give it usable wing area and low-speed behavior.

The original Shinden canard then evolves into a **small swept or delta foreplane**.

And suddenly the lineage is obvious without requiring anyone to mistake the new aircraft for the 1945 machine.

You could park them together and see:

> “Yes. That's what this became.”

That's exactly what I want out of an alternate aircraft family.

NASA's later synthesis actually describes why the combination is useful: delta wings offer relatively low wave drag over a broad Mach range but can suffer poor low-speed lift and high approach attitudes; adding a foreplane can improve lift distribution and usable takeoff/landing lift. citeturn520968search28

So Tsuruno's team isn't retaining the canard merely out of aesthetic pride.

The canard helps solve one of the delta's actual weaknesses.

---

# But I would *not* make it a 1980s-style close-coupled canard yet

This distinction matters.

The modern Gripen/Typhoon/Rafale sort of arrangement uses the foreplane and main-wing vortex systems very aggressively. That becomes much easier once you have sophisticated stability augmentation and eventually digital fly-by-wire.

Our 1950s Japanese fighter shouldn't magically have 1980s flight-control philosophy.

Instead, the first supersonic Shinden successor should still be **positively stable**.

The canards remain relatively far forward—recognizably descended from the old Shinden arrangement—and are designed principally for:

- pitch control;
- trim;
- low-speed lift;
- maneuver control;
- and managing the aircraft across the transonic shift in aerodynamic center.

NASA had tested canard aircraft at Mach 1.4–2.0 by this period, but those experiments also showed that the canard could alter directional stability differently at different Mach numbers. citeturn520968search9

So this is an airplane that requires **a lot of wind-tunnel work**, not a magical configuration whose problems disappear because it has canards.

That's actually perfect for Tsuruno's increasingly prestigious design bureau.

They become Japan's canard specialists because they've spent fifteen years discovering all the reasons canards are difficult.

---

# The nose is an enormous advantage—but put radar there, not most of the fuel

This is the one thing I'd change in your formulation.

You absolutely get a **huge useful nose**.

The engine is behind the pilot.

The intakes are alongside the fuselage.

So everything ahead of the cockpit is available.

But by the late 1950s, the single most valuable thing you can put there is increasingly:

> **radar.**

Shinden therefore gets a wonderful structural advantage over aircraft whose inlet lives in the nose.

The nose can grow naturally from the original blunt Ki-100 shape into a long pointed radome. Behind it sit radar electronics, gunsight/weapons computer, avionics, perhaps cannon ammunition farther aft, and eventually IR or electronic-warning equipment.

Fuel should principally remain **near the aircraft's center of gravity**.

Putting a giant primary fuel tank twenty feet ahead of the engine gives you an aircraft whose balance changes substantially as it drinks that fuel.

You can certainly have forward tanks, but they'd be used through a controlled fuel-transfer sequence.

The big tanks belong:

- around the main fuselage center;
- beside/between the inlet ducts where geometry permits;
- in the inner delta wing;
- and potentially in conformal spaces around the engine installation.

That gives us another advantage of the delta:

**a great deal of internal wing volume.**

So the supersonic Shinden can gain both radar and fuel without making the nose a flying petrol tank.

---

# The side intakes absolutely survive

They just become more complicated.

The simple Shinden-II/III intake doesn't remain a rounded hole in the fuselage when we're trying to do Mach 2.

By the supersonic generation, I'd expect something resembling:

> **two lateral variable-geometry ramp intakes**

feeding a single large turbojet/early turbofan aft.

That's still unmistakably Shinden.

Pilot in the center.

Intakes behind/beside him.

Engine aft.

Main wing surrounding the engine region.

Long clean nose ahead.

Canards forward.

Nothing about going supersonic requires abandoning that arrangement.

NASA actually tested a **60-degree delta-canard aircraft with twin side inlets from Mach 0.8 to 1.7** extremely early, which is almost eerily close to the configuration we're independently converging on. citeturn520968search10

For Mach 2, Japanese engineers then need shock control, intake ramps or equivalent geometry, boundary-layer management and a carefully designed duct.

That's a major engineering program, but not a conceptual problem.

---

# Now, the twin rudders

Here's the interesting answer:

## **Keep two. Move them.**

There is no aerodynamic rule saying a supersonic aircraft needs one vertical tail.

Twin vertical tails work perfectly well on supersonic aircraft, and NASA tested both **wing-mounted twin-tail canard configurations** and different tail placements precisely because location matters greatly to directional stability. citeturn180905search9turn180905search12 Even the Mach-3 XB-70 combined a delta wing, canards and twin vertical fins. citeturn180905search6

So the Shinden's visual signature can survive.

But I wouldn't keep the **1945 placement**.

The Ki-100-I's vertical fins are rather far outboard on the main wing. On the new thin delta, that becomes increasingly unattractive.

You'd be asking a very thin supersonic wing to carry substantial:

- fin bending loads;
- torsional loads;
- rudder hinge loads;
- and shock/vortex interference loads

well away from the fuselage.

And where the fins sit relative to canard and wing vortices can materially change their effectiveness. NASA's research on canard configurations specifically found vertical-tail location to be an important variable in directional stability. citeturn339325search0turn180905search14

So I think the tails **migrate inboard generation by generation**.

### Ki-100 Shinden

Two vertical fins well out on the straight main wing.

### Ki-100-III Shinden Kai Ni

Still twin-fin, but already perhaps slightly farther inboard as the jet installation and wing evolve.

### Supersonic Shinden successor

Two strongly swept vertical fins mounted on the **aft inner delta**, immediately to either side of the rear fuselage/engine bay.

Something roughly like:

```text
             /\ nose
          ==    ==     canards
             []
            /  \
          /      \     forward inner delta
        /          \
       /            \
      /   |      |   \
     /    |      |    \
    /_____|______|_____\
           [engine]
              >
```

Not literally that shape, obviously, but the relationship matters.

The fins are now almost **fuselage-mounted through the wing root** rather than genuinely wingtip-mounted.

That does four useful things.

It keeps the Shinden twin-tail identity.

It reduces structural penalty.

It keeps the vertical surfaces closer to the aircraft's central structure.

And it allows the designers to position them deliberately relative to the wing/canard vortex field.

I might even cant them outward slightly in later generations, though I wouldn't necessarily do that immediately.

So visually the evolution becomes wonderful:

> 1945 Shinden: **two fins standing on the wings.**

> 1958 Shinden successor: **two fins growing from the aft delta roots.**

> 1970s descendant: **twin canted tails integrated into the wing-body.**

You can watch Japanese aerodynamic knowledge accumulating just by looking at photographs.

---

# This also suggests when Ki-100 finally stops being Ki-100

I think the delta transition is the natural boundary.

Ki-100-I, II and III can remain variants because, despite increasingly large changes, they retain essentially the same airframe genealogy.

Once Tsuruno replaces:

- the entire main wing;
- the canard;
- the intake system;
- much of the fuselage;
- the landing gear geometry;
- and probably the engine;

we are no longer looking at another Ki-100 model.

We're looking at **the next Shinden**.

It can still publicly be *Shinden*.

It can even be *Shinden II*.

But it needs another Ki project number.

And **Ki-200 would be aesthetically gorgeous**:

> Ki-100 Shinden → Ki-200 Shinden II.

Unfortunately, there's one administrative loose end.

Historically `Ki-200` belonged to the Army's Shūsui rocket interceptor. The current older material still preserves Ki-200/J8M as an experimental program even though the B-29 emergency disappears. fileciteturn4file4

So if we want to lock **Ki-200 Shinden II**, we need to make one explicit alteration:

> **the Army never formally takes the Shūsui into the Ki registry as Ki-200.**

The Navy can still conduct J8M rocket experimentation. The Army may participate in testing. But without the homeland emergency, it never creates its own Ki-200 production project.

Then the number remains open.

Given how clean **Ki-100 → Ki-200** is, I actually think that may be worth doing.

---

# The likely Shinden transition

I'd currently put the development roughly here:

**1945 — Ki-100-I Shinden**  
Piston-powered proof aircraft; first flight 1 February.

**1946 — Ki-100-II Shinden Kai**  
Jet conversion; limited wartime operational service.

**c. 1948–49 — Ki-100-III Shinden Kai Ni**  
Purpose-built turbine Shinden: stretched fuselage, substantially more fuel, refined side intakes, improved fighter radius. This is the mature first-generation/early-1.5-generation fighter.

**c. 1951–53 — supersonic studies begin**  
Higher-powered engines push Ki-100-III into the transonic problem. Swept-wing variants are tested. Tsuruno's group concludes that merely sweeping the existing main wing produces too many compromises.

**c. 1953–55 — double-delta/canard demonstrator**  
Extensive wind-tunnel work and probably at least one subscale or dedicated flying research machine.

That timing is exceptionally plausible: Saab began what became Draken in 1949, used the Saab 210 research aircraft to investigate its unusual double-delta concept, and flew the full Draken in 1955. citeturn180905search20turn180905search19 Japan starting with a decade of Shinden-canard experience can credibly operate on a similar clock.

**c. 1956 — new Shinden prototype flies.**

**c. 1958–59 — operational service.**

And I would aim for something in the **Mach 1.8–2.0 class**, rather than immediately chasing absurd speed.

That already makes it a profoundly capable second-generation fighter.

---

# Which gives Japan two almost opposite aircraft philosophies

And this is what I think makes the whole Japanese air-development tree finally click.

The Navy's tradition becomes:

> **Add capability without throwing away the airframe.**

Keiun starts with two engines because early jets are weak. Later engines become powerful enough that the Navy could use one, but the Navy says: *why?*

Keep two.

Carry more fuel.

Carry more radar.

Carry bigger missiles.

Carry bombs.

Carry an extra crewman.

Come home if one engine quits over the Pacific.

The result eventually becomes Japan's Phantom-like multirole heavy fighter family.

The Army's tradition becomes:

> **Preserve the aerodynamic idea even if the airframe has to change completely.**

Shinden starts with a piston and straight wings.

Then a jet.

Then a better jet.

Then the old wing reaches its limit.

So Tsuruno throws away the wing but keeps the philosophy:

**canard ahead → pilot amidships → side intakes → engine aft → main lifting surface surrounding the propulsion section → unobstructed nose.**

And from that comes the double-delta Shinden II.

Eventually, once analog stability augmentation and then digital flight controls mature, the Army can begin moving the canards closer to the wing, deliberately exploiting their vortex interaction and relaxing static stability. That's when the Shinden lineage starts looking less like **“a futuristic 1945 aircraft”** and more like an independently evolved cousin of Viggen and eventually Gripen. NASA's work explains precisely why later close-coupled canards become attractive: their vortices can energize the inner delta wing and increase usable lift at high angle of attack. citeturn520968search28

So I think the visual ancestry can survive all the way into the fourth generation.

Not because Japan keeps building the same aircraft for forty years, but because **Japanese designers never receive the historical reason to abandon the design school that produced it.**

And the twin fins can absolutely remain part of that identity. They just slowly crawl inward until, by the supersonic generation, they're no longer “rudders attached to the wings” so much as **two aft vertical stabilizers emerging from the Shinden's inner delta/engine structure**. That is probably the cleanest technical and visual solution.

Yes. I think the missing aircraft is now fairly clear, and it also gives us a much cleaner IJN air arm than making Keiun do everything.

The basic answer I would use is:

> **R2Y/Keiun becomes the Navy's heavy carrier-capable strike, reconnaissance, interception, and eventually multirole lineage. Mitsubishi's A-series remains the dedicated carrier-fighter lineage.**

So the postwar IJN does **not** replace the A6M/A7M tradition with Keiun. It replaces the **B7A's operational place** with Keiun while allowing the old distinction between “fighter” and “attack aircraft” to blur as jets become multirole.

And conveniently, the old Aerospace Reference already contains the second aircraft in the Mitsubishi line: **A9M1 Shippū, entering service in 1956 as a carrier air-superiority fighter.** fileciteturn5file5 What it never had was a convincing ancestor between A7M Reppū and A9M.

I think that ancestor should be **A8M1**, Mitsubishi's first purpose-designed jet carrier fighter.

## First, I would slightly redefine what Keiun is replacing

I agree with your instinct about the B7A2, with one distinction.

R2Y2 doesn't necessarily become the bureaucratic successor to the **B-series**. It becomes its **functional successor**.

The B7A Ryūsei represents the mature piston-era idea that one carrier aircraft can combine dive bombing and torpedo attack instead of requiring separate attack types. Jet propulsion then makes the old distinction increasingly artificial. Keiun adds reconnaissance, interception and eventually guided weapons on top of that.

So by perhaps 1950 the IJN carrier deck increasingly has two principal combat-aircraft categories:

1. **A-series Mitsubishi fighter** — air superiority first.
2. **R2Y Keiun** — heavy strike/reconnaissance/all-weather/multirole aircraft that is carrier-capable by design.

That does not mean every Keiun squadron lives aboard a carrier.

Quite the opposite.

Your F-4 analogy is excellent here. The Phantom remained fundamentally a Navy aircraft and retained the structural consequences of that ancestry even when operated extensively from land; the Smithsonian describes it as qualified for both land and sea operations. citeturn284851search0turn284851search17

I'd make that an IJN institutional requirement:

> **Every frontline Keiun must remain capable of operating from the current full-size fleet carrier, whether or not its squadron is presently embarked.**

That means Keiun keeps paying the carrier tax:

- arrestor hook;
- very strong landing gear;
- low-speed handling requirement;
- folding surfaces where necessary;
- corrosion protection;
- carrier-navigation equipment;
- catapult attachment;
- restricted dimensions;
- and structural reinforcement for repeated arrested landings.

But an R2Y squadron stationed at Singapore might go years without seeing a flight deck.

**Carrier-capable, not carrier-bound.**

That is exactly the right distinction.

---

# Mitsubishi keeps the actual carrier-fighter inheritance

And I agree fairly strongly that this should remain Mitsubishi.

There's an industrial reason and an institutional reason.

The institutional reason is continuity. Mitsubishi produces A6M, then A7M. The Navy therefore already thinks of Mitsubishi as the house that knows what a **fleet fighter** is supposed to be.

The industrial reason becomes stronger with the jet transition, because Mitsubishi is also involved in turbine development. So keeping the carrier-fighter program there does not require the Navy to build an entirely new design/manufacturing ecosystem just as propulsion itself is changing.

Most importantly, I would preserve the **design philosophy** of Reppū rather than trying to preserve its literal silhouette.

That's how we avoid:

> “This is an F9F with Hinomaru painted on it.”

The Mitsubishi carrier-fighter tradition should mean:

> **range + excellent carrier handling + relatively low wing loading + good pilot visibility + clean aerodynamics + enough maneuverability that the pilot does not regard navalization as punishment.**

That's recognizably descended from the Zero/Reppū school even after the propeller disappears.

And that also distinguishes it wonderfully from Keiun.

---

# A8M1: the missing first-generation Mitsubishi jet

I think the first Mitsubishi jet fighter should be quite conservative.

Not a swept-wing miniature Sabre.

Not a delta.

Not VTOL.

Not an attempt to make a Mach 2 aircraft in 1948.

Something more like:

> **Take everything Mitsubishi has learned about making a good carrier fighter and redesign the aircraft around one turbine.**

So I would provisionally picture **A8M1** with:

- one engine;
- one pilot;
- straight or very mildly swept broad wings;
- folding outer wing panels;
- conventional tail;
- tricycle landing gear;
- reinforced arrestor structure;
- side or wing-root intakes;
- an engine mounted aft of the cockpit;
- guns concentrated in the nose;
- comparatively generous internal fuel;
- and an unusually low approach speed *for an early jet*.

Visually, there will inevitably be echoes of the **F9F Panther, Sea Hawk, Ouragan and similar early single-engine jets**, because there are only so many sensible ways to put a centrifugal-flow or early axial turbine into a compact aircraft.

But the **wing** is where I would make Mitsubishi's ancestry obvious.

Don't give it the smallest possible wing in pursuit of speed.

Give it a relatively broad, beautifully tapered carrier wing.

The Navy accepts several dozen kilometers per hour less top speed because the airplane:

- comes aboard more comfortably;
- has better low-speed control;
- carries useful internal fuel;
- turns well;
- and can still get off the deck in unfavorable conditions.

In other words, Japanese pilots getting out of an A7M and into A8M should say:

> “It's strange because it's a jet.”

not:

> “The Navy has forgotten how to build a fighter.”

That's the continuity we're after.

## And this isn't really the F2H/F9F “family”

There's a small historical correction worth making because it helps us.

The **F2H Banshee and F9F Panther were separate competing/parallel American designs**, McDonnell and Grumman respectively. The Banshee was twin-engined; Panther was single-engined. The U.S. Navy deliberately pursued several early carrier-jet solutions at once—Smithsonian notes four carrier-jet fighters were ordered in the 1944–45 period, while the FH-1 became the first U.S. jet to operate from a carrier. citeturn284851search18turn284851search7

That's actually the lesson to steal, rather than either airplane.

The IJN likewise shouldn't know in 1946 which arrangement wins.

It has:

**Kikka** — first jet and transitional technology demonstrator.

**R2Y2** — big twin-engine Navy machine.

**A8M** — compact Mitsubishi carrier fighter.

That's a perfectly healthy first-generation competition.

---

# I think the engine question gives A8M its character

A single early turbine sounds risky until you compare what the airplane is supposed to do.

Keiun takes **two Ne-330-class engines** because it is large and performance-hungry.

A8M doesn't need to carry the same fuel, cameras, strike load or future radar installation.

So Mitsubishi can effectively say:

> “Give us one good turbine and we'll build the lightest useful fighter around it.”

The first A8M may actually be somewhat underpowered.

That's fine.

Early American carrier jets weren't rocket ships either. The Navy itself described slow jet acceleration and short flight decks as the reason catapult assistance became necessary. citeturn321680search6

That gives A8M's pilots a very Japanese complaint:

> wonderful once it has energy, but don't throw that energy away casually.

And it creates a direct evolutionary path toward A9M.

The first large improvement in turbine thrust doesn't make Mitsubishi say:

> “Excellent, let's make A8M ten tonnes heavier.”

It says:

> “Excellent. Now we can sweep the wing.”

That gets us into the second generation.

---

# So I would preserve A9M1 Shippū

This is the nice part.

We don't need to throw away everything from the old Aerospace Reference.

It already gives us:

> **Type 16 A9M1 Shippū — 1956 — carrier air superiority — 1,180 km/h — 850 km radius.** fileciteturn5file5

The exact performance can be revisited later, but the **identity is excellent**.

Now it has an ancestry.

Something like:

**A7M Reppū**  
Last great piston Mitsubishi fleet fighter.

↓  

**A8M1 [name open]**  
First-generation straight-wing jet carrier fighter, perhaps entering service around 1949–50.

↓  

**A8M2 / Kai**  
Better engine, improved deck handling and armament, early 1950s.

↓  

**A9M1 Shippū**  
Clean-sheet or very heavily redesigned swept-wing second-generation carrier fighter, c. 1956.

↓  

**A10M**  
1960s supersonic successor.

↓  

**A11M / A12M**  
Third/fourth-generation fighter evolution.

And this means the old reference's later **A9M → A10M → A11M → A12M** sequence may actually be salvageable in broad form. fileciteturn5file9

What probably dies is the old **J14 Kairyū “heavy fleet-defense fighter”**, because we've just invented a much stronger historical reason for that role to belong to the maturing Keiun family.

That's good consolidation rather than loss.

---

# The resulting IJN air wing becomes much more comprehensible

By the mid-1950s, picture a Japanese fleet carrier.

Its fighter squadrons have **A9M Shippū**.

Their purpose is straightforward:

> get airborne quickly, intercept, escort, maneuver, win air superiority, come home.

Then the carrier has **R2Y3 Keiun Kai Ni**.

That aircraft is bigger.

It may increasingly be two-seat.

It carries more radar.

It goes farther.

It attacks ships.

It flies night interception.

It carries reconnaissance equipment.

It can haul a meaningful bomb load.

It can escort at long range.

It is still quite capable of killing another fighter, but that isn't the only thing its design has sacrificed everything else to do.

The difference becomes something like:

> **Shippū is what you send to kill the airplane. Keiun is what you send when you're not entirely sure what you'll need to kill when you arrive.**

That distinction can survive for decades.

Eventually technology makes both highly multirole, but their centers of gravity remain different.

---

# The French are actually useful here

Not as a first-generation model.

As a **philosophical confirmation** of the lightweight Mitsubishi route.

France's Étendard IV M was a compact, single-engine carrier fighter/attack aircraft. Dassault's own history explicitly describes navalization as requiring folding wings, a landing hook, reinforced fuselage and landing structure, and naval navigation/radar equipment. citeturn673354search2turn673354search9

And the French did that from comparatively modest carriers.

That's important.

It demonstrates that there is no universal law saying:

> jet carrier fighter → twin engines → enormous carrier → American aircraft.

A naval air arm can decide:

> **Our decks are expensive. Our airplanes should remain relatively compact.**

That is a very plausible Japanese instinct.

Indeed, with Japan operating **many carriers of different ages and sizes**, it has an even stronger reason than America to preserve a compact fighter.

Keiun may only operate comfortably from the large fleet carriers.

A8M should operate from **almost everything the Navy still considers a frontline carrier**.

That is an enormous procurement advantage.

---

# Your catapult intuition is also basically correct

Wartime Japanese carrier practice had been built around aircraft making rolling takeoffs using the deck run and wind over the deck; Japan did not structure ordinary fleet-carrier fighter operations around the sort of catapult-assisted launch cycle that later became standard for heavy jets. Its wartime carrier forces could put very large strikes into the air extremely rapidly under that system. citeturn759442search0

Jets break that model.

Not immediately, but progressively.

And we already have the same problem recognized in the German branch. *Peter Strasser* is now established as a **new post-divergence carrier conceived around future turbine aircraft**, with stronger catapults, arresting gear, deck structure, elevators, fuel and maintenance arrangements than *Graf Zeppelin*. fileciteturn5file3

Japan doesn't need to copy Germany.

In fact, I think there should be **two-way wartime technical exchange**.

Japan tells Germany:

> This is how you organize an actual carrier air group and deck cycle.

Germany tells Japan:

> This is what we've learned about catapult machinery and launching aircraft whose engines don't generate useful acceleration at walking speed.

Then both discover the jet problem themselves.

## I would give Japan a transitional carrier modernization

Something like:

### 1946–50: first jet adaptation

The largest Japanese carriers receive:

- stronger arresting gear;
- reinforced landing areas;
- jet blast protection;
- revised aviation-fuel systems;
- improved elevators;
- and powerful hydraulic/pneumatic catapults.

A8M can still make an unassisted rolling takeoff when lightly loaded with enough wind over deck.

But normal combat operations increasingly use the catapult.

R2Y2 at useful strike weight effectively **requires it**.

This creates a very useful fleet distinction.

Older/light carriers can operate:

- A7M;
- A8M;
- helicopters later;
- perhaps light attack aircraft.

Only the fleet carriers can efficiently operate **Keiun**.

That's another reason Mitsubishi's little fighter doesn't disappear.

### Early–mid 1950s: the real jet carrier

Then Japan hits the same technological wall everyone else does.

Historically, the steam catapult and angled flight deck were the great early-1950s answers to heavier, faster jets; the U.S. Navy's contemporary history describes the combination as the most important leap in carrier operating capability since the war. citeturn321680search2turn321680search4

Japan has more reason than almost anyone to pursue equivalent solutions.

So I'd expect its first major postwar carrier reconstruction to bring:

> **angled deck + steam catapults + optical/mirror landing aid + heavier arresting gear.**

Not in 1947.

But by the middle 1950s, absolutely.

And this couples nicely to the aircraft generations:

**A8M** is designed to survive on modified wartime carriers.

**A9M** is designed for the **modernized jet carrier**.

**A10M onward** assumes catapult operation as ordinary.

Keiun progressively assumes the biggest decks.

---

# This is where the Japanese supercarrier eventually comes from

And your current correction to the old naval ledger matters here.

The old Naval Reference should no longer control the late carrier-development story where it conflicts with what you've just established. It has a 76,000-ton Japanese *Hakuryū* but also assumes a more conventional American fleet-carrier buildup and needs a larger carrier rewrite anyway. fileciteturn5file10

The new broad outcome is:

- **Japan eventually builds true supercarriers.**
- **Britain eventually builds a true supercarrier.**
- **Germany eventually possesses a carrier of supercarrier scale**, though its fleet doctrine remains much less carrier-centric.
- **America does not make the supercarrier the center of its naval system**, because its naval doctrine remains institutionally divided much longer.

That makes Japan's path particularly coherent.

The supercarrier is not prestige appearing from nowhere.

It's the result of thirty years of the Navy repeatedly saying:

> Keiun is getting heavier.

Then:

> the next Keiun is getting heavier.

And:

> the new radar aircraft is enormous.

And:

> we need more fuel.

And:

> we need to launch all of these with useful weapons aboard.

Eventually someone realizes that continuously adapting 30,000–50,000-ton ships to increasingly large aircraft is more expensive than designing a flight deck around what naval aviation has become.

So the Japanese supercarrier is **an aviation requirement expressed in steel**, not a Yamato-style prestige project.

That's much stronger.

---

# VTOL should remain a side branch

I wouldn't make the Harrier idea central to Japanese carrier aviation.

Japan doesn't have Britain's strongest reason to love VTOL.

It has:

- many proper carriers;
- enormous numbers of island airfields;
- lots of coastline;
- a mature naval aviation establishment;
- and no recent war demonstrating that its runways are constantly being cratered.

So why accept the penalties in:

- range;
- payload;
- engine complexity;
- fuel consumption;
- and aerodynamic compromise?

But **experimental Japanese VTOL is extremely plausible**.

Maybe even more plausible than operational adoption.

The Navy would see obvious applications for:

- small escort carriers;
- helicopter carriers;
- isolated islands;
- emergency dispersion;
- reconnaissance;
- Marine landing support;
- and operating from damaged strips.

The historical Soviet path is actually instructive as a warning here: their first operational carrier jet solution was the **Yak-38 VTOL aircraft aboard Kiev-class ships**, rather than an early conventional fixed-wing carrier line. citeturn457715search0 Japan doesn't need to follow that route because it already possesses the thing the Soviets lacked: a large, experienced conventional carrier institution.

So the Soviets aren't a missing reference corpus. **There really isn't a Soviet equivalent to the 1950s American/British carrier-fighter story.** Their useful comparison begins much later.

---

# So I think we have the missing Japanese airplane

My preferred working reconstruction now is:

| Period | Mitsubishi fighter | Keiun | Carrier consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1945–47** | A7M Reppū | R2Y1/R2Y2 development | Piston carrier doctrine; jet trials begin |
| **c. 1949** | **A8M1 — first Mitsubishi carrier jet** | R2Y2 Keiun Kai | Largest wartime carriers receive jet modifications and catapults |
| **early 1950s** | A8M improved marks | R2Y2 mature | A8M broadly carrier-compatible; Keiun concentrated on fleet carriers |
| **c. 1955–56** | **A9M1 Shippū** | R2Y3 Keiun Kai Ni | Angled-deck/steam-catapult carrier generation |
| **1960s** | A10M supersonic fighter | next Keiun heavy multirole | Fighter/strike distinction begins blurring |
| **1970s** | A11M lightweight air-superiority family | Keiun becomes Phantom-like heavy multirole | Large fleet carriers increasingly optimized around mixed light/heavy air groups |
| **1980s** | A12M fourth-generation carrier fighter | fourth-generation Keiun descendant | Japanese proper supercarrier fully exploits the heavy-light pairing |

The important thing is that **the two lineages never really merge**.

Keiun keeps threatening to make the Mitsubishi fighter redundant.

Mitsubishi keeps proving that if all you need is a pilot, radar, missiles, fuel and an airplane capable of winning the air battle, carrying around the structural and systems burden of Keiun is unnecessary.

Then the Keiun bureau points out that the fleet never seems to need *only* that.

That procurement argument can continue for forty years precisely because **Japan never gets the catastrophic combat experience that would conclusively settle it**.

And I think **A8M is the piece that makes the entire lineage finally hang together**: not a Japanese Panther or Banshee, but the aircraft Mitsubishi would plausibly build when the company that produced Zero and Reppū is told, “All right. Now do it again without a propeller.”
