Yes. I think this gives the A8M a **very strong identity**, and most of what you're proposing can be made to work. The key is that its lightness should come from a genuine engineering crisis rather than the Navy formally demanding “build another Zero.” That lets Horikoshi repeat one of the A6M's virtues—ruthless mass discipline—without simply repeating all of its protection compromises.

The existing reference already leaves us exactly the right slot: the A7M remains the last major piston carrier fighter, while the later A9M1 is already provisionally established as Mitsubishi's 1956 carrier air-superiority fighter. fileciteturn7file0 So the A8M can be the missing first-generation bridge without disturbing the broader lineage.

And for the name, my preference is:

> **Mitsubishi A8M Senpū — 旋風, “Whirlwind.”**

It fits the IJN's established wind naming family for fighters, sounds sufficiently martial without being grandiose, and suits an aircraft whose defining reputation becomes exceptional lightness and agility. The existing Japanese naming framework already reserves wind and sea-weather names for carrier fighters. fileciteturn7file0

## Horikoshi's design logic works, with one correction about Raiden

I'd root the design philosophy somewhat more strongly in **Horikoshi's A6M experience** than in saying the J2M itself was exceptionally light.

The Smithsonian's account of the Zero is very explicit: Horikoshi's team deliberately attacked airframe weight because the Navy simultaneously demanded exceptional maneuverability and long range. The result was a remarkably light aircraft for its capability. citeturn348849search13turn348849search15

The J2M experience is still useful, but differently. It teaches Mitsubishi how tightly it can **package a powerful propulsion system into a compact fighter**, and how much fighter performance can come from making the aircraft relatively short, clean, and purpose-driven. So A8M becomes something like:

> **Zero weight discipline + Raiden packaging discipline + Reppū carrier-fighter experience + a turbine nobody initially believes is powerful enough.**

That's a very good Horikoshi culmination.

And because your post-1941 Japanese development methodology explicitly allows alternate programs to emerge from altered requirements rather than mechanically inheriting OTL equipment, we don't have to justify every detail by pointing to a historical A8M drawing. fileciteturn7file1

---

# I would slightly change the “wrong engine” story

The result is excellent. I'd just make the institutional mechanism less comical than somebody accidentally mailing Mitsubishi the wrong specification sheet.

The Navy begins the A8M program assuming that **Ne-330 is not available to Mitsubishi**.

The important context is that the Ne-20 is a genuinely small early engine producing only about **1,047 lbf / 475 kgf of thrust**, and the historical Kikka required *two* of them. Smithsonian gives the Kikka a planned 350-meter takeoff run even with rocket assistance. citeturn129747search8turn129747search12

So imagine the procurement argument around 1945–46.

Kūgishō says:

> Ne-330 belongs to Keiun. It is immature, scarce, and required in pairs for the Navy's priority heavy aircraft.

Mitsubishi asks what powerplant it should assume.

The answer is:

> **One Ne-20. If you want a carrier fighter, make one Ne-20 work.**

Perhaps the engine bureau expects a more powerful derivative eventually, but Mitsubishi is forbidden to design an aircraft whose minimum acceptable performance depends upon an engine that may never arrive.

That's the mistake.

Not an erroneous document.

An excessively conservative **engine-allocation assumption**.

So Horikoshi's group starts shaving kilograms because there is no other solution.

Then, late in development, Ne-330 matures much better than the Navy expected and the engine-allocation board decides that a single Ne-330 for each fighter is economically tolerable compared with **two per Keiun**.

Mitsubishi effectively receives almost three times the thrust it thought it was designing around.

And suddenly everybody looks very clever.

---

# But one Ne-20 should *not* give A8M a normal combat carrier takeoff

I'd resist that one.

Not because the aircraft cannot fly. It absolutely can.

But because the comparison with Kikka is brutal. Kikka had **two** Ne-20s and still had modest acceleration; its planned takeoff run was about 350 meters with rocket assist. citeturn129747search8 A single-engine naval fighter would have to weigh dramatically less than Kikka merely to reach a similar thrust-to-weight ratio, and carrier landing gear, folding wings, arrestor structure and fuel prevent Mitsubishi from reducing weight indefinitely.

So I would give Horikoshi a wonderful half-success.

### A8M1 with Ne-20

It **flies**.

It flies surprisingly well once airborne.

It can take off from a normal land runway.

It can even perform a carefully staged **carrier-equivalent launch** using:

- minimum fuel;
- no external stores;
- strong wind over the simulated deck;
- and small rocket-assist units.

Perhaps it later conducts one actual carrier launch under those conditions.

And the Navy records the wonderful bureaucratic phrase:

> **“Carrier operation technically demonstrated; tactical employment not recommended.”**

In other words, Mitsubishi wins the argument on a technicality.

Yes, the single-Ne-20 Senpū *can* get off a carrier.

No sane squadron commander wants to launch a combat formation that way.

Then the Ne-330 arrives.

And everything changes.

That is much more satisfying than making 475 kgf behave like 1,300 kgf.

---

# The Ne-330 version becomes absurdly lively

This is where your “jet engine with an aircraft attached” reputation becomes completely believable.

The engine is going to require some enlargement of the rear fuselage. We shouldn't pretend an engine producing roughly 1,300 kgf simply drops into exactly the same mounts as the Ne-20.

But Mitsubishi has already done the important work.

The airplane itself is:

- very small;
- single-seat;
- single-engine;
- simple;
- straight-winged;
- lightly armed;
- devoid of radar;
- devoid of a second crewman;
- designed around carrier folding;
- and ruthlessly weight-controlled.

So even after enlarging the ducting, tail structure, mounts and fuel system for Ne-330, it remains extremely light.

I'd expect the production aircraft to have a thrust-to-weight ratio startlingly good for its generation—good enough that the limitation stops being **“the engine can't accelerate the aircraft”** and increasingly becomes **“the straight wing won't let us use all this power as speed.”**

That leads beautifully toward A9M.

And this is where I'd qualify the pilot language.

It shouldn't have propeller-like **throttle response**. Early turbojets still take time to spool.

What pilots praise is propeller-fighter-like **airframe response**.

Roll it.

Pull.

Unload.

Accelerate.

Climb.

Change direction.

Once the turbine is already producing power, there isn't much airplane for it to push.

So Navy pilots say things like:

> “Kikka flies like a jet. Senpū flies like a fighter that happens to have a jet engine.”

That is exactly the reputation you're after without cheating turbine physics.

---

# And yes: make the armament embarrassingly light at first

I like this a lot.

The prototype's armament can absolutely be:

> **2 × 13.2 mm Type 3 machine guns.**

But I'd put them in the **nose**, not the wings.

That produces three advantages at once.

First, no convergence problem.

Second, removing guns and ammunition from the folding wing lets Mitsubishi make the wing structurally lighter.

Third, the entire nose has become available because there's no piston engine there.

So Horikoshi looks at all that empty nose volume and does the obvious thing.

Two guns, very close to the centerline.

Ammunition immediately behind them.

Simple access panels.

Very little structural penalty.

The problem is that two 13.2 mm guns are already **obsolescent fighter armament** by the late 1940s.

So Senpū immediately generates an ordnance requirement:

> **We require a 20 mm cannon light enough that two of them do not ruin the airplane.**

And there's an important point here: Japanese engineers do not need to invent the very idea of a light 20 mm. Existing Japanese 20 mm weapons are already relatively compact compared with some heavy cannon systems. The new requirement is more specifically for a **high-velocity, reliable, compact naval fighter cannon and feed system optimized for nose mounting**.

I like your proposed date-based designation.

Something like:

> **20 mm Type 7 aircraft cannon** — accepted 1947.

It could retain ammunition compatibility with the existing Navy 20×101RB family initially, while substantially improving:

- feed reliability;
- receiver mass;
- charging;
- cyclic rate;
- mounting;
- and nose installation.

The early production A8M then becomes:

> **2 × Type 7 20 mm cannon**, concentrated immediately beside the centerline.

That is enough gun.

Not Me 262 four-30-mm excess.

Not even four 20s.

The Japanese argument is:

> Two hits where you're aiming are preferable to four guns whose mass costs us climb, fuel and deck performance.

And *that* feels like an aircraft whose design bureau is obsessed with grams.

---

# But I would not let Horikoshi recreate the Zero's protection problem

This is an important brake.

By this point Japan has actually fought the southern war. The earlier equipment work already establishes that Malaya and the Indies expose the cost of inadequate protection, damage tolerance, rough-field durability and corrosion resistance. fileciteturn6file3

So when Mitsubishi says **light**, the Navy can answer:

> Not *that* light.

Pilot armor stays.

A protected windscreen stays.

Some degree of self-sealing or protected fuel tank construction stays.

The arrestor structure stays.

The wing-fold locking mechanism cannot be delicate.

The landing gear cannot be a racing-aircraft afterthought.

The weight has to come out of:

- aircraft size;
- excessive systems;
- armament;
- plumbing;
- unnecessary redundancy;
- wing-mounted equipment;
- cockpit luxuries;
- radar;
- bomb-carrying structure;
- and mission creep.

This is what distinguishes Senpū from “Jet Zero.”

The Zero was a lightweight airplane partly because Japan accepted protection compromises.

**Senpū is a lightweight airplane because Mitsubishi refuses to make it do anything except be a fighter.**

That's a much more mature doctrine.

And it sets up the comparison against Keiun beautifully.

---

# The rounded wing tips should stay

Absolutely.

Not because round tips possess some mystical Mitsubishi aerodynamic virtue, but because **visual lineage matters where it doesn't contradict engineering**.

A8M's main wing can remain:

- broad;
- moderately tapered;
- straight;
- low-to-moderate aspect ratio;
- with distinctly rounded tips;
- and folding outboard panels.

It therefore looks recognizably descended from A7M rather than from an American Panther.

And because the wing is deliberately generous for such a light aircraft, it gives Senpū the important carrier characteristics:

- relatively low approach speed;
- benign stall;
- strong turning capability;
- and enough wing area that early turbine thrust isn't fighting a tiny high-loading wing.

The price is compressibility.

By the time Ne-330 and later derivatives are installed, pilots are discovering that the engine wants to make the aircraft go considerably faster than the wing wants to go.

That is the correct technical reason for A9M.

Not:

> Senpū was bad.

Rather:

> **Senpū became so overpowered that its own successful design philosophy reached the transonic wall.**

---

# The nose should indeed remain bulbous—at first

This is another area where I think your visual instinct works.

Horikoshi has spent his career putting piston engines in noses. Suddenly there is nothing there.

I don't think the first instinct is necessarily to produce a long, Sabre-like pointed nose. There is no large radar.

So the A8M1 nose can retain something of the **rounded Mitsubishi fighter family face**, except now it becomes almost comically short and clean.

Looking head-on:

- rounded nose;
- two cannon or gun ports very close together;
- bubble/raised cockpit behind it;
- broad wing;
- and then this strange intake structure behind the cockpit.

It would look recognizably Japanese and also immediately strange.

Later A8Ms can gradually stretch the nose as gunsights, radio equipment, navigation equipment and eventually ranging radar demand volume.

Then A9M gets the proper longer jet-fighter nose.

Again, you can see the technological transition in photographs.

---

# And your ring intake can work—but don't make it flush

This is probably the most interesting visual idea in the whole proposal.

A literal **flush 360-degree slot around the fuselage** behind the cockpit would be troublesome.

The reason is boundary-layer ingestion.

Air moving immediately along the fuselage surface has already lost energy through skin friction. If the engine inlet simply sucks that slow, turbulent boundary layer directly into the compressor, pressure recovery and flow uniformity deteriorate. NACA experiments on fuselage-side inlets found exactly this problem; separating or removing the fuselage boundary layer substantially improved inlet behavior. citeturn129747search1turn129747search14turn129747search16

But that doesn't kill the visual.

It tells us how Mitsubishi makes it work.

## Give Senpū a raised **annular intake collar**

Immediately behind the cockpit, the fuselage narrows slightly.

Then there is a raised intake lip standing perhaps several centimeters away from the fuselage skin.

From the front, you see:

> fuselage → dark circular slot → outer intake collar

almost all the way around.

The small gap between the fuselage and intake lip acts as a **boundary-layer splitter/bypass** rather than allowing the slow fuselage air directly into the engine.

Inside, the intake feeds an annular plenum around the center structure and then gradually merges into the circular compressor face of the aft engine.

I might actually make it a **three-quarter annulus** rather than a perfect circle.

The intake runs:

> side → top → side

while the lower fuselage is interrupted by structural keel, fuel lines and landing-gear structure.

From most front-quarter views it still appears as the “ring intake.”

That is enough to make Senpū instantly recognizable.

And it gives Mitsubishi another development headache: uneven pressure around the annulus during high-angle maneuver.

Which is good.

An aircraft becomes memorable because its clever feature creates problems that engineers spend fifteen years fixing.

---

# Surprisingly, I think the taildragger can stay

I initially thought this was where I'd tell you no.

Then I checked the obvious British comparison.

**The Royal Navy actually operated a tailwheel jet fighter: the Supermarine Attacker.** The Fleet Air Arm Museum identifies the Attacker as the aircraft used to form the Royal Navy's first jet squadron in 1951, and Imperial War Museums preserves film of Attacker carrier trials aboard *Illustrious*. citeturn634618search8turn634618search17turn634618search24

So:

> **physically possible? Absolutely.**

And for A8M it has a stronger rationale than it did for Britain.

The IJN is transitioning pilots from A6M and A7M.

Its carriers are still straight-deck ships developed around piston aircraft.

Its deck crews understand tailwheel aircraft.

Its landing signals and handling practices assume that geometry.

And the aircraft's generous straight wing benefits from already sitting at a positive angle of attack during the takeoff run.

So Horikoshi can make the conservative argument:

> “The propulsion system is new enough. There is no reason to make the undercarriage new as well.”

I buy that completely for **A8M1/A8M2**.

But the Attacker also gives us the warning. The tailwheel configuration proved awkward enough in carrier use that it did not become the normal jet-carrier solution. citeturn634618search3

So I would make this another wonderfully temporary Japanese success.

### A8M1/A8M2 Senpū

Tailwheel.

Japanese carrier pilots love how familiar it feels.

### Late A8M development

Deck crews increasingly dislike it.

Forward visibility while taxiing is poor.

The tailwheel has annoying relationships with arrestor wires and deck obstructions.

Jet exhaust management is awkward in the nose-high ground attitude.

The stronger Ne-330 also means Senpū no longer needs the tail-down takeoff attitude nearly as badly.

### A9M

Tricycle undercarriage becomes standard.

So Senpū ends up remembered as **Japan's last taildragger fighter and first jet carrier fighter simultaneously**.

That is a superb transitional identity.

---

## I would even make the tail arrangement visually distinctive

Because the jet pipe occupies the centerline, don't put one ordinary little tailwheel directly beneath it.

Give A8M **two small retractable tailwheels**, one on either side of the exhaust structure.

The Attacker itself used twin tailwheels, so there is precedent for solving a rear-fuselage packaging problem that way. citeturn634618search41

Then add a heat shield underneath the tailpipe.

This does several things:

- clears the exhaust;
- gives redundancy aboard ship;
- spreads deck loads;
- and gives the airplane another characteristic shape when sitting on the ground.

You could identify a Senpū silhouette merely from:

**rounded nose + broad rounded folding wings + intake collar + twin little tailwheels + single central exhaust.**

That's an aircraft, not just a specification sheet.

---

# So I think the development story becomes something like this

### **Late 1945 — Mitsubishi receives A8M requirement**

Horikoshi's team finishes the major A7M work and receives the Navy's first clean-sheet carrier-jet fighter requirement.

The bureau is told to assume **one Ne-20**.

Nobody explicitly orders extreme lightness.

The performance requirement makes extreme lightness mathematically unavoidable.

### **1946–47 — A8M1 Senpū development**

Design characteristics:

- single Ne-20;
- broad straight folding wing;
- rounded tips;
- tailwheel undercarriage;
- two 13.2 mm nose guns;
- raised three-quarter annular “collar” intake;
- one pilot;
- minimal secondary mission equipment;
- essential armor and protected fuel retained.

The aircraft becomes a standing joke at Mitsubishi because every design meeting eventually reduces to:

> “How much does that weigh?”

### **1947 — first flight**

It flies.

And pilots like it.

The problem is power.

Land performance is acceptable for an experimental jet.

Normal loaded carrier operations are not.

Rocket-assisted carrier trials prove that the concept is technically possible but operationally unsatisfactory.

### **1947–48 — Ne-330 decision**

The engine situation changes.

Mitsubishi is ordered to adapt Senpū for the much more powerful Ne-330 family.

Rear fuselage, intake flow, mounts and fuel system require significant redesign.

The airplane gains weight.

It still remains extraordinarily light for the thrust available.

### **c. 1948–49 — A8M2 Senpū enters service**

Now the aircraft's reputation is established.

Excellent climb.

Excellent acceleration once the engine is spooled.

Excellent deck behavior for a jet of the period.

Good maneuverability.

Very modest radar/electronic capability.

Limited strike capability.

Reasonable but not extraordinary jet range.

And two new lightweight Type 7 20 mm cannon in the nose.

This becomes the first Japanese jet that ordinary Navy fighter pilots regard as a **fighter first and technological experiment second**.

---

And there's a lovely institutional irony buried in the whole program:

> **The A8M is successful because the Navy initially gives Mitsubishi an engine too weak to build the airplane it wants.**

Horikoshi's team responds by designing almost everything unnecessary out of the aircraft.

Then the Navy gives them nearly three times as much thrust.

Kūgishō's R2Y engineers look at the resulting performance figures and probably become slightly irritated, because they have spent years designing elaborate twin-engine inlet systems and a complex high-capability airframe while Mitsubishi has produced what amounts to **a seat, two guns, two wings and an Ne-330**.

And that becomes the philosophical divide between Japanese naval fighters for decades:

**Keiun asks how much capability can be put into an aircraft.**

**Senpū asks how little aircraft is necessary to put a fighter pilot into the sky.**

That is exactly the kind of rivalry that can naturally produce the A9M Shippū later, rather than having A9M simply appear in 1956 because the old reference said Japan needed another fighter. fileciteturn7file0

iturn752931image1

I think your instinct to **slow the Mitsubishi A-series down is right**, but not because a supersonic carrier fighter in the 1960s is technologically premature. The real-world F-8 Crusader is the important corrective here: the U.S. Navy asked for a supersonic day fighter in 1953, the prototype flew in 1955, and it was a **single-engine carrier fighter**. Its variable-incidence wing gave it workable low-speed carrier behavior without resorting to variable sweep. citeturn752931search0turn752931search6

So the question isn't “can Japan build a supersonic carrier fighter by 1966?” It absolutely could.

The better question is:

> **Why would this Japanese Navy pay to replace a perfectly satisfactory A9M with one?**

And given the long peace you've established, I think the answer may indeed be: **it doesn't, for quite a while.**

That gives us a much better division between Mitsubishi and Yokosuka.

## First: yes, I think R2Y should become B8Y

The current Aerospace Reference itself defines the Navy letters as:

- `A` — carrier fighter
- `B` — carrier attack/torpedo aircraft
- `D` — carrier dive bomber
- `G` — land-based attack
- `R` — land-based reconnaissance

and `Y` as Yokosuka Naval Air Technical Arsenal. fileciteturn9file0

Under the aircraft we've now created, **R is simply wrong for the production Keiun**.

But I wouldn't retroactively rename **R2Y1**.

That's useful ancestry.

R2Y1 really does begin as the land-based reconnaissance/aerodynamic test aircraft. Then the turbine program and carrier requirement transform what the Navy wants from its descendant.

So I'd make the break explicit:

> **R2Y1 Keiun** — piston reconnaissance/aerodynamic development aircraft.

> **B8Y1 Keiun Kai** — selected twin-engine jet carrier-attack aircraft descended from the R2Y program.

And this gives the transition historical texture. Engineering papers can continue referring casually to “R2Y2” during the early jet studies because everyone knows what they're talking about. But when the Navy decides, *this thing is going aboard carriers and replacing the B7A operationally*, it receives a proper carrier-attack designation.

That also means your V1/V2/V3 competition fits beneath **B8Y development**. The selected wing-root-intake V2 becomes B8Y1.

Then I agree with your next number:

> **B9Y1 Keiun Kai Ni**, circa 1955.

That's the genuinely next-generation Keiun resurrecting the nose-intake concept with new engines and redesigned structure.

After that we can have B9Y2/B9Y3 improvements before a B10Y clean-sheet aircraft eventually appears.

And I much prefer **B** to `D`. The B7A itself already represents the Navy's attempt to combine torpedo and dive-bombing functions into one carrier attack aircraft. Our Keiun simply carries that convergence much farther into the jet age.

So the lineage is conceptually:

**B7A Ryūsei → R2Y1 experimental bridge → B8Y Keiun → B9Y Keiun → later Yokosuka heavy multirole aircraft.**

That feels right.

---

# The Mitsubishi line does not need a new airframe every “generation”

This, I think, is where the old Aerospace Reference led us astray.

It currently says:

- A9M1 in 1956;
- A10M1 in 1966;
- A11M1 in 1978;
- A12M1 in 1983.

That's a suspiciously tidy **new generation → new designation → new generation → new designation** ladder. fileciteturn9file0

But aircraft generations are retrospective categories. Procurement offices don't say:

> “Second generation is over. Please issue third-generation airplane.”

They say:

> “The radar doesn't fit.”

> “Our landing speed is too high.”

> “We need another 150 kilometers of radius.”

> “This wing hits compressibility before the engine reaches full power.”

> “Enemy bombers are faster than us.”

And if you can fix the problem without replacing the aircraft, you do.

That becomes especially important in **this Japan**, because the wiki still defines Japanese technical power by carrier aviation, electronics and automation, but also gives it a comparatively narrow privileged technical-industrial core. Long-lived, progressively improved aircraft are entirely consistent with that structure. citeturn594483view2

So I'd let **A9M live a long time**.

Possibly twenty years.

---

# I would actually revise the A9M1 performance downward slightly

If we're saying A9M1 Shippū is fundamentally the **transonic successor to A8M Senpū**, then the old `1,180 km/h` number is misleadingly high unless we specify altitude.

Mach number is what matters here, not one naked kilometers-per-hour number.

I'd make the design intention roughly:

> **A9M1 Shippū — maximum level Mach approximately 0.95–0.98.**

It can go supersonic in a dive.

Perhaps exceptionally favorable test conditions flirt with Mach 1.

But it is not intended as a sustained supersonic aircraft.

That fits the development problem beautifully.

A8M says:

> We have more engine than the straight wing can exploit.

A9M says:

> Fine. Sweep the wing enough that we can actually use the engine.

That's a real reason to issue a new `A9` number: the wing structure, fuel arrangement, folding mechanism, landing gear relationship and probably much of the fuselage have been redesigned.

But it's still recognizably Horikoshi's successor to Senpū.

---

# Then A9M2 gets the radar

I agree almost exactly with this.

And because the engine is aft and the intakes aren't occupying the nose, Mitsubishi gets this beautiful luxury:

> **an empty nose waiting for electronics.**

So around 1959–61:

### A9M2 Shippū

The rounded A9M1 nose becomes longer and more pointed.

Inside it goes a relatively compact intercept/search radar.

That does not suddenly make A9M2 an F-14.

It allows:

- range-assisted gunsight/weapons computation;
- limited bad-weather interception;
- night interception with ground/fleet direction;
- early radar-supported missile employment;
- and much better target acquisition against the ocean/sky background.

The airplane gains weight.

Its center of gravity changes.

The electrical system gets substantially larger.

It probably loses some of A9M1's delightful lightness.

But the wing and engine remain fundamentally adequate.

So why replace the aircraft?

You don't.

---

# Then A9M3 gets the better engine

Now we're probably into the early-to-mid 1960s.

A newer turbojet, perhaps eventually early turbofan technology, gives the aircraft more thrust.

And this is where I think **A9 can technically become mildly supersonic without becoming a new aircraft**.

Something like:

> **A9M3 — Mach 1.1–1.2 class under favorable conditions.**

Not Mach 2.

Not a dedicated supersonic interceptor.

It has an afterburner or equivalent thrust increase, revised inlet geometry, stronger controls, better high-lift devices and improved missiles.

This is a very believable modernization of a swept-wing fighter.

And now we get a fascinating doctrinal division.

The A9M3 can go supersonic if necessary.

But that's not what it is **for**.

Its job remains:

> air superiority around the fleet.

---

# Because Keiun has already inherited the high-speed interception problem

This is the really important part.

Japan doesn't need the Mitsubishi fighter to do everything because **B9Y exists**.

By the late 1950s and 1960s, the Yokosuka aircraft can absorb:

- larger engines;
- larger radar;
- more fuel;
- a second crewman if desired;
- long-range radar missiles;
- anti-ship weapons;
- reconnaissance equipment;
- bigger electrical generators;
- heavier navigation equipment.

That is the aircraft for:

> “Unknown contact at 300 kilometers; go identify it and destroy it if necessary.”

A9 is the aircraft for:

> “There are enemy fighters over the fleet.”

This means B9Y can become **supersonic before A-series does so comfortably**.

And that's one of the strongest reasons the Navy doesn't panic about replacing A9.

The IJN already owns a fast interceptor.

It's called Keiun.

---

# This makes 1960s Japan wonderfully asymmetrical

Imagine a Japanese carrier group around 1965.

Its **B9Y2 Keiun** is the technologically impressive aircraft.

Big.

Twin-engine.

Two-seat, probably.

Serious radar.

Long-range missiles.

Mach 1.5-ish or perhaps eventually higher.

Large radius.

Useful strike load.

It is the airplane foreign magazines put on the cover.

Meanwhile its **A9M3 Shippū** is smaller, cheaper and slower.

But fighter pilots adore it.

It turns better.

It lands more comfortably.

It's cheaper to operate.

You can put more of them aboard ship.

It requires one engine rather than two.

And when the Navy asks whether it should replace Shippū, the carrier commanders respond:

> With what? The airplane already does its job.

That's exactly what a long peacetime procurement environment should produce.

---

# Variable sweep isn't the next necessary step

This is the big technical correction.

You were treating the progression roughly as:

> straight wing → swept wing → radar → variable sweep

because variable sweep appears to solve:

> good slow aircraft + good supersonic aircraft.

It does solve that problem. NASA's variable-sweep research describes exactly that attraction: low sweep provides good low-speed characteristics, while greater sweep supports high-speed flight. citeturn116763search1turn116763search10

But it isn't the **only** solution.

And for Mitsubishi's lightweight-fighter philosophy, it may be the wrong one.

The F-8 Crusader is almost uncannily useful here. It was:

- single-engine;
- carrier-based;
- supersonic;
- highly swept;
- and equipped with a **variable-incidence wing**, not a swing wing.

The entire wing could rotate upward for takeoff and landing, giving it better low-speed behavior and forward visibility while preserving a fixed highly swept planform for high-speed flight. citeturn752931search5turn752931search27

So Horikoshi's successors have a much simpler path available.

They don't need:

> wing sweep changes in flight.

They need:

> **a high-speed fixed wing whose low-speed carrier behavior has been deliberately engineered.**

That can be accomplished through some combination of:

- leading-edge slats;
- large flaps;
- boundary-layer control;
- variable incidence;
- good thrust-to-weight;
- and eventually increasingly sophisticated flight controls.

And that's much more consistent with the philosophical ancestry of Senpū:

> **Don't add machinery when clever aerodynamics can solve the same problem.**

---

# If Japan experiments with swing wings, I'd give them to Keiun

That's where I think the technology belongs institutionally.

Keiun is already:

- heavy;
- complex;
- expensive;
- twin-engined;
- radar-heavy;
- long-range;
- multirole.

Adding a variable-geometry wing to **that** aircraft is at least philosophically coherent.

You accept additional structural machinery because you're trying to make one large aircraft do:

- fleet interception;
- low-level maritime strike;
- high-speed dash;
- long-range cruise;
- carrier approach;
- heavy weapons carriage.

That's the F-14/F-111 end of the design problem.

NASA's own research history treats variable sweep as an attempt to combine otherwise conflicting low- and high-speed aerodynamic requirements. citeturn116763search1

But I wouldn't necessarily make Japan adopt it.

A mildly austere peacetime Navy can test a B9Y variable-sweep prototype, conclude:

> impressive, but the mechanism isn't buying enough capability for its cost and maintenance burden,

and keep fixed wings.

That would actually be quite believable.

---

# So when should A10 finally happen?

My answer would be **much later than 1966**.

Not because the old 1966 date was technologically impossible. It wasn't. A single-engine supersonic carrier fighter was flying in the real world in 1955. citeturn752931search6

It's because our Japan lacks the procurement shock that makes replacement urgent.

I would let A9 run approximately:

| Model | Working period | Main reason it exists |
|---|---:|---|
| **A9M1 Shippū** | c. 1955–56 | Swept-wing transonic successor to Senpū |
| **A9M2** | c. 1959–61 | Radar nose, improved electrical system, early missile integration |
| **A9M3** | c. 1963–65 | Better engine/afterburner, mildly supersonic performance, improved high-lift system |
| **A9M4** | c. 1968–70 | Mature missiles, naval data link, improved radar and carrier handling |

And now you've got a **1956 aircraft still entirely credible in 1970**.

That's not weird.

It's what successful fighter families do.

At that point the Navy asks what the next fighter should actually solve.

And *now* we get A10.

---

# A10 should be the first real break with Horikoshi's immediate architecture

I would put development beginning around **1968–72**, prototype sometime around **1973–75**, and initial operational service perhaps **1977–80**.

That puts it right around the technological neighborhood you were intuitively reaching for with F-16/F-18 comparisons.

And its requirement is no longer merely:

> go faster.

Keiun already does that.

Instead:

> **Can we produce a fighter with Shippū's carrier manners and low operating burden, but with genuinely supersonic maneuver performance and a modern radar/missile system?**

That's a much more interesting requirement.

The design probably remains:

- single engine;
- one pilot;
- fixed wing;
- carrier optimized;
- nose radar;
- lightweight relative to Keiun;
- very good instantaneous maneuverability;
- high thrust-to-weight;
- and increasingly dependent upon electronic flight control.

Now we are genuinely approaching the **F-16/F/A-18 generation of design thinking**—not because we're copying either airplane, but because the underlying technologies have finally changed enough that Japan can achieve both low-speed controllability and high-speed performance without mechanically changing the wing sweep.

That also fits the wiki's broader Japanese trajectory: by 1985 Japan's defining strengths include electronics, automation and carriers, while the postwar technical transition is described as being driven heavily by reliability engineering and control systems rather than spectacular novelty alone. citeturn594483view2

---

# And this fixes the generation problem

I would stop thinking:

> A8 = first generation  
> A9 = second generation  
> A10 = third generation  
> A11 = fourth generation

That's too neat.

Instead:

**A8M Senpū** is unmistakably a first-generation jet.

**A9M1 Shippū** is a classic second-generation swept/transonic fighter.

But then **A9M2/M3/M4 gradually accumulates some things people later associate with third-generation fighters**:

- radar;
- missiles;
- afterburner;
- limited supersonic performance;
- data links.

It does not magically become a new aircraft because a historian changes its generation label.

Then **A10M** is the genuine architectural break into the late-1970s/early-1980s high-energy, electronically controlled fighter.

That is much more believable.

---

## So I think the Japanese naval tree now wants to look roughly like this

| Date | Mitsubishi A-series | Yokosuka Keiun family |
|---|---|---|
| **1946–49** | A8M Senpū — ultralight first-generation fighter | R2Y1 development → **B8Y1 Keiun Kai** |
| **early 1950s** | Mature A8M marks | B8Y development and carrier integration |
| **1955–56** | **A9M1 Shippū** — swept/transonic fighter | **B9Y1 Keiun Kai Ni** — new high-speed twin-engine multirole |
| **1960** | A9M2 radar fighter | B9Y2 all-weather strike/interception |
| **mid-1960s** | A9M3 mildly supersonic lightweight fighter | B9Y/B10Y high-speed fleet-defense/multirole aircraft |
| **c. 1970** | A9M4 mature final Shippū | Keiun increasingly missile-, radar-, and strike-dominated |
| **mid/late 1970s** | **A10M prototype generation** | New Keiun generation, possibly including variable-geometry experiments |
| **c. 1978–80** | **A10M service** — true modern single-engine carrier air-superiority fighter | Heavy multirole counterpart |
| **1980s** | Progressive A10 upgrades rather than immediate A11 replacement | Progressive Keiun upgrades |

And I think that last row is important.

**We probably don't need A11M by 1978 and A12M by 1983 anymore.** Those came from the old reference's tendency to keep inventing a new airplane every few years. fileciteturn9file0

A successful A10 entering around 1978–80 could very plausibly remain Japan's principal lightweight carrier fighter through the entire 1980s with successive marks.

The same thing happens to Keiun.

That gives Japanese naval aviation a distinctive postwar character: **very long-lived families, conservative designation changes, aggressive subsystem modernization, and two procurement schools that spend decades trying to prove the other one unnecessary without ever quite succeeding.**

The A-series says: *the best fighter is the smallest airplane that can win the air battle.*

Keiun says: *the fleet never knows in advance which air battle it is going to need to win.*

That is a much stronger 1985 force than the old neat A9 → A10 → A11 → A12 ladder.

## Turn 1085 — Assistant

- Timestamp: 2026-08-14T04:38:11.510Z

iturn158396image2

Yes. I think **the F-2 is a very good visual reference for the A10M**, provided we are strict about what “reference” means.

The real Mitsubishi F-2 is not merely something that happens to resemble an F-16. Mitsubishi explicitly describes it as having been **designed on the basis of the F-16 through a US–Japanese joint program**; the November 1988 agreement begins that development chain, and the prototype first flew in 1995. citeturn257882view0 Lockheed likewise describes the F-2 as having roughly **25% more wing area than the F-16**, additional internal fuel and weapon stations, and a slightly longer fuselage. citeturn461570search3

So we can't literally say:

> “Mitsubishi independently invents the F-2 in 1977.”

That would be backwards.

But we absolutely can say:

> **Mitsubishi independently arrives at an aircraft occupying much of the same aerodynamic design space, for reasons internal to the A-series.**

And I think the really interesting thing is that **our A10M should probably look more like an F-2 than the historical F-2 looks inevitable**, because several of the changes that distinguish F-2 from F-16 are exactly what a carrier fighter descended from A8M/A9M would want.

## The trick is to derive the silhouette from the requirement

By the early 1970s, Mitsubishi has spent roughly a quarter-century learning one particular lesson:

> Don't make the fighter carry capabilities that another aircraft can carry better.

Keiun has become the big twin-engine systems aircraft.

So A10M does **not** need to become Japan's answer to every possible tactical-aircraft mission. Its requirement can be much narrower:

> **Build the smallest practical carrier fighter capable of genuine supersonic maneuver combat, modern radar/missile employment, and operation from the fleet's current carriers without sacrificing the excellent low-speed characteristics for which the Mitsubishi line is valued.**

That requirement immediately pushes several things in an F-2/F-16-ish direction.

One big engine rather than two.

One pilot.

A pointed radar nose.

A bubble canopy with excellent visibility.

A blended wing/fuselage rather than the old cylindrical fuselage with wings attached to it.

A relatively high thrust-to-weight ratio.

Electronic flight controls allowing the aircraft to become less conservatively stable.

And a broad, moderately swept wing optimized not merely for maximum Mach number but for maneuver and useful fuel volume.

That is already enough that a person from our world might look at it and say:

> “That looks vaguely like an F-2.”

But we haven't copied one thing yet.

---

# In fact, the big wing is *more* justified on A10M than on the real F-2

This is where I'd intentionally lean into the resemblance.

MHI emphasizes that the historical F-2 uses an enlarged, lightweight wing to improve maneuverability; Lockheed's published comparison puts its wing area about 25% above the F-16's, also providing additional internal fuel and weapon carriage. citeturn257882view0turn461570search3

Our A10M independently wants a **large wing for three Japanese reasons**.

First is carrier landing speed.

Second is range over the Pacific.

Third is maneuverability.

So Mitsubishi can arrive at almost exactly the same design observation:

> The engine is powerful enough. Stop spending thrust on another few kilometers per hour and buy wing instead.

That feels *extremely* consistent with the A-series lineage.

A8M Senpū had too much wing by the standards of someone optimizing solely for speed because Horikoshi cared about carrier behavior and maneuverability.

A9M swept that philosophy back to permit transonic flight.

A10M says:

> Fine. Now use modern controls and structural techniques to build a **large swept maneuvering wing** that works across the whole envelope.

So from above, A10M might genuinely have an F-2-like broad trapezoidal shape.

And because it's naval, I would make the outer portion fold.

That immediately produces a visual distinction the real F-2 lacks.

---

# But I would very deliberately **not give it the F-16 intake**

This is where we can make the lineage visibly Japanese.

The big chin inlet is probably the single strongest visual identifier of the F-16/F-2 family.

Our Mitsubishi lineage has no reason to develop exactly that arrangement.

A8M has its bizarre intake collar.

A9M probably transitions toward cleaner **lateral intakes**, because it needs a long unobstructed radar nose.

So keep that.

### A10M should have two side intakes feeding one engine.

Not two engines.

One large engine in the rear fuselage, with a duct entering from each side and merging around the centerline.

This costs some duct weight and complexity, but it gives us:

- the entire nose for radar;
- clean nose-wheel/catapult geometry;
- continuity with A9M;
- good separation between intake and carrier-deck debris;
- and, most importantly for worldbuilding, a recognizable Mitsubishi face.

So from above, somebody might mistake it for an F-2 cousin.

From the front, absolutely not.

Instead of:

> nose  
> cockpit  
> **giant mouth underneath**

you get:

> pointed radome  
> bubble canopy  
> **two dark intake mouths beside/behind the cockpit**

That alone changes the personality of the aircraft enormously.

And it gives you a visual genealogy:

**A8M:** intake collar behind pilot.

**A9M:** paired lateral intakes.

**A10M:** highly refined paired lateral intakes blended into the wing root.

You can see Mitsubishi learning.

---

# I would also make the wing root visibly different

This is where the fourth-generation transition really happens.

A9M probably still looks like:

> fuselage + swept wing.

A10M should look increasingly like:

> **one aerodynamic body whose fuselage happens to contain a pilot and engine.**

The leading-edge root blends forward toward the intake/cockpit region.

Not necessarily the enormous LERX of some later aircraft, but enough that Mitsubishi is deliberately using vortex lift at high angle of attack.

And because the actual setting gives Japan strong electronics, automation, carrier aviation and a narrow but sophisticated technical-industrial base by 1985, an aircraft program centered on flight controls, avionics and very refined naval aerodynamics fits the broader established Japanese technical character rather well. citeturn463965view0turn463965view1

This is also the point at which Mitsubishi can abandon the old belief that the airplane must naturally want to fly straight.

A8M needs aerodynamic stability.

A9M has stability augmentation.

A10M can be intentionally designed around **electronic control**.

That's the genuine generational break.

---

# And that is why A10M deserves a new number

Not because:

> “A9 is old.”

But because the basic relationship between pilot and airframe changes.

A9M's computer assists the pilot in controlling an aerodynamically conventional aircraft.

A10M's flight-control system becomes **part of the aerodynamic design**.

That lets Mitsubishi use a more aggressive center-of-gravity position and wing-body combination than it would willingly tolerate with mechanical controls alone.

That is much closer to the actual conceptual jump represented by aircraft such as the F-16. Lockheed describes the F-16's original development as a lightweight-fighter program and highlights fly-by-wire, longitudinal instability, wing-body blending and automatic variable-camber control among its defining technologies. citeturn461570search11turn461570search26

So our lineage becomes beautifully consistent:

> **A8M achieves agility by being extremely light.**

> **A9M achieves speed by reshaping that light aircraft.**

> **A10M achieves both by allowing electronics to control an airframe that would previously have been considered too aerodynamically aggressive.**

That's a genuine progression.

---

# But don't give 1978 A10M the real F-2's 1990s systems

This is the other important brake.

We can steal the **shape class** without stealing the technology date.

The historical F-2's development explicitly emphasizes its large lightweight composite wing, integrated electronic-warfare equipment and contemporary onboard electronics. citeturn257882view0 Its prototype doesn't fly until 1995. citeturn257882view0

Our first A10M, if we're putting it around **1978–80**, should therefore be materially cruder.

I'd expect:

**A10M1, c. 1979**

- single afterburning turbofan;
- analog/digital hybrid fly-by-wire;
- pulse-Doppler mechanically scanned radar;
- large but mostly metallic wing structure with selective composite parts;
- conventional head-up sight;
- naval data link;
- radar and infrared missiles;
- internal cannon;
- folding outer wing;
- arrestor hook;
- catapult nose gear;
- strong carrier undercarriage.

Then:

**A10M2, early/mid-1980s**

- increasingly digital flight-control computers;
- better pulse-Doppler radar;
- improved look-down/shoot-down;
- larger composite structural components;
- improved electronic warfare;
- better missiles;
- perhaps improved engine.

And only later does the family gradually acquire technologies approaching what we associate with the actual F-2.

This is important because it gives us somewhere to **develop**.

---

# I think it should also be somewhat larger than F-16 but not Keiun-large

The conceptual sweet spot is:

> **big lightweight fighter, not small heavy fighter.**

That distinction sounds contradictory, but it isn't.

A10M has a lot of wing and enough fuselage for fuel.

But it contains:

- one engine;
- one pilot;
- one radar;
- one cannon;
- no dedicated second crew station;
- no huge reconnaissance system;
- no enormous long-range interception radar;
- no requirement to carry every weapon in the Navy.

Keiun remains the airplane that gets large because people continually ask:

> “Can we put this in it too?”

A10M is protected institutionally from that process.

The Mitsubishi bureau should be almost fanatical about rejecting requirement creep:

> Anti-ship missile?

Keiun.

> Dedicated reconnaissance fit?

Keiun.

> Electronic-warfare operator?

Keiun.

> Twelve-hour patrol?

Keiun.

> Fighter radar, six missiles, cannon and enough fuel to defend the fleet?

Fine. That's ours.

That is how A10M remains something like an F-16/F-2 rather than becoming an F-14.

---

# There is also a wonderfully Japanese reason for the F-2-like large wing

**Deck spotting.**

This sounds backwards because bigger wings consume deck space.

But the wing folds.

So Mitsubishi can give A10M a very broad wing in flight while designing the **fold line from the beginning** around carrier elevator and hangar dimensions.

The outer panels fold vertically.

That means the aircraft's parked footprint isn't proportional to its flying span.

It gives us another instantly recognizable feature.

Imagine an A10M on deck:

- long pointed nose;
- bubble canopy;
- lateral intakes;
- broad root/chord;
- outer wings standing folded upward;
- single large swept fin;
- squat heavy carrier landing gear.

That doesn't look like an F-16 anymore.

It looks like something an observer might describe as:

> “an F-2 designed for a carrier by people whose grandfathers designed the Zero.”

Which is about perfect.

---

# I would probably preserve a single vertical tail

There's no need to get visually clever merely to make it different.

The Mitsubishi A-series has never had the Shinden lineage's twin-tail identity.

A large single swept fin is:

- lighter;
- mechanically simpler;
- perfectly adequate for a single-engine fighter;
- easier to fold and spot around;
- and visually connects A10M with A9M.

So Mitsubishi and the Army's Shinden lineage also remain visually different.

That gives Japan three very recognizable fighter traditions by the 1980s:

### **Army Shinden**

Canard + delta + rear engine + twin aft fins.

Alien, distinctive, recognizably descended from Ki-100.

### **Navy Mitsubishi A-series**

Single engine + conventional tail + broad maneuvering wing + pointed radar nose + lateral intakes.

Compact fighter.

### **Navy Yokosuka Keiun**

Twin engine + larger fuselage + heavy radar/weapons capacity + two-seat variants + long-range multirole emphasis.

Big fleet aircraft.

Now Japan has actual **design schools**.

That's much better than giving every Japanese fourth-generation aircraft some arbitrary weird feature merely to prevent convergence.

---

# And I'd probably move **Arashi** onto A10M

The outdated Aerospace Reference used `A11M1 Arashi` in 1978 and `A12M1 Arashi Kai` in 1983. fileciteturn0file7

Since we're eliminating that excessively rapid designation ladder anyway, I think the name is worth salvaging.

So provisionally:

> **A8M Senpū** — Whirlwind  
> **A9M Shippū** — Gale  
> **A10M Arashi** — Storm

That actually produces a nice escalation in the Mitsubishi wind-name tradition without sounding like somebody planned the names in 1946.

And **A10M1 Arashi, entering service around 1979–80**, feels much stronger to me than resurrecting the old A10M in 1966.

---

The broader point is that I wouldn't mourn fourth-generation convergence too much. **Convergence is itself worldbuilding.**

The interesting question changes.

In 1947, you can identify competing philosophies from wildly different silhouettes because nobody yet knows what a jet fighter ought to be.

By 1980, everybody has learned:

> pointed radar nose, high-thrust turbine, swept lifting surface, missiles, good visibility, electronic controls.

So the differences migrate from **“why does that airplane look insane?”** to smaller but still meaningful things:

> Where are the intakes?  
> How much wing does it have?  
> One engine or two?  
> One crewman or two?  
> How much fuel?  
> How does it land?  
> How much of the airframe exists to carry avionics?  
> What did the design bureau refuse to put aboard?

For the A10M, I think the answer is therefore:

> **Use the Mitsubishi F-2 as the broad visual reference, but replace the F-16-derived chin-intake/airframe ancestry with the A9M's paired lateral-intake lineage, navalize the wing and undercarriage from first principles, and give it late-1970s rather than 1990s avionics.**

Then an out-of-universe viewer can absolutely say:

> “Oh, it's kind of an F-2.”

But somebody who knows the setting can look at exactly the same airplane and see:

> **A6M → A7M → A8M → A9M → A10M.**

And that's the distinction we want.

---

Like if you're looking straight on at it, you might mistake it and think that this is some kind of oddly shaped air duct, or airbrake. But it's a, kind of blends in with the shape of the top, or the top shape of the airframe, and it raises up off the airframe about maybe one, two centimeters, maybe three at most, and then blends naturally in with the rest of the rear part of the hull behind the cockpit. And this intake, which is, it actually has about the same amount of area, like the actual looking straight on area of the air intake there, is the same that you would expect from two side mounts. It's just distributed very thinly across the body of the hull. That gives us a very distinct kind of appearance, and I think it would look very interesting. But most interestingly, it does something that the S-16 almost can't. In fact, in some sense, this is, this is a very interesting little shape that I'm designing in my head here. The bottom of the fuselage is available to host heavier things without having this really delicate intake to be worried about. That was what I was thinking about regarding the S-16. But the other thing is also that this design for the A-10M that we're describing, may be such that there never really ends up being an A-11. Because there isn't needed to be. If the system you want to upgrade to say, oh well, we want X, Y, Z on it, you can probably take the A-10M and modify it, and get your A-10M1, 2, 3, 4. I could imagine an A-10M-16 by the 2000s kind of situation, as it is just a very easily upgradable platform with a very long lifespan availability, if you think about it. And that is as a design.

## Turn 1088 — Assistant

- Timestamp: 2026-08-14T04:50:49.556Z
- Message ID: `2eb4550f-18d7-47fe-91e0-f4f1b53d4d6d`
- Source: ChatGPT shared conversation `Alternate J7W Jet Concept`
- Parallel branch: https://chatgpt.com/share/6a7eb2ea-137c-83e8-a9c8-b1fda9b3a455
- Relationship: parallel specialist continuation imported after the master project record through Turn 777

Yes. I think this is actually the point where the **A10M stops being merely “Japan's F-2-ish fourth-generation fighter” and acquires a silhouette of its own.** And I think the long-life conclusion follows naturally from the same design choices.

The intake can work. I would just make one technical distinction:

> **The 1–3 cm dimension should be the intake's stand-off from the fuselage boundary layer, not the total depth of the air passage.**

If the entire opening were literally only two centimeters high, even spread broadly across the upper fuselage, a large afterburning turbofan simply couldn't swallow enough air. But the visible lip can absolutely stand only a few centimeters proud of the fuselage while the duct **opens rapidly behind it** into a much larger internal plenum.

That preserves exactly the appearance you're imagining.

## The A10M gets a “black crescent”

I'd make the intake something like a very broad **dorsal crescent**, beginning behind and slightly below the rear edge of the canopy and sweeping around perhaps 220–260 degrees of the upper fuselage.

Viewed head-on, you see something like:

```text
               _______
             /         \
            /  radome   \
           |             |
            \  cockpit  /
             \_________/
          ___/█████████\___
        /                   \
       /                     \
      /                       \
```

The black area isn't an airbrake. It's the intake.

But because the lip lies almost parallel to the surrounding bodywork and stands only slightly proud, somebody looking at the aircraft parked might initially think:

> “What is that strange seam or brake panel behind the cockpit?”

Then they look directly into it and realize the entire dark crescent is feeding the engine.

That's an excellent visual signature.

NASA actually studied **top-mounted inlet systems for transonic/supersonic fighter applications**, so the general architecture isn't an aerodynamic fantasy. The studies treated inlet location, angle of attack, pressure recovery, and engine-face distortion as real design variables rather than dismissing dorsal inlets outright. citeturn131103search0turn150066search0

## Internally, the intake is much larger than it appears

I'd picture three layers.

The first is the visible **raised lip**, perhaps 20–30 mm off the skin. That allows the fuselage boundary layer to pass underneath or be bled away rather than feeding the slowest, dirtiest air directly into the compressor. NACA's side-inlet work found boundary-layer handling to be one of the central problems in fuselage-mounted induction systems. citeturn131103search1

Immediately behind that is the actual intake passage. It expands downward and outward beneath the skin, so the airflow area becomes considerably larger than the visible slot thickness suggests.

Then the left and right portions curve inward toward a large common plenum and compressor face behind the cockpit.

So:

> **externally shallow; internally deep.**

That makes the illusion possible.

And because the intake wraps broadly across the shoulders of the aircraft, it doesn't need one giant side scoop. The necessary capture area is distributed across a much wider arc.

---

# There is also a major naval advantage

Your point about the underside is good.

The A10M's lower fuselage is now extremely clean.

There's no F-16-style chin intake competing with:

- nose gear;
- catapult attachment hardware;
- centerline fuel tanks;
- reconnaissance pods;
- large missiles;
- bomb racks;
- landing gear doors;
- or deck servicing access.

For an airplane designed from birth as a carrier aircraft, that's valuable.

Especially because **the catapult structure is going through the lower forward fuselage anyway**. Mitsubishi gets to design a very strong keel without having to route the engine's principal intake directly through the same area.

So although the dorsal inlet creates aerodynamic complications, it simplifies the **naval structural problem**.

That's exactly the kind of trade I'd expect a carrier-aircraft design office to accept.

There's another minor advantage: a high-mounted inlet is comparatively sheltered from loose deck debris, although engine distortion and high-angle-of-attack behavior become the harder design problems instead.

---

# And high angle of attack is where the design earns its engineering pedigree

This shouldn't be an inlet that Mitsubishi draws once in 1972 and gets right.

It should consume years of wind-tunnel work.

The irony is that a dorsal inlet can actually have useful high-angle-of-attack characteristics because the nose pitches upward toward the incoming air. NASA's studies found top-mounted fighter inlets feasible and specifically investigated their changing flow field with angle of attack. citeturn131103search0

But now introduce **yaw**.

The aircraft is pulling hard, sideslipping slightly, perhaps rolling.

Suddenly one half of the crescent sees a different pressure field from the other half.

That's where the intake can send badly distorted flow toward the compressor.

So A10M probably needs an unusually sophisticated intake system for its time:

- left/right internal flow dividers;
- boundary-layer bleed;
- bypass doors;
- internal guide vanes;
- perhaps limited variable geometry at the inlet throat;
- and compressor controls specifically tolerant of transient distortion.

That becomes one of the reasons the aircraft takes until the late 1970s to mature.

And later digital engine control can improve it enormously without changing the external shape.

Which leads directly into your second point.

# Yes: A10M may very plausibly be the **last A-number for decades**

I think this is better than A11M and A12M appearing every few years.

The old Aerospace Reference's A11/A12 ladder was built before we'd established what the aircraft families actually were, so I would consider it superseded by this reconstruction. Its useful surviving principle is the Navy's `A` fighter designation system, not the exact old post-1978 type sequence. fileciteturn7file0

The aircraft we're creating has almost all the characteristics that make an airframe **upgrade unusually well**:

- generous wing area;
- substantial internal fuel volume;
- big unobstructed radar nose;
- a physically large engine bay;
- digital or hybrid digital flight controls from fairly early in life;
- broad electrical-generation margins;
- modular avionics bays;
- strong carrier landing structure;
- folding wings;
- enough payload capacity to accept new missiles;
- and an inlet sized with growth margin.

That last one matters enormously.

If Mitsubishi sizes the intake and engine compartment only for the original 1978 engine, later propulsion upgrades become miserable.

If the Navy instead pays a modest weight penalty and says:

> “The engine bay must accept the projected next engine class,”

then the 1995 A10M may have a completely different turbofan while retaining essentially the same aircraft.

Likewise, if electronics are built in replaceable racks rather than physically embedded wherever space happened to exist, you can replace almost everything the pilot interacts with.

The airframe becomes a **platform**, not an appliance.

---

# Your “A10M-16 in the 2000s” idea is completely believable in principle

Look at what happened to the real F-16.

The USAF received its first production aircraft in 1978–79, and the design subsequently accumulated major changes in radar, cockpit, weapons, structure, engine, flight-control software and mission capability. The Air Force itself described the original lightweight daytime fighter as having become a multirole, all-weather air-to-air and air-to-ground aircraft over the following decades. citeturn817817search1turn817817search4

Lockheed's later lineage runs through Blocks 10, 15, 20, 25, 30/32, 40/42, 50/52, 60 and 70, and later structural work extended some F-16s from an original 8,000-hour design life toward 12,000 hours. citeturn817817search12turn817817search15

So a Japanese aircraft entering service around 1979 and still existing in radically improved forms in **2000–2010** is not remotely excessive.

In this setting it may be *more* plausible because Japan has been especially conservative about replacing successful airframe families.

I wouldn't necessarily have **sixteen entirely different production models**, though.

I'd distinguish major airframe marks from modernization packages.

Something like:

| Variant | Approx. period | Principal change |
|---|---:|---|
| **A10M1 Arashi** | 1979 | Initial carrier fighter; hybrid digital FBW; mechanically scanned pulse-Doppler radar |
| **A10M2** | 1983 | Fully digital flight-control system, improved radar and missiles |
| **A10M3** | late 1980s | Improved turbofan, enlarged electrical system, better EW |
| **A10M4** | early 1990s | New radar generation, glassier cockpit, structural life extension |
| **A10M5** | mid-1990s | Major engine/intake-control modernization, expanded precision weapons |
| **A10M6** | c. 2000 | New mission computer, datalinks, modern electronic warfare |
| **A10M7+** | 2000s | Successive sensor, weapon, engine, structural and network upgrades |

Then there can be **Kai packages**, production lots, equipment configurations and export forms layered underneath those.

If we really want an `A10M16` by the 2000s, that's not inherently wrong. I just don't think every avionics revision needs to increment the final number.

The more important canon fact is:

> **There is no A11M simply because another decade has passed.**

---

# What would finally force an A11?

This is how I'd test the lineage.

Radar improvement?

No. New nose installation.

New missiles?

No.

More powerful engine?

Probably no.

New cockpit?

No.

Composite replacement wing?

Still perhaps no.

Completely new flight-control computers?

Definitely no.

New electronic-warfare suite?

No.

Conformal fuel tanks?

No.

Even a major inlet rework?

Potentially still A10.

The A10 lineage finally dies when the mission demands something that **cannot be fitted without changing the aerodynamic architecture**.

Candidates might be:

### 1. Low-observable shaping

If Japan eventually decides that major radar-signature reduction is essential, the dorsal crescent, exposed compressor path, existing wing planform and external stores may simply be incompatible.

Now we're talking A11.

### 2. Internal weapons

If missiles have to move inside the aircraft rather than hanging under the wing, everything changes.

A10 hasn't got the fuselage depth.

A11.

### 3. A genuinely new propulsion architecture

Vectored thrust, variable cycle, twin-engine requirement, or something of that magnitude.

A11.

### 4. Unmanned/optionally crewed architecture

Again, probably new aircraft.

A11.

But until one of those happens:

> **why throw away a superb carrier airframe?**

And because Japan experiences very little major combat, there is less chance of a war producing the institutional declaration:

> “Our current fighter is obsolete. Replace everything immediately.”

The absence of combat shock helps A10 live longer.

---

# The silhouette therefore becomes almost timeless

I really like where this leaves the aircraft visually.

Imagine an original **1979 A10M1** beside a **2003 A10M7 Kai**.

At first glance:

same airplane.

Same broad wing.

Same pointed nose.

Same canopy.

Same dorsal black crescent.

Same single vertical tail.

Same general carrier stance.

Then start looking closely.

The later one has:

- subtly reshaped leading-edge roots;
- composite outer wings;
- different radome;
- different exhaust;
- perhaps a slightly enlarged dorsal intake lip;
- completely different cockpit;
- embedded electronic-warfare antennas;
- new pylons;
- different navigation sensors;
- perhaps no visible external aerials;
- and substantially different weapons.

Then open the panels and virtually **nothing inside is the same**.

Different radar.

Different computer.

Different wiring.

Different engine.

Different fuel management.

Different flight-control computers.

Different defensive system.

Different displays.

Possibly even substantially replaced wing spars.

That is a very satisfying lineage because it makes the late Japanese aviation environment look culturally different.

Germany may periodically make more dramatic clean-sheet leaps.

The United States may have competing procurement schools.

Japan increasingly says:

> **“The airframe is fine. Modernize the system.”**

And the A10 becomes the purest expression of that philosophy.

---

There is one further consequence I particularly like: **the dorsal crescent intake becomes Mitsubishi's trademark.**

It begins on A8M as a desperate solution to feeding an aft-mounted Ne-20 while keeping the aircraft tiny.

A9M cleans it up.

A10M transforms it from the A8M's almost circular collar into a very shallow, wide **horseshoe/crescent scoop blended into the upper fuselage**.

So by 1985 somebody looking at a Japanese carrier deck can identify the Mitsubishi fighters from the front without knowing the model:

> pointed nose, bubble canopy, and that black crescent over the shoulders.

The technology has changed almost beyond recognition since Horikoshi's little Senpū, but one peculiar solution his team adopted in the late 1940s has survived because every succeeding generation found a better way to make it work.

**That**, more than making the aircraft visually bizarre, is what gives the A-series a genuine design language.

The Battle of Ceylon is often used as an argument of "this is why you need battleships" and the US Carrier doctrine never reaches the same Carrier primacy role it did historically, rather, instead, seeing a Carrier Subsidiary role as "Naval Aviation supports the fleet" not "Naval aviation is the principle arm of the fleet". Thus Battleships are genuinely developed in the US and the prospect of expensive ships remain a "Well that's just naval warfare for you" thing. The US submarine force also doesn't see a massive expansion (as it did historically).
