Yes. I think this substantially improves the missile genealogy, because it gives the Fi 103 and X-4 **institutional descendants** rather than treating them as prototypes that vanish once their immediate wartime purpose disappears.

There is also a historical coincidence almost too useful to ignore: the Fi 103 carried the cover designation **FZG 76, *Flakzielgerät 76***—literally an antiaircraft target device. citeturn891249search0turn891249search2 In our setting, the cover name can become the actual postwar mission.

## The Fi 103 becomes the ancestor of the German target-drone establishment

I would absolutely do this.

The original Fi 103 doesn't become some 1940s unmanned fighter. It isn't remotely capable of that. What Germany notices is much simpler:

> We already possess a cheap pilotless aircraft with an autopilot, propulsion system, launching apparatus, and enough payload capacity to carry test equipment. Why are we firing missiles at towed sleeves or relying entirely on mathematical interception exercises?

So perhaps as early as **1945**, Fi 103 airframes begin appearing at Wasserfall proving grounds with the explosive payload removed and replaced by ballast and instrumentation.

The first versions don't even have to be sophisticated remotely piloted drones. They fly a predetermined course, altitude, and speed. The missile battery knows approximately where they're supposed to be but still has to detect, track, engage, and hit them.

Then the test establishment starts adding capabilities.

A radio-command override lets controllers change heading or altitude. A telemetry package tells engineers what the drone was actually doing when the missile passed it. A transponder gives range-safety personnel a precise position. A destruct charge ensures a malfunctioning drone doesn't continue off the range.

And then you get the particularly useful versions you're describing: **emitter targets**.

One Fi 103 derivative carries equipment intended to approximate an H2S-like bomber radar. Another simulates Monica or some later airborne emitter. Another carries a radar reflector designed to reproduce a larger aircraft's return.

That immediately lets Germany test not just “can Wasserfall hit an aircraft?” but:

> Can the passive seeker distinguish an emitting target?

> Can it acquire through interference?

> What happens if two targets emit simultaneously?

> What happens if the emitter shuts off?

> Can the missile reacquire?

And because the target isn't carrying a pilot, they can deliberately create ugly test cases.

That is enormously important.

The Germans now have a **guided-weapons test culture based on instrumented unmanned aircraft** decades before anybody thinks of those aircraft themselves as frontline combat systems.

The lineage should therefore split fairly early:

| Line | Immediate purpose | Long-term consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Fi 103/FZG target line** | Expendable and later recoverable flying targets | Target drones, decoys, remote aircraft, eventually UAV institutional ancestry |
| **Fi 103 strike line** | Autonomous flying bomb | Cruise missiles |
| **A4 line** | Ballistic rocket and high-energy propulsion | Space launch, exoatmospheric interception, limited ballistic strike |
| **Fritz X/X-4 line** | Precision control and actuators | Guided air weapons, terminal control, antiship guidance |
| **Wasserfall line** | Integrated radar air defense | SAM networks and later exoatmospheric interceptors |

That gives the German guided-weapons ecosystem several connected branches rather than one magic family.

### But the Fi 103 eventually stops being a good target

This is an important limitation.

It's excellent for testing early SAMs against something resembling a bomber or flying bomb: modest speed, predictable flight, useful radar cross-section, and plenty of room for instrumentation.

Once Germany wants to test a 1960s missile against a Mach 2 fighter, the Fi 103 airframe is useless.

So the **airframe dies while the institution survives**.

By the 1950s, the *Flugziel* establishment starts developing small turbojet targets. By the 1960s, those targets can maneuver under radio control, present configurable radar signatures, emit specific frequencies, carry electronic countermeasures, and report miss distance.

And that is what gives Germany the later UAV connection.

I would deliberately prevent the Germans from immediately asking, “Why don't we put a camera and bombs on this?” Institutional categories are powerful. To the Luftwaffe, these are **targets**. They're range equipment operated by test organizations. They aren't aircraft flown by operational squadrons.

It probably takes much later advances in compact television, digital control, navigation, datalinks, and precision weapons before somebody finally says:

> “We're spending a remarkable amount of money making these things fly independently, navigate, maneuver, communicate, and avoid being shot down. Why exactly are we only letting the enemy shoot at them?”

That could make German armed UAVs of the later twentieth century feel like an almost embarrassingly obvious application of a technology family they've possessed for fifty years.

The setting's current technology reference already makes Germany's strength one of **integrated guided weapons, computing, sensors, and orbital infrastructure**, rather than merely better individual missiles, so this institutional lineage fits it extremely well. citeturn248589view1

---

## Your diagnosis of the X-4 problem is exactly right

The important failure isn't necessarily:

> **wire guidance doesn't work.**

It is:

> **manual command-to-line-of-sight guidance is a horrible workload for the man who is simultaneously flying a fighter aircraft.**

The historical X-4 really did use wire commands specifically because wire couldn't be jammed like a radio-command link. Its pilot steered the missile visually with a joystick, and test launches began in August 1944. Ruhrstahl actually built roughly a thousand airframes before the historical program collapsed. citeturn430878search2turn430878search8

So I wouldn't have the alternate German report say:

> “X-4 proves wire guidance is a dead end.”

It says something like:

> **“X-4 proves that the launch aircraft cannot also be the missile operator during fighter combat.”**

That is a considerably more consequential conclusion.

Wire guidance then remains alive.

It can migrate into antitank work because the operator there is standing or sitting behind cover and has several seconds to stare through a sight. It can remain useful for particular naval or ground weapons. It might even remain useful for specialized air weapons launched by a multi-crew aircraft.

What dies is **pilot-commanded fighter missile guidance**.

And this gives us two competing ways to solve it almost immediately.

## The passive-radar X-4 should exist before the infrared one

I think this is the simplest first attempt.

Take the existing X-4 control system and replace the pilot's guidance commands with a crude directional receiver.

The missile doesn't possess radar.

It just listens.

A British bomber transmits something within the receiver's frequency band. The missile senses that one side of its antenna system is receiving a stronger signal and generates steering corrections.

This would be **extremely stupid by later standards**.

It cannot meaningfully identify an aircraft.

It doesn't know that the strongest signal is necessarily the intended aircraft.

Signal strength isn't a clean measure of distance.

Several emitters can confuse it.

The target can shut its transmitter off.

Ground transmitters or decoys may attract it.

But that's fine.

The requirement is not:

> Produce Sparrow in 1945.

It's:

> **Demonstrate that an airborne weapon can steer itself toward an emitting aircraft after the pilot releases it.**

And now the Fi 103 target program becomes directly useful.

Put a representative bomber radar emitter on an FZG target.

Launch X-4 derivative.

Pilot releases.

Pilot turns away.

Missile follows the emitter.

If it passes within lethal radius, everyone at the range becomes considerably more interested.

That could plausibly happen in **1945–46**.

The operational descendant might become quite valuable specifically against large radar-equipped aircraft while remaining almost useless against a fighter whose radar is off.

So Germany learns something else quite early:

> **“Fire-and-forget” does not mean “fire-and-hit.”**

# Madrid is probably the better X-4 seeker than Hamburg

This is the one place I'd make a fairly definite historical correction.

Your underlying point about German infrared research is right, but the **Madrid** seeker is actually almost tailor-made for what you're proposing.

A declassified American account describes Madrid as an infrared seeker specifically intended for **small air-to-air missiles**, using an uncooled lead-sulfide detector. Another captured-technology report describes German homing-head work using lead-sulfide photocells. citeturn822106search0turn822106search1

Hamburg is still extremely valuable, but I would keep it principally in the larger guided-bomb/antishipping research branch.

So Germany ends 1945 with something like two related infrared schools:

**Hamburg:** larger-target/air-to-surface ancestry.

**Madrid:** compact anti-aircraft seeker ancestry.

That is actually even cleaner than forcing Hamburg onto X-4.

### The 1945–47 infrared X-4 therefore becomes very plausible

Not as a mature weapon.

As a **working experimental weapon**.

The development process is wonderfully straightforward conceptually and horribly difficult in practice.

The X-4 already possesses:

- an aerodynamic missile body;
- propulsion;
- control surfaces;
- control actuators;
- stabilization;
- a warhead;
- a proximity-fuze concept.

The engineers remove the wire-receiver commands and make **Madrid generate the steering commands instead**.

And then everything breaks.

The seeker sees the sun.

Cloud edges produce strange signals.

The detector's useful acquisition distance varies drastically with target aspect.

The missile sees the hot exhaust more readily from behind than it sees the aircraft from the front.

The seeker loses the target during maneuver.

The electronics shake.

The optical alignment shifts.

The rocket motor and missile body create their own thermal and vibration problems.

The seeker can acquire something on the test stand that it cannot reliably keep centered while the entire missile is accelerating through the sky.

That's exactly what 1946 should look like.

But Germany has two advantages our historical German program did not receive: **time and continuity**.

So I'd make the progression roughly:

**Late 1945:** first Madrid/X-4 bench integration.

**Early 1946:** captive and static seeker tests against aircraft engines and controlled heat sources.

**Mid-1946:** first free-flight attempts against cooperative FZG targets.

**Late 1946:** first successful self-guided interception passes under carefully controlled conditions.

**1947:** a small number of technically combat-capable evaluation missiles exist.

And I agree: **they don't go to Britain.**

---

# But secrecy needs to protect the seeker, not the idea of an AAM

This is the important qualification.

By 1947 Britain doesn't need to be completely unaware that Germany has experimented with guided air weapons.

Britain has already encountered German guided bombs. Fritz X used radio-command steering and itself became a direct technical ancestor of Ruhrstahl's later X-4 work. citeturn430878search6 British intelligence is perfectly capable of suspecting that Germany is investigating guided anti-aircraft weapons.

What Germany has a compelling reason to conceal is:

> **“We have achieved autonomous terminal homing in an aircraft-sized missile.”**

That's a much bigger secret.

If a test X-4 derivative is fired over Britain and fails intact enough to be recovered, Britain gets:

- detector material;
- optical arrangement;
- reticle geometry;
- amplifier technology;
- control circuitry;
- actuator arrangement;
- cooling or lack thereof;
- missile construction;
- perhaps even frequency/filter information.

And for what benefit?

A weapon that remains substantially less reliable than four 30 mm cannon.

Germany is winning the air campaign without it.

So the Luftwaffe's argument can be:

> **Don't trade a strategic technology for one Lancaster.**

That is entirely rational.

If Britain were on the verge of defeating Germany, they'd use it.

But they aren't.

Consequently, when early missile archives become accessible decades later, the revelation isn't:

> “Germany thought of an air-to-air missile in 1944!”

Everyone knows that.

It's:

> **“They had successful autonomous infrared interception trials in 1946?”**

That is the retrospective shock.

And I would keep the name of that weapon open for now. It could remain an X-4 development mark during trials rather than receiving a grand service designation for something never issued operationally.

---

# It also makes the later Luftlanze much better

The current reference has the **Luftlanze 55** as the first common missile carried by Germany's 1956–57 fighters. fileciteturn9file11

I think we now reinterpret that.

Luftlanze 55 isn't Germany's first AAM.

It is Germany's first AAM where the Luftwaffe finally says:

> **This is ordinary ammunition. Give squadrons thousands of them.**

That is a completely different milestone.

There's a decade of ugly experimental weapons behind it:

X-4 manual command → passive-emission X-4 → Madrid infrared X-4 → improved experimental infrared missiles → limited preproduction missile → Luftlanze 55.

That means the 1955 missile can be good without being miraculously invented in 1954.

And it can still be a fairly primitive weapon by later standards.

---

# The Fi 103 and A4 split gives Germany two kinds of long-range strike

I agree with your distinction almost completely, with the obvious dictation correction that this is the **A4** lineage and **Fi 103** lineage.

The A4's military problem becomes increasingly obvious in a non-nuclear world.

Germany can build something enormous that crosses a continent and puts a conventional warhead somewhere near Detroit.

Wonderful.

Now ask:

> **What did that cost, and what exactly did it destroy?**

If the answer is one factory building, a railway yard, or several city blocks, the economics become atrocious.

So long-range ballistic work isn't completely abandoned, but its strategic-strike prestige declines relative to **spaceflight**, where precisely the same high-energy propulsion and guidance technologies suddenly have extraordinary value.

The current canon already makes Germany's 1957 satellite the beginning of its public space lead and explicitly connects the space establishment to the German wartime rocket generation. citeturn248589view2

Meanwhile the Fi 103/Fritz X combination becomes the practical conventional-strike branch.

The ancestry is almost perfect:

> Fi 103 says **fly there autonomously**.

> A4 guidance research says **know where you are more accurately**.

> Fritz X says **correct the final approach**.

> Hamburg-style work says **recognize or home on the target**.

Replace the pulsejet eventually with a better turbojet, improve the inertial/navigation package, and add terminal guidance.

Now you have a recognizably modern **cruise missile**.

And because its propulsion and trajectory are much cheaper than an intercontinental ballistic rocket, Germany can build it in meaningful numbers.

That is probably where the postwar German surface-to-surface family truly becomes militarily important.

---

# The ASAT missile is where the ballistic branch gets back into weapons

This part of your model is particularly good.

Without nuclear weapons, an intercontinental ballistic missile carrying ordinary explosive has an awful cost-to-effect ratio.

An **anti-satellite missile does not**.

The target may itself represent years of work, enormous expense, a critical reconnaissance capability, or part of an entire military command network.

And unlike destroying Detroit, you don't require a multi-ton explosive effect.

You need to hit—or get sufficiently close to—one comparatively fragile object.

So the military rocket establishment suddenly has a target for which extreme altitude and velocity are not extravagances.

They're the entire point.

That means the German ASAT lineage is legitimately a descendant of **both** Wasserfall and A4.

Wasserfall contributes:

- interception mathematics;
- tracking;
- target prediction;
- guidance;
- proximity/terminal engagement;
- air-defense command culture.

A4/space launch contributes:

- staging;
- high-energy propulsion;
- upper-atmosphere flight;
- launch operations;
- orbital tracking.

So I wouldn't formally describe the mature weapon as merely a two-stage SAM.

I'd call it an **exoatmospheric interceptor descended administratively from air defense**.

That's exactly the sort of distinction German engineers themselves would make.

---

## And your “air-launched” asterisk works

The German engineering objection is correct.

Suppose the ASAT consists schematically of:

**large booster → upper interceptor stage → terminal kill package.**

The upper stage ignites after separation while already airborne.

Someone in the press therefore says:

> “Germany has demonstrated an air-launched orbital interceptor.”

And the engineers start grinding their teeth.

Because the upper stage didn't begin from an airplane doing Mach 0.9 at 15 kilometers.

It began after a first stage had already provided enormous velocity and altitude.

Those aren't remotely equivalent initial conditions.

So technically:

> **Yes, that stage was launched in the air.**

Operationally:

> **No, Germany has not demonstrated an aircraft-launched ASAT.**

But Japan notices something more subtle.

That upper package is already:

- compact enough to be treated as one flight vehicle;
- designed for ignition after release;
- capable of autonomous stabilization;
- equipped with terminal guidance;
- designed to operate without a fixed ground launcher once separated.

So Japanese engineers don't conclude:

> “Just put that under a fighter.”

They conclude:

> **“The first stage doesn't necessarily have to be a disposable ground rocket.”**

An aircraft could provide some initial altitude, some initial velocity, geographic flexibility, and a movable launch point. It would probably still need its own rocket booster after aircraft release.

But conceptually the architecture has changed from:

> ground missile climbing all the way to orbit

to:

> **carrier aircraft + booster + interceptor.**

That is a legitimate Japanese leap.

And it fits the currently established later orbital divergence nicely. The present wiki already has German anti-satellite research and orbital military infrastructure surviving into the 1980s, while Japan's following generation moves strongly toward unmanned orbital interception and distributed tracking. citeturn8file0 citeturn248589view1

## So I think the German lineage now has a remarkably clean shape

The part I would regard as effectively locked from what you've just established is this:

**Fi 103 does not die.** Its immediate postwar importance is actually greater as a target drone than as a weapon. Its descendants create Germany's permanent unmanned test-aircraft establishment, while a separate Fi 103-derived conceptual branch feeds the cruise missile.

**X-4 is built and tested but never becomes an operational wartime weapon.** Its lasting lesson is that pilot-guided MCLOS is unacceptable in fighter combat, not that wire guidance itself is useless.

**Passive-emitter homing is probably the first attempt at autonomous X-4 guidance.** It works only against cooperating or emitting targets and is horribly susceptible to ambiguity.

**Madrid-derived infrared guidance becomes the decisive second attempt.** Late-1945 integration leads to repeated 1946–47 trials and a technically combat-capable but secret pre-service AAM by 1947. The weapon isn't used over Britain because its battlefield value does not justify exposing autonomous seeker technology.

**Luftlanze 55 is therefore not the first German AAM.** It is the first mature, ordinary, mass-service German AAM.

**A4 largely escapes into spaceflight**, because conventional ballistic bombardment lacks an economically compelling strategic warhead.

**Fi 103 + A4 navigation + Fritz-X control + seeker research produces the practical German cruise-missile family.**

And then **ballistic military technology returns through exoatmospheric interception**, because satellites finally provide the kind of target against which a large high-energy missile is economically rational.

That also gives us a really elegant hidden continuity across sixty years: the 2000s German combat UAV doesn't descend principally from a fighter aircraft.

It descends, institutionally, from something whose name had once literally meant **“anti-aircraft target device.”**

That is exactly the sort of technology lineage that makes a setting feel as though it has history rather than merely a different equipment catalog. memcite

## Turn 1115 — Assistant

- Timestamp: 2026-08-14T16:37:34.954Z
- Message ID: `ad9dc134-a591-42ee-91c5-0bcbf40e7c4e`
- Source: ChatGPT shared conversation `Naval Doctrine Evolution`
- Parallel branch: https://chatgpt.com/share/6a80206d-15d0-83e8-b360-a8acc44d3025
- Relationship: parallel specialist continuation imported after the master project record through Turn 777

Yes. Once you separate **“America saw that this was possible”** from **“America physically acquired the foreign weapon and built from it,”** the American missile tree changes quite dramatically.

The central result is not that neutral America has no guided weapons. It is almost the opposite:

> **The United States retains a surprisingly rich domestic ecology of drones, guided bombs, target seekers, air-to-air experiments, JATO, sounding rockets, and antiaircraft-missile studies. What it loses most severely is the postwar German inheritance that historically accelerated large liquid-fueled ballistic rockets.**

That fits the setting's established American learning model: attachés, volunteers, British contacts, China, and commercial/intelligence reporting give Washington a real but incomplete view of the war, while America never receives the full institutional and industrial education of belligerency. fileciteturn10file17 It also fits the broader premise that Pearl Harbor never occurs and the United States never undergoes historical total-war mobilization. fileciteturn10file11

I'm going to use four labels:

- **Domestic** — the American project does not need a foreign weapon to exist.
- **Inspired** — a foreign capability created or accelerated the requirement, but Americans designed their own answer.
- **Exploited** — captured hardware, documents, components, or personnel materially shaped the actual historical project.
- **Contingent** — the design may be American, but its historical urgency depended upon American combat, nuclear weapons, or the particular Cold War.

The distinction between **Inspired** and **Exploited** is the one that matters most here.

---

# 1. The foundation America already has before the interesting divergence

American pilotless-weapon research is much older than the V-1.

The United States had the Kettering “Bug” aerial torpedo during the First World War. The Navy was operating radio-controlled target aircraft in the 1930s; an N2C-2 performed a simulated dive-bombing attack on *Utah* in 1938. Commander Delmar Fahrney had begun systematic Navy work on pilotless aircraft in 1936, initially for antiaircraft targets. citeturn447842search1turn447842search3turn447842search13

This matters enormously because it means:

> **The American unmanned-aircraft tree does not begin with the V-1.**

Likewise, American rocket research had an indigenous Caltech/GALCIT ancestry before captured V-2s. JPL's later wartime program grew out of that work, with Army interest increasing when reports of German long-range rockets demonstrated that the military application was real. citeturn543767search10turn543767search21

So there are two native roots already sitting there:

**Sperry/Kettering/Fahrney → autopilots, radio control, pilotless aircraft**

and

**GALCIT/Aerojet/JPL → JATO, solid/liquid rockets, guidance, sounding rockets**

Neither needs Germany to lose the war.

---

# 2. Wartime American drones and flying weapons, 1941–47

| Historical program | Real dependency | AltWWII judgment |
|---|---|---|
| **GM A-1 / revived aerial torpedo work** | **Domestic** | **Survives as research.** |
| **TDN/TDR assault drones** | **Domestic**, wartime funding accelerated | **Survives, smaller.** |
| **Interstate XBDR/BDR** | **Domestic** continuation of assault-drone work | **Survives as prototype/test family.** |
| **Glomb** | **Domestic** Navy guided-glider program | **Probably survives experimentally.** |
| **Bat** | **Domestic** radar-homing guidance | **Strong survivor.** |
| **Gorgon** | **Domestic** guided-missile experimentation | **Strong research survivor.** |
| **Gargoyle** | **Domestic** guided anti-ship weapon | **Likely survives experimentally.** |
| **JB-1** | **Inspired** by the flying-bomb problem, but American Northrop design | **Can survive.** |
| **JB-2 / Navy Loon** | **Direct Fi 103 exploitation** | **Does not exist.** |
| **JB-10** | Domestic derivative inside the V-1-response program | **Possible, but probably only experimental.** |

The TDR is especially important. Fahrney's pilotless-aircraft program predates American entry into the war, and by 1941 television plus radar-altimeter technology had made a practical assault drone possible. Interstate supplied the aircraft and RCA supplied television guidance. citeturn447842search0

So your XBDR example is exactly right. There is no need for an American engineer to see a Horten flying wing. Interstate's program has its own ancestry.

In this timeline I would expect something like:

> TDN → TDR → improved Interstate BDR/XBDR test articles → postwar target/research drones.

Production is vastly smaller because America isn't expending them against Japanese targets, but **the engineering survives**.

### Bat is another surprisingly important survivor

The Bat was a genuinely American active-radar-homing glide weapon. It had a radar guidance set in its nose and could seek a surface target after release. citeturn379806search0turn379806search2

That's an enormous thing for our purposes.

It means an alternate American engineer in 1945 does **not** need captured German homing technology to understand:

> radar can be placed inside the weapon and the weapon can steer itself toward a target.

He may not know what Germany has done with Wasserfall.

He doesn't need to.

America already possesses the conceptual building blocks.

The neutral-America difference is that perhaps twenty experimental weapons and a small service batch get built instead of the technology being validated by combat.

---

# 3. American guided bombs are much stranger and more advanced than the popular history suggests

This is probably the biggest correction to the intuitive picture.

The Army Air Forces historically had multiple independent guidance experiments:

| Weapon | Guidance | Foreign dependence | Alt fate |
|---|---|---|---|
| **VB-1 Azon** | Radio command, azimuth only | **Domestic** | Survives |
| **VB-3 Razon** | Improved radio command, range + azimuth | **Domestic** | Survives experimentally |
| **VB-6 Felix** | **Infrared/heat homing** | **Domestic** | Very important survivor |
| **VB-9 ROC** | Radar/remote guidance experiments | **Domestic** | Survives as research |
| **VB-10 ROC** | Television guidance | **Domestic** | Survives as research |
| **VB-13 Tarzon** | Razon control + British Tallboy body | **Mixed British/American**, later combat-contingent | Exact weapon uncertain |

Felix deserves emphasis. The National Museum of the USAF describes it as a 1,000-pound bomb equipped with an electronic nose that homed on sufficiently hot targets. It was cancelled before combat historically. citeturn890317search0

So in our timeline America can quite legitimately reach the early 1950s thinking:

> “What if we made an infrared-guided missile?”

without having the slightest idea that Germany had been testing Madrid-derived AAM seekers in 1946.

The Americans have **their own infrared family**.

What they're missing is the German operational insight:

> infrared guidance + small maneuvering rocket + aerial interception.

Felix people are thinking **bomb**.

German Ruhrstahl people are thinking **fighter weapon**.

That distinction alone can cost America several years.

Likewise, the VB-10 used a television camera in the bomb's nose, with the bombardier guiding it by radio. citeturn890317search2

So America's 1940s guided-weapons establishment is not technologically primitive. It's **fragmented**.

That's the word I would use.

There are people doing television.

There are people doing radar.

There are people doing infrared.

There are people doing radio command.

There are people doing autopilots.

There are people doing rockets.

What neutral America lacks is the war saying:

> **These five laboratories must be connected immediately because otherwise Hamburg burns tomorrow night.**

Germany gets that selection pressure.

America doesn't.

Interestingly, the historical Air Force itself notes that guided-bomb work essentially collapsed after World War II and had to be revived for Korea. citeturn890317search4 In AltWWII, there is neither American WWII combat experience nor the historical Korean War, so I would expect **continuing low-level laboratory work but even less urgency to procure the weapons**.

---

# 4. The JB-series: this is where the distinction becomes brutally clear

### JB-2 Loon: delete it

This is the easiest answer in the entire audit.

The JB-2 was an Americanized Fi 103/V-1. The June 1944 V-1 attacks caused Washington to make reproduction of the German flying bomb an extremely high priority. citeturn967969search23turn890317search24

No captured/crashed Fi 103 available to America means:

> **No JB-2. No American Loon.**

Not delayed.

Not renamed.

**Absent.**

And that has downstream consequences because historically the Navy used Loon for early submarine missile-launch experimentation. citeturn318502search7

So the American submarine-launched cruise-missile story loses one of its developmental stepping stones—which fits perfectly with the much weaker submarine prestige we're already establishing for this US Navy.

### JB-1: probably keep it

JB-1 was Northrop's own flying-wing jet-bomb approach. The broad **requirement** was stimulated by knowledge that pilotless long-range bombs were possible, but the vehicle wasn't simply a V-1 copy. NASA's historical treatment distinguishes the American Northrop winged JB work from the Americanized V-1 JB-2. citeturn300046search37

So:

> **German capability inspiration: yes. German hardware dependency: no.**

That means a neutral America can absolutely fund a Northrop pilotless-bomber demonstrator.

Probably not very aggressively.

But it can exist.

---

# 5. Unguided rockets survive almost untouched conceptually

This category is straightforward.

American research into:

- aircraft rockets;
- JATO;
- artillery rockets;
- naval bombardment rockets;
- folding-fin aerial rockets;
- antitank rockets;

doesn't need Germany or Japan.

Production quantities are another question. The historical war creates enormous demand for things like HVAR, Tiny Tim, FFAR families, and battlefield rockets. Neutral America doesn't need millions.

But the technology is domestic and sufficiently obvious that experiments continue.

GALCIT/Aerojet's JATO work is particularly safe because it sits at the root of the California rocket establishment rather than being a captured-A4 project. citeturn543767search10

So an AltWWII America should not mysteriously be deficient at **rocket motors**.

Its weakness is going to be in **large high-energy ballistic systems and integrated guided-weapon doctrine**, not in understanding solid propellants or small rockets.

---

# 6. The really consequential split: JPL rockets versus captured V-2 rockets

This is where America actually falls behind Germany badly.

The historical American Army rocket effort has **two branches that are often conflated**.

### Branch A: indigenous Caltech/JPL

This gives us:

- Private series;
- WAC Corporal;
- Corporal;
- later Sergeant ancestry;
- propulsion and guidance research;
- sounding-rockets.

The Army's ORDCIT effort begins in 1944. Reports of German long-range missiles helped justify it, but American engineers didn't need to disassemble a V-2 before building the WAC/Corporal line. citeturn543767search0turn543767search1

**This branch survives.**

Probably smaller and slower, but very definitely alive.

I would classify it:

> **German-inspired requirement, American technology.**

That is exactly the sort of program your America should possess.

### Branch B: captured A4/V-2 exploitation

This gives us a very different list.

| Historical program | German dependency | Alt fate |
|---|---|---|
| **Captured V-2 launches at White Sands** | Total | **Absent** |
| **Operation Paperclip rocket team** | Total | **Absent** |
| **Hermes V-2 exploitation work** | Very high | **Exact program absent/reconstituted** |
| **Bumper** | Captured V-2 + WAC Corporal | **Absent** |
| **Redstone** | Direct V-2/von Braun descendant | **Absent** |
| **Jupiter** | Redstone/von Braun institutional descendant | **Historical form absent** |
| **Juno launch vehicles** | Redstone/Jupiter descendant | **Historical form absent** |
| **Saturn lineage** | von Braun/ABMA institutional ancestry | **Historical form absent** |

This is the single biggest American technological casualty of the German victory.

Historical postwar America launched dozens of captured V-2s, interrogated and employed the Peenemünde team, and used that knowledge as part of its large-rocket development base. NASA's history explicitly describes Bumper as a captured V-2 carrying a WAC Corporal upper stage, while Army history identifies the German specialists brought under Paperclip as central to subsequent Army missile development. citeturn385174search0turn655756search11

Redstone is especially clear. The Army's own historical material places it in the Army missile lineage, while multiple official histories describe the American large-missile establishment as having directly exploited German V-2 technology. citeturn974123search23turn974123search14

So I would make this a hard canon rule:

> **There is no historical Redstone in AltWWII America.**

America will eventually build something occupying that performance category.

But it comes from an American tree.

That difference should ripple all the way into the American space program.

---

# 7. WAC Corporal, Aerobee and Viking give America a way back

This is important because we don't want to overcorrect and make America incapable of spaceflight.

**WAC Corporal survives.**

It came from the JPL/GALCIT program.

And that means the scientific sounding-rocket establishment survives too.

### Aerobee

Aerobee grew out of American high-altitude rocket research and was intended partly to provide scientists a practical sounding rocket rather than relying indefinitely on the finite stock of captured V-2s. citeturn385174search0

Without the V-2 stock, the reason to build an indigenous sounding rocket is actually **stronger**.

So I would preserve an Aerobee-like vehicle.

### Viking

Viking was a purpose-built Naval Research Laboratory sounding rocket rather than a V-2 copy. Historically, the Navy pursued it when it became obvious captured German rockets were finite. citeturn385174search0

Again, remove the captured rockets and the requirement does not disappear:

> “We need a high-altitude research rocket of our own.”

If anything, it becomes cleaner.

Thus I would retain **Viking or a recognizably similar NRL program**, though its schedule and dimensions should be reopened.

This means the American high-altitude family becomes:

> **GALCIT/JPL + NRL + Aerojet + domestic industry**

rather than:

> **GALCIT + captured V-2 + von Braun.**

America is behind.

It isn't helpless.

---

# 8. Atlas is a much harder case

I would **not** simply delete all American large-rocketry work after Redstone.

Convair's MX-774 contained substantial American engineering and became part of the ancestry of Atlas. But the historical postwar American ballistic-missile establishment was also explicitly exploiting what had been learned from the German missile effort. Air Force historical material describes postwar U.S. long-range missile development as leveraging the V-2 technology base. citeturn974123search8turn967969search3

So I'd classify Atlas as:

> **mixed ancestry, not a German copy.**

The decisive AltWWII problem is actually not technological.

It's doctrinal.

Why is America spending colossal sums to build a 5,000-mile ballistic missile?

Historically:

> nuclear warhead.

AltWWII:

> …a few tons of conventional explosive.

That does not remotely provide the same procurement argument.

So the likely answer is:

**MX-774-like research survives. Atlas-the-ICBM does not appear on the historical timetable.**

Its engineering instead filters into:

- high-altitude research;
- space launch studies;
- reentry research;
- possibly anti-satellite/interceptor work later.

When Germany launches Raumbote I in 1957, America suddenly has an excellent reason to pour money into that orphaned technology.

That is how America catches up.

Not because the nuclear deterrent demanded an ICBM in 1953.

---

# 9. Snark and Navaho are not the same category

This distinction is worth preserving.

### Snark

The Army Air Forces issued a requirement in August 1945 for a pilotless bomber with roughly intercontinental range. Northrop's answer was an American winged-missile design. Historically its ultimate purpose became nuclear strategic attack. citeturn595890search1turn967969search0

So Snark is:

**foreign-copy dependent? No.**

**nuclear strategic requirement dependent? Very heavily.**

In AltWWII, I could absolutely believe in an **experimental Northrop intercontinental pilotless bomber**.

I have much more trouble believing Congress buys operational squadrons of them to deliver conventional explosives.

So:

> **Snark survives as a prestigious, somewhat ridiculous test program; mass operational Snark probably doesn't.**

And that feels incredibly American for this setting.

### Navaho

Navaho is much more entangled with the German long-range rocket problem. The Air Force's official program history dates MX-770 to 1946 and makes it an ambitious supersonic long-range guided missile. citeturn967969search1 The broader postwar missile-development environment was explicitly shaped by German V-1/V-2 demonstration of long-range unmanned strike. citeturn974123search4

I would therefore **not preserve historical Navaho cleanly**.

American ramjet research certainly continues.

American supersonic missile work certainly continues.

North American Aviation certainly can propose something.

But without captured German rocket expertise and without a nuclear delivery mission, the historical:

> booster + Mach 3 ramjet + 5,000-mile strategic missile

program loses much of its reason for being.

So Navaho becomes either:

- a smaller high-speed research missile;
- a supersonic target;
- a propulsion demonstrator;
- or a much later conventional cruise-missile ancestor.

This is one of those cases where I'd preserve the **engineering questions**, not the historical weapon.

---

# 10. Air-to-air missiles: America gets here independently

This may be the most important answer to your specific hypothetical.

The United States does **not** need the Ruhrstahl X-4 to invent an air-to-air missile.

It had multiple domestic lines.

### Gorgon

The Navy had a wartime guided-missile program experimenting with air-to-air and other configurations. Navy historical surveys list Gorgon among the indigenous guided-weapons projects of the period. citeturn447842search16

### Firebird

The XAAM-A-1 Firebird began development in **1946**, evolving from American unguided air-to-air rockets. citeturn967969search14

That's nearly perfect for AltWWII.

I would retain Firebird.

It may actually become slightly more institutionally important because there is no captured X-4 sitting in a museum screaming:

> Germans already tried this.

The Americans can regard Firebird as an unusually novel American line.

### Falcon

Hughes's Falcon development began in the immediate postwar period as an American interceptor missile project. The broader interceptor/missile test infrastructure was already American. citeturn967969search18turn967969search20

Again:

> **keep.**

### Sparrow

Keep.

It's a Navy radar-guided AAM line built around American fleet-air-defense requirements and American radar expertise. Navy records show Sparrow testing at Point Mugu by 1949. citeturn318502search5

### Sidewinder

And most importantly:

> **Sidewinder does not need German Madrid.**

China Lake's Sidewinder was an indigenous American infrared missile effort.

This means one of the setting's most interesting intelligence ironies should be exactly what you suggested.

In, say, 1951–53, China Lake engineers may be immensely proud of solving the problem of making a compact infrared-homing fighter missile.

They might genuinely believe they are at or near the global frontier.

They have no reason to know that German engineers had achieved crude autonomous IR interception trials **six or seven years earlier**.

That isn't American stupidity.

It's secrecy.

The Germans never used the weapon.

Britain never captured one.

There was no Peenemünde occupation.

There was no Paperclip interrogation.

The intelligence picture says:

> Germany is known to have guided weapons.

It does not say:

> Here is the reticle geometry of their 1946 infrared AAM.

Thus I think the American AAM line becomes:

**Gorgon/Firebird experimentation → Falcon/Sparrow → Sidewinder-type IR weapon**

with **no German technical inheritance at all**.

The historical Sidewinder and Sparrow traditions remained thoroughly domestic Navy developments. citeturn318502search5turn318502search9

What changes is **timing and confidence**.

America probably gets there later because it has no air war forcing rapid solution.

# 11. And this means the first American “heat seeker” does not have to be Sidewinder

This is the strange bit I think is worth exploiting.

America already had Felix.

So the developmental narrative can be:

> 1944–47: infrared bombs work badly enough to be interesting.

> late 1940s: engineers experiment with using the same principle against aircraft.

> early 1950s: Navy/Army-Air-Corps programs independently converge on a practical small seeker.

The intellectual leap is **application**, not discovery of infrared detection.

This makes America's eventual shock upon seeing German archival Ruhrstahl/Madrid material even better.

The reaction isn't:

> “They knew infrared existed?”

It's:

> **“They put it in an air-to-air weapon in 1946?”**

That is much more credible.

# 12. SAMs: Nike is the major surprise survivor

A lot of people assume American SAM development is simply a response to the V-2 or German air-defense research.

It isn't.

An Army antiaircraft board called in January 1944 for a guided antiaircraft weapon against high-performance aircraft **without requiring a specific foreign weapon to prompt the requirement**. Bell Laboratories subsequently became involved in what became Nike. The historical record distinguishes this from separate V-2-driven ballistic-missile-defense work. citeturn180910view0

So:

> **Nike survives.**

And I think it survives quite strongly.

Neutral America still possesses:

- strategic cities;
- naval bases;
- factories;
- bombers getting faster and higher;
- radar;
- antiaircraft artillery establishments.

The question:

> “Can radar direct a guided projectile against a bomber?”

is entirely natural.

That means America may legitimately believe in 1946–48 that **Nike is one of the world's most advanced air-defense projects**, because Washington does not know how far Wasserfall has actually gone.

This is exactly the kind of parallel invention the setting needs.

### GAPA

The Army Air Forces' GAPA branch similarly survives as a domestic high-speed guided-antiaircraft project. Historically the Nike/GAPA split emerged from American institutional development, with GAPA later contributing to Bomarc. citeturn180910view0turn180910view1

So early postwar America has **two competing SAM cultures** without having copied Wasserfall.

That is excellent.

---

# 13. What does *not* survive cleanly: Thumper, Wizard and early ABM work

Historical American anti-ballistic-missile studies were very directly stimulated by the V-2.

The Army's wartime missile history separates the ordinary bomber-defense Nike requirement from projects intended to stop ballistic missiles like the German A4. citeturn554174view0turn180910view1

Thus:

**Nike:** survives.

**Thumper/Wizard as urgent V-2-defense programs:** much weaker.

America certainly knows that German ballistic rockets exist.

It can do paper studies.

But New York is not being bombarded by them.

There are no captured trajectory data sets.

There are no recovered guidance sections sitting at White Sands.

So I would put American ballistic interception before 1957 in the category:

> **interesting theoretical work with periodic funding, not a national program.**

Then Raumbote I changes the mood overnight.

If Germany can put an object into orbit, everybody in Washington understands that the energy problem behind a very long-range ballistic missile is solved.

Now missile defense becomes politically serious.

---

# 14. Navy SAMs split into two categories

This needs the same discipline.

### Bumblebee: foreign-capability inspired, but American technology

The Navy's Project Bumblebee emerged from concern over guided missiles attacking the fleet. Contemporary Navy/Army histories tie the 1944 requirement to defending task forces against guided weapons launched by aircraft. citeturn554174view0

That's **foreign inspiration**, principally the demonstrated German guided-bomb capability.

Fritz X and Hs 293 had shown Britain that an aircraft could release a guided weapon outside conventional gun-bombing geometry. Allied intelligence was actively developing jamming by 1943. citeturn379806search4

A neutral American Navy can learn **that much**.

Britain has every reason to tell Washington:

> “Germany has aircraft-launched guided bombs and they're dangerous.”

It does not have to give America every captured component.

Thus I would retain **Bumblebee**, but smaller and slower.

Its descendants—Talos, Terrier and later Tartar—can therefore still emerge as American naval SAMs.

Not copies of Wasserfall.

Not copies of anything Japanese.

Just an American answer to an observed foreign capability.

### Little Joe and Lark: delete or radically rejustify

These are the opposite.

The wartime emergency around close-in guided antiaircraft weapons was heavily connected to the kamikaze threat. The historical Navy record explicitly ties that late-war work to the Japanese suicide-aircraft problem. citeturn554174view0

AltWWII America has no kamikaze campaign.

So:

> **No historical Little Joe urgency. No historical Lark urgency.**

You could reuse those names later if you wanted.

But the historical programs should not simply appear because they're in a real-world equipment list.

---

# 15. The postwar target-drone program absolutely survives

And this is a really nice American parallel to the German Fi 103/FZG lineage we just established.

Historically, in 1948 the Air Force's Pilotless Aircraft Branch issued a requirement for a high-subsonic jet-powered aerial target. Ryan won it, producing the Q-2/Firebee family. citeturn414426search0

This requirement needs no war booty whatsoever.

In fact, AltWWII arguably makes it **more necessary**.

America has:

- Nike;
- GAPA;
- Sparrow;
- Firebird;
- experimental air-defense radars;

and no foreign war in which to test them.

So how do you prove your missile can hit something?

**Drones.**

Thus the United States and Germany arrive independently at almost the same institutional solution.

Germany:

> Fi 103 → *Flugziel* establishment → increasingly sophisticated target drones.

America:

> Fahrney/TDR → Pilotless Aircraft Branch → Ryan Firebee-type targets.

This is extremely useful because it means Germany doesn't get an automatic monopoly on later UAV development.

Both powers possess deep unmanned-test-aircraft cultures.

But neither necessarily recognizes them as future frontline aircraft.

Without Vietnam, America's Firebee probably remains a target/research platform much longer; historically, modified Firebees eventually became reconnaissance UAVs during Vietnam. citeturn414426search4

So both countries may independently reach the 1970s with engineers saying:

> “We have been flying unmanned aircraft for thirty years.”

and generals answering:

> “Yes. Targets.”

That institutional blindness is believable.

# 16. The American tactical missile tree mostly survives

This is where removing Germany matters less.

### Corporal

**Keep.**

### Sergeant

**Keep, probably delayed somewhat.**

It's fundamentally the American solid-propellant successor to Corporal and helped build indigenous large-solid-motor competence. citeturn437716search4

### Honest John

**Concept survives; exact historical program is weaker.**

An unguided battlefield rocket carrying conventional HE is completely plausible.

But much of the historical enthusiasm for very large battlefield rockets came from tactical nuclear delivery.

No nukes means the Army asks:

It can still be useful.

It just isn't automatically transformational.

### Little John

Same problem, only more so.

Possible conventional rocket.

Less important.

### Lacrosse

**Good survivor.**

A guided battlefield missile intended to deliver conventional precision against hard points has a real role even without nuclear weapons.

### Redstone

**Delete exact lineage.**

As above.

### Pershing

**Delete exact historical requirement.**

Pershing's historical job is inseparable from the theater nuclear ballistic-missile competition.

American rocketry can eventually produce something in that range category, but I would not carry Pershing across merely because the name exists.

### Lance

Same basic problem.

A conventional precision theater missile could arise.

Historical Lance as part of the tactical-nuclear artillery family does not have a strong reason to.

# 17. Antitank missiles produce another major divergence: France

This is one I would definitely change in the setting.

Historically, the United States **did** directly use foreign antitank guided missiles.

The Army followed the French SS.10 program, tested it in 1953, later purchased it, and also acquired ENTAC and SS.11 as interim weapons. The Army's own history says this explicitly. citeturn437716search0turn437716search1

But AltWWII doesn't have historical NATO France.

Therefore:

> **The SS.10 → ENTAC/SS.11 American interim path probably disappears.**

That matters because historically American dissatisfaction with those systems sits in the background of the domestic TOW solution.

Fortunately, America has its own branch.

### Dart

The Army began a domestic wire-guided antitank project after its early studies; the Dart used a wire command link unreeling behind the missile. citeturn437716search2

In this setting **Dart becomes more important**, because there isn't a friendly French arsenal ready to sell an interim weapon.

It might still fail.

In fact I'd rather it still have substantial problems.

But instead of:

> Dart fails → buy French missiles → build TOW,

we get:

> Dart struggles → continue American wire-guidance research → improved domestic follow-on → TOW-equivalent.

### TOW

Keep.

Its mature guidance architecture came out of American in-house development starting in the later 1950s/early 1960s. citeturn437716search0

And notice how well this complements what we've just done with Germany.

Germany concludes from X-4:

### Shillelagh, Dragon, Hellfire

These are all quite plausible domestic descendants once America has an antitank-guided-weapon establishment.

# 18. Bomarc, Hawk, Redeye and Stinger

These deserve separate treatment because none requires captured German technology.

### Bomarc

Bomarc evolves from American GAPA and missile-defense work. Historically it becomes part of the Cold War continental bomber-defense system. citeturn180910view1turn967969search9

So:

**historical schedule and massive deployment:** probably changes.

There is still a very real reason for America to fear high-speed German strategic aircraft.

Strong survivor.

# 19. Nuclear weapons eliminate an enormous amount of the historical missile tree

This is probably the single largest *doctrinal* edit after Paperclip.

These historical American systems are either absent or radically repurposed because their central mission is delivering nuclear weapons:

**Genie** — nuclear air-to-air rocket: **gone**.

**Nike Hercules nuclear role** — gone; an improved conventional Nike successor may retain the name.

**Thor IRBM** — historical strategic requirement largely gone.

**Jupiter IRBM** — historical requirement and Redstone ancestry both gone.

**Atlas ICBM deployment** — no nuclear rationale; research ancestry survives.

**Titan I/II strategic missile programs** — no historical rationale.

**Minuteman** — essentially no reason to build the historical silo force.

**Polaris/Poseidon/Trident** — no ballistic-missile submarine deterrent. The current naval reference already correctly excludes a strategically important SSBN force. fileciteturn10file7

**Skybolt** — gone.

**Hound Dog's historical nuclear penetration mission** — gone.

**SRAM** — gone.

**nuclear ALCM force** — gone.

This doesn't mean the technologies evaporate.

It means they appear where there is a conventional economic case:

- space launch;
- reconnaissance;
- ASAT;
- hard-target conventional attack;
- missile defense;
- long-range antiship strike;
- precision attack.

That is a fundamentally different rocket economy.

# 20. Matador and Mace are likely survivors—but as conventional weapons

The Air Force's Matador/Mace family is a domestic American winged-missile lineage. AFLCMC describes Mace as an improved Matador, using terrain-comparison navigation rather than the earlier radio-command scheme. citeturn967969search4turn967969search5

is entirely sensible in AltWWII—particularly once German cruise missiles become publicly known.

# 21. Regulus is where the missing JB-2 really bites

Historically, American submarines experimented with the Loon—the navalized JB-2—before the Navy moved into Regulus. citeturn318502search7turn318502search1

# 23. Harpoon is the archetype of a later “Inspired, not copied” program

for

# 24. Ballistic missile defense almost completely changes

Historical Nike Zeus → Sentinel → Safeguard is deeply tied to the nuclear ballistic-missile contest.

Without nuclear ICBMs, spending billions to intercept a conventional missile carrying a modest explosive load is much harder to justify.

So I would not preserve the historical American ABM complex.

Instead, the trigger becomes **space warfare**.

This is where the German path you just established gives America its later requirement.

Once Germany demonstrates:

- reliable orbital launch;
- orbital reconnaissance;
- exoatmospheric intercept technology;
- eventual ASAT capability;

the United States suddenly needs high-energy interceptors for targets that are genuinely worth the missile cost.

And America has an indigenous precedent for air-launched exoatmospheric experimentation. Historical American programs eventually demonstrated air-launched ASAT concepts, culminating in the 1985 F-15/ASM-135 satellite intercept. citeturn913978search0turn913978search1

So I'd expect an American ASAT program in AltWWII to be **domestic but foreign-triggered**.

The German demonstration says:

> capability required.

American engineers answer:

> aircraft + rocket stages + terminal seeker.

No captured German stage needed.

# 25. The American UAV story survives too

This deserves a final explicit note because of what we just did with Germany.

America has an entirely independent unmanned lineage:

> **Kettering Bug → N2C target drones → Fahrney → TDN/TDR → XBDR → postwar target drones → Firebee.**

Germany has:

> **Fi 103 → FZG target conversion → increasingly sophisticated *Flugziel* vehicles.**

So by the 1960s, both powers can possess very mature remotely piloted target-aircraft establishments.

Neither copied the other.

The difference is institutional ancestry.

Germany's comes from a **flying bomb turned target**.

America's comes from a **target drone turned assault drone turned target again**.

That is a fantastic piece of parallel technological evolution.

And without Vietnam, **both** may be surprisingly slow to make the final conceptual leap to:

> put a camera and weapons on it and deploy it operationally.

## The bigger conclusion

What this produces is, I think, **exactly the American technological position you've been aiming for**.

America is not backward in the sense that its engineers don't know how electronics work.

In some individual areas it is genuinely at the frontier.

By the late 1940s it can plausibly possess American laboratories working on:

- television-guided weapons;
- radar-homing weapons;
- infrared seekers;
- air-to-air missiles;
- radar-directed SAMs;
- remotely controlled aircraft;
- target drones;
- inertial/autopilot systems;
- solid rockets;
- liquid rockets;
- sounding rockets.

But these are **separate boxes**.

Germany has been forced by the war to combine the boxes.

The German night-defense establishment asks:

> radar sees bomber → computer predicts interception → missile flies there → seeker finishes interception.

An American engineer can understand every individual noun in that sentence while not realizing that Germany has already assembled the sentence.

And then there is the large-rocketry gap. America has JPL and NRL, but it never gets the extraordinary historical shortcut of:

> **“Here are intact A4s, the engineering records, and a large part of the team that built them.”**

So the real American lag after 1947 should be **least severe in small guided weapons and worst in integrated missile systems and large ballistic rockets**.

That creates a very good sequence of American shocks:

**late 1940s:** “We are doing remarkably advanced guided-weapon research.”

**early/mid-1950s:** evidence accumulates that German production weapons are ahead of American experimental ones.

**1957, Raumbote I:** “Their large-rocket program is much farther ahead than ours.”

**late 1950s:** American missile and space funding finally becomes systematic rather than laboratory-fragmented.

**1966, Maracaibo:** “The missile itself isn't the problem. Their whole detection-guidance-interception network is mature.”

That fits very neatly with the existing canon in which experimental rockets belong to a small joint establishment before the Philippine War, Raumbote and the Philippine experience create Aerospace Command in 1958, and Kennedy later turns it into the Aerospace Force. fileciteturn10file14

And there's one revision I would already make to our existing references because of this audit: **any early AltWWII American rocket chronology that casually imports Redstone, Jupiter, Juno, or a von-Braun-style launcher family needs to be treated as suspect.** America absolutely gets into space. But its launch-vehicle family needs to descend from **JPL, Aerojet, NRL/Viking, Convair/North American domestic research, and the 1957 German shock**, not from a German engineering team that it never captures.

## Turn 1118 — Assistant
