Yes. I think this works, and it gives the United States and Germany two answers to the same naval problem that are **genuinely incompatible without either being obviously foolish**.

There is one existing-canon collision worth cleaning up first. The current naval reference has *Admiral Scheer* publicly demonstrating German VLS technology in **1974**, while *Wotan* commissions in **1978** and *Siegfried* follows in **1982**. *Wotan* carries four 150 mm guns and 96 missile cells and is explicitly a *Großes Lenkwaffenschiff*, not a German battleship. fileciteturn14file4 I actually think we should preserve those dates. The 1978 shock doesn't need to be “America sees VLS for the first time.” It can be something more consequential:

> **In 1974 America sees VLS as a clever German cruiser weapon. In 1978 it realizes Germany has designed an entire 28,000-ton major combatant around it as the principal battery.**

That makes *Wotan* much more disturbing.

## The American “drone versus missile” distinction works

By the 1960s and 1970s, an outside weapons engineer may increasingly argue that some American naval assault drones **are functionally cruise missiles**. The United States Navy can nevertheless maintain a meaningful institutional distinction.

A German cruise missile is a **munition**. It lives in a container or cell, receives targeting information, is fired, navigates to its target, and is consumed.

The American naval assault drone remains an **unmanned aircraft**, even when expendable. It can have folding wings, receive continuous commands, send imagery back, loiter, change targets, abort, attack from an unexpected direction, and in more expensive forms return. It belongs to naval aviation. Its operator is thinking about a flying vehicle rather than a round of ammunition.

That distinction gets blurry, but bureaucratically it matters enormously.

The Navy therefore looks at a proposed shipboard cruise missile and asks:

> What does this give us that the assault-drone group doesn't already provide?

And for a long time the answer isn't sufficiently compelling.

The Germans answer the same question differently because their missile establishment is enormously more mature and their Kriegsmarine does not possess an American-scale carrier-drone establishment. German doctrine already says that the surface fleet fixes, threatens, and displays while the submarine arm actually destroys. fileciteturn14file4 Putting autonomous missiles into submarines and eventually surface ships therefore fits the institution naturally.

So this gives us two parallel families:

**Germany:** missile as stored naval ammunition.

**America:** unmanned aircraft as replenishable naval aviation.

That is an excellent divergence.

## The American advantage isn't exactly “200 versus 96”

It's **magazine depth versus salvo density**.

That distinction is important.

Suppose a mature American carrier can carry something on the order of 150–200 relatively compact folding assault drones under a heavy wartime load. I think that is entirely plausible as an eventual upper-end figure, especially if many are much smaller than manned jets. But I would not say that the carrier therefore possesses a 200-round missile battery.

Those 200 drones have to be brought from storage, inspected, fueled or powered, programmed, armed, moved to launching positions, launched, connected to control networks, and in many cases assigned operator or data-link capacity.

The *Wotan's* 96 cells are different.

Those are **96 immediately available launch positions**. fileciteturn14file4 The Germans can potentially throw a large proportion of the relevant strike load into the air in a short period.

So:

| German VLS | American assault-drone carrier |
|---|---|
| Very high immediate salvo density | Much deeper sustainable aviation magazine |
| High missile speed | Slower attack vehicles |
| Little launch preparation | Deck/rail launch cycle |
| Autonomous after launch | More operator/data-link dependence |
| Difficult at-sea rearm | Easier aviation-style replenishment |
| Limited retargeting/observation on early systems | Excellent human-in-loop flexibility |
| Expensive individual missiles | Potentially much cheaper expendable drones |
| Excellent surprise attack | Better persistence and repeated attack |

And the VLS reload criticism is real. Even the historical U.S. Navy only demonstrated reloading a modern VLS **while underway in open ocean in 2024**; before that, expended VLS ships normally had to return to a suitable rearming location. The Navy itself describes underway VLS rearming as a major increase in persistent combat power because it avoids withdrawing ships from the fight. citeturn445204search0turn445204search12

So an American admiral looking at *Wotan* in 1978 can make an entirely legitimate argument:

> “Those 96 weapons are terrifying. Then they're gone.”

Meanwhile his carrier may start with fewer immediately launchable weapons but can keep generating assault-drone sorties, receive replacement drones and ordnance from auxiliaries, rearrange payloads, and continue fighting.

The mistake would be assuming that therefore *Wotan* isn't dangerous.

## And that is exactly the mistake the American battleship school would be tempted to make

The American interpretation of *Wotan* practically writes itself.

Germany has removed the traditional heavy battery and produced a nuclear-powered, 28,000-ton ship with four 150 mm guns, 96 missile cells, helicopters, command spaces, and extensive electronics. fileciteturn14file4

The American battleship establishment looks at it and says:

> **“They've built a giant cruiser.”**

Or, less politely:

> **“They've spent battleship money on an air cruiser without airplanes.”**

That conclusion is not entirely wrong.

Under **American doctrine**, *Wotan* is a poor capital ship.

It cannot stand in a gun engagement with an American battleship.

It lacks battleship armor.

Its main offensive battery is finite.

Once its long-range magazines are empty, the remaining 150 mm battery is light-cruiser artillery by American standards.

An Iowa or later American BB can continue firing enormous quantities of conventional gun ammunition after the German missile battery is substantially depleted.

But the corrective is that **Germany didn't design Wotan to be an American battleship**.

Germany's doctrine doesn't expect *Wotan* to close with an American BB and exchange broadsides. The established German fleet model gives the destructive role primarily to U-boats and guided weapons. fileciteturn14file4

So the German argument is:

> “Why would we allow your battleship to reach gun range?”

And the American response is:

> “Because you eventually run out of missiles.”

And Germany responds:

> “You have to survive them first.”

That is a fantastic unresolved naval argument.

Neither navy gets the war necessary to prove which side has misunderstood the other.

## America therefore does **not** need to copy VLS

I agree strongly with this.

The 1974 *Admiral Scheer* demonstration produces technical interest. The Navy studies the launcher. Some ordnance people undoubtedly love it. There are probably American VLS experimental installations.

But the institutional response can be:

> **Interesting launcher. Wrong fleet.**

America already has trainable SAM launchers, deck-mounted weapons, aircraft, assault drones, guns and a very large carrier establishment. Nothing about seeing a German vertical cell forces the United States to reorganize its fleet around vertical magazines.

*Wotan* in 1978 intensifies the debate without resolving it.

This also lets us keep something visually distinctive about American ships through the 1980s. They don't suddenly acquire the giant rectangular VLS farms we're used to seeing on modern warships. Their decks retain:

- large gun turrets;
- trainable missile launchers;
- torpedo installations;
- drone-handling structures;
- radar directors;
- aviation facilities;
- and increasingly numerous close-defense guns.

They look like an evolutionary continuation of the mid-century warship rather than our familiar missile destroyer.

That's good setting design.

---

# But America absolutely still needs SAMs

I would resist one part of your proposed fork:

> **CIWS should not replace the interceptor missile. It should replace faith in the interceptor missile.**

America already has a domestic naval SAM lineage. We established that Project Bumblebee survives because it is an American response to the observed guided-air-attack problem, not captured German engineering.

And your existing American doctrine says AA is distributed across the fleet.

So the defensive model becomes layered:

**Carrier fighters** try to kill the launch aircraft, reconnaissance platform, or attacking drone before launch.

**Longer-range ship SAMs** try to kill aircraft and incoming missiles outside the formation.

**Guns and electronic countermeasures** deal with penetrators.

And then America develops a brutally effective **automatic terminal gun system** because admirals conclude that some missiles are inevitably going to leak through.

That last layer becomes distinctively American.

A nomenclature correction: **CIWS is Close-In Weapon System**, normally pronounced “sea-whiz,” rather than Close-In Weapon Support System.

Historically, the real Phalanx prototype was being tested on a ship in **1973**, and Phalanx entered fleet use around 1980. citeturn777488search2turn777488search7 So technologically, having an AltWWII American system mature during the later 1970s is entirely comfortable.

But I would start the American program **before Wotan**.

America already knows anti-ship missiles exist. Japan has them. Germany has them. American intelligence doesn't need to know about submerged German VLS to understand the terminal-defense problem.

My preferred sequence would be:

**late 1960s:** automatic radar-controlled terminal-defense experiments.

**early 1970s:** first serious gun-CIWS prototypes, tested heavily against America's own target/assault drones.

**1974:** *Admiral Scheer* VLS demonstration increases urgency.

**1978:** *Wotan* causes the “salvo problem” to become a major fleet-planning issue.

**c. 1979–82:** CIWS becomes standard on first-line American combatants.

This gives us something especially elegant: **America's drone establishment helps America learn to shoot down missiles.**

The Navy has decades of remotely controlled aerial targets. It can make them approach ships, maneuver, emit signals, dive toward the vessel, and eventually imitate cruise-missile profiles. That is exactly the kind of target infrastructure a CIWS development program needs. Modern Phalanx remains a radar-controlled Gatling-gun system whose purpose is precisely the last-ditch engagement of antiship missiles and aircraft. citeturn777488search1

## And the Americans would put CIWS on practically everything

This follows directly from the distributed-AA doctrine you established earlier.

The battleship doesn't have one CIWS.

It may eventually have **several**, because it has deck area, electrical power, fire-control capacity and an extraordinarily high strategic value.

The carrier has several.

Heavy cruisers have them.

Light cruisers become particularly sophisticated in coordinating the air-defense picture.

Destroyers absolutely have them.

Even frigates probably get one once the mount becomes compact and cheap enough.

The American answer to missiles therefore isn't:

> build our own Wotan.

It's:

> **make the fleet extraordinarily difficult to saturate.**

That's beautifully consistent with the battleship's broader American design philosophy.

The battleship's argument becomes:

> “The Germans assume their missiles will disable us before we reach effective range. Then our job is to make sure they don't.”

And now armor, compartmentation, electronic warfare, decoys, distributed SAMs and CIWS all become parts of the same capital-ship philosophy.

---

# Wotan creates a new American naval concept: surviving the first salvo

This may become one of the defining American fleet exercises of the 1980s.

The entire fleet is trained around a sequence:

**detect → disperse slightly while maintaining mutual defense → CAP intercept → electronic deception → area-defense fire → terminal gun defense → damage control → re-form → counterattack.**

The American battle fleet does not necessarily expect to prevent every hit.

That's important.

It expects to remain a functioning fleet **after being hit**.

And that connects directly back to why America still believes in battleships.

A missile cruiser doctrine places enormous value on preventing the hit.

The American capital-ship doctrine says:

> **Prevent as many as possible. Survive the rest.**

This may produce some very heavy later American ships.

Not because the US Navy hasn't noticed missiles.

Because it has noticed them and drawn a different conclusion.

---

# The carrier's drone magazine then becomes the American counter-salvo

Once the German attack has been survived, America doesn't necessarily respond with missiles.

It begins generating drone attacks.

And this is where the 200-drone idea becomes doctrinally meaningful even if the precise number stays open.

The carrier doesn't launch 200 simultaneously.

It may launch:

twenty;

then another twenty;

then thirty;

then another package several hours later.

Some are decoys.

Some carry radar emitters.

Some are reconnaissance vehicles.

Some are television-controlled assault drones.

Some later ones carry antiradar or antiship weapons themselves.

That is a **campaign magazine**, not merely a salvo magazine.

The Germans possess greater instantaneous violence.

The Americans possess greater persistence.

That's the naval analogue of what we've been doing with American drones on land.

And a carrier can be replenished much more naturally by the fleet train. Packaged drone airframes, engines, warheads, electronics and fuel can be transferred as aviation stores and assembled or prepared aboard ship. It still isn't effortless, but it belongs to an existing replenishment system. VLS canisters are a much more awkward geometry; the historical Navy's very recent effort to solve underway reloading demonstrates just how significant that distinction can be. citeturn445204search3

---

## There is one fleet-design consequence we should not miss: detached heavy cruisers need drones too

Earlier we established that an American **heavy cruiser is the smallest normal center of an independent task force**.

That creates a problem.

If long-range American naval attack increasingly belongs to assault drones, what happens when there's no carrier?

The CA needs a limited drone establishment.

Not 200.

Something like a modest hangar or packaged magazine for reconnaissance and assault drones becomes almost unavoidable.

The light cruiser probably carries reconnaissance drones heavily because that's already its information role.

The heavy cruiser carries enough **assault drones** to give a detached force limited reach beyond its guns.

The battleship does not need a large drone air group because the carrier normally accompanies the main battle fleet, although its expanding command facilities can control drone operations.

That reinforces the whole hierarchy rather neatly:

**BB:** commands.

**CV:** generates mass aviation and drone striking power.

**CA:** commands small task groups and possesses limited organic drone attack.

**CL:** finds and tracks things.

**DD:** fights anything that penetrates the screen.

**FF:** hunts submarines.

The same drone technology manifests differently at every echelon.

---

# And yes, the 1985 near-war fits extremely well—but it has an existing antecedent

There is already a canonical **1967–68 Iceland crisis**, in which German and American fleets confront one another in the North Atlantic. The resulting Mid-Atlantic Ridge Accord places Iceland on the European side of the strategic division and the Americas on Washington's side. citeturn578581view3

That actually makes your proposed 1985 incident better.

It isn't the first time the fleets have confronted one another.

It's:

> **the closest they have come since Iceland.**

And the Falklands context gives everyone a reason to be nervous. Germany is covertly sustaining Argentina with undersea logistics during 1984–85, while American armed mediation is explicitly intended to stop the war becoming an overt German-American or German-British escalation. fileciteturn14file2

So imagine a large German surface exercise moving west in 1985.

Not crossing the Accord line.

Just approaching it.

Perhaps *Wotan* or *Siegfried*, one of the *Europa*-class carriers, a cruiser group, escorts, and submarines are conducting what the Germans regard as an entirely normal long-range fleet exercise.

For Berlin, it tests:

- fleet communications;
- nuclear endurance;
- submarine coordination;
- missile-defense architecture;
- long-range reconnaissance;
- operations near the western edge of Germany's accepted Atlantic space.

The Germans know the Falklands War is underway, but the exercise isn't an invasion force.

Washington sees something rather different:

> A German fleet with enormous long-range missile capacity is approaching the 1968 strategic boundary while German submarines are covertly sustaining Argentina.

That is a very reasonable thing to become frightened about.

So an American battleship-centered force begins shadowing it.

And **this is where the doctrinal contrast becomes dangerous**.

The Germans see American ships approaching and think:

> “They are monitoring the exercise. Obviously.”

The Americans see Wotan's VLS and think:

> “If those cells open, we may have minutes.”

So the American commander needs authorization logic that operates **before** the German first salvo.

That's how you get the reverse-Able-Archer quality.

I wouldn't have the Americans continuously illuminate *Wotan* with fire-control radar while secretly preparing to shoot, because German electronic-support measures would notice something that overt.

Make it subtler.

American passive sensors, aircraft, satellites and light cruisers maintain the track. Fire-control solutions are prepared. CAP is armed. Drone strike packages are put on alert. Battleship turrets have planned firing data. CIWS mounts are in automatic or near-automatic readiness.

And the order becomes something like:

> **If the German formation crosses the agreed line, launches a mass missile salvo westward, or turns in a manner assessed as an attack approach, engage.**

Then the Germans execute their scheduled turn.

Five miles or twenty minutes before whatever American threshold exists.

Nobody fires.

German after-action reports say something like:

> American shadowing remained assertive but professional.

The classified American record says:

> **Weapons release authority had been delegated and firing solutions were active.**

Then, twenty or thirty years later, German archives or American declassification finally allow the two sides to compare records and somebody realizes:

> “They were going to shoot us?”

That has exactly the reverse-Able-Archer character you're after.

And it also provides a perfect end point for the American Navy we're building.

By 1985 it remains convinced that it has solved the German missile problem **without becoming German**.

It has armored command ships, big guns, aviation cruisers full of fighters and assault drones, layered escorts, excellent ASW, trainable SAMs, dense close-in gun defenses, and enormous replenishment depth.

Germany looks at that fleet and probably thinks:

> **“They are still designing to survive a battle we have no intention of fighting at their preferred range.”**

America looks at *Wotan* and thinks:

> **“They've built a ship that becomes progressively less dangerous every time it fires.”**

And neither side has enough combat evidence to realize exactly where its own doctrine is wrong. That is a much stronger basis for the 1947–85 American battle-fleet development than converging everything toward the historical missile/carrier navy. memcite

Yes. I think this now gives us a coherent **American surface-fleet architecture**, and the heavy-gun question has a much better answer than either “fire control fixes everything” or “the only way to shoot farther is a bigger gun.”

The central correction is:

> **Fire control increases usable range. Ammunition and gun design increase physical range.**

The United States can push both very hard, and its drone establishment makes the first half unusually powerful.

The newer wartime audit already gives us the right starting point: *Montana* and *Ohio* complete with the balanced-fleet school intact, while America avoids the historical wartime pressure that turned the carrier into the uncontested capital ship. fileciteturn15file16 The older Naval Reference, by contrast, now needs substantial supersession: it had American battleships carrying surface missiles and treated heavy/light cruiser distinctions as largely obsolete by 1985. fileciteturn15file7 Under what you've now established, **both distinctions remain very real**.

## The drone complement fits the whole hierarchy

I think you've now found the right relationship between drones and guns.

The battleship's drones are principally **eyes for its guns and command system**. A BB doesn't need 100 assault drones because a carrier normally accompanies it. It does need a small independent reconnaissance establishment so its defining weapon doesn't become blind merely because carrier aviation is unavailable. That means aft launch rails, several recoverable reconnaissance/spotting drones, perhaps some expendable electronic or decoy vehicles later, and enough control equipment to direct other ships' drones as part of the fleet command function.

That latter point matters. By the 1960s–70s, the battleship can be the place where the **gunfire solution is calculated**, while a light cruiser or drone 40 kilometers away actually sees the target.

Modern NAVSEA work demonstrates the same basic concept in another technological setting: unmanned aircraft have been integrated into naval gunfire-control loops to spot targets and feed corrections to shipboard gun systems. citeturn497434search2turn497434search6 Your Navy simply institutionalizes that relationship decades earlier.

The heavy cruiser then needs a stronger independent drone package because it can become a task-force flagship. Your **roughly 10–12 expendable combat drones plus reconnaissance machines** feels like an excellent design target for a mature CA. It isn't an aircraft carrier. But a cruiser detached with four destroyers and two frigates isn't confined to gun range either.

The light cruiser probably has the **largest reconnaissance-drone establishment relative to its size**. That's already its reason for being: find, classify, relay, scout, coordinate the screen, kill enemy scouts and destroyers, and remain fast enough to choose whether it continues an engagement.

The destroyer is where I'd make one qualification. I don't think drones immediately replace the surface torpedo, because a heavyweight torpedo offers something an airborne drone cannot: a stealthy underwater attack carrying an enormous warhead against the hull below or near the waterline. But as assault drones gain range and reliability, the **large antiship torpedo battery probably does disappear from most American destroyers**. ASW torpedoes remain. A minority of destroyer officers may keep pushing heavyweight surface-attack torpedoes, but by the 1960s–70s the ordinary DD probably spends that weight on drones, AA, sonar and guns instead.

The frigate is the one place I'd push back on a 20–40 mm *main* gun. A 20 or 40 mm weapon makes perfect sense as close defense, but a blue-water frigate that is actually part of the battle fleet still needs something capable of dealing with a patrol craft, surfaced submarine, small merchant vessel, shore position, or disabled destroyer without calling somebody else. I'd expect something in the **3-inch/76 mm class as the normal minimum**, with some larger frigates receiving a 5-inch weapon. Its real money still goes into sonar, quieting, ASW weapons and eventually helicopters/drones.

## The cruiser-gun evolution is especially plausible

The United States already had the beginnings of the exact direction you're describing.

The *Worcester* design process explicitly explored rapid-firing **6-inch/47** light-cruiser batteries, while the *Des Moines* design lineage was built around **rapid-fire 8-inch/55** heavy-cruiser guns. citeturn497434search13turn497434search24 NAVSEA still preserves examples of both an automatic 8-inch triple mount and a later 8-inch/55 major-caliber automatic gun. citeturn497434search15

So the alternate American lesson can become:

> **Don't necessarily add barrels. Make each barrel work harder.**

That is very attractive after 1947 because fire control is simultaneously improving.

A 1950s CL may still have several twin 6-inch turrets. A later CL can plausibly move toward fewer automatic mounts with much higher sustained fire, more room for radar, drones, SAMs and command electronics.

The CA follows the same pattern more conservatively. Heavy-cruiser officers care about **individual-shell destructive power and sustained medium-long-range fire**, so twin and triple 8-inch automatic turrets remain much more culturally attractive. I wouldn't automatically enlarge the CA gun beyond 8 inches yet. An exceptionally fast-loading, long-barreled 8-inch with advanced ammunition may be more useful than turning every CA into another Alaska.

That also leaves the Alaska family as an instructive upper limit:

> when your “cruiser” starts needing battleship displacement to carry cruiser armor around 12-inch guns, perhaps you've stopped solving the cruiser problem.

## Fire control can buy a lot—but not infinity

Your intuition is right that a range once regarded as “wasteful potshots” can become a legitimate fighting range as the fire-control system improves.

Dahlgren's actual history is useful here. The Naval Ordnance Research Calculator was used specifically for **naval gunfire spotting doctrine**, and modern Navy gun-control systems exist precisely to turn sensor tracks, ballistic corrections and ship motion into precise firing solutions. citeturn497434search0turn497434search1

The American progression can therefore attack nearly every deterministic source of error:

radar-derived target range and bearing; exact own-ship motion; barrel wear; muzzle-velocity measurement; propellant temperature; atmospheric density; wind at different altitudes; Earth rotation at extreme ranges; shell ballistic tables; drone observation of fall of shot; and increasingly good prediction of enemy course.

That does something enormously valuable:

**the first salvo becomes much better.**

And subsequent salvos converge on the target much faster.

But there are three things computation cannot wish away.

One is **dispersion**. Two nominally identical rounds do not emerge from enormous naval guns with perfectly identical velocity and attitude.

Another is **time of flight**. At very long range, you're shooting at where a maneuvering ship is predicted to be a considerable time later.

And the third is **the ballistic envelope itself**. If the barrel, elevation and projectile can only throw the round 43 kilometers, no fire-control computer can calculate its way to 60.

So I would describe the American postwar research program as attacking range in layers.

| Development | What it actually buys |
|---|---|
| Better radar/computers/drone spotting | Makes existing long range worth using |
| Better shell aerodynamics | Extends range without radically changing the gun |
| Higher elevation | Adds some range where the mount previously constrained it |
| Longer barrel/higher velocity | Extends range, but adds wear, pressure and machinery penalties |
| Subcaliber sabot projectile | Much more range at the cost of shell mass |
| Rocket-assisted projectile | Major range gain, increasingly blurs gun/rocket categories |
| Guided/terminally corrected shell | Makes extreme-range fire against moving targets practical |
| Electromagnetic gun | Eventually attacks the range problem at the propulsion level |

And the historical numbers are quite revealing.

An Iowa 16"/50 firing conventional ammunition reached about **23.4 nautical miles**, roughly 43 kilometers, during long-range experimentation. citeturn783633search0

The U.S. Navy's experimental **16"/56** was estimated to have a maximum range around **52,000 yards**, about 47.5 kilometers. citeturn783633search1 So simply making the gun longer and hotter does **not** turn a 16-inch weapon into a 100-kilometer gun. You pay a lot for another few kilometers.

But now look at ammunition.

During the real Navy's late-1980s 16-inch modernization work, Dahlgren was already developing a **subcaliber extended-range 16-inch projectile intended to exceed 30 nautical miles**. citeturn370986search0

That is extremely important for AltWWII.

With a continuous battleship establishment rather than a resurrected one, America doesn't begin thinking about this in 1988.

It begins thinking about it in the **1950s**.

## So I think the American gun-range progression can be quite dramatic

Not magical—dramatic.

The first step after Montana probably isn't a new gun. It's **better 16-inch ammunition and better firing solutions**.

The 1940s 16"/50 remains roughly a 20-odd-nautical-mile practical weapon.

By the later 1950s, radar/computer/drone integration makes engagements near the outer conventional envelope much more credible than they were in 1945.

By the 1960s, optimized long-range projectiles could plausibly push the old 16-inch guns into a **25–30 nautical mile useful family**, depending on projectile type.

By the 1970s, a dedicated subcaliber extended-range projectile passing **30 nautical miles** is entirely believable. Historically, Dahlgren was already pursuing that exact result with the same basic gun system. citeturn370986search0 In our timeline, it simply arrives much earlier because the Navy has spent twenty-five uninterrupted years asking for it.

And that's where I would draw a hard distinction:

> **Thirty-ish nautical miles can remain recognizably “naval gunnery.”**

Once the Navy wants reliable **40, 50, 60 nautical mile attacks against a maneuvering ship**, fire control alone isn't sufficient anymore. The target has too much time to alter course.

Then the projectile itself needs some ability to correct.

The gun establishment will probably accept this reluctantly because it can say:

> “It's still a shell.”

And the assault-drone people will reply:

> “That's adorable. You've invented an incredibly violent little drone that starts its flight inside a gun barrel.”

That bureaucratic argument should absolutely exist.

## The 18-inch gun makes sense—but primarily as the final caliber escalation

And this is where your instinct that the next battleship should at least match *Yamato* becomes very easy to justify.

The United States **already built and tested an 18-inch naval gun**. Dahlgren's official history traces the 18"/48 project back to 1917; the same experimental gun was later converted to 16"/56 and then back into an 18-inch test weapon, with 18-inch firing conducted during the Second World War. citeturn783633search1

So the American Navy does not need to discover that an 18-inch weapon is technically possible.

And note the useful political point:

**18 inches = 457.2 mm.**

*Yamato* is 460 mm.

For practical public purposes, an American 18-inch gun is *Yamato-class firepower*. You don't need to invent a 19-inch monster merely to win a measuring contest by a few millimeters.

My preferred development would therefore be:

> **Montana and Ohio are the last twelve-gun 16-inch battleships. The first true postwar American battleship adopts nine 18-inch guns.**

Three triple turrets.

That reduces barrel count while enormously increasing individual-shell effect and freeing some weight compared with trying to mount twelve 18-inch weapons.

And then **caliber escalation stops**.

The battleship school can say:

> We already possess a shell about as large as is operationally sensible. Now improve range and rate of fire.

That is exactly the doctrinal shift you're describing.

The next forty years are not 18 → 20 → 22 inches.

They're:

**18"/48 or /50 → improved loading → improved projectiles → higher useful elevation → better barrel metallurgy → range-optimized rounds → drone-integrated fire control → subcaliber/assisted ammunition.**

That's a much more credible technological lineage.

## Rate of fire then becomes the harder engineering problem

A battleship projectile is enormous.

You can automate shell rooms, hoists, ramming, propellant handling and loading sequence, but an 18-inch automatic cannon isn't just a scaled-up 8-inch mount. The masses and stored energies become extraordinary.

So I wouldn't expect a 1950s 18-inch battleship to suddenly deliver five rounds per minute per barrel.

But sustained **2–2.5 rounds per minute** from a highly mechanized postwar mount would already be terrifying if it can be made reliable.

Nine barrels at two rounds per minute means **18 roughly 18-inch shells every minute**.

And because fire control is better, that isn't simply a larger shotgun pattern.

That's where the battleship school gets its real “alpha strike.”

Not necessarily one salvo.

Rather:

> **the ability to put several enormous, tightly controlled salvos into the target before the opposing formation can escape the gun envelope.**

---

# The drone makes long-range battleship fire much more dangerous than the raw gun statistic suggests

This is where your BB drone rails stop being flavor.

At 30 nautical miles, the battleship itself may not have a useful direct radar horizon against a low surface target.

Its spotter drone does.

So the battle can look like this:

The CL's reconnaissance network acquires the German formation.

The BB's command system accepts the track.

A battleship spotting drone moves high enough to maintain continuous line of sight.

The firing computer solves from the drone's target track.

The first salvo goes out before the battleship itself can directly see the enemy.

The drone observes splashes.

Corrections return digitally.

Second salvo.

That is basically **over-the-horizon naval gunfire enabled by unmanned aviation**.

And it's very American.

The carrier still creates the genuinely long arm.

But the battleship's own drones ensure that its gun envelope is not artificially shortened by the curvature of the Earth.

This is also exactly the kind of integration that gives the light cruiser tremendous value. The CL doesn't have to destroy the enemy itself to decide the fight. It may be the ship that makes the battleship's first accurate salvo possible.

---

# This changes the post-Wotan doctrine too

Once *Wotan* appears, the United States doesn't abandon the gun.

It makes the gun doctrine more aggressive.

The American tactical model becomes:

> **survive the missile salvo → preserve the reconnaissance picture → enter the extended gun envelope → establish gunfire superiority before Germany can disengage or rearm.**

That explains why range becomes so politically important after 1978.

If an American 18-inch battleship can reliably engage at 30+ nautical miles, that's another 30 miles the German formation has to stay outside—not simply the old visual battle range.

And every additional five miles matters because it enlarges the area in which Germany cannot safely loiter after its missile salvo.

The American naval officer therefore isn't trying to out-range a cruise missile with a gun.

That's impossible and unnecessary.

He's trying to **shrink the German post-salvo sanctuary**.

That's a much more coherent requirement.

---

# Railguns then become almost inevitable as a serious research program

And I agree strongly with your later implication.

Historically, the U.S. Navy's electromagnetic railgun program advertised a 32-megajoule launcher capable, in principle, of firing a guided projectile over **100 nautical miles**, with Mach-5 terminal velocity and a desired rate of 6–12 rounds per minute. citeturn558215search5

In our setting, somebody in the American Battleship Bureau sees those numbers and does not think:

> “Interesting futuristic technology.”

He thinks:

> **“You finally solved the question we've been asking since 1948.”**

That changes the institutional support dramatically.

There are still enormous engineering problems—rail wear, projectile survival, pulsed-power storage, thermal load, electromagnetic stress and rate-of-fire durability. So I wouldn't automatically declare that America gets a perfect operational railgun simply because the battleship lobby likes it.

And one correction to the nuclear-ship idea: **a reactor by itself isn't enough**. An ordinary nuclear steam plant produces propulsion power; a railgun needs enormous bursts of electrical energy. The ship needs substantial generators, power conditioning and energy-storage architecture.

But a large nuclear battleship is about the best possible naval host from which to begin solving that problem.

It has:

space;

weight margin;

a huge electrical plant;

damage control;

large magazines and workshops;

and an institutional reason to accept a massive experimental mount.

So I'd expect the United States to treat naval railgun research much more seriously in the **1990s–2000s**, with a battleship serving as the natural full-scale test platform.

And if railgun technology ever matures enough for service in this setting, it does not replace the battleship tradition.

It becomes the culmination of it.

Chemical propellant had finally reached the point where getting another ten or twenty miles required increasingly strange shells.

The gun establishment changes the propellant.

---

## So I'd currently make the American gun doctrine this

The battleship is no longer trying to maximize **caliber** after the first postwar generation. An 18-inch weapon settles that question.

The long-term competition becomes:

> **How rapidly can I put very large projectiles onto a maneuvering target, and how far away can I do it while still calling the result deliberate gunfire rather than statistical bombardment?**

That creates an unusually clean lineage:

**1947:** Montana — twelve 16"/50s, excellent conventional battleship.

**1950s:** first postwar BB — probably nine 18-inch guns, 30-knot fleet standard, mechanized loading, drone spotting designed in from the outset.

**1960s:** digital/radar/drone fire-control revolution; old Iowas and Montanas gain vastly better useful gunnery without changing their barrels.

**1970s:** extended-range/sabot ammunition becomes a major capital-gun program; heavy cruisers and light cruisers increasingly adopt automatic high-rate guns.

**1980s:** 30+ nautical-mile battleship gunnery becomes credible; limited terminally corrected projectiles are debated but remain secondary because drones own precision attack.

**1990s–2000s:** conventional gun range begins approaching diminishing returns; electromagnetic-launch research gains unusually powerful institutional backing.

**2010s onward:** whether the railgun actually works becomes an engineering question rather than an institutional question—the Navy unquestionably wants it.

And that gives American naval technology a very distinct character. Germany asks, **“How far can the missile reach?”** America keeps asking, **“How far can we make the gun reach and still carry enough ammunition to keep firing?”**

The carrier-drone establishment then sits beside that rather than underneath it: the carrier fixes the enemy at long range, the cruisers find him, the battleship commands the fight, and the heavy gun exists to make the range at which the enemy can safely remain nearby progressively farther away.

---

Yes. At this point I would treat **everything in the old Naval Armaments Reference after the 1947–48 starting fleet as superseded for the United States**. The newer wartime audit gives us the usable starting condition: two *Montana*s, four *Iowa*s, two *Alaska*s, twelve fleet/light carriers with only five Essexes, and a much smaller escort/submarine establishment than the old mega-ledger assumed. fileciteturn16file15 From there, the fleet should grow out of the doctrine we've now established rather than converge back toward the historical USN.

There are also two preliminary points I'd lock.

First, **American carriers were not traditionally named after cities**. Cruisers were the type strongly associated with city names. Carrier naming historically emphasized famous names from the Navy list, famous ships, and important American battles or operations; the later tendency toward presidents was a much newer convention. citeturn588807search0turn588807search26 So I think this Navy should preserve the older carrier culture: *Enterprise, Saratoga, Lexington, Yorktown, Ranger, Wasp, Hornet, Kearsarge, Bonhomme Richard,* and so forth. The exact class lead names have to respect which legacy hulls are still commissioned, but **presidential carrier naming probably never becomes normal**.

Second, a ship authorized in 1989 because someone wants a future railgun is not joining the fleet in 1991. Battleships take years to design and build. So I think the late-1980s railgun question produces a **1990s battleship**, which is exactly what we want.

---

# I. The capital-ship cycle

I think American battleship construction falls naturally into four postwar phases.

| Program | Ordered | First service | Propulsion | Main-battery philosophy |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| **Montana class** | inherited | 1947–48 | Oil | Twelve 16-inch guns; final wartime battleship |
| **Kentucky class** | 1952–53 | c. 1959–61 | Oil | Nine 18-inch guns; first true postwar BB |
| **Maine class** | c. 1975–76 | c. 1983–86 | Nuclear | Mature nuclear command battleship; nine 18-inch guns |
| **Vermont class** | c. 1990–91 | c. 1998–2001 | Nuclear-electric | Railgun-ready electrical architecture; enters service with conventional heavy guns |

Those class names are **working proposals**, but the timing and functions are where I think the strongest answer lies.

## Montana: 1948 baseline

*Montana* and *Ohio* are not prototypes for the postwar Navy. They're the culmination of the prewar battleship argument.

Twelve 16-inch guns.

Excellent armor.

Large command spaces.

About 28 knots rather than the 30-plus-knot standard the Navy is going to want afterward.

Their first postwar modifications therefore focus on:

- radar;
- communications;
- AA;
- fleet command facilities;
- drone spotting;
- improved fire control;
- eventually SAMs and CIWS.

And *Montana's* speed becomes a mild doctrinal irritation.

She's extraordinarily powerful, but the fastest escorts and carriers continually remind the Navy that the capital ship is setting the fleet's speed downward.

That helps generate the next requirement.

---

# II. Kentucky: the battleship that settles caliber

I would open the successor requirement around **1949–50** and actually authorize construction around **1952–53**.

The Navy has now had several years to digest Ceylon, the survival of three Yamato-class ships, jet aviation, automatic major-caliber guns, better radar and its new fleet doctrine.

The requirement is approximately:

> **30-knot minimum; protection against existing capital guns; Yamato-class individual-shell effect; fewer but more productive barrels; designed from keel-up as a fleet command ship.**

The result is the proposed **Kentucky class**, with *Kentucky* and *Illinois*.

I'd use **nine 18-inch/457 mm guns in three triples**.

Not because 16-inch suddenly became inadequate, but because this is the one place where the United States accepts the prestige and tactical argument:

> Japan has 460 mm. We will not build the next generation with less.

After this, **caliber escalation ends**.

The whole subsequent American heavy-gun establishment becomes increasingly concerned with:

**range + rate of fire + accuracy + ammunition handling**, not 19-inch, 20-inch, 22-inch absurdities.

The 18-inch class is the answer.

The historical United States had actually manufactured and fired an 18-inch naval test gun, so this isn't a conceptual leap from nowhere; the alternate procurement decision is deciding to turn that research category into a fleet weapon. citeturn265547view5

I'd expect *Kentucky* around 1959 and *Illinois* around 1961.

That gives America, going into the 1960s:

- four Iowas;
- two Montanas;
- two Kentuckys;

with the older battle line rapidly leaving front-line service.

That is already enough capital strength that **there is no reason to order another battleship immediately**.

And that's important. These things are brutally expensive. Continuing the battleship tradition does not mean laying down a new class every five years.

---

# III. The 1960s are a refit decade for battleships

This is where I would place the nuclear experiment.

The setting explicitly makes civilian nuclear power a major **1960s** competition and has America catching up substantially in civilian nuclear investment during 1968–72 rather than inheriting the historical Manhattan-Project industrial complex. fileciteturn17file2 fileciteturn17file4

So I would not give AltWWII America a 1961 *Enterprise*-equivalent nuclear carrier merely because real America did. Historically, the real nuclear *Enterprise* was authorized in 1954 and commissioned in 1961; real America was operating an entirely different nuclear-industrial ecosystem. citeturn588807search3turn588807search21

Instead:

### First nuclear submarine

This is the easiest sell.

Authorize the first American naval-reactor submarine program in the **late 1950s**.

First practical boat perhaps **1963–65**.

Cheap petroleum doesn't answer:

> “How long can I remain submerged?”

So submarines get the reactor before the surface fleet.

The submarine arm remains relatively small because American submarine doctrine remains fleet-reconnaissance oriented, but its best boats go nuclear.

### Montana nuclear conversion

Then around **1967–68**, the Navy approves the experiment you've already suggested:

> **convert USS Montana to nuclear propulsion.**

I'd expect a monstrous rebuild lasting until approximately **1972–73**.

And *Ohio* remains conventional.

That gives the Bureau of Ships the comparison it wants.

The result is not:

> nuclear ships are five knots faster.

It is:

> ***Montana* can sustain fleet speed almost indefinitely from the propulsion standpoint, possesses enormous electrical margin, and barely cares about bunker-fuel calculations. *Ohio* can do exactly the same tactical maneuvers but eventually has to drink from an oiler.**

Historical Operation Sea Orbit demonstrated precisely the broader operational attraction of an all-nuclear surface group: *Enterprise*, *Long Beach*, and *Bainbridge* circumnavigated without propulsion refueling. citeturn588807search5turn588807search3

AltWWII America sees the same capability **later**, and reacts less enthusiastically because oil remains cheap.

The verdict becomes:

> **Nuclear power is not necessary for every ship. It may be worth paying for on the capital ships.**

That distinction controls everything afterward.

---

# IV. When nuclear becomes standard

I would place the actual doctrinal decisions like this:

### Submarines: c. 1960

For first-line long-endurance boats, nuclear power becomes clearly superior because it changes the mission itself.

### Battleships: c. 1974–77

*Montana's* nuclear trials prove the propulsion concept.

At the same time, the battleship is becoming the Navy's largest:

- C2 node;
- radar node;
- electronic-warfare node;
- SAM coordinator;
- fire-control computer center;
- drone-control center.

So the reactor is increasingly attractive **for electrical capacity as much as propulsion endurance**.

By the time the Navy authorizes its next clean-sheet battleship around 1975–76, I would make nuclear propulsion mandatory.

### Carriers: c. 1970s

The carrier case becomes compelling slightly earlier than the battleship-production decision, but for different reasons.

A CV repeatedly wants to:

- steam fast for flight operations;
- maneuver independently of tanker rendezvous;
- devote enormous internal volume to aviation fuel and ordnance;
- generate increasingly large electrical loads;
- operate a manned air group and a huge drone establishment.

So I'd authorize the first clean-sheet nuclear carrier around **1971–73**.

By the **early 1980s**, no new first-line American fleet carrier is ordered with conventional propulsion.

### Heavy cruisers: never quite mandatory

This is where I'd give America one experiment and then stop.

A nuclear heavy cruiser works beautifully.

The Navy asks:

> Does it work?

Yes.

> Is it worth the cost?

Usually no.

So nuclear power becomes an American **capital-ship characteristic**, not a general fleet characteristic.

That's one of the clearest distinctions between America and Germany/Japan.

---

# V. Carrier development

The carrier progression should be slower in hull count than historical America but no less sophisticated technically.

And the key point is:

> **The American “supercarrier” is not really a historical supercarrier conceptually.**

It becomes physically enormous because jets are enormous and flight decks are unforgiving. Historically *Forrestal* needed four steam catapults and an angled deck to generate a modern jet air operation. citeturn588807search1turn588807search19

But the American ship isn't built around:

> 90 manned strike aircraft constitute the Navy's principal offensive arm.

It's built around something more like:

> **50–65 manned aircraft defend and scout for the fleet, while a large secondary magazine of unmanned aircraft provides much of the expendable strike power.**

That's quite a different ship internally.

## First generation: the post-Essex fleet carrier

I'd begin the requirement in **1949–50** and authorize around **1951**.

Let's call it the **1951 Fleet Carrier** for now, because the eventual lead name should depend on which of the legacy carrier names have become free.

Rough character:

- 55,000–65,000 t full load;
- 31–32 knots;
- conventional steam;
- angled deck added either during late construction or as an immediate design revision;
- steam catapults;
- 55–65 manned aircraft;
- perhaps 50–80 folded assault/recon drones;
- dedicated drone magazines and preparation shops;
- deck-edge or specialized drone launching apparatus.

It should commission around **1957–59**.

Externally, foreigners probably call it an American supercarrier.

American officers probably roll their eyes and call it a fleet carrier or an aviation cruiser.

### Naming

I would retain the historical traditional pool:

- famous Navy names;
- famous former ships;
- important American battles.

That is exactly what NHHC records as the carrier naming tradition before the later presidential emphasis. citeturn588807search26

So something like **Kearsarge**, **Bonhomme Richard**, **Enterprise**, **Saratoga**, **Yorktown**, etc., recycled as previous ships retire.

Not *Dwight D. Eisenhower*.

Not *John F. Kennedy*.

The carrier simply never acquires the same quasi-monumental political status in this Navy.

---

# VI. Second carrier generation: the true jet/drone carrier

The first 1950s class still contains compromises inherited from the propeller-carrier world.

By around **1961–63**, jet weights, jet fuel, deck heating, larger radars, heavier AEW aircraft and increasingly numerous drones justify another clean-sheet carrier.

I'd order the second generation around **1962** and put the first in service around **1968–70**.

Call it provisionally the **Constellation class** if that name is available by then.

Roughly:

- 68,000–73,000 t;
- conventional propulsion;
- 32 knots;
- very large deck area;
- 50–60 manned jets and support aircraft;
- around 80–120 drones depending on mix;
- much larger drone-control and maintenance establishment;
- extensive fighter-direction/CAP facilities.

This is probably the last new conventional first-line American carrier class.

The Navy is not dissatisfied with it.

The reactor is simply starting to offer too much for the next one.

---

# VII. Enterprise: the nuclear American carrier

I'd reuse **Enterprise** for the first nuclear class once the old *Enterprise* has been retired long enough for the name to carry historical prestige.

Program authorization approximately **1971–73**.

First commission approximately **1978–80**.

That's roughly fifteen to twenty years behind the real nuclear *Enterprise*, which feels right given the setting's delayed American nuclear establishment and weaker fuel pressure. Historically CVN-65 was already capable of sustained 30-plus-knot operation and demonstrated the extraordinary endurance of nuclear surface propulsion. citeturn588807search4turn588807search3

The AltWWII **Enterprise class** is perhaps:

- 75,000–82,000 t;
- nuclear;
- 32+ knots sustained;
- about 55–60 manned aircraft;
- 120–160 drones under maximum combat loading;
- extensive drone launching/handling systems;
- excellent fighter direction;
- strong self-defense;
- no giant VLS battery.

This is the American carrier that outsiders properly start calling a **supercarrier**, but its hangar organization looks strange to our eyes.

A very large fraction of its aviation complement isn't made up of pilots and reusable combat jets.

It's boxes of folded aircraft.

## Next carrier

I'd order the next refined nuclear class around **1983–85**, commissioning around 1990.

Provisional lead name **Saratoga**, assuming the earlier *Saratoga* is long gone.

That gets us through 1985 without building nine giant carriers.

By 1985, I would expect perhaps **five or six genuinely first-line fleet carriers**, not nine:

- several late conventional ships;
- one or two nuclear *Enterprise*-generation ships;
- older carriers in training/reserve roles.

That matches the American balanced-fleet philosophy much better.

---

# VIII. Heavy cruisers

This line should stay very recognizable as a cruiser tradition.

## Des Moines generation

I would preserve a **Des Moines-like automatic 8-inch cruiser**, because practically everything about the concept fits the alternate Navy.

Automatic heavy gun.

Command capacity.

Good armor.

High speed.

Scouting capability.

It does not depend upon a carrier war to make sense.

So a reduced **Des Moines class** can enter around the early 1950s.

This becomes the bridge from wartime cruiser to postwar CA.

## 1960s heavy cruiser

Around **1960–62**, order the first cruiser designed from the keel up around:

- automatic 8-inch guns;
- secondary fleet C2;
- reconnaissance drones;
- perhaps ten or twelve expendable assault drones;
- substantial SAM battery;
- 32+ knots;
- protection against light-cruiser fire and partial protection against its peers.

Something around 17,000–20,000 tons initially seems plausible.

The important part isn't its exact displacement yet.

It's that the **CA stays a gun ship**.

## Nuclear CA experiment

Then, around **1967–69**, authorize one nuclear heavy cruiser.

And I would quite happily reuse **Long Beach**.

City name: correct for an American cruiser.

But unlike the historical *Long Beach*, ours is not a huge missile cruiser.

It's a **nuclear gun heavy cruiser**.

Automatic 8-inch battery.

Drones.

SAMs.

Excellent C2.

Very long endurance.

It commissions around **1973–75**.

And everybody loves operating it.

Then Congress sees the bill.

The Navy concludes:

> excellent ship; unjustifiable standard.

So the next heavy cruiser goes back to conventional power.

That gives the nuclear cruiser school an honorable defeat rather than making them fools.

---

# IX. The 1980s heavy cruiser

The appearance of *Wotan* in 1978 doesn't make America copy VLS. It does make the Navy want a new cruiser that is harder to kill and better able to contribute to layered defense.

So I'd order a new conventional CA around **1978–80**, entering service around **1985–87**.

Working name, say, **St. Louis class**.

Roughly:

- 20,000–24,000 t;
- 32+ knots;
- three twin or perhaps three triple automatic 8-inch mounts;
- 10–12 attack drones plus reconnaissance drones;
- trainable area-defense SAMs;
- several CIWS;
- substantial armor for cruiser combat;
- alternate fleet-command facilities.

This is the ship that shadows things.

An American admiral can detach a *St. Louis*, four destroyers and several frigates and say:

> “Go find out what the Germans are doing.”

It doesn't require a battleship.

---

# X. Light cruisers

The CL probably changes more visibly than the CA.

Its governing requirement is:

> **be faster than the battle fleet, see farther than the battle fleet, and kill whatever is trying to see the battle fleet.**

I'd give it three major generations.

### Worcester generation, early 1950s

Automatic 6-inch guns.

Heavy AA.

Early drone reconnaissance.

Around 33 knots.

### Second-generation scout cruiser, ordered c. 1961–63

Perhaps:

- 3×2 automatic 6-inch guns;
- 34–35 knots;
- much bigger radar;
- electronic intelligence;
- SAMs;
- drone hangar/rails;
- early ASW sensors without becoming an ASW hunter.

### Third generation, ordered c. 1974–76

Commission early 1980s.

The **information cruiser** fully emerges:

- perhaps only 2×2 or 3×2 rapid-fire 6-inch guns;
- 35 knots;
- very strong radar/EW;
- large reconnaissance-drone complement;
- trainable SAMs;
- several CIWS;
- fleet communications relay.

The CL is one of the classes most transformed by electronics without losing its gun identity.

And because cruisers conventionally use **city names**, this is where names like *Seattle, Phoenix, Denver, Cleveland,* and so forth belong—not on carriers. citeturn588807search0

---

# XI. Destroyers

I would expect new American destroyer classes roughly every twelve to fifteen years.

Not because every previous class instantly becomes obsolete, but because DDs are numerous enough that replacement is continuous.

### c. 1952 class

Classical fleet destroyer:

- 5-inch dual-purpose guns;
- heavyweight antiship torpedoes;
- sonar;
- ASW weapons;
- strong AA;
- 35+ knots.

### c. 1963 class

Same jack-of-all-trades identity, but:

- improved sonar;
- better radar;
- first small drone complement;
- increasingly automated 5-inch guns;
- some hulls sacrifice torpedo/drone capacity for expensive fleet SAMs.

This is probably the period when an explicit **AA destroyer subtype** becomes important.

### c. 1975 class

By now the torpedo question changes.

ASW torpedoes are non-negotiable.

Large surface-attack torpedo batteries are increasingly hard to justify against drones and improved gunfire.

So the ordinary destroyer becomes:

> **guns + AA + ASW + small drone complement**

while only specialized units retain large antiship torpedo batteries.

### 1980s

CIWS becomes standard.

The DD is still a battle-fleet combatant.

It absolutely still has a real gun—probably one or two 5-inch automatic mounts.

The American Navy never develops the cultural assumption that a destroyer with no missiles left should become a mostly unarmed radar platform.

---

# XII. Frigates

Frigates are actually the most demanding class to design under this doctrine because America insists they keep up.

They're ASW specialists, but they're **fleet ASW specialists**.

So:

### 1950s

Oil-fired steam, about 30 knots.

3-inch or perhaps 5-inch gun.

Very good sonar.

Ahead-thrown ASW weapon/depth weapons.

### 1960s

Much stronger quieting.

ASW helicopter or unmanned aviation begins becoming important.

Still about 30 knots.

### 1970s

76 mm–5 inch automatic gun.

Towed array.

ASW helicopter/drone.

Point-defense SAM becomes plausible.

CIWS appears later.

### 1980s

The mature American frigate is:

> quiet at hunting speed, capable of sprinting with the battle fleet, heavily optimized for sonar and ASW, and armed well enough that being “only a frigate” doesn't mean being helpless.

It still does **not** get the big trainable area-defense SAM installation unless some special subclass warrants the expense.

---

# XIII. Submarines

The submarine line remains comparatively small but technically excellent.

This is where nuclear power appears first because the reactor fundamentally changes submerged performance.

I would expect:

**1950s:** improved conventional fleet scout.

**c. 1963–65:** first nuclear fleet-reconnaissance submarine.

**1970s:** more mature quiet SSN built around shadowing enemy fleets and positioning for opening torpedo attacks.

**1980s:** highly sophisticated SSN reconnaissance/attack boats.

But perhaps only a couple dozen nuclear boats, not the enormous German submarine establishment.

And because the United States never develops a strategic nuclear deterrent:

> **no SSBN aristocracy ever displaces the fleet submarine.**

The torpedo remains the submarine's main weapon.

That's a very important continuity.

---

# XIV. The first clean-sheet nuclear battleship: Maine

Now back to the question that really determines the 1980s fleet.

I'd authorize **Maine** around 1975–76.

She is not a response to *Wotan*, because Germany hasn't shown *Wotan* yet.

She's the response to:

- aging Iowa/Montana hulls;
- successful nuclear *Montana* experiments;
- improving 18-inch gunnery;
- exploding C2 requirements;
- electrical demand;
- the desire for sustained 30-knot fleet operations.

Then *Wotan* appears in 1978 while *Maine* is under construction.

And suddenly the design office adds even more:

- electronic warfare;
- decoys;
- CIWS;
- missile-warning sensors;
- hardened command links;
- distributed damage-control systems.

But **no VLS**.

*Maine* commissions around 1984.

Her sister, perhaps **New Hampshire**, around 1986–87.

She is the mature American 20th-century battleship:

- nuclear;
- about 80,000 tons, give or take;
- 30–31 knots sustained;
- nine 18-inch guns;
- highly mechanized loading;
- trainable SAM battery;
- extensive CIWS;
- reconnaissance/spotting drones;
- huge fleet C2;
- very heavy armor;
- no major antiship missile battery.

She looks completely insane to a German naval architect.

Which is perfect.

The German looks at *Maine* and sees an enormous target designed around an engagement envelope the Kriegsmarine intends never to enter.

The American looks at *Wotan* and sees an underarmored missile magazine whose offensive power decreases every time it fires.

Neither side has enough war experience to settle the argument.

---

# XV. Then the railgun question arrives at exactly the right time

By around **1987–89**, American heavy-gun research is hitting diminishing returns.

You can:

- improve 18-inch projectiles;
- use subcaliber shells;
- use assisted projectiles;
- improve terminal correction;
- improve fire control.

But each extra increment of range is getting expensive.

Then electromagnetic-launch research starts producing serious laboratory numbers.

Historically, ONR was pursuing a 32 MJ railgun concept with a claimed goal of more than 100 nautical miles and 6–12 rounds per minute. citeturn265547view5

Your Navy has an institutional reaction to that which the real US Navy never had:

> **“That is a battleship gun.”**

Not:

> “Perhaps destroyers can carry this future weapon.”

The battleship establishment has spent forty years looking for precisely that answer.

So around **1988**, the Bureau of Ships issues the next capital-ship study.

And here's the important part:

> They do **not** require the railgun to be ready before authorizing the ship.

They require the ship to be **railgun-capable later**.

---

# XVI. Vermont: the electrical battleship

I would authorize the proposed **Vermont class** around **1990–91**.

Commissioning approximately **1998–2001**.

This is not yet “the railgun battleship.”

It is:

> **the first American battleship whose entire electrical architecture assumes a future main battery may consume enormous pulses of electricity.**

So she receives from the keel up:

- nuclear propulsion;
- integrated electric or nuclear-turboelectric architecture;
- enormously oversized generation capacity;
- dedicated high-voltage trunks;
- physically separated pulsed-energy rooms;
- space for capacitors, flywheels, compensated alternators, or whatever storage technology wins;
- cooling provision;
- reinforced gun foundations;
- large modular machinery spaces;
- very large electrical safety and damage-control zones.

And while waiting?

She enters service with **conventional 18-inch guns**.

Perhaps the existing mature gun in three turrets.

The ship is useful if the railgun program fails completely.

That's crucial.

No Pentagon-wars situation where the Navy spends fifteen years building a hull that has no functioning main armament.

If railguns work in 2012 or 2018, wonderful.

One turret—or eventually several—can be replaced.

If railguns remain laboratory toys, *Vermont* is still an extremely formidable conventional battleship.

That is the sensible procurement structure.

---

# XVII. So the class rhythm is actually fairly conservative

Once we step back, the American Navy is **not** building absurd numbers of clean-sheet classes.

For the most expensive types:

### Battleships

1948 — Montana  
1960 — Kentucky  
1984 — Maine  
1999 — Vermont

That's about one true generation every twenty years after Kentucky.

Perfectly sustainable for enormous ships expected to serve forty or fifty years.

### Fleet carriers

1958 — first jet/drone clean-sheet carrier  
1969 — larger conventional jet/drone carrier  
1979 — nuclear Enterprise generation  
1990 — refined nuclear carrier

Again, roughly ten-year design generations, with individual classes building for several years.

### Heavy cruisers

early 1950s — automatic-gun bridge generation  
mid-1960s — mature drone/C2 CA  
mid-1970s — nuclear experiment  
mid-1980s — mature conventional CA

### Light cruisers

early 1950s — automatic AA/gun cruiser  
mid-1960s — scout-information cruiser  
early 1980s — mature electronic/drone scout cruiser

### DD/FF

New generations every 10–15 years because they're the fleet's numerous working ships.

That gives us a fleet history rather than a technology-tree menu where a completely new class appears every time someone invents a radar.

---

# What the American fleet probably looks like in 1985

Not exact hull counts yet, but **qualitatively**:

**Battleships:** several Iowas/Kentuckys/Montanas still available, with *Montana* nuclear-converted and the first *Maine* newly operational. Some older hulls are reserve rather than permanently front-line.

**Carriers:** perhaps five or six first-line fleet carriers, one or two nuclear, with large assault-drone establishments. Older Essex-era ships survive only as training, reserve, drone trials, or secondary aviation ships.

**Heavy cruisers:** automatic-gun conventional CAs, one famous nuclear *Long Beach* experiment, and the first new 1980s class arriving.

**Light cruisers:** fast reconnaissance ships with automatic guns, large radar/EW systems, SAMs and substantial drone complements.

**Destroyers:** gun-armed general-purpose fleet combatants with AA, ASW and increasingly drones; some dedicated AA variants.

**Frigates:** fast ASW specialists with real guns and point defense.

**Submarines:** relatively small but increasingly nuclear first-line reconnaissance/attack force, still doctrinally oriented toward finding the enemy and opening the fleet engagement with torpedoes.

That is a fleet that looks recognizably American and yet would be almost impossible to mistake for our historical 1985 US Navy.

And I think the nuclear question now has a clean answer:

> **America does not become a nuclear Navy. It develops nuclear capital ships.**

Submarines get reactors because remaining submerged demands them. Battleships and fleet carriers get reactors by the late 1970s because endurance, sustained fleet speed, electrical load, and the capital value of the hull finally justify the cost. Heavy cruisers demonstrate that nuclear propulsion is possible and then mostly reject it economically. Destroyers and frigates never seriously need it.

Then the railgun question doesn't overturn that system. It simply makes the Navy discover, around 1990, that the decision to put nuclear reactors into battleships twenty years earlier has accidentally given the old heavy-gun establishment exactly the kind of ship it needs for the next experiment. memcite

---

## Turn 1139 — Assistant

- Timestamp: 2026-08-14T20:37:38.022Z
- Message ID: `aab52a72-5443-4a87-9bcf-0b65c6dfaf9c`
- Source: ChatGPT shared conversation `Naval Doctrine Evolution`
