Yes: **once the IJN nuclearizes a ship, the big propulsion smokestack essentially disappears.** A nuclear steam plant still produces steam and has to reject enormous quantities of waste heat, but after the steam passes through the turbines it is condensed back into water using seawater; it does not require a land-style cooling tower, and there is no combustion exhaust requiring a conventional funnel. citeturn624452search23turn624452search1

There can still be small exhaust trunks for auxiliary machinery, ventilation and emergency equipment. But visually, a Japanese nuclear carrier, cruiser, battleship or destroyer should have **no great oil-fired funnel**. That freed topside volume gets consumed by exactly the things the IJN cares about: radar, antenna arrays, SAM directors, aviation facilities and later integrated masts. The mature MSR generation gets cleaner still; its heat rejection remains principally through seawater heat exchangers below the waterline rather than giant structures above deck.

That means by the 1970s a very recognizable IJN visual distinction develops:

> **old route fleet: funnels; new fast fleet: masts.**

And by the 2000s, someone looking at a Japanese first-line battle group sees surprisingly few smokestacks at all.

## The two names

**USS Chicago** is an excellent lock for the American nuclear cruiser. Chicago Pile-1 achieved the world's first controlled, self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction under Stagg Field on 2 December 1942, led by Enrico Fermi. citeturn643925search0turn643925search2 It also conveniently obeys the American cruiser-city naming convention.

And because the historical Baltimore-class *Chicago* CA-136 belongs to the wartime production program we're already drastically reducing, we don't need that hull to exist in AltWWII. The name can remain available for the later nuclear cruiser.

For the Japanese destroyer, I think the exact answer is **Inazuma — 稲妻, “Lightning.”**

That is almost too perfect. It is a genuine traditional Japanese destroyer name, it belongs naturally to the meteorological naming culture you want, and it carries the electric association without using some artificial “Atomic” or “Radiant” name that doesn't sound like an IJN destroyer.

So my working recommendation is:

> **Inazuma-class nuclear fleet destroyer.**

Its sisters can continue the same family with names such as **Ikazuchi** (“Thunder”), **Arashi** (“Storm”), and **Hayate** (“Gale”). I would treat *Inazuma* itself as the strong proposal rather than silently make the exact name canon until you confirm it.

---

# Rebuilding the IJN from 1948

The corrected wartime audit is our starting point, not the old naval reference. Japan finishes 1947 with **thirteen fleet/light carriers afloat, ten operational; eleven capital ships afloat, nine operational; and roughly eighty ocean/fleet submarines, fifty-eight operational**. *Shinano* is unequivocally the third Yamato-class battleship. fileciteturn22file0

The controlling postwar doctrine is now carrier primacy. The Setting Bible's older language already described Japan as carrier-first, although its specific class ledger is superseded by what we're doing now. fileciteturn23file3

I think the mature organizational target is **four principal carrier battle divisions**, each normally built around two fleet carriers. A battleship serves as the heavy surface “big brother” for each division rather than being the formation's actual offensive center. That immediately explains why eight first-line fleet carriers and approximately four modern fast battleships make sense together.

Here is the principal postwar construction sequence I would use. The names and exact specifications remain working design choices except where we've already fixed the concept.

| Class | Type | Commissioning window | Built | Propulsion | Governing reason |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| **Yamato** | Battleship | inherited | 3 | Oil steam | Wartime heavy core; *Yamato, Musashi, Shinano* |
| **Kii** | Fast battleship | 1958–63 | **2** | Oil steam | First purpose-built carrier-guard BB; 460 mm battery, 31-knot class |
| **Shinano nuclear reconstruction** | Experimental BB | c. 1970–74 | **1 conversion** | PWR | First nuclear battleship experiment; propulsion/electrical testbed |
| **Suruga** | Nuclear fast battleship | 1977–82 | **2** | PWR | Mature carrier-guard battleship; replaces Yamato generation in fast fleet |
| **Hiryū II** | Jet fleet carrier | 1957–64 | **4** | Oil steam | First clean-sheet jet carrier |
| **Taihō II** | Nuclear fleet carrier | 1967–75 | **4** | PWR | First nuclear carrier generation; nuclear becomes mandatory for new fleet CVs |
| **Hakuryū** | Nuclear supercarrier | 1981–90 | **4** | PWR | Mature carrier-primary design; larger jet/AEW/missile air group |
| **Zuihō II** | Light carrier | 1962–69 | **4** | Oil steam | Regional air cover, ASW, training and secondary operations |
| **Takao II** | Carrier-group cruiser | 1959–66 | **4** | Oil steam | Fleet air defense, information coordination and task-group command |
| **Maya II** | Nuclear command cruiser | 1970–78 | **4** | PWR | First production nuclear cruiser; carrier-group radar/SAM hub |
| **Chōkai II** | Nuclear command cruiser | 1983–91 | **4** | Compact PWR | Second-generation nuclear cruiser with reduced plant burden |
| **Asakaze II** | Fleet destroyer | 1953–61 | **12** | Oil steam | First postwar carrier escort |
| **Amatsukaze II** | Fleet destroyer | 1962–70 | **14** | Oil steam | Mature conventional SAM/ASW carrier escort |
| **Inazuma** | Nuclear fleet destroyer | 1972–76 | **4** | PWR | First nuclear DD; deliberately oversized experimental escort |
| **Hatsuyuki** | Fleet destroyer | 1974–84 | **16** | Conventional | Economical mass escort while nuclear DD remains too expensive |
| **Shiranui II** | Nuclear fleet destroyer | 1980–89 | **12** | Compact PWR | Second nuclear DD generation; now recognizably destroyer-sized |
| **Shimakaze II** | Nuclear fleet destroyer | 1994–2006 | **16** | Fluoride MSR | Mature nuclear fleet escort; MSR becomes production standard |
| **Mikura II** | Ocean escort/FF | 1961–70 | **24** | Conventional | ASW and route defense |
| **Okinawa II** | Ocean escort/FF | 1973–85 | **24** | Conventional | Helicopter/sonar escort; standard late-century FF |
| **MSR fleet frigate, name TBD** | Nuclear FF | c. 2003–16 | **18** | Fluoride MSR | Final IJN miniaturization goal: normal frigate hull without reactor-driven gigantism |

I would **not** lock the submarines in this same pass because you've already flagged the Japanese submarine arm as deserving its own reconstruction. We need the wartime I-boat experiments before we can sensibly derive the SSNs. The only thing I'd preserve now is the requirement that Japan gets nuclear submarines early and treats them as forward carrier-fleet scouts.

## Why those carrier counts work

The **Hiryū II class** is the first truly new jet-carrier generation. Four ships are enough because Japan still has modernized *Taihō, Shōkaku, Zuikaku* and surviving *Unryū*s available during the transition. Japan isn't scrapping a perfectly functional fleet merely because a new airframe appeared.

By the mid-1960s, however, jet weight, radar aircraft, heavier strike aircraft and higher sortie rates have made the old carriers progressively less attractive. So the first nuclear **Taihō II class** begins replacing them.

I like four ships because this is the point at which nuclear carrier propulsion ceases to be experimental Japanese technology and becomes doctrine:

> **A first-line carrier shall not be limited by bunker fuel.**

Then **Hakuryū** becomes the true Japanese supercarrier. Four are ordered, but only the first two are operational by 1985. The remaining two arrive later in the decade.

That creates a very neat 1985 fleet-carrier picture:

**2 Hiryū II** still in first-line or high-readiness secondary service,  
**4 Taihō II** nuclear carriers,  
**2 Hakuryū** supercarriers,

for **eight first-line fleet carriers**.

That happens to resemble the old setting's eight-carrier scale, but the similarity is incidental; the old classes and logic are gone.

And these aren't American supercarriers. Japan believes the carrier is the **decisive fleet weapon**, so the large air group is the reason the ship exists. There is no American-style massive hidden assault-drone establishment taking up a large fraction of hangar volume.

## The battleships become much more sensible too

The Yamato trio's problem after 1955 isn't firepower.

It's **27-knot ancestry**.

That is increasingly unacceptable if the carrier they're supposed to protect can make 31–33 knots.

So **Kii** and her sister—I'd use **Owari**—become the first true postwar Big Brother battleships.

They retain nine 460 mm guns because Japan has no reason to begin a 500 mm caliber contest. Their design money goes instead into approximately 31 knots, better subdivision, radar, AA, eventually SAMs, and enormous protection.

That means Japan and America reach surprisingly similar caliber conclusions through different doctrines:

America says:

> “18 inches is enough. Now give us range.”

Japan says:

> “460 mm is already enough. Now make sure the carrier survives.”

Then the nuclear era arrives.

*Shinano* is an excellent experimental reconstruction precisely because she's the youngest Yamato hull. But putting reactors into her doesn't magically correct the hull's hydrodynamic limits. She becomes a useful technology and endurance demonstrator rather than the ideal carrier escort.

That lesson produces the **Suruga class**: two clean-sheet nuclear fast battleships, *Suruga* and perhaps *Echigo*, built expressly to stay with a nuclear carrier force.

By 1985 I would therefore have **four front-line carrier-guard battleships**:

two *Kii*-class conventionals;

two *Suruga*-class nuclear ships.

The Yamato trio remain enormously prestigious. *Shinano* is the nuclear experiment and reserve fleet asset; *Yamato* and *Musashi* increasingly move toward training, bombardment, mobilization reserve and state ceremony.

Japan hasn't “given up on Yamato.”

It has simply admitted that the jet carrier has outrun her.

---

# The cruiser line becomes simpler than America's

I would **not** preserve separate American-style heavy and light cruiser schools indefinitely.

Japan cares about the carrier-group requirement.

The postwar cruiser therefore becomes primarily:

> **large radar + fighter/air-defense coordination + missiles + command + aviation + enough surface armament to defend the screen.**

The **Takao II** class is the final conventional answer.

The **Maya II** is the first serious nuclear answer.

And the **Chōkai II** is the first one where foreign officers stop saying, “The reactor has forced them to build a ridiculous cruiser.”

Japan doesn't need fifteen different cruiser subtypes because a lot of scouting work migrates into aircraft, helicopters, satellites, submarines and the carrier's own airborne-warning establishment.

Four ships per major cruiser generation also fits carrier structure nicely. One cruiser can normally work with each major carrier division, while additional inherited or reserve cruisers cover detached formations.

---

# Inazuma should indeed be ridiculous

The first nuclear destroyer is where I think the setting gets one of its most memorable ships.

I'd provisionally put **Inazuma** around:

**9,500–10,000 tonnes full load**,  
roughly **32 knots**,  
two early compact PWRs or an equivalent redundant plant,  
a real 127 mm gun battery,  
large trainable area-SAM installations,  
heavy ASW sensors and weapons,  
anti-ship missiles,  
a helicopter hangar,  
and later multiple CIWS mounts.

No VLS initially. That's a later technology.

And, crucially:

**no large funnel.**

So she looks strange. She is big, clean amidships, heavily cluttered with radar and missile directors, and armed so densely that foreign recognition books simply call her a light cruiser.

The Japanese insist:

> **Destroyer.**

Because she exists to screen a carrier.

Even internally, I think sailors refer to her as something like “the great destroyer” rather than pretending she isn't enormous.

Her four ships would be:

**Inazuma** — Lightning  
**Ikazuchi** — Thunder  
**Arashi** — Storm  
**Hayate** — Gale

The reason only four are built is important: **the experiment succeeds technically and fails economically.**

The IJN loves the ships.

The Treasury despises them.

So Japan keeps building the conventional **Hatsuyuki** class alongside them.

That gives us an excellent 1970s procurement argument:

> Nuclear advocates: “One Inazuma can do the work of two escorts.”

> Opponents: “Two escorts can be in two places.”

Neither side is being stupid.

## Then Shiranui changes the argument

By around 1980 the second-generation PWR plant has materially improved.

The **Shiranui II class** comes down into roughly the **7,500–8,000-ton** region while retaining most of Inazuma's capability.

Now foreign navies no longer laugh when Japan calls it a destroyer.

They merely call it an **enormous destroyer**.

Twelve are built.

That is the point where nuclear fleet escorts stop being a scientific extravagance and begin becoming a real procurement option.

Then the **Shimakaze II** generation in the 1990s gets the mature fluoride MSR, and the displacement penalty falls again.

That's when the IJN finally wins its fifty-year argument.

---

# The frigate transition is deliberately much later

This is where I would resist rushing.

The conventional **Mikura II** and **Okinawa II** families remain extremely successful.

They are quiet.

Cheap.

Good at ASW.

And Japan needs large numbers of them.

That means the reactor bureau keeps arriving every five years saying:

> “We can nuclearize the frigate now.”

And the escort command replies:

> “At twice the price and 1,800 additional tonnes.”

No.

Then:

> “At fifty percent more and 900 tonnes.”

Still no.

Then around **2000–05**:

> “Same broad displacement class, acceptable crew burden, thirty-year fuel module, and the lifecycle cost closes because the whole fast fleet already has nuclear infrastructure.”

Now the answer changes.

That's how the nuclear frigate becomes meaningful. It isn't a prestige ship.

It is the moment nuclear propulsion becomes **boring**.

---

# What this gives Japan by 1985

I would aim for approximately this first-line combat force:

| Category | 1985 working strength |
|---|---:|
| Fleet carriers | **8** |
| Light carriers | **4** |
| Front-line fast battleships | **4** |
| Older Yamato-family heavy reserve/support | **3** |
| Carrier/command cruisers | **8–10** |
| Fleet destroyers | **about 38** |
| Fleet/ocean frigates | **about 46–48** |
| Nuclear attack / guided-missile submarines | **roughly low-20s combined**, details open |
| Conventional submarines | **substantial residual force**, details open |
| Kaibōkan, patrol and regional escorts | **additional**, outside the first-line fleet total |

Again, those numbers aren't being inherited from the obsolete naval document. They're falling naturally out of an eight-carrier force built as **four two-carrier battle divisions**.

A representative full-strength division might have two fleet carriers, one Big Brother battleship, two major cruisers, roughly six to eight destroyers/frigates in the inner fast screen, forward submarines, and additional support attached according to mission.

That gives Japan a naval establishment that can plausibly overtake Britain in front-line blue-water combat strength around the turn of the 1960s while still requiring a vast conventional route-defense fleet to police an empire running from the Russian Far East through Southeast Asia into the South Pacific. The corrected wartime audit explicitly notes that this geographic burden already constrains Japan from simply turning every wartime hull into a carrier. fileciteturn22file0

And visually, the progression becomes excellent:

**1955 Japanese fleet:** funnels everywhere.

**1975 carrier group:** nuclear carrier, nuclear cruiser and gigantic funnel-less *Inazuma* beside conventional escorts that still smoke.

**1985:** the elite carrier group is increasingly a collection of ships with radars and masts where funnels used to be.

**2005:** seeing a smokestack on a first-line IJN warship increasingly tells you that you're looking at an old ship, a cheap route escort, an auxiliary, or somebody else's navy.

That is a very distinctive way for the IJN's nuclear obsession to become visible rather than merely existing as a line in an engine specification. memcite

iturn753717image2

Yes. This can work, and I think it gives the IJN submarine arm a much more distinctive identity than simply becoming a Japanese version of Dönitz's force.

Also, you remembered the inspiration correctly: **_Konpeki no Kantai_**—*Deep Blue Fleet*. The OVA actually began in 1993 rather than the 1980s, according to J.C.Staff's own production history. citeturn177722search0turn177722search1

The important thing is that I would **not** treat the mature Japanese vessel as “an I-400, only gigantic.” The I-400 is the proof of concept. The mature strategic aviation submarine solves a rather different set of engineering problems.

## The I-400 concept is much less ridiculous than it sounds

The historical I-400-class boat already demonstrated three things that matter to us. It was a roughly 6,500-ton submerged submarine, carried **three M6A1 Seiran aircraft** in a pressure-tight hangar, and had enough range to contemplate attacks enormously distant from Japan. citeturn753717search2turn753717search3

Even more useful for our development history, the system exposed its central weakness. Launching all three aircraft took roughly **30 minutes with their floats**, or about **15 minutes without them**; removing the floats accelerated launch but eliminated ordinary at-sea aircraft recovery. citeturn284871search0

That is almost the entire postwar Japanese development requirement in embryo:

> **Reduce the time surfaced, increase the number and capability of aircraft, and solve recovery without sacrificing stealth.**

The historic boat proves that the basic thing isn't fantasy. The postwar program spends decades making it actually useful.

## In this timeline, the original program needs a different reason to exist

Japan isn't fighting the United States, so the historical rationale of secretly attacking American continental targets doesn't carry over.

Instead, I would derive the alternate **Sen-Toku experimental program** from the sheer geographical scale of the British war.

The IJN keeps encountering targets which are strategically interesting but don't justify moving a fleet carrier:

British rear-area airfields, isolated naval facilities, communications stations, ports, reconnaissance targets and Indian Ocean logistics points.

The requirement becomes:

> **Can one submarine penetrate somewhere nobody expects Japanese aviation, put three aircraft over a target, and disappear?**

That is already useful in a carrier-primary navy. It doesn't replace carriers. It gives the carrier school a way to **put aviation somewhere without putting a carrier there**.

So perhaps two or three experimental large aviation submarines complete by 1946–47. They conduct extensive exercises and perhaps one carefully selected combat operation—we don't need to lock the target yet—and the evaluation is essentially:

> This is expensive, slow and awkward.  
> It is also doing something no other Japanese ship can do.

Therefore the program survives.

---

# The submarine force then develops three principal identities

I would make this an explicit IJN doctrinal distinction.

**Fleet submarines** are the ordinary SS/SSN arm. They operate ahead of carrier forces as reconnaissance, tracking and ambush assets. Their torpedoes are particularly valuable for opening an engagement.

**Raiding submarines** operate independently against shipping, bases and isolated naval forces. Japan understands commerce warfare without turning the entire submarine service into a German-style trade-interdiction institution.

And then there is the **Special Submarine Force**.

That third branch owns aviation submarines, underwater transports, swimmer and landing operations, intelligence insertion, clandestine cargo and other things for which the useful characteristic of a submarine is simply:

> **It can arrive somewhere without anybody seeing it arrive.**

That's where your homage belongs.

And I'd make that branch prestigious but **tiny**.

---

# There should be two descendants of the Sen-Toku idea

This is the distinction that makes the whole program economically manageable.

### Aviation submarine

Carries aircraft and their weapons.

Mission:

- strategic reconnaissance;
- surprise conventional strike;
- electronic reconnaissance;
- attacks against airfields, headquarters, radar installations and ports;
- insertion of very small special-operations teams;
- occasional antishipping raids.

### Undersea assault transport

Carries people and cargo instead of a large aircraft establishment.

Mission:

- approximately a company of Special Naval Landing Force troops;
- combat swimmers;
- reconnaissance personnel;
- small boats or swimmer-delivery vehicles;
- demolition gear;
- communications equipment;
- perhaps a small number of vehicles or motorcycles on very large versions;
- several tens or hundreds of tonnes of specialist stores.

That is much more useful than trying to transport a division underwater.

And eventually **the two types should share substantial machinery**.

Same reactor family.

Same propulsion.

Same sonar.

Same navigation system.

Same major pressure-hull engineering.

The center mission section differs.

One has an aviation hangar.

One has troop accommodation, lockout chambers, boats and cargo spaces.

That makes a four- or five-hull strategic aviation fleet substantially easier to justify because it belongs to a larger **Special Submarine industrial family** rather than requiring its own boutique shipyard ecosystem.

---

# Aircraft recovery is the technology that defines the generations

This is where I would be quite strict.

A submarine can always make launching easier by getting bigger.

**Recovery is the problem.**

So I think the aviation history has three distinct eras.

## Era one: the Seiran solution, 1940s–50s

Use a specialized folding **floatplane**.

It is compact enough to store inside a cylindrical hangar, can be launched by catapult and can land beside the submarine for crane recovery.

That is slow and sea-state dependent.

But it actually works.

I would probably allow the postwar Aichi team to develop a much improved **turboprop Seiran descendant** in the 1950s rather than immediately demanding a submarine jet.

This aircraft would be an oddity in an IJN rapidly converting its normal carriers to jets.

But that doesn't matter.

Its mission values:

- compact folded dimensions;
- range;
- short preparation time;
- reliable water recovery;
- low-speed handling;
- payload.

Not dogfighting.

A 1958 submarine turboprop surrounded by jet fighters is perfectly plausible if it solves the submarine problem better.

And because it's principally attacking unsuspecting fixed targets, being somewhat slower than a frontline fighter isn't fatal.

## Era two: the awkward jet problem, 1960s

This is where the program nearly gets cancelled.

A normal jet fighter is a horrible submarine aircraft.

Launching one is solvable with catapults or rocket assistance.

Getting it back is horrible.

Jet seaplanes are possible but impose severe compromises. Building an actual arresting flight deck on a submarine rapidly turns the vessel into nonsense.

So the IJN spends much of the 1960s investigating:

- rocket-assisted launch;
- compact folding jets;
- jet seaplanes;
- capture systems;
- expendable reconnaissance drones;
- helicopters;
- vertical-flight research.

None is quite satisfactory.

And this is actually good for the setting because **Britain can still retain the prestige of demonstrating the first really convincing VTOL combat aircraft**.

Japan sees that and immediately realizes:

> “That technology solves a problem we've had for twenty years.”

The normal carrier fleet finds VTOL interesting.

The Special Submarine Force finds it transformational.

## Era three: VTOL makes the true submarine carrier possible

Now we get what you're imagining.

The aircraft no longer needs floats.

It no longer needs an arresting deck.

It requires a relatively small **launch/recovery pad**, a hangar elevator or transfer system, and enough clear space to avoid cooking the submarine with jet exhaust.

At that point the submarine can:

1. approach submerged;
2. verify weather and tactical conditions at periscope depth;
3. surface;
4. open aviation doors;
5. raise or move prepared aircraft;
6. launch four or six aircraft rapidly;
7. close everything;
8. submerge.

Recovery requires resurfacing again, but a vertical aircraft can land directly aboard rather than touching down on the water and waiting to be craned aboard.

That is the key breakthrough.

---

# The mature ship wants a broad multi-hull arrangement

This is where your Typhoon-scale comparison is useful **without copying Typhoon**.

The big problem with putting several aircraft into one cylindrical submarine pressure hull is geometry.

Aircraft want **wide rectangular volume**.

Submarines want **cylinders**.

Those shapes hate one another.

So I think the mature Japanese design eventually uses multiple major pressure bodies with the aviation facility occupying the central upper structure.

Conceptually:

```text
          aviation hangar / elevator / flight pad
             ┌─────────────────────┐
             │   A/C A/C A/C A/C  │
         ┌───┴─────────────────────┴───┐
        (  port main pressure hull       )
         \                              /
          \____________________________/

        ( starboard main pressure hull  )
```

Not literally that cross-section, but the principle is:

> **don't force all the habitable, reactor and aviation volume into one tube.**

The broad hull also creates something a submarine carrier desperately needs:

**deck area.**

That makes the mature strategic aviation submarine one of those vessels where enormous beam is a feature rather than an unfortunate side effect.

And yes, once we reach this design, **reactor miniaturization stops making the entire submarine much smaller**.

That's a particularly nice consequence of the MSR work we just established.

On a frigate, smaller reactor means smaller ship.

On a strategic aviation submarine, smaller reactor means:

> “Excellent. We can put another aircraft, another magazine or another special-operations compartment where the reactor machinery used to be.”

The **aircraft** become the displacement driver.

---

# I wouldn't give it twenty aircraft

This is where I think restraint will make the concept more impressive.

A genuinely useful submersible carrier carrying **six high-performance aircraft** is already extraordinary.

Trying to make it carry twenty turns it into an underwater conventional carrier and destroys the reason for submerging in the first place.

My preferred mature number is roughly:

> **4–6 manned strike aircraft**, initially.

Then later:

> **4–6 manned aircraft plus perhaps 6–12 much smaller unmanned vehicles**.

Or a mission-variable load.

A six-aircraft strike sounds tiny until you remember what the submarine is for.

It isn't fighting Midway.

It is suddenly putting six strike aircraft over a target whose defense plan assumed **zero enemy aircraft could possibly be coming from that direction**.

That's what makes the capability strategic.

---

# The scale probably develops like this

I would use this as a working developmental ladder:

| Period | Working type | Submerged scale | Aircraft | Character |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| **1945–48** | Sen-Toku experimental boats | ~6,000–7,000 t | 3 | Seiran-type floatplanes; proof of concept |
| **1950s** | Sen-Toku Kai | ~8,000–10,000 t | 3–4 | Turboprop strike/recon aircraft; faster launch and better hangar |
| **1960s** | Nuclear aviation experimental boat | ~12,000–18,000 t | 4 | Nuclear endurance, but aircraft recovery remains awkward |
| **1970s** | First true strategic aviation submarine | ~22,000–30,000 t | 4–6 | VTOL aircraft; rapid surface-launch/dive cycle |
| **1980s** | Mature strategic aviation submarine | ~30,000–40,000 t | 6 + drones | Strategic patrol force; modular aviation spaces |
| **1990s–2000s** | MSR successor | similar overall scale | 6–8 or mixed manned/UAV | Smaller machinery is traded for payload and mission flexibility |

Those displacement numbers are **design targets**, not canon yet.

But importantly, a very large nuclear submarine is not physically outside demonstrated submarine construction. The historical I-400 itself was already gigantic for 1945, and the world later demonstrated that submarines could grow to extraordinary dimensions. The issue for our Japanese boat isn't “can a hull this large be built?” It is whether the aviation benefit justifies the noise, cost and complexity.

For Japan, I think the answer can be yes for **four or five hulls**.

Not twenty.

---

# Four or five is exactly the number I would choose

By the mature 1980s generation, I'd aim for:

**4 operational strategic aviation submarines**, with perhaps  
**1 additional hull in major overhaul/training/trials**.

That gives the IJN enough to sustain something like:

- one Pacific patrol;
- one Indian Ocean/South Asian patrol;
- one available for contingency or another theater;
- one in training/refit;
- fifth as schedule/depot reserve depending on exact cycle.

This is where they become institutionally analogous to an SSBN force.

Not because they can end civilization.

Because they are:

- tightly controlled;
- strategically tasked;
- extremely secret;
- independent of local theater commanders;
- expensive;
- capable of being placed somewhere months before anybody knows they'll be needed.

A normal attack submarine is part of a naval campaign.

The aviation submarine is something Tokyo can move quietly as part of **national policy**.

That is a meaningful distinction.

---

# And the strategic mission is exactly what you're imagining

Your examples are good conceptually, with one qualification.

The submarine's best trick isn't necessarily penetrating all the way into a **heavily monitored enclosed sea** such as the Persian Gulf.

Every chokepoint it has to transit increases the chance somebody finds it.

Its stronger employment is usually:

> **remain in unexpected open water and let the aircraft supply the last several hundred kilometers.**

A boat off Baja can generate an attack from an axis from which American continental defense does not normally expect naval aviation.

A boat in the Arabian Sea can threaten installations that planners assumed were protected by their distance from Japanese land bases.

A boat in the South Atlantic can suddenly put Japanese reconnaissance over something Tokyo ordinarily cannot inspect.

Targets include:

- air-defense headquarters;
- early-warning radars;
- airfields;
- satellite ground stations;
- fleet headquarters;
- communications centers;
- ports;
- critical bridges;
- military-industrial installations;
- intelligence targets.

It is particularly good at attacking **systems whose protection depends on nobody being close enough to attack them**.

That is a uniquely useful capability.

---

# But recovery should remain optional in wartime

This is the biggest operational refinement I would make to the image.

The ship **can** recover its aircraft.

That is essential to calling it a true carrier.

But the commander should not always do it.

Launching requires one vulnerable surfaced interval.

Recovering six aircraft requires another, probably longer one, at a time when the enemy now knows somebody has just attacked him.

So Japanese doctrine probably distinguishes:

### Reusable mission

Low threat.

Reconnaissance.

Covert observation.

Limited strike against an opponent unable to search the launch area.

Aircraft return and are recovered.

### Strategic penetration mission

High threat.

The aircraft launch and **do not necessarily return to the submarine**.

They may:

- divert to a Japanese or associated-state airfield;
- land at a clandestine forward strip;
- rendezvous much later at another recovery point;
- in an extreme operation, be deliberately expendable after crew recovery elsewhere.

This echoes the original I-400 tradeoff. Historical boats could halve launch time by sending the Seirans without their floats, but that meant giving up normal at-sea recovery. citeturn284871search0

The mature Navy learns the same lesson at a higher technological level:

> **The submarine is more valuable than the aircraft. Don't risk the submarine merely because someone wants the airplanes back.**

That is very Japanese carrier logic applied underwater.

---

# The transport version can be smaller

The companion **submersible assault transport** does not need Typhoon scale.

I would expect perhaps:

**10,000–15,000 tons submerged**, eventually nuclear;

roughly **120–180 troops** for the normal mission;

lockout chambers;

several small landing/swimmer vehicles;

inflatable or semi-submersible boats;

communications/intelligence spaces;

perhaps 100–300 tonnes of mission cargo depending on configuration.

And there might only be **four to six** of these.

That's enough to put a company ashore unexpectedly without pretending the IJN can conduct an amphibious invasion through submarines.

Its strategic use is:

> seize or sabotage one thing.

Not:

> conquer the coast.

So the IJN Special Submarine Force can conduct operations such as:

- reconnaissance team insertion;
- sabotage;
- seizure of a small island or radar station;
- extraction of agents;
- emplacement of sensors;
- clandestine resupply;
- evacuation of important personnel;
- recovery of downed aviators.

That is an extremely useful capability for the vast Sphere.

---

# The aviation submarine becomes a secrecy problem too

Japan can hide **purpose** much more easily than **existence**.

By the satellite era, I would not claim that Germany, America or Britain have no idea that Japan possesses several huge submarines.

A 30,000-plus-ton submarine requires:

- specialized construction facilities;
- large dockyards;
- major reactor infrastructure;
- crews;
- tenders;
- maintenance;
- sea trials.

Foreign intelligence is going to notice something.

What Japan can plausibly conceal is:

> **what the central mission section contains.**

Foreign analysts may identify:

> “four exceptionally large nuclear special-purpose submarines.”

Then argue for twenty years about whether they are:

- missile boats;
- fleet-command submarines;
- transport submarines;
- electronic-intelligence boats;
- aviation boats;
- some combination.

And Japan never helps them.

Construction halls are enclosed.

Aircraft trials occur at remote facilities.

The boats don't conduct public port visits.

No convenient cutaway is released.

Even their dimensions can be uncertain.

That is more convincing than total invisibility and, frankly, more atmospheric.

American intelligence knows there's **something enormous** under the Pacific.

It isn't quite sure what Japan thinks it is for.

---

# And then drones make the concept even more dangerous

The irony is that Japan spends decades solving the impossibly difficult problem of putting **manned aircraft** on a submarine.

Then the unmanned-aircraft age arrives.

Suddenly the huge hangar can carry:

six manned aircraft **or**

four manned aircraft and eight drones **or**

twenty-plus small reconnaissance/strike drones **or**

a special-operations package.

Now the giant hull's inefficiency becomes flexibility.

And because Japan's broader military doctrine is already good at integrating distributed sensors, the aviation submarine becomes an extraordinary deep-ocean reconnaissance node.

By the 2000s it may be less accurate to call it a submarine aircraft carrier than a **submersible aviation and special-mission ship**.

But the institutional lineage remains completely clear:

> everybody can trace it back to three Seirans folded inside a tube.

---

## So I think the homage absolutely belongs

And I don't think we need to apologize for it as an eccentricity.

The trick is simply making the setting earn it.

The I-400 doesn't prove that submarine carriers are secretly better than normal carriers. It proves that **submarines can carry useful aviation at all**. The first postwar boats then spend years discovering why that capability is awkward. Jets nearly kill the concept. VTOL saves it. Nuclear propulsion gives it strategic endurance. Multi-hull construction gives it the required volume. Japanese compact-reactor research eventually frees more of that volume for payload. Drones then make the enormous aviation bay increasingly valuable rather than obsolete.

The result remains a tiny strategic force because it is **horrifically expensive per aircraft**.

And that's fine.

An eight-carrier IJN doesn't need twenty underwater carriers.

It needs four submarines that can make an enemy staff officer look at a map, point to somewhere hundreds of miles from any Japanese base, and still have to ask:

> **“Could Japanese aircraft appear here?”**

That's the strategic capability these ships buy. memcite

iturn290188image0

Yes. I think we can make this the **mission that saves the Japanese aviation-submarine idea from becoming an expensive wartime curiosity**. The broad result is strong enough to establish; the exact target is where I'd make one correction.

genui{"map_widget":{"points":[{"lat":22.0446,"long":64.2684,"name":"Dwarka–Al Ashkhara midpoint","category":"Original proposed patrol area"},{"lat":24.0,"long":60.0,"name":"Preferred I-400 launch box","category":"Working launch area"},{"address":"Al Mahatta Museum, Sharjah, United Arab Emirates","name":"RAF Sharjah","category":"Recommended target"},{"address":"Masirah Island, Oman","name":"Masirah","category":"Alternative target"},{"address":"Abadan, Iran","name":"Abadan","category":"Long-range strategic target"}]}}

### The geographical correction

The literal midpoint between Dwarka and Al Ashkhara is considerably farther east than I think you intended—roughly around 22°N, 64°E, in the Arabian Sea. From there, Dubai/Sharjah is about **525–530 nautical miles one way** by my calculation.

That doesn't work for a recoverable Seiran raid. The M6A1 had a stated maximum range of about **641 nautical miles with a torpedo or equivalent bomb load**. citeturn290188search0turn290188search3

Masirah, by contrast, is about 310 nautical miles from that midpoint. It is barely within a maximum-range out-and-back mission, but with very little reserve.

So if we want the more impressive **Persian Gulf surprise raid**, I would move I-400 west before launch, to approximately **24°N, 60°E**, still in the Gulf of Oman/Arabian Sea approaches rather than sending this enormous experimental submarine deep into the shallow Persian Gulf.

From there, historical RAF Sharjah is only about **260 nautical miles** away. That gives a roughly 520–530-nautical-mile round trip and leaves some reserve within the Seiran's nominal range.

And Sharjah is a much better 1946–47 target than Dubai.

### I would make the target RAF Sharjah

Dubai doesn't yet possess the sort of refinery complex you're imagining. More importantly, Britain already had a real strategic air infrastructure around the Gulf. An official RAF history describes the postwar network as stretching from Habbaniya and Basrah through **Bahrain and Sharjah**, with Masirah and Salalah serving as route stations farther south. citeturn537672search0

So I would make the raid something like this:

> **Late 1946. I-400 penetrates independently into the northwestern Arabian Sea, surfaces before dawn roughly 250–275 nautical miles southeast of Sharjah, and launches all three Seirans.**

The aircraft attack **RAF Sharjah**, concentrating on three functional targets:

1. one aircraft attacks the airfield's fuel/storage area;
2. one attacks hangars, parked aircraft, and maintenance facilities;
3. one attacks the wireless/navigation/operations complex.

The exact fuel-tank layout would be invented setting detail, but the presence of a British Gulf airbase and communications network there is historically grounded. citeturn537672search0

Then—and this is the part that matters most doctrinally—the three aircraft **come back**.

The historical I-400 system could carry and catapult three Seirans, and the aircraft were explicitly designed for submarine operation. citeturn290188search3turn290188search8 The operation therefore proves the whole system rather than merely demonstrating a one-way flying bomb.

### Why not Abadan or Kuwait?

They're excellent **later conceptual targets**, but bad choices for this proof mission.

Kuwait is particularly tempting because its first crude-oil export actually occurred in **1946**. citeturn290188search5 But Kuwait and Abadan are far enough up the Gulf that a three-aircraft recoverable raid from a submarine remaining outside the Strait of Hormuz doesn't fit the Seiran's range.

The IJN could send I-400 into the Persian Gulf itself, but that defeats much of the operational demonstration. The Gulf is constrained water. You have chokepoints, more traffic, less maneuvering room, and a much greater chance that Britain discovers the submarine.

The proof-of-concept mission should demonstrate:

> **The submarine can remain in oceanic water, beyond where Britain expects a Japanese carrier to be, and still put Japanese aircraft over a strategic British installation.**

Sharjah accomplishes that.

Masirah would be the safer alternative, and historically it was indeed part of Britain's route-station system. citeturn537672search0 But attacking Masirah proves merely that I-400 can raid an isolated Indian Ocean base.

Sharjah proves something psychologically larger:

> **The British Gulf system itself is reachable without the Combined Fleet entering the Gulf.**

That's the lesson that keeps the program alive.

## The damage should be useful, not spectacular

I would deliberately **not** make this a Pearl Harbor in miniature.

Three aircraft don't annihilate an airbase.

Maybe they destroy or damage several parked aircraft, ignite fuel stores, knock the wireless station temporarily offline, crater part of the field, and kill some personnel. One Seiran is perhaps damaged by AA fire on the way out. The British have the installation functioning again within days or weeks.

Tactically:

> interesting raid.

Operationally:

> irritating but not decisive.

Institutionally:

> **earthquake.**

Because the Naval Staff receives the report:

- submarine crossed an enormous distance independently;
- British reconnaissance never located it beforehand;
- three aircraft were launched successfully;
- all three reached the target;
- surviving aircraft returned to the submarine;
- the boat recovered them and disappeared.

The question after that isn't:

> “Was destroying those fuel tanks worth building I-400?”

It's:

> **“What happens when the submarine carries better aircraft?”**

And that's exactly the question we need Japan to keep asking.

I would therefore make the **Arabian Sea/Sharjah raid itself canon**, with the precise date and operation name still open unless you want to settle them later.

## It also explains why Britain doesn't immediately understand what happened

This could be one of the funnier intelligence episodes of the war.

British personnel at Sharjah see three Japanese aircraft attack from an approach that doesn't make immediate sense.

The RAF asks where they came from.

There is no known Japanese carrier force within useful range.

Maybe they flew from some clandestine forward strip?

Did Japan obtain airfield access somewhere in Persia?

Were they extremely long-range reconnaissance bombers?

Was there a carrier the Royal Navy had somehow lost?

The answer—**one submarine launched all three**—might take British intelligence some time to establish confidently.

The historical Seiran itself was sufficiently secret that Allied intelligence did not know of it until after Japan's surrender in our timeline. citeturn290188search0turn290188search8

In AltWWII Britain will eventually work it out, especially if wreckage or reconnaissance reports identify the strange aircraft. But the initial uncertainty is itself part of what demonstrates the weapon's value.

---

# And yes, I think these submarines should eventually receive names

I would make a distinction between **the wartime experiment** and **the postwar strategic institution**.

The wartime boats remain:

**I-400**  
**I-401**  
perhaps **I-402**

because they're still being procured within the ordinary submarine registry. They are officially *I*-boats despite being bizarrely large.

But after the Sharjah raid, the Navy effectively admits:

> These are not merely unusually large submarines.

The later strategic aviation submarine becomes sufficiently large, expensive and politically important that Japan creates a special naming convention while **retaining an I-number as its administrative hull designation**.

So you'd get something like:

> **I-500 *Ryūjin***  
> **I-501 *Watatsumi***

rather than abolishing the submarine numbering system completely.

The number tells the Navy what it is administratively.

The name tells everyone that this is a capital-grade strategic vessel.

## I like sea mythology for the naming family

We shouldn't steal:

- provinces from battleships;
- mountains/rivers from cruisers;
- weather from destroyers;
- the established carrier naming traditions.

The strategic aviation submarines are a genuinely new ship category, so they can receive a genuinely new naming family.

My preferred family would be **mythological sea beings, sea deities, and deep-ocean figures**.

The lead postwar class could therefore be the:

> **Ryūjin class**

after the dragon deity associated with the sea.

The individual ships could draw from that maritime mythological vocabulary rather than receiving ordinary submarine numbers alone.

And I think that fits culturally much better than calling them after modern abstractions like *Surprise*, *Stealth*, or *Strategic Deterrence*.

The ships are huge, secret, extraordinarily expensive, and spend months beneath the sea carrying aircraft intended to appear where Japanese aviation ought not exist.

A slightly mythic naming tradition is appropriate.

### Most importantly, though, the names should begin **after** I-400 succeeds

That's a good little institutional detail.

I-400 is a number because she's an experiment.

The successor is named because the experiment has created a **recognized strategic arm**.

So later historians can actually use the naming change as shorthand:

> **I-400 proved the idea. Ryūjin institutionalized it.**

That feels like a very clean transition into the postwar Japanese Special Submarine Force. memcite

The raid should be remembered by Britain **not as a damaging strike, but as an intelligence impossibility**: three Japanese attack aircraft appear over Sharjah from a direction that implies a carrier, yet the carrier simply does not exist on the reconnaissance picture. I’m checking the Seiran’s actual cruise/launch/recovery envelope so we can make the dawn timeline tight enough that the “another few minutes and they’d have seen I-400” beat is earned rather than cinematic luck.

Yes. This version is better, because **the raid's military effect should be nearly irrelevant while its intelligence effect is deeply unsettling**.

One correction to the British description: if the Seirans are going to return and be recovered, they need to retain their floats. Historically, I-400 could launch all three with floats in about 30 minutes, and the submarine carried a crane for recovery; removing the floats could halve launch time but sacrificed normal recovery. The Seiran was also a single-engine attack floatplane rather than a fighter. citeturn361507search0turn361507search1 So the first British reports probably describe something like **three unidentified or unfamiliar Japanese single-engine float attack aircraft**, not conventional carrier fighters. That actually makes the mystery better: did they come from a seaplane tender, a cruiser force, some secret Japanese airstrip, or something else?

I would make the raid almost embarrassingly unsuccessful as a bombing mission. One aircraft gets a respectable hit and sets a fuel tank or small fuel-storage area burning. Another damages perhaps a maintenance building or parked equipment. The third bomb misses its intended target entirely and explodes harmlessly enough that the later British history almost makes fun of it. A handful of personnel are wounded; perhaps nobody is killed. One Seiran takes a rifle-caliber or light-AA hit through the rear control surfaces—damaging an elevator trim tab or control linkage enough that the pilot has an unpleasant flight home, but not enough to lose the aircraft.

That gives Britain no reason to remember the raid as a great Japanese tactical achievement. What everyone remembers is the question:

> **Where did those airplanes come from?**

RAF Sharjah was a genuine British Persian Gulf staging station in precisely this period; a December 1945 RAF account describes Sharjah as one of the Gulf Stations on the important trunk route toward India and the Far East. citeturn361507search36 So three Japanese aircraft suddenly arriving at dawn is not merely an attack on some desert outpost. It is a violation of Britain's mental map of where Japanese aviation can exist.

The sequence I would use is approximately:

1. **Before dawn**, I-400 surfaces in the Gulf of Oman launch box. The crew assembles and launches all three Seirans with floats attached, accepting the roughly thirty-minute exposure required for a recoverable mission. Immediately afterward I-400 dives rather than waiting on the surface. citeturn361507search0
2. The aircraft fly roughly an hour or somewhat more toward Sharjah, staying low for much of the approach. They arrive around local dawn, make one quick pass each, drop their bombs, and leave toward the open Gulf. There is no prolonged strafing or second attack. The mission's whole logic is surprise.
3. Sharjah reports three Japanese floatplanes departing seaward. Available British aircraft are ordered to search the reciprocal bearing for whatever launched them. The first assumption is probably **surface aviation support**—a carrier, seaplane tender, cruiser group, or clandestine forward base—not an enormous submarine.
4. Meanwhile the Seirans rendezvous with I-400 at a prearranged recovery point displaced somewhat from the original launch position. I-400 surfaces in daylight. The aircraft alight alongside one by one and are craned aboard. This is the genuinely dangerous part; historical I-400 recovery was possible but difficult. citeturn361507search0
5. The damaged aircraft takes longest. Once it is secured, lookouts report an aircraft—or possibly merely something that could be an aircraft—approaching at the edge of visibility. The captain abandons any unnecessary topside work and orders an immediate dive. Historically I-400 could dive in roughly seventy seconds, so disappearing on this timescale is quite credible. citeturn361507search15
6. The British search aircraft reaches the area minutes later and finds **nothing**: no carrier, no cruiser, no seaplane tender. At most it sees a disturbed patch of sea, some oil or debris from recovery work, or a wake too ambiguous to establish what created it.

I particularly like the close escape because it gives the Japanese after-action report the opposite emotional character from the British report.

The British report says, essentially:

> Three Japanese floatplanes attacked Sharjah. Damage negligible. Origin unknown. Maritime reconnaissance found no carrier or tender.

The Japanese report says:

> **Three aircraft launched. Three reached target. Three returned. Three recovered. Submarine escaped before enemy reconnaissance reached recovery area.**

For the Japanese Naval Staff, that is an extraordinary technical success even if the bombs accomplished almost nothing.

And that's what preserves the program.

The evaluation isn't, “I-400 is an economical way of blowing up a fuel tank.” It obviously isn't. It's:

> **A single submarine placed a recoverable Japanese air strike over a British installation that British planners believed lay outside the practical reach of Japanese naval aviation, and Britain never located the launching platform.**

That is enough.

I would even have the IJN be somewhat irritated by the bombing results. The ordnance officers report poor accuracy, the aviation people complain about the damaged aircraft, the submarine commander complains that recovering three floatplanes in daylight nearly got everyone killed, and the financial people point out how absurdly expensive the entire exercise was.

And then somebody asks the decisive question:

> **“If the attack itself was poor, why did the British spend the rest of the morning searching hundreds of miles of sea for a carrier that wasn't there?”**

That's the conceptual victory.

It also gives the later program a very clean set of requirements derived directly from combat rather than from fantasy: **shorter surface exposure, faster aircraft preparation, better navigation and bombing accuracy, safer recovery, greater aircraft range, and eventually an aircraft that does not need to land on the sea at all.**

The raid therefore doesn't prove that I-400 is already a good strategic weapon. It proves that **the underlying capability is real enough to deserve another generation**. That is exactly the amount of success we need. memcite

## Turn 1168 — Assistant

- Timestamp: 2026-08-15T00:15:45.732Z
- Message ID: `73331952-daeb-4d42-a750-63b1ed275746`
- Source: ChatGPT shared conversation `Naval Doctrine Evolution`
- Parallel branch: https://chatgpt.com/share/6a80206d-15d0-83e8-b360-a8acc44d3025
- Relationship: parallel specialist continuation imported after the master project record through Turn 777

I think the Regia Marina ends up with a very strong identity precisely because **victory deprives it of the obvious enemy around which it had organized itself**.

The answer should not be “Italy becomes a small navy because the Mediterranean is safe.” Italy has acquired a maritime empire whose western and eastern halves are connected by sea, and the current setting explicitly describes Italy in 1947 as the dominant Mediterranean naval and logistical power while simultaneously burdened with Malta, Egypt, Suez, Sudan, and a politically difficult imperial corridor. fileciteturn21file10 The wiki likewise describes Italy as controlling the Mediterranean crossings while being strategically overextended. citeturn942566view0

So I think the postwar Regia Marina becomes something like:

> **A compact, extremely high-readiness sea-control navy designed to make Mare Nostrum a military fact rather than a slogan.**

It is probably the major navy that looks **most recognizably “modern” to us by the 1970s–80s**: missile-and-gun cruisers, excellent radar, helicopters, quiet conventional submarines, sophisticated frigates, amphibious ships, mine warfare, shore-based surveillance, and only a small number of very large prestige ships.

## The governing Italian question changes

During the war, the question was:

> How do we defeat or exclude the Royal Navy from the central Mediterranean?

After 1947, the question becomes:

> **How cheaply can we guarantee that nobody can reverse the Mediterranean settlement?**

That gives the Navy five enduring jobs.

The first is to keep the **three strategic approaches** under observation: Gibraltar in cooperation with Spain; the Turkish Straits and eastern Mediterranean; and the Red Sea outlet through **Bab el-Mandeb**. Gibraltar being held by an ally doesn't mean Italy ceases caring about it. Allies can change governments. Treaties can sour. Spain itself eventually becomes a major Latin naval power. The sensible Italian assumption is that the western gate should be friendly **and watched**.

Bab el-Mandeb is even more interesting because Britain still retains Aden in the setting. Italy possesses the Red Sea side through its East African system and Djibouti, but the southern outlet isn't simply an Italian lake. So the Red Sea Fleet remains a real operational command rather than ceremonial overseas basing.

Second, the Navy protects the **imperial artery**:

> Italy → Sicily/Malta → North Africa → Alexandria/Suez → Red Sea → Eritrea/Djibouti.

Third, it acts as the mobile heavy reserve behind Italian possessions and clients. If something goes wrong in Cyprus, Greece, Libya, Egypt, the Levant, or the Red Sea, ships can arrive quickly.

Fourth, it supplies naval air, gunfire, amphibious lift and command support to the Army. Italy's actual war has given it genuine amphibious and expeditionary institutional experience rather than merely theories about it. The wartime canon already has *Aquila* operational from 1944, *Sparviero* from 1946, and a growing Italian escort/amphibious establishment. fileciteturn21file14

And fifth, it prevents **another Matapan**.

That last one becomes almost a religion.

## “Never the blindfolded navy again” is probably the defining technical doctrine

I think your Matapan instinct is exactly right.

The modern Italian Navy's own historical account identifies Matapan as exposing serious deficiencies in **night fighting and aeronaval cooperation**, while its radar-history material says the losses at Matapan finally broke through resistance and accelerated Italian radar work. citeturn981974search9turn981974search5

Our Italy then spends another six victorious years learning how expensive poor information can be.

So the postwar Regia Marina's obsession becomes:

> **See first. Identify first. Establish the firing solution first. Fire first.**

That produces an Italian technical ecosystem focused disproportionately on:

- surface-search and air-search radar;
- fire-control radar;
- electronic support measures;
- night optics;
- command-information centers;
- automatic plotting;
- datalinks between ships and shore;
- radar-controlled guns;
- increasingly compact guided missiles;
- highly automated medium-caliber artillery.

And the geography helps.

The Mediterranean is almost ideal for a **shore-assisted naval sensor network**. Italy can build radar and communications stations across Sicily, Sardinia, Pantelleria, Malta, Tunisia, Greece, Cyprus, Egypt, Suez and East Africa, while coordinating westward with Spain.

An Italian warship therefore often fights as one node of a regional network rather than as a self-contained blue-water island.

That is a major reason it doesn't need to be Japanese.

It doesn't need a nuclear cruiser capable of sailing from Tahiti to Kamchatka.

It needs a cruiser that leaves Taranto and is already plugged into the Mediterranean battle picture.

## This probably makes Italy an early missile-and-automatic-gun navy

And this is where your suggestion that it becomes surprisingly familiar to modern eyes works extremely well.

Historically, postwar Italy really did develop a strong automatic naval-gun tradition. The Italian Navy's history records the introduction of the 76/62 family in its 1950s ships, followed later by the 76/62 **Compatto**; Italian experimental ships also tested both the Compact gun and short-range surface-to-surface missiles in the 1960s. citeturn114158search0turn114158search5turn114158search1

In AltWWII, that development gets an uninterrupted victorious industrial base and a much stronger institutional reason to pursue it.

So I would make one of the characteristic Italian postwar weapons a lineage of **exceptionally good automatic 76 mm naval guns**, with larger automatic 127 mm weapons occupying the destroyer/cruiser surface-fire role.

By the missile age, an Italian frigate might look much more familiar to us than an American one:

> one excellent automatic gun forward,  
> trainable or later vertical SAMs,  
> antiship missiles,  
> helicopter,  
> sophisticated radar,  
> compact hull.

That isn't because Italy has abandoned naval gunnery. Quite the opposite: **the gun is being made into part of the sensor system**.

Later real-world Italian 76 mm systems ultimately became capable of extremely rapid fire and guided anti-air/anti-missile ammunition, so there's an obvious long-term technological direction here. citeturn114158search12turn114158search13

That is very Matapan:

> the answer isn't simply a bigger shell.  
> The answer is getting the right shell onto the right target before the other man understands what is happening.

---

# The battleship survives, but I don't think Italy builds another battleship class

This is where I would distinguish Italy sharply from America and Japan.

Italy finishes the war with a very respectable battle line. The existing 1947 inheritance gives it *Littorio, Vittorio Veneto, Roma, Impero, Andrea Doria,* and *Caio Duilio*, with *Giulio Cesare* lost during Torch. fileciteturn21file12

The two old *Doria*-class ships are retirement candidates almost immediately.

That leaves **four Littorio-class battleships**.

What strategic problem would justify spending a fortune replacing them in 1955?

There really isn't one.

Britain has been expelled from the Mediterranean.

France has been partitioned.

Spain is friendly.

Turkey cannot challenge four Littorios.

Germany isn't a Mediterranean naval competitor.

Therefore, unlike the Americans, the Italians don't need another caliber race. Unlike Japan, they don't need a 30-knot nuclear Big Brother to chase carriers across the Pacific.

They can say:

> **These four ships are perfectly capable of killing anything likely to enter our sea. Modernize them.**

That feels very Italian and very economically sensible.

I'd therefore make the Littorios some of the most extensively reconstructed capital ships in the setting.

Their evolution probably looks something like:

**late 1940s:** wartime radar/AA completion;

**1950s:** radically improved fire control, modern AA, command spaces;

**1960s:** SAM installation, helicopter/reconnaissance facilities, new electronics;

**1970s:** removal of some secondary battery, modern close defense and electronic warfare;

**1980s:** perhaps two remain truly front-line while two have become reserve/training/bombardment ships.

That happens to get us toward the old reference's **two active Italian battleships in 1985** without requiring its old class assumptions. fileciteturn21file1

And I would probably make **Roma and Impero** the final two because they're the youngest hulls.

They become enormous Mediterranean gun-and-missile flagships.

No nuclear conversion.

No need.

They can refuel in Taranto, Palermo, Malta, Alexandria, Suez, Massawa or Djibouti.

## The carrier survives for almost the opposite reason

Italy's carriers aren't needed to dominate the Mediterranean under normal conditions because Italy has **land airfields everywhere**.

That makes *Aquila* and *Sparviero* useful, but it also prevents the carrier faction from becoming the IJN.

The postwar Italian carrier argument becomes:

> **Land aviation controls the normal Mediterranean. The carrier brings aviation to the place where the normal system has failed or does not reach.**

That means:

- rapid crisis response;
- Red Sea and northwest Indian Ocean operations;
- amphibious support;
- mobile fighter cover if a land base is damaged;
- intervention outside the normal Italian airfield chain;
- prestige and bloc leadership.

So I would absolutely build more Italian carriers.

Just not supercarriers.

Perhaps by the 1960s–80s the ideal Regia Marina is something like:

**two medium fleet carriers**, perhaps 35,000–45,000 tonnes;

plus **one smaller assault/light carrier** primarily oriented around helicopters, Marines and later VTOL aircraft.

That's enough to project a serious aviation force without pretending Italy wants to fight Japan east of Singapore.

And historically Italy's wartime carrier turn was already a response to combat lessons; the actual Regia Marina ordered *Roma* and *Augustus* converted to *Aquila* and *Sparviero* in 1942, although our historical ships never became operational. citeturn981974search0 In the setting, their successful wartime service gives a completely natural institutional foundation for a small permanent carrier arm.

---

# Cruisers probably become the real center of the postwar fleet

This is where I'd put Italian shipbuilding prestige.

The battleships are powerful but old.

The carriers are valuable but few.

The **cruiser is where Italy can demonstrate that it understands modern naval war better than it did in 1941**.

A postwar Italian cruiser should be:

- very well sensored;
- fast;
- heavily automated;
- extremely good at night fighting;
- capable of directing smaller ships;
- equipped with good SAMs;
- armed with effective medium-caliber automatic guns;
- later armed with antiship missiles;
- able to coordinate helicopters and shore-based aviation.

This is where German missile technology can enter without Italy becoming German.

Italy initially **imports or licenses individual German missile technologies**, but then Italian and Occitan electronics firms turn them into Latin naval systems.

That makes the 1958 **Latin Naval Materiel Board** especially valuable. It already exists in canon as the institution standardizing replenishment, communications, missile/torpedo interfaces, rescue equipment and deck practice. fileciteturn21file16

The natural division is:

**Italy:** ships, naval guns, Mediterranean doctrine, carrier experience.

**Spain:** Atlantic endurance, shipbuilding, Gibraltar/Atlantic operations.

**Occitania:** guidance, electronics, aerospace and sensor integration.

**Portugal:** Atlantic route expertise and smaller-ocean navy experience.

That lets the Latin Bloc build excellent systems without every state reproducing an entire military-industrial ecosystem.

---

# Destroyers and frigates become disproportionately important

Because Italy doesn't need eight capital ships.

It needs to be able to **close the sea**.

That means lots of relatively compact, high-readiness ships.

Destroyers are fleet air-defense/surface-combat escorts.

Frigates become ASW and patrol workhorses.

And unlike Japan's frigates, they don't need extreme endurance.

A Mediterranean frigate can trade enormous fuel bunkers for:

- radar;
- weapons;
- crew habitability;
- helicopter facilities.

That makes them compact and heavily armed for their displacement.

This could become another visual Italian signature:

> **Italian ships look slightly too heavily armed for their size.**

Because the designer knows the ship can be back at a friendly port much sooner than a Japanese or British vessel can.

A British frigate has to cross oceans.

An Italian frigate has another naval base over the horizon.

---

# The submarine force probably becomes excellent precisely because it stays conventional

I agree completely that Italy doesn't become German underwater.

Wolfpack doctrine solves the German problem:

> How do we destroy Atlantic commerce with submarines acting as the principal strategic offensive fleet?

That isn't Italy's problem.

The Italian submarine asks:

> **How do I make a narrow sea or chokepoint dangerous?**

This should produce a first-class **SSK navy**.

Quiet diesel-electric boats.

Good sonar.

Good torpedoes.

Later wire-guided weapons.

Excellent mine capability.

Shorter endurance than German ocean boats because it doesn't matter.

Very good shallow/enclosed-water tactics.

And I'd keep Italy largely **out of nuclear submarines**, or at most give it one expensive experimental program that doesn't become standard.

Nuclear propulsion's greatest strengths—very long submerged endurance and oceanic strategic mobility—are least valuable in Italy's normal operating environment.

A smaller battery boat sitting quietly outside Alexandria, Gibraltar or Bab el-Mandeb may actually be the more dangerous local weapon.

So Italy could paradoxically be technologically first-rate while remaining one of the last great powers to say:

> **No, we do not actually need to put a reactor in this.**

---

# Mine warfare should be much more important than we've treated it

This is almost unavoidable.

Italy's entire strategic position revolves around chokepoints.

Gibraltar.

The Sicilian narrows.

The approaches to Malta.

Suez.

Bab el-Mandeb.

The Aegean and Turkish approaches.

That means offensive mining and mine countermeasures should be prestigious Regia Marina specialties.

Not glamorous in popular culture.

Extremely glamorous to naval planners.

If Italy can mine a gate faster than an enemy can clear it, that enemy's theoretical fleet strength becomes irrelevant for the first several days of a crisis.

So I'd expect Italy to maintain one of the world's most sophisticated mine-warfare establishments, perhaps alongside Britain.

And this is also a cheap way to defend an imperial maritime perimeter without permanently stationing a battleship everywhere.

---

# Amphibious warfare becomes the other unexpectedly important branch

This is the piece I think the old reference accidentally got right when it gave Italy a fairly substantial amphibious fleet. fileciteturn21file1

The postwar Italian empire contains islands, North Africa, Egypt, Red Sea possessions and politically unstable dependent territories.

That demands:

- Marine/Navy infantry;
- landing ships;
- helicopter assault;
- repair ships;
- transports;
- hospital ships;
- coastal landing craft.

Italy's great naval operation after 1947 is probably much more likely to look like:

> land a brigade somewhere in the eastern Mediterranean under cruiser and carrier cover

than:

> fight the Japanese Combined Fleet.

So the Regia Marina becomes unusually competent at **short-range amphibious concentration**.

Because again, geography helps it.

Italian transports don't need to cross the Pacific.

They need to move troops from Taranto to Crete, or Alexandria to Cyprus, or Massawa to somewhere around the Red Sea.

That is a very different design requirement.

---

# This leaves Italy with a remarkably modern-looking 1985 fleet

I would not lock exact classes yet, but the **shape** I now find most plausible is something like:

| Type | Approximate first-line 1985 objective | Character |
|---|---:|---|
| Battleships | **2** | Extensively reconstructed Littorio hulls |
| Fleet carriers | **2** | Medium conventional jet carriers |
| Assault/light carrier | **1** | Helicopters, Marines, VTOL |
| Large missile/command cruisers | **4–6** | Core high-end surface combatant |
| Destroyers | **10–14** | Fleet AA/surface escort |
| Frigates | **16–24** | ASW/patrol backbone |
| Corvettes/missile craft | **20+** | Mediterranean littoral denial |
| Conventional submarines | **10–14** | Quiet chokepoint ambush force |
| Nuclear submarines | **0–2 experimental**, possibly zero | Never central |
| Major amphibious ships | **8–12** | Imperial crisis-response force |
| Mine-warfare ships | **12–20** | Major doctrinal specialty |

That isn't necessarily **small** in raw numbers.

But it is compact relative to the empire's status and very different from Japan's enormous blue-water system or Britain's oceanic convoy architecture.

And I would make readiness unusually high.

Italy can concentrate a large percentage of that fleet inside the Mediterranean relatively quickly because the operating theater is small.

So the Regia Marina's strength isn't:

> “We have 300 warships.”

It's:

> **“How many first-rate combatants can we put between Sicily and Alexandria within forty-eight hours?”**

That is the metric Italian admirals care about.

## Which makes the Italian Navy's technological personality very clear

America says:

> **Survive, command, and keep firing.**

Japan says:

> **Keep the carrier able to launch the next strike.**

Germany says:

> **Remain hidden and destroy from outside the enemy's preferred fight.**

Britain says:

> **Keep the routes open.**

Italy says:

> **Know exactly what is inside our sea, concentrate before it can act, and make every approach expensive.**

That is a very strong doctrine.

And it means I agree with your instinct that Italy may become the navy that looks **least retrofuturistic** to us.

No nuclear destroyers.

No underwater aircraft carriers.

No eighty-thousand-ton railgun battleships.

Instead, somebody from our world looks at a 1985 Italian task group and thinks:

> *That looks surprisingly normal.*

A medium carrier.

A missile cruiser.

Several destroyers and frigates with excellent automatic guns.

Helicopters.

Antiship missiles.

A very quiet diesel submarine underneath.

A shore radar network telling all of them where the target is.

What the observer misses is that Italy arrived at that shape through **Matapan, Malta, Torch, Suez, and the political problem of turning Mare Nostrum from a wartime aspiration into a peacetime system of control**.

That gives the Regia Marina a reason to remain first-rate without needing to pretend it still has 1942's strategic problem. memcite
