## Turn 1171 — Assistant

- Timestamp: 2026-08-15T00:31:51.310Z
- Message ID: `fb26f590-8f79-4d5a-bcb9-37f2c8338190`
- Source: ChatGPT shared conversation `Naval Doctrine Evolution`
- Parallel branch: https://chatgpt.com/share/6a80206d-15d0-83e8-b360-a8acc44d3025
- Relationship: parallel specialist continuation imported after the master project record through Turn 777

I think the British answer is actually beginning to emerge fairly clearly, and it is **not carrier primacy, battleship primacy, or submarine primacy**.

The postwar Royal Navy becomes a **communications-and-sea-lane navy**.

The controlling question is no longer:

> What wins the decisive fleet battle?

It is:

> **What prevents Britain and the Commonwealth from being cut into isolated pieces?**

That is already very close to the surviving canon. The old Naval Armaments Reference calls the Royal Navy the “armed infrastructure of the Siege Commonwealth,” with priorities of sea-lane survival, ASW, expeditionary logistics, carrier air cover, defense of Canada and Atlantic possessions, and enough heavy surface power that Germany cannot simply dismiss Britain as defeated. fileciteturn22file0 The wartime reconstruction independently reached essentially the same conclusion: by 1947 the Royal Navy's first job is keeping Britain supplied, then preserving Commonwealth communications, while retaining enough carriers and heavy ships that Germany or Italy cannot exploit an escort-focused Britain. fileciteturn22file15

I think we should keep **that strategic character**, while being willing to rebuild almost all of the old class details later.

## Britain learns the opposite lesson from America

America finishes the war without testing its fleet doctrine properly and continues asking:

> “How do we build the strongest battle fleet?”

Britain has just spent years discovering that even a powerful fleet can lose strategically when it has **too many things that must be protected simultaneously**.

Torch is especially formative. The Royal Navy can screen the invasion force against submarines, or concentrate destroyers around the battle fleet, or protect the merchant convoys—but the same destroyer cannot be in three places at once. The wartime transcript already identifies this as one of Torch's central lessons. fileciteturn22file1

So the British do not conclude:

> battleships were wrong.

Or:

> carriers were wrong.

They conclude:

> **we did not possess enough usable naval capacity to cover every obligation simultaneously.**

That is exactly the kind of conclusion a defeated institution could carry for generations because it is both partly true and politically useful.

And it makes your proposed **fleet-in-being argument** very plausible.

The surviving heavy fleet says:

> “When we still had enough force concentrated, the enemy had to respect us. Every time we stripped the fleet to cover another convoy, expedition, or theater, we created a vulnerability somewhere else.”

The escorts answer:

> “And whenever you demanded another capital-ship screen, there were fewer destroyers protecting the food ships.”

Neither side wins completely.

That becomes the British naval argument.

---

# The British doctrine is therefore two layers

I would define the mature Royal Navy through a distinction between the **Standing Fleet** and the **Route Fleet**.

Not necessarily those exact formal names, but that's the concept.

### The Standing Fleet

This is the fleet-in-being component.

Its purpose is to make sure Germany cannot suddenly decide that Britain has reduced itself to an escort service and send major surface forces into the Atlantic.

It contains:

- battleships;
- fleet carriers;
- major cruisers;
- first-line destroyers;
- nuclear attack submarines;
- fleet auxiliaries.

It is comparatively concentrated.

Britain does **not** try to distribute every valuable capital ship around the entire Commonwealth.

The standing fleet remains primarily Atlantic-oriented, because Germany is the immediate existential naval threat.

### The Route Fleet

This is the enormous distributed system that actually keeps the Commonwealth alive.

It contains:

- frigates;
- corvettes;
- escort carriers/light carriers;
- maritime-patrol aviation;
- minesweepers;
- repair ships;
- oilers and stores ships;
- conventional submarines in some regional roles;
- locally based Commonwealth squadrons.

These are spread along:

> Britain → Canada/Newfoundland → West Africa → Cape → Indian Ocean → Ceylon/Aden/southern India → Australia/New Zealand.

The existing political canon already makes the Cape route “sacred” after Britain's Mediterranean losses, while Canada becomes an indispensable arsenal and Australia/New Zealand are deliberately tied into British equipment and defense systems. fileciteturn22file3

So the Royal Navy is not really one fleet anymore.

It is a **network of fleets connected by standardized logistics**.

That is its distinctive answer.

---

# ASW absolutely becomes the British obsession

I agree very strongly with your “traumatic overcorrection” language.

Germany ends 1947 with the world's most formidable submarine establishment, and the final Atlantic crisis specifically ends Britain's decisive cryptographic advantage against the U-boats. The postwar British government therefore cannot tell itself:

> “We beat the submarine problem once and for all.”

It knows the opposite.

It knows the Germans eventually adapted.

So virtually every serious British naval procurement after 1947 gets asked:

> **What does this contribute to ASW?**

Not every ship becomes an ASW specialist, because that would be wasteful.

But the capability is distributed extraordinarily widely.

### Battleship

Sonar doesn't become its defining sensor, but the battleship has an excellent submarine warning picture, torpedo defense, helicopters later, decoys, and extensive command integration with the ASW screen.

### Fleet carrier

This becomes one of the biggest differences from America's carrier.

The British fleet carrier carries fighters and strike aircraft, certainly.

But it also carries **serious ASW aviation**.

Helicopters.

Fixed-wing patrol/ASW aircraft where practical.

Sonobuoys.

Submarine-tracking command facilities.

The carrier is valuable partly because it can put a search pattern hundreds of miles around the force.

### Cruiser

Strong command-and-control for ASW groups, helicopters, good sonar on some classes, long-range communications and enough endurance to coordinate hunter groups.

### Destroyer

Real dual-purpose fleet escort.

Air defense plus ASW.

### Frigate

This is where Britain becomes obsessive.

The frigate is not a junior destroyer.

It is essentially:

> **a machine for making a submarine captain miserable.**

Quiet machinery.

Excellent sonar.

Later variable-depth sonar.

Then towed arrays.

ASW mortars.

Light torpedoes.

Helicopters.

Eventually increasingly sophisticated passive processing.

And Britain builds **a lot** of them.

The old reference already pointed in this direction with Whitby → Rothesay → Leander → Broadsword, every active frigate carrying a serious ASW suite. fileciteturn22file7 I wouldn't preserve those exact class numbers blindly, but the lineage logic is probably right.

## Britain probably becomes the world's best ASW navy

Germany may build better submarines.

Britain becomes the power most institutionally dedicated to finding them.

That's a useful distinction.

The German submarine officer asks:

> How do I become quieter?

The British admiral asks:

> **How many independent ways can I detect you?**

Hull sonar.

Passive arrays.

Towed arrays.

Variable-depth sonar.

Maritime-patrol aircraft.

Helicopters.

Sonobuoys.

SOSUS-like fixed hydrophone networks around important routes.

Intelligence.

Traffic analysis.

Satellite ocean surveillance later.

Nuclear hunter-killers.

Convoy geometry.

The whole system matters.

This gives British electronics and computing another strong military use because ASW increasingly becomes a **signal-processing problem**.

---

# The British submarine arm can become very important without becoming “the submarine navy”

I think this solves another part of the problem.

Britain does not perform an Uno reverse and become Germany.

But Germany's submarines create one extremely compelling British submarine mission:

> **hunt the hunters.**

That makes the British SSN a natural prestige weapon.

Not principally commerce raiding.

Not strategic missile attack.

Not an independent submarine war.

The British nuclear attack submarine is an **offensive ASW asset**.

It operates around:

- German U-boat exit routes;
- Iceland/Norway approaches;
- Atlantic chokepoints;
- likely German patrol areas;
- important Commonwealth convoy corridors.

That has an excellent doctrinal logic:

> The best thing we can do to a German submarine is kill it before it reaches the convoy.

So Britain is one of the first powers that can justify serious nuclear-submarine expenditure even while money is scarce.

And because Britain's civilian nuclear doctrine already frames atomic power as **“atoms against blockade”**, submarine nuclear propulsion has enormous political resonance. The wider canon already has Britain deepening nuclear power and ASW together through the 1950s Siege Commonwealth. fileciteturn22file16

Nuclear surface ships are harder to justify.

Nuclear hunter-killer submarines are easy.

---

# Carriers become more important than in America, but not supreme

I agree with your instinct here.

Britain has learned too much from Ceylon and the Indian Ocean to pretend carrier aviation is secondary.

At the same time, the Royal Navy has learned too much from years of convoy warfare to believe the carrier alone constitutes the fleet.

The carrier's role is best described as:

> **mobile air superiority and surveillance for a globally dispersed maritime system.**

That makes it extremely important.

Britain has lost a lot of overseas territory and airfield access.

The Cape route is enormous.

A carrier can put fighters, reconnaissance and ASW aircraft where there is no friendly runway nearby.

So I'd say Britain develops something like **carrier equality**, not carrier primacy.

The battleship, carrier and escort establishments all have credible claims to indispensability.

The British answer to “What is the principal arm of the fleet?” may actually be:

> **The fleet is the principal arm.**

That sounds tautological, but institutionally it is very British.

No single weapon system gets to define naval power.

The fleet is valuable because the pieces support one another.

That is a continuation of fleet-in-being thought, but modified by defeat.

---

# Lion survives because heavy ships still have one unique job

The current source material already preserves *Lion* as one of Britain's visible emergency responses to accumulated capital-ship losses rather than a casual postwar prestige project. fileciteturn22file2

I think that's exactly right.

The battleship establishment's postwar argument isn't:

> “Battleships won the war.”

Clearly they didn't.

It's:

> **“When an enemy heavy surface force appears, you either have something that can confront it or you surrender that ocean area until somebody else arrives.”**

Britain cannot afford that.

Germany retains major surface units.

Italy has a strong Mediterranean fleet.

Japan has Yamatos and eventually carrier-guard battleships.

So Britain keeps perhaps **two modern Lions**, not eight.

That's enough to constitute a credible fleet-in-being.

This actually makes their psychological role larger.

A Lion is not merely an artillery platform.

It is the physical statement:

> **Britain still has a battle fleet.**

And that matters enormously after 1947.

The old naval reference's later Lion reconstruction—guns plus SAMs, helicopters and command spaces—is broadly consistent with that role even if we later redo the exact specification. fileciteturn22file7

---

# But the frigate may become the culturally defining British warship

This is where I think the setting gets something particularly British.

America has the battleship.

Japan has the carrier.

Germany has the U-boat.

Italy has the missile/gun Mediterranean cruiser.

Britain may have the **frigate**.

Not because it's glamorous.

Because Britain discovers that the strategically decisive ship is often the one escorting a refrigerated merchant ship four thousand miles from home.

And that feels exactly right for the Siege Commonwealth.

A frigate commander can reasonably believe:

> “If I do my job, nobody writes about it because the convoy arrives.”

That's the Royal Navy's postwar professional ethos.

It also creates a prestige inversion.

The surface-war officers still want carriers and Lions.

But within the service, commanding an elite ASW frigate or hunter-killer group becomes a **serious career track**, not second-rate escort duty.

By the 1960s–70s, some of Britain's most technically capable naval officers come out of ASW rather than capital ships.

That is a major institutional difference from 1939.

---

# Britain also needs enormous maritime-patrol aviation

This almost becomes part of the Navy even if institutionally it remains split with the RAF.

Long-range patrol aircraft are indispensable because the distances are absurd.

Canada and Newfoundland patrol the North Atlantic.

West African and Cape stations cover the long southbound route.

Ceylon/Aden/Australia cover the Indian Ocean.

The aerospace reference already gives Britain powerful maritime and strike aircraft, and Harrier becomes valuable specifically because the Siege Commonwealth expects dispersed bases, island defense and small carriers. fileciteturn22file10

I think Britain may end up with the world's most mature **ship-aircraft ASW coordination doctrine**.

The frigate hears something.

The helicopter localizes it.

The patrol aircraft extends the search.

The SSN moves toward the predicted escape route.

The convoy changes course.

This is one weapons system spread across an ocean.

---

# Commonwealth standardization is what makes the geography even remotely affordable

This is the part I think has to be emphasized much more than in the other navies.

Britain alone cannot build and crew enough escorts after 1947.

So it doesn't try.

Instead it increasingly builds **Commonwealth naval families**.

Canada builds British-standard or jointly designed frigates.

Australia does the same.

New Zealand operates smaller numbers.

South African yards maintain and eventually build regional escorts.

Perhaps Indian Ocean associated states operate simplified export versions.

Britain supplies:

- sonar;
- radar;
- turbine/engine standards;
- weapons;
- command doctrine;
- officer schooling;
- technical specifications.

The Dominions supply:

- hulls;
- crews;
- local yards;
- regional maintenance;
- their own design improvements.

The current setting already has a Commonwealth Standard Ship Programme for merchant shipping and a permanent Commonwealth Council of Defence and Reconstruction. fileciteturn22file16 Extending the same industrial logic into naval escorts is almost unavoidable.

This lets Britain solve its biggest problem:

> **distance.**

Not every frigate guarding Australia has to sail from Portsmouth.

Some are built and based in Australia.

The Royal Navy becomes the lead service of a **distributed Commonwealth naval architecture**, not merely a British fleet visiting colonies.

That also complicates the “when does Japan surpass Britain?” question.

Japan may surpass the **Royal Navy proper** in blue-water combat power around the late 1950s or early 1960s.

But the entire Commonwealth maritime system remains broader.

That's a much more painful and interesting prestige decline than Britain simply becoming weak.

---

# I would expect three principal British fleet types

By perhaps the 1960s, British planning naturally divides its forces according to mission.

### Home/Atlantic Fleet

The hardest force.

- Lions;
- major carriers;
- best destroyers;
- SSNs;
- advanced ASW frigates.

Mission:

> deter Germany, protect Britain, cover Atlantic approaches.

### Route Groups

Smaller carrier/escort formations distributed along the Cape and Indian Ocean system.

- light or escort carrier;
- cruiser/destroyer leader;
- many frigates;
- auxiliaries;
- maritime patrol aviation.

Mission:

> keep the commercial artery alive.

### Expeditionary Groups

Amphibious/mobile intervention forces.

- light carrier or assault carrier;
- landing ships;
- destroyers/frigates;
- Royal Marines;
- supply ships.

Mission:

> Indian crises, Gulf, Africa, islands, Commonwealth emergencies.

That is much more useful than pretending one generic Royal Navy task force covers everything.

---

# Light carriers become disproportionately attractive

This follows immediately from the geography and from ASW.

Britain can't afford a Malta-sized carrier everywhere.

But it **can** put a smaller carrier with:

- ASW helicopters;
- several fighters;
- perhaps VTOL aircraft later;
- airborne radar;
- command facilities

into a route group.

This is where Britain's later VTOL lead becomes exceptionally important.

The existing aerospace canon already makes Harrier unusually valuable because Britain expects damaged runways, island warfare and **small carriers**. fileciteturn22file10

So unlike the historical debate where small carriers eventually become substitutes produced by budget pressure, AltWWII Britain has a positive doctrinal argument for them:

> **A 20,000–30,000-ton carrier with helicopters and VTOL fighters can put useful aviation on three different Commonwealth routes for the cost and manpower of fewer giant fleet carriers.**

That doesn't replace fleet carriers.

It produces **two carrier tiers**.

And that seems very British.

---

# Britain probably doesn't nuclearize surface ships very much

Despite the enormous distances.

Money is the reason.

The Royal Navy needs **numbers**.

If a nuclear cruiser costs enough to prevent two frigates from being built, the Admiralty has a hard time justifying it.

Japan can say:

> fuel independence is worth the premium.

Britain says:

> **the U-boat doesn't care how your frigate is propelled if you only built half as many frigates.**

So I would put British nuclear money principally into:

1. SSNs;
2. civilian power / blockade resilience;
3. perhaps eventually one prestige or experimental surface ship if desired.

But not wholesale nuclearization.

Conventional surface propulsion remains normal because Britain possesses the Commonwealth fuel network and needs hull count more than propulsion elegance.

---

# “Paranoia” also changes ship survivability

There's another consequence we shouldn't miss.

British ships don't only carry ASW sensors.

They are designed around the assumption that **a torpedo is eventually going to get through**.

So postwar RN design might place unusual emphasis on:

- machinery separation;
- double bottoms;
- flooding control;
- shock hardening;
- emergency electrical systems;
- duplicated sonar/control facilities;
- damage-control parties;
- rapid towing capability;
- helicopter rescue;
- anti-torpedo decoys;
- eventually active or hard-kill torpedo defenses if technology allows.

America's survivability culture is battleship-centered.

Britain's is **submarine-centered**.

The nightmare scenario for an American admiral is a missile salvo smashing his battle fleet.

The nightmare scenario for a British admiral is three quiet German submarines getting inside the convoy screen without anyone noticing.

Those different nightmares should shape their ships.

---

# So I think the British doctrinal formula is this

Not carrier primacy.

Not battleship primacy.

Not submarine primacy.

> **Route primacy.**

Everything is judged by whether Britain can maintain maritime communication despite Germany.

The **battleship** ensures the enemy cannot exploit Britain's escort dispersal with a heavy surface sortie.

The **fleet carrier** supplies mobile air cover, reconnaissance and strike.

The **light carrier** supplies route-level aviation and ASW.

The **cruiser** commands dispersed groups.

The **destroyer** covers high-threat fleet tasks.

The **frigate** is the central ASW workhorse.

The **submarine** hunts enemy submarines before they reach the route.

The **RFA** makes all of it mobile.

And the **merchant ship** is ultimately the thing the Navy exists to deliver safely.

That's why I think the old line describing the Royal Navy as the **armed infrastructure of the Siege Commonwealth** is probably one of the strongest things in the otherwise outdated naval reference. fileciteturn22file0

If we want a more doctrinal in-setting phrase, something like **“Continuity of Communications”** or **“Maritime Continuity Doctrine”** could eventually emerge, but I wouldn't force a formal label yet.

The important point is that the British fleet's center is not a ship.

It is a **route**.

And that gives Britain perhaps the most defensive-looking naval doctrine of the great powers while still requiring carriers, battleships, SSNs, and first-rate surface combatants. It also makes Japanese overtaking of the Royal Navy deeply humiliating without making Britain incompetent: Japan can build the stronger concentrated battle fleet, while Britain has spent its money making sure grain from Canada and Australia still reaches Liverpool when German submarines are trying to make that impossible.

- Relationship: parallel specialist continuation imported after the master project record through Turn 777

Yes. **1966 is entirely defensible**, and it is much less aggressive than it first sounds.

The main correction is that the historical Harrier did **not** enter RAF service in 1976. The Harrier GR.1 entered service in **1969**; No. 1 Squadron became the world's first operational Harrier squadron that year. citeturn189020search3turn189020search5 The P.1127 had already begun hovering trials in 1960, the Kestrel flew in 1964, and nine Kestrels were being operated in near-service conditions by the Tripartite Evaluation Squadron in 1965. citeturn311416search1turn311416search5

So what you're actually proposing is:

> **move operational service from 1969 to about 1966—not from 1976 to 1966.**

That is only a three-year acceleration.

And in AltWWII Britain, I think the institutional conditions justify it very comfortably.

The present Aerospace Reference has the Harrier GR.1 entering in 1970 and already explains its importance through damaged runways, island defense, dispersed operations, and small carriers. fileciteturn23file17 I would now regard **1970 as superseded if you want to make 1966 the date**.

## The engine is the real constraint

You cannot get a Harrier simply by asking Hawker for one earlier. The decisive piece is the **Pegasus concept**: one engine whose thrust can be vectored through four rotating nozzles, combined with reaction-control jets in the extremities so the pilot still has attitude control while there is little or no aerodynamic control authority. Rolls-Royce describes Pegasus as the world's first STOVL engine, and its own history traces the relevant experimental work back into the 1950s. citeturn189020search1turn311416search8

That is the bottleneck.

But the historical chronology actually gives us enormous room:

- British VTOL engine/airframe experimentation is underway in the **1950s**. citeturn311416search1turn311416search8
- P.1127 hovers in **1960**. citeturn311416search5
- Kestrel is flying in **1964** and doing quasi-operational evaluation in **1965**. citeturn311416search1turn311416search3
- Harrier is operational in **1969**. citeturn189020search16

You only need to move that chain left by perhaps **three to five years**.

That is very different from saying Britain invents a 1980s turbofan in 1955.

## And AltWWII gives Britain exactly the right pressure

Historically, Hawker's P.1127 began substantially as a private venture before government interest became strong enough to produce Kestrel evaluation. citeturn311416search1

Your Britain is the opposite environment.

By 1946–47 it has direct experience of:

- German attacks on airfields and communications;
- southeastern bases becoming vulnerable;
- aviation having to operate from dispersed or damaged infrastructure;
- enormous imperial distances;
- carriers which cannot all be giant fleet carriers;
- the need to put useful airpower on small islands and improvised forward bases.

So the Air Ministry and Admiralty can write a formal requirement **years before historical official enthusiasm really matures**.

The requirement does not need to say:

> “Build Harrier.”

It says:

> **We want a jet strike/fighter aircraft capable of operating from extremely short or damaged runways and from naval platforms substantially smaller than a conventional fleet carrier.**

Then British industry starts exploring several answers.

Most fail.

One branch eventually becomes the P.1127/Pegasus arrangement.

That is a much healthier alternate history than having somebody sketch the historical Harrier in 1947.

## My preferred development clock

I would make the British path something like:

| Date | Development |
|---|---|
| **1947–49** | RAF/FAA issue dispersed-jet and small-deck operating studies after the late war |
| **1950–52** | serious lift-jet, deflected-thrust and vectored-thrust experimental programs |
| **1953–55** | Bristol/Rolls-Royce and Hawker converge on the single-engine vectored-thrust solution; competing concepts continue |
| **1956–57** | first dedicated Pegasus-like bench engines and thrust rigs |
| **1958** | P.1127-type prototype begins tethered/hover work |
| **1959–60** | transition from hover to conventional/transitional flight |
| **1961–63** | Kestrel-like preproduction aircraft; dispersed-base and shipboard trials |
| **1964–65** | operational evaluation squadron; production configuration frozen |
| **1966** | **Harrier GR.1 enters limited RAF service** |
| **1967–68** | first fully operational squadrons and serious Fleet Air Arm deployment |
| **late 1960s** | improved GR/Sea variants, weapons expansion and larger carrier/light-carrier integration |

That's completely believable.

In fact, I would probably make **1966 initial operational capability rather than universal maturity**.

Maybe one squadron is operational in 1966.

By 1968, Britain can actually deploy them confidently.

That's conservative enough to respect the technology.

## The 1966 Harrier should also be a little worse than our familiar Harrier

This is where we should resist giving the acceleration away for free.

If Britain pushes the program harder and gets it into service three years earlier, the first aircraft should probably be somewhat less mature.

The original reference currently gives the 1970 GR.1 about 1,175 km/h maximum speed, 600 km combat radius, two 30 mm ADENs and 2,300 kg of stores. fileciteturn23file6

I'd reopen those numbers.

A **1966 GR.1** could plausibly have:

- somewhat lower thrust;
- weaker hot-and-high performance;
- shorter combat radius;
- lower useful vertical-takeoff payload;
- more maintenance;
- less mature navigation/attack electronics;
- more restrictions on shipboard vertical landing;
- perhaps significantly less weapon load if doing a true vertical takeoff.

That last distinction becomes central British doctrine.

The Harrier is **capable of vertical takeoff**, but carrying meaningful fuel and weapons usually means **short takeoff**.

Britain learns very quickly that VTOL is not:

> “hover everywhere because that looks impressive.”

It is:

> **use a short rolling takeoff whenever you can; preserve vertical landing and zero/near-zero runway dependence for the circumstances where they matter.**

That is exactly what STOVL means operationally.

## It also explains why Harrier becomes Britain's iconic postwar aircraft

Not because it is Britain's objectively best fighter.

It probably isn't.

A Lightning will massacre it in the appropriate interceptor problem.

A proper carrier fighter will have advantages in speed, radar and range.

A Buccaneer carries far more useful strike load.

But Harrier does something those aircraft **cannot do at all**.

That gives Britain its first genuinely distinctive postwar aviation capability.

An RAF squadron can disperse away from major runways.

The Royal Navy can put jets aboard a ship too small or too cheap for catapult/arrestor operations.

A Commonwealth island with a short strip can suddenly host tactical jets.

A damaged airfield doesn't necessarily cease being an airfield.

And once Britain is building the **Route Fleet** we just discussed, Harrier becomes almost a perfect aircraft for it.

The fleet carrier still carries conventional high-performance fighters.

But a 20,000–30,000-ton route carrier can carry:

- Harriers;
- ASW helicopters;
- airborne-warning helicopters/aircraft;
- Marines or support aviation.

That means Britain's global naval problem and its aviation problem solve one another.

## I would actually make the Fleet Air Arm adopt it extremely quickly

Historically, the RAF got Harrier before the Sea Harrier became a Royal Navy system.

In AltWWII I think that separation narrows considerably.

The Admiralty has a far stronger reason to care from the start because it is actively looking for **useful fixed-wing aviation on smaller route carriers**.

So perhaps:

**1966 — Harrier GR.1, RAF.**

**1967–68 — navalized Harrier FRS.1-equivalent enters Fleet Air Arm service.**

That version gains:

- folding or otherwise carrier-conscious components where useful;
- corrosion protection;
- maritime navigation;
- fleet communications;
- air-search/intercept radar either initially limited or introduced in the next mark;
- stronger emphasis on air defense.

That might make the **naval Harrier almost as important as the land Harrier**, much earlier than in reality.

And Britain now has a capability nobody else quite possesses for several years.

Germany has better high-speed fighters.

Japan has better conventional carrier aviation.

America has more advanced unmanned assault aviation.

But only Britain can casually put a useful jet fighter on a small flat-deck ship or a rough dispersed strip.

That is exactly the sort of **narrow but strategically consequential first** that each bloc should occasionally get.

### So my recommendation

I would change the current canon from:

> **Harrier GR.1 — 1970**

to:

> **Harrier GR.1 — 1966 initial service; 1967–68 mature operational deployment.**

And I would make the British V/STOL program a **formal late-war/postwar requirement rather than a 1950s private curiosity**.

That requires no impossible materials, electronics, or engine science. It mostly requires Britain to spend serious money on a technological path that historically reached operational service only three years later anyway.

So, yes: **1966 is not merely possible. Given this Britain's strategic experience, I think it is probably preferable.** memcite

## Turn 1177 — Assistant

- Timestamp: 2026-08-15T01:03:40.102Z
- Message ID: `49ed1be3-8545-45ff-8a1b-e17dcec880e3`
- Source: ChatGPT shared conversation `Naval Doctrine Evolution`
- Parallel branch: https://chatgpt.com/share/6a80206d-15d0-83e8-b360-a8acc44d3025
- Relationship: parallel specialist continuation imported after the master project record through Turn 777

Yes. I think this should become one of the defining peculiarities of British postwar aviation.

But I would phrase the doctrine as **“dispersed airpower” rather than “everything must hover.”** The RAF's traumatic conclusion from the Second Battle of Britain is that a combat aircraft whose existence depends on a handful of long paved runways is strategically fragile. Harrier proves that this dependency can be broken. After that, every new British tactical-aircraft requirement gets asked some version of:

> **Why does this aircraft need a runway? And if it does need one, prove that there is no reasonable way around it.**

That is much stronger than simply producing lots of Harriers.

## A VTOL interceptor is absolutely possible

In fact, Britain historically tried to build almost exactly the aircraft you're imagining.

The Hawker Siddeley **P.1154** was a proposed **supersonic V/STOL fighter** using the BS100, a more powerful Pegasus-derived engine with plenum-chamber burning. It won the technical side of NATO's NBMR-3 competition. Britain then tried to turn it into a common RAF/Royal Navy aircraft: the RAF wanted a low-level supersonic strike aircraft, while the Navy wanted a **supersonic fleet-air-defense fighter**. Those conflicting requirements, cost, and service politics helped kill the project—not a conclusion that a supersonic VTOL fighter was physically impossible. citeturn916447view0

That is almost a gift to AltWWII.

Your Britain has a much stronger reason than historical Britain to prevent its air-defense force from depending on fixed runways. So the P.1154-equivalent doesn't encounter an RAF asking whether V/STOL is worth prioritizing. It encounters an RAF saying:

> **“Harrier demonstrated the principle. Now make it supersonic and give it radar and interception weapons.”**

There are still ugly engineering compromises. But the mission itself is absolutely feasible. Later NASA studies repeatedly found supersonic STOVL fighter configurations technically viable, although propulsion integration, hover control, weight, and performance penalties remained difficult. citeturn989953search0turn989953search6

So I would divide British postwar fighter development into **generations**, rather than turning the original Harrier into everything.

### Harrier I: the aircraft everyone abuses

The 1966 Harrier begins as the ground-attack/dispersed-support aircraft we've already established.

Then success creates scope creep immediately.

The RAF wants reconnaissance.

The Army wants better CAS.

The Royal Navy wants fleet defense.

Coastal and Commonwealth commands want maritime strike.

The air-defense establishment starts wondering whether it can provide local interception from dispersed sites.

And the Harrier gets repeatedly modified to do jobs that the original airframe was not really optimized for.

That fits the aircraft exceptionally well as a cultural object. It becomes ubiquitous partly **because it is uniquely deployable**, not because it's the best aircraft in every category.

A Sea Harrier-type derivative can absolutely become a competent point-defense fighter. Historically the Pegasus family ultimately supported radar-equipped Harrier II+ aircraft carrying BVR missiles, demonstrating that STOVL and serious radar air combat aren't inherently incompatible. citeturn116384search3

But an early Harrier still isn't a Lightning.

The English Electric Lightning was designed specifically around climb rate, acceleration, and speed as an interceptor; its original operational radius was only about 150 miles because those characteristics mattered more than endurance. citeturn916447view2 Trying to make the 1966 Harrier equal that performance by adding another suffix to the name is how procurement programs become disasters.

So Britain eventually says:

> **We need another V/STOL aircraft. Not another Harrier modification.**

## Harrier II, conceptually, should be the supersonic generation

I'd put the serious requirement quite early—perhaps around **1965–67**, almost immediately after the first Harrier squadrons demonstrate that dispersed operations are practical.

The resulting aircraft could plausibly enter service somewhere around **1972–75**.

It doesn't have to literally retain the P.1154 designation, but P.1154 should be its historical ancestor. The requirement combines:

- supersonic interception;
- substantially better radar;
- air-to-air missiles;
- useful strike capability;
- short rolling takeoff at combat weight;
- vertical recovery;
- dispersed ground operation;
- naval operation from smaller carriers.

And this aircraft is probably where RAF and Fleet Air Arm requirements align **better** than they did historically.

Historically the RAF and RN wanted rather different things from P.1154, with the Navy specifically emphasizing fleet air defense and even preferring a twin-engine solution. citeturn916447view0 In AltWWII, both services have spent twenty years living under the same strategic principle:

> Don't let destruction of a runway or flight deck end the air battle.

That doesn't eliminate disagreements, but it gives them a shared premise.

The second-generation aircraft will almost certainly be **STOVL rather than routinely VTOL**. That's an important language distinction throughout British doctrine. Vertical takeoff with useful fuel and weapons is expensive in thrust. The normal combat technique is:

> short rolling takeoff → conventional flight → vertical or very short landing.

Britain wants the ability to hover because it eliminates landing dependence. It doesn't insist that every combat sortie begin by hovering wastefully over a concrete pad.

## Then something fascinating happens in the 1980s: your idea almost occurred historically

This is the strongest support for making STOVL Britain's long-term institutional obsession.

In **1982**, the historical RAF genuinely debated whether STOVL should be a prime requirement for the aircraft intended eventually to replace **both the Jaguar ground-attack aircraft and the Tornado F3 air-defense fighter**. There were senior Air Staff advocates for it, and Hawker's Kingston team had promising designs, including **P.1216**. Britain ultimately backed away largely because a national program was unaffordable and its prospective European partners would not accept STOVL. citeturn481685search36

That is almost literally your proposal.

So in AltWWII, where Britain has:

- a much stronger historical trauma around vulnerable airfields;
- a twenty-year successful Harrier establishment;
- a large Route Fleet requiring small-deck aviation;
- no historical NATO/EFA political structure forcing it toward the same compromise;
- a Commonwealth industrial system capable of sharing costs;

I think **Britain absolutely insists on STOVL for its fourth-generation tactical fighter**.

That might become one of Britain's most expensive and difficult postwar procurement programs.

The engineers repeatedly say:

> “We can give you Mach 2, excellent radar, long range and tremendous payload much more easily if you stop asking us to make it hover.”

The Air Staff replies:

> **“No.”**

Because from their perspective the runway vulnerability isn't a specification detail. It is one of the reasons Britain lost the war.

That gives the program exactly the sort of scope creep you're looking for.

## Where I would draw the line

I would not make literally **every RAF aircraft VTOL**, because some missions punish the requirement far more severely than others.

The British distinction should become something like this:

| Mission | British expectation |
|---|---|
| CAS / tactical strike | **STOVL effectively mandatory** |
| Fleet fighter | **STOVL mandatory** |
| Tactical air superiority | **Strong STOVL requirement** |
| Interceptor | **STOVL highly desirable; eventually achieved** |
| Reconnaissance fighter | **STOVL preferred/normal** |
| Light tactical transport | STOL/VTOL where practical |
| Heavy transport | **Conventional/STOL** |
| Tanker | **Conventional** |
| Large AEW aircraft | Conventional, with helicopter/STOVL alternatives on small carriers |
| Maritime patrol | **Conventional long-range aircraft** |
| Very large strategic bomber | **Conventional** |

The reason is basic thrust and weight.

A tactical fighter already needs an enormous thrust-to-weight ratio, which is why turning engine thrust downward can conceivably support the aircraft.

A 150-ton tanker carrying tens of tons of transferable fuel would require an absurd vertical-lift installation whose weight would then be hauled around uselessly for the rest of the mission.

So Britain's doctrine is not:

> Everything shall hover.

It's:

> **Every tactical combat aircraft shall be independent of a major prepared runway unless the Air Staff accepts an explicit exception.**

That's an unusually strong and plausible doctrine.

## This probably kills the historical British Tornado/Typhoon path anyway

Not necessarily the *missions*, but the exact aircraft.

Britain isn't collaborating with historical West Germany in Panavia in this world, so there's no reason to preserve historical Tornado as a procurement program.

Britain still needs:

- low-level interdiction;
- long-range strike;
- air defense;
- eventually fourth-generation air superiority.

But those requirements go through an indigenous/Commonwealth aerospace establishment already obsessed with V/STOL.

So the British 1970s–90s tactical-aircraft family may look much more like:

**Harrier I** — subsonic first-generation STOVL workhorse.

**Supersonic V/STOL fighter** — P.1154 descendant, 1970s.

**Advanced STOVL fighter/attack aircraft** — P.1216-type development generation, 1980s.

**Digital fourth-generation STOVL fighter** — late 1980s/1990s, increasingly one aircraft replacing separate strike/interceptor families.

And ultimately you get exactly what you suggested:

> **Britain tries to build the F-35B idea before anyone else has a reason to.**

Not literally the F-35.

But the philosophical requirement:

> supersonic, advanced radar, excellent air-to-air capability, precision strike, low-observable work eventually, and STOVL as a fundamental—not optional—design characteristic.

Historically, the actual F-35B demonstrates that a supersonic STOVL fighter is achievable; its LiftSystem uses a forward lift fan, swiveling rear nozzle, and roll-control posts rather than the Harrier's pure Pegasus architecture. citeturn116384search2turn481685search12 Britain reaching toward a comparable *architectural idea* earlier is reasonable once its engineers have concluded that simply making Pegasus bigger is producing diminishing returns.

And that means British propulsion research becomes fascinating. It doesn't remain married to one solution merely because Pegasus worked.

## Harrier's unpleasant handling should accelerate flight controls too

This is another excellent consequence.

If British planners decide STOVL isn't one exotic aircraft but the **future of tactical aviation**, then making vertical flight less dependent upon an exceptionally skilled pilot becomes strategically important.

The early Harrier can remain notoriously demanding.

The second generation receives stronger stability augmentation.

By the 1970s–80s, increasingly sophisticated analog and then digital control laws can coordinate:

- engine thrust;
- reaction controls;
- nozzle angle;
- aerodynamic controls;
- transition between wing-borne and powered-lift flight.

By the time Britain reaches its fourth-generation STOVL fighter, the pilot should no longer be personally micromanaging powered lift in the manner expected from the first-generation Harrier.

That is also a useful technology spillover into British **fly-by-wire** development.

The modern F-35 STOVL experience gives the endpoint of that development: British official material explicitly contrasts advanced STOVL control technology with the much more complicated Harrier operating experience. citeturn481685search39

So ironically, Harrier being difficult to fly becomes one reason Britain becomes exceptionally good at making later unstable/complex aircraft **easy to command**.

## And yes, helicopters get pulled forward too

This is an easy consequence because Britain already had a serious early helicopter foothold historically.

The first RAF helicopter unit existed by **1950**, the British-designed Bristol Sycamore first flew in 1947 and entered RAF service in 1953, and rotary-wing flying expanded substantially thereafter. citeturn558999search0turn558999search6

Your Britain has even stronger requirements:

- ASW;
- casualty evacuation;
- supply to dispersed Harrier sites;
- moving radar and missile teams;
- Royal Marine operations;
- vertical replenishment;
- Route Fleet aviation;
- operating where roads/runways have been destroyed.

So I would expect the RAF and Royal Navy to become unusually enthusiastic helicopter adopters during the **1950s**, rather than merely waiting for the technology to become obviously mature.

This links perfectly to the British naval doctrine we just established.

The British answer to geographic overextension becomes:

> **frigates, light carriers, helicopters and STOVL fighters.**

Those four technologies all solve the same underlying problem: Britain cannot afford to require a massive fixed base everywhere it has an obligation.

## The cultural outcome is probably exactly what you're imagining

Harrier becomes something like the **Spitfire of the postwar Siege Commonwealth**.

Not because it has the world's best kill ratio.

Not because every pilot loves flying it.

Not because every role assigned to it makes sense.

Quite the contrary.

It becomes famous because whenever somebody tells Britain:

> “You cannot operate combat aircraft from there,”

the British answer is:

> **“Why not?”**

And that attitude survives the airframe.

By the 1980s, an RAF requirement that does **not** include some discussion of dispersed or short/vertical operation would almost look negligent.

Which produces a very British procurement pathology:

> **Harrier did it, therefore you must explain why your aircraft cannot.**

Sometimes that demand produces extraordinary innovation.

Sometimes it adds five years and several tonnes to a fighter that would have been perfectly good without it.

That's exactly the kind of institutional legacy I would want this setting to preserve.

iturn781316image0

Yes. **P.1214 can plausibly beat P.1216**, and I think there is a particularly good way to make it happen without declaring the stranger-looking airplane superior by authorial fiat.

The key is that P.1214 should win because **AltWWII Britain asks a slightly different question from historical Britain**. Instead of selecting the lowest-risk route to a supersonic STOVL fighter, the RAF and Fleet Air Arm place unusually high value on dispersed operation, low-speed/high-angle controllability, small-deck operation, and air combat after the Harrier has made runway independence part of British doctrine.

And there is one wonderful historical fact underneath this. In 1982 the real RAF genuinely considered making **STOVL a prime requirement for the aircraft that would replace both the Jaguar in ground attack and Tornado F3 in air defense**. The official RAF Historical Society account explicitly says the Kingston design office had promising concepts, “notably the P1216.” Britain backed away because it could not afford the national program and failed to convince its European partners to accept STOVL. citeturn346913view0

So we're not inventing the procurement argument. We're changing which Kingston concept wins it.

## First, P.1214 really does belong in this competition

There is a source-quality problem worth flagging. The accessible official RAF history discusses **P.1216** specifically, but does not describe P.1214 or P.1219. The detailed online documentation for those two is mostly later project histories rather than original RAF/BAe documentation. So I don't want to silently canonize questionable exact specifications for either aircraft.

What we can evaluate confidently is the configuration you're interested in: a **supersonic STOVL fighter built around a forward-swept wing**, competing against the more conservative P.1216 approach.

And forward sweep was technologically credible by exactly this period. NASA's X-29 work used graphite-epoxy composite wing skins and deliberate **aeroelastic tailoring** to control the major structural problem of a forward-swept wing: divergence. NASA's research also found potential benefits in high-angle-of-attack lateral control. citeturn338699search0turn338699search15

So the strange silhouette isn't science fiction.

The price is that Britain has to earn it.

---

# Why P.1214 is the riskier aircraft

Forward sweep creates an unpleasant structural feedback.

As aerodynamic load bends a conventional aft-swept wing, its geometry tends to behave relatively benignly. With a forward-swept wing, bending can twist the wing in a direction that **increases local angle of attack**, creating more lift, creating more twisting force, and potentially driving the structure toward divergence.

Historically, this was precisely why serious forward-swept fighters had to wait for advanced composite structures and aeroelastic tailoring. NASA was still treating divergence as the central forward-sweep engineering problem around the beginning of the 1980s. citeturn338699search23turn338699search25

So if Britain chooses P.1214, it is buying three difficult technologies simultaneously:

**supersonic flight + STOVL propulsion + a structurally tailored forward-swept wing.**

P.1216 is attractive because the procurement office can quite reasonably ask:

> Why are we solving three hard problems when two will do?

That's the case P.1214 has to overcome.

## But Britain has a reason to accept that risk

Because the RAF does **not** think this is merely another fighter.

It thinks this aircraft is supposed to replace a large portion of Britain's tactical aviation system.

Under the doctrine we've just established, it has to be able to:

- launch from dispersed wartime sites;
- recover without an intact runway;
- defend those sites against German attack;
- provide fleet air defense;
- operate from smaller British carriers;
- conduct tactical strike;
- fight enemy fighters well enough that the RAF doesn't need to pair every dispersed squadron with a conventional interceptor squadron.

That last requirement is what helps P.1214.

The first Harrier proved runway independence.

The second-generation British machine proves **supersonic STOVL**.

This generation has to prove that STOVL does not condemn Britain to having an inferior air-combat fighter.

So suddenly the aerodynamic advantages of the forward-swept configuration have a constituency.

---

# The RAF requirement should stop demanding “Mach 2 at all costs”

This is probably the single most important way P.1214 wins.

If the competition is:

> **Which design gives us the cleanest Mach 2 interceptor?**

I would lean toward P.1216.

If the competition becomes:

> **Which design gives us the best deployable fighter that can get supersonic quickly, fight effectively, carry serious missiles, operate from short strips and small decks, and survive after our airfields have been bombed?**

P.1214 becomes much more interesting.

Britain could deliberately accept something like **Mach 1.6–1.8 class performance** rather than insisting on Mach 2-plus.

That isn't technological regression.

By this period increasingly capable guided missiles and radar mean absolute top speed is only one part of interception performance. For Britain's peculiar mission, **acceleration, climb, readiness, missile reach, sensor quality and the ability to launch from wherever the aircraft survived last night's bombing** may matter more than whether the specification sheet says Mach 2.05.

That is a very plausible RAF conclusion after the Second Battle of Britain.

---

# What forward sweep buys P.1214

It doesn't improve hover. That's important.

When the aircraft is hovering on engine thrust, the wing's sweep is largely irrelevant.

The benefit arrives during **transition and wing-borne combat**.

NASA's forward-sweep research found that the configuration could retain useful lateral control at high angles of attack, while composite structures offered a way around the divergence problem. citeturn338699search15turn338699search18

For our British aircraft, that translates into a potential advantage in three places.

First is **slow transition flight**. As the aircraft transitions from powered lift into aerodynamic lift, predictable control at low speed and high angle of attack is extremely valuable.

Second is **short takeoff**. It doesn't magically create thrust, but an aerodynamically effective wing in the low-speed regime helps the aircraft get onto its wing sooner once it begins its rolling departure.

Third is **air combat**. Britain desperately wants its post-Harrier fighter to stop carrying the stigma of:

> marvelous trick airplane, mediocre fighter.

If P.1214 demonstrators show markedly better controllability in high-angle maneuvering than the P.1216 demonstrators, the RAF can regard that as worth paying for.

Not because turning tightly automatically wins every dogfight.

Rather because P.1214 would finally demonstrate:

> **STOVL capability need not be purchased by accepting second-class fighter aerodynamics.**

That is politically enormous.

---

# But P.1214 should not win unchanged

This is the part that makes the procurement history feel real.

I would not have Britain fly P.1214 and P.1216 against each other and then say:

> P.1214 wins. Build the drawing.

Instead:

> **P.1214 wins the competition. P.1216 wins a great deal of the engineering argument.**

The production P.1214 incorporates things discovered during P.1216 development.

So the final aircraft retains the feature we actually care about visually:

**the strongly forward-swept main wing and the extraordinary X-like planform.**

But development tones down whatever parts of the original study prove unnecessarily ambitious.

Perhaps the forward sweep becomes somewhat less extreme.

Perhaps the fuselage gets deeper for fuel.

The inlet geometry changes.

The twin-boom/tail arrangement is refined.

The powered-lift system adopts improvements demonstrated on P.1216.

The landing gear gets widened and brutalized for rough-field operation.

The original sleek concept acquires all the ugly access panels, sensors, antennas, pylons, vents and structural reinforcement that distinguish a beautiful design study from an aircraft the RAF actually abuses in Scotland for twenty years.

That is exactly how I'd want it.

From above, however, it remains unmistakably **P.1214**.

---

# The decisive technology is composites

If we want P.1214 to win, Britain should deliberately make **aeroelastic composite structures** one of the development program's principal investments.

The X-29 research is particularly helpful here. NASA did not simply make a forward-swept metal wing exceptionally thick and heavy. It used composite layups so structural stiffness could be oriented to make the wing twist in more favorable ways under aerodynamic load. citeturn338699search0turn338699search4

That is exactly the road Britain needs.

And it fits the setting.

The current technology canon already characterizes Britain and the Commonwealth as particularly strong in **aerospace, scientific integration and interfaces**, despite limited capital. citeturn715166view0

So I would make this aircraft one of the reasons British composite aviation becomes unusually mature.

The Harrier's legacy wasn't only vectored thrust anymore.

It creates:

> advanced engine controls;  
> digital flight controls;  
> composite aeroelastic structures;  
> high-temperature materials;  
> dispersed maintenance systems.

P.1214 pulls all of them together.

---

# Fly-by-wire becomes almost mandatory

This is another place where the bizarre airplane produces useful industrial consequences.

A forward-swept, high-performance STOVL fighter asks the pilot to manage several very different aerodynamic regimes:

**hover → transition → conventional flight → supersonic flight → high-angle maneuver → transition → vertical recovery.**

That is not something Britain should solve indefinitely by giving the pilot six more levers.

The official RAF Harrier history itself emphasizes how elegantly the original P.1127 reduced the pilot's additional vectored-thrust control to essentially one nozzle lever, which was one of the great successes of the concept. citeturn879906view0

P.1214 needs to take that philosophy much farther.

So by the production aircraft, the pilot isn't really commanding nozzle positions individually.

The pilot commands:

> **what the aircraft should do.**

The flight-control computers coordinate aerodynamic surfaces, thrust vectoring and reaction controls.

That would make the P.1214 program one of Britain's great fly-by-wire accelerators.

Which is another reason the airplane can look preposterous without flying preposterously.

---

# I can see the procurement fly-off very clearly

I'd run the final competition across **four categories**, because that's what makes the winner defensible.

| Criterion | P.1214 | P.1216 |
|---|---|---|
| **Structural/development risk** | Worse | **Better** |
| **High-speed aerodynamic conservatism** | Worse | **Better** |
| **High-AoA / agility potential** | **Better** | Good |
| **RAF doctrinal distinctiveness** | **Excellent** | Excellent |
| **Rough-field/STOVL suitability** | Comparable after development | Comparable |
| **Growth margin** | Questionable initially | **Better initially** |
| **Production cost** | Worse | **Better** |
| **Technical payoff if successful** | **Much higher** | Lower-risk |

P.1216 wins every Treasury briefing.

P.1214 wins just enough flight tests to stay alive.

And then the deciding event needn't even be spectacular.

Perhaps during a 1982–83 evaluation one P.1214 demonstrator conducts repeated short-strip interceptions against conventional fighters. It consistently leaves a dispersed strip faster than expected, transitions cleanly, and proves startlingly good in the high-angle portion of mock engagements.

P.1216 is faster at altitude.

P.1214 is slightly shorter-ranged.

P.1216 is cheaper.

But the operational evaluation concludes that **P.1214 is the better fighter**.

The Air Staff has spent twenty years being told:

> STOVL is wonderful, but if you want a *real* fighter you need a normal aeroplane.

P.1214 breaks that argument.

That's enough for the RAF to take the risk.

---

# There is also an institutional reason the Navy might prefer P.1214

The Fleet Air Arm doesn't principally care whether the airplane wins a beautiful high-altitude Mach-number contest.

It cares about how much fighter capability can be generated from a **small deck**.

So its questions are more like:

- What's the minimum launch run with combat fuel and missiles?
- How rapidly can I recover four aircraft?
- How tolerant is it of rolling/pitching deck recovery?
- How much deck area does one aircraft consume?
- Can it fight immediately after taking off with a useful load?
- How many maintenance hours does its lift system consume?

If P.1214's wing/control characteristics produce better low-speed handling and transition margins, the Fleet Air Arm becomes its strongest political patron.

That could actually settle a close RAF competition.

The Navy says:

> P.1216 may be a slightly cleaner interceptor.

> **P.1214 is a better Commonwealth fighter because it can defend Britain, Ascension, Ceylon, Australia and a 25,000-ton carrier with the same basic airframe.**

That's an extremely persuasive argument in this setting.

---

# And aesthetically, yes, we should preserve the X

I agree with you completely on the visual side.

There is something particularly useful about P.1214 because it does **not** look like:

> “another 1980s delta fighter.”

Viewed from above, the forward-swept wings crossed against the rear structures give it this almost science-fiction X-planform.

And in this setting that can become part of Britain's technological visual language.

American fourth-generation fighters still tend toward recognizable conventional fighter forms.

Japanese aircraft develop their own canard and carrier-driven ancestry.

German fighters have their own priorities.

Then a British squadron appears with these things.

You immediately know whose aircraft they are.

That is excellent worldbuilding because the silhouette is caused by a **doctrine** rather than by decorative weirdness.

Britain refuses to depend on runways.

Therefore Britain keeps investing in powered lift.

Powered lift creates unusual propulsion integration.

That integration gives Kingston unusual freedom and unusual constraints.

Britain also wants first-class dogfighting performance.

That makes the forward-swept solution attractive enough to investigate.

Composite technology makes it structurally possible.

And suddenly your Ace Combat airplane has an actual institutional genealogy.

---

## P.1219 is the one I would hold open

I looked specifically for it because your uncertainty was warranted.

The official RAF Historical Society material I can access identifies **P.1216** by name as a promising Kingston STOVL fighter concept in the 1982 Air Staff debate. It does **not** mention P.1219, and I couldn't find an accessible BAe/RAF primary source that gives me enough information to confidently characterize the P.1219's propulsion and operating concept. citeturn346913view0

So I would not presently say:

> “P.1219 definitely was X.”

The later project literature apparently contains more, but for canon I'd rather source that properly before building off it.

And we don't really need it yet.

I think the **P.1214 versus P.1216 competition is already enough**.

## My preferred AltWWII outcome

I would provisionally structure it as:

**1966 — Harrier I enters service.**

**early/mid-1970s — first-generation supersonic STOVL successor**, descended from the P.1154 problem, proves that the concept can go supersonic but remains expensive and temperamental.

**late 1970s — RAF and Fleet Air Arm jointly issue the next advanced dispersed-combat-aircraft requirement.**

**1979–82 — P.1214 and P.1216 receive parallel serious development rather than remaining paper exercises.**

**1982–84 — both fly as demonstrators/prototypes.**

**1984 — P.1214 wins**, principally on fighter handling, dispersed operations and naval suitability despite greater structural risk and cost.

**1987–89 — production P.1214-derived fighter enters service.**

And the service aircraft is not simply the 1979 drawing. It is a **P.1214/P.1216 synthesis in which P.1214 wins the silhouette and aerodynamic philosophy while P.1216 donates many of the practical engineering solutions**.

That, to me, is the sweet spot.

We get the wonderfully bizarre forward-swept British fighter you want without requiring the Admiralty and Air Staff to ignore everything the more conservative P.1216 teaches them. The aircraft looks like it came out of *Ace Combat*, but its development history reads like something produced by a painfully real British procurement committee.

Yes. I think this works extremely well, with one adjustment that makes the politics more believable:

> **The public does not force the RAF to declare P.1214 technically superior. It makes cancelling P.1214 politically harder than continuing it.**

That difference is enough to produce the drama you want without turning aircraft procurement into a popularity contest.

And given the setting's Falklands War runs from April 1984 into 1986, with the disastrous Second Torch in July 1984 and a prolonged naval-air campaign afterward, you've almost accidentally picked the perfect moment for such a competition. citeturn971129view0

## I would absolutely build both prototypes

In fact, I'd go slightly further than one of each.

By the time Britain has reached this generation, the RAF and Fleet Air Arm are asking for an aircraft they expect to carry British tactical aviation into the next century. That is too important a decision to make from drawings and wind-tunnel models.

So the competition probably reaches something like:

**P.1214 programme**
- one aerodynamic/flight demonstrator;
- one full mission-system/propulsion prototype.

**P.1216 programme**
- same.

Four flying aircraft total is still a tiny programme compared with producing either type, but it gives Britain enough hardware that a single accident doesn't decide the competition.

Historically P.1216 got as far as extensive model work and a full-scale mock-up, and people involved in the programme later considered the configuration technically achievable. The real project never received the sustained state commitment required to build flying prototypes. citeturn146582search0turn146582search5

Our Britain does.

And that means around **1983–84**, there are two extremely strange-looking British STOVL fighters actually flying.

That is very difficult to keep invisible.

## I wouldn't make the P.1216 automatically bad at rolling

Your visual intuition gets us toward a useful difference, but I'd express it more carefully.

The P.1216's planform does look like a machine built around a comparatively disciplined high-speed configuration. But static lateral stability doesn't directly tell us roll rate. Roll response also depends upon:

- moment of inertia;
- control-surface area and leverage;
- differential tail control;
- flight-control laws;
- thrust vectoring;
- aerodynamic behavior at the particular speed and angle of attack.

The historical P.1216 concept had all-moving tail surfaces and a sophisticated vectored-thrust arrangement, so there is no reason it must be a truck in roll merely because its planform looks stable. citeturn146582search5

But we **can absolutely make the two prototypes develop distinguishable flying personalities**.

And that's much more interesting.

### P.1216: the RAF officer's fighter

The P.1216 demonstrator proves exceptionally good at:

**acceleration → climb → supersonic dash → missile engagement → disengagement.**

It achieves the RAF's coveted **Mach 2-class requirement**, perhaps around Mach 2.0–2.1 in the clean/interceptor configuration.

It has excellent directional stability.

It's an extremely good missile platform.

It behaves predictably at high speed.

It probably carries somewhat more fuel internally.

Its radar installation is easier to accommodate.

And an RAF interceptor pilot flies it and comes back saying:

> **“This is what replaces Lightning.”**

Not literally the same mission by then, but psychologically that's what he means.

The Air Staff loves it.

### P.1214: the pilot's fighter

P.1214 doesn't quite get there.

Let's say its practical top end is around **Mach 1.75–1.85**.

That's not slow.

It's emphatically supersonic.

But every RAF specification sheet has this slightly embarrassing line where P.1216 says `M2+` and P.1214 doesn't.

Then the pilots start fighting them.

And P.1214 is wonderful.

NASA's actual X-29 forward-swept-wing research gives us a strong physical basis for that possibility. The X-29's combination of forward sweep, canards, active flight controls and tailored structure produced exceptionally good control response at high angle of attack; later flight tests retained significant controllability at angles where conventional fighters were in serious difficulty. citeturn346680search1turn346680search0

That doesn't automatically mean “forward sweep wins every dogfight.”

But it gives us grounds for a P.1214 whose strongest regime is:

> **rapid attitude changes, strong low-speed authority, excellent high-alpha control, and unusually good maneuverability through the transition between fast and slow combat.**

Its roll response can also be tuned to be excellent without claiming the wing magically provides it. The flight-control system, differential controls and low enough roll inertia do that.

So the pilots' shorthand becomes something like:

> **1216 goes where you point it.**

> **1214 points wherever you want it.**

That's exactly the kind of oversimplification the press would adore.
