# Then the Falklands turns an internal competition into national entertainment

This is where I think your idea becomes especially strong.

The programme begins as a fairly ordinary classified procurement competition.

The Ministry expects:

> prototypes tested quietly → Air Staff report → Cabinet decision → polished unveiling of winner.

Then Argentina invades the Falklands in **April 1984**. Britain suffers severe naval-air losses, Second Torch fails in July, and the war becomes a prolonged national ordeal extending through 1985 and into 1986. citeturn971129view0

Suddenly anything associated with the future of British naval aviation becomes news.

And these aircraft are impossible-looking.

People already know what Harrier means.

Now somebody photographs this:

> forward-swept wings, canards, strange powered-lift configuration, British roundels.

The newspaper headline practically writes itself.

**SON OF HARRIER?**

Then somebody photographs the other one.

And now Britain discovers there are **two**.

That's when the problem starts.

## The RAF doesn't have to leak very much

This is important for plausibility.

We don't need some clerk to steal a `SECRET – P.1214 PERFORMANCE ENVELOPE` binder.

Most of the public information can be obtained through **observation plus inference plus selective leaks**.

Aviation enthusiasts near British test establishments are going to notice:

- which aircraft flew;
- how often;
- which prototype was grounded;
- external stores;
- approximate dimensions;
- nozzle arrangements;
- extraordinarily short takeoffs;
- vertical landings;
- formation flights with known aircraft;
- whether one seems to accelerate substantially harder;
- whether one demonstrator repeatedly performs spectacular maneuvering trials.

And Britain has a mature television and enthusiast-magazine culture.

Somebody gets 8 mm or videotape footage.

Someone else has a long-lens camera.

A retired RAF pilot appears on television and explains what he thinks he's seeing.

*Flight* or the setting's equivalent starts publishing speculative drawings.

A defence correspondent gets told by an unnamed Ministry source that:

> “One aircraft has already achieved the required supersonic performance.”

The paper converts that into:

> **NEW BRITISH JUMP JET BREAKS MACH TWO**

The RAF spokesman refuses to confirm.

Now everyone assumes it definitely happened.

That is much more believable than civilians accurately calculating Mach numbers with wristwatches.

---

# Though I desperately want the stopwatch men anyway

Just not as reliable intelligence.

They should absolutely exist.

You get men standing near a permitted viewing area with:

- binoculars;
- cameras;
- notebooks;
- stopwatches;
- radio scanners where legal;
- aircraft-recognition books;
- very strong opinions.

One says P.1216 just did Mach 2.3.

Another writes a furious letter to the aviation press explaining why this is physically impossible and that his own calculations prove Mach 1.94.

A third insists the P.1214 outran it last Thursday.

All three are wrong.

The RAF internally knows:

> P.1216: Mach 2.06.  
> P.1214: Mach 1.81.

Or whatever numbers we eventually choose.

But because it won't publish either figure, mythology fills the vacuum.

That's fantastic texture.

---

# And the war creates factions

You could have the British public assign personalities to the aircraft before the Ministry ever names them.

### The P.1216 camp

Usually:

- RAF traditionalists;
- interceptor enthusiasts;
- engineers impressed by raw performance;
- people worried about German high-speed aircraft;
- readers who obsess over specifications.

Their case is simple:

> **We're building a fighter. The faster fighter is better.**

P.1216 becomes “the thoroughbred.”

### The P.1214 camp

- Fleet Air Arm supporters;
- Harrier enthusiasts;
- younger pilots;
- people following Falklands air combat;
- people who like the extraordinary appearance;
- the broader public once television shows its demonstrations.

Their case becomes:

> **If we're replacing Harrier, build the aeroplane that can actually fight.**

And P.1214 has an enormous unfair advantage:

**it looks fantastic on television.**

A Mach 2 intercept at 50,000 feet is strategically useful and visually rather dull.

A P.1214 doing a violent low-altitude break, pointing its nose at an absurd angle, transitioning to a short landing and dropping vertically onto a pad is spectacular.

NASA's later X-29 research demonstrates why a forward-swept/canard machine could genuinely produce remarkable high-alpha demonstrations rather than this being merely theatrical. citeturn346680search1

So public opinion naturally gravitates toward the aircraft whose best characteristics can be **seen**.

That doesn't mean the public understands fighter performance.

That's precisely the problem facing the RAF.

---

# The Falklands makes P.1214 nearly impossible to kill

This should be the decisive political mechanism.

Suppose that in late 1984 the Air Staff's preliminary conclusion is:

> **P.1216 preferred. P.1214 development to terminate after current trials.**

Perfectly defensible.

P.1216 meets the Mach requirement.

It has better range.

Its interceptor characteristics fit RAF planning.

Then that recommendation leaks.

And it detonates.

Because Britain is simultaneously fighting a war in which:

- carrier aviation is nationally visible;
- dispersed aviation matters;
- aircraft and ships are being lost;
- the Harrier family is heavily identified with Britain's ability to keep fighting far from home.

The setting already establishes the Falklands conflict as a major test of Commonwealth naval-air endurance and one that becomes politically inseparable from questions of preparedness, reserves and procurement. citeturn971129view0

So the story becomes:

> **RAF TO SCRAP “NEW HARRIER” DURING FALKLANDS WAR**

Whether technically accurate is irrelevant.

Members of Parliament start asking questions.

Fleet Air Arm officers quietly tell journalists that P.1214 has performed extremely well.

Some RAF test pilots defend it.

Hawker/BAe employees in Kingston know which programme disappears if P.1214 dies.

Opposition politicians demand to know why Britain is cancelling a promising domestically designed fighter *while British pilots are fighting in the South Atlantic*.

Now the Air Staff faces a different calculation.

It can still kill P.1214.

But it has to kill it **publicly**.

That's a much higher threshold.

---

# And I think the correct outcome is not quite “buy both”

At least not as two equal fleets.

Britain we've established is **financially constrained and geographically overcommitted**. It cannot casually maintain two unrelated advanced STOVL fighter production systems because the public likes both.

The better compromise is more British.

### P.1214 wins the common fighter programme

This becomes the true **Harrier successor**.

I'd probably avoid literally calling it Harrier II if we want the visual break to feel enormous. The public might call it the “Super Harrier” throughout development, but it receives its own service name.

It becomes:

- RAF tactical fighter;
- Fleet Air Arm fighter;
- strike aircraft;
- dispersed air-defense aircraft;
- Commonwealth export/common fighter.

P.1214 wins **the large production order**.

That means you get your preferred design as the aircraft that defines British aviation going into the 1990s.

### P.1216 gets a limited RAF order

This is where I'd indulge the Air Staff.

They were not wrong.

P.1216 really **is better at the requirement they originally considered most important**.

So Britain purchases perhaps:

> **24–36 P.1216 interceptors.**

Maybe two operational squadrons plus development/reserve aircraft.

These are stationed primarily in Britain.

Their mission is:

> rapid home-defense interception against high-speed German reconnaissance, bombers, and strike aircraft.

They use the same missiles, much of the same radar family, perhaps substantial engine commonality and as many subsystems as practicable with P.1214.

That limits the logistical penalty.

The RAF gets its Mach 2 machine.

The Navy gets P.1214.

The Treasury complains correctly that Britain has somehow managed to turn a competition intended to choose **one** aircraft into a contract for **two**.

Kingston has the decade of its life.

---

# And P.1216 becomes Britain's “other fighter”

This produces lovely cultural consequences.

P.1214 is famous.

Children have models of it.

It's on recruiting posters.

It's in Falklands-victory documentaries even though it didn't actually fight in the war.

It becomes the symbol of British aerospace recovery.

P.1216 is respected by people who know aircraft.

Pilots love its acceleration.

RAF home-defense crews insist:

> “Ours is faster.”

P.1214 pilots answer:

> “Yes, provided nobody turns.”

That probably isn't entirely fair to P.1216.

Which is exactly why the joke persists.

You can have a thirty-year internet argument in-setting over which aircraft was “actually better.”

Perfect.

---

# The network part works, but I would scale it correctly for 1984

This is where the current technology canon gives us a very nice boundary.

By **1977–83**, personal computing has already created mass software-reading publics, and by 1980–85 electronic offices, fax, paging and personal machines are increasingly ordinary. But the affluent household is still described as **largely offline** in 1985. citeturn402170view1turn402170view2

Meanwhile, Weltnetz exists in the early 1980s as a developing international transport concept and trial system; it doesn't become the normal common civilian network until the **mid-1990s**. citeturn268219view3

So I would **not** make the P.1214/P.1216 rivalry a 1985 Twitter equivalent.

Instead, it becomes one of the first British defence controversies to develop an **electronic enthusiast subculture** alongside conventional media.

Most people encounter it through:

- BBC television;
- newspapers;
- aviation magazines;
- radio;
- photographs;
- home video;
- pub arguments.

But engineers, students and serious aviation enthusiasts begin circulating:

- digitized performance tables;
- typed sightings;
- crude line drawings;
- flight logs;
- scanned or retransmitted photographs;
- arguments on university, engineering and specialist bulletin-board systems.

A man photographs P.1214 on Tuesday.

A university student digitizes the photograph on Wednesday.

By Friday, somebody in Canada is arguing about its wing sweep on a Commonwealth technical board.

For **1984**, that feels startlingly modern.

But it doesn't require the setting to have a universal public Internet fifteen years early.

And because the international Weltnetz transport is only entering trials around this period, the aircraft controversy might become one of those stories later network historians cite as an early example of:

> **a national news story escaping the newspaper cycle and acquiring a persistent electronic discussion community.**

That's even more interesting than simply saying “people posted about it online.”

---

# There can be a genuine security scare

Not because the public discovers the exact maximum speed.

Because dozens of individually harmless observations get aggregated.

One enthusiast reports:

> P.1214 flew with two missiles and external tank.

Another:

> P.1216 launched at 09:14 and returned at 10:37.

Another:

> aerial refueling trial yesterday.

Someone else identifies which radar company has engineers visiting Kingston.

Another notices test sorties stop for eleven days.

Individually useless.

Collected together, British intelligence realizes:

> **Good Lord, they're reconstructing our flight-test programme.**

This would be an excellent early lesson in what we would now call open-source intelligence.

Nobody stole anything.

Nobody committed espionage in the classic sense.

Thousands of citizens merely looked at things they were legally allowed to see and then **combined their observations electronically**.

That can cause a very British 1985 security controversy:

> Is telling other enthusiasts when an aeroplane flew a breach of national security?

The government discovers that its secrecy procedures were designed around protecting documents, not around hundreds of people collectively producing a picture from public fragments.

That is extraordinarily well matched to the setting's emerging network age.

---

# I think the final chronology should look roughly like this

| Date | P.1214 / P.1216 programme |
|---|---|
| **1978–80** | competing advanced STOVL configurations mature |
| **1980** | government orders parallel flying demonstrators |
| **1982–83** | first prototypes assembled; ground and powered-lift tests |
| **late 1983** | first P.1214 flight |
| **early 1984** | first P.1216 flight |
| **Apr. 1984** | Falklands war begins; programme abruptly becomes politically interesting |
| **summer 1984** | both enter intensive comparative tests as Second Torch turns British airpower into national news |
| **late 1984** | leaked preliminary RAF preference for P.1216 creates political controversy |
| **1985** | televised/photographed demonstrations turn P.1214 into public favorite; specialist electronic discussion becomes a security concern |
| **1985–86** | Ministry delays final cancellation decision during the war |
| **1986** | decision: P.1214 becomes common RAF/FAA next-generation fighter; limited P.1216 interceptor procurement authorized |
| **1988–90** | first production P.1214-derived squadrons enter service |
| **similar window** | first small P.1216 home-defense force becomes operational |

I wouldn't push the production versions into the Falklands War itself. That would cheapen the development drama.

They should remain tantalizingly **almost ready** while British pilots are fighting with the aircraft they will eventually replace.

That gives the newspapers another angle:

> *Britain is fighting today's war while tomorrow's fighter circles over Wiltshire.*

And after victory, both aircraft become attached to the national recovery story even though neither fired a shot.

## So I prefer limited dual procurement

It gives every side something without erasing the competition.

**P.1214 wins historically.** It becomes the famous aircraft, the major production type, the Fleet Air Arm's choice and the ancestor of Britain's later STOVL fighter lineage.

**P.1216 wins the specification.** It demonstrates the speed and interception performance the RAF originally demanded and survives as a small specialized home-defense fleet.

That's a much more interesting outcome than declaring either design a loser.

And decades later, historians can still argue over the counterfactual:

> Had the Falklands War not occurred—and had the British public never seen P.1214 fly—**would the RAF have cancelled the aircraft that eventually became Britain's definitive fighter?**

I think the answer would probably be **yes**.

That makes the public drama consequential without making public taste itself an aerodynamic test standard.

---

## Turn 1187 — Assistant

- Timestamp: 2026-08-15T01:59:10.074Z
- Message ID: `4edf2f8f-be28-4c30-ba92-77e416a76c30`
- Source: ChatGPT shared conversation `Naval Doctrine Evolution`

- Relationship: parallel specialist continuation imported after the master project record through Turn 777

Yes. I think this is the best outcome, and I would keep **both P.1214 and P.1216 in canon**.

The important technical qualification is that Kingston cannot economically make them “the same aircraft under different skins.” Their aerodynamic layouts are too different. But it can make them **two airframes built around one common systems architecture**. That is enough to turn what would otherwise be an extravagant dual procurement into something Britain can defend.

Historically, the RAF really was considering STOVL for the future Jaguar/Tornado-F3 replacement role in 1982, with Kingston's P.1216 specifically identified as one of its promising designs. The historical program died primarily because Britain could not afford to pursue the national STOVL route and its European partners wouldn't accept it—not because the RAF had concluded the concept was useless. citeturn975243search36 In AltWWII, Britain has both the strategic requirement and the industrial reason to keep Kingston's work alive.

## The Kingston compromise

I would make the decisive event something like **1985–86**, after both prototypes have flown and after it has become increasingly apparent that neither service wants the same winner.

The Fleet Air Arm says:

> **P.1214.**

It likes the aircraft's low-speed behavior, maneuverability, deck operating characteristics, and the fact that it is an excellent *fighter* rather than merely a supersonic aeroplane that can land vertically.

The RAF says:

> **P.1216.**

It gets closer to the original high-speed requirement, has the better interceptor profile, and gives Air Defence Command the Mach-2-class aircraft it wanted.

The Treasury's answer is:

> “Choose one.”

And Kingston's answer becomes:

> **“What if you don't actually have to support two aeroplanes?”**

Not literally, of course. But close enough.

### What becomes common

I would aim for extremely high commonality in the expensive **line-replaceable systems**, rather than structural parts.

Both production aircraft use the same:

- engine core and accessory package;
- radar hardware family;
- mission computer;
- inertial/navigation system;
- radios and datalink;
- electronic-warfare suite;
- cockpit displays;
- HOTAS controls;
- ejection seat;
- oxygen/environmental-control equipment;
- generators;
- hydraulic pumps;
- fuel pumps and valves;
- sensors and diagnostic equipment;
- weapons-management computers;
- missile interfaces and pylons where practical;
- standardized maintenance connectors;
- software architecture.

That means a technician trained to replace the radar power-supply unit on P.1214 already knows how to replace it on P.1216.

A warehouse in Scotland doesn't need two unrelated sets of pressure regulators.

A Rolls-Royce depot overhauls **one engine family**.

A weapons update written for one aircraft can usually be ported to the other rather than beginning from zero.

And eventually both use the same training simulators for large parts of systems instruction.

That is an enormous saving.

## What cannot sensibly be common

This is where I would keep the engineering grounded.

The two aircraft still need different:

- wing structures;
- wing actuators in some positions;
- fuselage frames;
- flight-control laws;
- intake geometry;
- powered-lift ducting;
- nozzle extensions/installation plumbing;
- tail structures;
- landing-gear geometry;
- control surfaces;
- fuel-tank shapes;
- aerodynamic fairings.

And probably different naval reinforcement.

The **engine itself can be common**, but its installation isn't necessarily identical.

Think:

> same engine on the shipping pallet;

but

> different intake, duct and nozzle installation kits once it goes into the aeroplane.

That preserves the performance difference.

P.1216 doesn't suddenly lose its high-speed advantage because it shares the P.1214's engine. Its lower drag, different internal arrangement, inlet design and aerodynamic profile still determine what it does with that thrust.

Likewise P.1214 retains its maneuvering characteristics because those belong principally to its aerodynamics and flight-control system, not to some unique set of fuel valves.

Rolls-Royce's actual STOVL history reinforces how much performance depends on the integration of propulsion, nozzles, controls and airframe rather than merely possessing an engine that can vector thrust. citeturn975243search0turn975243search1

---

# This produces a very convincing service split

I would make the distinction quite clean.

### P.1214 — Fleet Air Arm

This becomes Britain's principal **naval STOVL fighter**.

Its priorities are:

1. fleet air defense;
2. fighter maneuverability;
3. small-deck operation;
4. maritime strike;
5. short-field expeditionary operation.

It is the prettier, stranger and more famous one.

This is the aircraft children recognize.

It is the one on recruiting posters.

It is the one that gets filmed hovering over a carrier deck.

And because of the Falklands-era public controversy, it acquires a mythology before it ever reaches squadron service.

### P.1216 — RAF

This becomes the **land-based dispersed interceptor/fighter**.

Its priorities are:

1. rapid climb;
2. supersonic dash;
3. long-range radar interception;
4. missile employment;
5. dispersed STOVL basing;
6. secondary strike.

It is probably slightly less spectacular at airshows and substantially more satisfying to the Air Staff.

If P.1214 is roughly a **Mach 1.8-class** aircraft, I am comfortable giving mature P.1216 something around **Mach 2.0–2.1 clean**, assuming its propulsion and inlet development are successful.

And because Britain's entire tactical-air doctrine has become hostile to major-airfield dependence, even the RAF's home-defense interceptor retains STOVL.

That's a wonderfully strange consequence:

> Britain's fastest interceptor can be hidden next to a farm.

---

# Kingston wins enormously

And this is absolutely what the company would try to do.

The two design teams aren't enemy tribes who desire the extermination of the other office.

They work in the same company.

People transfer between them.

They drink in the same places.

Their managers know that if one airplane wins completely, an enormous number of highly specialized engineers on the other program are going to become redundant.

So once the political situation develops into:

> FAA wants 1214; RAF wants 1216; Treasury wants one aircraft,

the company's rational response is to construct a **commonality proposal**.

Kingston management goes to the Ministry and essentially says:

> You are not buying two fighter systems.

> You are buying **one British STOVL combat-aircraft family with two aerodynamic variants**.

This is marketing language.

But it isn't fraudulent.

The common systems make it partly true.

And the stronger the commonality, the stronger Kingston's argument becomes.

---

# The engine becomes the heart of the family

I would especially insist on one common engine family because otherwise the support savings begin collapsing.

The original Harrier was unusually identified with Pegasus, and Rolls-Royce continued developing that engine family through substantial thrust and durability improvements. citeturn975243search0 In this timeline the British STOVL establishment has been continuously funded since the 1950s, so an advanced 1980s successor to Pegasus can reasonably be designed from the outset as a **common fighter powerplant**.

Let's provisionally call it something generic like the **Pegasus successor** rather than assign the engine designation yet.

Both aircraft use the same basic engine.

P.1214 tunes its installation around:

> transition control, responsiveness and naval reliability.

P.1216 uses an installation optimized more aggressively around:

> inlet performance, supersonic efficiency and high-altitude thrust.

Same engine core.

Different aircraft.

That is a very useful distinction.

---

# Common radar hardware, different software

This is another place I think Britain saves enormous money.

The radar itself doesn't need to be two entirely unrelated sets.

Both aircraft can have the same basic radar family—antenna technology, transmitter, receiver, processor and maintenance modules—with mission software diverging.

The FAA version emphasizes:

- look-down maritime air defense;
- low-altitude fighter detection;
- fleet datalink integration;
- antiship modes.

The RAF version emphasizes:

- long-range interception;
- high closing-speed target processing;
- home-defense network integration;
- BVR missile control.

So the P.1214 pilot and P.1216 pilot may see different menus and have different tactical procedures while the avionics technician sees essentially the same boxes.

That is exactly the kind of commonality that matters financially.

---

# The cockpit could be almost identical

I'd go quite far here.

Sit a pilot in either aircraft and the controls should feel deliberately familiar.

Same:

- instrument layout;
- displays;
- throttle;
- stick;
- nozzle/STOVL controls;
- warning system;
- navigation page;
- radar controls;
- weapons logic.

The flying qualities differ enormously once the aircraft moves.

But conversion training from one to the other is much easier than switching unrelated fighters.

That creates another interesting consequence:

**RAF and FAA pilots can cross-qualify.**

Not casually.

But if Britain suddenly needs additional naval pilots during a crisis, an RAF P.1216 pilot already knows eighty percent of the aircraft's systems before ever entering a P.1214 conversion course.

Given Britain's Falklands trauma, that personnel flexibility would be considered genuinely valuable.

---

# I would let the airframes remain visibly unrelated

This is important aesthetically.

We shouldn't make commonality slowly erase what makes the two aircraft interesting.

From twenty meters away, the cockpits may look related.

Open an avionics bay and the components are cousins.

Talk to the mechanic and he'll tell you half his tools work on either aircraft.

But from above:

> **you cannot mistake them.**

P.1214 has that extraordinary forward-swept/X-like planform.

P.1216 has its strange but more high-speed-oriented configuration.

Britain therefore ends up with something almost no other air force has:

> **two frontline fighters from the same technological family that look radically different because each service optimized the same machinery around a different kind of fight.**

That is a very strong visual expression of the RAF/FAA distinction.

---

# The Treasury can actually accept this

There is still a penalty.

Britain must maintain:

- two production jigs;
- two structural supply chains;
- two sets of aerodynamic spares;
- separate wings;
- separate tail assemblies;
- separate flight testing;
- separate airworthiness certification;
- somewhat different training.

So this isn't as cheap as building only P.1214.

The honest argument is:

> **dual procurement costs appreciably more than one aircraft, but dramatically less than maintaining two unrelated fighter programs.**

And Britain doesn't need both in equal numbers.

I could see something like:

### P.1214
**roughly 180–240 British/Commonwealth aircraft initially**

because the Fleet Air Arm needs them and Commonwealth route forces can use them from dispersed strips and smaller carriers.

### P.1216
**perhaps 100–150 RAF aircraft**

because Britain needs fewer dedicated high-performance air-defense aircraft than multi-role naval/tactical fighters.

Those are only scale estimates—we shouldn't lock production totals until we establish British carrier and RAF squadron strength.

But the ratio makes sense.

And export customers complicate it further.

Some Commonwealth states probably prefer P.1214 because naval/expeditionary flexibility matters more.

Others with major continental air-defense requirements may prefer P.1216.

Suddenly Kingston can amortize the common engine, radar and avionics across **hundreds of both airframes**.

Then the dual program stops looking quite so insane.

---

# The two branches should also converge over time

This is another reason the commonality decision pays off.

The first production aircraft may only be, say, **60–70 percent common by expensive systems**, while structurally they remain very different.

Then modernization increases commonality.

When Britain introduces a new radar in 1994:

both get it.

New missile:

both.

New mission computer:

both.

New digital engine control:

both.

New defensive suite:

both.

New helmet sight:

both.

So by the late 1990s the pilots joke that:

> everything behind the cockpit software is trying to become the same airplane,

while aerodynamicists point out that this is obviously nonsense.

And then the eventual **next-generation British fighter program** inherits an enormously useful industrial lesson.

The RAF and FAA no longer begin by developing independent airplanes.

They begin with:

> **one propulsion, sensor, software and weapons architecture—then determine how many airframe variants are actually necessary.**

That's a very believable precursor to Britain's eventual attempt at an F-35-like family.

---

# It also resolves the Falklands procurement story beautifully

The public story has an apparent winner:

**P.1214.**

The newspaper readers, aviation enthusiasts and Fleet Air Arm partisans get their futuristic fighter.

The RAF technically loses the competition.

Then, six months later, the Ministry announces that it is ordering **P.1216 as the RAF member of the same combat-aircraft family**.

Air Staff officers who had privately preferred it are delighted.

Treasury announces that extensive component standardization has reduced the cost of maintaining two variants.

Kingston announces that employment at the works is secure.

The government declares the entire thing a brilliant compromise.

Opposition MPs point out, not incorrectly, that the competition was originally supposed to select **one aeroplane**.

And everyone involved conspicuously avoids discussing that.

That feels almost painfully plausible.

## So I would lock the relationship as:

**P.1214**
- Fleet Air Arm primary fighter;
- more maneuver-oriented;
- ~Mach 1.8 class;
- better suited to small-deck/naval operations;
- public favorite;
- larger production family.

**P.1216**
- RAF primary interceptor/fighter;
- Mach-2-class;
- better acceleration/high-speed interception;
- smaller but still substantial production run;
- Air Staff's preferred design.

**Both**
- same advanced British STOVL engine family;
- same broad cockpit architecture;
- same radar/avionics hardware families;
- same weapons ecosystem;
- same electronics and maintenance standards;
- substantial common accessories and LRUs;
- radically different aerodynamic structures and installation geometry.

So Britain doesn't choose which one was “really better.”

It concludes that the answer depended on the question.

And Kingston gets to build both. memcite

## Turn 1190 — Assistant

- Timestamp: 2026-08-15T02:08:58.192Z
- Message ID: `70f96fb8-6432-41db-bd34-2bed6bd3ebf2`

- Relationship: parallel specialist continuation imported after the master project record through Turn 777

Yes. Your commonality concept works, and I would formalize it as **three different kinds of commonality**, because that gets Kingston much closer to what you're imagining than a simple percentage-of-identical-parts figure.

The first is **literal interchangeability**: engine, radar boxes, mission computers, displays, pumps, valves, bearings, wheels and brakes where loads permit, actuators, connectors, fasteners, weapons interfaces, batteries, generators, and so forth. The second is **common repair stock**: tubing, hose, wiring, duct sections, conduit, sheet material, insulation, seals, and standardized stock that can be cut, bent, terminated, or machined to a marked P.1214 or P.1216 dimension. The third is genuinely **airframe-specific geometry**: wing spars, major frames, inlet lips, landing-gear attachment structures, control surfaces, and the pieces whose loads or shapes are fundamentally different.

So a box can very plausibly arrive marked something like:

> **P.1214/P.1216 — DUCT, AIR, No. 38**  
> P.1216: use full length.  
> P.1214: trim at marked station and fit adaptor B.

For pressure-critical tubing, structural members, and landing-gear components, I'd normally push the cutting/forming work up to a properly equipped depot rather than letting an ordinary squadron mechanic attack a certified flight-critical part with a hacksaw. But the principle is exactly right. The goal is not “every part physically identical.” It is:

> **one supply system should be able to repair either fighter.**

That could become one of the cleverest parts of the Kingston compromise.

## And I think I have the names

My strongest pairing is:

> **P.1214 — BAe Sea Fury F.1**  
> **P.1216 — BAe Tempest F.1**

I like this considerably more than inventing two entirely new names.

There is a historical reason that makes the pairing almost absurdly appropriate. **Tempest and Sea Fury were themselves closely related Hawker aircraft.** Hawker developed the Sea Fury/Fury concept from a lighter derivative of the Tempest, and the RAF and Fleet Air Arm variants were originally being developed in parallel. citeturn270629search0turn270629search1

So forty years later, Kingston deliberately resurrects **the same two family names for another pair of related-but-different RAF and FAA fighters**.

That's excellent institutional continuity rather than just nostalgia.

### P.1214 — **Sea Fury**

This is the Fleet Air Arm machine.

The name fits it almost perfectly. It is the more maneuver-oriented aircraft, designed around naval operation, and it becomes the machine that the public falls in love with during the Falklands-era competition.

The original Sea Fury was itself a Fleet Air Arm fighter, so the name carries naval pedigree. citeturn270629search0

And importantly, I would **not** call it *Sea Fury II* officially.

Your existing British designation system uses **public name + role mark + mark number**—Meteor F.3, Javelin FAW.1, Lightning F.3, Buccaneer S.2, Harrier GR.1, and so on. fileciteturn24file0

So this is the new:

**Sea Fury F.1**

The forty-year gap tells people which Sea Fury they're discussing.

A historian says “1947 Sea Fury” or “1989 Sea Fury.” A mechanic says F.1. The public just says **Sea Fury**.

And I can easily imagine the unveiling language deliberately invoking the old fighter:

> *The Fleet Air Arm has carried the name Sea Fury before.*

That would play extremely well after the Falklands.

## P.1216 — **Tempest**

This one may fit even better.

The historical Tempest was explicitly a **high-speed fighter**, which is precisely the personality we've given P.1216. citeturn270629search1

So:

**Tempest F.1**

is the RAF's Mach-2-class dispersed interceptor.

Sea Fury wins the dramatic low-speed demonstration.

Tempest goes upstairs faster.

Sea Fury wins the public beauty contest.

Tempest satisfies the Air Staff.

Sea Fury lands on the carrier.

Tempest disappears over the horizon during an interception trial.

And because the two old Hawker names were historically connected, Kingston gets to present the production settlement not as:

> “We failed to choose between two prototypes.”

but as:

> **“We have developed the new Tempest/Sea Fury combat-aircraft family.”**

That is precisely the sort of reframing a company would want.

## It also gives the rivalry much better language

During development, the newspapers call the entire thing the **Harrier II competition**, because nobody outside the program knows what Britain's next STOVL fighter will actually be called.

Then the names leak—or are officially announced.

And suddenly the national argument stops being the rather bloodless:

> P.1214 versus P.1216.

It becomes:

> **Sea Fury versus Tempest.**

That is much better television.

You'd get headlines like:

**SEA FURY STEALS THE SHOW**

and the following week's aviation magazine:

**TEMPEST: THE RAF'S FASTER ANSWER**

The enthusiast subculture would immediately acquire tribal identities.

“Fury men” think the Navy has the real fighter.

“Tempest men” think the Fury enthusiasts are impressed by airshow maneuvers while ignoring interception performance.

Actual test pilots think both groups are oversimplifying.

Perfect.

## The family relationship also becomes visible when you open them

Externally, they look almost unrelated.

That is part of the charm.

But remove the access panels and suddenly the relationship becomes obvious.

Same black boxes.

Same labels.

Same connector standards.

Same cockpit.

Same engine accessories.

Same hydraulic components.

Same brake assemblies.

Same missile electronics.

The maintenance manuals might even deliberately use shared volumes:

**Air Publication 121 — Common Equipment, Sea Fury and Tempest**

followed by:

**AP 1214 — Sea Fury Airframe**

and

**AP 1216 — Tempest Airframe**

That would be a very British way of expressing the relationship.

The commonality becomes most obvious at a Commonwealth depot. An Australian or Canadian maintenance unit can receive one broad inventory marked for the **Sea Fury/Tempest family**, with smaller sets of airframe-specific components for whichever type it operates.

That matters more than being able to claim “72.4 percent parts commonality.”

## And the names say something about the services

This is the bit I particularly like.

**Sea Fury** is overtly naval. It sounds aggressive, close, maneuverable, and tied to the Fleet Air Arm.

**Tempest** sounds fast, violent, and slightly impersonal. It fits an RAF interceptor launched from a concealed dispersal site to climb rapidly into an incoming German formation.

So their silhouettes and names reinforce the service distinction:

> **Fleet Air Arm — Sea Fury:** strange forward-swept fighter, deck fighter, knife-fighter.

> **Royal Air Force — Tempest:** straighter high-speed machine, dispersed interceptor, missile fighter.

Yet both are unmistakably children of Harrier once somebody watches either one make a short takeoff and vertical recovery.

Harrier therefore doesn't need to donate its **name** to them.

It donates the **idea**.

And I think that's stronger. Harrier becomes remembered as the aircraft that changed what Britain believed a tactical aircraft should be. Sea Fury and Tempest are what Britain built once that belief stopped being experimental and became doctrine.

So I would lock **Sea Fury F.1** for P.1214 and **Tempest F.1** for P.1216. They are distinct names, historically British, unusually well matched to their respective missions, and—best of all—already belong to the same Hawker family tree in the real historical lineage. memcite

Instead, it creates an aerodynamic school whose first great postwar victory is the strategic bomber, and whose second great victory, decades later, is low observability.

That also means parts of the present Aerospace Reference are now scaffolding rather than final canon. Its basic 1948 register and the Me 262/HG research ancestry remain useful, but the old `Ho 505`, `Ar 503`, `Ju 506`, and later neat one-house-per-role sequence should be rebuilt around the design-school model we're establishing now. fileciteturn27file0

## The German firms should have philosophies, not monopolies

I would define six surviving schools this way:

| Design house | Its recurring argument | Fields where it tends to win | Characteristic failure |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Messerschmitt** | *Make it faster; reduce everything that prevents speed.* | Interceptors, high-speed reconnaissance, fast strike | Range, low-speed handling, maintenance burden, over-specialization |
| **Focke-Wulf** | *Make the pilot able to use more of the flight envelope.* | Air superiority, maneuver fighters, close support, later exotic aerodynamics | Structural/control complexity; sometimes sacrifices outright dash performance |
| **Horten-Gotha** | *Don't push unnecessary airplane through the air.* | Long-range penetrators, flying-wing bombers, reconnaissance, later low-observable aircraft | Stability/control, internal arrangement, developmental risk |
| **Junkers** | *Build the aircraft around the mission system and keep improving the platform.* | Maritime patrol, EW, AEW, transports, tankers, long-endurance multirole aircraft | Weight growth and less spectacular headline performance |
| **Heinkel** | *Make difficult flight conditions technologically manageable.* | Night/all-weather combat, advanced propulsion, specialized interceptors, high-altitude and experimental aircraft | Expensive sophistication and frequent competition with simpler alternatives |
| **Arado** | *Reach the target before interception becomes practical.* | Schnellbomber, reconnaissance, theater strike | Increasingly overlaps Messerschmitt until corporate independence stops making sense |

The historical ancestry supports those last two especially well. The Ju 88/188/388 family operated across bombing, reconnaissance, and fighter roles, which gives Junkers a very natural institutional memory of designing adaptable **platforms** rather than one exquisitely specialized mission aircraft. citeturn454595search6 Heinkel, meanwhile, backed the He 178, which made the world's first turbojet-powered aircraft flight in 1939, while the He 219 became an unusually sophisticated dedicated night fighter. That gives Heinkel a believable postwar culture built around propulsion, radar, crew systems, and operating in difficult conditions. citeturn454595search4turn454595search0

But none of these are fenced-off preserves. Messerschmitt will absolutely submit a dogfighter. Focke-Wulf will submit an interceptor. Horten will repeatedly try to convince the Luftwaffe that its latest strange wing can be a fighter. Junkers will occasionally attempt another bomber. Heinkel will try to steal an interceptor contract.

The point is that when two firms answer the same requirement, **they instinctively answer different questions**.

---

# Horten XVIII should beat Me 464

The wartime starting condition is already fixed. The Me 364 is Germany's late-war **Höhenbomber**, and it is the aircraft involved in the May 1947 White Parachutes episode. fileciteturn26file11 That gives Messerschmitt enormous prestige entering the postwar strategic-bomber competition.

So the competition around 1946–50 isn't:

> Can Horten build a bomber while Messerschmitt doesn't know how?

It's:

> **Does the next strategic bomber look like a conventional swept-wing jet descendant of Me 364, or does Germany commit to the all-wing solution?**

Messerschmitt's answer is the Me 464 proposal: swept wing, multiple jets, high altitude, technically conservative by the standards of what Germany has just learned.

Horten-Gotha says the Me 464 is solving the wrong problem.

Why carry a long fuselage, large tail and separate aerodynamic surfaces across intercontinental distances if most of the airplane can be **fuel volume, structure and lifting surface at the same time**?

And we have an excellent real-world plausibility check. The American YB-49 was already flying in **1947** as an eight-turbojet flying-wing bomber. The USAF records generally good performance, about a 4,000-mile range with a 10,000-pound bomb load, and a 42,000-foot ceiling. Its serious problem was stability during simulated bombing runs, not that an all-jet strategic flying wing was physically impossible. citeturn980948view0

That is almost exactly the technical argument we need.

### So Horten does not win because it is “stealthy”

Not yet.

Horten wins because it offers:

**less parasitic drag → better fuel efficiency → better strategic radius for a given engine/fuel generation.**

The bombs and most of the fuel remain internal.

Its enormous wing gives good high-altitude characteristics.

And Germany already has an industrial organization comfortable with unusually integrated aircraft structures.

The price is that it is harder to aim accurately, harder to trim, harder to control in yaw, and much less forgiving when something in the control system isn't behaving.

That makes the Horten victory **conditional**.

The Luftwaffe says, in effect:

> The range advantage is worth the control problem, provided you solve the control problem.

And that becomes Horten-Gotha's great postwar engineering project.

## I would not force the first bomber to use primitive Jumo 004s

The wartime design work can absolutely contemplate six engines. But the production aircraft should wait for the better second-generation German turbojets coming out of the late-war engine programs.

That also keeps the timing sane.

A working developmental sequence would be approximately:

| Period | Strategic-bomber development |
|---|---|
| **1945–47** | Horten XVIII and conventional Messerschmitt successor studies compete while Me 364 remains operational |
| **1948–49** | full-scale Horten prototype/testing; longitudinal and yaw-control work becomes the primary difficulty |
| **1950–52** | second-generation engines, automatic stabilization, bombing autopilot and navigation system mature |
| **c. 1952–54** | first operational Horten strategic flying-wing bomber enters service |
| **later 1950s** | second production mark gets considerably better engines, electronics and control augmentation |

The exact dates are still working figures. But **early 1950s service is quite reasonable** considering that the YB-49 was already flying in 1947. citeturn980948view0

The Me 464 becomes the famous loser.

And it shouldn't contribute nothing. Messerschmitt's pressure-cabin work, high-altitude systems, navigation, engine integration and aerodynamic research can all migrate into other aircraft. There may even be one or two flying Me 464 prototypes.

But there is no German B-52 equivalent because **Germany chose the other road**.

That also leaves America free to develop its own genuinely American bomber personality rather than having everybody independently build Stratofortresses.

---

# The Ho 229 then becomes Horten-Gotha's founding legend

The Ho 229 itself is a genuine basis for this. The surviving V3 is the world's only surviving example of the first all-wing jet-aircraft family, and the actual project encountered substantial technical difficulties rather than being a magically mature 1945 stealth fighter. citeturn303088search4turn303088search16

I would divide its postwar history into three phases.

### 1947–mid-1950s: prestigious specialist

This is closest to what we've already established.

Ho 229 derivatives serve in limited numbers as:

high-altitude escort, fast reconnaissance, penetration strike, and perhaps specialized night/intruder aircraft.

They are famous.

Pilots volunteer for them.

Propaganda loves them.

They are **not** what the average Jagdgeschwader flies.

The reason isn't that the airframe is useless. It's that a conventional fighter gives the Luftwaffe much easier stability, better low-speed behavior, simpler training, easier maintenance, and more predictable weapons employment.

Messerschmitt and Focke-Wulf can manufacture fighters that ordinary squadron pilots can use without every unit becoming a flying-wing experimental establishment.

That makes the Ho 229 more credible, not less important.

### Late 1950s–1960s: the radar question appears

This is the point at which I'd make a very deliberate distinction.

The Luftwaffe does **not** discover in 1945 that the Ho 229 is secretly invisible.

The Smithsonian's technical investigation of the surviving aircraft notes that the famous claim about charcoal deliberately producing radar absorption lacks tangible evidence one way or the other. We should therefore keep the setting away from the later mythology. citeturn303088search14

Instead, German radar tests in the 1950s begin revealing something much more modest:

> Horten aircraft sometimes present **less radar return than a conventional aircraft of similar physical size**, particularly from useful aspects.

That's interesting.

Not magical.

And now the Luftwaffe starts asking a new question:

> Can we deliberately make that advantage larger?

That is the moment Horten-Gotha changes schools.

The firm was founded intellectually on **aerodynamic economy**.

During the 1960s it begins becoming the German authority on **electromagnetic economy** too.

Now Horten engineers study:

engine-face shielding;

inlet geometry;

buried engines;

panel joints;

antenna placement;

edge alignment;

radar-transparent and radar-absorbing materials;

weapons carried internally;

and what vertical control surfaces do to radar return.

Suddenly the weird characteristics they've spent twenty years learning to manage become valuable for an entirely different reason.

---

# Fly-by-wire gives the Ho 229 philosophy its second life

This is where your favorite finally gets its revenge.

Through the 1950s and much of the 1960s, Horten's fighter proposals keep losing because the Luftwaffe reasonably asks:

> Why accept those handling compromises when Messerschmitt and Focke-Wulf give us extremely capable conventional fighters?

Then flight-control computers improve.

That fundamentally changes what shapes are acceptable.

NASA's later X-36 is a useful demonstration of the principle: a tailless fighter configuration that was unstable in both pitch and yaw could nevertheless be stabilized by digital fly-by-wire, while split control surfaces and thrust vectoring provided directional control. citeturn845869search0

AltWWII Germany reaches that general technological category earlier than the X-36 because its Horten program never stops demanding it. I still wouldn't give it mature digital FBW in 1958. But by the **1970s**, analog augmentation transitioning into digital controls means Horten can suddenly submit fighter designs whose control problem is being solved in software rather than entirely by passive aerodynamics.

That is enormous.

The competition changes from:

> “Horten's airplane is weird and difficult to fly.”

to:

> “Horten's computer is flying a weird airplane and the pilot merely tells it what maneuver he wants.”

And now low signature matters too.

So around the 1970s–80s, **Horten gets back into the fighter business seriously**.

It may still not win every competition.

But Messerschmitt and Focke-Wulf now have an actual third competitor.

---

# The eventual B-2-looking Horten is therefore completely justified

But I wouldn't make it literally a stretched Ho 229.

The family resemblance is philosophical and aerodynamic.

The mature low-observable Horten strategic bomber of the 1980s should have:

a broad tailless flying-wing planform;

engines deeply integrated into the body;

internal stores;

careful inlet and exhaust treatment;

digital flight controls;

signature-aware surface geometry;

and considerably more sophisticated construction than the wooden Ho 229.

So to somebody from our world it produces the immediate reaction:

> **“That looks disturbingly like a B-2.”**

But in-setting, nobody thinks Northrop has been copied because Northrop isn't the genealogy.

They see:

> **Ho 229 → Horten XVIII → thirty years of German flying-wing bombers → low-observable Horten.**

And the historical American YB-49/B-2 sequence gives us an important reality check: flying wings really did possess enough efficiency to keep the bomber concept attractive, while later flight controls allowed a much more sophisticated realization of it. The USAF itself notes that the flying-wing bomber idea disappeared for decades after the YB-49 before reappearing with B-2. citeturn980948view0

Germany simply never has that forty-year interruption.

That is one of the strongest alternate-technology divergences we've developed.

---

# Messerschmitt gets the supersonic fighter instead

This is where I would give Messerschmitt its consolation prize—and a very substantial one.

The Me 262 lineage absolutely survives.

But I wouldn't take a 262, stretch it, install bigger engines and call it the world's first proper supersonic fighter.

The current development we've already established is better:

> **Me 262 → HG-I → HG-II → HG-III → clean-sheet postwar Messerschmitt fighter.**

The HG-III matters because it asks what happens when the nacelles stop hanging underneath the wing and the engines move inward, while the entire airframe gets redesigned around higher speed. Our earlier transcript already established it as research rather than merely another production 262. fileciteturn26file1 The present Aerospace Reference similarly makes HG-III research feed the later clean-register fighter. fileciteturn27file0

I would keep that.

What I would change is the **date**.

The old reference puts the Me 501 Falke in 1956 at 1,620 km/h. fileciteturn27file0 Given the German technological head start we're now preserving, I think that's unnecessarily late.

A plausible progression is:

| Date | Messerschmitt high-speed branch |
|---|---|
| **1948** | Me 262F/HG-II-class transonic production fighter |
| **1947–50** | HG-III and related engine/inlet/wing research |
| **1951–52** | clean-sheet postwar supersonic prototype |
| **1953–54** | first operational Messerschmitt supersonic interceptor |
| **late 1950s** | second-generation machine reaches genuine Mach-2-class performance |

For comparison, the historical F-100 prototype first flew in 1953 and the supersonic production fighter entered service in 1954. citeturn980722search0turn980722search25

So Germany getting an operational supersonic fighter in **1953 or 1954** is aggressive, but not technologically absurd. It has operational jet combat behind it in 1944 and an uninterrupted high-speed research establishment.

I would be comfortable making Germany the first power in the setting with a **production fighter capable of sustained level supersonic flight**.

Not necessarily Mach 2 immediately.

Mach 1.2–1.4 is enough to make the historical first.

Then comes Mach 2.

## And yes, it can absolutely carry wing fuel

The part I'd change is **thickening the wing substantially**.

That works against Messerschmitt's objective because transonic and supersonic drag strongly rewards thinner sections.

Instead:

> thin swept wing + integral inboard wing tanks + substantially larger fuselage fuel volume + better-specific-fuel-consumption engines.

The longer fuselage you've suggested is useful.

More internal fuel also naturally follows from bringing the engines inward and cleaning up the nacelle arrangement.

The result remains recognizably descended from Me 262 in design philosophy without pretending an Me 262A wing can simply be pushed to Mach 1.5.

And under the existing 1948 German registration scheme, I would **not call that clean-sheet aircraft Me 362 or Me 363**. Clean-sheet postwar operational aircraft begin in the 500 block. fileciteturn27file0 So `Me 501` remains a very good candidate; we merely move and redesign it.

That is a useful formal-versus-functional distinction:

> **Functionally:** the Me 501 is the descendant of Me 262.

> **Formally:** it is not an Me 262 variant.

---

# Focke-Wulf should become Germany's control-authority school

I think “maneuverability” is correct, but I'd broaden it slightly.

Focke-Wulf's question becomes:

> **How much control can we give the pilot over where the airplane points?**

Sometimes that produces maneuverability.

Sometimes it produces excellent low-speed handling.

Sometimes rough-field operation.

Later it produces relaxed stability, unusual control surfaces, thrust vectoring, canards, and eventually your **forward-swept-wing fighter**.

That distinguishes it more usefully from Messerschmitt than merely “turning versus speed.”

And this is where we need to fix an old piece of provisional canon.

The current Aerospace Reference still has the **Ju 287/EF 131 forward-swept evaluation program**. fileciteturn27file0 If your statement that the first German forward/reverse-swept wing belongs to Focke-Wulf means **literally the first flying German example in-setting**, that old Junkers line has to be superseded. That's entirely permissible because the Ju 287's historical flight was after our 1941 divergence.

I think the cleaner compromise is:

> Junkers may conduct theoretical/wind-tunnel work, but **Focke-Wulf produces Germany's first serious flying forward-swept combat-aircraft program**.

That preserves the authorial identity you want.

### But the really radical Focke-Wulf shouldn't arrive in 1955

Forward sweep has a nasty aeroelastic problem: wing loading twists the wing in ways that can increase its aerodynamic load still further. NASA's X-29 solved this much later using aeroelastically tailored composite structure and digital flight control; the resulting aircraft demonstrated excellent control response at very high angles of attack. citeturn303088search2turn303088search5

That tells us what Germany needs.

So I would have Focke-Wulf **experiment** with moderate forward sweep during the 1960s.

The really spectacular reverse-swept fighter arrives with composites and digital flight controls in the **late 1970s or 1980s**.

Then Germany gets something visually just as strange as Britain's P.1214, but produced by a completely different institutional logic:

Britain wants runway independence.

Focke-Wulf wants control authority.

Same decade.

Very different airplane.

---

# Junkers has a very strong niche once we stop trying to make it another fighter company

I think Junkers should become Germany's **platform house**.

That's not a consolation prize.

Its basic question is:

> **How many missions can this airframe support over twenty years without becoming a maintenance disaster?**

The historical Ju 88 family already demonstrated exactly this sort of institutional versatility, with descendants serving as bombers, reconnaissance aircraft, and day/night fighters. citeturn454595search6

So postwar Junkers becomes very strong at:

maritime patrol;

electronic reconnaissance;

airborne early warning;

tankers;

transports;

long-range communications aircraft;

missile-control aircraft;

perhaps large battlefield-surveillance machines later.

This also fits Germany's empire.

The Reich has a huge amount of coastline, overseas administration, northern approaches, African geography and naval infrastructure to watch.

A Messerschmitt interceptor flying Mach 2.3 is spectacular.

It is a terrible aircraft in which to spend twelve hours listening for submarines.

Junkers makes the aircraft that does that.

And Junkers still submits occasional bomber and fighter designs. It simply has a consistent tendency to win when **endurance, internal volume, maintainability, crew space and mission-system growth** matter more than spectacular aerodynamic purity.

That keeps it relevant forever.

---

# Heinkel should own “difficult conditions”

This is the one I like most after thinking through the historical ancestry.

Heinkel doesn't need to become “Junkers but smaller.”

Its design philosophy can be:

> **The airplane should still work when the environment is trying to make ordinary aviation fail.**

Night.

Cloud.

High altitude.

Short warning time.

Difficult propulsion requirements.

Unusual basing.

The He 219 gives it an institutional ancestry in radar-heavy dedicated night fighting, while Heinkel's support for von Ohain's turbojet work gives it an unusually early propulsion pedigree. citeturn454595search0turn454595search4

So the postwar Heinkel bureau becomes particularly interested in the **whole technical system surrounding the pilot**:

radar;

automatic interception;

navigation;

pressurization;

de-icing;

crew workload;

advanced engines;

automatic landing;

later infrared;

perhaps lift jets or VTOL experiments;

high-altitude reconnaissance;

special-weather strike.

Heinkel therefore competes very seriously against Messerschmitt for **all-weather interceptors**.

Messerschmitt says:

> Mine is 180 km/h faster.

Heinkel says:

> Mine finds the bomber in cloud, carries more radar, keeps two crewmen useful for four hours, and can land in miserable weather.

Now the Luftwaffe has an actual decision to make.

Sometimes Messerschmitt wins.

Sometimes Heinkel does.

That is what we want.

---

# Arado can disappear as a corporation without disappearing intellectually

I agree with your merger instinct.

Arado's great postwar problem is that its strongest argument is:

> **fast strike and reconnaissance.**

Messerschmitt eventually says:

> That's also our argument.

The Ar 234 lineage gives Arado enough prestige to survive through the 1950s, and there may be one successful postwar Blitz generation.

But as Messerschmitt moves from pure interception into high-speed penetration, the duplication becomes increasingly hard to defend.

So sometime around the **late 1950s or 1960s**, I would have Messerschmitt absorb Arado or establish a corporate combination in which the Arado design bureau becomes Messerschmitt's **Schnellangriff/strike division**.

That is better than simply firing everyone.

The name gradually disappears from aircraft designations.

The engineers don't.

Thirty years later, a Messerschmitt strike aircraft may contain a recognizable Arado design ancestry even though there hasn't been an `Ar` number for decades.

---

# This produces a much more interesting 1980s Luftwaffe

Instead of one German company suspiciously producing every good aircraft, the fleet has visible intellectual genealogies.

A **Messerschmitt** is usually fast, clean, powerful, and somewhat contemptuous of fuel.

A **Focke-Wulf** tends to have extraordinary control authority and may look increasingly bizarre because Kurt Tank's institutional descendants keep asking whether the pilot can exploit another part of the envelope.

A **Horten-Gotha** increasingly looks like somebody has been trying to make parts of the aircraft disappear. Its strategic bombers have been flying wings for thirty years, and its fighters begin following them once computers make tailless control less punishing.

A **Junkers** tends to be the airplane that's still flying twelve hours later with six operators and three tonnes of electronics.

A **Heinkel** is the thing you'd rather have when it is midnight, raining, the runway is terrible, and somebody has just told you the target is at 60,000 feet.

And an **Arado** after the 1960s is less an aircraft badge than a group of engineers inside Messerschmitt who keep proposing that the solution to every strike requirement is another 300 km/h.

That also explains why Germany deliberately retains multiple specialized combat-aircraft fleets. The old Aerospace Reference already has separate interceptor, air-superiority, strike, close-support and maritime branches; what we're changing is **why those branches keep remaining technologically distinct**. fileciteturn27file0

## The Horten result, specifically

I don't think you have to concede very much on the Ho 229 at all.

What you have to concede is only this:

> **Ho 229 does not become Germany's universal fighter.**

Everything else can survive.

It becomes one of the most famous wartime jet families.

Its aerodynamic philosophy wins Germany's strategic-bomber competition.

That victory keeps Horten-Gotha rich, prestigious and institutionally permanent.

Its fighter branch continues as an experimental and specialist line.

Radar turns one of its incidental properties into a serious military advantage.

The 1960s create deliberate signature reduction.

The 1970s give it flight controls good enough to reopen the fighter question.

And by the 1980s, Horten-Gotha can be fielding an aircraft whose silhouette makes a modern observer think **B-2**, while simultaneously submitting smaller low-observable fighters against Messerschmitt and Focke-Wulf.

That's much more satisfying than having Ho 229 replace Me 262 in 1949.

Messerschmitt wins the **speed race**.

Focke-Wulf wins much of the **maneuver race**.

Horten wins the **shape of the future**.

And those three firms spend the next forty years trying to prove that their particular victory is the one that matters most. memcite

Yes. I think the Ho XVIII can converge on a **YB-49-like stabilization solution without simply becoming the YB-49**, and the eight-engine choice actually helps make the comparison more convincing.

There is one useful correction first. The YB-49 did have **four inboard vertical fins**, but these weren't its whole yaw-control system. Northrop also relied on split/drag-rudder arrangements in the wing; earlier Northrop flying-wing experiments had already used split drag rudders near the tips. NACA testing of the YB-49 specifically records its dorsal fins, while later NASA material describes four inboard vertical fins as part of the jet-powered configuration. citeturn892383search0turn892383search1 So the lesson Horten can take from Northrop is not simply “put four conventional rudders on it.” It is **combine passive directional stability with active differential-drag control**.

That gives us a better Ho XVIII.

## I would use the four central fins, not four wingtip fins

The wingtip-fin version could fly, but I think it creates more problems than it solves on an aircraft this large.

A vertical fin produces yaw stability primarily because its aerodynamic force acts **behind the center of gravity**. Putting it far outboard does not automatically multiply its yaw authority in the same way that putting a drag brake far outboard does. A wingtip vertical surface also applies its side force a long way from the aircraft centerline, which creates more roll–yaw coupling, and on a huge flexible flying wing it puts additional mass and aerodynamic loads exactly where the structure is already most sensitive.

That isn't fatal. Wingtip fins and winglets are perfectly real aerodynamic devices. But on the first production Ho XVIII, they buy us relatively little compared with the structural and flutter work they impose.

The **drag rudders**, however, belong farther out.

When you open a drag surface on the right wing, you're deliberately generating additional drag far to the right of the centerline. That gives you a very useful yawing moment. Northrop's flying-wing lineage made exactly this kind of split-surface control practical. citeturn302288search1turn718108search1

So my preferred Horten solution becomes:

> **four relatively small vertical stabilizing fins in the central wing, plus split drag rudders/elevons farther outboard.**

That gives the bomber both passive directional damping and strong active yaw control.

And it avoids turning the wingtips into giant loaded structures.

## Your engine-side fin arrangement is almost exactly where I would put them

The production Ho XVIII has **eight second-generation turbojets**, buried in the thick central wing as four engines on each side of the aircraft centerline.

I would then place the four vertical fins approximately like this from above:

```text
                         COCKPIT
                           ▲
                    ┌─────────────┐
               fin  │ ● ●   ● ● │ fin
                  \ │             │ /
                   \│ ● ●   ● ● │/
                fin \             / fin
                     \           /
                      \         /
                       \       /
                        \     /
```

Not literally between every engine—the thermal and maintenance geometry has to remain sensible—but in **two paired stations flanking the main engine installation**.

Something like:

> inner port fin  
> outer port fin  
> inner starboard fin  
> outer starboard fin

all located far enough aft on the central wing to provide useful directional stability.

That is strikingly similar in concept to the YB-49's four inboard fins, which is reasonable because both design teams are confronting the same underlying problem: a huge flying wing has no conventional vertical tail. citeturn892383search1

But the Ho XVIII gets there independently through its own development program.

## I would keep all four on top

The top-and-bottom arrangement is aerodynamically interesting, but I don't think it's worth the operational cost.

In principle, having matched dorsal and ventral surfaces gives you a nicely symmetrical side-force arrangement. You reduce some of the rolling moment that comes from having the entire vertical tail area above the aircraft's center of gravity.

But the lower surfaces create three unpleasant problems.

First, **ground clearance**.

A flying wing already wants to sit relatively close to the ground. Large ventral fins force longer landing gear or much smaller lower fins, and the moment somebody lands nose-high or compresses the gear hard, you've created something expensive to scrape off the aeroplane.

Second, they complicate precisely the underside of the center section where we want:

landing gear, bomb bays, access panels, antennas, and the bombardier station.

Third, they make maintenance unpleasant. A dorsal fin can be surrounded by scaffolding. A ventral rudder lives underneath a strategic bomber weighing many tens of tonnes.

So I'd turn your idea slightly:

> instead of two fins piercing completely through the wing and extending equally above and below, give Ho XVIII **four fairly shallow dorsal fins**, structurally rooted deeply into the central wing.

Their internal spars can indeed pass down through much of the wing depth. Visually, however, only the upper surfaces protrude.

This is also a nice technological marker. The first Ho XVIII needs four fins because 1950s control technology isn't yet good enough to make the aerodynamics disappear. Later Horten bombers progressively shrink them.

Eventually Horten engineers say:

> “Every one of those things is drag, weight, and radar return.”

And forty years later, the mature low-observable Horten has **none**.

That's a very clean evolutionary story.

---

## The eight engines work unusually well for this first generation

I like eight better than six for the initial operational model.

Not because eight engines are inherently desirable. They're expensive to maintain and eight engines mean eight opportunities to develop a fault.

But **early jet thrust is the constraint**.

The historical YB-49 itself flew using eight Allison J35 turbojets. citeturn718108search4 So an eight-engine early-1950s German strategic flying wing is entirely within the period's engineering envelope.

And this gives Horten an excellent development sequence.

The first operational Ho XVIII has:

> **8 turbojets.**

The next major generation gets sufficiently powerful engines that Horten says:

> “We can now obtain the required thrust from six.”

Then eventually:

> **4 large engines.**

And every reduction pays twice.

You remove engines and their accessories, but you also remove intakes, exhaust paths, fuel plumbing, maintenance doors and engine-control equipment.

That frees internal wing volume for fuel.

So the bomber gets longer ranged even before improvements in engine efficiency are counted.

By the time Horten starts seriously caring about radar signature in the late 1950s and 1960s, reducing the number of engine openings also becomes useful for an entirely different reason.

---

# The four fins plus drag rudders probably solves enough of the early handling problem

Not perfectly.

That's important.

The YB-49's actual difficulty wasn't merely that someone forgot to install enough rudders. Its flight-test program found serious pitch/yaw and bombing-stability problems, and even its early stability-augmentation system didn't make it as stable a bombing platform as the conventional B-29. One YB-49 test pilot later described the fundamental problem as the aircraft demanding control responses beyond what a human pilot could comfortably provide without a more anticipatory control system. citeturn718108search1turn718108search2

That's almost perfect for Horten-Gotha.

The production Ho XVIII therefore gets three layers:

**The fins** make it less directionally wandering.

**The split drag rudders** give the pilot strong yaw control.

**The automatic stabilization system** continually makes small corrections that the pilot doesn't want to spend six hours making manually.

That last one should be primitive by later standards—electromechanical/analog stabilization rather than digital fly-by-wire—but Germany can absolutely build an autopilot/stability-augmentation system by the early 1950s.

And because this bomber actually enters service, Horten gets decades to improve it.

The Ho XVIII may consequently become one of the Luftwaffe's great drivers of automatic flight-control research.

---

# Your cockpit arrangement works, with one adjustment to the gunner

I like the center section having a recognizable inhabited “head” rather than giving the aircraft an utterly seamless B-2 cockpit immediately.

The **pilot and copilot sit side-by-side forward**, under a fairly low blended canopy.

Immediately behind them is the defensive gunner.

Below and slightly forward is the bombardier's station.

That gives the early Ho XVIII a crewed-machine quality that distinguishes it visually from the later Horten lineage.

But I would separate the **gunner's observation blister** from the gun mount.

A full rotating bubble turret large enough to contain the gunner is aerodynamically expensive. On a flying wing whose entire sales pitch is aerodynamic efficiency, Horten engineers are going to hate it.

Instead, I'd give the gunner a small, heavily glazed **dorsal observation dome immediately behind the flight crew**, blended into the cockpit hump.

Then give him a remotely controlled dorsal barbette farther aft.

The B-29 had already demonstrated during the 1940s that remote defensive gun turrets were practical technology, so we don't need to invent anything futuristic here.

Visually:

```text
side profile

                 pilot/copilot
                     ___
               _____/   \_
______________/          ( )\________________
                         ^ 
                    gunner blister

                            ___
___________________________/   \______________
                          remote
                          turret
```

The turret can remain almost flush when stowed and elevate when needed.

That matches the image you're after much better:

> ordinarily, the Ho XVIII remains very aerodynamically clean;

but

> when threatened from behind, this little dorsal weapons installation suddenly rises out of the wing.

And because the actual gunner is forward of it, you aren't trying to cram a human being, seat, ammunition feed and traverse mechanism into the turret itself.

## The jet exhaust creates one firing limitation

We should deliberately include this.

With eight engines buried in the central wing, the direct six-o'clock firing arc is full of hot turbulent exhaust flow.

We don't necessarily want cannon shells being fired straight through the exhaust plume, and we definitely don't want the turret traversing downward into parts of the aircraft.

So the defensive installation has a **computer/mechanical firing interrupter** that prevents it from firing into prohibited arcs.

Its best coverage is:

> high six, high quarter, and lateral rear hemisphere.

The absolute low-six position is weaker.

That's a real limitation rather than a reason to abandon the arrangement.

And it gives enemy interceptor pilots something to learn.

---

# I like the bombardier station almost exactly as you've described it

Do **not** put a B-17-style glass nose on this thing.

That would defeat the Horten aesthetic and add unnecessary drag.

The bombardier sits inside the lower forward center section with a relatively small **flush optical panel** beneath him.

I'd actually give the window an external shutter.

During takeoff, cruise and combat maneuvering:

> closed → smooth metal skin.

During the bombing run:

> shutter retracts → optically flat glazing exposed.

The bombardier looks through that using a stabilized optical bombsight.

That gives the early bomber a very 1940s/1950s human bombing arrangement without forcing the aircraft to wear the technology permanently on its exterior.

And later the evolution is obvious.

**Ho XVIII A:** optical bombardier window essential.

**Ho XVIII B:** radar bombing increasingly important, window retained as backup.

**Ho XVIII C:** optical station smaller.

**later strategic Horten:** bombardier as a separate crew role disappears; electro-optical/radar sensors replace the literal man looking through the floor.

Eventually even the window disappears.

Again, every generation becomes a little smoother.

---

# So I think the first production Ho XVIII now has a pretty coherent silhouette

From above, you see the enormous swept flying wing, but its central section is busier than the later stealth bombers it eventually produces.

There are **eight buried jets**, four per side.

Four small vertical fins rise from the central/aft wing around the engine installation.

The outer trailing edges carry elevons and split drag rudders for pitch, roll and yaw control.

Forward is a modest cockpit blister.

Immediately behind it is the gunner's smaller transparent dome.

Farther aft is a low retractable defensive barbette.

Underneath the forward center section is the shuttered bombardier's optical window.

And everything that can possibly go inside the wing—fuel, bombs, landing gear, engines, most crew accommodation—does.

That aircraft is **not yet stealthy**.

It's not even especially inconspicuous on radar.

But it is already obeying the design principle that later lets Horten become the low-observable house:

> **if something does not need to stick out into the airflow, put it inside.**

I think that's the right first operational Horten strategic bomber. It resembles the YB-49 enough that a modern observer recognizes that both engineering teams discovered some of the same answers, but the cockpit, defensive system, German propulsion installation, and later uninterrupted development give it its own genealogy.

---
