## Turn 1229 — Assistant

- Timestamp: 2026-08-15T07:11:11.892Z
- Message ID: `d8561b01-8200-4153-937d-ace6f799d81f`
- Source: ChatGPT shared conversation `Naval Doctrine Evolution`
- Parallel branch: https://chatgpt.com/share/6a80206d-15d0-83e8-b360-a8acc44d3025
- Relationship: parallel specialist continuation imported after the master project record through Turn 777

Yes. I think the earlier conclusion was **too conservative**, and I can see why we reached it: we were asking whether an underwater freighter could compete economically with an ordinary merchant ship. The answer to that is still mostly **no**. But that is not the requirement Germany now has.

The actual requirement is:

> **If the Atlantic surface route to Mittelafrika becomes temporarily untenable, how much of the imperial connection can Germany preserve without first defeating the enemy at sea?**

Once that is the question, an *Unterseefrachter* begins making considerably more sense.

And there is surprisingly strong historical support for taking the concept much farther than our old 500–1,000-ton transports.

## We overcorrected the old concept

The old naval reference explicitly replaced “transport submarine as underwater merchant freighter” with “special strategic transport for small, decisive, high-value cargo,” and consequently ended up with four 500-ton Type XXVIIIs followed by only a handful of 800–1,050-ton later transports. fileciteturn36file0 That logic subsequently became important to Operation *Nachtbrücke*, where the boats move missiles, electronics, engines, ammunition, and specialists rather than attempting to sustain Argentina's whole war effort. fileciteturn37file0

I would **not throw that latter concept away**.

Rather, I think we accidentally combined **two different submarine logistics requirements** and then chose the smaller one.

Germany can have both:

> **Unterseefrachter** — a genuinely large blockade-running cargo submarine intended to preserve strategic sealift to Mittelafrika.

and

> **Unterseetransportschiff** — the smaller, quieter special-mission transport carrying high-value cargo, technicians, special forces, and politically deniable material.

*Nachtbrücke* uses the second.

Mittelafrika is what justifies the first.

That distinction resolves most of the problem.

---

## A Liberty-ship-order submarine is not physically absurd

This surprised me when I checked the historical design work.

A Liberty ship was roughly a **10,000–10,800-deadweight-ton cargo ship**. U.S. government material gives the standard Liberty design about 10,000 tons deadweight, while the National Park Service gives about 10,800 tons. citeturn713949search48turn713949search2

Now look at what General Dynamics was studying in **1958**.

The U.S. Maritime Administration commissioned an actual engineering feasibility investigation of nuclear-powered submarine tankers with **20,000, 30,000, and 40,000 tons deadweight**, at submerged speeds ranging from 20 to 40 knots. Twenty-seven parametric designs were examined, including conventional practical hull arrangements and hydrodynamically ideal bodies of revolution. citeturn911298view0turn911298view1

The conclusion wasn't:

> impossible.

It was:

> **technically feasible, economically questionable.**

A contemporary engineering paper likewise concluded that nuclear cargo submarines were technically feasible but unlikely to compete in ordinary commercial trade because the slight hydrodynamic advantage did not offset the much higher capital and operating cost. citeturn911298view2

There was even a 1958 Electric Boat study whose representative concept displaced about **50,000 tons submerged while carrying roughly 30,000 tons of oil**. citeturn889600search2

So your proposed German discussion in the 1960s isn't:

> “Can human beings build a cargo submarine the size of a merchant ship?”

That was already being seriously studied historically.

The German discussion is:

> **“Can we afford enough of them that their military utility matters?”**

That's a much more favorable question for AltWWII Germany.

## Dry cargo is considerably harder than oil

This is the limiting qualification.

A tanker gets a huge advantage because its cargo is liquid.

Oil doesn't care whether the tank is cylindrical.

It doesn't require aisles.

It doesn't need individual crates moved through hatches.

Some liquid cargo can even occupy tanks incorporated into the space between pressure and hydrodynamic hulls.

A dry freighter has to provide enormous **dry pressure-protected volume** and somehow get thousands of tonnes of cargo into and out of it.

So I would not take:

> 50,000-ton submarine → 30,000-ton tanker payload

and conclude:

> 50,000-ton submarine → 30,000 tons of trucks, ammunition crates, machine tools, and canned food.

No.

For our *Unterseefrachter*, something like **6,000–10,000 tonnes of normal dry cargo** becomes a much more believable mature target.

And that is already enormous.

---

# The mature ship is probably a 30,000–45,000-ton submarine

This is where I think your “submersible Liberty ship” image becomes accurate **in purpose**, even though the physical shape can't literally be a Liberty hull with ballast tanks welded underneath.

A surface merchantman likes a broad box containing huge rectangular holds.

A submarine likes pressure-resistant cylinders inside a streamlined body.

So German naval architects probably end up with something conceptually closer to the architecture later used for unusually broad submarines:

> **multiple parallel pressure cylinders inside one hydrodynamic outer hull.**

One relatively narrow central hull contains:

- control spaces;
- reactor spaces;
- crew accommodation;
- navigation;
- machinery.

One or two enormous parallel cylindrical pressure holds contain cargo.

Then everything sits inside a free-flooding streamlined outer casing.

That gives you a very **wide submarine**, because width is useful here.

Something in the broad order of:

**150–180 meters long**,  
perhaps **20–25+ meters overall beam**,  
**30,000–45,000 tonnes submerged**,  
**6,000–10,000 tonnes normal dry payload**,  
roughly **15–20 knots economical submerged transit**,

is the kind of mature 1970s–80s design I'd investigate.

Those are working ranges, not specifications yet.

And there is another useful reality check: proposals in the late 1990s/early 2000s to convert historical Typhoon-class submarines into cargo vessels estimated **10,000–15,000 tonnes of cargo** in roughly a 48,000-ton submerged vessel. citeturn392958search8

So an AltWWII German 1980s *Unterseefrachter* carrying something like eight thousand tonnes is not remotely outside physical plausibility.

It's merely **expensive**.

And Germany has a strategic reason to pay.

---

# Nuclear propulsion changes the argument completely

The first experimental *Unterseefrachter* does not necessarily need nuclear propulsion.

In fact, I'd keep the old Type XXVIII concept as a useful first step.

### Type XXVIII generation — late 1950s

This is still recognizably an enormous conventional submarine rather than a true underwater merchant ship.

Maybe:

**4,000–6,000 tonnes submerged**,  
**500–1,000 tonnes cargo**,  
diesel-electric/Schnorchel,  
perhaps two to four built.

That boat answers:

- How do you load a cargo submarine?
- How large can the hatches safely be?
- How do you arrange cranes?
- How do pallets and vehicles fit through cylindrical pressure holds?
- How do you trim the submarine as thousands of kilograms are removed from one part of the vessel?
- How do you unload at an African port?
- How long does turnaround actually take?

It is primarily a **cargo-handling experiment**.

The Navy discovers that the concept works and is horribly inefficient in some completely unexpected ways.

Good.

Then Type XXX nuclear propulsion appears in the combat force around the early 1960s.

Now the transport designers look at the reactor and say:

> **That's what we've been waiting for.**

Because if the freighter is supposed to remain underwater for most of northern-Europe-to-Africa transit, nuclear power solves its most awkward problem.

A diesel-electric cargo submarine could hide intermittently.

A nuclear *Unterseefrachter* can make:

> **submerged passage the normal passage condition.**

That's when it stops being an enlarged blockade-runner and becomes the thing you're actually imagining.

---

# It should still surface for cargo operations

I agree completely there.

Trying to make the entire commercial port system operate underwater adds an enormous second technological project for little gain.

The boat sails submerged until it reaches the controlled approach to one of its African deep-water ports.

Then:

> friendly maritime patrol aircraft have swept the area;

> German ASW units control the approach;

> mine-clearance forces maintain the channel;

> local coast-defense aviation is available;

> the submarine surfaces;

> pilot comes aboard;

> it enters harbor like an extremely peculiar ship.

The 1958 American feasibility work explicitly investigated giant submarine tankers **with a surface-draft limitation of 34 feet**, which tells us designers were already thinking about how such vessels would interact with conventional ports. citeturn911298view0

Germany would therefore invest in a few specialized *Unterseefrachter* berths in Europe and Mittelafrika:

deep channels;

wide turning basins;

enormous gantry cranes;

secure handling facilities;

dedicated maintenance;

perhaps sheltered pens.

It does **not** need to rebuild every African harbor for them.

Only the strategic terminals.

---

# And I would change how they're escorted

This is one place where I would modify your image slightly.

Near port, absolutely:

> frigates, patrol aircraft, helicopters, mine warfare, shore radar.

Once the *Unterseefrachter* goes down, however, having three surface destroyers follow directly above it partly defeats the point.

They tell the enemy:

> **there is something worth protecting right here.**

The natural blue-water escort is another submarine.

So German wartime doctrine could use:

> **one or two Jagd-U-Boote running ahead and abeam of the freighter**, rather than sitting beside it visibly.

Maritime-patrol aviation periodically sanitizes areas farther ahead.

Surface escorts handle the approaches.

Fixed sensors watch likely British interception corridors.

The freighter itself carries:

- excellent passive sonar;
- decoys;
- torpedo warning;
- countermeasures;
- perhaps a minimal self-defense torpedo battery, depending on whether Germany classifies it as a naval auxiliary or merchant vessel.

It isn't nearly as stealthy as an attack submarine.

It's huge.

But “huge underwater object whose approximate route is unknown” is still a different problem from “15,000-ton merchantman on the surface continuously available to radar, aircraft, surface ships, and visual reconnaissance.”

## And your survivability distinction is correct

Submerging does not make it invulnerable.

It makes entire **categories of attack irrelevant**.

When submerged, the enemy can't ordinarily kill it with:

- cruiser gunfire;
- destroyer gunfire;
- most antiship missiles;
- strafing;
- ordinary bombing;
- surface raiders.

The remaining threat set is concentrated into:

- enemy attack submarines;
- ASW torpedoes;
- depth weapons;
- mines;
- specialized ASW aircraft and helicopters;
- fixed acoustic networks.

That is a major benefit.

A German transport submarine doesn't need to be as quiet as a Lauerboot to be useful.

Its value is partly simply:

> **you must bring ASW equipment to kill it.**

A British cruiser that finds a German merchant convoy can destroy freighters.

A British cruiser that finds the approximate location of a submerged *Unterseefrachter* has found **an ASW problem**.

That's a meaningful change.

---

# The important issue is how many

I agree that **two is not enough** if Dönitz's argument is Mittelafrika.

Two boats are a curiosity.

Four are strategic special transports.

To have a genuine **minimum wartime sealift capability**, Germany needs a class large enough that boats can simultaneously be:

- loading;
- outbound;
- unloading;
- inbound;
- undergoing maintenance;
- unavailable after casualty.

I think the mature force wants something like:

> **8–12 large Unterseefrachter.**

That feels like the correct scale.

Not fifty.

Not two.

Suppose, merely as a design exercise, the mature boats average around **8,000 tonnes useful cargo**.

Eight boats represent 64,000 tonnes if every hull makes one delivery.

Twelve represent 96,000 tonnes.

A single Liberty ship could carry about 10,800 deadweight tons. citeturn713949search2

So Germany's entire astonishing, enormously expensive undersea-freighter fleet can move approximately the cargo of only **six to nine Liberty ships per complete cycle**.

That tells us immediately what it cannot do.

It cannot replace German merchant shipping.

It cannot carry the entire civilian economy of Mittelafrika through a total blockade.

It cannot make surface sea control irrelevant.

But it can keep an extraordinary quantity of **strategically important cargo** moving.

If the round trip including loading, unloading, routing, and maintenance is around a month or somewhat longer, we're looking at broadly **tens of thousands of tonnes per month** reliably getting through even under extreme pressure.

For:

- precision machine tools;
- ammunition;
- aircraft engines;
- missile systems;
- replacement vehicles;
- pharmaceuticals;
- communications equipment;
- engineers;
- military personnel;
- specialist industrial components,

that is significant.

Especially because Mittelafrika is not an empty island that has to import every calorie and liter of water from Germany.

The submarine bridge doesn't have to sustain **Africa**.

It has to sustain the things Africa **cannot make for itself**.

That's a much easier requirement.

---

# This is why ordinary convoys still matter

And this prevents the concept from becoming magical.

Germany still escorts conventional merchant ships because their economics are overwhelmingly better.

A convoy of ten Liberty-sized ordinary freighters can put **100,000-plus tonnes of deadweight capacity** at sea using comparatively cheap hulls. citeturn713949search2

Losing one hurts.

Building another is manageable.

The *Unterseefrachter* is the opposite:

much more expensive;

much harder to build;

far more technically sophisticated;

limited cargo fraction;

specialized docks;

nuclear-trained crew on mature versions.

Therefore German wartime logistics has **layers**.

### Normal conditions

Ordinary merchant traffic.

### Elevated crisis

Escorted convoys.

### Major Atlantic war

Heavily escorted convoys plus rerouting and concentrated ASW.

### Surface route temporarily unacceptable

> **Unterseefrachter bridge.**

The big cargo submarines ensure that “Britain has closed the surface route” does not immediately mean:

> “Mittelafrika has been severed from Germany.”

It means:

> **“Mittelafrika is now receiving a fraction of its normal tonnage, so prioritize ruthlessly.”**

That is strategically valuable.

---

# And then retain the smaller special transport

This is the piece I would keep from the previous version.

The giant *Unterseefrachter* is **not** what Germany sends covertly to Argentina during *Nachtbrücke*.

That would be like conducting covert arms smuggling with a container ship painted black.

The special **Unterseetransportschiff** remains a different animal:

smaller;

quieter;

lower cargo capacity;

designed to unload quickly at primitive or clandestine sites;

capable of moving technicians and specialist personnel;

perhaps carrying a few hundred to roughly a thousand tonnes.

That's exactly why the earlier Falklands logic still works: *Nachtbrücke* is a high-value bridge whose cargo is selected because a small amount can keep much larger Argentine systems operating. fileciteturn37file4

So rather than delete that canon, I'd revise the old supersession rule from:

> ~~transport submarine as underwater merchant freighter~~ → special strategic transport

to:

> **bulk Unterseefrachter and special Unterseetransportschiff are separate branches.**

That is, I think, the cleaner answer.

## And historically, Dönitz has an institutional precedent stretching back before him

Germany had already built the merchant submarine **Deutschland** during the First World War specifically to carry valuable cargo through a blockade. Its designers expected roughly **750 tons of freight**, and it successfully crossed the Atlantic without escort. citeturn911298view3

The United States, notably, also took the cargo-submarine concept seriously enough after World War II to create dedicated `SSA` cargo-submarine and `SSO` submarine-oiler classifications and experimentally convert *Barbero* for cargo transport. citeturn911298view4

So a victorious German Navy led by the man whose entire professional reputation rests on exploiting the undersea domain, while Germany possesses a vulnerable overseas colony, has **more reason than either historical country did** to keep asking the question.

That makes a progression from:

**Deutschland — hundreds of tonnes**,  
to **XXVIII — roughly a thousand**,  
to **nuclear Unterseefrachter — several thousand**,  
to **mature Liberty-order underwater freight — perhaps 8,000–10,000 tonnes**

feel like a genuine German institutional lineage rather than a bizarre technology suddenly appearing because we wanted it.

And I think the result is better than our original two-ship solution.

The Kriegsmarine does not build an underwater merchant marine.

It builds something much stranger and more specifically German:

> **a strategic reserve merchant route that exists beneath the Atlantic.**

Most of the time, Germany sends cargo to Mittelafrika on ordinary ships because ordinary ships are vastly cheaper.

But in a general war, Dönitz's successors can tell Berlin:

> *The surface route may be closed. The African connection is not.*

That is enough reason to have **a real squadron of Unterseefrachter rather than two curiosities**. memcite

Yes. I think the current **“everything new starts at 500” system should be discarded outright**. It solves the problem for about five minutes and then recreates exactly the same problem at a higher number. The old reference explicitly does that, and the wiki has inherited it almost verbatim. fileciteturn38file0 The current Germany article even defines the 1948 reform principally around “reserving the 500 block,” so that section is definitely one of the pieces we should eventually rewrite. citeturn524794view0

There is also one historical correction that actually helps us: the wartime RLM number wasn't literally “this is the 262nd German aircraft.” Internally the Me 262 appeared as `8-262`, and type numbers were centrally allocated rather than forming a clean chronological count; blocks and occasional reused assignments make the sequence even less informative. citeturn445817search43turn445817search18 So by 1947 Germany doesn't so much **run out** of numbers as recognize that the old number has become nearly useless as information.

I think the postwar answer should be a **role-series register**, and our newly established German procurement culture makes it especially elegant.

# The new format

I'd keep the name **Reichsluftgerätordnung 1948** if you like it; the name isn't really the problem. Rewrite what the regulation does.

The new operational designation would be:

> **`Me J4B-2`**

Read it as:

- **Me** — design authority: Messerschmitt
- **J** — primary aircraft family: *Jagdflugzeug*
- **4** — fourth fighter type accepted under the postwar register
- **B** — second major production series/redesign
- **-2** — second standardized subvariant of that series

Then separately:

> **W.Nr. 438217**

is the individual aircraft's *Werknummer*.

That last separation matters. Don't make the type designation tell you which physical airplane came off the line. That's what the serial number is for.

So you can look at `Me J4B-2` and learn almost everything useful about **what kind of aircraft it is** without turning it into a twenty-character database key.

## It is essentially the useful part of the Japanese idea, Germanized

The Japanese naval designation you like does four things very cleanly:

> role → ordinal within that role → designer/manufacturer → variant.

Germany can achieve essentially the same informational density while retaining its traditional habit of putting the design house first.

So:

> **`Fw J5A-1`**

immediately means:

> Focke-Wulf; fifth postwar service fighter; first major series; first production standard.

And:

> **`Ho B2C-3`**

means:

> Horten-Gotha design authority; second postwar bomber type; third major series; third production standard.

You no longer need to know whether `521` happened to be a fighter and `523` happened to be a bomber.

---

# The role codes should be broad

This is important because otherwise we reinvent the clutter.

I would use something approximately like:

| Code | German category | Covers |
|---|---|---|
| **J** | *Jagdflugzeug* | Fighter, interceptor, air-superiority, escort |
| **S** | *Schlachtflugzeug* | Ground attack, close support |
| **B** | *Bombenflugzeug* | Tactical through strategic bombers |
| **A** | *Aufklärungsflugzeug* | Reconnaissance, surveillance |
| **Se** | *Seeflugzeug / Seeaufklärer* | Dedicated maritime patrol/attack |
| **T** | *Transportflugzeug* | Cargo, troop transport, tanker derivatives |
| **Sch** | *Schulflugzeug* | Trainers |
| **H** | *Hubschrauber* | Helicopters/rotary wing |
| **Vb** | *Verbindungsflugzeug* | Liaison/utility if a separate category is actually needed |

I would **not** make separate basic classes for:

night fighter;

all-weather fighter;

point-defense interceptor;

fleet fighter;

high-altitude interceptor;

long-range escort.

Those are all **Jagdflugzeuge**.

That means Messerschmitt and Focke-Wulf can answer the same `J` requirement with completely different philosophies without the designation bureaucracy pretending they're different species.

Likewise *Schnellbomber* and *Fernbomber* can both belong to `B`. Their actual mission classification lives in staff documentation.

## And the number is national, not manufacturer-specific

This part is worth locking.

Suppose the postwar sequence goes:

> `Me J1`  
> `Fw J2`  
> `He J3`  
> `Me J4`

That means J4 is literally the **fourth fighter design accepted into the new Reich register**, regardless of manufacturer.

That's much more useful than having:

> Me J1, Fw J1, He J1

all existing simultaneously.

It also creates historical meaning. German aviation historians can say:

> “J7 was the last fighter accepted under Göring.”

And everybody knows approximately where it sits in the development sequence.

The number is an **acceptance ordinal**, not a project ordinal.

---

# This meshes beautifully with the strange German procurement culture we just established

This may actually be the strongest reason to use this system.

German companies can build astonishing numbers of projects without polluting the service designation list.

Messerschmitt develops:

> `Me P.1147`

Focke-Wulf develops:

> `Fw P.312`

Horten-Gotha develops whatever internal project designation its designers use.

Those are **company projects**.

They can reach:

paper;

wind-tunnel model;

engine rig;

full-scale mock-up;

even the single privately financed flying demonstrator

without receiving a `J` number.

That means the German experimental zoo can be enormous.

The operational register remains tiny.

### A typical history becomes:

Messerschmitt begins `P.1147`.

It builds one `P.1147 V1`.

The Luftwaffe watches it.

Messerschmitt spends three more years improving it internally into `P.1147/III`.

Then the Luftwaffe finally decides:

> Yes, we actually want this.

**Only then** does the Reich type office assign:

> **`Me J6A-0`**

to the pre-series batch.

And:

> **`Me J6A-1`**

to the first service standard.

That is much cleaner than giving every prototype some permanent RLM number.

It also produces a wonderful intelligence problem.

Foreign intelligence might know Germany has observed:

> Me P.1147  
> Fw P.319  
> Ho P.82  
> He P.611

and have absolutely no idea which one will become **J6**.

---

# The variant hierarchy can also be made sane

I'd preserve the useful German wartime letter/number hierarchy while stripping out some of its accumulated clutter.

### Major series: letter

`A`, `B`, `C`, etc.

A new letter means something substantial has changed:

- major wing redesign;
- substantially different engine installation;
- major structural revision;
- radically revised avionics/weapons architecture;
- enough change that conversion and maintenance documents genuinely differ.

So:

> `Me J4A` → first major production architecture  
> `Me J4B` → substantially revised aircraft

### Production standard: number

`-1`, `-2`, `-3`.

These are less fundamental changes:

- new radar;
- improved engine mark without major installation changes;
- revised armament;
- fuel changes;
- avionics modernization.

Thus:

> `Me J4B-1`  
> `Me J4B-2`

### Preproduction: `-0`

This is worth retaining because it is already German and useful:

> `Fw J5A-0`

is the evaluation/pre-series aircraft immediately preceding A-1.

### Prototypes: `V`

Also retain this **before service acceptance**:

> `Fw P.319 V1`

Once J5 exists, a developmental prototype of the production family might be referred to as `Fw J5 V3` internally, but I would generally keep the company project history intact.

---

# I would drastically simplify `/R` and `/U`

The wartime system gets increasingly obnoxious here.

I'd say the 1948 regulation establishes:

> **If a factory modification changes the permanent aircraft standard, give it a new `-number`.**

No more trying to hide a materially different production aircraft behind a forest of `/U` codes.

So if a new radar installation requires factory rebuilding:

> `J4B-1` → `J4B-2`.

A **Rüstsatz** survives only for genuinely removable mission equipment.

For example:

> long-range reconnaissance camera package;  
> external ferry tanks;  
> specialized electronic receiver;  
> temporary maritime kit.

Then a unit may record:

> `Me J4B-2/R3`

but `/R3` is not treated as a new aircraft type.

And I'd make `/R` kit numbers **type-family specific**, because pretending one universal `R3` kit can fit Horten and Messerschmitt airframes would be bureaucratic theater.

---

# The manufacturer prefix should actually mean “design authority”

This solves another future problem.

Suppose three factories build the same Focke-Wulf fighter.

It does **not** acquire three manufacturer codes.

`Fw` means:

> **Focke-Wulf owns the basic design authority.**

The actual factory that physically assembled airframe W.Nr. 481552 is recorded in production documentation.

That also handles corporate mergers.

Old:

> `Ar B2A-1`

stays an Arado type forever.

After Arado's military design bureau is absorbed by Messerschmitt, a new design emerging from the combined organization receives:

> `Me ...`

even if half the engineers used to work for Arado.

Likewise we can decide whether Horten-Gotha's military design-authority code remains traditional **`Ho`** or becomes **`HG`**. My inclination is actually `Ho`, because the military design school is identified with the Hortens even while the civilian public thinks of the company as Gotha.

---

# Grandfather absolutely everything before the reform

This is where the old reference had one good instinct.

Do **not** rename Bf 109 or Me 262.

The regulation says:

> Existing registered aircraft retain their existing designations until retirement.

So the late-1940s Luftwaffe has an intentionally mixed nomenclature:

**Me 262A-1**  
**Ho 229**  
**Ar 234C**

alongside eventually:

**Me J1A-1**  
**Ho B1A-1**  
**Fw J2A-1**

That is exactly what a real nomenclature reform looks like.

Nobody repaints thousands of technical manuals because the bureaucrats have discovered a better filing system.

Twenty years later the old system has simply died naturally with the old aircraft.

## This also gives the reform a real historical trigger

By 1947 the RLM register has become full of:

- legacy aircraft;
- abandoned projects;
- numbers that tell you nothing about role;
- design-house changes;
- prototypes;
- recycled or oddly allocated numbers;
- increasingly large numbers that aren't meaningfully chronological anyway.

The historical RLM really did use centrally assigned airframe numbers such as `8-262`; the modern summary of the historical system notes that numbers were not a clean chronological sequence and could occasionally be reassigned. citeturn445817search43

Then postwar German industry becomes even more **prototype-heavy** than wartime industry.

That is the moment where somebody in the RLM says:

> *We're not assigning a permanent national type number to every strange airplane Horten decides to fly on a Wednesday.*

Exactly.

---

# One important consequence: we should not assign the numbers yet

This is where I think the old Aerospace Reference made its second large mistake after the 500 block.

It invented a nice tidy sequence:

> Me 501, Ho 505, Ju 506...

and thereby accidentally **canonized aircraft we hadn't actually designed yet**. fileciteturn38file1

With the new system, we shouldn't say what `J1`, `J2`, `B1`, etc. are until we've actually reconstructed the German postwar aircraft chronology.

We already know enough to make some likely predictions, but not to lock them.

For example, if the Horten XVIII-derived strategic bomber is the first **clean-sheet bomber accepted after the regulation**, then it becomes:

> **`Ho B1A-1`**

But if an Arado production bomber beats it into formal acceptance by six months, Horten becomes `B2`.

Likewise the clean-sheet supersonic Me 262/HG descendant might be `Me J1`, but we shouldn't declare that until we've decided whether some other postwar fighter is accepted first.

That makes the designation system **follow canon instead of creating canon**.

Which is exactly what we want.

---

## So I would rewrite the 1948 rule approximately this way

The **Reichsluftgerätordnung 1948** abolishes the old monolithic RLM airframe-number sequence for newly accepted aircraft while grandfathering all existing designations. New service aircraft receive a designation consisting of **design-authority prefix + role-series code + major-series letter + production-standard number**.

Thus:

> **`Me J4B-2`**

means a Messerschmitt-designed aircraft, the fourth fighter type accepted under the postwar register, in its second major series and second standardized production form.

Private and company-financed designs retain internal `P.`, `Entwurf`, `EF`, Horten, or equivalent project numbers until the Luftwaffe formally accepts them. Individual aircraft are identified separately by **Werknummer**.

That system can survive essentially indefinitely.

Even if Germany accepts **one entirely new fighter every two years for fifty years**, you're only at roughly `J25`.

Bombers might be at B8.

Maritime aircraft at Se6.

Transports at T12.

There is no looming `Me 987` problem because there is no single bucket whose number has to represent every airplane Germany has ever considered.

And it has another advantage I think you'd appreciate: **the designation immediately tells the reader what they're looking at.**

If I write:

> `Ho B3C-2`

you do not need me to remind you whether that is a fighter, transport, or bomber.

You know it's Horten's third accepted postwar bomber family, late enough in life to have reached its C-series and second C production standard.

That is the thing the old German system never gave us, and the thing the 500-block solution completely failed to fix. memcite

- Timestamp: 2026-08-15T08:04:58.987Z

Yes. I think the cleanest thing is to lock two separate layers of nomenclature:

> The Reich standardizes what an aircraft is called after the Luftwaffe accepts it. The companies absolutely do not standardize how they name things while inventing them.

That is actually more historically German than forcing every design office into the same internal scheme. German manufacturers already used different project systems: Heinkel used P. project numbers, Arado used E. numbers, and Junkers maintained a separate EF development-project sequence that was explicitly independent of the later aircraft type designation.  Junkers' historical EF numbers were assigned chronologically to advanced projects, with parallel versions such as EF 24/1 and EF 24/2.

So I would make that diversity a deliberate feature of the postwar German industry.

The six-house system

Design house Internal project form Internal branches Example

Messerschmitt Me P.#### /I, /II, /III; then V# Me P.1147/III V1

Focke-Wulf Fw P.### Entwurf I/II/III; then V# Fw P.312, Entwurf II, V1

Horten-Gotha H XIX, H XX, etc. A/B/C; then V# H XXIV B V1

Junkers Ju EF ### /1, /2, /3; then V# Ju EF 151/2 V1

Heinkel He P.#### A/B/C; then V# He P.1126C V1

Arado Ar E.### -1, -2, -3; then V# Ar E.612-2 V1

Once the Luftwaffe actually adopts one, this project identity is supplemented by the national service designation we just established. So Me P.1147/III V1 might eventually become something like Me J[n]A-0, with the exact J ordinal depending on where it falls in the real acceptance chronology.

The internal project number does not determine the service number.

That distinction is critical.

---

Messerschmitt — P.####

Messerschmitt should simply continue what it was already doing.

Historical Messerschmitt projects include P.1101, P.1110, P.1111, and P.1112; P.1101 itself reached prototype construction.  So there is no reason for Messerschmitt to reinvent its own internal filing system merely because the Luftwaffe reinvents the national one.

The number is a chronological company project number, not a mission code.

Thus:

P.1143 might be a fighter.

P.1144 could be a transport proposal.

P.1145 could be a high-speed reconnaissance aircraft.

Messerschmitt doesn't care that the sequence tells an outsider nothing. It's an engineering ledger.

For substantially different approaches within the same project, Messerschmitt uses Roman branches:

> P.1147/I

P.1147/II

P.1147/III

Once something physical flies:

> Me P.1147/III V1

This fits Messerschmitt's culture particularly well because the company is constantly iterating one high-speed idea into another.

And your original Me P.1147 example therefore works perfectly.

---

Focke-Wulf — P.### plus Entwurf

Focke-Wulf gets a somewhat different culture.

Historically, the aircraft eventually associated with Ta 183 was being developed as Project VI, with later references also identifying Project VII and multiple design configurations.

I would have Focke-Wulf decide after the war that Roman numerals alone are becoming irritating and introduce its own three-digit project ledger.

So:

> Fw P.312

means Focke-Wulf Project 312.

Where it keeps the old house tradition is in the aerodynamic configuration:

> Fw P.312, Entwurf I

Fw P.312, Entwurf II

Fw P.312, Entwurf III

The project number identifies the problem being worked on.

The Entwurf number identifies which aerodynamic answer the design team is currently pursuing.

That's wonderfully suited to Focke-Wulf because we've made it the company most prone to asking:

> “What if we change the wing?”

And once one actually flies:

> Fw P.312, Entwurf II, V1

Incidentally, I would grandfather wartime Ta aircraft, but new post-1948 service aircraft use Fw, not Ta. The new Reich designation is supposed to tell you the design authority/company, not commemorate the individual chief designer.

---

Horten-Gotha — keep the Roman numerals

This one I would make deliberately eccentric.

Reimar Horten really did privately identify his designs with Roman numerals: the aircraft later known as Ho 229 was Horten's H IX. The Smithsonian explicitly notes that Horten preferred H IX V3, and that he used Roman numerals for his various designs.

So don't rationalize it.

Let Horten refuse.

After:

> H IX

H XVIII

come:

> H XIX

H XX

H XXI

H XXII

and eventually increasingly silly things like:

> H XLVII

Everyone else has computers by then.

Horten's design office is still writing Roman numerals on the cover sheet because that is how Horten aircraft are numbered.

Major configurations become:

> H XXIV A

H XXIV B

H XXIV C

and a flying aircraft is:

> H XXIV B V1

The important corporate distinction is exactly the one you gave:

Gotha Flugzeugwerke is the company. Horten is the design authority.

Therefore the military prefix is:

> Ho

not Go.

If the two ever separated, Gotha would naturally receive Go and Horten retain Ho, but they do not separate in the setting.

That also gives civilian aviation its charming double identity. An airline passenger buys a ticket aboard a Gotha Weltblick. An aeronautical historian may tell you that the actual design lineage inside Gotha was H XXVII or whatever we eventually establish.

Both are correct.

---

Junkers — EF ###

Junkers should preserve the most bureaucratically satisfying system of all.

EF means Entwicklungs-Flugzeug—development aircraft—and Junkers historically maintained this project sequence separately from the final type designation. The ADL reconstruction explicitly describes the EF numbers as chronologically assigned project numbers and notes that they were not themselves the eventual aircraft type numbers.

So:

> Ju EF 151

is an aircraft development project.

Alternative layouts are:

> EF 151/1

EF 151/2

which even has direct historical precedent in Junkers' earlier EF bookkeeping.

A prototype becomes:

> Ju EF 151/2 V1

I would also let Junkers formalize a separate EFo research register after the war.

EFo is for things that are not yet really aircraft programs:

advanced wing research;

control systems;

unusual propulsion integration;

new structural concepts.

If an EFo project matures into something Junkers intends to build as an aircraft, it receives a new EF number.

That fits Junkers beautifully because it makes the firm feel like the most systematic research establishment of the major German houses.

---

Heinkel — P.####, but letters rather than Roman branches

Heinkel also historically used P. numbers. The P.1078 program, for example, contained distinctly different A, B, and C configurations.

So Heinkel retains:

> He P.####

but its internal grammar differs from Messerschmitt's.

Messerschmitt:

> P.1147/I

Heinkel:

> P.1126A

P.1126B

P.1126C

That is enough distinction without inventing a new tradition Heinkel never needed.

The flying machine becomes:

> He P.1126C V1

One important rule: the C is an internal design branch. If the Luftwaffe eventually accepts that machine, the national production-series letters begin independently.

So:

> He P.1126C V1

could become:

> He J[n]A-0

rather than somehow being forced to become a C production series.

That prevents company paperwork from contaminating the national designation logic.

---

Arado — E.###

Arado gets perhaps the cleanest system.

German manufacturers historically varied their project nomenclature, and contemporary historical reconstruction specifically identifies Arado's use of an E prefix for internal designs.  The surviving project lists include E.555, E.580, E.581, and E.583, while the Arado E sequence was independent of the eventual RLM type number.

So Arado keeps:

> Ar E.###

and uses numbered alternatives:

> E.612-1

E.612-2

E.612-3

A demonstrator is:

> Ar E.612-2 V1

This makes Arado's documents immediately recognizable.

And it gives us a very clean endpoint when Messerschmitt eventually absorbs the military design bureau.

The Arado E-series simply stops.

An Arado project already flying can complete evaluation under its existing designation.

An unbuilt project transferred into Messerschmitt might be archived as something like:

> Me P.12xx — vormals Ar E.6xx

But all new military development uses the Messerschmitt P-register.

The civilian Arado brand can continue independently, which lets executive jets remain “Arados” long after Ar E. disappears from military project documentation.

---

One thing is common across everybody: V

I would keep V—Versuchsmuster, effectively the experimental/prototype airframe marker—as the common cross-industry convention.

That means the companies can argue about everything else and the Luftwaffe test establishment can still say:

> “Send V1 to Rechlin.”

Usually the speculative German system we've established produces only V1 at company expense.

If the Luftwaffe becomes interested, it might fund:

> V2

V3

V4

for proper weapons, maintenance, climate, and operational evaluation.

That also gives us a useful way of telling how serious an experimental aircraft really became.

A project that ended with:

> Fw P.318, Entwurf IV

never left paper.

A project ending with:

> Fw P.318, Entwurf IV, V1

flew once as a company demonstrator.

A project with:

> V1–V6

was being taken quite seriously by the Luftwaffe even if it ultimately lost.

And an aircraft with:

> Fw J[n]A-0

has crossed the line entirely: the Reich has now accepted it into the service register.

So the whole German nomenclature hierarchy becomes

Conceptually:

> company project

→ company prototype

→ Luftwaffe acceptance designation

→ production series

→ individual Werknummer

For example:

> Me P.1147/III

→ Me P.1147/III V1

→ Me J[n]A-0

→ Me J[n]A-1

→ [W.Nr](http://W.Nr). 48xxxx

And another manufacturer moves through the exact same institutional stages without using the same internal language:

> H XXIV B

→ H XXIV B V1

→ Ho J[n]A-0

→ Ho J[n]A-1

→ [W.Nr](http://W.Nr). ...

That is the part I think makes the system work so well.

The state's nomenclature is rationalized.

The German aerospace industry absolutely is not.

And because our German procurement culture deliberately rewards firms for developing unsolicited aircraft, that mess of P., EF, E., Entwurf, and Roman-numeral projects becomes a visible part of the setting rather than an administrative inconvenience we need to edit away.

I would treat these six internal systems, along with Ho rather than Go for the combined Horten-Gotha military design authority, as settled going forward.

## Wiki naming rule

In wiki articles on German airframes, both the internal project number and the RLM/post-RLM designation are given when both exist. The RLM/post-RLM designation is the aircraft's primary name whenever one has been assigned. The internal designation is used as the primary name only when the design never reached the RLM or post-RLM service register and therefore never received a service designation.

Yes. And after going through the engine genealogy, I think the American aviation track is **considerably easier to make coherent than it initially looked**.

The mistake is to look at the J67 and conclude that the Century Series depended on Britain for the engines America couldn't build. That isn't really what happened. The better model for AltWWII is:

> **British technology gets the United States into the jet age; American industry then becomes increasingly indigenous, with foreign licenses used as accelerators and insurance rather than as the foundation of the mature high-performance fighter fleet.**

And that gives us a very good setting model: **pre-Philippine-War America is prototype-rich but squadron-poor.** It can have very sophisticated engines and experimental aircraft on test stands and at Edwards while remaining embarrassingly slow about actually putting jets into operational squadrons.

## The Century-Series engine problem is smaller than it looks

First, one period correction: the J67 wasn't originally a "Rolls-Royce Olympus" in contemporary terms. Wright licensed the **Bristol Olympus** in 1950, alongside Armstrong Siddeley's Sapphire, which became the American J65. Wright didn't merely assemble crates of British parts either; the production J65 underwent further American compressor and turbine development. citeturn729283search0turn359379search5

Now look at the actual propulsion behind F-100 through F-108:

| Aircraft | Intended/important engine | Origin |
|---|---|---|
| **F-100** | Pratt & Whitney J57 | **American** |
| **F-101** | Pratt & Whitney J57 | **American** |
| **F-102** | Pratt & Whitney J57 | **American** |
| **XF-103** | Wright XJ67 + XRJ55 dual-cycle installation | **Licensed Bristol core + American integration** |
| **F-104** | J65 prototypes → GE J79 production | **British-derived prototype engine → American production engine** |
| **F-105** | Pratt & Whitney J75 | **American** |
| **F-106** | Pratt & Whitney J75 | **American** |
| **F-107** | Pratt & Whitney J75 | **American** |
| **F-108** | General Electric J93 | **American** |

The J57 was a Pratt & Whitney design begun as the X-176 in 1948 and became the first successful twin-spool turbine engine; it powered the F-100, F-101 and F-102. citeturn729283search6 The J75 was developed from that American J57 family specifically for the next generation of supersonic fighters and powered the F-105, F-106 and F-107. citeturn780014search0turn780014search2 The J79 was a GE program selected in 1952 around a high-thrust Mach-2 requirement and introduced its very important variable-stator compressor. citeturn359379search6 And the J93 was another GE engine, designed specifically around the F-108/XB-70 Mach-3 regime. citeturn791682search8

So if we're talking about the **mature intended propulsion of the nine F-100 through F-108 designs, eight of the nine are principally running on indigenous American engine families.** The XF-103 is the conspicuous foreign-derived exception. The F-104 briefly makes it look worse because the two XF-104 prototypes used the Wright J65/Sapphire, but the YF-104A and production machine switched to the domestic GE J79. citeturn359379search0

That completely changes my view of the problem.

## The American engine story should begin in 1941 almost exactly as it historically did

And wonderfully, this happens **before or right on top of our divergence**.

Arnold asked NACA to create its Special Committee on Jet Propulsion in February 1941. He saw the British Gloster/Whittle work that spring, and British-American technical discussions were already underway by July 22. Historically the September 1941 decision was then made to have GE build Whittle-derived engines and Bell build the aircraft. citeturn729283search2turn729283search5

Our divergence is around August 1941.

So we don't have to invent some later British technology transfer despite American neutrality. **The process is already in motion.**

I would preserve the September agreement almost unchanged. Britain has every reason to want American industrial assistance, and Washington has every reason to want to know what Germany and Britain are doing with this revolutionary propulsion system even if it intends to stay out of the war.

The difference comes afterward.

Historical America pours wartime money, production capacity and manpower into aviation. AltWWII America doesn't. So the **research clock stays surprisingly close to history while the production clock falls behind it**.

That's the fundamental correction I'd make to our American aviation chronology.

A P-80 can therefore exist as a developmental aircraft years before the **P-80A-5 enters Army service in 1952**. Likewise the F-86 project can exist long before its currently canonical 1957 operational introduction. An engine can have accumulated hundreds of test hours while nobody has appropriated money for fifteen operational squadrons.

That gives us exactly the America we've already been describing: technically capable, economically enormous, but strategically complacent and poorly mobilized until events finally force the issue.

## There is one other hidden problem: the F-86

This is actually more dangerous to continuity than the engines.

Historically, North American's XP-86 benefited enormously from captured German aerodynamic research after Germany surrendered in May 1945. Smithsonian explicitly notes that the 35-degree swept wing came after North American received German data showing how sweep delayed compressibility effects. citeturn996807search0

Germany never surrenders in AltWWII.

But we can save the Sabre without cheating, because **NACA was independently researching swept wings anyway**. There are NACA swept-wing wind-tunnel reports from 1946, free-flight work on 42-degree sweep in 1947, and supersonic investigations shortly afterward; NASA also specifically notes that NACA conducted independent variable-sweep research in 1945. citeturn996807search2turn996807search4turn996807search18

So I would deliberately change the Sabre's ancestry.

The AltWWII XP-86 initially remains a straight-wing or modestly swept proposal longer than historically. North American then works with NACA through roughly 1946–49 and independently converges on a strongly swept wing. Intelligence photographs and reports about operational German high-speed aircraft can tell the Americans *that* sweep works without handing them the engineering calculations.

That probably delays the polished Sabre prototype, which is **perfect**, because we've already delayed its service introduction to 1957.

And then the F-86 becomes an important institutional lesson:

> America discovers that waiting until an aircraft is ready for mass procurement before starting its successor is much too slow.

That lesson produces the Century Series.

---

# What the American engine industry becomes

I would **not** rewrite America as refusing foreign licenses. That removes a very realistic feature of the period. Instead, the government begins treating licensed engines as **technology-acquisition programs** rather than permanent dependencies.

### General Electric becomes the high-speed compressor house

GE starts with Whittle, but it doesn't remain there. Its J35 axial-flow program began in 1943, Allison later significantly redesigned that engine, and GE's indigenous J47 followed in 1946–47. citeturn780014search1turn780014search5

Then comes the important GE high-speed lineage:

**J35 → J47 → J79 → J93.**

The J79 is the crucial step because variable compressor stators let the engine operate efficiently over a much wider range of airflow conditions. Historically GE hired **Gerhard Neumann**, a German war refugee, in 1948; his work was central to that variable-stator development. citeturn158572search0turn158572search14

That's a continuity item we should deliberately preserve. He doesn't require Operation Paperclip or an American occupation of Germany—he was a refugee. His precise route to America will be different in AltWWII, but I think we should explicitly have him ultimately arrive and join GE around 1947–49.

So GE becomes America's **Mach-2/Mach-3 specialist**.

### Pratt & Whitney starts foreign-assisted and then becomes overwhelmingly domestic

This is another place where the historical record can give the misleading impression you were worried about.

Pratt & Whitney initially entered postwar turbojets by licensing the Rolls-Royce Nene as the J42 and collaborating with Rolls-Royce on the Tay/J48. citeturn875686search0

But then P&W starts the X-176 in **1948**.

That becomes the J57, the first successful twin-spool turbojet and the 10,000-pound-thrust-class engine behind an enormous proportion of advanced American aviation. citeturn729283search6

Then the J75 is developed from 1951–54 for still larger supersonic fighters. citeturn780014search2

So P&W's AltWWII trajectory should be:

**Nene/Tay license → learn high-volume jet production → J57 → J75 → increasingly advanced domestic turbofans.**

British licensing is the apprenticeship, not the permanent condition.

### Allison is the production and development second line

Allison is particularly useful because historically it wasn't just bolting together other people's engines. It inherited GE designs and then substantially reworked them.

The J35 is the best example: Allison took a roughly 3,700-pound-thrust GE design, pushed it toward 5,000 pounds and developed an afterburner. citeturn780014search1turn780014search4

I would make Allison the American government's preferred **industrial redundancy house**: medium/high-thrust engines, afterburners, durable production engineering, second-source development, and engines for aircraft which don't justify an entirely bespoke GE or P&W program.

It doesn't need to defeat P&W or GE technologically. It needs to keep America from having one engine failure kill three aircraft programs.

### Curtiss-Wright is the company we actually need to save

This is where I think the setting should diverge more deliberately.

Historically Wright entered turbines in 1950 by licensing both the Sapphire and Olympus. citeturn158572search7 That's not evidence that Wright engineers were hopeless; the J65 alone became a major American production engine, with more than 10,000 built, and it received significant American compressor/turbine development. citeturn729283search4

Rather than making Wright suddenly invent a better J79, I'd give it a distinctive niche:

**Wright becomes America's high-temperature combined-cycle and ramjet integration house.**

The J65 teaches production. The J67/Olympus gives it a large high-performance axial core. The XF-103 program forces Wright into inlets, afterburners, ramjets, hot structures and engine-transition control.

Now the foreign license has produced something indigenous that Britain didn't simply hand to them.

That is much more satisfying.

### Westinghouse should survive—but not by pretending the J40 wasn't a disaster

Westinghouse is particularly interesting because it had one of the strongest claims to a genuinely indigenous American jet tradition. Its early line produced the first all-American-designed turbojet family, and roughly 5,000 J34s were eventually built. citeturn729283search12

Then the J40 went badly wrong.

The J40 was initially extraordinarily promising—it was at one point the most powerful American turbojet qualified for production—but it suffered inadequate thrust, serious reliability problems, crashes and schedule delay. NACA actually managed to cure an important compressor-surge problem, but Westinghouse still couldn't get the required overall thrust performance, and the engine was canceled in 1955. citeturn158572search4turn158572search9

I wouldn't magically make the J40 perfect.

Instead, AltWWII procurement people learn from it:

**don't let one ambitious engine become an all-or-nothing bet.**

Westinghouse survives as a smaller specialist in compact axial engines, auxiliaries, experimental propulsion and perhaps later VTOL engines. It remains technologically useful without becoming the company that somehow beats GE at the J79.

There is even an optional sixth player: Packard developed the **first American turbofan**, the XJ49, in 1947, before the government canceled its funding and Packard exited aircraft engines. citeturn158572search10 If we ever want another American engine firm for the 1960s–70s, **saving Packard's turbine division is an extremely tempting divergence**. I wouldn't make that necessary for the Century Series, though.

---

# So how do all nine Century Series aircraft fly?

This is where the problem gets unexpectedly easy.

Under your definition—**F-100 through F-108 inclusive**—there are nine numbers.

Historically, **seven of the nine already flew**.

The F-107 wasn't a paper airplane. Three prototypes flew beginning in September 1956, and one reached Mach 2 within months. It lost a production competition to the F-105. citeturn791682search5

The two actual holes are:

**XF-103 — never flew.**

**F-108 — never flew.**

The Air Force got as far as a metal XF-103 mockup and a detailed F-108 mockup; the F-108 was actually expected to make its first flight in March 1961 before funding killed it. citeturn791682search2

That means we don't need nine miracles. We need **two successful rescues and one procurement divergence**.

I would use this working flight chronology:

| Program | Proposed AltWWII first flight | Functional place |
|---|---:|---|
| F-100 | 1954 | First-generation supersonic Army fighter |
| F-101 | 1955–56 | Long-range fighter/interceptor-recon branch |
| F-102 | 1955 | Delta interceptor |
| F-104 | 1956 | Extreme point-interceptor branch; service 1958 |
| F-105 | 1956–57 | Heavy Army strike fighter |
| F-107 | 1957 | High-speed strike/research competitor |
| F-106 | 1957–58 | Mature delta interceptor |
| **XF-103** | **1959** | Mach-3 combined-cycle research interceptor |
| **XF-108** | **1961** | Long-range Mach-3 strategic interceptor |

Those dates are **my proposed working chronology**, not established canon.

Notice that F-103 flies after F-107 despite having the lower designation. That's completely fine. The numbers identify programs, not a neat sequence of first flights.

And it gives the 1950s American aircraft industry exactly the feel I think we've been looking for: multiple companies simultaneously trying radically different solutions to the same rapidly moving problem.

---

# The XF-103 is the most interesting rescue of the lot

Historically the XF-103 wasn't killed because someone suddenly proved ramjets impossible.

It accumulated failures **around the airplane**.

The Air Force's own history says Republic claimed Mach-3-plus cruise, while Air Materiel Command thought sustained performance would be only a little over Mach 2.5. It required extensive titanium construction, a flush canopy/periscope arrangement, an escape capsule and the extremely ambitious XJ67/XRJ55 propulsion installation. Then funding remained low. Worse, the original MA-1 fire-control system was replaced by ASG-18/GAR-9, which demanded a major nose redesign. By 1957 it had been reduced to one experimental aircraft—and then both the XF-103 and its Wright engine programs were canceled. citeturn791682search2

So the way to save it is **not** "give Republic more money until the complete weapons system magically works."

We separate the aircraft from the weapons system.

In AltWWII, around 1956–57, intelligence concerning German high-altitude work and impending satellite capability makes the Americans unwilling to discard high-speed propulsion research. When the interceptor requirement changes, the Army/joint board says:

> Fine. The XF-103 no longer has to be the operational interceptor. But Republic is finishing the flight vehicle.

That is the critical decision.

The **XF-103A** therefore flies around 1959 with a simplified developmental nose, instrumentation instead of the final radar installation, and only enough combat equipment to establish weight and aerodynamic behavior.

Now it needs to prove four things: the inlet, the dual-cycle propulsion transition, the hot structure, and pilot survival.

That is a much more achievable program.

## And the ramjet actually gives us the aerospace connection we want

A ramjet can't take off under its own power because it has no compressor. It uses the aircraft's forward motion to compress its intake air, so it needs some other means of accelerating to the point at which the ramjet begins producing useful thrust. citeturn772177search0

That's exactly why the XF-103 arrangement is interesting.

The turbojet does the low-speed work. As velocity rises, the inlet itself does more and more of the compression. At sufficiently high speed the machinery in the turbojet becomes less important, and the downstream duct/combustion system can increasingly function as a ramjet. The Air Force's historical description specifically envisioned shutting down the turbojet above Mach 3 and operating the system as a pure ramjet. citeturn791682search0

That makes the XF-103 almost a primitive ancestor of the **multi-cycle propulsion philosophy we've already established for Pathfinder**.

Turbojet → ramjet → eventually rocket.

That connection is too useful not to exploit.

---

# About Mach 5: keep it, but change what it means

I wouldn't canonize the historical XF-103 as a "Mach 5 fighter," because the official record doesn't support that. Republic was talking about Mach 3-plus cruise, and Air Materiel Command was skeptical even of that. citeturn791682search0

But **Mach 5 absolutely can become an XF-103 program objective in AltWWII.**

And this isn't as speculative as it sounds.

The unmanned Lockheed X-7 ramjet program reached Mach 4.31, and a Marquardt ramjet reportedly accelerated an X-7 test vehicle to about **Mach 4.7**. citeturn771246search9turn771246search3 NACA engineers in 1957 were explicitly discussing turbojet applications approaching Mach 4 and ramjets for the Mach-5 region. citeturn771246search13

So I'd split the 103 program.

The **XF-103A** is the manned Mach-3-class interceptor demonstrator.

Then the **XF-103B/C research series** chases Mach 4 and ultimately a short-duration Mach-5 objective in the early 1960s.

And here we can make it even more important.

NACA historically ran a Wright J65 on liquid hydrogen in 1955, successfully flew a B-57 with one hydrogen-fueled engine in February 1957, and published *Hydrogen for Turbojet and Ramjet Powered Flight* that April. citeturn771246search0turn771246search1

So an early-1960s **hydrogen-assisted XF-103 research derivative** is not science-fiction grafted backward into the 1950s.

It would have terrible fuel-volume problems and very short useful endurance. But that's okay. It isn't an operational interceptor anymore.

Strip radar and weapons. Add cryogenic tanks. Use hydrogen both as fuel and as a heat sink around the hottest inlet/engine structures. Use special nickel alloys or stainless structures at the worst thermal points rather than pretending the original titanium airframe can casually live at Mach 5. NASA notes that heating beyond Mach 5 becomes severe enough to drive special high-temperature materials and, potentially, fuel cooling. citeturn772177search10

Now we have two contemporary American high-speed laboratories:

**X-15:** rocket-powered, extreme altitude, reaction controls, very high Mach.

**XF-103 research family:** airbreathing, inlet compression, turbine-to-ramjet transition, hydrogen cooling/fueling, sustained atmospheric high-speed flight.

And twenty years later Pathfinder engineers can quite literally say:

> We need the 103's inlet and transition logic, the X-15's high-altitude controls, and a rocket engine behind both.

That is an excellent genealogy for American orbital aviation.

---

# F-107 requires almost no engineering rescue

The F-107 is the easy one.

It flew. It worked. It reached Mach 2. Its variable-area dorsal intake was genuinely interesting. The Air Force simply selected the F-105 instead, and two F-107s went to NACA for high-speed research. citeturn791682search5

So I would **not cancel the F-105 to save it**.

That's exactly the kind of false choice AltWWII America doesn't need.

Let Republic's F-105 become the Army's major heavy tactical strike fighter.

Let North American receive a **small F-107 service-test/operational batch**—perhaps thirty-six to sixty aircraft—for high-speed reconnaissance, special strike development and flight research.

That makes it an expensive piece of American platform fragmentation, which is already part of the setting's institutional character, but not an absurd second thousand-aircraft fleet doing exactly the F-105's job.

It survives.

Pilots fly it.

A few squadrons use it.

NACA/Aerospace Command gets its hands on several.

And the dorsal variable-area inlet contributes directly to America's increasingly sophisticated inlet-control work.

That is probably all we need.

---

# F-108 is practically asking to survive in this setting

This is the easiest rescue conceptually, because **we have already canonized the F-108A Rapier entering service in 1966.**

We just haven't explained why.

Historically, North American was making real progress. The aircraft shared its **J93 engine, escape-system technology and other high-temperature development with the XB-70**, and the first flight was projected for March 1961. It died principally because the Air Force couldn't afford the program. citeturn791682search1turn791682search4

Well, AltWWII has removed the main reason to kill it.

Germany is not a defeated power whose bomber threat can increasingly be replaced in American planning by Soviet ICBMs. It is a technologically advanced continental empire pushing into satellites, high-altitude reconnaissance and eventually aerospace vehicles.

Then **Raumbote I happens in 1957**.

Then **Aerospace Command appears in 1958**.

Then the new organization desperately needs something that proves it isn't simply a renamed collection of old fighter commands.

The F-108 is almost made for it.

And because our B-70 also survives, its J93 doesn't become an orphan engine. North American can distribute development cost across both aircraft exactly as it historically hoped to do. The J93 itself was designed for the two programs. citeturn791682search8

So I would lock in:

**XF-108A first flight: 1961.**

**Systems maturation: 1961–65.**

**F-108A operational: 1966**, as already established.

The F-106 remains the shorter-range continental interceptor. The Rapier is the enormous long-range northern/oceanic interceptor that goes out to meet high-speed intruders far from the defended target.

Then the F-12 Blackbird follows in 1970 as the next, more exotic branch rather than making the Rapier redundant before it ever arrives.

---

# And then there's the “XF-109”

This one needs a designation caveat.

Contemporary NASA material calls the aircraft the **Bell D-188A**, not XF-109. Its 1/8-scale free-flight model successfully hovered and transitioned into forward flight, although NASA found a serious directional divergence above about sixteen degrees angle of attack. citeturn542599search0

So I wouldn't say "historically, the XF-109 was canceled."

I'd say:

**AltWWII is where Bell's D-188A actually receives the X(F)-109 designation.**

That makes the designation itself part of our divergence.

And despite how bizarre it looks, it isn't really a rocket aircraft. It is a **jet VTOL aircraft** using tilting engine nacelles plus additional fuselage engines. citeturn542599search0

Its contribution to the aerospace lineage is therefore different from the XF-103.

The 103 teaches:

**high-Mach inlet + propulsion-mode transition + thermal management.**

The 109 teaches:

**thrust vectoring + propulsion/flight-control integration + transition between radically different flight regimes.**

That's still tremendously valuable.

I wouldn't try to make the D-188A a successful frontline fighter. Its complexity, engine count, transition handling, engine-out problem and weight penalties are exactly the sort of things that should prevent it from becoming the next F-104.

But I'd absolutely let Bell build two or three full-scale machines around **1962–64**.

It becomes the **X-109A**, a VTOL/supersonic research fighter.

It may be tactically mediocre.

Technologically, it becomes priceless.

And now America's eventual aerospaceplane engineers inherit three different experimental traditions rather than one miraculous breakthrough:

**XF-103:** airbreathing combined-cycle propulsion.

**X-15/NF-104:** rocket propulsion, reaction controls and near-space human factors.

**X-109:** thrust vectoring and propulsion-coupled flight control.

Those eventually converge.

---

# The resulting American development model

So I think the correct reconstruction is **not** an America that somehow avoids foreign technology and independently invents everything.

It's more interesting than that.

From roughly **1941–52**, America builds a technically vigorous but poorly mobilized research establishment. British licenses give GE, Pratt & Whitney and Wright shortcuts. Westinghouse and GE simultaneously develop indigenous axial-flow experience. NACA supplies the national test infrastructure. Operational procurement remains frustratingly slow.

From **1953–57**, the Philippine War turns "interesting laboratory machinery" into an urgent military-industrial problem. Reliability, afterburners, high-temperature alloys, inlet control, missiles and maintainability start receiving wartime attention. America suddenly has to turn prototypes into squadrons.

Then **1957–62** is the real Century-Series explosion. The German space shock moves continental defense, strategic interception and high-altitude research into a new institutional home. Aerospace Command stops canceling unusual aircraft simply because they aren't immediately economical weapons systems.

And I'd give that system one procurement rule which probably becomes the most important mundane reform of the entire American aerospace story:

> **No critical propulsion program is allowed to depend upon one airframe.**

If its intended fighter is canceled, the engine keeps a flying testbed.

If a new radar changes the interceptor requirement, the propulsion demonstrator doesn't get redesigned around it before it has even flown.

If an engine is supposed to enable three future aircraft, it is funded as an engine family rather than as an accessory to whichever airframe currently owns the contract.

That single institutional change explains how the United States gets from the J67 fiasco to Pathfinder much better than simply saying "American companies built better engines."

It means the Americans begin treating **propulsion itself as a strategic technology**.

And once we do that, I think we can comfortably have **every F-100-through-F-108 design fly, F-107 survive in limited service, F-108 enter service in 1966 as already canonized, and Bell's D-188A become the additional X-109 flight program**—while the XF-103 becomes arguably the most important apparent "failure" in the entire family, because its descendants provide the missing airbreathing half of the American road to orbit. memcite
